De apoios de cabeça a emissões do V8, entenda o que é avaliado na homologação do SUV americano e quais adaptações podem ser necessárias O Tribunal de Haia, nos Países Baixos, definiu a primeira derrota da Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) na disputa judicial contra a BYD envolvendo o SUV híbrido BYD Ti7. A corte holandesa determinou que a fabricante britânica destrua imediatamente todos os documentos e arquivos digitais apreendidos em agosto nos escritórios da montadora chinesa nas cidades de Schiedam e Hoofddorp. A decisão atendeu integralmente aos protestos da BYD, que classificou a operação dos oficiais de justiça como uma invasão excessiva. Leia Também: Pela sentença, a JLR tem o prazo de 24 horas após a notificação formal para eliminar os dados. O descumprimento acarretará multa de cerca de € 50 mil por hora de atraso, com teto fixado em € 500 mil, além da condenação da britânica ao pagamento de € 25.376 em custas processuais. A origem do caso e a suspeita de engenharia reversa O conflito começou quando a JLR acusou a rival asiática de infringir direitos de propriedade intelectual do Land Rover Defender no desenvolvimento do BYD Ti7. A fabricante britânica suspeitava que a concorrente tivesse recorrido à engenharia reversa — desmontando uma unidade do Defender — para reproduzir soluções técnicas do utilitário. Essa desconfiança motivou as buscas nas sedes da marca chinesa na Europa. Contudo, o tribunal concluiu que a apreensão configurou uma busca indiscriminada e sem alvo definido, conhecida como fishing expedition. Segundo o magistrado, os arquivos recolhidos — que incluíam planos de lançamento e dados financeiros — não eram necessários para comprovar uma eventual cópia, sobretudo porque o SUV sequer era comercializado na União Europeia à época. Histórico de disputas da JLR na China Este não é o primeiro embate da JLR com uma fabricante do país asiático. Em 2019, a companhia obteve uma decisão favorável na China contra a Jiangling Holdings, responsável pelo Landwind X7, cujo alvo da cópia era o Range Rover Evoque. O Tribunal Distrital de Chaoyang, em Pequim, reconheceu que o modelo chinês reproduzia características do Evoque e determinou a interrupção de sua fabricação e vendas. Por outro lado, a relação da JLR com a indústria chinesa também é marcada por parcerias estratégicas. Em 2012, a britânica uniu-se à Chery em uma joint venture e, em 2024, as empresas avançaram para licenciar o nome Freelander e desenvolver elétricos com arquitetura da Chery, gerando frutos como o Freelander 8, produzido em Changshu. Futuro do BYD Ti7 e chegada ao Brasil Mesmo com o resultado desfavorável nos tribunais da Holanda, o veredito não define se o BYD Ti7 infringiu ou não as patentes de design da JLR. Portanto, há muito mais para se desenrolar neste caso. Não à toa, o CEO da fabricante britânica, PB Balaji, reforçou que a empresa não abrirá mão de proteger juridicamente suas criações contra plágios. Enquanto a briga jurídica avança, o modelo expande sua presença internacional. No Reino Unido e em mercados europeus, o Ti7 é comercializado na versão Excellence AWD, equipada com tração integral e conjunto híbrido plug-in (sistema DM-p) que entrega 408 cv de potência combinada, associado a um motor 1.5 turbo a gasolina. A BYD divulga aceleração de 0 a 100 km/h em 4,8 segundos e bateria Blade de 35,6 kWh, que garante autonomia elétrica de aproximadamente 119 km. No mercado britânico, o utilitário tem preço anunciado de 47.995 libras (cerca de R$ 342,8 mil em conversão direta), posicionando-se consideravelmente abaixo do Defender 110 equivalente. Para o mercado brasileiro, a estreia do BYD Ti7 foi confirmada durante uma convenção de concessionários em Mendoza, na Argentina, conforme revelou o jornalista Jorge Moraes, da CNN. A expectativa é que o Brasil receba a configuração de cinco lugares, distinguindo-se da versão Excellence AWD europeia, que leva sete assentos. Na China, onde é comercializado pela submarca FangChengBao, essa variante de cinco lugares mede 5 metros de comprimento, 2 m de largura, 1,86 m de altura e 2,92 m de entre-eixos (enquanto a versão internacional com três fileiras é maior, com cerca de 5,15 metros). Além disso, o modelo traz uma vasta lista de equipamentos, que inclui central multimídia de 15,6 polegadas, painel digital de 10,25 polegadas, som com 18 alto-falantes, ar-condicionado de três zonas, teto panorâmico e refrigerador no console. Com esse pacote, o utilitário tem tudo para agitar o segmento nacional em 2027.

artigo.texto: BYD is making its presence felt as much as possible just about everywhere, including the Land Down Under. They say that models like the Sealion 7 benefit the people who need them the most, including in rural areas; they joined forces earlier this month with the AFL (Australian Football League) by signing a major partnership with the Hawthorn Football Club, and back in October already celebrated 150k unit sales in the region. As far as models are concerned, BYD made available in September the smaller ATTO 2 DM-i featuring the Dual Mode 4.0 Super Hybrid platform and the Blade battery using Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) chemistry, as well as the ATTO 3 featuring the new e-Platform 3.0 EV architecture with 800 volts. Now it’s time for a proper flagship of the people mover variety – the company first confirmed the all-new BYD M9 minivan was coming to Australia back in August and then announced the pricing configuration in September, with the model starting from AU $61,990 for the base eight-seat M9 Dynamic model and from AU $72,990 (over $48k) sans OTR for the seven-seat M9 Premium variant. The Chinese brand now announces the arrival of the BYD M9 on the market, with BYD's first new energy people mover bringing together the “brand's expertise in new energy vehicle mobility with the versatility Australians expect from large and well-appointed mobility.” Initially, the first version touching down in the Land Down Under is the top-spec seven-seat Premium grade, featuring a 2+2+3 configuration with luxurious leather-appointed and second-row captain’s chairs, a 15.6-inch rear entertainment screen and a 12-speaker audio system among the highlights. The more versatile eight-seat M9 Dynamic featuring a 2+3+3 seating arrangement will come before the end of the year, and both share the latest DM-i Dual Mode 5.0 Super Hybrid system, three-zone air-conditioning, and 470 liters (16.59 cu. Ft.) for luggage with all seats raised. With the rear seats folded, the M9 has 2,036 liters of space – or 71.9 cubic feet of storage. The Dynamic grade has Frequency Selective Damping technology, while the Premium gets BYD's DiSus-C Intelligent Damping Body Control system, but the intelligent plug-in hybrid system is common to both. It consists of a 1.5-liter turbocharged Xiaoyun gasoline engine and a permanent magnet synchronous electric motor with a combined output of 191kW for Dynamic and 218kW for Premium – that’s 256 hp or 292 horsepower. The Dynamic features a 20.4kWh BYD Blade Battery offering up to 80 km of pure electric range or 50 miles, while the Premium version is even more capable thanks to its larger 36.6kWh battery – EV range soars to 145 km or 90 miles. Total combined range is 790km and 850km, respectively, based on WLTP – or 491 and 528 miles, respectively. Both the M9 Dynamic and Premium are solely available with front-wheel drive, though, and feature three intelligent operating modes: EV Pure Electric, HEV Series, where the gasoline engine only acts as a power generator, and HEV Parallel, where both the gasoline and electric motor work together. Inside, BYD gives the driver a 12.3-inch digital instrument display and a 15.6-inch infotainment touchscreen with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

artigo.texto: Portugal e mais sete países da UE exigem entrada em vigor sem atrasos de novo mercado de carbono - Portugal e outros sete Estados-membros defenderam a entrada em vigor do mercado de carbono europeu sobre emissões de edifícios e transporte rodoviário, sem atrasos. - Numa carta ao comissário europeu do Clima, Wopke Hoekstra, os ministros do Ambiente de vários países manifestaram forte apoio ao CELE 2. - O CELE 2, criado em 2023, é crucial para a descarbonização e segurança energética da Europa, reduzindo a dependência de combustíveis fósseis. Feedback Se consideras que o resumo não está claro ou não reflete bem o conteúdo, envia o teu feedback. A tua opinião é importante para ajudar a melhorar esta funcionalidade! Partilhar Numa carta dirigida ao comissário europeu do Clima, Wopke Hoekstra, os ministros do Ambiente da Dinamarca, Finlândia, Alemanha, Luxemburgo, Países Baixos, Portugal, Espanha e Suécia manifestam “forte apoio” ao Sistema de Comércio Europeu de Licenças de Emissão 2 (CELE 2). Portugal e outros sete Estados-membros defenderam hoje a entrada em vigor, sem novos atrasos, do mercado de carbono europeu sobre emissões de edifícios e transporte rodoviário, numa altura em que vários países contestam a aplicação do mecanismo. Numa carta dirigida ao comissário europeu do Clima, Wopke Hoekstra, os ministros do Ambiente da Dinamarca, Finlândia, Alemanha, Luxemburgo, Países Baixos, Portugal, Espanha e Suécia manifestam “forte apoio” ao Sistema de Comércio Europeu de Licenças de Emissão 2 (CELE 2). O CELE 2 é um mercado de carbono complementar ao CELE original. Enquanto o CELE original abrange as emissões da produção de eletricidade e de calor, da indústria pesada, da aviação e do transporte marítimo, o CELE 2 incide sobre novos setores, como as emissões criadas pela utilização de combustíveis em edifícios e no transporte rodoviário. Criado em 2023, o CELE 2 tinha entrada em vigor inicialmente prevista para 2028, mas países mais dependentes dos combustíveis fósseis, como a Itália ou a Polónia, têm apelado a que essa data seja adiada ou que o sistema seja aligeirado. Foi perante esta pressão que, na cimeira do Conselho Europeu de outubro, os líderes da União Europeia (UE) comprometeram-se a avaliar o impacto do CELE 2 antes da sua entrada em vigor em 2028. Na carta hoje dirigida ao comissário europeu do Clima, que partiu da iniciativa da Dinamarca, os oito ministros frisam que o CELE 2 é hoje “mais importante do que nunca”, numa altura em que “a perturbação dos fluxos de energia através do Estreito de Ormuz voltou a expor a vulnerabilidade da Europa”. “É evidente que temos de reduzir a nossa dependência dos combustíveis fósseis importados, de modo a diminuir a nossa exposição às tensões geopolíticas e aos choques de preços, que prejudicam a competitividade europeia, afetam negativamente as empresas e as famílias, colocam em risco a nossa segurança energética e nos tornam vulneráveis a pressões políticas”, defendem. Os ministros consideram, por isso, que, “ao proporcionar um meio economicamente eficiente de acelerar a descarbonização dos setores dos transportes rodoviários e dos edifícios”, o CELE 2 “reforça a segurança energética da Europa, reduzindo a dependência das importações de combustíveis fósseis e promovendo a eletrificação”. “O CELE 2 desempenha, assim, um papel fundamental no reforço da resiliência da Europa e da sua autonomia estratégica aberta”, insistem. Os ministros recordam ainda que o CELE 2 é “parte integrante de um compromisso mais amplo, que procura alcançar um equilíbrio delicado entre ambição, eficiência em termos de custos e solidariedade”. Dirigindo-se ao comissário europeu do Clima, os ministros manifestam-se “disponíveis para trabalhar de forma construtiva com a Comissão”, para garantir que o CELE 2 entra em vigor “em conformidade com o calendário já acordado”.

artigo.texto: EVE Energy Unveils Full-Scenario Energy Storage Solutions for AI Data Centers at RE+ 2026 New solutions address power needs across the source-grid, power-distribution and cabinet-side layers of AI data center infrastructure LAS VEGAS, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As AI workloads scale, data centers are placing new demands on power infrastructure, making reliable electricity supply essential to continuous operations. At RE+ 2026, part of North America's Smart Energy Week, EVE Energy introduced a full-scenario energy storage portfolio for AI data centers (AIDC), with solutions designed to support power requirements from the source-grid side through power distribution to cabinet-level backup. The company also showcased energy storage solutions for commercial and industrial, residential and telecommunications applications, alongside emerging all-solid-state and sodium-ion battery technologies. From the source grid to the cabinet: an integrated AIDC power architecture During the exhibition, EVE held a dedicated AIDC product launch and presented solutions for three application layers: the green zone, or source-grid side; the gray zone, or power-distribution side; and the white zone, or cabinet side. The portfolio includes rack-level battery backup solutions and is designed to address requirements ranging from millisecond-scale load smoothing to long-duration energy management. Source-Grid Side: High-Power Energy Storage and Frequency Regulation. On the green zone's source-grid side, EVE Energy introduced the 1P 5MWh ESS, which the company describes as the industry's first 20-foot, 5 MWh, 1P high-rate energy storage system. The system balances 5 MWh of energy capacity with 1P power capability in a standard 20-foot container. It is rated at 1P, with a peak rate of up to 1.2P, and delivers 20,000 equivalent cycles in frequency-regulation applications. System efficiency reaches 93.6%, while auxiliary power requirements are reduced by 20%, according to EVE. The solution integrates DC, AC and EMS capabilities at the plant level. At a 100 MWh project scale, the configuration can reduce the number of cabinets by three, lower transportation costs by more than 40% and reduce land use by more than 13%. EVE reports annual system availability of 99%, along with higher returns over the system's full lifecycle. The system is equipped with what EVE describes as the industry's first 300+ Ah dedicated frequency-regulation cell, featuring a capacity of 315 Ah and a volumetric energy density of 395 Wh/L. According to EVE, no lithium plating occurs at the cell interface under high-rate operating conditions, helping ensure cell safety and long service life. Also on display was Mr.Giant 3.0, EVE Energy's flagship long-duration energy storage system. Following 700 days of demonstrated operation, the system achieved efficiency of more than 95.5% and a cycle count reaching 10,000 cycles. EVE says the system can deliver lifecycle benefits equivalent to an additional two years. Power-distribution side: backup for transient loads. EVE presented its Fortron 6C/10C backup power cabinet, designed to support short-duration, high-power load events. The cabinet supports continuous discharge at up to 10C and can deliver 660 kW for five minutes. It has a 15-year design life and is compatible with uninterruptible power supply (UPS) backup systems, with support for high-voltage direct current (HVDC) applications. The modular architecture is designed for factory pre-integration and rapid deployment. Safety provisions include a reinforced cell design, compartmentalized thermal isolation, staged overcurrent protection and coordinated fire-suppression systems. These features are intended to help protect the system while supporting fast-response backup applications. Cabinet side: rack-level support for dynamic AI loads. EVE also introduced a rack-level energy storage system combining a battery backup unit (BBU) with a capacitor backup unit (CBU). The BBU uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) high-power cells in a high-density 3U form factor and supports discharge rates of up to 48C. The system is designed to smooth load fluctuations across a 1-millisecond-to-10-second window, while providing backup power transfer in less than 2 milliseconds. According to EVE, The LIC hybrid supercapacitor has a response time of 1 millisecond or less. Building a full-scenario energy storage platform for AIDC Spanning the green zone on the source-grid side, the gray zone for power distribution and the white zone at the rack level, EVE Energy's newly launched AIDC energy-storage portfolio reflects years of sustained investment, development and expertise across the company's full range of battery products. With one of the world's most comprehensive lithium battery product portfolios, EVE Energy is among the few companies capable of directly supplying both battery cells and systems across the entire AIDC power chain. The company's end-to-end capabilities extend from battery cell development through system integration. The integrated approach is intended to simplify procurement and operations for customers. A single-source offering can reduce the number of vendor relationships and streamline purchasing and project decisions. Coordinated development of cells, BMS and system integration can also clarify accountability when issues arise. A unified technical platform and service contact are designed to reduce maintenance complexity and operations and maintenance (O&M) costs for data centers that operate around the clock. EVE says it ranked No. 2 globally in energy-storage cell shipments in the first half of 2026. The company reports cumulative global shipments of 230 GWh and inclusion in S&P Global's Tier 1 list of energy storage system integrators. Building on its strategy of "global manufacturing, global cooperation and global service," EVE says it will continue developing grid-forming capabilities and energy storage products for the full range of AIDC application

artigo.texto: If a qualifying data center opens in your county, a Texas lawmaker wants the company behind it to pay you every year. You could qualify even if you live on the other side of the county. Your kids could qualify, too. So what might that actually pay? Under House Bill 1273, a data center authorized to draw 100 megawatts of power would owe at least $1 million for a full year of operation. Split that among 100,000 eligible residents and it comes to $10 per person before administrative costs. The payment could be higher depending on how much money the facility brings in and how many residents qualify. Recommended Videos Democratic state Rep.-elect Cecilia Castellano filed the bill Nov. 20. It would also pause covered construction for two years and give voters a direct role in approving projects. The annual payments would apply only to qualifying projects that first receive a permit under the proposed law after it takes effect. Who would get paid? Your primary home would have to be in the county that hosts the data center for at least 183 days of the year. Renters would qualify, and a parent or legal guardian would receive a child’s payment on their behalf. Income and citizenship status would have no bearing on eligibility. The developer and operator would each be legally responsible for the full amount owed. The annual payment would be whichever of the following is higher: - 2% of gross receipts from services provided using the facility, such as data processing, computing capacity, AI training and data storage. - $10,000 per megawatt of power the facility is authorized to draw at its peak. Eligible residents would receive equal shares by June 1 each year. The bill allows up to 2% of the fund to go toward administrative costs. What would voters get to decide? Under the bill, a project outside city limits would need a majority vote in a countywide election. A project inside city limits would have to win two separate votes, one in the city and one countywide. The ballot would show how much power the facility expects to draw at peak demand and how much water it expects to use each year. Which data centers would the bill cover? The rules would apply to new data centers designed to draw at least 20 megawatts or with at least 50,000 square feet devoted primarily to computing equipment. The bill would also cover expansions that increase a data center’s maximum power demand by at least 10 megawatts or add at least 25,000 square feet of space for computing equipment. Along with voter approval, the projects would need a state permit backed by studies on water use, electricity demand, noise and emissions. The bill would also repeal certain data center sales tax exemptions. When would the bill take effect? If passed, HB 1273 would take effect Sept. 1, 2027. It could take effect immediately if at least two-thirds of the elected members of each chamber vote for it. The two-year pause on covered projects would begin on whichever date the law takes effect.

artigo.texto: CASPER, Wyo. — A recently founded corporation is looking to breathe new life into data center and power generation projects on Falls Ranch property near Casper. Western Power Development LLC wants to rezone 1,275 acres to use for data center halls and on-site power. A legal notice published Tuesday announcing a 5:30 p.m. Dec. 8 public hearing before the Natrona County Planning and Zoning Commission does not state where specifically on the sprawling Falls Ranch land the project will be. Oil City News is awaiting a response from Natrona County on a public records request for the company’s application and supporting documents. Per the legal notice, the company seeks to establish the Falls Ranch Industrial Park by setting up a Planned Unit Development overlay zoning district from vacant land currently zoned as Ranching, Agriculture, and Mining. The Natrona County Development Department is accepting written comments prior to the meeting; however, anyone wishing to do so has only until Friday, Nov. 27 to submit. Although the county’s legal notice states that comments will be accepted via email, mail or in-person delivery, county staff confirmed that offices will be closed Thursday and Friday for the Thanksgiving holiday. The Planning and Zoning Board meets in the County Courthouse in District Courtroom 1 in Casper. According to the Wyoming Secretary of State’s Office, Western Power Development LLC is a new corporation, having submitted its initial filing on Nov. 2. Named as one of two organizers on the document is Sharin A. Scott, who is also listed as chief financial officer and treasurer for SG Interests. Both SG Interests and Falls Ranch are owned by Texas oilman and billionaire Russell Gordy. Gordy previously partnered with Trenton Thornock, founder of Prometheus Hyperscale, by offering the Falls Ranch land for Prometheus’s planned $500 million computing campus. Prometheus began publicly pitching its 1.5-gigawatt project in the spring. Initial plans called for a 940-acre development between Casper and Glenrock, with data center halls in Converse County and power generation in Natrona County. After pushback from neighbors and a reversal on the Converse County Board of Commissioners industrial park zoning decision, Prometheus changed the location to Falls Ranch property south of Interstate 25 and proposed building both the data center halls and power generation facilities entirely within Natrona County. On Sept. 1, Thornock and Eric Schlidt with Prometheus’s Build Wyoming officially pitched the project to the Natrona County Board of Commissioners, asking for industrial park zoning. However, the company never filed paperwork to get that process started before its Oct. 28 announcement that it was walking away from the project. Prometheus executives said the company would focus its efforts on building a data center campus in Uinta County on Thornock’s family ranchland. That same day, Falls Ranch representatives said they were moving forward with project plans under a new development company. “This recent shift will expedite and elevate this project for Natrona County, and we couldn’t be more excited about it,” Robert Hand, representative for Falls Ranch, said at the time. “Falls Ranch will remain committed to agricultural stewardship and will continue to honor Wyoming’s ranching legacy.” Oil City News will update this story with information and documents received as a result of the public records request filed with Natrona County.

artigo.texto: EVE Energy's Comprehensive AIDC Energy Storage Portfolio Makes Its Global Debut at RE+ 2026 New portfolio for AI data centers spans source-grid, power-distribution and cabinet-side applications LAS VEGAS, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- EVE Energy showcased its full-scenario energy storage solutions for AI data centers (AIDC) at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas, alongside emerging all-solid-state and sodium-ion battery technologies. The company also held a product launch during the event, introducing an integrated portfolio designed to address data center power requirements from the source-grid connection through power distribution to cabinet-level backup. As demand for AI computing capacity accelerates, energy storage is moving beyond auxiliary backup to become an essential part of data center power infrastructure. With AIDC projects advancing toward large-scale deployment, EVE says its portfolio is designed to address needs across the data center power chain. Drawing on experience in power, energy-storage and consumer batteries, together with coordinated development across lithium, sodium and hydrogen technologies, EVE says it can provide both cells and systems for AIDC applications through an integrated offering. Its three-layer architecture covers source-grid, power-distribution and cabinet-side applications, supporting needs from millisecond-scale load smoothing to long-duration energy management. Three-layer product portfolio makes global debut, addressing AIDC power challenges At RE+ 2026, EVE placed its AIDC energy storage portfolio at the center of its exhibit, while also showcasing solutions for commercial and industrial, residential and telecommunications applications. Products highlighted at the event included the 20-ft, 5 MWh, 1P S5-1P high-power ESS; a dedicated 315 Ah frequency-regulation cell; the Fortron backup power cabinet; and a high-rate, rack-level BBU+CBU energy storage system. EVE says the portfolio is intended to provide the reliable power infrastructure needed as AIDC deployments scale. The S5-1P is designed to deliver 5 MWh of energy capacity with 1P power capability in a standard 20-ft container. Its dedicated 315 Ah frequency-regulation cell has a volumetric energy density of 395 Wh/L. The company also reports no lithium plating at the cell interface under 1P charge/discharge and 1.22P frequency-regulation conditions, supporting safety and long service life in high-rate applications. Designed for transient, high-power loads, the Fortron 6C/10C backup power cabinet supports continuous discharge at up to 10C and can deliver 660 kW for five minutes. It has a 15-year design life and is compatible with uninterruptible power supply (UPS) backup systems and high-voltage direct current (HVDC) applications. Its modular architecture is designed for factory pre-integration and rapid deployment, with layered cell, thermal and fire-safety protections. At the cabinet side, EVE's rack-level BBU+CBU system is designed to smooth power fluctuations across a 1-millisecond-to-10-second window. The BBU uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) high-power cells in a high-density 3U form factor and supports discharge rates of up to 48C. According to EVE, the LIC hybrid supercapacitor responds in 1 millisecond or less and is rated for more than one million high-rate pulse cycles. The company lists autonomous system response at 2 milliseconds or less, helping maintain stable power delivery as AI computing loads change. Integrated, full-chain delivery simplifies procurement and operations Unlike project configurations assembled from multiple vendors, EVE's integrated AIDC energy storage offering is designed to deliver three customer benefits. First, it simplifies procurement through a single-source solution, reducing the need to coordinate multiple cell manufacturers and system integrators while helping shorten project timelines and lower decision-making costs. Second, it provides clearer accountability: battery cells, the battery management system (BMS), system integration, thermal management and fire protection are developed within a coordinated architecture, helping address responsibility gaps that can arise in multi-vendor systems. Third, it reduces operations and maintenance (O&M) complexity through a common technical platform and a single service point of contact, supporting AIDC facilities that operate 24/7 while helping lower lifecycle O&M costs. EVE says it is committed to building the energy foundation for the AI era through full-scenario AIDC energy storage products and to becoming a trusted global energy partner for AI computing infrastructure. At RE+ 2026, the company presented its solutions to customers in China and international markets as it looks to accelerate AIDC energy storage deployments. Its stated goal is to provide safe, efficient and lower-carbon power support for AI infrastructure worldwide, helping keep computing operations and token generation reliable.

artigo.texto: The Uttar Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission (UPERC) has approved power procurement agreements and tariffs for 375 MW/1,500 MWh of standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in Uttar Pradesh. The projects will be developed with viability gap funding (VGF) support under the Power System Development Fund (PSDF) and are expected to strengthen the state’s electricity supply management, support renewable energy integration and improve grid stability. In orders dated November 19, 2026, the commission approved the tariffs discovered through a competitive bidding process conducted by Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited (UPPCL). The projects will supply stored energy on demand for 15 years from their respective commercial operation dates. Their scheduled commissioning date is December 7, 2027, with VGF support of Rs. 18 lakh per MWh. The procurement process attracted 13 bidders, of which 12 qualified during the technical evaluation. Eleven bidders subsequently participated in the electronic reverse auction conducted on May 2, 2026. Following the auction, UPPCL allocated the total capacity of 375 MW among three successful bidders based on the lowest discovered tariffs and the applicable bucket-filling mechanism. Under Petition No. 2404 of 2026, UPERC approved a tariff of Rs. 6.45 per kWh for KCC BESS Private Limited, a special purpose vehicle of KCC Buildcon Private Limited. The company will develop a 187.5 MW/750 MWh standalone battery storage project. The commission also approved the power procurement agreement signed between UPPCL and the company on June 1, 2026. In Petition No. 2405 of 2026, the commission approved the same tariff of Rs. 6.45 per kWh for Agastya Solar UP1 Private Limited, a subsidiary of Agastya Green Energy Limited. The company has been awarded 62.50 MW/250 MWh of storage capacity under a power procurement agreement dated June 8, 2026. Meanwhile, Petition No. 2403 of 2026 involved the 125 MW/500 MWh project awarded to MKC Kashivisvanath Ji Energy Private Limited, a subsidiary of MKC Green Energy Limited. UPERC approved a slightly higher tariff of Rs. 6.46 per kWh and cleared the power procurement agreement signed on June 3, 2026. UPPCL informed the commission that the discovered tariffs of Rs. 6.45 and Rs. 6.46 per kWh were competitive compared with previous procurement benchmarks. The corporation highlighted its earlier procurement through NTPC Vidyut Vyapar Nigam Limited (NVVN), where tariffs ranged between Rs. 6.71 and Rs. 6.72 per kWh. The newly discovered rates therefore offer a lower procurement cost for the approved storage capacity. During the hearing held on October 1, 2026, the commission raised concerns over UPPCL’s failure to initially submit the complete set of bidding documents along with its petitions. UPERC expressed displeasure over the omission and directed the corporation to provide the missing records. UPPCL subsequently apologised and submitted the required documents through an additional affidavit filed on October 23, 2026. After examining the submitted records, bidding process and applicable guidelines, the commission was satisfied that the procurement had followed the approved competitive bidding framework. It consequently approved the discovered tariffs and power procurement agreements for all three projects. The approved battery storage capacity is expected to help Uttar Pradesh manage peak electricity demand, improve the utilisation of renewable energy and provide greater flexibility in grid operations. UPERC has directed the concerned parties to take timely action to ensure that the projects achieve their scheduled commissioning deadline of December 7, 2027. artigo.texto: - Power - 2 min read Battery price rebound, rupee fall threaten viability of India’s BESS projects: ICRA The rating agency flags procurement costs, currency movements and execution delays as key risks despite policy support and a growing tender pipeline. India's rapidly expanding battery energy storage system (BESS) market is facing fresh financial viability challenges as a rebound in battery prices, rupee depreciation and aggressive project bidding put pressure on developers' returns, according to a report by rating agency ICRA. While strong policy support and a growing tender pipeline are driving the sector's expansion, the ability of developers to procure batteries at competitive prices and execute projects within stipulated timelines will remain critical to their financial sustainability, ICRA said in its November 2026 report on the Indian renewable energy sector. ICRA's sensitivity analysis indicates that at a battery pack cost of $70 per kWh, BESS projects would generate a cumulative debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) of 1.17-1.27 times at capacity tariffs of ₹2.60-2.80 lakh per MW per month. The DSCR measures a project's ability to generate sufficient cash flows to meet its debt repayment obligations. A relatively narrow coverage margin could leave developers with limited financial flexibility if battery procurement costs rise further or project execution faces delays. Battery procurement costs and currency movements have emerged as key variables determining the viability of aggressively bid projects, the rating agency said, underlining the importance of competitive procurement strategies and protection against cost escalation. ICRA also highlighted the need for robust long-term service agreements (LTSAs) and firm offtake arrangements to safeguard project economics. The concerns come as India's battery storage market moves from the tendering stage towards actual project execution. Rising renewable energy capacity, which continues to outpace transmission augmentation, particularly in resource-rich states such as Rajasthan and Gujarat, is increasing grid congestion and the need for storage infrastructure. Battery storage systems are expected to play a crucial role in absorbing surplus renewable generation during solar hours and shifting electricity supply to periods when solar generation declines. Government support through viability gap funding (VGF) schemes announced in 2023, 2025 and 2026, covering a cumulative 135.8 GWh of storage capacity, is providing significant capital support to the sector. However, policy incentives and lower initial funding requirements alone may not eliminate the financial and operational risks associated with BESS projects. ICRA cautioned that developers also need to account for eventual duty payments under the MOOWR scheme, performance penalties, additional battery requirements and post-warranty maintenance expenses. These costs may not necessarily be covered by supplier guarantees. The rating agency said project assessments should examine whether supplier guarantees adequately cover developers' commitments to power buyers, particularly in cases where equipment performance falls short of contractual requirements. With battery costs, currency movements and execution timelines becoming increasingly important to project economics, timely procurement and adequate financial safeguards will be crucial for developers navigating India's expanding energy storage market.

According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Formation Chambers market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global formation chambers market represents a critical, high-value segment within the broader advanced materials processing and semiconductor fabrication equipment industry. As of the 2026 analysis period, the market is characterized by robust demand driven by relentless technological advancement, particularly in next-generation electronics and energy storage. The convergence of megatrends in artificial intelligence, 5G/6G infrastructure, and the green energy transition is fundamentally reshaping demand patterns, pushing the capabilities of formation chamber technology to new limits. This report provides a comprehensive, data-driven assessment of the current market landscape, its underlying dynamics, and a strategic forecast through 2035. Supply chains for formation chambers are complex and concentrated, with a handful of technologically dominant players controlling a significant share of the market. These suppliers are engaged in intense competition through R&D, striving to meet increasingly stringent specifications for precision, yield, and process integration. The market's evolution is not merely a function of volume growth but is increasingly defined by a shift towards more sophisticated, integrated, and often customized solutions that command premium pricing. This creates both significant opportunities for innovators and high barriers to entry for new participants. The outlook to 2035 points towards sustained, albeit cyclical, growth, punctuated by technological disruptions and evolving trade policies. Regional investment patterns in semiconductor and battery manufacturing capacity will be a primary determinant of demand geography. Success for industry stakeholders will hinge on strategic positioning within high-growth application niches, deep technical partnerships with leading manufacturers, and resilience in navigating an increasingly fragmented global trade environment. This report serves as an essential tool for understanding these multifaceted dynamics. The baseline scenario for the formation chambers market anticipates a 6.2% CAGR from 2026 to 2035, with the market index rising to 182 (2025=100). This outlook is supported by sustained capital expenditure in semiconductor fabrication and advanced battery manufacturing, where formation chambers are indispensable for thin-film deposition, annealing, and sintering processes. The baseline assumes a moderate cyclical recovery in semiconductor capex following the 2024-2025 inventory correction, followed by steady growth as node shrinkage to 2nm and below drives demand for more precise and integrated chamber systems. In the battery sector, the scale-up of solid-state and next-generation lithium-ion production is expected to create a new wave of demand for thermal and pressure formation chambers, particularly in Asia-Pacific and North America. The baseline also incorporates a gradual increase in replacement and upgrade activity as existing installed bases age and manufacturers seek to improve yield and reduce downtime. Geopolitical factors, including export controls and regional subsidy programs, are expected to reshape supply chains but not derail overall growth. The market is projected to remain concentrated, with the top five suppliers accounting for a significant share of revenue. Pricing is expected to remain firm for advanced systems, while standard chambers face moderate price pressure. The forecast horizon to 2035 sees the market evolving towards higher integration of process control software and data analytics, creating value-added opportunities for system integrators and service providers. Semiconductor fabrication remains the largest end-use sector for formation chambers, accounting for an estimated 45% of global demand in 2026. The ongoing transition to smaller process nodes, such as 3nm and below, necessitates chambers capable of atomic-level precision in deposition and etching. Additionally, the adoption of 3D NAND and gate-all-around transistor architectures requires more complex and integrated chamber systems. Demand is also supported by the expansion of foundry capacity in Asia-Pacific and the United States, driven by government incentives and national security concerns. Through 2035, the demand for formation chambers in this sector will be increasingly driven by the need for higher throughput, lower defect rates, and enhanced process control. The shift towards 2nm and 1.4nm nodes will require new chamber designs with improved plasma uniformity and temperature control. Furthermore, the integration of AI and machine learning for process optimization will drive demand for chambers with advanced sensors and data analytics capabilities. The replacement cycle for existing chambers, typically 5-7 years, will also contribute to steady demand. Key demand-side indicators include semiconductor capex, wafer fab equipment spending, and node transition timelines. Current trend: Growing demand for advanced nodes and 3D architectures. Major trends: Transition to 2nm and below nodes driving demand for advanced deposition and etch chambers, Rising adoption of 3D NAND and gate-all-around transistors requiring complex chamber systems, Government incentives and geopolitical factors spurring new fab construction in the US, Europe, and Asia, Integration of AI and machine learning for process control and predictive maintenance, and Increasing focus on sustainability and energy efficiency in chamber design. artigo.texto: FERNANDA BRIGATTI, MARCOS HERMANSON E JOÃO GABRIEL FOLHAPRESS A política de incentivo a data centers virou lei há dois meses, mas até agora os interessados em usar os benefícios fiscais que ela criou ainda não sabem quais são as regras de habilitação, os prazos, como será o uso de energia e até mesmo quais serão os equipamentos comprados com isenção de PIS, Cofins e IPI. O principal entrave para a regulamentação é o uso do gás natural como fonte de energia nessas estruturas, o que opôs os ministérios da Fazenda e do Meio Ambiente -contrários à ideia- ao de Minas e Energia -a favor. Segundo pessoas que participam das negociações, as pastas envolvidas chegaram a um acordo sobre todos os outros pontos da regulamentação há mais de um mês. O que atrasou o avanço da proposta durante esse tempo foi o debate sobre o combustível fóssil. A brecha para o uso do gás foi aberta por uma negociação costurada pelo presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União Brasil-AP), a partir de um lobby do setor. O texto original previa que os data centers teriam de ser abastecidos por energia limpa ou renovável. O Senado mudou a obrigação para fontes renováveis ou de “baixa emissão”. Após uma discussão técnica que envolveu quatro ministérios e a Casa Civil, caberá ao presidente Lula bater o martelo sobre o tema. Os ministérios do Meio Ambiente e da Fazenda são contrários à liberação do gás por entenderem que ele contradiz o propósito original do projeto, que vinculava o incentivo tributário ao uso de fontes renováveis. As pastas chegaram a apresentar uma proposta de regulamentação que criava tantas condicionantes ao uso do combustível fóssil que, na prática, ele se tornava inviável. O Ministério de Minas e Energia, por sua vez, defende o gás como fonte para data centers. No dia em que a lei do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenters) foi sancionada, a pasta divulgou nota na qual defende a presença do gás e informa que o combustível foi “classificado pela Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA) como de baixa emissão de carbono e de transição energética.” O setor de gás afirma que a demanda por energia dos data centers será alta e terá de ser estável, sem riscos de intermitências, o que termelétricas a gás podem oferecer. Entre as empresas que acompanham a regulamentação da política de incentivo, a fonte de energia é vista como uma questão secundária e que poderia ser tratada em uma norma separada. Também se discutiu a possibilidade de a regulamentação prever que o gás natural só seria usado quando outras fontes não estiverem disponíveis. TRATATIVAS Após a aprovação do projeto, o governo reuniu integrantes do Meio Ambiente, Indústria, Fazenda, Minas e Energia e Casa Civil para definir o critério técnico de fonte de “baixa emissão”, necessário para definir quais fontes entram e quais ficam de fora da lista. As partes avançaram em acordo sobre essa definição, segundo um integrante do governo ouvido pela reportagem, mas agora aguardam um despacho com o presidente Lula, que é quem vai dar a palavra final sobre quais fontes entrarão no programa. Os membros do grupo envolvido na discussão técnica esperavam apresentar o decreto ao presidente nesta semana, após o retorno de Lula ao Brasil, o que ocorreu na noite de segunda (16). Um integrante desse grupo, ouvido pela Folha, avalia que a regulamentação segue importante, mesmo com a demora e a mudança do arcabouço tributário a partir de 2027, porque garante o imposto de importação zerado e viabiliza potencialmente a isenção do ICMS. A preocupação de representantes de entidades é a de que o fim do ano se aproxima e, com isso, o incentivo fiscal previsto na legislação praticamente chega ao fim. Para 2026, o governo federal previu na Lei Orçamentária uma reserva de R$ 5,2 bilhões em isenções de PIS, Cofins e Imposto sobre Produtos Industrializados. No próximo ano, esses tributos serão extintos e substituídos pela CBS (Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços). Mas as empresas que aderirem ao Redata ainda terão garantia de cinco anos de isenção do imposto de importação para produtos sem similar nacional. A isenção vale mesmo que produtos hoje isentos passem a ser fabricados no Brasil. A regulamentação do Redata também é considerada importante para que o setor conquiste a isenção do ICMS (Imposto sobre Consumo, Mercadorias e Serviços) no Confaz, o conselho que reúne os secretários estaduais de Fazenda. Entidades organizadas no Fórum das Associações do Setor Elétrico (Fase) enviaram cartas aos ministérios se posicionando pela regulamentação da política. “Cada mês sem regulamentação representa, portanto, não mera postergação, mas perda efetiva de capacidade de atração de investimentos, sem ganho arrecadatório, uma vez que os equipamentos não adquiridos tampouco gerarão tributos.” O setor elétrico vê no Redata também a possibilidade de dar vazão aos excedentes de geração eólica e solar, uma vez que cerca de 20% dessa produção foi cortada em 2025 para evitar sobrecarga do sistema integrado. “Os data centers que o Redata busca atrair estão entre os principais vetores de crescimento da carga [demanda] do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), e sua regulamentação é indispensável para que os investidores conheçam as condições e os procedimentos de implantação dos projetos”, diz a carta. A demanda de data centers deve passar de cerca de 0,3 GW médio em 2026 para 5,7 GW médios em 2030, ou quase um terço do crescimento da carga do SIN no período. As entidades defendem a publicação imediata da regulamentação. Além do impasse dentro do governo quanto aos parâmetros do uso do gás natural nesses projetos, a lista de equipamentos beneficiados sem similar nacional também é frente de embates. Uma minuta de decreto de regulamentação que circula entre entidades de tecnologia acendeu um alerta em algumas delas, que consideraram o rascunho muito restritivo, dizendo que ele inviabilizaria praticamente a política de incentivo. artigo.texto: Regulamentação do Redata e PL do marco de IA: relator na Câmara cobra agilidade e prioridade do Governo Ao participar do Fórum Dig.ia, que acontece em Brasília, o deputado Aguinaldo Ribeiro (PP/PB), disse que tem quatro semanas para tratar do marco legal da inteligência artificial. "Mas o texto só vou apresentar à medida que houver espaço para votação. Temos o PL do Mercado Digitais para ser votado. O texto de IA requer requinte porque a regulação tem de ter longevidade. Tem de ter vontade do Governo e do Congresso", afirmou. Ao participar do Fórum dig.ia, da Aliança pela Infraestrutura Digital e Internet Aberta, realizado nesta quarta-feira, 25/11, em Brasília, o deputado Aguinaldo Ribeiro (PP/PB) disse que vai cobrar agilidade e prioridade do governo com relação à regulamentação do Redata – ainda pendente – e sobre o PL do Marco Legal de Inteligência Artificial. Ele não quis dar prazos, mas diz que há quatro semanas para se votar o PL de IA. “Mas temos de saber se é prioridade do Governo e do próprio parlamento. O meu texto será apresentado conforme o interesse de votação. Nós estamos tratando de um tema complexo, que requer requinte de texto para produzir o que se quer para o Brasil”, afirmou Ribeiro, ao falar com o Convergência Digital, sem adiantar detalhes das mudanças no texto para adequar todos os pleitos do ecossistema digital. “Temos agora que tratar também da cibersegurança. A infraestrutura digital ganha uma relevância e um papel estratégico”, adicionou. Aguinaldo Ribeiro definiu o ano de 2027 como um ano difícil do ponto de vista global, fiscal e econômico e é preciso aguardar o desenho do governo Lula 4. Mas fez uma mea culpa. Disse que o governo e o parlamento são reféns das circunstancias. “Tudo é movido pelo hoje. Falta um olhar mais para frente. O nosso desafio é legislar para antecipar as decisões. E hoje ainda somos muito pelo hoje”, completou.

artigo.texto: The Real Economics of AI Infrastructure: Power, Cooling and the Price of Growth Key Highlights - The WEF argues that AI campuses should be assessed as part of the wider power, water, land, fiber and community systems they depend on. - Nuclear uprates, existing powered sites and new generation agreements offer potential supply pathways, but differ in timing, cost and execution risk. - Utilities and regulators are increasingly addressing who pays for new infrastructure and how existing customers are protected from large-load expansion. - Workload management and flexible demand could help campuses deliver more computing within constrained power supplies, though gigawatt-scale performance remains to be proven. - Water availability, cooling choices and the ability to retrofit for future hardware are becoming central to permitting, resilience and long-term investment decisions. A data center can have an excellent power usage effectiveness (PUE) rating and still be a poor infrastructure investment. It may be located on a grid that cannot deliver additional power, rely on increasingly contested water supplies, or require extensive reconstruction to accommodate the next generation of AI hardware. None of those shortcomings will necessarily register in conventional facility-efficiency metrics. That is the argument underlying the World Economic Forum’s September 21 report, Data Centre Sustainability and Resilience: A Decision Playbook for AI Infrastructure, developed in collaboration with Marsh. Rather than defining sustainability primarily through the performance of an individual facility, the report examines an AI campus in the context of the power generation, transmission, cooling, water, land, fiber, supply chains and communities on which it depends. The scale of the challenge was reinforced by the International Energy Agency’s November release of its World Energy Outlook 2026, which projects that global data center electricity consumption will approximately double to 1,000 terawatt-hours (TWh) by 2030 under its Stated Policies Scenario. Since the WEF report’s publication, announcements from hyperscalers, utilities and infrastructure suppliers have begun to put its recommendations to the test. Google has entered into a major nuclear uprate agreement and a separate set of power arrangements in Wyoming, while Amazon is supporting the evaluation of nearly a gigawatt of advanced nuclear generation in Indiana. NVIDIA is placing greater emphasis on computational output relative to power consumption and the ability to dynamically manage an AI factory’s electrical load. OpenAI has outlined a program intended to make future campuses responsive to grid constraints. Meanwhile, regulators, communities and utility customers are increasingly questioning who should bear the costs and risks of AI infrastructure expansion. A Trillion-Dollar Opportunity, With an Important Qualification The WEF estimates that more sustainable and resilient development practices could help unlock $700 billion to $1 trillion in global data center investment through 2030 by reducing project delays and cancellations. It is a substantial figure, but one better understood as an indication of the scale of investment potentially at risk than as a forecast of recoverable capital. The estimate is based on applying an assumed 10%–15% exposure to project delays and cancellations against a projected $7 trillion in investment. Delayed investment, however, is not necessarily lost investment. Projects can also be derailed by deteriorating economics, financing constraints, equipment availability or changing demand assumptions that better environmental and infrastructure planning alone cannot resolve. For a developer unable to establish when utility service will be available, the financial consequences of delayed energization can easily outweigh modest improvements in facility efficiency. A campus that requires unanticipated transmission or water infrastructure may face a substantially different capital budget from the one originally presented to investors. Given the pace of technological change, a facility design that cannot accommodate successive generations of processors may also strand mechanical and electrical investments long before the building reaches the end of its useful life. Against this backdrop, the WEF’s central recommendation is not simply to spend more money on sustainability initiatives, but to identify the constraints that could undermine a project’s financial returns before making commitments that are expensive to reverse. Its framework encompasses development pathways, common decision principles, recommended metrics and market-specific constraint profiles, with guidance for developers, operators, enterprise customers, financial institutions and policymakers. For developers, that means evaluating whether a proposed site can support both the initial project and subsequent expansion. For investors, it means looking beyond conventional construction costs and projected returns to assess exposure to delays, regulatory uncertainty and infrastructure dependencies. The framework does not prescribe a single solution. Its value lies in identifying the trade-offs that could undermine a project’s economics while there is still an opportunity to address them. Nuclear Uprates Show the Appeal of Existing Infrastructure One of the clearest examples came on October 6, when Google and Constellation announced a 20-year agreement supporting 890 MW of additional nuclear generating capacity at 11 operating reactor units in Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Constellation outlined more than $4.3 billion in planned investments to increase the thermal and electrical output of existing facilities, with the first uprate expected in 2028. The approach aligns with the WEF’s emphasis on evaluating infrastructure as a system. artigo.texto: Veto session: Advocates hope lawmakers pass data center regulation, Bears stadium, reentry housing bills next week Illinois lawmakers will be in session Dec. 1-3 SPRINGFIELD, Ill. (WAND) – State lawmakers will return to Springfield for the final week of veto session right after the holiday weekend. Many hope the General Assembly passes data center regulations and a bill to keep the Chicago Bears in Illinois. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle agree that Big Tech companies need to bring their own energy sources, pay their fair share for power, and use closed-loop water systems. Advocates say the POWER Act could also establish consumer protection and pollution control policies. “People are tired of waiting for the state to protect our local water supplies and from the dirty fossil fuel plants powering them,” said Springfield environmental activist Lori McKiernan. “People are tired of fighting against backroom deals without a real seat at the table.” The Illinois Environmental Council said communities have been trying to make major decisions about data centers on their own without proper resources. The Power Act could ban NDAs for data centers and require full and transparent access to any agreements. Lawmakers could finalize data center regulations during the lame-duck session in early January if they fail to pass a bill next week. Chicago Bears fans are excited to watch their team battle against the Detroit Lions on Thursday, but they are also pleading with lawmakers to keep the Monsters of the Midway in Illinois. Top lawmakers and Bears leadership want to create a stadium authority to own the property, while the Bears pay for the stadium. “I can’t guarantee anything the legislature will or won’t do,” said Gov. JB Pritzker. “What I can do is make sure that there is a piece of legislation that would work for the Bears. Then, it’s up to the Bears where they want to put their stadium. We want to make sure that the opportunity for them is in the state of Illinois.” State senators could also vote on legislation to improve housing and support services for people returning home from prison. The Home for Good plan calls for rental subsidies and wraparound services for returning residents. “Coming home from incarceration should mean a real second chance,” said Maritza Albarran, the regional coordinator for Live Free Illinois Lake County. “It shouldn’t be something that you’re just left to figure out all by yourself. That’s why Home for Good matters.” The Illinois House will also continue its special investigation into Rep. Carol Ammons. The Urbana Democrat is accused of using her position to get state grants for organizations she and her daughter profited from. The committee hopes to hear from William Brown, CEO of Hood Vote Community Transformation; Charise Williams, former acting director of the Illinois Criminal Justice Information Authority; Barner Hill, former ICJIA grant manager for Hood Vote; and Shai Hoffman, former ICJIA violence prevention grant manager. “Despite recent developments, I remain committed to the work ahead and look forward to allowing due process to take its course,” Ammons posted on Facebook. artigo.texto: Battery energy storage systems (“BESS”) have become an increasingly vital part of New York’s electric grid. They charge when power is cheap or plentiful, including surplus solar and wind output, and discharge when demand peaks or generation falls short. The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (“NYSERDA”) credits battery storage with making New York’s grid more flexible, efficient, and resilient. On June 20, 2024, the New York State Public Service Commission adopted an updated goal of deploying 6,000 megawatts (6 GW) of energy storage statewide by 2030—enough to power between 4.5 million and 6 million average homes. The order authorized programs for 4,700 megawatts of new capacity (3,000 MW large-scale, 1,500 MW commercial and community, and 200 MW residential); the balance of the goal comprises roughly 1,300 MW already procured or under contract. NYSERDA estimates that this build-out will reduce projected future statewide electric-system costs by nearly $2 billion. BESS development is proceeding alongside ongoing local concerns about safety and environmental impacts. This past September, NYSERDA announced awards for eight bulk energy storage projects, including two in the Bronx and two in Suffolk County. The 950 MW awarded would, by NYSERDA’s account, more than double the utility-scale storage now operating statewide. NYSERDA’s announcement touts the awards as showing New York’s commitment to “locally produced clean energy,” but BESS can pose environmental risks. A May 2023 fire at NextEra Energy’s East Hampton battery facility was followed by the detection of perfluoropropionic acid (PFPrA) in nearby drinking-water wells. The New York Department of Environmental Conservation’s (“NYDEC’s”) preliminary analysis pointed to the facility’s Novec 1230 fire-suppression agent mixing with firefighting water, not the batteries themselves. Early this past October, NextEra suspended operations at its East Hampton and Montauk facilities, which use the same agent, pending its removal. These developments illustrate the tension between statewide energy policy and municipal land-use authority. That tension is increasing; according to media reports, nearly 100 municipalities had adopted BESS moratoria by early 2026. Recently, a Westchester County Supreme Court decision, In the Matter of the Application of Yorktown ESS, LLC v. Town of Yorktown Zoning Board of Appeals, No. 58158/2026 (July 16, 2026), addressed a central question municipalities and BESS developers face when attempting to develop a BESS site: when the latter seeks a use variance, does the application face the traditional unnecessary-hardship standard or the more flexible standard governing public-utility infrastructure? The court held that the public-utility standard applies. In doing so, it provides a sense, at least for now, of how municipalities and BESS developers should approach BESS site development. The Public Utility Variance Standard Ordinarily, applicants seeking a use variance for their real estate project under Town Law § 267-b(2)(b) must establish unnecessary hardship, as do those seeking ones under Village Law § 7-712-b(2) and General City Law § 81-b(3). An applicant must show that, for each permitted use in a district, it cannot realize a reasonable return, the hardship is unique, the variance will not alter the essential character of the neighborhood, and the hardship was not self-created. For the last five decades, courts have evaluated variances for public-utility infrastructure projects under a different standard, commonly known as the Public Utility Variance Standard (“PUVS”). In Matter of Consolidated Edison Co. of New York v. Hoffman, 43 N.Y.2d 598, 611 (1978), the Court of Appeals explained that a utility seeking to modify an existing facility must demonstrate that the modification is a public necessity required to render safe and adequate service and that compelling reasons, economic or otherwise, make the site more feasible than alternatives. The court also stated that where the intrusion or burden on the community is minimal, the required showing should be correspondingly reduced. Notably, Hoffman involved modification of an existing power plant, a proposed cooling tower at Con Edison’s Indian Point Unit 2 in Buchanan, not the siting of an entirely new facility. A decade and a half later, the Court of Appeals applied the public-utility framework to the siting of a new cellular telephone facility, holding that a cellular provider is a public utility for zoning purposes. In Matter of Cellular Telephone Co. v. Rosenberg, 82 N.Y.2d 364 (1993), the court reinforced the Hoffman court’s view that a zoning board may not exclude a utility—even a non-traditional, competitive one—from a community when the utility demonstrates a need for its facilities. Appellate Division decisions have addressed the limits of a utility’s site-selection discretion. In Matter of United Water New Rochelle, Inc. v. Zoning Board of Appeals of Town of Eastchester, 254 A.D.2d 490 (2d Dep’t 1998), the Second Department granted a use variance for a proposed water facility after finding public necessity, compelling economic reasons, and minimal community impact. Conversely, in a pre-Hoffman decision, Matter of Niagara Mohawk Power Corp. v. City of Fulton, 8 A.D.2d 523 (4th Dep’t 1959), the Fourth Department reversed an order directing issuance of a building permit for an electrical substation in a residential district because the utility had not shown that its chosen site was reasonably necessary or that less disruptive alternatives were unavailable. More recently, the Third Department applied the public-utility variance framework to a proposed solar facility in Matter of Freepoint Solar LLC v. Town of Athens Zoning Board of Appeals, 234 A.D.3d 127 (3d Dep’t 2024). artigo.texto: Transmissoras de energia sinalizam que não vão participar dos leilões de baterias marcados para os próximos dias 2 e 4 de dezembro, a despeito de terem se engajado há anos em estudos e projetos pioneiros de baterias instaladas na Rede Básica. O motivo é a possibilidade de terem de compartilhar com os consumidores a receita proveniente dos sistemas de armazenamento, para fins de modicidade tarifária. A Taesa já anunciou que não vai participar do certame, mesmo após ter cadastrado diversos projetos para a disputa. A diretora Financeira da empresa, Catia Pereira, explicou à Coluna que o principal motivo da desistência é a insegurança regulatória e citou dúvidas relacionadas à “modicidade tarifária”. “Pensando em disciplina de capital, pensando em ter clareza sobre essa questão regulatória que vem para as baterias, dado que estamos em um setor regulado e muito previsível, temos um cuidado maior, então decidimos tirar o pé desse leilão e continuar estudando, continuar contribuindo com essa discussão regulatória, mas não participando”, afirmou. Já a Isa Energia, detentora do primeiro projeto de baterias do Brasil, instalado junto à subestação Registro, no Estado de São Paulo, afirmou, também no início do mês, que analisava a potencial participação no leilão de baterias “com cautela”. A diretora executiva de Finanças, Relações com Investidores e Desenvolvimento de Negócios da companhia, Silvia Wada, também justificou a prudência adotada pela existência de “incertezas” sobre o certame, incluindo a questão da modicidade tarifária e rateio do encargo que custeará os sistemas contratados no leilão. Pela lei em vigor, o custo será arcado exclusivamente pelas geradoras, em um formato ainda sujeito a regulamentação da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). A regra desagradou as geradoras, que tentam alterar a norma no Congresso e entraram na Justiça para tentar suspender o leilão e tornar a regra inconstitucional. Durante videoconferência com analistas e investidores, Wada afirmou que o potencial compartilhamento de receita poderia reduzir a competição no certame, uma vez que inviabilizaria a participação das transmissoras. Regulação O tema do compartilhamento de receitas não consta no edital do leilão, mas chegou a ser comentado em reunião de diretoria da Aneel, durante a deliberação sobre esses documentos. O assunto veio à tona após a Taesa fazer uma consulta ao regulador sobre a necessidade de alteração do Estatuto Social da companhia caso viesse a participar do certame e obtivesse outorga independente na condição de armazenador. As áreas técnicas da agência indicaram que a transmissora poderia disputar o leilão e constituir uma Sociedade de Propósito Específico (SPE) sob controle direto, mas teria a captura de parte da receita para modicidade tarifária para os usuários conectados no segmento de transmissão. Durante a reunião da Aneel, um representante da Taesa criticou a orientação e defendeu que a participação da transmissora deveria ser em “igualdade de condições, em benefício da isonomia e da livre concorrência”, portanto sem a captura de receitas do novo segmento, mas como atividade segregada. “Aqui a transmissora não está prestando serviços de engenharia dentro de seu contrato de concessão, mas sim como empreendedor único e independente de armazenador de bateria, para participar desse leilão, com objetivo de ter uma outorga de armazenamento”, argumentou Rafael Janiques, advogado que falou em nome da empresa. Ele lembrou que já existe no mercado estrutura de modelo de negócios em que um mesmo CNPJ opera concessões de transmissão e separadamente usinas de geração ou concessões de distribuição, sem compartilhamento de receitas, e citou empresas como Axia, Copel e EDP. O procurador geral junto à Aneel, Eduardo Ramalho, explicou que a procuradoria qualificou a atividade de armazenamento como conexa aos contratos de concessão existentes, o que permitiria o compartilhamento de receitas. Já o diretor relator do processo sobre o edital do leilão, Gentil Nogueira, avaliou que o regulador não controla todas as formas possíveis de participação de uma transmissora no certame e em que medida algum ativo poderia ser compartilhado, por isso não poderia fazer uma análise genérica sobre o tema. Com isso, a questão ficou em aberto. Com a palavra Procurada pela reportagem, a Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Transmissão de Energia Elétrica (Abrate) disse entender que o compartilhamento para a modicidade tarifária só se justifica quando há aproveitamento de ativos já remunerados pelos consumidores via Receita Anual Permitida (RAP). “Esse pressuposto não se aplica a projetos de armazenamento estruturados de forma autônoma - com outorga própria, patrimônio, financiamento e contabilidade segregados, investimentos integralmente novos, riscos assumidos pelo investidor e sem uso de bens reversíveis ou recursos da RAP”, disse, por meio de nota. Diante da indefinição, a entidade apresentou uma carta à Aneel solicitando à Secretaria de Leilões e às áreas técnicas da agência uma manifestação conclusiva que sinalizasse para a não aplicação do mecanismo de captura de receitas para a modicidade tarifária nos casos de Sistemas de Armazenamento estruturados com outorga própria, patrimônio, financiamento e contabilidade segregados, sem utilização de bens reversíveis, recursos das concessionárias de transmissão ou custos imputados a essas concessões. No entanto, até o momento nenhuma comunicação oficial foi divulgada pelas autoridades setoriais. artigo.texto: Power Latin America Speeds Up Battery Storage: Brazil Auctions in December, Mexico Extends Registration Battery storage projects are gaining traction throughout Latin America. Released Wednesday, November 25, 2026 Written by Leonardo Aguirre for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary Battery storage projects are gaining traction throughout Latin America. Brazil to Hold BESS Auctions in December After Brazil's National Electric Energy Agency (ANEEL) approved the bidding documents on October 27, the country will hold its first auction dedicated exclusively to battery energy storage systems (BESS) on December 2 and 4. The results are expected to be approved in April 2027 and the 15-year supply contracts to take effect on August 1, 2028. Interest was record-high: the Energy Research Company (EPE), the planning agency for the region, received 6,091 proposed projects totaling about 297 gigawatts, while the government plans to contract between 5 and 6 GW. The system operator (ONS) identified more than 50 GW of remaining capacity in 373 substations and blocks across 25 states and the Federal District. The Northeast concentrates 71% of the registered capacity, but 41 of its blocks are listed as lacking capacity for this auction. The main risk is who pays the bill: a legislative change regarding the distribution of the contract would require modifying the bidding terms and could postpone the auction. Mexico, for its part, has extended the registration of storage projects in its strategic call until March 1, 2027. The Ministry of Energy published its call on May 15 and set a reference of 935 megawatts (MW) of storage not associated with generation plants, distributed by regional control management: North (245 MW), East (180 MW), Northwest (160 MW), Baja California (140 MW), Peninsular (140 MW), Baja California South (50 MW) and Western (20 MW). In this case, a different scheme was chosen, since there is no award date: each project must pass studies by the National Center for Energy Control of Mexico (CENACE) and the decision of the state-owned Federal Electricity Commission (CFE), to then be developed in partnership with the latter. The operating rules and remuneration for storage have not yet been published, which conditions the financing. Elsewhere in Latin America, Argentina and Colombia have already allocated capacity, and the region doubled its storage capacity in one year. On July 3, Argentina awarded, through Resolution 155/2026, 700.5 MW of batteries in 20 AlmaSADI projects: 185 MW in the province of Buenos Aires, 211.5 MW in the Northeast, 150 MW in the Northwest, 86 MW in the Littoral and 68 MW in the Pampa. All are outside the Buenos Aires Metropolitan Area, which had already received 713 MW in AlmaGBA. The target date for the contracts is January 1, 2027, and the maximum commercial authorization is December 31, 2029. Colombia awarded nearly 100 MW of batteries at the end of July, associated with solar projects and deliveries between 2030 and 2035, despite buyers expressing interest in a much larger amount. Although no specific auctions are recorded in Chile, the country is a pioneer and absolute regional leader in the development of BESS projects, concentrating two-thirds of the total regional capacity. The Industrial Info Resources Power Project (IIR) database reflects this asymmetry: while for Latin America it has 721 active projects involving the installation of BESS systems (both in stand-alone installations and support in generation plants and electrical substations), only 88 of these projects are in Mexico, compared to 409 in Chile. The Global Market Intelligence (GMI) project database offers a list of detailed project reports. The recent acceleration in the development of BESS projects in the region is mainly due to a grid problem. In Brazil, cuts in wind and solar generation for energy reasons totaled 18.67 terawatt-hours (TWh) between January and September 2026, 52.7% more than a year earlier, with estimated losses of R$15.5 billion (US$2.7 billion). The Northeast accounted for nearly 83% of the curtailment up to August, and the ONS estimates that storage could reduce these cuts by between 40% and 50%, depending on the auction results. The intermittency explains the design of other mechanisms. Colombia included a supply product from 6:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. (local time), the peak demand slot when solar power falls. In Chile, most batteries are in the north and take advantage of solar energy, which the system does not consume. The demand for data centers adds pressure on the nodes themselves. Industrial Info Resources is tracking 71 active data center projects in Mexico, led by the CloudHQ campus in Colón, Querétaro, and 277 in Brazil, with Dataspots in Nova Iguaçu and Terranova in Praia Grande. Key Takeaways - Brazil will hold its first auction dedicated exclusively to BESS projects on December 2 and 4. - Mexico has extended the registration of storage projects in its strategic call until March 1, 2027. - Chile is the regional leader in the development of BESS projects. artigo.texto: The global transition towards electric mobility is creating demand for affordable, sustainable and safer alternatives to conventional lithium-ion batteries. For metal producers, this presents an opportunity to diversify beyond traditional industrial applications and enter emerging energy storage markets. Hindustan Zinc is looking to capitalise on this opportunity by developing new applications for zinc through its research collaboration with IIT Madras. Meanwhile, shares of Hindustan Zinc Ltd. were trading at Rs. 531.35, up 2.24 percent from their previous closing price of Rs. 519.70. The stock opened at Rs. 528.00 and reached an intraday high of Rs. 533.20 and a low of Rs. 527.00. The company's estimated market capitalisation stood at Rs. 2,24,512 crore. What's the news Hindustan Zinc Limited announced on November 26, 2026, that it has unveiled an electric three-wheeler prototype in collaboration with IIT Madras, featuring an approximately 1 kWh zinc-air battery designed to function as a range extender. The prototype, unveiled at the IIT Madras Energy Summit 2026, features a dual-battery configuration in which the zinc-air battery contributes nearly 10 percent of the vehicle's total energy requirements. While the existing lithium-ion battery supports acceleration and peak power requirements, the zinc-air battery provides a steady supply of energy during operation. The research collaboration, initiated in 2024, has progressed from laboratory-scale research to vehicle-level demonstration, marking an important milestone in the development of indigenous battery technology. Zinc-air batteries generate electricity using zinc and oxygen from the surrounding air. The technology uses a non-flammable, water-based electrolyte and recyclable zinc, offering potential advantages in affordability, safety and environmental sustainability. Financial & Business analysis Looking at the quarterly results of Hindustan Zinc, the company's consolidated revenue from operations increased by 76.55 percent YoY, from Rs. 8,549 crore in Q2 FY26 to Rs. 15,093 crore in Q2 FY27, and increased by 9.79 percent QoQ from Rs. 13,747 crore in Q1 FY27. The company's consolidated net profit increased by 142.05 percent YoY to Rs. 6,412 crore from Rs. 2,649 crore, while increasing 17.24 percent QoQ. EBITDA grew 108 percent YoY to a record Rs. 9,285 crore, with an EBITDA margin of 62 percent. On the operational front, refined metal production increased 7 percent YoY to 264,000 tonnes, while silver production grew 20 percent to 173 tonnes. Zinc production costs, excluding royalty, declined 29 percent YoY to $703 per tonne, supporting profitability. The collaboration with IIT Madras forms part of the company's broader HZL 2.0 growth and diversification strategy, which aims to expand zinc applications into value-added segments such as electric mobility and renewable energy storage. Successful commercialisation of zinc-air batteries could create an additional source of demand for Hindustan Zinc beyond conventional industrial applications. However, the technology remains at the prototype stage, with no commercial orders, revenue guidance or mass-production timelines disclosed. Company overview Hindustan Zinc Limited, a Vedanta Group company, is the world's largest integrated zinc producer and among the top 5 silver producers globally. The company operates across mining, smelting and refining, supplying products to more than 40 countries and commanding roughly 75–77 percent of India's primary zinc market. The company is also expanding into sustainable and value-added metal applications, including low-carbon zinc, renewable energy storage and next-generation battery technologies, as part of its long-term diversification strategy.
