artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Sérgio Leverdi – A desinformação tem custo: o que os mitos sobre data centers fazem com a economia brasileira Publicado 24/11/2026 • 21:48 | Atualizado há 10 horas Foto: Divulgação/Ascenty A nova geração de data centers combina eficiência, energia limpa e rigor regulatório. Debater o tema com fatos é condição para que o investimento chegue ao país. Por Sérgio Leverdi, CEO da LAWINFRA A história da indústria é, em boa medida, a história da busca por fazer mais com menos. Cada salto tecnológico trouxe consigo a pressão por economizar energia, usar a água com mais inteligência e reduzir o impacto sobre o meio ambiente: dos motores mais eficientes à iluminação que consome uma fração do que consumia, das fábricas que reaproveitam seus insumos às cidades que medem o que gastam. Não será diferente com os data centers e a inteligência artificial. A modernização, bem entendida, nunca foi inimiga do meio ambiente nem da qualidade de vida e é justamente o conceito que permite combinar produtividade, preservação e bem-estar. É dentro dessa lógica que nasce a nova geração de data centers. Desinformação não é apenas um problema de reputação. Ela encarece o capital, atrasa decisões e afasta investimentos que geram emprego, arrecadação e capacidade tecnológica. Quando um investidor lê que o Brasil vai repetir os problemas americanos ou que data centers consomem toda a água e a energia limpa, o risco percebido sobe, e o dinheiro vai para onde o debate é menos ruidoso. Um relatório recente, "Data centers no Brasil: mitos e fatos", reúne dezesseis dessas ideias equivocadas e as confronta com dados. Vale olhar para as mais frequentes. A comparação com os Estados Unidos ignora a escala. O mercado brasileiro soma cerca de 1 GW de capacidade; os americanos têm cerca de 60 GW em operação, com projeção de chegar a 150 GW em 2030, segundo a S&P Global. Lá, a demanda cresceu mais rápido que a rede e a geração, com filas de conexão e projetos que passaram a gerar a própria energia. Aqui, o acesso à rede é planejado e autorizado de forma centralizada pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) e pela ANEEL, e há sobra de geração renovável, que hoje é cortada. Quanto ao carbono, a pegada de um data center depende da eletricidade que ele consome. Em 2025, 86,8% da eletricidade ofertada no Brasil veio de fontes renováveis, segundo o Balanço Energético Nacional da EPE. Os operadores ainda contratam energia renovável no mercado livre, por contratos de longo prazo e certificados de origem que permitem rastrear cada MWh. Processar dados aqui, e não em mercados de matriz fóssil, reduz as emissões associadas ao mesmo serviço digital. Esta é, talvez, a maior contribuição que o país pode dar ao debate global sobre data centers sustentáveis. Há ainda um benefício pouco discutido. No Nordeste, parte da geração eólica e solar é cortada por falta de demanda ou de capacidade de escoamento, o chamado curtailment. Um data center instalado perto desses parques transforma em processamento de dados uma energia limpa que hoje se perde, sem retirá-la de nenhum outro consumidor, e ajuda a viabilizar usinas renováveis existentes e futuras. A imagem do data center que "bebe" água vem de projetos antigos ou de resfriamento evaporativo. No Brasil, mais de 80% dos data centers operam com refrigeração em circuito fechado, e os novos projetos o adotam por eficiência, por compromisso ambiental e para atender ao regime especial do setor. A água entra na carga inicial e circula sem evaporar, como no radiador de um carro, com reposição apenas pontual em manutenção. Depois disso, o consumo equivale ao de um pequeno escritório. Os geradores a diesel, por sua vez, funcionam como seguro: só entram em operação se a rede falhar. Fora das emergências, são testados por cerca de 15 minutos por trimestre, um equipamento por vez, e os limites de emissão são fixados no licenciamento ambiental. Já a conta de luz não sobe por causa deles: o data center paga pela própria conexão, aporta garantias financeiras e recolhe as tarifas de uso da transmissão como qualquer usuário. Como sua carga é grande e constante, ele dilui custos fixos do sistema e tende a reduzir o custo por MWh para os demais. Nenhum data center de grande porte se conecta à Rede Básica sem estudos do ONS e autorização da ANEEL, e todos passam pelo licenciamento ambiental, em licenças sucessivas, com condicionantes e documentos públicos. O país tem regulação madura em zoneamento, setor elétrico e meio ambiente, construída ao longo de décadas de hidrelétricas, grandes plantas industriais e mineração. O risco existe e precisa ser planejado, inclusive diante do crescimento da demanda por inteligência artificial, mas o setor elétrico tem instrumentos para isso. Cada nova geração de equipamentos processa mais dados por unidade de energia, e os projetos novos são construídos com refrigeração e distribuição elétrica mais eficientes que os antigos. Dizer que data centers geram poucos empregos é medir uma estrada pelas vagas da praça de pedágio. Bancos, varejo, saúde, agronegócio, indústria e governo dependem de processamento de dados para operar e crescer. Hoje, boa parte do processamento consumido no Brasil acontece fora do país, o que significa importar serviços e deixar investimento, empregos e arrecadação em outros lugares. O regime especial – REDATA - desonera os equipamentos em troca de contrapartidas, como energia limpa, eficiência no uso da água e pesquisa e desenvolvimento local. Dados processados aqui ficam sob a jurisdição brasileira, com menor latência para pagamentos instantâneos, telemedicina e serviços públicos digitais, e menor dependência de infraestrutura estrangeira em situações de crise. O Brasil tem a vantagem do momento, com mercado ainda está em formação, cerca de 60 vezes menor que o americano, e as regras de rede, zoneamento e meio ambiente já existem antes de a escala chegar. artigo.texto: A chegada de dezenas de unidades do BYD Dolphin GT a um pátio no Espírito Santo mostra que o novo híbrido plug-in (PHEV) já entrou na reta final antes da estreia, prevista para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. Flagras recentes mostram o modelo em estoque após testes com camuflagem pesada. Com esse movimento, o veículo deve assumir o posto de híbrido mais barato da montadora chinesa no Brasil, ficando posicionado abaixo do SUV Atto 2 e do sedã King. As imagens do desembarque são da Auto Rod Motors, enquanto os primeiros registros nas ruas foram feitos pelo perfil @placaverde. Leia também - Híbrido mais barato da BYD, Dolphin GT já tem dezenas de unidades no Brasil esperando a estreia - O dia que eu passei mal dentro do Porsche 718 mais potente de todos os tempos - “Não tenho medo dos carros chineses”, dispara presidente da General Motors Esse posicionamento mira uma faixa de preço sensível do mercado, entre R$ 130 mil e R$ 140 mil. O valor fica abaixo do Dolphin elétrico atual e invade o território de hatches compactos topo de linha e SUVs de entrada. Na prática, o BYD Dolphin GT entra no radar de quem avalia opções a combustão ou híbridas convencionais nessa faixa de valores, ampliando a ofensiva da fabricante entre os modelos eletrificados. O que já se sabe sobre o projeto e o visual do BYD Dolphin GT Embora carregue o nome Dolphin, o modelo não é apenas uma variação híbrida do hatch elétrico já vendido no país. Trata-se de um projeto com carroceria própria, revelado no Festival de Goodwood, na Inglaterra, e comercializado na Europa como Dolphin G DM-i. O novo híbrido adota linhas mais limpas e menos curvas em comparação ao irmão 100% elétrico. A dianteira traz faróis afilados interligados por uma barra preta, a traseira mantém as lanternas conectadas e as rodas variam de 16 a 18 polegadas, conforme a versão. Por dentro, o hatch segue a identidade recente da marca, com central multimídia giratória, quadro de instrumentos digital, teto solar panorâmico e bancos com ajustes elétricos. Nas medidas, soma 4,16 metros de comprimento e 2,61 metros de entre-eixos, com porta-malas de 425 litros — chegando a 1.225 litros com o banco traseiro rebatido. Motorização: o que muda no BYD Dolphin GT em relação à Europa A BYD ainda não confirmou oficialmente a mecânica do carro no Brasil, mas o conjunto deve seguir um caminho distinto do europeu. Lá fora, o modelo utiliza a quinta geração do sistema híbrido plug-in DM-i, unindo motor 1.5 aspirado a gasolina (95 cv) a um propulsor elétrico dianteiro (163 cv). No mercado europeu, a potência combinada varia de 176 cv nas opções de entrada a 212 cv nas configurações de topo. As baterias Blade, de 7,42 kWh a 18,3 kWh, permitem rodar entre 40 km e 105 km apenas no modo elétrico (ciclo WLTP) e ultrapassam 1.000 km de autonomia total. No Brasil, o BYD Dolphin GT deve estrear com o sistema híbrido flex da fabricante (DM-i Flex), adaptado para rodar também com etanol. Os modelos da marca por aqui costumam combinar um motor 1.5 a outro elétrico, mas o conjunto local pode ganhar calibração e números próprios de potência e consumo. Expectativa de preço e produção na fábrica de Camaçari Sem preços divulgados oficialmente para o mercado nacional, o hatch custa 25 mil euros na Europa — cerca de R$ 150 mil na conversão direta. Por aqui, a projeção indica valores abaixo do Dolphin elétrico atual, situados entre R$ 130 mil e R$ 140 mil. A formação de estoque com unidades importadas deve sustentar o início das vendas no primeiro trimestre de 2027, enquanto a montadora avança na ampliação da fábrica de Camaçari (BA). Em outubro, a empresa informou que as áreas de soldagem e pintura estavam na fase final de testes operacionais e que a estamparia seguia em construção. Como o sistema híbrido flex foi desenvolvido para o Brasil e equipa veículos montados localmente, a nacionalização do modelo na unidade baiana tende a ocorrer na sequência. Principais rivais e impacto do Dolphin GT no mercado Se confirmar um preço competitivo na faixa de R$ 130 mil, o BYD Dolphin GT passa a pressionar diferentes segmentos. De um lado, ameaça hatches compactos topo de linha a combustão; de outro, atinge SUVs compactos de entrada e intermediários, além de elétricos de acesso e híbridos leves ou convencionais. Para o consumidor brasileiro, o grande atrativo está em unir a recarga na tomada para o uso urbano diário com a flexibilidade do motor flex na estrada. Tudo isso em um pacote que entrega nível de tecnologia e espaço interno superiores à média da categoria nessa faixa de preço. Carregando ofertas...

artigo.texto: Loudoun’s Board of Supervisors wants more authority from the General Assembly this year, particularly relating to the data center industry. Each year, county supervisors adopt a legislative agenda that lists priorities and specific issues they want their representatives to support during the session. This year’s additions to that wish list include a focus on energy, data centers and transmission lines. One item requests authority to deny land use applications because of local power grid constraints. That was included in last year’s requests as well. During rezoning applications for data centers, supervisors are not allowed to consider the building’s impacts on the electric grid since the application is a land use request. This would change that. Another item requests authority to require that data centers provide a comprehensive list of their tenants at the request of the Commissioner of the Revenue. Supervisors also support legislation that would allow a locality to implement a pause on data center applications, although the board already approved a pause last week during its Nov. 17 meeting. Supervisor Koran T. Saines (D-Sterling) also earned support to add an item requesting permission for the county to restrict data centers’ use of generators. This comes as Saines has been working to reduce impacts from a turbine-powered data center in his district that has garnered public pushback. He earned support in July to have staff find ways to regulate generator use. Supervisor Laura A. TeKrony (D-Little River) also successfully moved to add support for legislation that would allow a jurisdiction to issue fines on data centers if they did not notify the locality of backup generator use during emergencies. “Loudoun County has 6,200 diesel generators,” she said. “If some, or all of these generators are used during an emergency, it will be a public health emergency, not just a grid emergency.” The longer the generators are used, the higher the impact, and residents deserve to know when that is happening, she said. Supervisors also opted to add support for legislation that would allow localities to increase fines against data centers for violations of noise ordinances. The request seeks authority to impose fines of $5,000 for first offenses, and $10,000 for subsequent violations. Currently, fines can be implemented at $250 and $500, Saines said. Supervisors are also looking for more of a say in where transmission lines are built, another issue garnering significant public input. Becker & Poliakoff Senior Government Relations Consultant Clarence Williams said the county’s lobbying team is working on a “smorgasbord” of policy options on that issue. “I’m looking for any and all ideas if we possibly can,” Supervisor Caleb A. Kershner (R-Catoctin) said. A proposal by County Chair Phyllis J. Randall (D-At Large) to support any legislation that would shift the cost of new energy transmission infrastructure to high energy rate classes, protect conservation easements and historic landmarks, protect landowners, increase transparency from utilities, make existing transmission corridors priorities for new lines, expand participation in load forecasting, establish pilot programs for underground transmission lines, and improve demand management. Randall said she’s contacted Sen. Russet Perry (D-31) and Del. John McAuliff (D-30) about sponsoring legislation on those issues in response to concerns from residents in western Loudoun, particularly about the Valley Link transmission line. However, residents across the county would be impacted if this legislation passed, she said. Randall said large load transmission through conservation easements and the taking of private property owner’s land for the lines are especially concerning to her. “If you put your land in conservation easement, you do not expect to get a transmission line through your land. That’s the point of doing a conservation easement. … These are the things we’re trying to respond to,” she said. TeKrony also earned support during a Nov. 5 meeting to request legislation that would remove a utility’s obligation to provide power to high facilities using more than 100 megawatts of energy in Northern Virginia if the local power grid is constrained, a viable transmission line corridor or substation does not exist, or if there’s an energy service backlog of more than three years. “Loudoun County has a severely constrained grid,” she said. “The number of data centers in the queue and the duty to provide power to these extremely high load users is unsustainable.” Utilities may delay service to users if needed, but currently they have a legal obligation to eventually provide that power. This year’s agenda also includes support for a work group to study the health impacts of transmission lines, substations and generators. Changes to this year’s agenda also included language to continue supporting Oak Hill’s establishment as a state park; to extend the timelines for residents to appeal corrections to local tax assessments; to allow local oversight for animal releasing agencies, pet shops and boarding facilities; to extend absentee voting; to provide collective bargaining legislation that protects local government authority; to permit more housing regulations on landlords; to expand tax-setting authority; to support traffic calming and to make several environmental protection changes. The board adopted the full agenda during its Nov. 17 meeting. The 2027 General Assembly session is set to begin Jan. 13.

artigo.texto: Moradores de Atibaia (SP) querem barrar data center de R$ 3 bilhões por questões ambientais Ação na Justiça pede suspensão de licenças, enquanto abaixo-assinado aponta para problemas do projeto Um projeto de data center de R$ 3 bilhões em Atibaia (SP) enfrenta a resistência de moradores, que pedem a apuração de possíveis irregularidades no licenciamento ambiental da obra. Nesta segunda (23), uma ação popular apresentada na Justiça de Atibaia pediu a suspensão de qualquer licença, alvará ou autorização municipal que permita a construção do data center. O projeto pertence à DataSpots, empresa do Grupo ON comandada por Luiz Fernando Ortega. O plano prevê investimento de R$ 3 bilhões no Data Center Alfa, um complexo com capacidade de 50 megawatts (MW) e conexão em 138 kV, que ocupará uma área equivalente a 50 campos de futebol no Bairro do Tanque. A operação está prevista para começar entre 2029 e 2030. O empreendimento faz parte de um pacote nacional da companhia que soma R$ 39 bilhões em oito projetos. Em agosto de 2025, ele obteve parecer de acesso do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), que prevê a expansão de cerca de 15 km de linha e dois módulos de entrada em 138 kV, além de tratativas com a distribuidora Elektro. Embora o portfólio oficial da DataSpots apresente o projeto como "aprovado e estruturado", a ação popular afirma que a Prefeitura de Atibaia recebeu apenas "consultas preliminares, sem processo formal de licenciamento ambiental ou urbanístico". Por isso, a ação pede que o município entregue, em dez dias, cópias dos documentos relacionados ao projeto e identifique as empresas interessadas e os servidores responsáveis pelas decisões. Em nota, a prefeitura de Atibaia afirmou que não há, até o momento, "nenhum projeto de implantação de data center formalmente protocolado junto à Administração Municipal para fins de análise e aprovação". "Não existe qualquer processo em andamento ou análise técnica realizada pela Prefeitura relacionada à implantação desse tipo de empreendimento, tampouco qualquer processo de licenciamento ambiental neste particular", diz o documento. A prefeitura confirmou que houve uma reunião sobre o tema. Porém, afirma que o encontro "não representou qualquer compromisso ou tratativa formal, nem deu início a processos de análise ou autorização de empreendimentos, pois não houve qualquer protocolo para aprovação de projeto neste sentido". A reportagem procurou a Prefeitura de Atibaia e a DataSpots, mas não obteve resposta. Já o ONS confirmou que emitiu, em agosto de 2025, o Parecer de Acesso para o Data Center Alfa, com previsão de atendimento de carga de até 25 MW a partir de 2029 e de até 50 MW a partir de 2030, condicionado a reforços e ampliações previstos no sistema elétrico. Segundo o operador, a análise concluiu pela viabilidade do empreendimento, conforme os critérios e procedimentos vigentes para acesso às instalações de transmissão. Sobre outras questões, o operador declarou em nota: "O ONS ressalta que questões relacionadas ao licenciamento ambiental, estudos de impacto, uso e ocupação do solo e demais aspectos socioambientais são de competência dos órgãos responsáveis por essas análises e autorizações". Argumentos contra o projeto Antes da ação popular, o movimento Fora Data Center criou um abaixo-assinado que já reúne mais de 4 mil assinaturas pedindo a proibição desse tipo de estrutura na cidade. Entre os argumentos dos moradores contra o projeto estão os impactos ambientais, como o alto consumo de água e de energia elétrica, o ruído contínuo, a poluição luminosa, as bolhas de calor e o tráfego pesado nas rodovias. Eles também contestam a promessa de desenvolvimento econômico: apesar de o setor contar com incentivos federais bilionários, a operação, altamente automatizada, gera apenas de 50 a 200 empregos permanentes depois das obras (que mobilizam de 150 a 500 trabalhadores temporários), enquanto o ônus ambiental e viário fica com o município. "A implantação de complexos industriais que demandam água e energia em escala massiva, produzem poluição sonora perene e desfiguram o ordenamento territorial colide frontalmente com a vocação turística, ecológica e residencial que define o município", diz o abaixo-assinado. Em 27 de agosto, a Associação Salve Atibaia e o Movimento dos Atingidos por Subestação em Atibaia (MAS Atibaia) protocolaram representação na Promotoria de Justiça de Atibaia (MPSP) pedindo a apuração de irregularidades no licenciamento ambiental da infraestrutura elétrica associada ao data center: o Projeto Fernão Dias, da ISA Energia Brasil. Com investimento superior a R$ 300 milhões, 33 km de linha de transmissão e ampliação da Subestação Fernão Dias, o projeto obteve Licença Prévia em junho de 2025 e tinha energização prevista para o segundo semestre de 2026. Em julho de 2025, o diretor de Projetos da ISA Energia, Dayron Urrego, afirmou: "O Projeto Fernão Dias contribuirá para a transição energética no Brasil. O empreendimento é essencial para o crescimento econômico no Estado de São Paulo, em especial para data centers que contarão com o fornecimento energético ainda mais seguro e eficiente para avançar em suas operações". Em janeiro deste ano, Urrego voltou ao tema: "Com o Projeto Fernão Dias, avançamos na transição energética do Brasil e impulsionamos o desenvolvimento de São Paulo. O fornecimento de energia mais seguro e eficiente será decisivo para que data centers e outras operações alcancem novos patamares de inovação e crescimento". Segundo os moradores, porém, na audiência pública do Estudo de Impacto de Vizinhança, realizada em 17 de junho de 2026, a concessionária não esclareceu a ligação entre os ramais de transmissão e a instalação do complexo da DataSpots. Procurada pela reportagem, a ISA Energia Brasil se distanciou dos projetos de data center e afirmou que atua "exclusivamente" na infraestrutura de transmissão de energia elétrica e que "não possui responsabilidade sobre os data centers eventualmente projetados

artigo.texto: UTICA — The Utica Common Council discussed proposed legislation to regulate battery energy storage systems (BESS) at a Monday, Nov. 23 Committee of the Whole meeting. The council currently has a moratorium on BESS in Utica, having passed several extensions, with the most recent extension set to expire Saturday, Dec. 5. The council’s next regular meeting is Wednesday, Dec. 2. At the Nov. 23 meeting, the councilors reviewed legislation that Assistant Corporation Counsel Stephanie DiGiorgio prepared. The legislation split BESS into three tiers: Tier 1 for systems at one to two-family dwellings that do not exceed 40 kilowatt-hours within utility closets and storage space, and 80 kWh in detached garages, exterior walls or outdoors on the ground, or those that have an aggregate energy capacity less than or equal to 80 kWh Tier 2 for systems that have a capacity of less than 300 kWh or comprise more than one battery storage technology in a room or enclosed area. Such systems would require site plan approval from the Planning Board. Tier 3 for systems that greater than or equal to 300 kWh or are composed of have more than one storage battery technology in a room or enclosed area. These systems could be built in industrial or mixed-use industrial zones, and would need a special use permit to be built. Tier 3 systems are large-scale battery energy storage systems. The councilors debated whether or not they’d like to allow Tier 3 systems with the regulations, or ban them altogether, with Councilor-at-Large Jack LoMedico arguing strongly in favor of prohibiting them, due to the lithium battery fires that have occurred at such installations. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, lithium battery fires can be very hard to extinguish and could reignite, can release harmful gases, and require specialized procedures for cleanup and disposal. “I think we should ban it. I think let’s just get it by us,” he said. We don’t need battery storage areas in the city. I’ve seen what they’ve done and they’re a mess. Maybe 50 years from now or 20 years from now, if we want to take another look at it, but I don’t want to be responsible,” LoMedico said. “Have you ever seen one catch fire?” Sixth Ward Councilor Joseph Betrus, whose district includes many industrial and mixed-use industrial zoned areas, said that he is also not in favor of large-scale BESS, but expressed hesitance about closing the door entirely on such developments. “In my opinion, if that’s the case, we should go with the top two [tiers] and don’t do three right now, because I don’t think we know enough about it,” Betrus said. “But I don’t want to shut anybody off either down the road.” The council does have the ability to revisit the legislation after its passage, and could go through the process to amend the ordinance by adding in the section allowing Tier 3 systems if so desired. Betrus said he would be satisfied with this. First Ward Councilor Katie Aiello said that while she was hesitant about BESS at first, she’s since learned more about the world’s increasing reliance on electricity. BESS draw electricity from the grid during periods of low demand, and then stores it until it’s needed, according to the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority. These systems provide backup during power outages from severe weather or accidents, and stabilize the grid during peak demand times, like during the summer when everyone is running their air conditioners, according to NYSERDA. “It’s just the way the world is going. There’s pros and cons. We’re up front, we don’t know all the risks, and we’re setting ourselves up, some people are feeling through the dark on this one,” she said. “But there’s also, you get ahead of it, and we can position ourselves. There are things that I’d like that other cities have done, if they do it. … I just don’t want us to get short-sighted and not be prepared.” After discussion, the councilors decided that Tier 3 systems should not be allowed at all, and so DiGiorgio said she would remove it from the proposed ordinance, to prohibit them from the city. After a lengthy discussion about putting further limitations on the number of electric vehicle charging stations that can be placed outside buildings and facilities, they decided to exclude home and business charging stations from the legislation, so that the regulations would not apply. She said she would also amend the Tier 2 definition to reflect that it would be for accessory use to a building. The council scheduled a special meeting from 5 p.m. on Monday, Nov. 30 to introduce its BESS legislation.

artigo.texto: CHESAPEAKE, Va. — A new announcement about the future of the former Frank Williams Farm property in southern Chesapeake is renewing questions about whether data centers could eventually become part of the massive development. Praetorian Fund, the private investment firm behind the proposed 4,000-plus-acre Praetorian Park off Highway 17 near the North Carolina border, announced it has selected engineering and planning firm Kimley-Horn to help advance planning for the property. The announcement comes after News 3 Chesapeake reporter Erin Holly first reported in September on Praetorian's plans for the property and neighbors' concerns about its future, including questions about possible data center development. Watch previous coverage: Investment firm purchases Chesapeake's 4,000-acre Frank Williams Farm for multi-billion dollar hub Praetorian envisions the property as a multi-phase innovation hub that could include advanced manufacturing, defense technology, energy, sports, entertainment and what the company describes as "modern digital infrastructure." The company says Kimley-Horn will support design, infrastructure coordination, entitlements and planning, helping establish a framework for land uses, parcel configurations and connections between different development areas. Kimley-Horn has an established practice working on data centers and other "mission critical" facilities. The firm's website says its work in that field includes site planning, power and cooling infrastructure, utility coordination, zoning and permitting. News 3 also found recent examples of Kimley-Horn working on major proposed data center developments in Ohio and Texas. That experience does not establish that Kimley-Horn was selected to plan a data center in Chesapeake, or that one will ultimately be built at Praetorian Park. However, city records reviewed by News 3 show data centers have been contemplated as one possible use for a portion of the property since years before Praetorian Fund became involved. In November 2022, Chesapeake City Council approved the rezoning of approximately 1,420 acres of the larger property from agricultural land to a Planned Unit Development Industrial Park, or PUD-IP. The development criteria approved as part of that process specifically state that the proposed industrial park could accommodate several types of employment uses, including advanced manufacturing, corporate headquarters and offices, medical campuses and higher-learning centers. The document then states: "The PUD contemplates the inclusion of light fabrication and assembly ancillary to a research and development use, as well as data centers." Elsewhere in the document, data centers are described as an appropriate use alongside advanced manufacturing, research and development and other employment uses. The distinction is important: those documents apply to roughly 1,420 acres, not the entirety of the 4,000-plus-acre property, and they identify data centers as one of several possible uses. They do not establish that a data center is currently planned. The city has been laying the groundwork for large-scale development here for years. In 2016, City Council identified the Williams property as a target for economic development. In 2018, Council changed the city's long-term plan for part of the property, opening the door to industrial and other non-residential uses. The next major step came in 2022, when Council approved the Coastal Virginia Commerce Park rezoning. At the time of the 2022 rezoning, city staff described the project as a "mega site industrial park" designed for a small number of large users. During a presentation ahead of the rezoning, city staff said parcels within the park would have a minimum lot size of 100 acres and that individual users were expected to occupy even more land. City staff also acknowledged at the time that there was not yet a detailed master development plan because the eventual users and their needs would help determine the layout of the park. News 3's review found another connection between the old plans and the new Kimley-Horn involvement announcement. Kimley-Horn was already working on the Frank Williams Farm property years before Praetorian Fund's involvement. The 2022 PUD documents identify Kimley-Horn as the firm that prepared the Master Land Use Plan associated with the project and the property's traffic impact study. The firm also prepared a preliminary engineering report studying water and sewer service to the Williams Tract. Public utilities were a major issue during the 2022 planning process. City staff said the property's lack of public utilities had prevented its economic potential from being fully realized. The PUD documents describe extending public water and sewer to the commerce park as "critical," with the applicant or property owner responsible for continuing that infrastructure south from the Chesapeake Regional Airport area to the property. The criteria also contain environmental and military-related development requirements. The property lies within the Northwest River Watershed Protection District, which protects a drinking-water source for Chesapeake. The criteria require additional review related to runoff and development within that watershed. The site is also near Naval Support Activity Northwest Annex and within an area where development can potentially create electromagnetic interference with military equipment. The approved criteria call for future development plans to be provided to the Navy for review and recommendations on mitigating that interference. In announcing Kimley-Horn's newest role, Randy Royal, a principal with the firm who has previously worked on the property, said the firm's job will be to turn the larger vision into a workable plan. artigo.texto: The village has approved a building permit for a second building at a massive $18 billion data center campus in Grayslake where residents suing to stop the project are awaiting a judge’s ruling. The Village of Grayslake said Monday it issued a building permit for the second facility at the T5 campus within the Cornerstone property along Peterson Road. The second building will span 456,270 square feet and is part of an estimated $18 billion private investment, village officials said. The village issued the first building permit for the T5 @ Chicago IV data center campus on September 1 for an 800,000-square-foot building. The village said in a statement that the development, like all buildings in the village, must “strictly adhere to Grayslake’s high standards, rigorous local codes, and state environmental regulations.” “As the building activity progresses, the Village will conduct stringent oversight. In all the Village development projects, preserving natural resources and protecting surrounding neighborhoods remain absolute priorities every step of the way,” the village said. Village officials said the project was secured without local municipal tax incentives, tax exemptions or TIF subsidies and the current campus plan is projected to generate $1.4 billion in property tax revenue over 20 years across local taxing bodies. “Because the Village of Grayslake operates with a balanced budget with zero debt, new revenues from the campus offer unmatched potential to directly benefit local households by the Village Boards established goal of Giving Back to residents and Doing Big Things for the community,” the village said. Village officials said operating with zero municipal debt allows the village to explore “creative ways to return revenue directly to residents” and that new commercial revenue could fund projects such as downtown investment, expanded open space and trails, advanced infrastructure and community amenities “that were previously unimaginable without borrowing.” The village is conducting a feasibility study for a possible community recreation center. The Preservation of Community Well-being Collective LLC and nine Lake County residents filed a lawsuit on July 31 in Lake County Circuit Court against the Village of Grayslake, T5 Data Centers, LLC, and Alter Asset Management Company challenging the village’s 2024 to 2025 approvals of the campus. The lawsuit asks the court to declare the approvals invalid, void the development agreement between the village and T5 and permanently bar the village from issuing further permits in reliance on the approvals. The village and T5 have asked the court to dismiss the case, arguing the residents filed it long after the deadline to challenge the approvals. Lake County Judge Janelle Christensen heard arguments on the motions on November 6. She said she was concerned there could be a due process violation if residents were kept from a September 2024 zoning hearing on the project, though she said she was not saying the village concealed anything. Christensen said she would issue a written ruling no later than December 30. T5 Data Centers CEO and Chairman Pete Marin said in September that the company voluntarily withdrew its application to remediate local wetlands in July after hearing from residents. The campus as approved by the Grayslake Village Board between September 2024 and May 2025 calls for up to 472 acres of development, more than 10 million square feet of buildings and approximately 1.55 gigawatts of electrical demand. The village’s latest plans call for 6,750,000 square feet of building space across 11 buildings, which is 33% less than previous plans, according to a village FAQ released in September. The village expects the data centers to be built over the next seven to 10 years, according to the FAQ. The campus is part of Cornerstone, a $750 million, 641-acre mixed-use development near Peterson Road and Alleghany Road. The Lake County Board voted on September 8 to ban new data centers from being approved in unincorporated Lake County until May 2027, but the county has said the village, not the county, has jurisdiction over the T5 project. It is unclear when construction on the second building would begin.

artigo.texto: Kalamazoo seeks resident input on zoning rules for data centers, battery energy storage KALAMAZOO, Mich. — How should data centers and battery energy storage systems be regulated in Kalamazoo? That's the question the City of Kalamazoo is asking residents as city officials study up on the facilities and develop zoning regulations. According to city officials on Wednesday, a group of neighborhood residents, environmental representatives, industry experts and city staff convened to help with this process. A community open house and workshop has also been scheduled for Dec. 15 at the Crosstown Community Room: 150 E. Crosstown Pkwy in Kalamazoo. During this event, community members are invited to learn more about the facilities, as well as their potential impacts. They can also ask questions, and can share concerns or priorities, according to city officials. "This is the first of several planned opportunities for public input. Your feedback will help inform the development of proposed regulations," officials said. - Oshtemo Township: considers extending moratoriums on energy projects, data centers Wednesday's update comes over a month after the Kalamazoo City Commission adopted a temporary moratorium Oct. 5. While in effect, the moratorium pauses acceptance and applications for data centers, battery energy storage systems, cryptocurrency mining systems and artificial intelligence data centers until 2027, unless new regulations take effect or the moratorium is extended, according to city officials. More information about the moratorium, working group and the ongoing review can be found online.

artigo.texto: Sodium vs. Lithium: New Economics Challenge Lithium-Ion's Proven Resilience in Next-Gen Energy Storage Markets Key Highlights - Wood Mackenzie reports more than 70 GWh of sodium-ion supply agreements across the U.S., China and Europe. - Sodium-ion cells could reach LFP-level production costs by the end of 2026, while grid-ready systems may not match LFP upfront pricing until after 2030. - Passive cooling, extreme-weather durability and fewer mid-project battery replacements are among potential SIB advantages. - Global markets are evaluating 21% lower total ownership costs over a 20-year SIB project lifespan, despite higher upfront cell costs than LFP. In the race for next-generation grid power, lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries (SIB) are increasingly competing in the global energy storage market. Amid this shifting landscape, SIB developers like Alsym Energy are advancing non-lithium-ion and advanced battery energy storage systems (BESS) across multiple use cases like mining. The safety performance of lithium-ion is significantly stronger in newer systems than in vintage BESS designs. As EnergyTech previously reported, the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) highlighted in an October white paper that BESS failures per deployed GWh declined 98% between 2018 and 2025. For years, however, lithium-ion batteries in legacy systems were prone to catastrophic fires. That same seven-year span includes separate fire events at the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, and a 2019 thermal runaway event that severely injured eight firefighters in Surprise, Arizona. These incidents exposed critical safety risks in early-vintage BESS—just as large-scale energy users race to bring record capacity online for AI data centers and next-gen industrial electrification. That behind-the-meter and grid-scale surge has prompted the industry to look for safer alternatives. Beyond safety: The commercial surge of sodium-ion Although newer lithium-ion battery designs have largely addressed these safety concerns, sodium-ion batteries are still surging into commercial production for the global energy storage sector. This includes production of the TENER Sodium Energy Storage System from Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL), which debuted in Munich, Germany. The company claims it is a field-validated sodium-ion energy storage solution. In early market deployments, sodium-ion batteries are demonstrating their potential viability for long-duration storage, weather resistance and safety in next-gen operations. Yet this momentum isn’t directly linked to thermal runaway in vintage lithium systems. According to a recent Wood Mackenzie (WoodMac) report, sodium-ion's improving economics stem from its 20-year lifecycle math, extreme-weather durability and broader shifts in global trade policy. In WoodMac’s November report, “Sodium-ion batteries: commercialisation begins, economics to follow,” the global research firm noted that sodium-ion batteries are now entering commercial production with over 70 GWh of supply agreements already secured across China, the U.S. and Europe. Tracking market trends in China, the U.S., Germany and India, the report found that sodium-ion is establishing itself as “the most cost-effective emerging alternative” to lithium-ion battery storage. Top manufacturers are on track to produce raw sodium-ion battery cells as cost-effectively as lithium iron phosphate (LFP) by the end of 2026. However, WoodMac noted that grid-ready sodium-ion BESS won't match the upfront pricing of comparable LFP systems until after 2030. “The 2030-2035 window is where the economics decisively shift,” said WoodMac senior research analyst Priya Shrivastava in a statement. “For projects being deployed today, LFP remains the bankable choice for two- to four-hour duration assets.” China, which dominates early manufacturing in this sector, is projected to achieve an 18% to 20% "learning rate" between 2026 and 2035. WoodMac explains that this means China will have the ability to drop its production costs by roughly one-fifth every time its cumulative sodium-ion output doubles. “While SIB offers manufacturers a valuable alternative, the chemistry still faces material challenges: scaling production, refining cell materials and establishing a track record of consistent performance,” added Shrivastava. Today, sodium-ion chemistries account for less than 1% of global battery production for EVs and energy storage, according to WoodMac, and still cost more overall than lithium-ion for an equivalent storage capacity. Yet sodium is the sixth-most common element available to miners, roughly 1,000 times more abundant than lithium. Shrivastava explained that the most probable outcome WoodMac views is a sodium-ion battery market served by different technologies, each optimized for distinct applications and duration profiles. Passive cooling and the 20-year lifecycle math LFP, a lithium-ion battery chemistry, uses iron phosphate as its cathode material and can store up to 205 watt-hours per kilogram in each cell. Major manufacturers like CATL have unveiled LFP architectures that meet this threshold to boost energy capacity for large-scale stationary storage. However, as WoodMac previously highlighted, LFP requires energy-intensive active cooling to maintain safe operating temperatures in standard energy storage tech built around its chemistry. U.S. companies like battery storage developer Peak Energy are developing passively cooled BESS tech to deploy next-gen sodium-ion battery cells, built for stationary grid storage applications. By eliminating active cooling systems, Peak Energy claims its sodium-ion BESS reduces lifecycle energy storage costs by 20% (compared to conventional systems) while delivering more than 99% uptime. artigo.texto: Governo vê risco de "dano severo" ao sistema elétrico se leilão de baterias for adiado A AGU alertou que adiar o leilão de baterias pode causar dano severo ao sistema elétrico brasileiro, gerando risco de déficit de potência e apagões até 2027. O posicionamento rebate ação da ABEEólica para suspender o certame de dezembro, motivada por discordâncias sobre o custeio imposto aos geradores. Enquanto tramita no Congresso projeto para transferir essa conta aos consumidores, entidades do setor defendem a manutenção do leilão para assegurar a estabilidade energética nacional. Um adiamento do leilão para contratação de baterias de armazenamento de energia marcado para a próxima semana gera perigo de "dano concreto e severo" para o sistema elétrico brasileiro, que pode ter déficit de potência já a partir do próximo ano, disse a União, com base em informações do Ministério de Minas e Energia. A declaração consta em defesa da Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU), vista pela Reuters, em um processo judicial movido pela associação da energia eólica ABEEólica que tenta suspender o certame, em meio à insatisfação dos geradores com o pagamento dos custos das baterias. Segundo a AGU, estudos do governo identificaram, já para 2027, "violações aos limites regulatórios de garantia de suprimento de potência" -- uma situação que, na prática, pode desestabilizar o sistema elétrico nacional e levar a apagões. O leilão de baterias ajudaria a recompor a margem de segurança operativa, defendeu a União, ressaltando que o grande certame voltado à contratação de termelétricas e hidrelétricas em março deste ano não foi suficiente para suprir toda a necessidade do sistema elétrico. O Ministério de Minas e Energia já havia dito anteriormente que calibrou sua demanda de contratação em leilões neste ano para que parte da necessidade fosse atendida pelas baterias, justamente para abrir espaço para essa tecnologia e evitar uma sobrecontratação de capacidade. Ainda de acordo com a AGU, um adiamento do leilão da próxima semana poderá comprometer a conexão dos projetos vencedores à rede elétrica nacional, conforme as regras da nova Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão (Pnast). "Suspender os leilões às vésperas de sua realização inviabiliza o cronograma, compromete a entrega da potência na data planejada pelo setor e frustra investimentos já realizados pelos proponentes habilitados que aportaram garantias", diz o documento. Programado para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro, o certame de baterias foi judicializado na semana passada pela ABEEólica, que ingressou com ações na Justiça Federal e no Supremo Tribunal Federal questionando a alocação dos custos dessa contratação aos geradores de energia. A entidade sustenta que a lei que impôs o ônus da contratação aos geradores é inconstitucional, e também aponta "vícios" na estruturação do certame de baterias pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel), citando a falta de uma regulamentação sobre o rateio dos custos entre os diferentes geradores. A AGU pediu que a cautelar de urgência solicitada pela ABEEólica para suspender o certame seja indeferida, afirmando que os efeitos da medida seriam irreversíveis sobre toda a licitação. Disse ainda que os geradores não são "meros financiadores" das baterias, visto que esses sistemas também os beneficiariam ao, por exemplo, reduzirem o desperdício energético dos cortes de geração atuais. Uma discussão sobre os custos do certame também corre em paralelo no Congresso, por meio de um projeto de lei que tramita em regime de urgência na Câmara. A proposta retira dos geradores a obrigação do custeio total das baterias e redistribui esse ônus aos consumidores de energia. A Frente Nacional dos Consumidores de Energia (FNCE) estimou que essa mudança da lei poderia resultar em custo extra de até R$6,26 bilhões por ano na conta de luz dos consumidores de energia. Em nota, a entidade também defendeu a manutenção do leilão e disse que considera "irresponsáveis" as tentativas de suspensão do certame. "Atrasar o leilão pode comprometer o enfrentamento dos cortes de energia e dificultar o equilíbrio do sistema", apontou o presidente da FNCE, Luiz Eduardo Barata. Já a Absae, entidade que representa o segmento de baterias, também se posicionou a favor da realização do certame na próxima semana, mas rechaçou os cálculos da FNCE, afirmando que, se mantido com os geradores, esses custos serão repassados aos consumidores "acrescidos de tributos, custos financeiros e prêmio de risco".

artigo.texto: RTX 5090 desaparece de lojas na crise de preços causada por data centers de IA Placa topo de linha da Nvidia vira símbolo da disputa por memória, e lojas de PC gamer como a 4Gamers revisam compras e preços A GeForce RTX 5090, placa de vídeo mais potente da linha para jogos da Nvidia, tornou-se o sinal mais visível da crise de preços no mercado de hardware. Em outubro, o modelo deixou de aparecer na loja online da fabricante nos Estados Unidos, num ano em que a disputa por chips de memória entre data centers de inteligência artificial e fabricantes de computadores encareceu peças de PC no mundo todo. Na 4Gamers, loja de computadores e PC gamer com e-commerce e loja física na Vila Leopoldina, em São Paulo, o efeito aparece na reposição de memória RAM, SSD e placas de vídeo, segundo o fundador e CEO, Rodrigo Bariani. A Nvidia nega que a placa tenha saído de linha. Em 16 de outubro, em Taipé, o vice-presidente sênior Jeff Fisher afirmou que a RTX 5090 não foi descontinuada e que os envios continuam, mas reconheceu que a capacidade da cadeia de suprimentos está restrita. No Brasil, a loja da Nvidia ainda listava 20 modelos da placa no mesmo dia, com preços entre R$ 23 mil e R$ 57 mil, segundo levantamento do Canaltech. Parte da explicação está na memória. A RTX 5090 usa 32 GB de memória GDDR7, tipo que enfrenta o mesmo aperto dos chips usados em servidores. Segundo a consultoria TrendForce, os fornecedores vêm reduzindo a produção de GDDR6, e a GDDR7 tem fabricação limitada porque as fábricas mais avançadas priorizam memória para data centers. O movimento atinge todo o computador. Os preços contratuais da DRAM convencional, o tipo de memória usado nos pentes de RAM, subiram entre 93% e 98% no primeiro trimestre de 2026 sobre o trimestre anterior, de acordo com levantamento da TrendForce. A consultoria atribui a escalada à decisão dos três maiores fabricantes de chips de memória de concentrar produção e embarques em servidores, produtos de preço e margem mais altos, num momento em que provedores de nuvem ampliam a infraestrutura voltada à IA. A pressão perdeu velocidade, mas não mudou de direção. Para o quarto trimestre, a TrendForce projeta reajuste de 10% a 15% nos contratos de DRAM convencional e de 13% a 18% na memória destinada a PCs. A consultoria informa ainda que os fabricantes trabalham com planos preliminares de reduzir a oferta de DRAM para computadores em 2027, já que a demanda ligada à IA segue firme. No Brasil, o varejo de hardware também lidou com o vaivém tributário. Em fevereiro, a Resolução nº 852 do Gecex (Comitê-Executivo de Gestão da Câmara de Comércio Exterior) elevou o imposto de importação de mais de mil itens de informática e telecomunicações. No fim do mesmo mês, a Resolução Gecex nº 866 devolveu placas de vídeo, processadores e placas-mãe às alíquotas anteriores. "Existe um intervalo entre a mudança de custo e o reflexo no varejo. Importação, transporte, desembaraço aduaneiro e estoques já nacionalizados fazem a alta demorar para chegar à prateleira, mas ela chega", afirma Bariani, cuja loja trabalha tanto com importação quanto com distribuidores oficiais. A procura segue firme mesmo com peças mais caras. Em setembro, o volume de vendas do segmento de equipamentos e material para escritório, informática e comunicação cresceu 19,5% em relação ao mesmo mês de 2025, segundo a PMC (Pesquisa Mensal de Comércio) do IBGE (Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística). Foi o maior avanço entre as atividades do varejo na comparação anual. "A RTX 5090 é o termômetro. Quando a placa mais cobiçada do mercado fica difícil de achar até na loja do próprio fabricante, o recado para o varejo é claro: a memória passou a ser disputada com os data centers", diz Bariani. Para ele, a cadeia de componentes funciona de forma interligada. "Quem entende minimamente de hardware sabe que, se o SSD sobe, tudo sobe. A loja que não acompanha isso de perto perde margem ou perde cliente." A 4Gamers tem respondido com ferramentas que ajudam o cliente a gastar melhor. No Monte seu PC, o comprador escolhe cada componente do computador com checagem de compatibilidade. No Troque seu PC, o equipamento usado entra como abatimento na compra de um novo. "Quem vai comprar PC gamer hoje está mais atento a cada real. Nosso papel como loja é ajudar o cliente a chegar na configuração certa para o uso dele, sem pagar por peça que não vai aproveitar", afirma o executivo. Para Bariani, a gestão de compra e de preço deve pesar cada vez mais na competitividade das lojas de computador nos próximos trimestres, com projeções que indicam reajustes menores, mas ainda positivos, e oferta de memória para PCs mais restrita em 2027. O perfil da loja no Instagram reúne as configurações e as ofertas da 4Gamers.

artigo.texto: New solutions address power needs across the source-grid, power-distribution and cabinet-side layers of AI data center infrastructure LAS VEGAS, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As AI workloads scale, data centers are placing new demands on power infrastructure, making reliable electricity supply essential to continuous operations. At RE+ 2026, part of North America's Smart Energy Week, EVE Energy introduced a full-scenario energy storage portfolio for AI data centers (AIDC), with solutions designed to support power requirements from the source-grid side through power distribution to cabinet-level backup. The company also showcased energy storage solutions for commercial and industrial, residential and telecommunications applications, alongside emerging all-solid-state and sodium-ion battery technologies. EVE Energy AIDC Full-Scenario Energy Storage Solutions During the exhibition, EVE held a dedicated AIDC product launch and presented solutions for three application layers: the green zone, or source-grid side; the gray zone, or power-distribution side; and the white zone, or cabinet side. The portfolio includes rack-level battery backup solutions and is designed to address requirements ranging from millisecond-scale load smoothing to long-duration energy management. Source-Grid Side: High-Power Energy Storage and Frequency Regulation. On the green zone's source-grid side, EVE Energy introduced the 1P 5MWh ESS, which the company describes as the industry's first 20-foot, 5 MWh, 1P high-rate energy storage system. The system balances 5 MWh of energy capacity with 1P power capability in a standard 20-foot container. It is rated at 1P, with a peak rate of up to 1.2P, and delivers 20,000 equivalent cycles in frequency-regulation applications. System efficiency reaches 93.6%, while auxiliary power requirements are reduced by 20%, according to EVE. The solution integrates DC, AC and EMS capabilities at the plant level. At a 100 MWh project scale, the configuration can reduce the number of cabinets by three, lower transportation costs by more than 40% and reduce land use by more than 13%. EVE reports annual system availability of 99%, along with higher returns over the system's full lifecycle. The system is equipped with what EVE describes as the industry's first 300+ Ah dedicated frequency-regulation cell, featuring a capacity of 315 Ah and a volumetric energy density of 395 Wh/L. According to EVE, no lithium plating occurs at the cell interface under high-rate operating conditions, helping ensure cell safety and long service life. Also on display was Mr.Giant 3.0, EVE Energy's flagship long-duration energy storage system. Following 700 days of demonstrated operation, the system achieved efficiency of more than 95.5% and a cycle count reaching 10,000 cycles. EVE says the system can deliver lifecycle benefits equivalent to an additional two years. Power-distribution side: backup for transient loads. EVE presented its Fortron 6C/10C backup power cabinet, designed to support short-duration, high-power load events. The cabinet supports continuous discharge at up to 10C and can deliver 660 kW for five minutes. It has a 15-year design life and is compatible with uninterruptible power supply (UPS) backup systems, with support for high-voltage direct current (HVDC) applications. The modular architecture is designed for factory pre-integration and rapid deployment. Safety provisions include a reinforced cell design, compartmentalized thermal isolation, staged overcurrent protection and coordinated fire-suppression systems. These features are intended to help protect the system while supporting fast-response backup applications. Cabinet side: rack-level support for dynamic AI loads. EVE also introduced a rack-level energy storage system combining a battery backup unit (BBU) with a capacitor backup unit (CBU). The BBU uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) high-power cells in a high-density 3U form factor and supports discharge rates of up to 48C. The system is designed to smooth load fluctuations across a 1-millisecond-to-10-second window, while providing backup power transfer in less than 2 milliseconds. According to EVE, The LIC hybrid supercapacitor has a response time of 1 millisecond or less. Building a full-scenario energy storage platform for AIDC Spanning the green zone on the source-grid side, the gray zone for power distribution and the white zone at the rack level, EVE Energy's newly launched AIDC energy-storage portfolio reflects years of sustained investment, development and expertise across the company's full range of battery products. With one of the world's most comprehensive lithium battery product portfolios, EVE Energy is among the few companies capable of directly supplying both battery cells and systems across the entire AIDC power chain. The company's end-to-end capabilities extend from battery cell development through system integration. The integrated approach is intended to simplify procurement and operations for customers. A single-source offering can reduce the number of vendor relationships and streamline purchasing and project decisions. Coordinated development of cells, BMS and system integration can also clarify accountability when issues arise. A unified technical platform and service contact are designed to reduce maintenance complexity and operations and maintenance (O&M) costs for data centers that operate around the clock. EVE says it ranked No. 2 globally in energy-storage cell shipments in the first half of 2026. The company reports cumulative global shipments of 230 GWh and inclusion in S&P Global's Tier 1 list of energy storage system integrators. Building on its strategy of "global manufacturing, global cooperation and global service," EVE says it will continue developing grid-forming capabilities and energy storage products for the full range of AIDC applications. artigo.texto: Quinta-feira, 26 de novembro de 2026 Por Redação O Sul | 25 de novembro de 2026 A FCC (Comissão Federal de Comunicações dos Estados Unidos) autorizou a SpaceX a lançar uma constelação de 1 milhão de satélites para instalar data centers no espaço, informou a agência nessa quarta-feira (25). No início do ano, a empresa de Elon Musk havia solicitado autorização para colocar em órbita os módulos, capazes de processar grandes volumes de dados, para serem utilizados na Terra. A FCC afirmou que aprovou a constelação, batizada de “Starmind”, para ajudar a atender à demanda crescente por capacidade computacional para inteligência artificial. Pela licença, a SpaceX deverá iniciar o lançamento dos satélites até novembro de 2033. A empresa terá de colocar em órbita 10% do total autorizado, ou 100 mil unidades, até novembro de 2035, e metade da constelação até novembro de 2038, informou a FCC. A aprovação permitirá à SpaceX “desenvolver tecnologias emergentes que ampliem a liderança americana no espaço e na inteligência artificial”, acrescentou a agência. Os data centers são a infraestrutura física que sustenta a inteligência artificial e exigem grandes quantidades de energia. “Com o aproveitamento direto da energia solar, disponível quase continuamente e com baixos custos operacionais e de manutenção, esses satélites alcançarão ganhos transformadores de eficiência energética e de custos, além de reduzir significativamente o impacto ambiental associado aos data centers terrestres”, afirmou a SpaceX à FCC. Ainda não está claro se a empresa pretende colocar 1 milhão de satélites em órbita. Atualmente, existem cerca de 17 mil satélites no espaço. Operadoras do setor às vezes solicitam autorização para lançar um número maior de unidades do que planejam efetivamente colocar em operação, a fim de ter flexibilidade no desenvolvimento dos projetos. A SpaceX pediu autorização para lançar 42 mil satélites Starlink antes de começar a implantar o sistema. A rede, que continua em expansão, conta atualmente com pouco mais de 11 mil unidades em órbita. O pedido da empresa depende, em grande parte, da redução dos custos de lançamento da Starship, foguete reutilizável de nova geração que está em desenvolvimento e deverá ajudar a colocar os satélites no espaço. A unidade de satélites Leo, da Amazon, e outras empresas criticaram o projeto. Elas argumentam que a SpaceX dificilmente conseguirá lançar todas as unidades previstas e que a operação poderia levar séculos. Em março, o presidente da FCC, Brendan Carr, rejeitou as críticas. “A Amazon deveria se concentrar em organizar sua própria operação de lançamentos e sua própria constelação de satélites, em vez de se preocupar com outras empresas que estão efetivamente lançando satélites no ritmo e na frequência em que a SpaceX está”, afirmou Carr. A FCC informou ainda que aprovou pedidos da SpaceX para reforçar sua rede óptica, autorizando recursos adicionais de comunicação.

artigo.texto: Battery storage system could power 170,000 homes Plans to build a battery storage system capable of powering more than 170,000 homes have been recommended for approval. CONNECTID 2 Ltd has applied to install the infrastructure on land west of the A140 at Red House Farm in Yaxley, near Eye, Suffolk. However, the application has been opposed by Yaxley, Thrandeston and Mellis parish councils over concerns including flooding and fire safety. Mid Suffolk District Council will make its final decision at a planning meeting on 2 December. Blueprints showed the storage system would consist of 448 battery container units and be built on 10.4 hectares (25.7 acres) of mostly agricultural land. The facilities enable electricity from renewable sources, such as solar and wind, to be stored outside of national and local networks and then released into the grid when power is required. According to planning documents, the development would have 520MW of storage - enough energy to power 176,100 homes a day. If permission is granted, the site will be returned to agricultural use after 40 years or if it goes six months without operating. Similar proposals at land south of Eye Airfield Industrial Estate were approved by the council in July 2025. The local authority is run by a Green, independent and Liberal Democrat coalition. artigo.texto: The American public really hates data centers. We should know. Over the past year, we’ve watched data center fights flare up in hundreds of towns nationwide and dominate the midterm elections. Our polling shows that 71% of Americans would now oppose a data center being built near their home — up from 42% last year. So it’s little wonder that data centers have become a big part of the debate over the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, the permitting reform bill that now awaits a vote in the House of Representatives. BAAJA would make it easier to build many types of big and small projects in the United States, including transmission lines, pipelines and public transit. But when criticizing the bill, opponents have fixated on one type of project in particular: data centers. Earthjustice, an environmental litigation group, has warned that the bill will “fast-track the dirty data center buildout.” In an interview last month, a powerful House Democrat claimed that the bill is really “about” data centers and the energy infrastructure needed to power them. This didn’t happen by accident. Within hours of the bill’s release, opponents planned to link it to data centers in their messaging criticizing the legislation, according to a transcript leaked to Punchbowl News. In response, the bill’s supporters have argued that BAAJA penalizes data centers and would force them to protect Americans from higher electricity bills — a policy that many winning Democrats just ran on. Some supporters have gone further, asserting that the bill won’t help data centers in any way. That isn’t true. But it’s also not true that the bill would be an unqualified gift to the data center industry. The big four policies While BAAJA is a long bill, it has four big policies that would affect data centers in some way. It’s worth holding all four in your head at the same time. First, it would build out the country’s electricity transmission grid, requiring utilities and grid operators to plan and build a much larger grid than exists right now. This would help data centers because data centers need a lot of electricity. But it would also help everything else that uses electricity, too — including the electric vehicles, heat pumps, and electric infrastructure essential to fight climate change. And it would help renewables, whose growth is limited by insufficient power-line capacity to bring electricity to cities and suburbs. For this reason, some green critics of the overall bill, such as Earthjustice, “strongly support” the transmission section. Second, BAAJA would write tough new ratepayer protection provisions applying to data centers and crypto mines into federal electricity law. If BAAJA passes, then the Federal Power Act would discriminate against AI and crypto data centers as it discriminates against no other type of industrial energy user. These policies aim to protect Americans from seeing their electricity bills rise due to data centers, and they go much further than President Trump’s voluntary “pledges.” They would force data center developers to pay for grid upgrades upfront, so that if a project requires grid infrastructure improvements and then fails, it doesn’t impose costs on everyone. These provisions would allow states or utilities to write their own stricter rules and, for instance, auction off spare capacity on the grid to data centers instead of giving it away to whoever is first in line. States could then use those savings to cut Americans’ power bills further. On top of these rules, the bill would require data centers, crypto miners, and other large computing facilities to report their energy use to the federal government. This has been a longstanding priority for climate groups; disclosing this information is already required for most other kinds of large energy consumers, but it has been voluntary for the AI and crypto industries. Third, the bill would ease permitting for natural gas pipelines at a time when new ones are being developed specifically to serve data center demand growth. BAAJA would narrow and limit states’ ability under the Clean Water Act to block permits for natural gas pipelines that cross major rivers or wetlands, and it extends permits granted under the law from five to 10 years. It also significantly curtails a provision that has allowed some Democratic governors to block gas pipelines that pass through their states. Data centers run on electricity, not natural gas. But because it has been so hard for new facilities to connect to the electricity grid, many data center developers have planned to build big on-site natural gas plants to power their projects. The bill’s changes could make it easier for gas pipelines to expand to service these planned facilities. Finally, the bill would make it easier to build big projects of all kinds that have any kind of federal permitting nexus. BAAJA limits the scope of certain environmental review laws, such as the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act. It imposes new deadlines on outside litigants’ ability to sue under those laws. And it limits the scope of Clean Water Act wetlands permitting and allows states to take over Endangered Species Act reviews. The bill also makes it much harder to undo permitting decisions lawfully made by a previous president. This last set of changes, taken together, would make it easier for large construction projects of all kinds to break ground and reach completion, especially in places where federal wetlands and species permitting could take a long time. That could help factories, wind and solar farms, mines, transmission lines, public transit, pipelines, warehouses, retailers, and — yes — data centers. What this all means The bill, in other words, isn’t simply good or bad for data centers. artigo.texto: Car battery gigafactory builder drops out - Published The company building the UK's biggest electric vehicle (EV) battery factory has said its opening remains "on track", despite a major contractor stepping away from the project for the second time in six months. The gigafactory near Bridgwater in Somerset, is being led by Agratas and built on the site of a former ordinance factory, creating around 4,600 jobs once open. Contractor TSL, which is building the factory's exterior, will step down, external once that work is complete, but the company has declined to say why and it is unclear if it had planned further involvement. Buckinghamshire-based TSL only joined the project in June after previous lead contractor Sir Robert McAlpine ended its involvement. Agratas, part of the Tata Group which owns Jaguar Land Rover, said it will not need to replace TSL as it is already working with another contractor - NG Bailey - who will carry out the remaining work fitting out the inside of the factory. More from Somerset - 'Stunning' sculpture could replace M5 Willow Man - Published20 hours ago - Hopes damaged tower could reopen to visitors - Published21 hours ago - Loss of farm school land to have 'massive impact' - Published1 day ago A spokesperson for Agratas said: "We are on track to meet our customer requirements. "The Somerset site is a large and complex industrialisation project, and all of our supplier partners are supporting us well as we prepare for the facility's launch phase." Construction of the factory on the 616 acre (249.2 hectare) brownfield location near Bridgwater was expected to take two years, with about 2,000 people working on site this year. Project leader Agratas said in the summer the original 2026 factory opening date had been pushed back to 2027, and has now confirmed it will be the end of that year. The company said 1,500 operational jobs would be created in 2027, with 4,600 jobs on offer once it expands across the whole site. artigo.texto: Data center surge powering questions of who pays electricity bills Q. Electricity demand has increased after years of little change. What is driving this? Average annual change in electricity consumption in the U.S was about 0.1 percent from 2005 through 2020—hardly any change whatsoever. The economy [had become] less energy intensive and more efficient. Manufacturing moved offshore and everyone knows light bulbs changed. Refrigerators and dishwashers and other sorts of heavy electrical, durable goods in the household became more energy efficient. Even though we were growing, the economy became less energy dependent. What's changed very recently? I would say two things. One is data centers. Second, we didn't have electric vehicles in large numbers 20 years ago. Now, we have millions of electric vehicles that are on the grid. Q. How big a contributor are data centers? Data centers aren't new. We've had data centers around as long as we've had the internet and computers. For example, Netflix’s streaming service has to store things on the cloud and make them available to access at any given time. But data centers for this were smaller, maybe 10 to 25 megawatts [each]. Now with the boom in artificial intelligence, we have to train these [computing] models in what's called inference. These AI models require significantly higher amounts of computation and hence, power. These types of data centers are a lot more energy intensive and can be upward of one gigawatt or multiple gigawatts. (One gigawatt equals 1,000 megawatts.) This is equivalent to a medium-sized U.S. city, about 250,000 households, which can use about one gigawatt of electricity at peak demand. Q. For context, what’s the maximum amount of electricity on a summer day that we can produce and consume in Texas? We just set records this year. We went over 90 gigawatts for the first time during a handful of days in the summer [of 2026]. Before that, the record was 85 gigawatts. That’s a 5 to 7 percent increase in the peak load just from one year to the next in the service area of ERCOT [the Electric Reliability Council of Texas]. We're going from 90 gigawatts as the peak load last summer and potentially adding 60 gigawatts of data centers on top of that within a handful of years. You can see how we would need to be building out a lot of electricity supply. Q. How is this new electricity demand likely to be met? Natural gas is far and away the answer in the moment as far as what we see in the pipeline of what is being built [for generation] over the next handful of years, as well as solar. There's been a conversation from the federal government about extending the life of coal plants that were supposed to be retired. That can bring some relief. The other piece is nuclear. I think there's been a resurgence in the role that nuclear can play on the grid, but it's a very long timeline for permitting and construction. Q. What about data center operators creating “behind-the-meter,” off-the-grid power supplies? I don't see that much behind-the-meter generation powering data centers. It's extremely difficult to run your own power grid. There's a lot that goes into also having a power supply onsite. It's also not as reliable [as grid power]. The grid offers reliability, and that partners well with what a data center requires. Data centers need to have “five nines” reliability. That means that their up-time is 99.999-plus percent of the time. They can only be offline for a single digit of hours throughout the year. When you run your own power plant, all that risk of making sure that your electricity grid does not fail is on you as the island behind the meter. If you lose your power plant and then can't guarantee reliability to your customers, that's a big problem. But also, because you want to guarantee this reliability, you have to either do many smaller power generation units or you need to build in redundancy called “N plus one.” You basically have to overbuild your power capacity. The estimate I see usually is around 30–40 percent more power built onsite than you'll consume, because you need to make sure that in case one of those goes down, you can continue. It's costly for companies to do this. What behind the meter offers is that you don't have to wait for the regulators. These grid interconnections can take a long time depending on where you're trying to locate. There's conversation about whether some data centers in the next number of years might start off as behind the meter while they're waiting for an interconnection. There's not too many data centers currently operating fully behind the meter. I think some estimates show that maybe 30 percent of what's in the pipeline over the next three to five years would be behind the meter. But it's unclear if that's going to materialize or pan out. Q. What's going to be the impact of all this extra electricity demand on prices? We have a good sense of how power plants work and the way that the grid operates. We have less visibility into how a data center is going to be operating from hour to hour or whether they're going to actually be constructed. Starting first off with what data centers have already cost so far, [we have] an average of about a 7 percent increase nationally in the wholesale [electricity] price compared with a world in which data centers don't exist. If you were just to strip out the demand from data centers and set the price at that point, cost increases [would] vary from month to month, from around 4 percent to 8 percent depending on the time of year.
