artigo.texto: As the midterm results rolled in a few weeks ago, making clear that Democrats were headed for a huge night, the world’s richest person, the largest individual midterm donor, and one of X’s most relentless posters was focused on his latest extraterrestrial scheme: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Elon Musk wrote on the social media platform he owns. It was his first public reaction to the election results, which amounted to a harsh rebuke of the MAGA messaging he’d spent the past four years underwriting. A self-serving take? Absolutely. SpaceX aims to launch a huge amount of AI processing capacity into orbit, with the goal of eventually deploying 100 gigawatts of solar-powered computing satellites every year. But does Musk have a point? Maybe. As the midterms proved — and as Heatmap has long been tracking — anti-data center sentiment is exploding. Our most recent polling found that 71% of survey respondents would oppose a data center near where they live, which is actually down slightly from 75% a few months earlier. The overwhelming majority of congressional and gubernatorial candidates who won this year favored cracking down on these facilities through stronger regulations or even moratoria. That’s all to say that Musk is hardly the only entrepreneur betting the moment is ripe for AI infrastructure to reach far flung corners of the planet and beyond. So far, the middle of the ocean and low Earth orbit look like the leading frontiers. Wave energy startup Panthalassa, for instance, is building ocean-based data centers, while other space-based data center hopefuls such as Cowboy Space, Starcloud and Orbital are also jockeying for a share of the market alongside bigger players like Google and Blue Origin. “When we first embarked, there was probably more skepticism than there was conviction,” Joseph Yaffe, COO of data center startup Cowboy Space, told me. “Now I think the balance has changed, and there’s more conviction than there is skepticism.” Yaffe originally founded the startup with the goal of beaming solar power down to Earth, but pivoted to data centers this spring when the company raised a $275 million Series B at a $2 billion valuation. Unlike other startups in this industry, Cowboy Space doesn’t want to rely on SpaceX to get its satellites into orbit — it plans to build its own rockets. While taking on Musk’s nearly $2 trillion rocket-slash-AI company may sound like a fool’s errand, Yaffe sees this as the startup’s edge, in part because the midterms revealed the deep unpopularity of Musk’s priorities. “We’re operating in an industry that’s dominated by one single polarizing company, or really a company with a polarizing leader. His side lost,” Yaffe told me. “People who are thinking a lot about space as a new commercial frontier would like to have other ways to get access to space.” Cowboy Space’s rockets are purpose-built to house its 1-megawatt orbital data centers, with an upper section designed to detach and double as the GPU-packed satellite. By contrast, Starship, Musk’s next-generation rocket, still requires a separate satellite to house AI chips. And if an outside company wants to hitch a ride, they’ll have to pay SpaceX for the privilege; if Cowboy Space’s rocket design proves skyworthy, it avoids that. The company thinks these advantages will eventually make its computing as cheap as anything on Earth, if not cheaper in the long run. “But not 20 years — we think five years,” Yaffe told me. It’s targeting first launch by the end of 2028. No major customer has yet committed to buying compute from orbital data centers at scale, though some are testing the waters. Starcloud says its next satellite, slated to launch by year’s end, will run workloads for Crusoe, and it has partnerships with AWS and Google Cloud. But Yaffe expects to see more action within the next year. “People, understandably, are now in the place of, Well, do we wait and see if they can put a one-megawatt data center in orbit, or do we commit and try to at least have first dibs on the first 10 gigawatts in orbit now?” Orbital, a pre-seed space-based data center startup founded earlier this year, also sees the midterms as a gift of sorts. “I guess folks are going down the same research journey that I did like a year ago, and realizing that this is not at all that crazy of an idea,” Euwyn Poon, the company’s CEO, told me. Orbital is targeting its first launch for next summer, aboard a SpaceX rocket, with plans to begin scaling by the end of the decade. Neither Yaffe nor Poon, however, views community opposition as the primary constraint on the AI buildout. Both support building on land, they just don’t think terrestrial energy supply can keep pace. But they’re split on what comes next. Poon thinks orbit will become “the dominant way of capturing energy and running AI compute,” while Yaffe expects the majority of computing capacity to stay on Earth. In the broader context of the industry, however, this is a fairly minor point of disagreement. After all, plenty of investors still view the prospect of scrappy startups building orbital data centers as a wildly expensive and exceedingly unlikely proposition in the first place, including Mike Schroepfer, founder of Gigascale Capital and former Meta CTO. “It’s a trap. I’m just amused by how many people are falling for it,” Schroepfer told me. “Elon’s so good at this. He’s convincing everyone this is the thing, so everyone’s going to invest in it and build the supply chain. And he is best positioned to build space-based data centers, so I don’t know how anyone’s going to compete against SpaceX on this.” Schroepfer thinks Musk will put AI infrastructure in orbit, but that the economics of this approach will still look pretty poor compared with his favored alternative: deploying data centers in the open ocean. artigo.texto: AI's next data center boom is moving into cities, and into people's homes As demand for computing power grows, developers are finding ways to install servers in office towers, industrial buildings and even private residences. The shift promises faster connections and new revenue streams, but also raises questions about electricity, noise, water consumption and regulation. In recent weeks, residents of the Colonial Hills neighborhood in Southaven, Mississippi, have been receiving unexpected house calls. Real estate agents hired by xAI, Elon Musk's artificial intelligence company, have been going door to door, offering to buy residents' homes and urging them to leave the area quickly. The logic behind the move is as straightforward as it is ruthless: in an effort to prevent homeowners from joining a lawsuit already filed against the company over noise generated by a power plant supplying electricity to a nearby xAI data center, Musk has apparently decided that buying their homes would be cheaper. According to one recorded conversation, the company aims to acquire 418 homes in the neighborhood. So far, 18 homeowners have agreed to sell. This remarkable story is just one example of the unusual challenges arising from the ever-growing demand for the computing resources that power the artificial intelligence revolution. To generate responses quickly, AI models require ever-increasing numbers of servers. The result is a global construction boom in massive data centers, typically built in remote areas or on the outskirts of towns, whose construction and operation can take a toll on the environment, wildlife and local communities. In Finland, Google was ordered last month to halt infrastructure and construction work on two data centers after it emerged that the company had illegally felled approximately a quarter of a million trees to clear the sites. In Talavada, India, local residents are campaigning against the construction of a massive data center, a joint project by Google and the Adani Group, arguing that it threatens the local water supply and regional wildlife. Meanwhile, in the United States, Republican voters are increasingly paying attention to environmental issues, in this case because of the impact data centers are having on their own communities. Residents are complaining about the constant "white noise" generated by data centers and their adjacent power plants, as well as the enormous quantities of water consumed to cool the servers inside them. And what about Israel? The Electricity Authority was recently forced to intervene and regulate the flood of applications to establish data centers. While the Authority sought to manage the facilities' electricity consumption, setting a limit of 200 megawatts for each new facility, one question remains unresolved: how much land is actually available in such a small, densely populated country to accommodate these enormous server complexes? These challenges have helped drive a new development in the industry: the construction of data centers within urban areas. Some are designed to meet the computing needs of an entire building, reducing reliance on remote server farms; others occupy entire floors of office towers. Some companies are even offering to install servers in vacant rooms in residential buildings, generating rental income for apartment owners. The shift is already underway and is expected to accelerate. The main reason for bringing data centers into cities is that building them in remote locations can take years, due to the need to establish transmission infrastructure, clear land, navigate regulatory hurdles and contend with public opposition. Cities, by contrast, already have established power infrastructure. Integrating data centers into existing buildings through mixed-use development can also help overcome planning and land-acquisition barriers. The trend is also being driven by forecasts about how the technology industry will evolve. Until now, much of the AI industry's focus has been on training models, a process that requires enormous computing power but does not necessarily require servers to be close to end users. Consulting firm McKinsey predicts that the industry's focus will increasingly shift toward "inference": the actual execution of models when a user asks a question, an autonomous vehicle detects a pedestrian or a robot makes a decision. Unlike training, inference often requires rapid response times, making it advantageous to locate computing infrastructure closer to users. A server for every tenant The trend is still in its early stages, but research firm The Insight Partners estimates that approximately $10.9 billion was invested in urban data centers in 2025. It projects that the figure will reach $118.8 billion by 2034, representing annual growth of about 30%. According to the study, spatial constraints will be a key driver, with a shortage of available sites accelerating the migration toward urban centers. The EdgeUp AI project by Switchup, a company that manages approximately 300,000 square meters of office space, is among the first attempts to bring this model to Israel. The complex, currently under construction in Tel Aviv, is expected to combine office space with infrastructure facilities, including data centers. Ben Braverman, a managing partner at Switchup, says the company is building a facility in which parts of the space were initially allocated to 16 servers. Their computing power will be made available to companies renting offices in the building. According to Braverman, having servers nearby will significantly reduce the gap between simulation and real-world execution while lowering costs for tenants. Braverman says the model will spare companies the need to establish and operate their own server infrastructure. He describes a broader vision: "We will take a floor or half a floor in a building, divide it into units of about 50 square meters, and companies that rent labs from us will get server farms

artigo.texto: U.S. data centers are driving greater power demand, and with it, more pollution from coal and gas power plants. Researchers estimate that worsening pollution is leading to hundreds of early deaths. The new modeling study finds that, in 2023, the added power demand from data centers led to an estimated 650 early deaths across the U.S. Given the rapid buildout of data centers, their impact would likely be even greater today, authors say. The study further suggests that pollution is often intensifying far from where data centers are located. For instance, data centers in Virginia — which are connected to a large regional power grid — might spur power plants in the Midwest to ramp up. As their power output grows, so does particulate pollution, a contaminant linked to heart attacks, strokes, and lung disease. “Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” said coauthor Noelle Selin, head of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy at MIT. The findings were published in Environmental Research Letters. A separate study, published this month in Nature Sustainability, looks at the impact of more than 400 hyperscale data centers across the U.S. It found the facilities are using as much electricity as 8 million homes. In Oregon and Virginia, two data center hotspots, they are consuming more than 15 percent of the electricity sold in each state. artigo.texto: A Tecto Data Centers anunciou nesta quarta-feira, 25, a construção de seu primeiro data center em Pernambuco. Localizado em Recife, o empreendimento, denominado TREC1, terá capacidade inicial de 1 MW, com possibilidade de expansão para até 6 MW. O início das operações está previsto para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. O projeto integra o plano de investimentos de US$ 2 bilhões da companhia, anunciado em abril deste ano, que contempla obras e novos empreendimentos até 2028. O valor destinado especificamente à unidade pernambucana não foi divulgado. A instalação atenderá operadoras de telecomunicações, hyperscalers, provedores de nuvem e de conteúdo, além de clientes corporativos. Entre os serviços previstos estão colocation, interconexão e serviços gerenciados. Integração O novo data center será interligado à infraestrutura da companhia em Fortaleza (CE), um dos principais pontos de chegada de cabos submarinos internacionais ao Brasil. A integração permitirá que clientes distribuam suas operações entre as duas capitais, inclusive para recuperação de dados em caso de desastres e continuidade dos negócios. "Com o TREC1, a região passa a contar com dois polos da nossa rede, afinal, acreditamos que Recife está para Fortaleza, assim como o Rio de Janeiro está para São Paulo. Essa é a lógica da nossa estratégia AI Grid, que conecta data centers, levando capacidade de processamento para perto das empresas e complementando as grandes estruturas do AI Factory", afirmou Tito Costa, CRO da Tecto Data Centers. Com a unidade de Recife, a companhia prevê alcançar oito data centers em operação na América Latina até 2027, sendo cinco no Brasil e três na Colômbia. A empresa também desenvolve outros dois projetos no mercado brasileiro: um de 200 MW em Santana de Parnaíba (SP) e outro de 20 MW em Porto Alegre (RS).

artigo.texto: EU and UK Finalize Deal to Link Emissions Trading Systems, With Interchangeable Allowances From January 2028 Why It MattersLinking the two carbon markets shifts airline compliance toward one pooled allowance market with a single UK authority, while the EU's separate plan for long-haul flights keeps its external reach contested. What happened The European Union and the United Kingdom have finalized negotiations to link their respective emissions trading systems (ETS), with the deal announced at the EU-UK summit in Brussels on Nov. 20, 2026. The UK ETS was created in 2021 following Brexit, and businesses called for it to be linked to the EU ETS from the outset. Negotiations began in late 2025. The European Commission's Directorate General for Climate Action said the agreement will ensure the same set of climate rules related to emissions trading applies in the EU and the UK. If ratified on both sides, the deal is expected to simplify airline compliance and create a larger market with more stable carbon pricing. The UK will also introduce a "one-stop shop," so airlines deal with a single authority for both schemes rather than separate UK and EU regulators. Work is underway to operationalize the agreement, with any necessary legislation to be passed in 2027 and procedures to be enacted in January 2028. According to the UK government, from Jan. 1, 2028, UK and EU allowances can be used interchangeably across both schemes. The first surrender deadline at which allowances from both systems will be accepted is Sept. 30, 2028, covering operators' obligations for the 2027 compliance year. The two systems will continue to operate separately, with "dynamic alignment," and the UK government said it will have an early "decision-shaping role" when the EU develops new EU ETS policies. The aviation scope dispute In July 2026, the European Commission announced plans to extend the EU ETS to cover flights between the EU and non-EU countries within a 5,000 km (3,100 mi.) range. The proposal drew strong opposition from aviation stakeholders, who view it as extraterritorial and as undermining global efforts through Corsia, the International Civil Aviation Organization's program to stabilize net CO2 emissions from international flights. The UK Department for Transport acknowledged the draft EU proposal and said it is aligning with "elements" of the EU ETS, including the scope of aviation coverage. The EU ETS has been linked with Switzerland's ETS since Jan. 1, 2020. Industry impact & what to watch For airlines and business-aviation operators flying between the UK and the EU, the practical change is administrative as much as financial. Two separate carbon regimes, each with its own regulator and allowance pool, are set to become one interchangeable pool with a single UK point of contact. Operators that today hold and track allowances separately for each scheme would be working from a common stock, and a larger linked market is expected to steady carbon pricing. The link also ties UK aviation policy more closely to Brussels. With dynamic alignment, the UK follows the EU's rule changes while keeping a separate system, and its early role in shaping new EU policy sits alongside its stated alignment with elements of the EU's aviation coverage. That makes the EU's July proposal on flights to non-EU countries within 5,000 km a live question for UK-linked operators, and it keeps the objections tied to Corsia in play. The next dated milestones are legislation in 2027, procedures in January 2028, and the Sept. 30, 2028 surrender deadline for the 2027 compliance year. Ratification on both sides is the condition on which the deal's benefits depend.

artigo.texto: SpaceX gets FCC approval for 1 million satellites to build data centers in space, Brendan Carr says The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday greenlit SpaceX's request to put 1 million satellites in space that will create orbital data centers, bringing CEO Elon Musk closer to his goal of harnessing the sun to generate computing power. "Today, in a historic first, the FCC approved SpaceX's request for 1 million satellites (orbital compute modules) to create data centers in space," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a post on X. Musk responded by saying, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world." SpaceX's satellites will conduct telemetry, tracking and command operations, and will connect with other satellites, including those in SpaceX's Starlink system, the FCC said in a February filing. SpaceX filed a request with the FCC to put data centers in space in January. In its application, it said that deploying data centers in space would be the "first step towards becoming a Kardashev II-level civilization," referring to a threshold Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev proposed at which a civilization could tap the entire energy output of its star. When it filed its initial public offering in May, SpaceX said that orbital data centers would be able to handle intense demand from the AI sector and generate energy more efficiently than land-based facilities, which have become a flashpoint across the U.S. Thousands of data centers are being built, sparking backlash from communities who argue the facilities will transform their cities, create unwanted noise and drive up electricity and water use. In the midterms, American voters approved dozens of proposals aimed at restricting data centers. In its IPO filing, SpaceX said it expects to begin deploying orbital AI compute satellites as early as 2028.

Resumo e áudio gerados por inteligência artificial a partir do texto desta matéria. A WEG obteve o credenciamento de seu pack de baterias de lítio junto ao Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social, o BNDES, e chega habilitada ao primeiro leilão de armazenamento de energia do Brasil, que começa na próxima quarta-feira (2). Com o registro, investidores que adotarem a solução da fabricante de Jaraguá do Sul (SC) passam a ter acesso a condições diferenciadas em linhas, como a de Financiamento de Máquinas e Equipamentos, e a do Fundo Clima. O Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade de 2026 será dividido em duas etapas. Em 2 de dezembro ocorre a disputa de armazenamento nacional, restrita a soluções que cumprem requisitos de conteúdo local. Entre no grupo Em 4 de dezembro, a modalidade de armazenamento geral abre espaço também para sistemas sem nacionalização. Os contratos dos vencedores terão duração de 15 anos, com início de operação previsto a partir de agosto de 2028. Diferença no financiamento A WEG foi enquadrada na rota 2 de credenciamento, mais complexa que a rota 1, por exigir etapas de fabricação dos packs no Brasil. Dentro dessa classificação há diferenças de profundidade industrial: parte das soluções se limita a integrar módulos e conjuntos já montados, enquanto outras partem das células para processos mais complexos de fabricação e montagem. “É justamente nessa segunda abordagem que nos diferenciamos estrategicamente no mercado. A WEG está indo além da estratégia de nacionalização a partir das células e do atendimento regulatório, pois está contribuindo para estabelecer uma indústria brasileira de armazenamento com maior conteúdo tecnológico, competitividade e autonomia ao mercado”, diz o diretor de Vendas Solar, BESS e Building da WEG, Harry Schmelzer Neto. A classificação pesa no custo dos projetos. Pelo Fundo Clima, empreendimentos na rota 2 podem financiar até 100% dos itens elegíveis, ante o limite de 80% na rota 1. Em projetos de grande porte, nos quais custo de capital, prazo de financiamento e previsibilidade de receitas são determinantes, a diferença tende a influenciar a escolha de fornecedores. “Nossa participação no leilão terá grande importância, pois contribuiremos para atender o sistema energético naquilo que ele precisa, aumentando sua estabilidade e garantindo o uso das fontes renováveis para a transição energética”, completa Harry Schmelzer Neto. Nova fábrica em Itajaí Para atender à demanda por sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, conhecidos pela sigla BESS, a WEG amplia o parque fabril de Itajaí, no Litoral Norte catarinense, com uma nova fábrica de 4 GWh de capacidade anual. O investimento de R$ 330 milhões é feito por meio do programa BNDES Mais Inovação, e a operação deve começar no segundo semestre de 2027, cerca de um ano antes do início previsto dos contratos do leilão.

artigo.texto: In Eatonville, Florida, America’s first all-Black municipality, the Hungerford School taught generations of Black students how to build a life in a country determined to limit their futures. The Florida boarding school for Black students built in 1897 paired academics with skilled trades, making it an engine of Black self-sufficiency. Now, 17 years after the school was shuttered, part of its former property holds a project that some residents and advocates argue could limit the futures of its Black children: a data center. The facility, which began construction in 2019, came with grand promises that have only shrunk as time goes on. In the early stages, HostDime, the developer, pledged to set up the town’s residents with free at-home Wi-Fi. As construction costs have nearly doubled and the open date keeps being delayed, the company’s CEO, Manny Vivar, said its original promise of free at-home wifi is “not sustainable.” The company also said it would provide scholarships, programs, and STEM training for Eatonville students and residents upon completion of the facility. It is not clear if that will move forward. HostDime has now said it will offer “public” Wi-Fi through an antenna atop the building. Without any binding agreements or clear enforcement from local officials, those commitments have faded. Meanwhile, residents are left without access to the land and the memory of their self-reliance, and now, potential pollution from the data center. “That’s just been the story of Eatonville,” said Julian Johnson, an Eatonville resident. “It’s almost like the norm to be on defense and fighting because of the valuable land.” The fight in Eatonville reaches far beyond the 5 acres where HostDime is building its data center. Across the country, the artificial intelligence race is raising questions about who makes the deals, controls the land, and must live with the demands for electricity and the threat of pollution. For many Black communities, it is also a question of whether land that sustained generations can remain a foundation for their futures. “We don’t have anybody to stand for us,” resident Chad McKendrick said at a recent town council meeting about the data center. The situation in Eatonville is “another example of data centers making these promises and offering community benefits, but then failing to deliver on those benefits,” said Shelby Green, the research and communications manager at the Energy and Policy Institute. In Eatonville, the average household income is less than $33,000. It is located in Orange County, where the average income is roughly 2.5 times higher than that at $80,000. Green said this disparity in wealth is seen in data center placement. “This data center expansion is almost replicating the failures of urban renewal back when the federal government through state governments was acquiring land from Black communities and building highways over them in service of white or wealthier communities,” she said. At a recent town council meeting, Vivar said that offering Wi-Fi to the community “came from a pure heart.” “Do I regret saying it the way I said?” he added, “Probably, because there was no technicality behind it.” A century-long fight over Black land At one point, the land in question was owned collectively by the town’s residents before being donated for the school through a trust. Nearly 50 years after the school was built, Orange County Public Schools acquired the property from the trust following a court battle. In its 1951 order, the Florida Supreme Court required the school board to only use the land to educate Black children. But over the next half century until the school was closed, the school district had regularly tried to sell the property, prompting continued backlash from Eatonville’s Black community. “You see, somebody is going to make money off Eatonville and that’s because Eatonville is such a precious commodity. The people of Eatonville are the ones who should be able to benefit and build a lasting legacy and lasting economic legacy,” said N.Y. Nathiri, the executive director of the Association to Preserve the Eatonville Community, or PEC. HostDime’s 5 acres are only one part of a broader dispute over the former school property, where residents are also contesting how the remaining 100-plus acres of land should be developed. For years, residents called on the city government to buy the land from the school district. Instead, former Mayor Angie Gardner supported selling land to the data center developer and to Sovereign Land Co., which attempted to build a shopping and entertainment district. Eatonville’s need for investment is urgent. The town has remained under a state financial-emergency designation for more than two decades and is at threat of running out of money because of a dwindling tax base. Residents and town council members understand this, but want more say in how to address the crisis. Some accused Gardner of advancing these projects without proper council approval and public input, raising concerns about a lack of transparency and oversight. Gardner “sat out there and essentially sold this town out,” said Councilman Tarus Mack. “I have always been saying give us the property or let us buy it back.” Gardner did not respond to Capital B’s request for comment before publication. Following the accusations made during a town council meeting, Gardner said there were several constituents and officials who supported the sale and development of the former school property, and others could have voiced concerns but did not. In 2023, PEC challenged the effort by Orange County Public Schools to sell roughly 100 acres to Sovereign Land Co. The lawsuit argued that the proposed sale violated restrictions intended to preserve the land’s educational purpose. Sovereign Land Co. subsequently withdrew from the deal. Now, PEC is suing again, challenging the process behind a new agreement to transfer the property to Dr. Phillips Charities. Plans by the charit

artigo.texto: Korean POSCO Group has strengthened its relationship with battery manufacturer CATL through a long-term lithium supply agreement covering the 2026-2028 period. The deal will see POSCO supply lithium for use in electric vehicle battery production, further deepening cooperation between the two companies as demand for battery raw materials continues to grow. Supporting Battery Production CATL is the world’s largest EV battery producer, accounting for around 40% of the global electric vehicle battery market. The company supplies batteries to major vehicle manufacturers in China and international markets. Under the agreement, POSCO Group will provide lithium required for CATL’s battery manufacturing operations between 2026 and 2028. The companies have also committed to strengthening their long-term partnership and cooperating to support a stable supply of battery raw materials. According to the announcement, deliveries under the contract have already begun. Expanding POSCO’s Lithium Business The agreement forms part of POSCO Group’s broader strategy to grow its lithium business, building on capabilities developed through its long-standing experience in securing and developing raw materials for its steel operations. The company has established a production base through the early acquisition of high-quality lithium resources and believes the CATL agreement will reinforce its sales position in China while enhancing its standing in the global lithium market. The deal also aligns with the strategic direction of POSCO Holdings Chief Executive Chang In Hwa, which focuses on securing high-quality resources and developing long-term relationships with leading global customers. Focus on Supply Chain Stability POSCO said it plans to continue improving the production stability and sales competitiveness of its lithium resources in an effort to strengthen profitability. The company also highlighted its role as a major Korean supplier of critical minerals, stating that it aims to contribute to greater stability across global supply chains for key battery materials. For the battery sector, the agreement underlines the importance of long-term raw material partnerships as manufacturers and suppliers seek to secure reliable lithium supplies to support continued growth in electric vehicle battery production.

artigo.texto: The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk's SpaceX to put 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites in orbit, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday. Carr said in a post on X, the social network owned by SpaceX, that the company's Starmind constellation, and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead" in AI. Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world." The FCC, in its authorization filing, noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC (Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)." In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan." The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims." The petition resulted in a rebuke from Carr, who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone. Amazon declined to comment on the FCC's approval. Other companies have also set their sights on orbital data centers. Google last year announced Project Suncatcher, which it describes as a "moonshot to put AI in space," and launched its first chips into space on a SpaceX rocket and Planet Labs satellite in October. In March, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin petitioned the FCC to let it launch up to 51,600 satellites as part of a low Earth orbit satellite constellation dubbed "Project Sunrise." The constellation would work in tandem with Blue Origin's planned TeraWave satellite internet service, announced in January. Astrophysicist and author Adam Becker was critical of the FCC move in an email to CNBC on Wednesday. "Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," he wrote. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense." SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. A senior attorney with Earthjustice, Jan Hasselman, criticized the FCC for issuing its decision on a holiday week, and approving the SpaceX proposal without any environmental review, which he said was required by the National Environmental Policy Act. The FCC said in its authorization that it dismissed "comments and concerns raised regarding topics over which the Commission has no authority, including environmental concerns," and concerns about its impact on "optical astronomy."

artigo.texto: O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, afirmou que a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata) está em fase final de conclusão e deve sair "nos próximos dias". A expectativa foi sinalizada em conversa com jornalistas, durante o Fórum dig.ia, realizado em Brasília, nesta quarta-feira, 25. "O mais difícil foi conseguir aprovar [o Redata] no Congresso Nacional. Está agora na fase final do processo de regulamentação. É uma discussão entre ministérios, Casa Civil e presidência da República. A gente acredita que nos próximos dias isso será resolvido, até pela importância do tema", disse o ministro. A lei do Redata foi sancionada em setembro. A regulamentação, que deve trazer uma lista de equipamentos contemplados com redução de impostos, é aguardada pelo mercado como forma de ampliar os investimentos no setor de infraestrutura digital aproveitando o benefício fiscal. "Sabemos que é muito importante para atração de novos data centers. A gente vai assumir esse papel de ser um grande hub de data centers para inteligência artificial", destacou Siqueira Filho. Políticas adiadas para 2027 Se a regulamentação do Redata pode sair em breve, o mesmo não se pode dizer das políticas nacionais de cabos submarinos e data centers. Ambas eram esperadas para este ano, mas o ministro, questionado por TELETIME, confirmou que vão ficar para 2027. "Isso vai ficar para 2027. A política de data centers se soma ao Redata, justamente por reduzir a burocracia e favorecer a interação com estados e municípios com relação aos licenciamentos. É isso que estamos propondo para dar mais visibilidade e segurança jurídica para quem decide investir no Brasil", pontuou. Norma 4 O ministro também afirmou que ainda deve conversar com a Anatel sobre a extinção da Norma 4. A previsão é de que a medida que distingue serviços de telecomunicações do Serviço de Conexão à Internet (SCI) seja revogada em janeiro de 2027, o que contraria entidades de provedores de Internet. "Não tratei desse assunto particularmente ainda. Em breve, a gente vai conversar com a Anatel para entender quais são as motivações, o que a Anatel está pensando, qual o objetivo disso. E também ouvir o mercado, os provedores, as empresas que fazem acontecer no nosso setor para que a gente tenha uma posição que seja justa no tempo correto atendendo a todos", disse Siqueira Filho.

artigo.texto: China's Arcfox Teams Up With CATL to Push Battery Swapping for the Masses: Can a $7,500-Class Swap Car Crack the Recharging Market? The battery-swap race heated up abruptly in the autumn of 2026. Geely and NIO took cross-shareholdings in each other, Huawei Yinwang and CATL connected the Qiankun intelligent-driving system with the Chocolate battery-swap network, BAIC signed a million-vehicle swap agreement with CATL, and Chery, GAC and Changan joined the ranks one after another. Against this backdrop, Arcfox Auto on Nov. 13 launched its "Arcfox + Era" mass-market battery-swap ecosystem strategy, announcing it would work with CATL to build a swap ecosystem network and push for unified swap standards, while simultaneously launching two new models: the Arcfox Beta S3 535ULTRA laser swap version and the Arcfox Beta T1 swap version. According to a report by 36Kr, the Beta S3 swap version measures more than 4.9 meters in length with a wheelbase exceeding 2.8 meters, approaching C-segment dimensions. Under a battery-vehicle separation and battery-rental plan, the bare-car price drops to just over 50,000 yuan (approximately $7,500). A 50,000-yuan budget previously covered only A0-segment small cars, and this pricing directly rewrites the segment's price anchor. Prices disclosed by Arcfox show the Beta S3 535ULTRA laser swap version starts at 78,800 yuan (approximately $12,000) under a battery-rental plan after a limited-time subsidy, while the Beta T1 swap version starts at 52,000 yuan (approximately $7,800) under a rental plan. The two cars stake out the B-segment spacious family market and the A0-segment entry-level commuter market respectively, contributing volume models to the Chocolate swap network. Two swap paths advance in parallel Battery swapping is not a new concept. Tesla demonstrated a 90-second swap in 2013 but abandoned it two years later. Its business logic relies heavily on network effects: station density, model supply and traffic volume reinforce one another. The industry currently has two representative paths. One is led by vehicle manufacturers that build their own networks and refine the experience around their own brands, with NIO as the exemplar. The other centers on cross-brand collaboration and standardized openness, pushing for unified standards in battery dimensions, interfaces and locking mechanisms so more brands can plug into the same network, with CATL providing support in battery standardization and network construction. The industry often compares the two to "Apple and Android." The focus of Arcfox's partnership this time is no longer simply supplying batteries for a single model, but jointly advancing ecosystem building around standardized batteries, the swap network and vehicle products. CATL's Chocolate swap system currently offers standard No. 20 and No. 25 swap blocks, has deployed more than 2,520 swap stations, and covers 31 provinces and 200 cities. The two sides plan to jointly build 30,000 swap stations in the future, strive to cover all cities nationwide within two years, form a 10-minute recharging circle in core areas, and leave room for more brands to join. On product strategy, the entire Arcfox lineup natively supports swapping, but the company is not going all-in on swapping; it advocates "chargeable and swappable," with its own charging network and CATL's swap network forming a "two networks in one"—charging where plugs exist, swapping where they don't. Swap versions account for 70% of orders Market data offers preliminary validation of the model. During the Beta S3 pre-sale period, swap-version orders accounted for 76%, and six months after launch they remain stable at around 70%. With charging and swap versions sold side by side, consumers have made their choice through orders. NIO's data offers a reference point. After adopting the BaaS battery-rental plan, the NIO ES8's entry threshold fell from 406,800 yuan (approximately $61,000) to 298,800 yuan (approximately $45,000), a one-time difference of 108,000 yuan (approximately $16,000); the model remains the sales leader in the 400,000-yuan-class large SUV market. The 2026 halved purchase-tax policy further amplifies the swap advantage, as swap models use the body price excluding the battery as the tax base. Recharging efficiency is another practical advantage. The Beta S3's standard swap time is 99 seconds, with users averaging 90 seconds in practice, and 99.9% of orders swap immediately upon arrival with zero queuing. NIO user surveys show swap satisfaction at 9.29 points with a 90.9% satisfaction rate, and 57.3% of owners say they will definitely choose a swappable model on their next purchase. A deeper shift lies in where battery-asset risk sits. Buying the battery outright means users bear the degradation and depreciation themselves, while renting transfers that uncertainty to the operator: each swap doubles as a battery health check, battery health is centrally managed by the platform, and selling the car no longer means absorbing a discount for an aging battery. According to estimates by the China Passenger Car Association, by the end of 2026 about 2.6 million new-energy vehicles will be more than eight years old, and by 2032 nearly 20 million NEVs will successively cross the battery warranty line—while cases of a battery replacement quote starting at 80,000 yuan (approximately $12,000) against a vehicle residual value of only 30,000 yuan (approximately $4,500) are not rare. Network density remains a hard constraint The appeal of swapping also has clear limits. China has built about 6,862 swap stations nationwide, while the total number of EV charging infrastructure connectors (guns) reaches 25.391 million—a stark gap in network density. Swap stations are heavy-asset investments, and a single station needs 60 to 70 swaps per day on average to break even; currently only about 20% of stations meet that bar, with most still relying on continued investment to stay afloat. artigo.texto: Justiça nega suspensão do leilão de baterias Justiça Federal nega suspensão do leilão A Justiça Federal do Distrito Federal negou nesta quarta-feira (25) um pedido de tutela de urgência que buscava suspender a realização do primeiro leilão para contratação de baterias para o setor elétrico brasileiro, marcado para a próxima semana. A decisão foi proferida pelo juiz Diego Câmara, que analisou a ação civil pública apresentada pela Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica (ABEEólica). O magistrado entendeu que não estavam presentes no caso os requisitos para a concessão da medida, como perigo de dano ou o risco ao resultado útil do processo. A negativa mantém o cronograma do certame, que é aguardado com expectativa pelo setor elétrico. A decisão representa um revés para a entidade eólica, que buscava barrar a realização do leilão antes mesmo de sua ocorrência. Com isso, o processo segue seu curso normal, e a disputa deverá ocorrer conforme planejado pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). ABEEólica questionava custeio das baterias Na ação civil pública, a ABEEólica questionava principalmente o custeio da contratação das baterias, que por definição legal foi imputado aos geradores de energia. Segundo a entidade, a lei que impôs o ônus aos geradores é inconstitucional. Esse ponto central da argumentação da associação eólica não foi acolhido pelo juiz, que considerou ausentes os requisitos para a tutela de urgência. Além disso, a ABEEólica apontava “vícios” na estruturação do certame de baterias pela Aneel, citando a falta de uma regulamentação sobre o rateio dos custos entre os diferentes geradores. A entidade defendia que, sem essa definição prévia, o leilão não poderia ser realizado de forma justa e transparente. No entanto, o juiz entendeu que não há norma legal ou regulamentar que condicione a realização do leilão à definição prévia pela agência reguladora do rateio do encargo. Decisão destaca ausência de dano iminente O juiz considerou ainda que não há dano iminente aos geradores associado ao leilão, já que a disputa marcada para a próxima semana não corresponde ao início da cobrança de encargos. Segundo a decisão, a cobrança somente ocorreria com a entrada em operação dos projetos, em 1º de agosto de 2028. Esse entendimento foi fundamental para afastar o perigo de dano alegado pela ABEEólica. Dessa forma, o magistrado concluiu que a realização do leilão não traria prejuízos imediatos aos geradores, uma vez que os efeitos financeiros só seriam sentidos anos depois. A decisão reforça a ideia de que o certame é uma etapa necessária para garantir a segurança energética do país, sem antecipar ônus indevidos aos agentes do setor. Governo cita risco de déficit de potência O juiz citou ainda em sua decisão elementos trazidos em defesa da manutenção do leilão pelo governo, como o risco de déficit de potência já a partir do próximo ano. Esse argumento foi apresentado pelo poder público para justificar a urgência na contratação de baterias, que são vistas como essenciais para garantir a estabilidade do sistema elétrico diante do crescimento da geração intermitente, como a eólica e a solar. A menção ao risco de déficit de potência reforça a importância do leilão para o planejamento energético nacional. A decisão judicial, portanto, alinha-se à necessidade de assegurar o suprimento de energia no curto e médio prazo, evitando possíveis crises de abastecimento que poderiam afetar consumidores e empresas em todo o país. Impacto para o setor elétrico e consumidores A manutenção do leilão de baterias tem implicações diretas para o setor elétrico brasileiro. A contratação de sistemas de armazenamento é considerada estratégica para dar flexibilidade ao sistema, especialmente com o avanço das fontes renováveis. Para os geradores, a decisão significa que deverão se preparar para participar do certame e, futuramente, arcar com os custos definidos em lei, ainda que a discussão sobre a constitucionalidade continue em tramitação. Para os consumidores, especialmente os empresários e comerciantes do interior paulista, a realização do leilão pode trazer benefícios a longo prazo, como maior confiabilidade no fornecimento de energia e redução de riscos de interrupções. No entanto, há também a preocupação com o repasse dos custos dos encargos, que podem impactar as tarifas de energia. A decisão judicial não encerra o debate, mas garante a continuidade do processo de contratação, que é visto como essencial para a modernização do setor. A fonte não detalhou os próximos passos da ação civil pública, mas a decisão desta quarta-feira representa um marco importante para o leilão de baterias, que segue confirmado para a próxima semana. O setor elétrico acompanha atentamente os desdobramentos, enquanto a ABEEólica avalia as possibilidades de recurso. Perguntas Frequentes Por que a Justiça Federal negou o pedido de suspensão do leilão de baterias? O juiz Diego Câmara entendeu que não estavam presentes os requisitos para a concessão da medida, como perigo de dano ou risco ao resultado útil do processo. Quais eram os principais questionamentos da ABEEólica contra o leilão de baterias? A ABEEólica questionava o custeio da contratação das baterias imputado aos geradores de energia, alegando inconstitucionalidade da lei, e apontava vícios na estruturação do certame, como a falta de regulamentação sobre o rateio dos custos. Quando os geradores começarão a pagar os encargos das baterias contratadas no leilão? A cobrança de encargos somente ocorrerá com a entrada em operação dos projetos, em 1º de agosto de 2028.

artigo.texto: China's EV battery market shifts: CATL's share slips quarter by quarter as second-tier makers rise The rankings in China's power battery market are being reshuffled below the leader. A Nov. 23 analysis of the October new-energy vehicle lithium battery market by Cui Dongshu, secretary-general of the China Passenger Car Association, shows CATL still leads with a 44.0% share but has declined quarter by quarter, falling to 40.5% in the fourth quarter (through October); BYD edged up to 19.1%. Meanwhile, second-tier players such as Gotion High-tech (6.1%), EVE Energy (5.5%) and Geely Yaoning (2.5%) posted clear share gains, while tail-end companies have largely exited the competition. This is not an isolated event. Two years ago, in 2024, CATL and BYD together accounted for nearly 70% of China's power battery installations, forming a "two-strong" structure. According to statistics from the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance, in the first 10 months of 2026 the two leaders' combined installation share had fallen to 62.3%, while the top 10 still held 94%; 41 companies achieved supporting installations, 10 fewer than a year earlier. The reordering of orders is mainly happening among companies with scale and customer bases, rather than a broad dispersion. Looking globally, the picture is the opposite of China's domestic market. According to SNE Research, global EV power battery installations reached 994.5GWh in January-September 2026, up 19.7% year on year, with September alone hitting a monthly record of 145.1GWh. CATL led with 389.2GWh and a 39.1% share, up 1.6 percentage points from a year earlier; BYD was second with 150.9GWh and 15.2%, putting the two at 54.3% combined. Seven of the top 10 are Chinese companies, with a combined 73.0% share, up another 3.5 percentage points in a year; the three South Korean majors (LG Energy Solution, SK On and Samsung SDI) fell to 12.6% combined, down 4.1 percentage points. LFP batteries' share of global installations also rose to 57.7% from 52.5% a year earlier, in line with the LFP-led direction in China. Note: Panasonic Energy's share is calculated as installations divided by total global installations of 994.5GWh; the remaining top-10 spots are held by Chinese manufacturers including CALB and Gotion High-tech. In other words, China's domestic share is dispersing beyond the leaders while the global share is concentrating among Chinese manufacturers — and the two are not contradictory: second-tier players are grabbing domestic orders, while the leaders rely on overseas automaker customers and the cost advantage of LFP. For the Japanese supply chain, the direct effect of this reshuffle is share dilution — Panasonic Energy installed 35.6GWh in January-September, down 0.8% year on year, with supplies highly concentrated on Tesla; as global low-priced models keep shifting to LFP, suppliers tied to a single customer and the ternary route will see their share left behind by market growth. North America was the only major market to contract in the period (down 24.3% year on year), which is where the pressure on Japanese and South Korean battery makers comes from. Total installations are still expanding, but growth has clearly shifted gears. China's October power battery installations were 99GWh, up 18% year on year and approaching the 100GWh mark; January-October cumulative installations were 676GWh, up 17%. By contrast, output expansion has been more aggressive: October power battery output was 245.1GWh, up 44% year on year; January-October cumulative output was 2,078.1GWh, up 61%. With output growth far outpacing installations, the monthly installation-to-output ratio was just 41%, and the cumulative ratio fell to 33%, highlighting destocking pressure across the supply chain. Note: LFP accounted for 83% of January-October installations and 87% in October alone. Changes in demand structure give supply-chain adjustments a landing point. In October, LFP accounted for 86.9% of China's power battery installations, while monthly ternary lithium installations fell 22% year on year, leaving the market in a pattern of "absolute LFP dominance and continued ternary shrinkage." Companies with existing LFP expertise can participate in more model development around cost, fast charging and lifespan. Gotion High-tech also disclosed that its standardized battery packs have been supplied in batches to customers including SANY Heavy Truck and Geely Remote. Commercial vehicles focus more on charging efficiency, cycle life and whole-life costs, offering second-tier companies a niche in which to build scale. Second-tier expansion first benefits from changes in automakers' procurement strategies. When new-energy vehicles were rapidly scaling up, adding suppliers could ease supply-guarantee pressure; as price competition intensifies, automakers also want multiple suppliers to gain more room for cost negotiation and order allocation. Whether second suppliers can pass validation and achieve stable mass production determines whether this procurement choice is truly effective. This year, automakers' moves to bring in second suppliers have extended further into in-house development and capital cooperation. In September, Li Auto disclosed that the 5C fast-charging cells for its 2026 Li i6 are developed in-house by Li Auto and contract-manufactured by Sunwoda and CALB, with the battery pack produced by Li Auto. The same month, Sunwoda disclosed that Li Auto plans to invest 2.65 billion yuan (approximately $397.7 million) to increase capital in Sunwoda Power; at the end of October, it disclosed a 1.7 billion yuan (approximately $255.1 million) capital increase plan by Xiaomi's Hanxing Venture Capital. Automakers are beginning to participate more deeply in battery development and to strengthen cooperation with suppliers through equity ties. artigo.texto: POSTECH Develops Solid-State Battery That Runs at Room Temperature Without Pressure Equipment South Korean researchers have demonstrated an all-solid-state lithium metal battery that operates at room temperature under low pressure, without heavy pressurization equipment. The achievement sharply lowers the high-pressure operating conditions long seen as the biggest obstacle to commercializing solid-state batteries, opening a path to reducing the weight and volume of battery packs. POSTECH announced on the 26th that a research team led by Park Soo-jin, a professor in the Department of Chemistry, together with Dr. Lee Hyung-seok and integrated-program student Sung Ji-hoon, developed the all-solid-state lithium metal battery in collaboration with researchers from Chung-Ang University, the Korea Basic Science Institute (KBSI) and Southern Methodist University (SMU) in the United States. The battery operates stably at room temperature under pressures of 0.3 MPa (megapascals) or less. The results were published on the 7th (local time) in the international journal Nature Communications. Solid-state batteries are a next-generation technology that replaces flammable liquid electrolytes with solid ones, lowering the risk of fire. Using a lithium metal anode can significantly boost energy density, but during charging, deposited lithium causes the electrode to expand in volume, opening gaps between the electrode and the electrolyte. Needle-like lithium crystals known as dendrites grow through these gaps and, if they pierce the electrolyte, can cause internal short circuits. Previously, preventing such gaps required pressing the battery firmly with massive equipment at high temperatures. The pressurization equipment itself was a major contributor to the weight and volume of battery packs. The research team tackled the two problems — electrolyte cracking and lithium expansion — with separate materials. First, they added thioctic acid (TA) to the sulfide-based solid electrolyte, which is vulnerable to impact, to form a dense polymer network structure. This network binds tightly with the electrolyte and holds cracks together like safety glass in automobiles, suppressing cracking and dendrite penetration, the team confirmed. The expansion problem was solved by using a porous carbon material with numerous microscopic pores as the anode current collector. In effect, the collector is pre-equipped with buffer space inside to accommodate the lithium that swells during charging. According to the team, the force of the expanding lithium is not concentrated toward the electrolyte but is distributed evenly through the pores of the current collector. The team used the Pohang Light Source (PLS-II) to observe the interior of the battery in three dimensions in real time during charging and discharging. They confirmed that expansion stress is absorbed as lithium fills and empties the pores of the current collector, and that repeated charge-discharge cycles produced no short circuits or distortion at the electrode-electrolyte interface. Cells using the technology operated stably at room temperature and pressures of 0.3 MPa or less even in a full-cell configuration with an NCM811 ternary cathode, widely used in actual electric vehicles. The team said this is the first time such low-pressure operation has been achieved in a sulfide-based all-solid-state lithium metal full cell with a capacity of 2.4 mAh/㎠. "The limitations of brittle sulfide-based solid electrolytes were addressed with a polymer network, and the expansion stress of lithium with a porous current collector," Park said. "These results came from close collaboration with South Korean researchers." Dr. Lee Hyung-seok, a co-first author, said, "Eliminating the massive pressurization equipment makes it possible to reduce the volume and weight of battery packs," adding, "It is expected to be recognized as a core mechanism that accelerates the commercialization of solid-state batteries." Solid-state batteries are regarded as a technology that can secure both energy density and safety at the same time, and global automakers and battery companies are competing to commercialize them. However, the brittleness of sulfide-based electrolytes, the expansion of lithium metal anodes and high-pressure operating requirements have been cited as bottlenecks for mass production. Because this study lowered the pressure requirement through material combinations alone, it is expected to serve as a reference for future cell design and pack lightweighting research on solid-state batteries. Still, as the work is at the laboratory-scale full-cell validation stage, further verification is needed for scale-up, long-term cycle life and application to production processes. The researchers expect the achievement to help bring forward the commercialization timeline for sulfide-based solid-state batteries. artigo.texto: Battery energy storage is playing an increasingly strategic role within Spain's energy system. Its development will depend not only on technological advances, but also on factors such as regulation, revenue mechanisms and investor appetite. Arup's Energy, Business & Investor Advisory and Foresight teams analyse the current state of Spain's energy storage market and explore how it could evolve by 2036. Combining sector analysis, international market comparisons and strategic foresight, the report examines the key challenges, opportunities and business models that are likely to shape the sector's growth. Through four possible scenarios for 2036, we explore different futures for Spain's energy storage market, defined by who assumes investment risk and how value is distributed across the market. These range from Regulated Champions, where growth is driven primarily by regulated mechanisms and large operators, to The Algorithmic Bazaar, a more distributed market in which data-driven optimisation plays a central role. The report also considers Competition by Design, characterised by broader participation from independent developers, aggregators and industrial consumers, and Guardians of the Spread, where value is concentrated among players able to integrate generation, storage and energy retail activities. More than an assessment of current market conditions, the report offers a strategic perspective on the factors that will shape the future of energy storage in Spain. It helps developers, investors, energy companies and policymakers identify opportunities, anticipate risks and prepare for the decade ahead.

artigo.texto: Eight EU countries join forces to defend carbon market against calls for delay The eight countries warn that further delays to the EU's expanded carbon market would undermine energy security, prolong dependence on fossil fuel imports and jeopardise investment in clean technologies. Eight European Union countries have joined forces to defend the bloc's expanded carbon market, warning against any further delays or changes to its implementation. In a letter to Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra, seen by Euronews, the climate ministers of Denmark, Finland, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden argue that the EU's dependence on imported fossil fuels is a major economic and security vulnerability. They see the new Emissions Trading System (ETS2) as part of the solution, pushing governments and businesses to accelerate the shift to electrification. "By providing a cost-effective means to accelerate the decarbonisation of the road transport and building sectors, ETS2 strengthens Europe's energy security by reducing dependence on fossil fuel imports and promoting electrification," reads the letter dated 23 November. Related The intervention comes amid mounting political pressure from the four-nation Visegrad Group, Italy and Greece to soften or delay the system following the 15-16 October EU summit in Brussels. Resisting calls to scrap ETS2, EU leaders instead agreed to assess its impact ahead of its introduction in January 2028, after it was already delayed by a year. ETS2 will put a carbon price on fuels used for road transport and heating, with energy suppliers expected to pass the additional costs on to consumers through higher bills. The scheme has become increasingly politically sensitive as EU governments grapple with high energy costs and growing concerns about the impact of climate policies on households and businesses. Energy security before climate goals In their letter, the eight ministers invoke the disruption of energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz to argue that reducing fossil fuel consumption is no longer simply a climate objective, but a matter of strategic autonomy. The EU imported €340 billion worth of fossil fuels in 2025, the ministers noted. Since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year, the additional cost of imports resulting from higher prices has reached €127 billion. The ministers warn that Europe's continued dependence on imported oil and gas leaves its economies exposed to geopolitical tensions, volatile prices and political pressure from suppliers. They argue that the ETS2 can help reduce that vulnerability by accelerating electrification in buildings and road transport, reducing fossil fuel imports and creating demand for clean technologies manufactured in the EU. Danish Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa said ETS2 was essential to the EU's electrification ambitions. "We need to accelerate the clean transition so the EU can reduce its dependence on expensive and unreliable fossil energy imports. That is crucial for lowering energy prices, strengthening our long-term competitiveness and stepping up our efforts to combat climate change," Nawa reacted. A warning against reopening the ETS2 The eight governments also warn against allowing the Commission's review of ETS2 to become an opportunity to reopen the legislation and water down its provisions. They argue that the system is part of a carefully balanced climate framework, combining emissions reductions with financial support for those most affected by the transition. Central to that balance is the Social Climate Fund, designed to cushion vulnerable households and businesses against higher heating and transport costs. Changing ETS2 in isolation, the ministers warn, risks undermining that broader agreement. They also insist that sticking to the agreed timetable would provide businesses with the regulatory certainty needed to invest in cleaner technologies, while generating revenues for national governments. Related "A strong implementation of ETS2 without further delays provides regulatory certainty and investment signals that are crucial to ensure the necessary investments towards decarbonisation and electrification," reads the letter. Czech Deputy Prime Minister Karel Havlíček said the energy crisis, Russia's war in Ukraine and continued geopolitical tensions have let to "exceptionally high energy costs" for households and businesses across the EU. "Implementing ETS2 under these circumstances, when the system was designed and agreed upon under completely different geopolitical and economic conditions, simply does not seem reasonable to us," Havlíček told Euronews. "It will also be increasingly difficult to explain to our citizens across the EU why additional costs should be imposed at a time when many households are already struggling with high energy prices and the cost of living."

artigo.texto: The Global AI Data Center Debate, Explained As countries race to build the infrastructure behind artificial intelligence (AI), the electricity, water, and land that data centers demand are shaping who can compete. By experts and staff - Published - Emilyn LarsonIntern, Digital Content, Editorial Global construction of data centers is accelerating as the race to lead in AI development heats up. These facilities have the computational and physical infrastructure needed to train and run large-scale AI models, making them a critical part of countries’ efforts to drive AI expansion. However, while technology companies are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into building these facilities, countries’ approaches to their construction differ, shaped by energy supply, land availability, and economic capital. Data centers consume enormous amounts of electricity and water, and communities have pushed back over concerns about rising power bills and strained resources. In response, some countries have restricted new construction, while others have taken action to fast-track projects with the goal of attracting investment. These differing approaches reflect broader uncertainty about AI proliferation. “It’s not really about energy or water so much as people’s concerns about AI,” David Hart, CFR senior fellow for climate and energy, said of the backlash to data center construction. “It’s very hard to tackle that directly because it’s a very abstract, amorphous thing, but if the data center is right there, then it’s a much easier target.” CFR unpacks what data centers are, the debate surrounding them, and how different countries and regions are approaching their development. What are data centers, what do they do, and how do they work? Data centers are large facilities filled with servers that store and process the data behind nearly everything people do online. Traditional data centers run mainly on central processing units and were built to supply roughly five to ten kilowatts of power per rack—the cabinet that holds a stack of servers. These centers use air cooling systems to prevent servers from overheating. AI data centers, however, rely mostly on graphics processing units (GPUs)—specialized processors that can run thousands of calculations simultaneously, making them well suited to building and running large-scale AI models. These systems require substantially more power: A single rack of Nvidia’s GB200 NVL72 system, for example, draws approximately 120 kilowatts per rack, equivalent to the average electricity demand of one hundred American homes. To manage the added heat, AI facilities primarily use liquid cooling systems that pipe coolant directly to the chips. AI’s growing power demands are driving a rapid consumption of electricity. Data centers consumed an estimated 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024—about 1.5 percent of all electricity consumed worldwide that year—and the International Energy Agency estimates that figure will more than double by 2030, primarily due to the increase in AI use. Much of that electricity demand is a result of how AI models are built and used. Before an AI model can be deployed, it needs to be trained, a process that involves feeding enormous amounts of data through many thousands of GPUs at once. Because these models run around the clock, AI data centers require a reliable, continuous power supply that renewables such as wind and solar alone cannot provide, causing developers to look increasingly to natural gas and nuclear energy. How many data centers are in the United States and globally? The United States has more data centers than any other country, with more than five thousand operational and planned facilities of varying sizes listed across the country, according to Data Center Map. Globally, more than 13,000 planned or operational data centers are listed across over 180 countries. Beyond the United States, these centers are clustered primarily in major European economic hubs, such as France and Germany, as well as large Asian markets such as China and India. Why do data centers use so much water? Data centers use water directly to cool their servers and indirectly through the power plants that generate their electricity. Many still rely on evaporative cooling, which requires a constant water supply because lost water cannot be immediately reused. In 2025, global data centers used almost 1.2 trillion gallons of water, according to a report [PDF] by the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment, and Health—enough to meet the annual basic household water needs of more than six hundred million people in sub-Saharan Africa. AI expansion could drive water consumption much higher. By 2030, the UN report projects that AI-related water consumption could reach nearly 2.5 trillion gallons annually. Where data centers are built also matters: S&P Global estimates that 43 percent of data centers worldwide face high water stress, including 38 percent in the United States and roughly 60 percent in China. Why are data centers controversial? Concerns about AI infrastructure center on two major issues: Environmental. In addition to concerns over water usage, AI data center growth is driving up carbon emissions and increasing demand for coal and natural gas, which still power many facilities. AI-related carbon dioxide emissions could reach four hundred million tons annually by 2030—roughly what the entire United Kingdom emitted in 2025. AI’s expansion is also challenging tech companies’ climate goals. Microsoft, which has promised to become carbon negative by 2030, saw its emissions rise 25 percent in fiscal year 2025, largely because of data center development. Data centers can also pose health risks to nearby communities. artigo.texto: CONWAY — At the ninth hearing on BlueWave Solar’s proposed solar array on Roaring Brook Road, Planning Board members and residents voiced concerns with the fire safety of the proposed battery energy storage system. After the company agreed to revise its original application to remove 20% of the panels, the proposed solar array’s updated design entails a 4.05-megawatt, dual-use system, allowing landowner Ronald Boyden to continue using the site for farming, with animals able to graze under the panels. “I believe the decision that’s before this board is going to be the most consequential land-use decision this town has made,” Selectboard Chair Christopher Waldo said at the start of the Nov. 18 public hearing. “It’s going to set a precedent for how industrial developers look at Conway. It’ll set a precedent for how we as board members, committees [and] citizens protect Conway.” Waldo said the town lacks the infrastructure to respond to fires originating at battery energy storage systems, including the water supply and force of firefighters, given that the Conway Fire Department consists of volunteers. “Where are we going to get that water supply? Where are we going to get the firefighters?” Waldo asked. “We all support green energy, we all support solar. … Unfortunately, Conway cannot be a host to such an industrial facility, because we can’t in good conscience say that we could protect our citizens and our schoolchildren if a fire breaks out.” Kevin LaMalva, an engineer at Fire & Risk Alliance working with BlueWave Solar, said using water to extinguish a battery energy storage system fire is discouraged and would only exacerbate the issue. Fire Chief Christopher Herrmann clarified that the firefighters would use water to control the fire if it spread to surrounding areas, like the nearby barn. With water being discouraged, “You’re pretty much stuck with, like Chris [Waldo] said, letting the battery burn out,” Herrmann said. For the fire chief, his concerns relate to the potential of a fire releasing harmful chemicals from the batteries into the air and water. According to LaMalva, the levels of hydrogen fluoride, one of the chemicals in the lithium-ion batteries, that would be released in a fire would be similar to a structure fire igniting from “ordinary items.” “That’s when the emergency response plan comes in,” LaMalva said. According to LaMalva, the emergency response plan for the battery energy storage system, which BlueWave Solar has not yet created, will recommend air monitoring after a fire to track any gasses from the fire’s plumes. In response to Herrmann and Selectboard member Elaine Campbell’s concern about emissions from the fire reaching the Conway Grammar School — the town’s emergency shelter — across the street from the proposed solar array, LaMalva said the school sits outside the area that would raise concern based on plume modeling data from other projects. “That is truly a worst-case outcome, because these are highly, highly regulated and tested pieces of equipment,” LaMalva said. “The system itself is intrinsically designed to burn itself out safely without leading to further fire spread.” He described the battery energy storage system’s fire safety system as a “defense and depth” approach, with multiple layers of prevention. A battery management system and thermal management system monitor the batteries for signs of thermal runaway and adjust the voltage and temperature. Thermal runaway occurs when a battery overcharges, short-circuits or undergoes damage that heats up the battery and can cause fires or explosions. If thermal runaway does occur, pressure relief vents in the cells work to stop the runaway. To prevent an overheated cell from overheating another nearby cell, insulators also separate the cells within the module. If thermal runaway spreads to other cells, an explosion control system within the battery energy storage system container kicks in. Other safeguards are in place if the runaway continues to escalate, LaMalva said. “It’s not relying on one safety system to prevent the bad outcomes,” LaMalva said. “It’s a series of barriers that are in place to prevent that really bad outcome. It starts at the micro-level and it gets more macro-level.” According to the Electric Power Research Institute, while battery energy storage systems continue to experience safety failures, the rate of safety failures has decreased by 98% between 2018 and 2025. Nevertheless, residents have heard of fires at solar projects close to home, including in Shutesbury, where a fire started in an inverter at a 5.6-megawatt solar array in April. Along with recommended tactics, the emergency response plan will list critical firefighting equipment if the battery energy storage system catches fire. After Campbell mentioned that Conway firefighters recently had to wash their uniforms at another town’s fire station due to the department’s low budget, BlueWave Solar’s Senior Director Steve McDonough said BlueWave Solar would work with the town to secure the right equipment. An expert on battery energy storage systems will be available to help train firefighters and familiarize them with the emergency response plan. While LaMalva said the systems typically contain around 100 cells in each of the 20 modules, McDonough said the company is still considering two different types of batteries and the size depends on the availability of the suppliers. The solar company will settle on the exact system and size if the Planning Board grants the special permit and it receives a building permit. “The Planning Board’s supposed to vote on something they don’t know the size or scope of?” Campbell asked.
