artigo.texto: A discussão em torno do modelo de financiamento para o armazenamento de energia no Brasil coloca em evidência os impactos econômicos e regulatórios das regras de custeio. Enquanto fontes tradicionais dividem despesas entre os consumidores, a legislação recente aplicou uma dinâmica diferente para as baterias. A situação gera debates sobre a transparência dos preços e a segurança jurídica para os investidores do setor. A diferença no modelo de financiamento Historicamente, a reserva de capacidade destinada a garantir potência nos horários de maior demanda utiliza recursos rateados entre os consumidores de forma direta. No entanto, a Lei 15.269/2025 estabeleceu que o custo das baterias seja suportado exclusivamente pelos geradores. Especialistas e agentes do setor questionam a coerência de adotar critérios distintos para serviços com a mesma finalidade no sistema elétrico nacional. Impactos na formação de preços O deslocamento da cobrança para os geradores não significa a eliminação do gasto para o consumidor final. Todo novo encargo inserido na cadeia produtiva acaba por influenciar a formação do preço do produto. Nos contratos do mercado livre, o investimento sofre forte pressão, enquanto nos leilões regulados a Aneel já projeta o repasse às distribuidoras, resultando em reflexos nas tarifas de energia elétrica. Incerteza regulatória e novos leilões Com os leilões de baterias agendados para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026, o mercado lida com um cenário de indefinição. Tramita no Congresso Nacional o Projeto de Lei 3.716/2026, de autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania/SP), que visa revogar a exclusividade do custeio pelos geradores. A dualidade entre a lei vigente e a proposta legislativa adiciona riscos para empreendimentos de longo prazo, que dependem de contratos de 15 anos e de receitas previsíveis para atrair financiamento. Desafios para a competição e a modicidade tarifária A inclusão do risco regulatório nas propostas tende a encarecer os projetos e pode afastar potenciais investidores, reduzindo a competitividade dos certames. A tentativa inicial de proteger o consumidor de cobranças diretas corre o risco de produzir o efeito oposto, encarecendo a energia por vias indiretas. Garantir segurança regulatória é apontado por analistas como um passo fundamental para viabilizar o armazenamento de energia no país sem elevar os custos finais.

artigo.texto: Data centers: o que aprender com Singapura? A seleção de projetos em Singapura traz lições e alertas sobre eficiência e valor econômico para a infraestrutura digital no Brasil. Por Victor Arnaud* – Um data center pode atrair investimento e disputar energia, água e espaço com outras atividades. Singapura decidiu comparar as propostas pelo que entregariam ao país. Ao Brasil, interessa entender essa escolha e seus riscos. Na inauguração da primeira instalação, Tan Kiat How, ministro de Estado sênior para Desenvolvimento Digital e Informação de Singapura, defendeu gerar mais valor com a capacidade computacional, em vez de apenas aumentar seu volume. Após pausar a expansão em 2019, Singapura lançou o piloto do Data Centre Call for Application, o DC-CFA, em 2022. EDB e IMDA, agências de desenvolvimento econômico e digital, compararam eficiência, conectividade e contribuição econômica. Em julho de 2023, alocaram provisoriamente cerca de 80 MW a quatro propostas. A primeira instalação do piloto foi inaugurada em 6 de novembro de 2026, com 8 MW iniciais e até 20 MW previstos na expansão completa. A segunda chamada abriu em dezembro de 2025 e alocou provisoriamente 200 MW a quatro operadores em agosto de 2026. O PUE máximo caiu de 1,3 para 1,25, ambos a plena carga de TI. Esse índice mede o consumo total da instalação por unidade de energia usada pela TI. Exigiu-se também abastecer ao menos metade da nova capacidade por vias elegíveis de baixo carbono. Os selecionados deverão informar o consumo e comprovar essa parcela. O mérito é explicitar a relação entre acesso a recursos e compromissos de entrega. O risco aparece quando “contribuição econômica” se torna um critério tão amplo que favorece quem promete o maior pacote. Sem justificativas claras e possibilidade de contestação, a seleção pode proteger empresas estabelecidas. Um projeto eficiente no papel também precisa demonstrar desempenho em operação. O Digital Infrastructure Act, aprovado em 2026, permitirá incorporar compromissos da candidatura às condições de licença. A vigência é esperada para 2027, com implantação gradual. Os próximos passos serão executar os projetos e detalhar as regras. Outra rodada poderá ser considerada, mas não está garantida. Singapura tem pouco território e depende fortemente de gás importado para gerar eletricidade. O Brasil tem matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável e gargalos distintos entre regiões. Energia disponível não significa conexão pronta no local do projeto. Transmissão, água e autorizações exigem avaliação local, em vez de uma restrição nacional copiada de outro contexto. No “AI Cake”, Jensen Huang descreve cinco camadas: energia, chips, infraestrutura, modelos e aplicações. A imagem ajuda a pensar a política brasileira: como os data centers permitirão desenvolver e usar modelos, formar profissionais e levar aplicações às empresas e aos serviços públicos? Essa ligação deve orientar a expansão. O Redata é uma das peças desse esforço. A Lei 15.504/2026 prevê suspensão de tributos sobre bens elegíveis, nos termos legais, com contrapartidas de energia, eficiência hídrica, pesquisa e atendimento ao mercado interno. Exige relatório público de sustentabilidade e atribui ao MDIC e à Fazenda a avaliação dos benefícios. Até 25 de novembro, o regulamento operacional não havia sido localizado nos registros oficiais consultados. A lição de Singapura deve orientar o conjunto da política de infraestrutura digital: coordenar recursos, definir critérios e acompanhar a entrega. O cuidado é evitar exigências vagas que acrescentem espera e favoreçam poucos. Para o Brasil, o resultado precisa aparecer no acesso à capacidade computacional, no desenvolvimento tecnológico e no uso produtivo dessa infraestrutura. O Redata deve ser avaliado por sua contribuição a esses objetivos. A qualidade da política estará na ligação entre os projetos aprovados e o que empresas, pesquisadores e serviços públicos conseguem realizar com eles. *Victor Arnaud, presidente da Equinix no Brasil, escreve mensalmente a Coluna do Arnaud no Tele.Síntese, com sua visão sobre presente e futuro da infraestrutura digital, soluções e IA .

For Use in Drones a The complaint in a patent lawsuit filed by U.S. battery company SES AI against South Korean battery company BEI. View original image U.S.-based battery company SES AI has filed a lawsuit against South Korean battery company BEI, alleging that BEI infringed its patents for anode-free lithium-metal batteries. According to the battery industry on November 25, SES AI filed a patent infringement lawsuit against BEI under U.S. patent law in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on November 18. SES AI alleges that at least two products developed by BEI, including the "Maximus UL17B" and "Maximus UL20A," infringe its anode-free lithium-metal battery technology. The two patents SES AI claims were infringed are a patent on "the design and performance of a battery in which the anode capacity is lower than the cathode capacity" (U.S. Patent No. 9,887,415) and a patent on "a high-capacity battery in which a metal coating forms on the anode surface during initial charging" (U.S. Patent No. 10,727,483). Both concern anode-free lithium-metal battery technology. Images and specifications of BEI-developed batteries "MUL 17B" and "MUL 20A." Screenshot from BEI's website. View original image The patents were registered to Singapore-based Viking Power Systems Pte. Ltd., a wholly owned subsidiary of SES AI. The second patent is also registered with the Korean Intellectual Property Office as "Electrochemical Cell and Method for Manufacturing the Same" (Registration No. 1025884540000). Lithium-metal batteries, which use lithium metal instead of graphite for the anode, are lighter and have a higher energy density than conventional lithium-ion batteries, and are being developed primarily for aerial mobility applications such as drones. Anode-free lithium-metal batteries, which have recently attracted attention as a next-generation battery technology, are exactly what their name suggests: batteries without an anode material. During charging, lithium ions from the cathode combine with electrons and plate directly onto the current collector as lithium metal, thereby forming the anode. During discharge, the lithium metal loses electrons and moves back to the cathode in the form of lithium ions. The battery operates through an electrochemical process in which the anode forms and then disappears. Because anode-free lithium-metal batteries do not contain an anode material, they can have thinner cells and store more energy in the same volume. They can also simplify the manufacturing process and reduce costs. Since its establishment in 2020, BEI has manufactured batteries for drones, defense applications, and robots. In particular, the company is expanding its business, including through an MOU signed in March with POSCO Future M and Kumho Petrochemical to jointly develop anode-free lithium-metal battery technology. BEI is preparing for a KOSDAQ listing in 2028 and has selected Samsung Securities and Mirae Asset Securities as lead underwriters. Posco Future M signed an MOU with Kumho Petrochemical and BEI at the POSCO Center in Seoul on March 25 to jointly develop anode-free lithium metal battery technology. (From left) Ko Younghoon, head of Kumho Petrochemical’s Central Research Institute; Hong Youngjun, head of Posco Future M’s Technology Research Institute; and Bae Changdeuk, CEO of BEI. View original image SES AI has also recently been expanding its drone battery business. In 2021, SES AI established a lithium-metal battery production facility at its plant in Chungju, North Chungcheong Province, and is developing it into a key production base for drone batteries. The company is reportedly planning to expand the plant's annual production capacity from around 200,000 units to 1 million units by the end of 2026. In its complaint, SES AI alleged that "some of BEI's employees were former senior executives of SES AI" and that they would have been familiar with SES AI's patents. According to LinkedIn, at least four BEI employees previously worked at SES AI. SES AI's patent lawsuit appears to signal its determination to actively protect its intellectual property, as anode-free lithium-metal batteries have recently drawn attention as a next-generation battery technology. SES AI said, "SES AI has groundbreaking proprietary technology and patents that can enhance the competitiveness of military drones and drone batteries, and plans to strongly protect its intellectual property rights." It added, "If infringement is confirmed in the future, we will continue to take active steps to protect our intellectual property rights." BEI also said it would contest the matter through legal channels. BEI said, "We are currently reviewing the scope of the claims and the technical specifications of the patents in question," adding, "We are consulting with a U.S. law firm specializing in patent litigation on how to respond." artigo.texto: On Battery Storage Facilities To the editor: Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) installations are vital for stabilizing and reducing the cost of power. For example, during the short period of the 2024 winter freeze, BESS facilities saved about $750 million in day-ahead market costs (Aurora Energy Research), helped maintain normal levels of service and prevent outages. Scare tactics in communications against BESS installations are deplorable. BESS facilities need to be distributed in order to provide the most benefit. Centralizing them does NOT provide the ability to relieve transmission bottlenecks, reduce grid power losses, stabilize local voltage, and eliminate single points of failure across the entire grid. The Warda BESS connects to the LCRA 138 kV transmission system at the Warda substation. The LCRA T170 138 kV Transmission Circuit, rated at 580 MVA, directly connects the Warda Substation to the Winchester Substation. Both the Warda and Winchester substations have stepdown transformers providing 12.7 kV power for the distribution networks for both the Bluebonnet Electric and Fayette Electric cooperatives. The Winchester Volunteer Fire Department normally receives power from the Winchester Substation via Bluebonnet. Both the St. Mark’s Medical Office Building and the new Progressive Health of Fayette hospital receive power from the Fayette Electric Cooperative through the connections to these two substations. To better understand how power from the Warda BESS powers local loads, consider a simple example of 100 MW flowing into the Warda Substation on one 138 kV line and 100 MW exiting on another 138 kV line while the BESS is putting 25 MW into the substation at 138 kV and Bluebonnet and Fayette together are withdrawing 25 MW via 12.7 kV interconnections. Thus, the BESS is supplying the entire local load of 25 MW in this example. Through the T170 interconnect, the BESS also helps power loads in the Winchester area, including the Winchester Volunteer Fire Department. When the Warda BESS produces more power than the immediate area is consuming, it also supports the grid for other counties. Weirdly, we hear some say that because people in adjoining counties to Fayette County can benefit, that makes the BESS a bad thing for Fayette County. Please reference Matthew 22:39 “Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself.” A prime source of inexpensive charging power for the BESS is the 7V Solar Ranch with an output of 240 MW nearby in Muldoon here in Fayette County. There are other solar facilities reasonably close, for example: Bastrop County has the Big Star Solar near Rosansky with an output of 200 MW (plus it has an old 80 MW/120 MWh BESS with it); The Weberville Solar Farm output is 30 MW; and Milam County has more than 1400 MW of solar capability interconnecting with LCRA. The claim that “there isn’t enough water in the area to fight a fire in the area” is absurd. Not much water is needed following a thermal event because the batteries used are Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFe-PO4 or LFP).

artigo.texto: Coweta County voters will decide in January whether to overturn the rezoning that approved Project Sail and prohibit future data center development throughout unincorporated Coweta County. On November 23, Coweta County Probate Court Judge Carrie B. Markham issued two orders clearing the way for a January 12, 2027, special election, following months of organized opposition to the proposed data center campus in western Coweta County. While opposition to Project Sail initially centered on the rezoning of approximately 829 acres of Rural Conservation land near Welcome to Sargent Road and Wagers Mill Road, the referendum extends well beyond that particular development. The proposed changes to Coweta County’s zoning ordinances would prohibit data centers even in areas already zoned for industrial use. More than 11,000 signatures verified The citizens’ petition, filed October 16, was brought under Article IX, Section II, Paragraph I(b)(2) of the Georgia Constitution, which provides a mechanism for citizens to bring county government decisions before voters. In counties with populations exceeding 50,000, the process requires signatures from at least 10% of the registered voters in the last general election. In Coweta County, that meant petitioners needed 10,971 valid signatures. As of November 20, county election officials had reviewed 11,551 signatures and certified 11,065 as valid, with additional signatures remaining to be reviewed. Markham declared the petition valid and ordered the special election, the expense of which will be borne by Coweta County. In a separate order, Markham dismissed an objection filed October 23 by Atlas Development LLC. The judge cited a 2023 Georgia Supreme Court decision involving Camden County establishing that parties do not have legal standing to object to this type of citizens’ petition in Probate Court. A ban beyond Project Sail The referendum combines the repeal of the Project Sail rezoning with changes to the county’s zoning ordinances in a single ballot question. According to the court order, the question will read: “Shall the action of the Coweta County Board of Commissioners on April 7, 2026 approving REZONE 24-019 be repealed, and Appendix A. Zoning and Development of the Coweta County Code of Ordinances be amended to delete data centers and data center campuses as permitted and conditional uses in all zoning districts and to prohibit data centers, data center campuses, cryptocurrency data centers, and cryptocurrency mining operations in all zoning districts of Coweta County?” Voters will not be asked to decide separately whether to reverse the Project Sail rezoning and whether to prohibit future data center development. The two proposals are combined. The ballot language does not distinguish between Rural Conservation land and existing industrial areas. It remains unclear what effect the measure would have on previously approved data center projects other than Project Sail. Months of organized opposition The Coweta County Commission approved the Project Sail rezoning in a 3–2 vote on April 7. Commissioners Al Smith, Jeff Fisher, and John Reidelbach voted in favor, while Chairman Bill McKenzie and Commissioner Bob Blackburn voted against it. The decision followed months of public meetings and organized opposition, with residents raising concerns about water and electricity consumption, traffic, environmental impacts, property values, and the preservation of Coweta County’s rural character. In May, a group of residents filed a separate lawsuit in Coweta County Superior Court seeking to invalidate the rezoning. Steve Swope, co-founder of Citizens for Rural Coweta, welcomed Monday’s Probate Court rulings in an email. “The Coweta County Commission does not have the last vote on the massive data center called Project Sail in an area of our county that has long been zoned for Rural Conservation, we the Citizens do!” Swope wrote. From restricting locations to prohibiting development In a March interview with The Citizen, Swope distinguished his organization’s opposition to Project Sail from opposition to the data center industry itself. “We’re not opposed to AI and we’re not opposed to data centers,” Swope said at the time. Swope advocated locating data centers in existing industrial corridors, including areas along Interstate 85, rather than converting rural conservation land to industrial use. The proposed zoning changes, however, would prohibit data centers in both. In an extensive June interview with The Citizen, Fisher discussed his reasons for supporting Project Sail, including his concerns that Coweta could lose the opportunity to benefit financially from data center development if opposition extended to existing industrial areas. Fisher estimated that Project Sail could eventually generate more than $100 million annually in combined county and school property tax revenue. Swope has previously disputed the scale of those projections, citing tax revenues generated by existing Georgia data centers. Fisher also argued that industrial tax revenue could reduce the county’s reliance on residential growth and provide funding for infrastructure, public safety, and land conservation. In August, Fisher joined the other four commissioners in unanimously rejecting another proposed data center, Project Oak, on property already zoned industrial. “I’ve tried to look at each data center proposal on its own merits,” Fisher wrote in a statement published by The Citizen. The proposed ordinance changes would remove data centers as an allowable land use throughout the county’s zoning districts rather than leaving future proposals to be considered individually by commissioners under the current ordinances. The Citizen reached out to Fisher and Reidelbach late Wednesday for comment on the court rulings. Neither had responded as of publication. The decision goes to voters The January special election will precede the next regularly scheduled elections for the three commission

artigo.texto: A Telebras, empresa estatal de telecomunicações, estima iniciar a operação de um novo data center voltado para o uso de inteligência artificial no fim de 2027. Com custo estimado de R$ 375 milhões, o projeto será financiado pela EAF, Entidade Administradora da Faixa de 3,5 GHz. Mesmo com a liberação dos recursos, a Telebras ainda precisa definir como será mantida a operação do empreendimento. De acordo com Albuquerque, a estatal não concluiu um levantamento dos custos de manutenção, mas vem trabalhando na elaboração de um plano para que o data center comece a funcionar com geração de receita operacional. O local de construção do empreendimento também não foi definido ainda. Em entrevista ao Poder360, Albuquerque mencionou Brasília como uma das possibilidades. Fundada em 1972, a Telecomunicações Brasileiras (Telebras) é uma empresa estatal federal vinculada ao Ministério das Comunicações, sendo responsável por implementar as Políticas Públicas de Telecomunicações do Brasil. Em 2022, a Telebras registrou um receita líquida de R$ 491 milhões e um lucro líquido de R$ 140,5 milhões. Atualmente, a estatal conta com cinco data centers próprios, localizados em Brasília, Rio de Janeiro, Campo Grande, Salvador e Florianópolis.

artigo.texto: Dear reader: unless you are like RANGE writer Aaron Hedge who doesn’t have a life, you may be about to sit down at a glorious Thanksgiving feast with family. Congratulations. But implied in that eventuality is a poison pill: you will get sucked by your “just asking questions about people’s right to bodily autonomy” Uncle/Granddad/Father-figure Bill/Dave/Jim-Bob or your delusional Hillary dead-ender aunt into a … POLITICAL DEBATE, dun, dun, duuuuunnnn!!! (Yeah, we know: family bigots can come in all shapes, genders, sexual preferences, colors and ages.) What we’re saying is: no matter how much we all do the performative “no politics around the turkey!” thing, someone always ends up throwing just a little bit of shade from last night’s episode of Maddow or Gutfeld! (his exclamation, not ours), and then we’re racing to the bottom. But really, how many more times can we all endure that? We’re now entering year 12 of Trump’s stranglehold on the discourse, and your friends at RANGE are more than a little tired of reheating the same family discourse the way America is about to reheat all this damn stuffing. So what’s a locally engaged civic edgelord like you to do?Well, you can just wait around for Grandpa Bob to start asking your genderfluid niece, “what’s up with girl's sports?" Or, as a die-hard RANGE reader, you can short-circuit the national partisanship that we all find so exhausting by bringing up some local controversies that have much more complicated and interesting lines of discussion than just “Boy, Elon sure spent a lot of money in Texas, huh, kid?”And — bonus! — not only are the local issues below the sorts of things people like second cousin Cletus could actually work to change, they are the kind of things you, as your family’s RANGE reader (who’s about to convert the entire unit), already know like the back of your hand. This vaunted status places you in an ideal position to Dungeon-Master tomorrow’s little table-top brawl. That way, your antifa-loving ass can *team up* with your back-to-the-gold-standard uncle to mock your meme-stock cousin who is really dying to just “turn down the heat on the whole data center controversy” because his whippets dealer dared him to buy a bunch of Avista stock. In doing so, you may learn a little something about that uncle (other than why he doesn’t trust the World Bank) and, if you’re lucky, you’ll delay the evening’s annual title-card rematch — the battle for the most reasonable centrist: your never-Trump uncle (who likes to trot out the old saw about how Obamacare is basically just right-wing Romneycare) and your mom, who is still listening to “Mueller, She Wrote,” for some reason — juuuuuust long enough that one of them falls asleep in grandpa’s favorite recliner. (Again, if it makes you feel any better, Hedge does not have to worry about this.) Here, we’re suggesting five RANGE stories/products with which you can gird your rhetorical loins on a number of salient issues in prep for your inevitable fight with your familial political nemeses. Here they are: Who doesn’t want to be a millionaire? Daniel Walters explains why Washington’s new so-called “millionaire’s tax” will probably not affect you unless you are a *captain of industry* in “Who Wants to Tax a Millionaire.” This might come up because lots of influential folks want to convince you that the state government is coming for you, the average person who might own a small business or make a decent salary. There was even a ballot measure backed by similar talking points attempting to repeal the tax that failed in the last election. Curley Qs Next, the media industry is embroiled in a turmoil that has come home in the form of Spokane’s most visible Disney stan, Rob Curley. Curley, the now-former editor of The Spokesman-Review, is no longer at the paper after a lengthy process that has thrown the paper of record and the nonprofit that was supposed to absorb it into a stage of intense uncertainty. Read Daisy Zavala Magaña’s and Wilson Criscione’s initial investigation, showing the newsroom had lost faith in Curley, accusing him of a history of abuses, here. Read the current status of the newspaper’s transfer to the Comma Community Journalism Lab here. (Spoiler: it’s kinda dead.) Eat your heart out, Schwarzenegger The artificial intelligence revolution has come for our souls, but it isn’t the inefficient slugfest between Arnold and Robert Patrick everyone used to think it’d amount to. It’s a lot dumber than that. And while President Donald Trump thinks anyone who opposes infrastructure that supports AI is a troglodyte (we’d love to hear him try to say that word), RANGE has covered the trend in-depth, calling out public officials and, yes, other journalists, for using the technology without disclosing it. Brush up on it with in-depth articles by Erin Sellers and Walters Power politics Not unrelated to the AI stuff, some Spokane County officials and the local power utility have been trying to bring a large data center to the environmentally beleaguered West Plains and the area northeast of Spokane, saying it’ll benefit the economy. (That’s probably not true.) Local folks are furious about it and have been calling for accountability for the secretive conversations power brokers are having with developers. Read our stories, starting with rumors of Avista Corp.’s mysterious “large-load customer,” then uncovering the backroom talks between commissioner Al French and data center developers over the last two years and then read about how our community feels about data centers. Kingdom to the snood We did it again: launched a newsletter! And unlike the good public service we do every week with CIVICS and Wide RANGE, this one, titled “Principalities & Pastors” targets a specific topic: Christian nationalism, the idea that Christians should be in control of the most influential sectors of society. Hedge has been accused of a weird fixation on it, but he’s not the only one. His colleagues Walters and Hay

artigo.texto: Consumo de energia – A expansão da inteligência artificial (IA) deve provocar um aumento de 70% nas emissões de carbono dos data centers até 2030. A projeção é da Agência Internacional de Energia (AIE), que relaciona o crescimento à necessidade de ampliar a infraestrutura tecnológica para atender à demanda por processamento de dados, principalmente nos Estados Unidos e na China. De acordo com o relatório anual da agência, o consumo de eletricidade dessas estruturas deve dobrar até o fim da década, em comparação com os níveis atuais. A inteligência artificial será responsável por aproximadamente três quartos desse crescimento, devido à necessidade de maior capacidade computacional. LEIA: Jensen Huang retorna ao comando da Nvidia após suspeita de espionagem A estimativa da AIE é que os data centers voltados à IA consumam 350 terawatts-hora (TWh) adicionais de eletricidade por ano até 2030. O volume supera o consumo anual de energia do Reino Unido. O avanço acontece em um cenário de mudanças no setor energético mundial, que também enfrenta pressões sobre o abastecimento e precisa atender a outras necessidades, como climatização e crescimento populacional. Combustíveis fósseis devem abastecer data centers Mesmo com os investimentos de grandes empresas de tecnologia em fontes renováveis, a geração de eletricidade por meio de combustíveis fósseis deve avançar em ritmo mais acelerado para acompanhar a expansão dos data centers. Na China, a previsão é que aproximadamente metade da eletricidade consumida por essas instalações venha de usinas a carvão até 2030. A parcela restante será fornecida principalmente por fontes renováveis, com participações menores de energia nuclear e gás. Nos Estados Unidos, o gás natural deve representar cerca de 60% da eletricidade destinada aos data centers até o fim da década. Em agosto de 2026, os projetos anunciados para novas usinas a gás vinculadas a essas estruturas somavam aproximadamente 180 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade, número próximo ao de toda a geração a gás atualmente disponível na União Europeia. Infraestrutura mundial cresce com avanço da IA O levantamento da AIE também aponta uma rápida expansão da capacidade global de data centers. Nos últimos dois anos, o indicador aumentou dez vezes, chegando a 17 GW. Com os projetos que estão em construção, a expectativa é alcançar aproximadamente 50 GW. Atualmente, a capacidade instalada mundial é de 120 GW. Outros 120 GW devem ser acrescentados até 2030, sendo que três quartos dessa expansão serão destinados a instalações voltadas à inteligência artificial. artigo.texto: Moment Energy has unveiled Nova, a battery energy storage system (BESS) built using repurposed electric vehicle batteries and designed for commercial, industrial and utility-scale applications across North America. The company said Nova is the first BESS based on second-life EV batteries to achieve both UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification. Production is already underway at Moment Energy’s Megafactory 1, with the system intended to help customers lower energy costs, improve reliability and integrate renewable energy into their operations. Second-Life Batteries for Energy Storage Nova has been developed around a flexible architecture capable of integrating batteries from multiple EV platforms. The system uses the company’s AI-powered battery management system (BMS), which continuously evaluates batteries in different states of health to optimise performance, efficiency and reliability throughout their operational life. Each Nova unit delivers 200kW of power and 500kWh of energy within a footprint measuring 2.94m by 1.80m. The scalable design is intended for space-constrained commercial sites while also supporting larger installations reaching tens of megawatt-hours. A key feature of the platform is its swappable battery architecture. Individual battery packs can be replaced as they age rather than requiring the entire energy storage system to be removed. Moment Energy said this approach can extend operational life beyond 20 years when combined with its capacity augmentation service. North American Supply Chain Focus The company said Nova is manufactured in North America and has been independently verified as compliant with Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements. Moment Energy has also been verified as a non-Prohibited Foreign Entity. According to the company, repurposing retired EV batteries creates a domestic battery supply chain while helping retain the value of batteries beyond their automotive use. The approach also supports circular economy objectives by extending battery lifetimes before recycling. Edward Chiang, Co-Founder and CEO of Moment Energy, said: “We see a future where reengineered EV batteries become essential infrastructure for powering businesses and onshoring manufacturing and supply chain. Nova brings that vision to life, combining safety, engineering and North American manufacturing to deploy what we believe are the safest and highest-performance batteries ever made: EV batteries to supercharge our aging grid.” Safety Certifications and Commercial Deployment Nova has achieved UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification and has also been tested to UL 9540A standards for thermal runaway fire propagation. Megafactory 1 is certified to UL 1974, covering the sorting, grading and repurposing of electric vehicle batteries. The system incorporates liquid cooling, smoke, heat and flammable gas detection, as well as an integrated deflagration prevention system. Additional features include a Type 3R enclosure, operation across temperatures from -25°C to 50°C, and compatibility with grid-tied, grid-forming and virtual synchronous generator operating modes. Moment Energy said first deliveries are planned for the first quarter of 2027.

artigo.texto: City staff estimate a 50 megawatt data center would use as much electricity as 25,000 new homes. San Francisco’s moratorium on new data centers has been extended to next fall, Mayor Daniel Lurie’s office said Tuesday. In extending the moratorium, San Francisco — like Oakland and Seattle — is giving city staff more time to study data centers and their impacts. “We will continue listening to our communities and labor partners, collaborating across city government, and drawing on the best available data to develop a policy that keeps electricity rates low, protects the clean water and air our residents deserve, and supports the technology infrastructure our hospitals, universities, and government rely on,” Lurie said in a statement. The Board of Supervisors last week unanimously approved an extension to the zoning moratorium until September. Lurie signed the moratorium Monday, his office said. Although the Planning Department shared some of its findings with the public in a report two weeks ago, it was only an initial assessment identifying areas needing more research. That includes understanding how many data centers there are citywide — besides three “standalone” facilities — as well as how much water they use. The initial report did have some clarity, though. It found that San Francisco’s electricity transmission is near capacity and that data centers would be competing with other developments that also need electricity, including housing. The report estimated that a 50 megawatt data center in San Francisco would demand the same electricity as 25,000 new homes. Additionally, two of the three “standalone” data centers in San Francisco identified by city staff are in the Bayview, and one of them has “five active notices of violation” issued this year by the Bay Area Air District over diesel-powered generators out of compliance with permit conditions, operating with expired permits, and exceeding run-time limits of 35 hours. Southeast San Francisco, with its industrial zoning, has been identified as a part of the city that faces environmental burdens and elevated levels of air pollution. The initial 45-day moratorium, as well as the extension (opens in new tab), were proposed by Supervisor Shamann Walton. He terms out in January, making his efforts to curb and study data centers among his final actions as supervisor. He will be replaced on the board by Theo Ellington. While campaigning, Ellington endorsed the idea of a data center moratorium specifically for District 10, which stretches from Dogpatch and Potrero Hill to the Bayview and Visitacion Valley. Land in District 10 has been the subject of speculation. The lobbyist for a private equity firm known for developing data centers met with city officials in August about building and planning permits for a big plot of land in Dogpatch. The moratorium doesn’t allow for the city to process building or planning permits to establish new data centers. Right now, there are no such applications before the city’s Planning Department. “The absence of pending applications is not a reason to let the moratorium expire,” Walton said at a Nov. 16 committee meeting. “The city must proactively evaluate future development and its potential impacts.” More about the author Omar Rashad reports on San Francisco government and politics.

artigo.texto: Chint Power announced an investment of 821 million yuan to install a plant in China uninterruptible power supply systems (UPS) the high-power factory will have a capacity of 2 GWh per year and will meet the backup power demands of data centers. EVE Energy, for its part, will redirect a ternary cylindrical battery project towards the manufacture of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries the revised plan provides for a capacity of 8 GWh for storage and light mobility applications. Chint Power will invest 821 million yuan in a UPS plant The investment, equivalent to approximately $122.9 million, will see the plant located in Haining, Jiaxing City, Zhejiang Province, To begin operations, the company will lease and adapt existing industrial facilities. Construction is expected to take two years. The project, titled Haining Chint Digital Intelligence Energy Co., Ltd. 2GWh Annual High-Power UPS Project, will be carried out by the subsidiary Haining Chint Digital Intelligence Energy Co., Ltd. According to company documents, the subsidiary was established on July 7, 2026, with a share capital of 100 million yuan. Chint Power owns 100 % of the company, and the project marks Chint Power’s entry into the data center backup power market. The expansion of these facilities is increasing the demand for systems that can keep critical loads powered during power outages. With this plant, the company aims to expand its product portfolio, generate new revenue streams, and strengthen its presence in the high-power UPS market. EVE Energy modifies its cylindrical battery project On November 20, EVE Energy informed the Shenzhen Stock Exchange of changes to several capital-funded projects, one of which involved manufacturing large-format ternary cylindrical batteries, the company will now dedicate that production line to LFP cylindrical batteries. The revision reduces the planned capacity from 21 GWh to 8 GWh and the total investment from 5.203 billion to 2.801 billion yuan, the project will now be called the Chengdu EVE Energy High-Energy Density Cylindrical Battery Industrialisation Project. EVE Energy will allocate 1.871 billion yuan to the revised plan, which had been left unallocated in the original project, the rest of the investment will be covered with its own resources, the new line will be geared towards low-power equipment, light electric vehicles and small-scale storage, among the intended uses are residential storage and power backup for base stations. LFP technology expands its industrial applications According to EVE Energy, LFP batteries are gaining market share compared to lead-acid and nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) batteries. The company highlights their competitive costs, extended lifespan, and safety level. It also points out that this chemistry facilitates the standardization of cylindrical cells. One of the challenges in large-format LFP cells is improving electrical conductivity EVE Energy it uses a full-tab design to reduce internal resistance, according to the company. This configuration allows large-diameter cells to support sustained fast charging and deliver high currents. These features open up applications in energy storage and light mobility, as well as their use in electric passenger vehicles. Two strategies to expand the energy storage industry The two projects respond to different demands of the Chinese market; Chint Power is directing its new manufacturing capacity to support critical loads in data centers, while EVE Energy is adjusting the production volume and chemistry of its cells to serve light mobility and small-scale storage. artigo.texto: Rolling Meadows approves data center tax incentive for development over residents' objections The Rolling Meadows City Council approved support for the county to give a data center a tax incentive to develop land, despite passionate opposition from residents at their meeting Tuesday night. The meeting exemplified the different approaches Chicago suburbs are taking different to the data center dilemma, with one facing opposition to a project while another welcomes the developments. In Rolling Meadows, neighbors brought signs and packed city chambers as its city council weighed bringing in a data center. A former office space that sits on 40 acres off the tollway on Route 53 has been vacant for years, and that's where the Rolling Meadows data center would end up if approved. But residents raised many questions at Tuesday night's meeting, including the impact to nearby Bussey Woods and its wildlife. But the biggest concern is about nearby homes. "To also state the nearest home is 2,000 feet away is also a huge dismissal," one resident told the council at the meeting. "Two thousand feet isn't far." Residents are worried about the noise, environmental issues both known and unknown, and what a data center could do to the community. Most of the residents in attendance said they believed they should have a vote and a voice in whether the data center is built. While the vast majority wanted the Rolling Meadows City Council to vote against the project, some in the room showed support, saying they would bring jobs and economic benefits. Other communities are not willing to close the door completely to data centers. In Zion on the North Shore, Mayor Billy McKinney said nothing is off the table. He pointed out the village was approached previously about a data center but that deal lacked vision. "I want to make this point, being cautious does not mean that we are opposed to progress. That is the big key," he said. "The plan was so inconclusive, and it raised more questions." McKinney said he understands community concerns, but is not willing to implement a data center ban. "But also know that whatever decision we make, it has to protect our community and future generations," he said. In the end, the Rolling Meadows City Council voted four-two to approve their support for the county giving a tax incentive to develop the land with a data center.

artigo.texto: The growing demand for electric vehicles, renewable energy storage and reliable power backup solutions has increased the importance of battery manufacturing in India. From automotive batteries used in conventional vehicles to advanced lithium-ion systems powering electric scooters, cars and industrial equipment, battery manufacturers play an important role in the country’s energy and mobility ecosystem. As the country moves towards domestic battery manufacturing, companies are expanding their capabilities across battery cells, packs, energy storage systems and recycling. Here is a look at some of the leading battery manufacturing companies in India, their products and their presence across different battery segments. Top Battery Manufacturing Companies in India: Quick Overview These companies operate across different parts of the battery value chain. Their manufacturing capabilities, technology and target applications vary. 1. Exide Industries Founded in 1947, Exide Industries is one of India’s most established battery manufacturers. The company has a significant presence in automotive, industrial and stationary energy storage markets. Its product portfolio includes automotive batteries for two-wheelers and four-wheelers, industrial batteries, inverter batteries and energy storage solutions. Exide also operates multiple manufacturing facilities across India and serves both original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and replacement markets. The company is expanding into lithium-ion battery manufacturing through its wholly owned subsidiary, Exide Energy Solutions Limited (EESL). Its planned lithium-ion manufacturing ecosystem includes a cell manufacturing facility in Bengaluru and battery module and pack manufacturing capabilities at Prantij, Gujarat. According to its FY2025-26 annual report, the Bengaluru cell facility progressed through installation, process validation and customer sampling activities. This investment reflects Exide’s strategy to expand beyond conventional lead-acid batteries and participate in India’s growing electric mobility and energy storage markets. 2. Amara Raja Energy & Mobility Amara Raja Energy & Mobility is another major name among Indian battery manufacturers. The company operates under the Amara Raja Group and is widely recognised for its automotive battery brand, Amaron. Its business includes automotive batteries, industrial energy storage, UPS batteries and advanced lithium-ion battery solutions. The company’s lithium-ion expansion is being undertaken through its Giga Corridor project in Telangana. In July 2026, Amara Raja commissioned a Customer Qualification Plant for lithium-ion cells with an investment of approximately ₹500 crore. The facility supports the development and qualification of different cell formats and chemistries. The company has targeted commercial-scale cell production beginning in 2027. Amara Raja is also developing battery packs and charging solutions for electric mobility applications. Its established automotive battery distribution network and investment in advanced cell technology position it as an important participant in India’s evolving battery industry. 3. Tata AutoComp Gotion Green Energy Solutions Tata AutoComp Gotion Green Energy Solutions is a joint venture between Tata AutoComp Systems and China’s Gotion. Established in 2020, the company focuses on designing and manufacturing lithium-ion battery packs for electric mobility and energy storage applications. Its product portfolio covers several segments: - Electric two-wheelers and three-wheelers. - Passenger electric vehicles. - Commercial vehicles and electric buses. - Industrial equipment. - Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). The company uses lithium-ion technology, including Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) chemistry, with integrated battery management systems and thermal management solutions. An important distinction is that Tata AutoComp Gotion focuses on battery pack manufacturing rather than being India’s primary lithium-ion cell manufacturing business. Battery packs combine individual cells with electronics, safety systems and protective enclosures. Its capabilities make it an important supplier within India’s electric vehicle battery supply chain. 4. Ola Electric Ola Electric has entered the battery manufacturing industry through its gigafactory in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu. The company is developing indigenous lithium-ion cell technology under its Bharat Cell programme. Its manufacturing ambitions include producing advanced 4680-format cells for electric mobility applications. Ola’s investment in battery production is intended to strengthen its control over the electric vehicle supply chain and reduce dependence on externally sourced battery cells. The company’s battery operations are particularly relevant to the electric two-wheeler market, where battery cost, energy density, charging performance and safety influence vehicle economics. However, announced manufacturing capacity should not be confused with actual commercial output. The Ministry of Heavy Industries reported that Ola had installed 1 GWh of capacity and started pilot production, while working towards stabilising full-scale commercial operations as of December 2025. 5. TDS Lithium-Ion Battery Gujarat (TDSG) TDS Lithium-Ion Battery Gujarat is a joint venture between Toshiba Corporation, Denso Corporation and Suzuki Motor Corporation. The company manufactures automotive lithium-ion batteries in Gujarat and supports India’s domestic hybrid and electric mobility ecosystem. TDSG began cell-level battery production in India in 2021. Its operations have subsequently expanded, including local production of hybrid battery electrodes in 2025. The company supplies automotive battery systems for Suzuki’s vehicle programmes, including hybrid applications. artigo.texto: Alguns credores adiaram a decisão enquanto fazem uma análise mais detalhada de um empréstimo ampliado de US$ 6,6 bilhões pedido pela Bridge Data Centres (BDC), controlada pela Bain Capital, segundo pessoas envolvidas nas negociações. Os data centers da empresa na Malásia atendem clientes como a ByteDance. A Bain encaminhou as perguntas à BDC, que não quis comentar. A ByteDance não respondeu ao pedido de comentário. Um banco desistiu de participar de um empréstimo de US$ 372 milhões, com subscrição integral, para a Digital Halo, apoiada pelo Partners Group, e outros estão fazendo mais perguntas, segundo pessoas a par das conversas. Os recursos são para um data center na Malásia que atende a Alibaba e outros clientes. Vários bancos também estavam reavaliando um empréstimo de US$ 480 milhões para a Aolani, neocloud com sede em Singapura que tem a ByteDance como cliente, disseram outras pessoas a par do assunto na semana passada. Digital Halo, Aolani e Alibaba não responderam às perguntas. O Partners Group não quis comentar. Novas regras incluem o Brasil As restrições impostas em 2022 pelo governo Biden à exportação de chips americanos avançados deram origem a um ecossistema de empresas no Sudeste Asiático que ajudam companhias chinesas de tecnologia a acessar esse hardware remotamente. Os empréstimos a data centers na região dispararam nos anos seguintes, e o financiamento de chips começou a ganhar força mais recentemente, à medida que os bancos passaram a aceitar operações mais arriscadas. Isso mudou depois que os EUA anunciaram, na semana passada, que empresas de Singapura, Malásia, Indonésia, Tailândia e Brasil vão precisar de licença do governo americano para comprar chips avançados de IA de fabricantes do país. No mundo todo, data centers que já alugam capacidade de computação relevante para empresas chinesas vão precisar de uma licença específica para continuar com esses contratos e terão 90 dias para obtê-la. Mais de uma dúzia de banqueiros disseram que suas equipes aguardam respostas sobre como as novas restrições vão afetar os tomadores de crédito, o que deve no mínimo atrasar o fechamento de operações. Credores como Citigroup e Standard Chartered, além dos principais bancos de Singapura, iniciaram uma revisão ampla de seus clientes do setor de data centers, segundo pessoas a par do assunto. Bancos tentam reduzir exposição Alguns bancos querem diminuir parte da exposição a dívidas de IA e de data centers, inclusive com a venda de empréstimos no mercado secundário e com operações de transferência significativa de risco (SRT, na sigla em inglês). O United Overseas Bank (UOB), de Singapura, busca uma operação de SRT de cerca de US$ 1 bilhão para repassar riscos ligados a empréstimos para data centers e infraestrutura, entre outros setores, segundo pessoas a par do assunto. Uma delas disse que o noticiário atual está atrasando o andamento e que os detalhes ainda não estão definidos e podem mudar. Um representante do UOB não quis comentar, citando a confidencialidade da operação. Os credores privados, que eram os mais agressivos na busca pelos retornos mais altos do financiamento de GPUs, também estão mais cautelosos. Pelo menos um fundo decidiu não participar de um empréstimo de US$ 300 milhões para a GMI Cloud, parceira de nuvem da Nvidia, destinado à compra de chips para um data center na Tailândia que seria usado pela Tencent, segundo uma pessoa a par do assunto. GMI Cloud e Tencent não responderam aos pedidos de comentário. O efeito vai além do crédito. A DayOne Data Centers, que tem a ByteDance como maior cliente, suspendeu os planos de abrir capital nos EUA, segundo pessoas a par do assunto. Um consórcio que inclui a BlackRock avalia reduzir sua oferta por uma carteira de data centers na Ásia-Pacífico, segundo outras fontes. Para Ben Kostrzewa, advogado de comércio internacional do Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, não é ruim que as novas restrições tenham forçado uma reavaliação ampla das operações. Desde 2023, os empréstimos a empresas de data center na Ásia-Pacífico saíram de praticamente zero para mais de US$ 49 bilhões, segundo dados compilados pela Bloomberg. “Pode ser uma boa pausa para fazer um balanço e revisar esses projetos, considerando o quanto o mercado está aquecido há algum tempo”, disse Kostrzewa. “Isso não vai impedir a construção desses data centers nem parar o mercado, mas vai desacelerar tudo.”

artigo.texto: Nocera Inc (Nocera), a construction engineering company, has signed a binding letter of intent (LOI) to invest US$ 22 million in Calgary-based BitRock Ltd., an AI data center developer. The proposed investment would give Nocera 44 percent stake in BitRock, based on a post investment valuation of US$ 50 million, along with the right to appoint directors and participate in major corporate decisions. According to a press release, the funds will support construction of BitRock’s first AI data center in Alberta, Canada, with 10 MW of IT capacity across four 2.5 MW computing modules. The company plans to expand the site to 200 MW in additional 10 MW phases based on customer demand. The facility will operate under a colocation model, providing powered data hall space and operational services to customers supplying their own computing equipment, and has reported signing memoranda of understanding (MoU) for hosting services. Andrew Teng, Asia Director, Nocera, said, “Power is the scarce asset in AI infrastructure, and BitRock is built around its, we are putting capital into a facility designed to generate its own electricity, in a province that has asked developers to do exactly that, and we are doing it one 10 MW unit at a time. This is a measured entry into North American compute with a meaningful ownership position and a voice on the board.” The investment comes as Alberta faces constraints on grid capacity for large-scale data center projects. The province’s interim allocation of 1,200 MW for large-load developments has been fully committed, increasing the importance of alternative power sources. The LOI was signed on November 19, 2026 and the investment remains subject to due diligence, a definitive agreement, required approvals and other closing conditions while both companies have not guaranteed that the transaction will be completed.

artigo.texto: Virginia data center deals face transparency tests BOTETOURT COUNTY, Va. (WDBJ) - From Botetourt County to Northern Virginia, fights over how local governments approve data center projects are playing out in court. In Botetourt, one such challenge has brought construction on Google’s data center to a halt. The cases involve different projects and different alleged violations, but they raise a common question: Did local governments give the public the access and notice required by law before making decisions? Megan Rhyne, executive director of the Virginia Coalition for Open Government, said challenges to government decisions have focused on alleged Freedom of Information Act and public notice violations. “There already are lawsuits around the state that are trying to change this, change decisions based on either FOIA violations or public notice violations,” Rhyne said. “Most well known is up in Prince William County.” A public notice case in Northern Virginia In Prince William County, a court threw out rezonings for the Digital Gateway data center project after finding that the county had not properly advertised the public hearing. The Court of Appeals upheld that ruling, and the last developer pursuing an appeal later dropped it. Rhyne said transparency rules apply regardless of what a government decides. “These rules of transparency exist no matter what the decision is,” she said. “All decisions that the government made have to follow these procedures and these rules.” In Botetourt, a judge found that supervisors agreed to the Google data center deal behind closed doors and then failed to adequately identify it when they voted in public. Court records say the Board of Supervisors discussed a performance agreement with Google in closed session in June 2025, then returned to open session and approved what board members called “walk-on item number one.” Google’s announcement followed the vote. The judge voided the initial action on procedural grounds and ordered new construction to stop. Crews had begun grading the site and moving dirt in September. Rhyne said the violation affected the public’s ability to see its government make decisions. “This technical violation has resulted in undermining the very thing that FOIA is supposed to protect, which is their access, the public’s right to see their government making its decisions that impact them,” she said. On Tuesday, the Board of Supervisors took action to stop items related to Google’s investments, including a museum and library renovations, while the county evaluates its next steps. The agreement also included investments in first responder equipment and athletic infrastructure; some projects have already been completed. Questions about another project Tim Dooley, the attorney who represented the plaintiff in the Botetourt case, said the ruling raises questions about the process used for another data center project at Wood Haven in Roanoke County. “I think if you scrutinize the process the Western Virginia Regional Industrial Facility Authority, the process they used, you’ll see some striking similarities between that and what happened in Botetourt,” Dooley said. Rhyne said the Botetourt ruling is not binding on other judges, although they could look to it for guidance in future cases. Botetourt County could appeal. The judge also said the board could hold a new public hearing that follows the law. Copyright 2026 WDBJ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: A Tecto anunciou nesta quarta-feira, 25, a implementação de seu primeiro data center no Recife. Inicialmente, o centro de dados tem capacidade de 1 MW, mas pode ser expandido para 6 MW. Com começo das atividades no primeiro trimestre de 2027, o data center foi batizado como TREC 1 e atenderá hyperscalers, operadoras, provedores de nuvem, provedores de conteúdo e empresas de enterprise. Entre os serviços que disponibilizará estão colocation, interconexão e serviços gerenciados. O TREC1 faz parte da estratégia de AI Grid da empresa. Ou seja, a criação de uma rede de centro de dados regionais interligados, mas descentralizados. A ideia da companhia é formar um eixo no nordeste brasileiro com o TFOR3 de Fortaleza para garantir distribuição de operação de seus clientes, inclusive sendo alternativa para redundância em casos de disaster recovery. Com o centro de dados no Recife, a companhia passa a ter oito data centers na América Latina, sendo cinco no Brasil (três em Fortaleza, um no Rio de Janeiro e um no Recife) e três em Barranquilla, na Colômbia. Anunciado em abril de 2026, o TREC1 faz parte de uma série de obras e novos projetos que acumularam US$ 2 bilhões de investimentos da Tecto até 2028. Entre os próximos locais estão o TGRU1 em Santana de Parnaíba/SP e o TPOA1 em Porto Alegre. Juntos, os novos projetos ampliaram a capacidade da empresa para 220 MW, sendo 200 MW na região metropolitana de São Paulo e 20 MW na capital gaúcha.

artigo.texto: Korean researchers have developed an all-solid-state lithium-metal battery that operates reliably at room temperature under low pressure. The technology could ease the high-pressure requirements that are one of the barriers to commercializing all-solid-state batteries and could be used to reduce their weight and size. A team led by Park Su-jin, a chemistry professor at Pohang University of Science and Technology POSTECH, said on the 26th that it had developed an all-solid-state lithium-metal battery that operates at room temperature under pressure of 0.3 megapascals (MPa) or less. The team worked with researchers at Chung-Ang University, Korea Basic Science Institute (KBSI) and Southern Methodist University (SMU) in the United States. The findings were published in the international journal Nature Communications on the 7th, local time. All-solid-state batteries are attracting attention as a next-generation technology that can reduce fire risks by using a solid electrolyte instead of a liquid one. Using lithium metal in the anode can increase energy density, but the lithium expands during charging, creating gaps between the electrode and the electrolyte. In this process, branchlike growths called lithium dendrites can penetrate the electrolyte and cause an internal short circuit. High pressure has been applied to batteries to prevent this, but the equipment needed adds weight and bulk. The researchers addressed the problem by preventing cracks in the solid electrolyte and distributing the pressure caused by lithium expansion. They added thioctic acid (TA) to a sulfide-based solid electrolyte to form a polymer network, suppressing cracks in the electrolyte and the penetration of lithium dendrites. They also applied a porous carbon material with many tiny holes to the anode current collector to provide space for lithium to accumulate. The design distributes the force generated by lithium expansion during charging within the current collector, reducing the strain on the electrolyte. The researchers used the Pohang Light Source to observe the inside of the battery in 3D during charging and discharging. They found that stress from expansion was relieved as lithium filled and left the pores of the current collector. A battery using the technology operated reliably at room temperature and under pressure of 0.3 MPa or less, even in a full cell using a ternary cathode material (NCM811) for electric vehicles. The researchers said it was the first time in the world that such low-pressure operation had been achieved in a sulfide-based all-solid-state lithium-metal full cell with an areal capacity of 2.4 mAh/㎠. "We addressed both the limitations of the brittle sulfide-based solid electrolyte with a polymer network and the stress caused by lithium expansion with a porous current collector," Park said. "This result came from close collaboration with Korean researchers." References Nature Communications(2026), DOI: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-79393-w

artigo.texto: Polarium Energy Solutions AB has been declared bankrupt by the Stockholm District Court The company more than halved operating expenses since 2024 but remained under financial pressure Chairman Harald Mix is exploring a potential acquisition by his private investment company Mounting financial pressures have forced Swedish battery energy storage company Polarium Energy Solutions AB into bankruptcy. The Stockholm District Court declared bankruptcy after the company concluded that it could not continue operating in its current form. The company attributed its bankruptcy to several factors, including sharply declining battery prices amid growing competition from Chinese suppliers, reduced investments by telecom operators and tower companies, and delays in some distributed BESS development projects. Overcapacity from the Chinese suppliers and a shift to cheaper battery chemistry is pushing down prices for every player in the supply chain leading to sharply lower gross margins. “Like the auto industry, several European battery and energy storage companies have been hit hard by the dramatic increase in competition from Chinese players, and a number of European manufacturers have been forced to file for bankruptcy or restructure financially,” said Harald Mix, Chairman of Polarium. Morrow Batteries and sonnen are some of the European battery companies to have walked the same path (see Germany’s sonnen GmbH Faces Insolvency As US Business Expands and Europe’s Morrow Batteries Files For Bankruptcy). Earlier another Swedish battery manufacturer Northvolt filed for bankruptcy. Its recycling patents were acquired by Refinyx (see Refinyx Acquires Northvolt’s 134 Battery Recycling Patents). These developments, explains Polarium, weakened its financial position despite efforts to reduce costs and restructure its operations. The company claims it had more than halved its operating expenses since 2024, but demand remains “too low relative to costs” leading to an unstainable financial situation. It also made changes to its strategy, business model and organizational structure in an effort to improve profitability. The company had explored options to secure its future, including finding a buyer for all or parts of the business and a court-supervised reorganization, but concluded that bankruptcy was the only remaining option. Polarium’s bankruptcy follows a strategic transformation initiated in 2025. In August 2026, Polarium announced a sharper focus on telecom power solutions and distributed energy storage, areas it identified as having stronger growth and profitability potential. The company also sought to reduce costs, improve margins, strengthen its presence in local markets and move closer to key suppliers. As part of the transformation, Polarium reported that its 2025 net sales declined to SEK 896 million from SEK 1.332 billion in 2024. However, gross profit improved to SEK 114 million from a loss of SEK 46 million, while its EBITDA loss narrowed to SEK 61 million from SEK 270 million. The decision to file for bankruptcy follows the October 1, 2026 appointment of company EVP and Head of the Residential and C&I business segments Pontus Winberg as Polarium’s new CEO. Winberg succeeded Leif Ottosson who retired after leading the transformation and strategic renewal of Polarium. Polarium Chairman Harald Mix said he intends to engage with the bankruptcy trustee to explore whether parts of the business can continue. He has also indicated that he is prepared to consider financing a potential acquisition by his private investment company. According to the company’s announcement, the bankruptcy trustee, Mikael Kubu of Ackordscentralen, has now taken over the company and will determine how its assets and business will be handled, including the possibility of a sale and continued operations.

artigo.texto: By Andrew Blakers, Australian National University The final cost estimate for Snowy 2.0 has been released. The conversion of the original Snowy hydroelectric scheme to a large pumped hydro energy storage scheme will cost A$22-25 billion and will be completed in late 2029. Much media coverage has focused on the major blowouts in cost and time. When the scheme was announced in 2017, then-Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull gave a rough costing of just $2 billion – extremely low for a project this size – and said it could be finished in four years. Engineering issues, stalled tunnelling machines and surging costs of construction all contributed to the blowouts. The project has endured a remarkable amount of negative press, including from renewable energy advocates. Some of it is warranted – early cost estimates were overly optimistic. Some is debatable, such as claims it won’t work as advertised. But let’s zoom out. Snowy 2.0 is about 80% done. It will likely be finished within three years. Once up and running, it will convert the original Snowy scheme into a giant rechargeable battery, able to back up solar and wind overnight and during calm and cloudy weather. It will arrive in time to allow ageing coal plants to retire. Once up and running, it will last 150 years. $22 billion sounds like a lot – but it translates to about $5 per Australian per year of operation. As more and more renewables enter Australia’s power grids, we will need much more energy storage. Building grid-scale batteries with the same energy storage as Snowy 2.0 would cost three times more than the final cost ($22 billion). But batteries last 20 years, while Snowy 2.0 will last for 150 years. Why do we need so much energy storage? Renewables currently provide about 50% of the power in the National Electricity Market, Australia’s largest power grid. The government’s target is 82% by 2030 (mostly solar and wind). Reaching this goal will require much more storage. That’s because over half the demand for electricity is overnight (defined as 4pm to 8am). During these hours, solar output is minimal or nonexistent. Wind provides some power, but not enough. Coal plants currently meet most of the overnight demand. But Australia’s coal fleet is ageing rapidly and will not be replaced. Almost all will close over the next ten years. How can we keep the lights on overnight as coal exits? We can use wind (which is intermittent), gas (expensive and responsible for high emissions), or store energy for use overnight and on cloudy days. Energy storage has shot to prominence in recent years, driven by rapid falls in battery costs. Home batteries and battery-electric vehicles are surging in popularity for consumers. In the grid, batteries are muscling in and taking a role once occupied by gas-powered plants to cover short spikes in demand. Because batteries can do this job more cheaply than gas, electricity costs are falling for everyone, not just the owners of batteries. So why do we need pumped hydro? Batteries are an increasingly cheap way to store energy short term, meaning minutes to hours. But they’re an expensive way to cover longer periods, such as overnight and during cloudy days. This is where pumped hydro can help. Pumped hydro turns a normal hydroelectric plant into a giant water battery. When power prices are low, water is pumped uphill to a high reservoir. When power prices rise, water is run downhill through turbines to produce power. These schemes excel at long-duration storage, as very large volumes of water can be kept in dams and released as needed. Every year, Australia’s science agency, CSIRO, releases GenCost, an update on changes to the costs for all components of the clean energy transition. The latest figures show pumped hydro can store and release power much more cheaply than batteries can. The cost advantage is highest now, but it will still be there in ten and 20 years time. That’s because the steep falls in battery costs are expected to taper off. Pumped hydro typically lasts five to ten times longer than batteries. Keeping water behind a rocky dam is an extremely cheap and durable way to store energy long term compared to extracting metals to make batteries. Pumped hydro also stimulates the local economy more, compared to imported batteries. Time to take a longer view Once up and running, Snowy 2.0 will roughly quadruple Australia’s total rechargeable electricity storage. Behind the 45-metre high wall of its upper reservoir, Tantangara, is up to 254 gigalitres of water. That’s about 50% of the water in Sydney Harbour (500GL). This enormous volume of water represents 350 gigawatt-hours of storage – the equivalent of the energy available in the batteries of seven million electric vehicles. To stop climate change from worsening, we have to stop burning fossil fuels. To do that, we have to triple or quadruple how much electricity we produce so that we can electrify transport, heating, industry and other sectors. Almost all of this new electricity will come from solar and wind. We will also need large-scale energy storage so renewable power can be released at night or as needed. Energy storage is becoming a solved problem. Batteries and pumped hydro can do the job of storing power over shorter and longer periods. As electrification gathers pace, Australia will need more pumped hydro projects – some as large as Snowy 2.0. The good news is that the technical issues and tunnelling problems Snowy 2.0 has faced have taught us a great deal about how to overcome them. The key challenge the engineers of Snowy 2.0 faced is the need for a 27-kilometre-long tunnel. Australia has hundreds of excellent options for off-river pumped hydro sites between Brisbane and Melbourne, located close to transmission lines and away from national parks and rivers. These options require much shorter tunnels compared to Snowy 2.0, meaning they would be much quicker to build. Snowy 2.0 is no longer a bargain. But it’s still a very good long-term inve

artigo.texto: As the data center boom draws intense backlash across Pennsylvania, the state’s consumer advocate wants to ensure existing customers aren’t saddled with higher costs and increased risk of outages. In a legal complaint filed with the Public Utility Commission in October, the consumer advocate argues that PPL Electric Utilities’ rules don’t adequately protect customers from the potential negative consequences of data centers connecting to the grid. There’s already broad agreement among government officials that data centers should pay for the extra costs they cause and bear the risk of reliability problems if the grid becomes overwhelmed, the complaint says. Major tech companies and utilities, including PPL, have publicly committed to following these principles. But the legally binding rules that cover how the company sets prices and delivers power don’t fully reflect those aims, the consumer advocate argues. “We just want to make sure these pledges and promises actually have teeth to them,” said Consumer Advocate Darryl Lawrence. “What we’re trying to do is get this enshrined in regulation.” PPL has forecast more demand from data centers than any other electric company in Pennsylvania, according to the complaint. “This is going to be the case that should pretty much set the guiding principles for everyone else,” Lawrence said. One indicator of the proceeding’s significance is that Gov. Josh Shapiro’s office has filed to intervene as a party in the case. It’s been at least 15 years since the governor has taken that step in a utility proceeding. Intervening in the case gives the Democratic governor another avenue to set the terms for data center development and its impact on residents. In August, Shapiro signed an executive order incentivizing data center developers to meet certain standards, including securing their own supply of electricity and paying the full cost of grid upgrades necessary to serve them. The case is progressing as state and federal officials weigh legislation and regulations. Regulators are grappling with the new challenges posed by data centers in the face of widespread public opposition. “There is a level of bipartisan consensus on the idea that Grandma should not be subsidizing Big Tech’s electricity bill that I don’t see in any other facet of American life,” said Abe Silverman, an energy researcher at Johns Hopkins University. Even with residents, elected officials and utilities agreeing on the wider issues cited in the consumer advocate’s complaint, disputes could still surface as details are hashed out. There are different ways to define the costs at issue, legal filings show. Anticipated demand from data centers has already driven up electricity bills across Pennsylvania, after record price spikes at the auctions where utilities secure their power supply. Going forward, the consumer advocate wants data centers to shoulder more of those costs. PPL agreed to some changes around data centers, including long-term contracts and exit fees, as part of a settlement in its most recent rate case that state regulators approved in June. More recently, the company also proposed a plan to insulate existing customers from transmission costs associated with data centers. The consumer advocate argues that neither effort goes far enough. In a statement, a PPL spokesperson said the company is “committed to protecting customers, maintaining reliability and ensuring that large-load customers pay the costs associated with their projects.” The case, which will include public hearings as well as extensive testimony, is still in its early stages. A final decision from the utility commission is not due until next July. A new paradigm Data centers need massive amounts of power, consuming as much as thousands or even millions of homes. To accommodate the extra demand, utilities must spend millions of dollars upgrading their networks. Data centers use so much electricity and want to connect to the grid so quickly that they upend old assumptions about how to share those costs fairly, experts told Spotlight PA. For instance, utilities typically spread the cost of upgrading transmission lines — which transport electricity across long distances — across all their customers, because everyone benefits from a more reliable system. In guidance issued in May, however, state regulators concluded that data centers require a different approach. If network upgrades would not have been necessary “but for” the interconnection of a data center, the utility commission concluded, the data center should pay for them — even if other customers also benefit. In some cases, it’s straightforward to determine which costs have been triggered by a data center; in others, it can quickly become complicated, said Ted Kury, director of energy studies at the University of Florida’s Public Utility Research Center. Even with a “but for” standard in place, “it will be up to the regulator to decide what that standard means,” he said. Most electric utilities haven’t yet indicated how or whether they will adopt the commission’s recommendations, which are not binding. PPL’s current rules — updated as part of a settlement negotiated before the guidelines were finalized — still allow other customers to share increased transmission costs caused by data centers, the consumer advocate says. The complaint cites a planned transmission line in Luzerne County that’s needed to serve a potential data center campus. The project drew national attention after the developer offered residents $10,000 payments if the data center were built. The planned transmission upgrades will cost about $178 million, legal filings show. PPL plans to recover only 12% of that from the data center itself — “the cost causer and the primary beneficiary of the network upgrades,” the consumer advocate’s complaint says.
