artigo.texto: A instalação de mega data centers em Campinas e seus possíveis impactos ambientais, econômicos e sociais foram discutidos nesta terça-feira (24) durante um debate público na Câmara Municipal. Especialistas e ambientalistas questionaram a capacidade da legislação vigente de regulamentar empreendimentos desse porte e alertaram para consequências que vão além do elevado consumo de água e energia. - Clique aqui para fazer parte da comunidade do Porque Campinas no WhatsApp e receber notícias em primeira mão. Mediado pelo vereador Wagner Romão (PT), o encontro teve como um dos principais pontos de discussão o Campus Campinas, mega data center voltado à inteligência artificial da Terranova em parceria com a gestora britânica Actis, previsto para a Fazenda Pau d’Alho, em Barão Geraldo, dentro do Polo de Inovação para o Desenvolvimento Sustentável (PIDS). Presidente do Instituto Brasileiro de Proteção Ambiental (PROAM), Carlos Bocuhy chamou a atenção para a dimensão física da infraestrutura necessária ao funcionamento das ferramentas de inteligência artificial e seus impactos sobre o meio ambiente. “A inteligência artificial, da forma como ela se insere, precisa de gigantescos data centers, e ela não está nas nuvens. Ela precisa de uma base física. Ela estimula a mineração, a construção de novos chips, materiais. Data centers consomem energia, consomem água”, afirmou. Ruídos de baixa frequência preocupam especialistas Professora titular da Faculdade de Engenharia Civil, Arquitetura e Urbanismo da Unicamp, Emília Rutkowski destacou a necessidade de diferenciar os centros de processamento de dados convencionais dos megaempreendimentos destinados a atender grandes operações tecnológicas. Durante sua apresentação, a pesquisadora reproduziu uma gravação do ruído emitido por um mega data center e explicou que equipamentos como ventiladores de resfriamento, transformadores elétricos e geradores de emergência são fontes de sons de baixa frequência. “Esse é o grande problema, porque a gente vai ficar ouvindo isto 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana, 365 ou 366 dias por ano”, afirmou. Segundo Emília, as características de propagação desses ruídos representam desafios tanto para a instalação de barreiras acústicas quanto para a fiscalização dos empreendimentos. A professora também questionou os possíveis efeitos sobre a fauna, a vegetação e as comunidades próximas. A pesquisadora ressaltou que os data centers são estruturas fundamentais para a produção de conhecimento, mas questionou a concentração dessas operações em empreendimentos de grandes dimensões. “Não vamos discutir ‘não quero data center’. Eu não quero mega data center, porque o que ele está fazendo é economia de escala para quem detém essa informação de nuvem, ou para quem quer treinar a sua IA”, declarou. Proximidade com o Sirius gera questionamentos A localização do empreendimento também foi alvo de preocupação durante o debate. Além de áreas residenciais de Barão Geraldo, como Jardim Miriam, Guará e Alphaville, o entorno reúne importantes instituições de ensino, ciência e tecnologia, entre elas Unicamp, PUC-Campinas, CPqD e o Centro Nacional de Pesquisa em Energia e Materiais (CNPEM), onde está instalado o acelerador de partículas Sirius. Wagner Romão destacou a sensibilidade dos equipamentos científicos do CNPEM a interferências externas e lembrou que, durante as discussões sobre a implantação do PIDS, até mesmo a circulação de caminhões nas proximidades da instituição foi motivo de preocupação. O parlamentar questionou a compatibilidade entre a instalação do mega data center e as atividades científicas desenvolvidas na região, além dos possíveis efeitos sobre a ocupação urbana prevista para o entorno. Legislação ambiental e benefícios fiscais são questionados Outro ponto levantado por Romão foi a regulamentação ambiental desses empreendimentos. O vereador apresentou uma resposta da Companhia Ambiental do Estado de São Paulo (Cetesb) a um inquérito civil do Ministério Público, segundo a qual a atividade de data center não está entre as fontes de poluição previstas em um decreto estadual de 1976 e, por essa razão, dispensa licenciamento ambiental no âmbito da companhia. “O mega data center, sobretudo, expõe não uma lacuna. É uma gigantesca cratera de meteoro na nossa legislação e na capacidade do poder público de regular esse tipo de empreendimento”, afirmou o parlamentar. Romão também questionou a inclusão dos data centers no programa municipal de incentivos fiscais destinado à atração de investimentos e à geração de empregos. Já o advogado Leonardo Pilon, mestre em Direitos Digitais e Sustentabilidade pela Universidade Federal de Santa Maria (UFSM), chamou a atenção para os possíveis impactos térmicos dessas estruturas e defendeu que o planejamento urbano priorize a adaptação das cidades às mudanças climáticas. “A corrida que a gente realmente deveria estar correndo é a adaptação à emergência climática”, afirmou. Conselho de Meio Ambiente acompanha o caso Conforme noticiado anteriormente pelo Porque Campinas, o Conselho Municipal de Meio Ambiente de Campinas (Comdema) busca a participação de instituições científicas e tecnológicas na avaliação dos possíveis impactos do empreendimento. Entre as preocupações estão a demanda por água e energia, a emissão de calor, os ruídos e as vibrações, além de eventuais interferências nas atividades desenvolvidas pelos centros de pesquisa instalados na região. O debate desta terça-feira foi transmitido pela TV Câmara Campinas e está disponível na íntegra no canal oficial do Legislativo no YouTube.

artigo.texto: AI has turned data centers into one of the fastest-growing electricity users on the planet. In its Energy and AI report, the IEA estimates that data centers used about 415 TWh in 2024, around 1.5% of the world’s electricity. In its Base Case, this becomes about 945 TWh by 2030 and about 1,200 TWh by 2035. In the US, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory counted 176 TWh in 2023, 4.4% of the country’s electricity, and expects 325 to 580 TWh by 2028. That would be 6.7% to 12% of all US electricity. Every one of those kilowatt-hours goes through power supplies before it reaches a chip, usually more than one. So here is a question I keep asking: who checks how efficient those power supplies really are? The honest answer is the manufacturer itself, or a voluntary label it chose to apply for. As far as I can find, no law anywhere requires an independent lab to verify the efficiency of a data center PSU. Someone buying an 850 W PSU for a gaming PC has more independent efficiency data to choose from than an operator buying thousands of server modules that run 24/7. Before I go further, you should know where I stand. I run HWBusters and the Cybenetics lab, and Cybenetics would gain from what I propose here, because we test and certify power supplies for a living. Keep that in mind and check my sources. Every number below is linked. Where the power goes In a typical data center, electricity from the grid passes through a transformer, an uninterruptible power supply (UPS), and power distribution units (PDUs). Then the server PSU, or a power shelf that feeds a whole rack, converts it to a low DC voltage, and converters on the board step it down again for the CPU or GPU. Every step loses a little. The server PSU is the one stage that every server has, and it never switches off. The diagram shows the uncomfortable part. Transformers have mandatory EU efficiency rules. The UPS has only voluntary programs. The server PSU has a minimum in the EU that the manufacturer declares itself, and nothing mandatory in the US. DC and high-voltage DC (HVDC) supplies, where the industry is heading, have no rules at all. What the rules already do Credit where it is due. The EU has had minimum efficiency rules for server PSUs since 2020, in Regulation (EU) 2019/424. Since 1 January 2023, a single-output server PSU must reach 90% efficiency at 10% load, 94% at 20%, 96% at 50% and 91% at 100%, with a power factor of at least 0.95 at half load. Multi-output units need 90%, 94% and 91% at 20%, 50% and 100% load. Those are demanding numbers. Three details matter, though. Compliance is self-declared under CE marking, so no independent lab has to confirm the numbers before a product goes on sale. The PSU limits exclude DC-powered servers. And the regulation exempts several server types, including servers with more than four processor sockets, large servers, fully fault-tolerant servers and network servers. The Commission was supposed to review the regulation by March 2022. More than four and a half years later, its own website still lists it as “under review”. In the US, I could not find any federal minimum for server power supplies. ENERGY STAR includes PSU efficiency and power factor tables in its Computer Servers v4.0 specification, and it requires independent certification: an EPA-recognized certification body accredited to ISO/IEC 17065 by an IAF MLA signatory, using data from an ISO/IEC 17025 lab. That is the right model. The catch is that it is voluntary, and it nearly disappeared. The administration’s FY2026 budget request zeroed the program, and Congress restored full funding in a law signed on 23 January 2026, with votes of 397-28 in the House and 82-15 in the Senate. In March 2026, EPA and DOE signed an agreement that makes DOE the lead agency. Then there is 80 PLUS, run by CLEAResult. It is voluntary too, but it has categories for 230 V, 277 V, 480 V, and 380 V DC redundant data center PSUs, and a new Ruby level that CLEAResult describes as ultimate efficiency for AI data centers. I found no 800 V DC category. Its test method comes from the EPRI/Ecova Generalized Internal Power Supply Efficiency Test Protocol, which checks a handful of fixed load points. China went another way. Its GB 43630-2023 standard sets mandatory efficiency limits and grades for tower and rack servers, and servers now need a China energy label. But it rates the whole server with a benchmark; it does not test the PSU on its own, and it covers general-purpose one- and two-socket machines. Blade, multi-node, full-cabinet and HPC systems are left out. Facility rules are moving faster. Germany’s Energy Efficiency Act requires new data centers that start operating from 1 July 2026 to reach a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.2 or better, with limits of 1.5 from July 2027 and 1.3 from July 2030 for existing sites, although an amendment that may relax them is being debated. In the EU, data centers with at least 500 kW of IT power already report their energy performance, and on 21 September 2026 the Commission adopted an A to G rating and label based on PUE, water use and other indicators. The first labels are expected in 2027. Three blind spots The first is the metric itself. PUE, defined in ISO/IEC 30134-2, divides the total energy of the facility by the energy of the IT equipment. The PSU is part of the IT equipment. So a watt wasted inside a server PSU counts as IT energy, exactly like a watt spent on computing. PUE tells you how efficient the building is. It cannot tell you how much your power supplies waste, and neither can a label based on it. The second is how efficiency is measured. The EU rule and 80 PLUS check a few fixed load points. That is fine as a minimum, but redundant PSUs share the load with a partner module, so they can spend long periods at light load, and nothing below 10% load is checked at all. In our redundant server PSU protocol, we apply more than 1,450 load combinations from 2% to 100% of the operating range in a hotbox

artigo.texto: BOTETOURT COUNTY, Va. – Construction on Google’s planned data center campus in Botetourt County has been halted following a circuit court judge’s ruling Monday evening, a decision that some residents are celebrating as a victory for transparency and government accountability. The ruling has drawn praise from residents who have opposed the project since its inception. “He (plaintiff Robert Dallas) basically gave Google a black eye. He hit a giant in the face and knocked him down. So that’s something important,” said Chad Bean, a Botetourt County resident. The decision comes after county resident Robert Dallas sued Botetourt County and a company associated with Google, arguing that county officials failed to adequately disclose that they were voting on the project’s performance agreement during a June 2025 meeting. Transparency has been a central concern among opponents of the project. “FOIA does matter. And we showed that. There is a desperate need for transparency with the county,” Bean said. The judge’s ruling halts construction, voids the performance agreement and rescinds all actions taken on the data center since the June 2025 meeting. The decision creates new complications for the county and Google, as construction has already begun and money has changed hands. Dr. Mac Scothorn, chair of the Botetourt County Board of Supervisors, provided an update on the project during a regularly scheduled board of supervisors meeting Tuesday. “The county is reviewing the ruling carefully with our legal counsel. Construction activities will be minimal for destabilization into the holidays to ensure this site is in compliance with the permits,” Scothorn said. Google also responded to the ruling Tuesday, saying their considering their options moving forward. “We are evaluating yesterday’s ruling by the court. We remain committed to working transparently with Botetourt County and the community in full compliance with all legal and regulatory requirements,” a company spokesperson wrote. While many celebrate, Botetourt County resident Danny Goad says this isn’t the end of the fight. “I think over the next three or four weeks, you’re going to see many things come out of the groups that oppose this. We want the people’s voice to be heard,” Goad said. The ruling does not necessarily mean the data center project is dead. The county could move forward by holding a public hearing and taking another vote on the performance agreement.

artigo.texto: The U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has approved SpaceX’s request to launch as many as 1 million satellites for the creation of a network of data centers in orbit for complex artificial intelligence computing. The agency’s first-ever authorization of data centers in space makes way for a concept that was central to Elon Musk’s pitch to investors ahead of SpaceX’s initial public offering in June. The company has cautioned that orbital AI data centers rely on unproven technologies and may never be commercially viable. “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said Wednesday in a statement. He has frequently praised SpaceX and attended a test launch of the company’s new Starship rocket earlier this month.

artigo.texto: O Ministério das Comunicações (MCom) trabalha no desenvolvimento de um projeto para facilitar os investimentos em cabos submarinos no Brasil. A intenção é catalogar todas as autorizações necessárias para ancoragem de cabos na costa brasileira, substituindo, assim, o atual modelo marcado por medidas esparsas. A ideia foi comentada pelo diretor do Departamento de Investimento e Inovação do MCom, Marcelo Alves da Silva, nesta quarta-feira, 25, durante o Fórum dig.ia, realizado em Brasília. Em linhas gerais, o projeto chamado de Zona de Interesse de Ancoragem envolve realizar um mapeamento de todas as licenças e autorizações necessárias para a instalação de cabos no litoral brasileiro, incluindo obrigações exigidas por todas as esferas de governo. Com isso em mãos, a pasta acredita que poderá disponibilizar um pré-projeto aos operadores de infraestrutura. A expectativa é de que a modelagem facilite os negócios envolvendo infraestruturas subaquáticas no País. "Isso vai ser resultado de todas as tomadas de subsídios e workshops que fizemos [sobre cabos submarinos]. Ter esse mapeamento é um projeto que estamos trabalhando dentro do ministério", afirmou Silva. Falta de governança Suzana Rodrigues, conselheira substituta da Anatel, comentou que o setor de cabos submarinos carece de governança. Segunda ela, os órgãos públicos envolvidos com o segmento precisam ter uma coordenação para que o operador "não fique correndo atrás de diversos organismos". Na prática, apesar de o Brasil ser atrativo ao segmento, até pelo posicionamento geográfico, o modelo atual atrasa os investimentos. "Fazer esse balanceamento entre segurança jurídica e as necessidades de um setor altamente tecnológico é sempre um desafio. Estamos falando de infraestruturas críticas, e o nosso olhar tem que ser para o operador de uma infraestrutura privada que está pensando em um retorno econômico", avaliou a conselheira substituta da Anatel. Energia para data centers A coordenadora-geral de Planejamento da Transmissão do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), Thais Ingrinde de Souza Araújo, disse que a pasta está adotando um novo modelo de acesso à rede elétrica para facilitar a contratação de energia por data centers. O modelo antigo funcionava como uma fila, com cada solicitação sendo analisada em ordem cronológica pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS). Contudo, agora a entidade trabalha com um sistema chamado de "temporada de acesso", no qual diversos pedidos são analisados conjuntamente. "Para os locais em que há muita competição – ou seja, tem mais projetos cadastrados do que a rede consegue absorver –, abre-se um procedimento competitivo com base no sinal econômico: quem der o maior bônus, quilowatt por reais, fica apto a conseguir assinar o seu contrato e seguir com o seu processo de conexão naquele barramento", explicou. De acordo com Thais, a mudança de modelo reduz o tempo de análise e favorece projetos "mais maduros". Além disso, o setor elétrico consegue direcionar investimentos para obras com as quais já tem assinatura de projeto com um provedor de data center. "Com isso, a gente conseguir garantir que nenhuma estrutura de transmissão fique ociosa", resumiu.

artigo.texto: Regulating carbon emissions is complex. Digital tools developed through Imperial Consultants will help Malaysia's policymakers decide how to establish the country's first emissions trading system. Malaysia is preparing to introduce a domestic carbon emissions trading system (ETS) as a way of persuading its companies to reduce the amount of greenhouse gases they produce. Researchers at Imperial College London, working through Imperial Consultants, are supporting that process with two digital tools that will help regulators and businesses see how the new scheme might play out once it is in operation. Climate policy is becoming a data challenge as much as a policy-design challenge. Dr Gbemi Oluleye Centre for Environmental Policy "Climate policy is becoming a data challenge as much as a policy-design challenge," says Dr Gbemi Oluleye of the Centre for Environmental Policy, who led the Imperial team. "Governments need to assess thousands of installations, firms and products while understanding implications for emissions coverage, revenues, trade exposure and regulated entities." These questions operate at different scales but are increasingly interconnected. "Digital tools can help shift policymaking from policy evidence to policy intelligence. They enable policymakers to identify exposure, compare policy configurations, test decisions under uncertainty and connect policy domains supporting the design, operationalisation and institutionalisation of market-based solutions." Emissions trading systems are among a range of market-based solutions that use prices, markets and financial incentives to encourage emission reductions, while giving businesses flexibility over how, where and when they decarbonise. Under an ETS, the government sets a limit (or cap) on the total emissions permitted from covered activities, typically reducing this cap over time. Emissions allowances are then allocated to companies, either free of charge or through auctions. Each allowance generally represents permission to emit one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. Companies must surrender sufficient allowances to cover their verified emissions. Those that reduce their emissions below their allowance holdings can sell their surplus allowances to companies that need additional allowances, for example because reducing emissions from their activities is more technologically challenging or costly. This creates a financial incentive to reduce emissions while ensuring that total emissions remain within the cap. Some ETS regimes also allow companies to use carbon credits generated through eligible projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gases, such as afforestation or certain carbon capture and storage activities. These projects may be located domestically or internationally, depending on the rules of the scheme. Tools for policymakers The first tool that Imperial's researchers helped develop is an ETS Threshold Calculator. This enables users to explore how different emissions thresholds influence the design and coverage of an ETS, including the installations covered, emissions brought within the scheme, administrative burden and potential revenue from auctioning carbon credits. "Higher thresholds can reduce administrative burden, but may lower emissions coverage and auction revenues," Dr Oluleye explains. "Lower thresholds increase coverage but can bring more small emitters into the system for limited additional benefit. The ETS Threshold Calculator enables policymakers to explore these trade-offs by testing different thresholds and sector combinations and examining their implications for coverage, regulated entities and indicative revenues." The second tool addresses an international aspect of carbon emissions, since any national approach to the issue will also be affected by what neighbouring countries and significant trading partners have decided to do. For example, the European Union has operated an ETS since 2005, with increasingly ambitious carbon reduction targets. This has driven up the cost of emitting carbon within the bloc, giving companies an incentive to move carbon-intensive production elsewhere. To address this risk of "carbon leakage" the EU has created a Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which makes importers pay a tariff on the carbon emitted during the production of goods outside the EU. Regardless of whether emissions have leaked from the EU or not, this exposes countries such as Malaysia to additional costs on their exports to Europe. So, the Imperial team developed a CBAM Viability and Liability Assessment Tool, which integrates trade information with relevant EU methodologies to help users estimate potential exposure, embedded emissions and carbon-related liabilities. It does this across all relevant product codes within the six CBAM sectors (iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity) and allows users to incorporate verified company-specific emissions data for more accurate, tailored analysis. Digital tools are not intended to replace policymaker judgement. Instead, they create an interactive policy laboratory, making the consequences of different assumptions and decisions more visible. Dr Gbemi Oluleye Centre for Environmental Policy "Our Malaysia assessment estimated approximately 2.56 million tonnes of embedded CO₂ across assessed CBAM-covered exports, with aluminium accounting for around 87%," Dr Oluleye says. Wider analysis also identified substantial exposure elsewhere, with Russia and China recording the highest estimated EU CBAM liabilities. "Exposure therefore varies considerably across countries, sectors and products. Understanding where exposure lies, why it arises and how different policy choices could change it requires moving beyond static analysis towards interactive decision-support tools." artigo.texto: CATL remained China’s largest power-battery supplier by installations in October 2026, with 39.60 GWh and a 40.00% market share. CnEVPost reported the figures on November 19, attributing them to the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance (CABIA). CATL’s share fell 0.93 percentage points from September even as its installation volume increased. CATL led China’s October battery market BYD ranked second with 21.36% of China’s October power-battery installations, leaving an 18.64-percentage-point gap between the two companies. CATL’s lead narrowed from September, when the gap was 19.83 points, according to CnEVPost’s CABIA-attributed figures. Market share is a company’s portion of all installations in the market. It can fall even when a company installs more batteries, if total installations grow faster. Rising installations do not guarantee a rising market share: the total market sets the pace. Why CATL’s share fell as its installations rose CATL’s installations increased about 11.6% month over month, from 35.49 GWh in September to 39.60 GWh in October. China’s total power-battery installations grew faster, rising 14.0% month over month to 99.4 GWh. That difference in growth rates explains how CATL could add installation volume while losing 0.93 percentage points of share. CATL’s LFP and ternary shares moved in opposite directions The change varied by battery chemistry. CATL’s share of China’s LFP installations edged up, while its share of ternary-battery installations fell. The segments have separate totals, so each share describes CATL’s position within that chemistry rather than within the whole market. The reported decline extended through October On November 20, the South China Morning Post reported that October marked CATL’s sixth consecutive monthly decline in China market share. It linked the trend to domestic automakers diversifying their battery suppliers. CATL’s January–October position remained stronger than its October-only share Across January to October 2026, China’s power-battery installations totaled 675.6 GWh, up 16.9% from the same period a year earlier. CATL accounted for 293.28 GWh and a 43.55% share; its cumulative share was 0.76 percentage points higher than a year earlier. BYD recorded 127.58 GWh and an 18.94% share over the same period.

artigo.texto: The midterm elections — with data centers a key issue in many races — helped provide clarity around the environment for data center development, James Burke, Vistra president and CEO, said on an earnings call earlier this month. “Before the elections, in many markets, we were seeing concerns about data centers in the way that the public was reacting to the pace of development, who had control over those decisions, what impact could it have on electric prices, water, all of that,” Burke said on the Nov. 6 call. “Moving past this election is a positive just in terms of being able to understand what's at stake, and now how do we move forward?” So far, the key messages from Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa have been “very similar to some of the key messages that Governor Abbott had expressed and … consistent with messages we've been expressing, which is there has to be some guardrails on this development,” Burke said. Vistra wants tougher requirements for data center interconnection, including higher collateral requirements and take-or-pay agreements for transmission charges, according to Burke. “As we've said for some time, load interconnect queues were overstated across the country and especially in [the Electric Reliability Council of Texas footprint], driven by speculation from developers,” Burke said. Even with the midterm elections and regulatory actions around data centers, through 2030 Vistra expects load to grow by 4% to 6% a year in ERCOT and by 2% to 3% annually in the PJM Interconnection footprint, according to Burke. Despite Vistra’s expectations for load growth in ERCOT, power prices there have been trending lower due to some crypto mining facilities coming offline so they can convert into data centers, and the state’s data center audit and permitting pause, Burke said. “We do not see this as a long-term impact,” he said, noting that ERCOT hit a 91 GW peak demand record this year. Vistra’s fleet has grown to about 50 GW with its Oct. 30 Cogentrix acquisition, Burke said. The fleet includes combined cycle and peaking power plants that are running more often, according to Burke. “As renewable penetration continues throughout the country, you're seeing these assets get called on more,” Burke said in response to an analyst question about potentially selling off parts of the fleet. “So we've been bullish on dispatchable. We've been bullish on flexibility … So as a long-term owner-operator, we like the fleet.”

artigo.texto: A Victorian homeowner paid $74,000 AUD ($49,000 USD) for an off-grid setup with 65 solar panels and 46 kilowatt-hours of battery storage, according to a 2024 report cited by Dubbo Photo News. Here's what to know Household self-sufficiency can extend beyond electricity to supplying water and managing wastewater, making owners responsible for those services. Going off-grid can involve disconnecting a home from the electric grid and other public utilities. For most properties, a grid connection remains the cheapest electricity option, the Australian Government's energy.gov.au website explained. But off-grid power can make financial sense for remote properties where connecting to the network would be expensive or impractical. Household electricity use determines the cost of a stand-alone solar installation. For homeowners comparing solar options, EasyHome is a user-friendly marketplace offering solar shoppers exclusive pricing and unique deals from trusted partners. More background Construction detritus, wildlife droppings, and other debris can contaminate collected rainwater, so owners disconnecting from public water need to manage those risks. With proper installation and maintenance, however, rainwater tanks can provide a safe supply, NSW Health noted. NSW Health emphasized cleaning gutters every three to four months for water-independent homes, as well as regularly checking water storage tanks for cleanliness. Owners must keep household sewage systems working properly and obtain council permission both to install and to operate them, the NSW Office of Local Government says. What can be done? Rooftop solar panels are the most effective solution to rising energy prices, and solar leases offer those savings with no upfront costs. Homeowners can go solar without taking on the full responsibilities of an off-grid home. Prospective buyers and builders should check local code requirements before committing, assess their home's needs, and seek expert guidance when planning such a system. For households dealing with high electric bills, EasyHome is like Groupon for home energy, negotiating exclusive offers for its large user base. It also offers special battery deals: pairing solar with storage boosts savings and provides backup electricity during outages — useful benefits for households that decide to keep their grid connection. Energy used for heating and cooling can be reduced through intentionally deployed insulation, glazing, and shading, the Australian Government's Your Home guide advised. artigo.texto: TAMPA, Fla. — The debate over how to regulate data centers is moving from unincorporated Hillsborough County to Tampa City Hall. Tampa City Council approved a resolution advancing a proposed temporary moratorium on data center development, giving city staff time to review Tampa's Comprehensive Plan, Land Development Code and City Code and recommend potential regulations. WATCH REPORT FROM JADA WILLIAMS: The council's action does not enact the moratorium itself. Instead, it moves the proposed ordinance toward the public hearing process. Susan Johnson-Velez with Tampa's Legal Department told council members that the proposal stems from a motion made in late October. "Council asked staff to bring back a resolution doing a number of things related to data centers, among them preparing an interim development control or moratorium ordinance to allow staff time to review the Comprehensive Plan, the Land Development Code, and the City Code so that we could come back to council with recommendations on regulations for data centers," Johnson-Velez said. Hillsborough County has been considering the same questions for months Tampa's action comes as Hillsborough County has spent months examining how it could regulate data centers before significant development occurs. On Aug. 5, county commissioners directed staff to evaluate a potential framework for future data center regulations, including whether to limit or prohibit the use of county drinking water for cooling. The county's subsequent November report says modern data centers associated with artificial intelligence can involve very large buildings with significant demands on power and water. Cooling and backup power equipment can also produce persistent noise, according to the report. Commissioner Harry Cohen told Tampa Bay 28 in August that the county wanted to proceed cautiously. "We're going to do some study. We are going to assess what the impacts of these centers could be, and we're going to proceed very, very cautiously before we even entertain the idea of allowing anything like this to be built," Cohen said. During that August meeting, members of the public also urged commissioners to act before projects begin moving forward. "It's clear that we need to hit the brakes on explosive growth and data center projects," one speaker told commissioners. Another urged the board to "protect our communities until thorough research and safeguards are in place." What could Hillsborough County's rules look like? By November, the county's Development Services staff had outlined several potential approaches. The framework includes requiring planned-development zoning or allowing data centers as conditional uses only in certain zoning districts. It also considers separation requirements designed to address potential noise impacts on residents, livestock and sensitive wildlife. Other possibilities include: - Enhanced screening around data center sites - Architectural requirements intended to break up large, monolithic building faces - Limits on the use of potable, or drinking, water for cooling - Requiring the use of reclaimed water Data centers are not currently listed as permitted uses within Hillsborough County's standard zoning districts, according to the county report. That means a data center development would currently need to be specifically approved through planned-development zoning. The county also identified electricity demand as a significant consideration, including possible cost impacts on other customers. However, its report does not propose regulations addressing electricity rates because those are regulated by the Florida Public Service Commission. County moratorium proposal deferred Hillsborough County has also considered a temporary moratorium of its own. On Nov. 10, commissioners had an item before them that would have declared "zoning in progress" and scheduled public hearings for consideration of an ordinance establishing a one-year temporary moratorium on AI data centers in unincorporated Hillsborough County. However, commissioners deferred that item to a date to be determined. View more - Skanska booked the award as new contracted work rather than revenue already earned. - The latest award mirrors an earlier Georgia project in capacity and footprint. - Skanska's Georgia announcements represent separate awards rather than one cumulative project value. Skanska announced on November 26, 2026 that it had received an additional $275 million award from an existing client to build a new 48 MW data center in Georgia, USA. The award is worth about SEK 2.8 billion and will be included in Skanska’s US order bookings for the fourth quarter of 2026. That classification matters: the announcement adds contracted work to the order book, rather than reporting the full amount as revenue already earned. Building Scope and Delivery Schedule The main facility will total 244,730 square feet, approximately 22,700 square meters. Skanska’s scope covers construction of the shell and interior fit-out for technical spaces, support areas and office functions. An 860-square-foot, approximately 80-square-meter, ancillary water-treatment building is also included. Although small beside the main facility, it places supporting utility infrastructure within the award. Construction began in November 2026, and Skanska expects completion in October 2028, meaning work was already underway when the additional award was announced. September Award Provides a Close Comparison Skanska’s September 22, 2026 announcement described an $84 million contract with an existing client, assigned to US order bookings for the third quarter. It listed the same 48 MW capacity and 244,730-square-foot footprint as the latest project, while specifying five colocation data halls and administrative space. The September project was scheduled to begin in November 2026 and finish in the third quarter of 2028; the latest release gives October 2028 as the expected completion month. September’s delivery scope included civil, structural, utilities, electrical, mechanical, security, interior amenities and fit-out work, plus commissioning of major equipment through completion. Earlier Awards Establish a Sequence of Georgia Work An April 9, 2026 release disclosed a $75 million contract, booked in the first quarter, for a 22,700-square-meter, 244,090-square-foot facility. Its scope included associated site work, underground utilities, administrative space and five data halls. Construction began in March 2026, with completion scheduled for the first quarter of 2028. A June 23, 2026 announcement followed with a $255 million supplemental contract, booked in the second quarter. That project covered approximately 245,000 square feet, associated site work and underground utilities, administrative space and five data halls, with the same stated March 2026 to first-quarter 2028 construction schedule. These releases establish a sequence of Georgia data-center awards during 2026, but not one aggregate project value. Skanska identifies the customers only as existing clients and does not explicitly connect every announcement to the same facility. The values should therefore be read as separate awards, not as a documented cumulative cost for a single project. The latest award’s significance is split between two timelines: a fourth-quarter 2026 booking for Skanska’s US business and a construction program extending to October 2028. The first measures new work secured; the second will track how that booked work becomes a completed 48 MW facility with its supporting water-treatment infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Sungrow Renewables and Actuate Energy have agreed to develop a 380MW/1.5GWh portfolio of battery energy storage systems (BESS) in Spain. The seven-project deal, involving sites in A Coruña, Almería, Castellón and Navarra, is anticipated to bring new energy storage capacity online from 2027 to the first half of 2028. Discover B2B Marketing That Performs Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms. The transaction, said to be the largest BESS deal in Spain, establishes a long-term partnership to develop, build and operate the stand-alone BESS projects. Sungrow Renewables is a subsidiary of Sungrow Power Supply Group, while Actuate is an energy storage platform backed by private equity firm NGP. The portfolio includes stand-alone battery installations, some of which are already under construction, while others are scheduled to reach ready-to-build (RtB) status by 2027. Specific sites in the agreement include the Valencia Cluster in La Vall d’Uixó (Castellón), Santiago in Lousame (A Coruña), Berja in Almería, and the Navarra Cluster in Olite and Cordovilla. Sungrow Renewables Western Europe Daniel Sánchez said: “This transaction marks a major milestone for Spain’s BESS market. “With 380MW and 1.5GWh, it is the largest battery energy storage transaction completed to date in Spain and, crucially, is backed by an advanced-stage portfolio of projects already moving into construction. Energy storage in Spain is moving from ambition to execution.” The agreement could lead to further collaboration, as both companies aim to expand their presence in the energy storage sector and help stabilise Spain’s electricity network. According to Sungrow Renewables, it has previously delivered hybrid solar photovoltaic (PV) and stand-alone battery storage projects in Spain and currently operates in over 20 countries. Actuate Energy invests in and operates energy storage assets to support renewable power and grid stability across Europe. The company has chosen Spain as its first European market, citing the country’s significant renewable energy uptake and established project opportunities. Actuate Energy CEO Ben Skinner said: “Spain is a market leader in deploying renewable energy, but battery storage has not kept pace. “This portfolio marks a real step forward for the Spanish grid, adding flexible assets that respond in seconds to keep the system stable, allowing more renewables to come online.” Last month, Sungrow announced plans to partner with ENGIE and Elecnor to advance the 150MW/300MWh Hazelwood BESS in Victoria, Australia.

artigo.texto: que são mega data centers de Inteligência Artificial, onde estão projetos no Brasil e por que precisamos de leis rigorosas para conter as Big Techs Por Andressa Santa Cruz – Greenpeace Brasil | A era da Inteligência Artificial (IA) virou uma corrida desenfreada que exige cada vez mais territórios, recursos e dados. No Brasil, mega projetos das gigantes da tecnologia avançam em meio a isenção de impostos, enquanto comunidades e consumidores enfrentam os prejuízos. Mas dá tempo de agir antes que os danos se tornem irreversíveis. “Antes de seguir expandindo os data centers de IA que só aumentam os lucros bilionários das Big Techs, o Brasil deve saber o custo e definir as regras para que o povo brasileiro não pague a conta dos impactos” explica Julia Catão, especialista em Tecnologia do Greenpeace Brasil. O que são Mega Data Centers de IA? São centros de dados de hiperescala para desenvolver modelos de Inteligência Artificial (IA), concentram milhões de servidores para processar, armazenar e transmitir enormes volumes de dados, podendo consumir energia equivalente a países inteiros e milhões de litros de água potável. A diferença está no tamanho e na capacidade: data centers tradicionais operam os serviços digitais que usamos no dia a dia (enviar mensagens, assistir a vídeos e acessar plataformas); já mega data centers de IA são instalações computacionais de escala e impactos industriais e atendem sobretudo às Big Techs. Quais os impactos dos Mega Data Centers de IA? - Aumento na conta de luz: usam a rede local e elevam os custos da energia nas residências – nos EUA, as tarifas chegaram a triplicar para mercados, custo que é repassado aos consumidores. - Consumo de água: apesar de existir “circuito fechado”, há perdas e reposição; nos EUA, o consumo anual chegou a 1 trilhão de litros d’água. - Poluição sonora: geradores fazem ruído insuportável, alto e constante, afetando a qualidade de vida das famílias vizinhas. - Emissões de gases de efeito estufa: a possibilidade de usar fontes fósseis, ampliando as emissões que agravam a crise climática. - Pressão sobre os territórios: ocupam áreas enormes que podem chegar a mais de 100 campos de futebol, disputando terras, água e energia com comunidades locais. - Concentração de poder: domínio de empresas estrangeiras sobre o mercado e as infraestruturas impede o avanço tecnológico no país. Nos EUA, onde mais tem data centers no mundo, a população fez vários protestos contra e o tema foi decisivo nas eleições. Nova York suspendeu novas instalações de hiperescala até ter leis mais rígidas e países europeus também pausaram projetos como Irlanda, Holanda e Dinamarca. Quais são os projetos de Mega Data Center no Brasil? O Brasil já possui data centers (cerca de 225 e quase metade fica no estado de São Paulo), mas os mega projetos para desenvolver IA estão começando a chegar em todo país. O mais avançado está em construção no território indígena do povo Anacé, em Caucaia (CE), região metropolitana de Fortaleza. Segundo o Governo do Ceará, abrigará as tecnologias de IA do TikTok e a previsão é começar a operar no segundo semestre de 2027. Confira abaixo projetos de mega data centers em andamento no Brasil. Lei Redata e a importância de regular data centers no Brasil No Brasil, o Redata (Lei 15.504/2026), sancionada em setembro, criou o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter. Na prática, concede isenções de impostos para atrair centros de dados ao país — uma renúncia fiscal estimada em R$ 7 bilhões, segundo Secretaria Especial da Receita Federal, ou seja, recursos públicos que deixam de ser arrecadados. Aprovado sem participação social ou diálogo com as comunidades atingidas, o Redata abre brechas preocupantes, como o incentivo à combustível fóssil. O desenho da lei favorece as Big Techs em detrimento do povo brasileiro e do clima global. Enquanto estados norte-americanos e países europeus discutem limites rígidos, o Brasil se torna alvo da expansão acelerada. O que são Big Techs e quem controla a corrida da Inteligência Artificial? As Big Techs são gigantes da tecnologia que estão entre as empresas mais ricas e influentes do mundo, como Google, Amazon, Meta, Nvdia, Microsoft e TikTok – seus fundadores e administradores ocupam o topo da lista de bilionários da Forbes. São exemplos de como a “inovação” acontece quando é controlada por poucos: lucros recordes, cortes de empregos e a falsa promessa de que automação trará benefícios, porém na prática acumulam infrações trabalhistas, sociais e ambientais. Por que regular Big Techs e Data Centers? Regular não é censurar ou frear o desenvolvimento tecnológico, é assegurar que a população faça parte com salvaguardas que respeitem os ciclos da natureza, o bem-comum e que tragam retorno para a sociedade. Para isso, precisamos de criar regras: - Regulação das Big Techs (ambiente digital e democracia): estabelece limites e responsabilidades para as grandes empresas de tecnologia, incluindo transparência sobre algoritmos, proteção de dados e direitos digitais. - Regulação de data centers (infraestrutura física e recursos naturais): impõe análise de riscos e leis firmes para a construção e operação desses empreendimentos, considerando os impactos socioambientais. Parem os mega data centers! Nove organizações — Instituto Terramar, Amazônia Sem Data Center, CTRL+Z, Data_Labe, Instituto Decodifica, Mulheres pelo Clima do Vale do Paraíba, Coding Rights, Filha do Sol e Greenpeace Brasil – se uniram para frear o avanço de mega data centers de IAs no Brasil até que sejam assegurados: - Consentimento e Transparência: Participação social ativa e consulta livre, prévia e informada para as comunidades tradicionais. - Licenciamento Ambiental completo: Estudo e relatório de impacto assegurando transição energética justa e proibindo instalação em áreas de importância ecológica. - Fim da isenção de impostos: Quem lucra com infraestrutura digital em larga escala deve se responsabilizar pelos custos e impactos, e investi

artigo.texto: Midea has launched its Energy Storage business in Australia expanding its local product portfolio. Already an established and trusted presence in many Australian homes across air conditioning, heating, refrigeration, laundry and other smart household appliances, Midea’s local expansion into residential energy storage comes as Australian households look for ways to take greater control of electricity use, maximise rooftop solar investments and reduce reliance on grid electricity. Leading the new Australian portfolio is PowerInfi, an all-in-one residential energy storage system designed to bring energy storage functionality together in a single solution. When paired with a suitable solar installation, residential batteries can store surplus electricity for use later, reducing reliance on grid purchases and reducing energy costs over time. PowerInfi also reflects Midea’s broader approach to home energy, with energy storage sitting alongside technologies such as air conditioners, heat pumps and other major household appliances in its portfolio that use energy throughout the home. Midea is also introducing Omni X, a standalone energy storage solution showcased with a 7kWh battery configuration. Designed for flexibility, the Omni X offers installers and homeowners another option to meet differing household energy requirements. Midea Energy Storage showcased its local range for the first time at the recent All Energy Australia 2026, held in Melbourne last month. PowerInfi and Omni X were displayed alongside Midea air conditioners and heat pumps, illustrating the breadth of the company’s home energy and climate technology portfolio, and provided installers, industry partners and other stakeholders an opportunity to explore the solutions and learn about Midea’s plans for the market. Midea Australia and New Zealand general manager, Ivan Ma, said Australia is an important market for Midea Energy Storage. “There is strong rooftop solar adoption here and a growing interest in household energy independence, so it is a natural next step for us to be able to offer our residential energy storage technologies to Australian homeowners,” Ma said. "Australians already know Midea through the many appliances and climate control solutions they use every day. “We're building on that familiarity and trust in energy storage, which will increasingly become an important part of the modern connected home of the future.” Ma said choosing a residential energy storage system is a significant investment. “Consumers are making a long-term decision about how they power their homes, and they need confidence in the company standing behind that investment,” he said. “We see enormous potential to bring greater confidence and choice to this market, and to consider how energy storage, heating, cooling and appliances can work together to deliver a better experience for consumers.”

artigo.texto: A estimativa atribuída à Epoch AI coloca o data center da Huawei em Horinger, na Mongólia Interior, em cerca de 81 mil equivalentes H100 — aproximadamente 7% da capacidade computacional estimada de Colossus 2, associado à xAI. Um equivalente H100 expressa capacidade computacional em relação ao acelerador Nvidia H100. Portanto, os 81 mil equivalentes não representam uma contagem de GPUs Nvidia instaladas. Como Horinger se compara a Colossus 2 As estimativas usam a mesma unidade, o que permite comparar a escala computacional dos dois campi: A estimativa de Horinger equivale a cerca de 7% da estimativa para Colossus 2. É uma comparação entre capacidades computacionais estimadas, não entre contagens verificadas de aceleradores físicos. Para comparar a escala de data centers, use a mesma unidade: equivalentes H100 expressam capacidade computacional estimada, não o número de GPUs instaladas. Como a estimativa foi calculada O método atribuído à análise combina observações de infraestrutura com estimativas de chips. Imagens de satélite permitem identificar equipamentos de refrigeração; a partir deles, estima-se a dissipação de calor e a capacidade do campus. Para estimar a quantidade de aceleradores, o cálculo também considera as vendas de chips da Huawei e o intervalo entre a venda e a implantação. A estimativa atribui ao campus cerca de 105 mil chips Ascend 910C e 8 mil Ascend 910B. Em um relato publicado em novembro de 2026, quatro edifícios de refrigeração densa somavam uma capacidade estimada de 286 MW; três eram descritos como operacionais naquele relato. A mesma análise cita uma subestação de 304 MW e geradores de reserva de 230 MW como referências para conferir a estimativa. Esses valores se referem a infraestruturas distintas dos 286 MW atribuídos aos quatro edifícios.

artigo.texto: Energy Vault Closes $78 Million Financing for Texas Battery Storage Project The financing will support construction of the SOSA Energy Center, with commercial operations expected in Q3 2027 November 24, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights Energy Vault, a utility-scale energy storage project developer, has closed $78 million in construction and bridge financing for its 150 MW/300 MWh SOSA Energy Center battery storage project in Madison County, Texas. The bridge financing will be repaid through an $80 million preferred equity investment already committed upon project completion. Energy Vault said the construction financing, preferred equity investment, and a draw on the OIC preferred facility are intended to fund the project through construction and commercial operations on a non-recourse basis. The SOSA Energy Center was the first energy storage asset formally acquired and placed into development under Asset Vault, Energy Vault’s platform for owning and operating energy storage and artificial intelligence infrastructure assets. Once completed, the project will operate on a merchant basis in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas North market. Energy Vault said the project will retain the flexibility to enter into a contracted offtake agreement as market conditions change. Construction began in the fourth quarter of 2025 after the company secured site control and reached environmental and interconnection milestones. Civil work has been completed, and a substation has been installed. Energy Vault is handling the project’s engineering, procurement, and construction. Major equipment is expected to arrive at the site in the coming months. Commercial operations are scheduled for the third quarter of 2027. The company said the SOSA Energy Center represents an investment of approximately $100 million in Madison County. Energy Vault estimates that the project will generate $9.3 million in tax revenue for North Zulch Independent School District and Madison County over 10 years. Construction is also expected to create 65 local jobs. In September 2026, the company acquired more than 2.3 GW of U.S. battery energy storage development projects from Colorado-based developer and operator of utility-scale battery storage projects, Goshe Energy Storage. In the first nine months of 2026, publicly announced energy storage project funding increased by 197% year over year, compared to 9M 2025, according to Mercom’s recently released 9M 2026 Funding and M&A for Energy Storage report.

artigo.texto: Sungrow Renewables and Actuate Energy have agreed to develop a 380MW/1.5GWh portfolio of battery energy storage systems (BESS) in Spain. The seven-project deal, involving sites in A Coruña, Almería, Castellón and Navarra, is anticipated to bring new energy storage capacity online from 2027 to the first half of 2028. The transaction, said to be the largest BESS deal in Spain, establishes a long-term partnership to develop, build and operate the stand-alone BESS projects. Sungrow Renewables is a subsidiary of Sungrow Power Supply Group, while Actuate is an energy storage platform backed by private equity firm NGP. The portfolio includes stand-alone battery installations, some of which are already under construction, while others are scheduled to reach ready-to-build (RtB) status by 2027. Specific sites in the agreement include the Valencia Cluster in La Vall d'Uixó (Castellón), Santiago in Lousame (A Coruña), Berja in Almería, and the Navarra Cluster in Olite and Cordovilla. Sungrow Renewables Western Europe Daniel Sánchez said: "This transaction marks a major milestone for Spain's BESS market. "With 380MW and 1.5GWh, it is the largest battery energy storage transaction completed to date in Spain and, crucially, is backed by an advanced-stage portfolio of projects already moving into construction. Energy storage in Spain is moving from ambition to execution." The agreement could lead to further collaboration, as both companies aim to expand their presence in the energy storage sector and help stabilise Spain's electricity network. According to Sungrow Renewables, it has previously delivered hybrid solar photovoltaic (PV) and stand-alone battery storage projects in Spain and currently operates in over 20 countries. Actuate Energy invests in and operates energy storage assets to support renewable power and grid stability across Europe. The company has chosen Spain as its first European market, citing the country's significant renewable energy uptake and established project opportunities. Actuate Energy CEO Ben Skinner said: "Spain is a market leader in deploying renewable energy, but battery storage has not kept pace. "This portfolio marks a real step forward for the Spanish grid, adding flexible assets that respond in seconds to keep the system stable, allowing more renewables to come online." Last month, Sungrow announced plans to partner with ENGIE and Elecnor to advance the 150MW/300MWh Hazelwood BESS in Victoria, Australia. "Sungrow and Actuate sign 380MW battery storage deal in Spain" was originally created and published by Power Technology, a GlobalData owned brand.

artigo.texto: In summary Some colleges are setting up their own data centers and designing AI products to rival ChatGPT. The community colleges and the UC systems are both discussing expanding these AI alternatives, even as they continue to work with commercial providers. On Thursday, the University of California announced another deal with OpenAI to give ChatGPT to students. At the same time, California’s higher education systems are considering building their own data centers and creating in-house alternatives to ChatGPT, Claude, and other commercial AI products. College administrators say they want to explore all options without limiting themselves to just one vendor. Some tech leaders say these alternatives to ChatGPT are not only possible but would save money and avoid data security risks. The California Community Colleges system — the largest higher education system in the country — is asking the state for $21 million next year to develop a more independent AI network that would, according to the proposal, be a “fraction of the cost of commercial solutions.” The University of California is considering doing something similar, though the system has yet to put forward a formal proposal. California State University spokesperson Amy Bentley-Smith said the 22-campus system is having “initial conversations” with the UC and community colleges about collaboration on AI but did not share other details. While they discuss designing their own AI, the UC, Cal State and community college systems continue to use commercial providers. UC spokesperson Stett Holbrook told CalMatters the purchasing amendment of the new OpenAI agreement isn’t finalized yet, even though the university has already announced the deal. That disclosure emerged after reporters for CalMatters repeatedly asked for a copy of the purchase agreement. The previous OpenAI contract requires the UC to pay a minimum of $10 per user per month for ChatGPT EDU licenses and a minimum of $30 per user per month for another advanced ChatGPT platform. The Cal State system signed contracts with OpenAI that extend through 2029 for roughly $56 million. The community colleges’ chancellor’s office has AI cooperation agreements with Google, Microsoft, Adobe and IBM but no systemwide financial arrangement with any AI company. University-designed AI models are cheaper and ensure more privacy, but they’re “not quite necessarily as intuitive,” said Craig Hayward, a strategic advisor to the community college chancellor’s office on AI. “Your prompting game needs to be more on point to get the value out of them.” Locally, individual universities are already moving forward with their own AI plans. This month, Cal Poly San Luis Obispo announced the creation of its AI data center, which is intended to serve the whole campus, according to Chris Lupo, the director of the university’s school of applied computing. The most advanced, university-controlled AI platform is at UC San Diego, where university IT services collaborated with its supercomputing center to create TritonGPT, a nod to the campus mascot and OpenAI’s ChatGPT. The San Diego platform has licensed or shared aspects of its AI development with other UC campuses to help them develop their own chatbots, including BearGPT at Berkeley and SCOUT at Merced. UCSD was also cited as a partner in the community college system’s AI proposal. “This is the model that the higher education system in the state of California is trying to expand,” said Zachary Johnson, the senior director of AI strategy for UCSD. Why sovereign AI is gaining popularity For the community college system, developing an independent or sovereign AI system comes with three main benefits, Hayward said. The first is cost. While tools such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini are the most popular examples of AI, they’re expensive, with individual plans reaching $200 per month and incurring further costs to go beyond usage limits. To develop their own AI systems, colleges don’t work from scratch — they use other AI tools, known as open-weight models, including Chinese products such as Kimi or DeepSeek or American ones such as Llama and Gemma. Getting these products up and running can be costly, but once operational, they are often not only cheaper than ChatGPT or Claude but also give schools more control. The code behind these low-cost models is typically free to use or change, allowing colleges to rename and rebrand the AI or even repurpose it entirely. The second benefit is control. The Cal State contract with OpenAI specifically says that the company cannot use student data to train its models, but Hayward said these kinds of agreements still have risks and unknowns. “There’s just this concern that somehow it’s going to leak,” he said, adding that internally developed AI tools give colleges “end-to-end control” over the data. That control is helpful for research and for operations. Campuses can develop AI uses that are tailored to help with other projects that commercial models like ChatGPT or Claude aren’t necessarily built for, such as using AI to help with admissions or course enrollment. Lupo at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo said these more independent AI models also allow computer science professors and students to design their own AI experiments without having to worry that a third-party might change its model in the middle of an experiment. Hayward said the last benefit is environmental. The community college system has lofty climate goals, including reducing potable water usage by 50%. He said that by adapting open-access or open-weight AI models, colleges take on more of the burden of AI computing internally, which means they can more closely track the power and water demands of these systems. “We can better monitor and know our AI footprint,” Hayward said. “It’s somewhat obscured when you use big vendors like Anthropic and Google.” Pushback to OpenAI For many UC and Cal State leaders, however, big vendors still hold a lot of sway. “OpenAI models are more ad

artigo.texto: Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Uzbekistan will receive an US$8.5 million grant from the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) to prepare for trading carbon credits with South Korea. The documents were signed on 25 November during a meeting between Umid Abidkhodjaev, Deputy Minister of Economy and Finance, and representatives of KOICA and the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), the ministry said. The grant is being provided under KOICA's technical assistance programme for a project titled "Supporting Uzbekistan's Implementation of the Paris Agreement and Joint Actions with the Republic of Korea under Article 6". The project will be implemented jointly with GGGI. The talks were attended by Kim Myung Jin, head of KOICA's office in Uzbekistan, Stella Seung Yeon Lee, head of GGGI's office in Uzbekistan, and specialists from both organisations. The parties discussed Uzbekistan's transition to a green economy and the regulatory and institutional framework for carbon credit trading. The project will involve developing rules, guidelines and a joint action plan for carbon credit trading between Uzbekistan and South Korea. The grant will also support the establishment of a training centre for specialists involved in preparing and managing carbon projects. The centre will be equipped with the necessary facilities and offer training programmes. Another component will involve pilot projects to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in agriculture, energy and water management. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement allows countries to cooperate voluntarily in meeting their climate commitments. Under Article 6.2, one country can transfer verified emissions reductions generated by projects within its territory to another country. These transfers are known as internationally transferred mitigation outcomes (ITMOs). The purchasing country can count them towards its national climate targets, while the selling country must exclude the same reductions from its own accounting to prevent double counting. Article 6.4 establishes an international carbon credit mechanism supervised by a United Nations body, while Article 6.8 covers non-market approaches to cooperation. Countries agreed on the main rules for implementing Article 6 at the COP26 climate conference in Glasgow in 2021. In 2025, GGGI, with financial support from KOICA, implemented the Green Restoration of the Aral Sea Region project in Karakalpakstan. It focused on developing climate-resilient agriculture, introducing water-saving technologies and attracting green investment. The new project continues KOICA and GGGI's cooperation in Uzbekistan on green development, climate change adaptation and sustainable finance. According to the ministry, it will expand Uzbekistan's opportunities to participate in the international carbon market and help the country achieve its climate goals.

artigo.texto: A Justiça Federal do Distrito Federal negou, nesta quarta-feira, 25 de novembro, o pedido de tutela de urgência apresentado pela Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica) para suspender os leilões de reserva de capacidade destinados à contratação de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias, previstos para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro. Na decisão, o juiz Diego Câmara, da 17ª Vara Federal Cível do Distrito Federal, entendeu que não foram demonstrados os requisitos necessários para a concessão da medida, considerando que a cobrança do encargo dos geradores terá início somente em agosto de 2028 e que a suspensão dos certames poderia comprometer a segurança do suprimento de energia elétrica. A decisão foi proferida no contexto da ação civil pública ajuizada pela Abeeólica em 16 de novembro, contra a União e a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). A entidade questiona a constitucionalidade da regra que atribui exclusivamente aos geradores o custeio da contratação das baterias e a realização dos leilões sem a regulamentação definitiva do rateio do encargo. Para o magistrado, a atribuição dos custos aos geradores decorre de uma escolha expressa do Legislativo,e não de uma decisão da Aneel ou do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME). O juiz também avaliou que uma eventual declaração de inconstitucionalidade do dispositivo não implicaria necessariamente a invalidação dos leilões ou dos contratos deles decorrentes, mas uma alteração na base de agentes responsáveis pelo pagamento do encargo. “O § 6º disciplina apenas quem custeia o encargo. Eventual reconhecimento de sua invalidade repercutiria, portanto, sobre a definição da base pagante, e não sobre a validade da licitação ou dos contratos”, afirmou o magistrado. Com o indeferimento da tutela de urgência, a ação civil pública seguirá em tramitação. O juiz determinou a citação da União e da Aneel para apresentação de suas defesas, com posterior manifestação do Ministério Público Federal (MPF). Regulamentação do encargo não condiciona leilões Outro argumento afastado pelo juiz foi o de que os leilões não poderiam ser realizados antes da definição da metodologia de rateio dos custos entre os geradores. Segundo a decisão, não há norma legal ou regulamentar que condicione a realização dos certames à conclusão da regulamentação pela Aneel, que deverá estar operacional antes do primeiro ciclo de apuração do período de suprimento. Em sua manifestação à Justiça, a Aneel lembrou que o primeiro leilão de reserva de capacidade na forma de potência, realizado em dezembro de 2021, antecedeu em quase três anos a publicação da resolução normativa que disciplinou o rateio do respectivo encargo. Em relação à proposta de diferenciação da cobrança conforme a flexibilidade das fontes de geração, questionada pela Abeeólica, o magistrado ressaltou que ainda não há uma metodologia definitiva aprovada pela diretoria da agência. A decisão também registra que a Aneel está avaliando uma proposta alternativa apresentada pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS). “Eventual ilegalidade do ato normativo que vier a ser editado poderá ser submetida ao controle jurisdicional antes de qualquer cobrança, sem que seja necessário paralisar a contratação”, declarou o juiz. Risco à segurança do suprimento Ao negar o pedido de urgência, o magistrado considerou que não há risco de dano iminente aos geradores, uma vez que a cobrança do encargo está prevista para começar em 1º de agosto de 2028. Para o juiz, há tempo suficiente para a conclusão da regulamentação do rateio, a análise do mérito da ação civil pública e o julgamento da ação direta de inconstitucionalidade (ADI) apresentada pela associação ao Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF). Por outro lado, o magistrado destacou os riscos associados ao adiamento dos leilões, com base em informações apresentadas pelo MME. Segundo a pasta, o Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia 2036 (PDE 2036) e o Plano da Operação Energética 2026 identificaram violações dos critérios de garantia de suprimento de potência a partir de 2027, mesmo após as contratações realizadas nos leilões de reserva de capacidade de março deste ano. O adiamento dos certames também poderia comprometer o enquadramento dos projetos nas temporadas de acesso ao sistema de transmissão e, consequentemente, a entrada em operação dos empreendimentos na data em que serão necessários ao sistema elétrico. “O dano alegado é patrimonial, futuro e passível de reparação pela eventual realocação do encargo, caso acolhida a tese da autora”, afirmou o magistrado. Discussão no STF e no Congresso O juiz também considerou o fato de que a própria Abeeólica submeteu o questionamento sobre a constitucionalidade da cobrança exclusiva dos geradores ao STF. A ADI nº 8.050 foi ajuizada em 19 de novembro e está sob relatoria do ministro Cristiano Zanin, que solicitou informações antes de analisar o pedido de medida cautelar. Até a decisão desta quarta-feira, o pedido ainda não havia sido apreciado pelo Supremo. Para o magistrado, não seria prudente antecipar, em uma decisão provisória com efeitos de alcance nacional, a análise sobre a validade de uma lei federal que já está sendo questionada diretamente no STF. A decisão também menciona a tramitação do Projeto de Lei (PL) nº 3.716/2026 no Congresso Nacional, que propõe revogar o dispositivo que atribui exclusivamente aos geradores o custeio das baterias, como um elemento adicional a recomendar cautela na atuação do Poder Judiciário.

artigo.texto: China fixes solid-state battery marketing myths From July this year, if a battery loses more than 0.5% of its mass during a vacuum bake test at {{120ºC}} for six hours, you can't legally call it an all-solid-state unit - at least not in China. That single metric matters more than any press release we've read this decade. For the last five years, automakers have put the "solid-state" label on anything with slightly less liquid sloshing around inside. China closed that marketing loophole with the rollout of GB/T 43568-2026. It establishes a formal threshold that strips away the PR fluff and forces OEMs to show actual factory readiness instead of optimistic lab charts. To secure an official all-solid-state designation, the liquid electrolyte must sit below 5% of the total cell weight. In August 2026, the International Electrotechnical Commission officially approved a China-led proposal to establish global testing and application guidelines for automotive solid-state batteries. The implications stretch into how legacy brands engineer their upcoming platforms. China is effectively shaping global markets without exporting a single battery. If you're a Chinese manufacturer already dominating the electric vehicle supply chain, aligning your export models with a domestic standard reduces compliance friction to zero. Foreign competitors face a reverse burden. European and American automakers now have a choice - they can either adapt to a framework designed without their input, or they can spend years trying to draft a new standard from scratch while the market moves on. There is no dedicated European solid-state standard published yet. Japan has advanced R&D, but lacks an equivalent national mandate to enforce it. We're already seeing the results of this regulatory clarity on the ground. Doctex spun up a manufacturing facility in Tianjin producing certified solid-state cells with an energy density of 350 Wh/kg. Far from being some fragile lab prototypes - they are going straight into production vehicles, offering a 15% to 20% bump in real-world driving range. Not everyone is moving at the same pace. Geely is working to complete full vehicle validation and pack layout integration by the third quarter of 2026. BYD has mapped its solid-state development timelines closer to 2027. Saike Power is still pouring concrete for its 0.1 GWh sulfide pilot line down in Yibin, pushing actual machine testing to the final months of 2026. It highlights the massive capital divide between battery suppliers who are fully industrialized and those still chasing the chemistry. State-backed Dongfeng Motor is prepping a 0.2 GWh plant to integrate its own oxide-polymer hybrid cells into a fleet of 100 demonstration vehicles across Hubei province. They're targeting driving ranges pushing toward the 620 miles mark, which sounds absurd until you look at the validation data. During winter testing up in Mohe - one of the coldest places in China - these cells kept 72% of their energy capacity. They also survived high-temperature {{170ºC}} oven bake evaluations without losing structural integrity. That kind of thermal stability addresses the strict thermal runaway and single-cell failure requirements laid out in the mandatory GB 38031-2025 EV safety rules that arrived this summer. The hardware needed to build these cells is also changing. Gotion High-Tech validated a pilot line using 100% locally manufactured machinery, integrating domestic slot-die coaters and high-pressure rollers into the factory floor. This cuts their reliance on international procurement entirely. When you eliminate overseas logistics bottlenecks and geopolitical tariff friction, the cost of scaling drops dramatically. Upgrading production lines with domestic equipment is projected to save the industry billions. It shifts initial factory budgets down to between RMB 400,000,000 and RMB 500,000,000 (roughly £42,900,000 to £53,900,000) per GWh. That financial insulation gives domestic brands a huge buffer against price wars. Western automakers simply don't have that localized machinery leverage yet. But having machinery readily available is only one part of this monumental shift. China is building a layered regulatory framework that scrutinizes every single component inside the pack. The new GB/Z 214-2026 guidance document issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology targets the solid electrolytes themselves. It establishes a uniform vocabulary and strict material parameters for suppliers, ensuring everyone evaluates the same physical characteristics in the exact same way. If an electrolyte material doesn't meet the baseline, it doesn't get CCC certification, and it won't be sold or imported into China. This prevents cell producers from swapping in cheaper, unverified electrolyte compounds to hit cost targets. It treats individual chemical components as distinct product categories with their own (enforceable) technical expectations. But even with this much manufacturing progress, we need to stay realistic about the timelines. CATL has openly acknowledged that widespread commercialization of true all-solid-state batteries will likely be restricted until 2030 due to anomalies in solid-interface resistance. The physics of moving ions through a solid medium at scale without degradation is still a big problem. For now, conventional liquid setups will continue to reach high-volume delivery records. That is the reality of mass manufacturing - the transition simply won't happen overnight, but the technical and safety definitions are now set in stone. By drawing a hard line with the GB/T 43568-2026 classification and pushing it through the IEC, China has ended the era of vague battery marketing. The unified safety standards are next, and it won’t be long before China gets those rubber-stamped.
