artigo.texto: Tecto anuncia data center expansível a 6 MW no Recife Primeira unidade da empresa em Pernambuco começará a operar em 2027 e será integrada à infraestrutura instalada em Fortaleza. A Tecto Data Centers anunciou hoje (25) a implantação de seu primeiro data center em Pernambuco. Batizado de TREC1, o empreendimento terá capacidade inicial de 1 MW, expansível a 6 MW, e previsão de entrada em operação no primeiro trimestre de 2027. O projeto integra o plano de investimentos de US$ 2 bilhões anunciado pela companhia em abril deste ano, destinado a obras e novos empreendimentos até 2028. O TREC1 oferecerá serviços de colocation, interconexão e serviços gerenciados para hyperscalers, operadoras de telecomunicações, provedores de nuvem e conteúdo e empresas do segmento corporativo. A instalação será integrada às operações da Tecto em Fortaleza, onde a companhia possui três data centers, entre eles o TFOR3, inaugurado em 2025. A capital cearense é um dos principais pontos de chegada de cabos submarinos internacionais ao Brasil. Segundo a empresa, a conexão entre os dois polos permitirá aos clientes distribuir operações entre diferentes localidades do Nordeste, inclusive para estratégias de recuperação de desastres (disaster recovery) e continuidade dos negócios. “O Nordeste reúne conectividade internacional e uma demanda crescente por infraestrutura digital, por isso tem papel estratégico na nossa expansão”, afirmou Tito Costa, CRO da Tecto Data Centers. Processamento regional O empreendimento no Recife integra a estratégia AI Grid, que prevê a distribuição da capacidade de processamento por meio de data centers regionais interligados, aproximando a infraestrutura dos locais onde os dados são gerados e consumidos. Essa frente complementa a estratégia AI Factory, composta por instalações de grande porte e alta densidade, destinadas ao treinamento de modelos de IA e ao processamento intensivo de dados. “Com o TREC1, a região passa a contar com dois polos da nossa rede, afinal, acreditamos que Recife está para Fortaleza, assim como o Rio de Janeiro está para São Paulo. Essa é a lógica da nossa estratégia AI Grid, que conecta data centers, levando capacidade de processamento para perto das empresas e complementando as grandes estruturas do AI Factory”, acrescentou Costa. De acordo com o relatório Data Center Brasil 2026, elaborado pela JLL e citado pela Tecto, a taxa de ocupação dos data centers brasileiros atingiu 96% no primeiro semestre deste ano. Expansão no Brasil e na Colômbia A Tecto prevê encerrar 2027 com oito data centers operacionais na América Latina. Serão cinco no Brasil, distribuídos entre Fortaleza (3), Rio de Janeiro (1) e Recife (1), além de três em Barranquilla, na Colômbia. A companhia também desenvolve outros dois empreendimentos no mercado brasileiro: o TGRU1, em Santana de Parnaíba (SP), com capacidade projetada de 200 MW, e o TPOA1, em Porto Alegre (RS), com 20 MW. (Com assessoria de imprensa)

artigo.texto: Em Atibaia, no interior de São Paulo, a promessa de um investimento de R$ 3 bilhões em infraestrutura digital tornou-se motivo de conflito. Moradores da região do Bairro do Tanque organizaram o movimento "Fora Data Center" para barrar a instalação de um complexo de processamento de dados de hiperescala, o Data Center Alfa, previsto para operar entre 2029 e 2030. O cerne da disputa não é apenas o tamanho do empreendimento — que ocuparia uma área equivalente a 50 campos de futebol -, mas a forma como ele chega à cidade. Para a comunidade, há um abismo entre a burocracia oficial e a realidade dos fatos. A contradição é clara. De um lado, a Prefeitura de Atibaia afirma que não há pedidos de licenciamento ambiental nos registros da Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente e que qualquer projeto precisará passar por rigorosos estudos da Cetesb e outros órgãos. Do outro, a infraestrutura elétrica já está sendo moldada para receber o gigante. Documentos da concessionária Isa Energia e do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) revelam que já houve autorizações para a expansão de 15 quilômetros de linha de transmissão e a implantação de módulos de entrada de 138 kV, especificamente para atender ao Data Center Alfa. Para os moradores, isso indica que o projeto está muito mais avançado do que a administração municipal admite publicamente. Enquanto a empresa DataSpots (do Grupo ON) mantém silêncio e não responde a questionamentos, quem vive no Bairro do Tanque lida com a incerteza sobre recursos básicos. A maior preocupação é a água. Em uma região onde não há rede de abastecimento público ou saneamento básico, as famílias dependem inteiramente de poços artesianos e "caipiras". Gabriel Tonobohn, morador do bairro há mais de três anos, relata a fragilidade do sistema: "A maioria usa um poço caipira e já está ficando sem água na época de seca". A chegada de um complexo que exige volumes massivos de água para resfriamento de servidores pode, na prática, secar a única fonte de sobrevivência da comunidade. Além da água, a qualidade de vida está sob ameaça por três fatores: Para as famílias que residem no local há décadas, o risco não é a desapropriação formal com indenização, mas a desvalorização total de seus imóveis. Se o bairro se tornar barulhento, quente e sem água, as casas perdem o valor de mercado. "Se torne esse bairro inabitável… elas vão ser obrigadas a sair dali. E elas não vão conseguir vender ou alugar essa casa para ninguém", explica Gabriel. É a perspectiva de ter que recomeçar a vida do zero, sem a compensação financeira que acompanharia uma obra pública. Até o momento, o movimento "Fora Data Center" já reuniu mais de 4 mil assinaturas e pressiona a Câmara Municipal para alterar o Plano Diretor e o Código de Obras, tentando criar barreiras legais contra a instalação de complexos de hiperescala antes que a primeira pedra seja lançada. artigo.texto: Sodium-ion batteries are rechargeable batteries made of a cathode, anode, electrolyte, separator, and current collectors that move sodium ions between the cathode (positive electrode) and anode (negative electrode) during charging and discharging. The movement of sodium ions changes between the cathode and anode during charging and discharging. Sodium ions move from the cathode to the anode through the electrolyte and vice-versa during the discharging state. Electric mobility conventionally uses lithium-ion batteries to provide power for the majority of electric vehicles. Lithium-ion batteries provide higher energy density, and they are lightweight and have a compact design, making the device easier to fit and move. The reason for shifting from lithium-ion batteries to sodium-ion batteries is to achieve overall improved performance of energy storage devices, which could also enhance affordability, safety, and supply chain security. As consumer demand for electric vehicles increases, manufacturers began exploring sodium-ion batteries as an alternative option to reduce reliance on costly lithium-ion batteries and replace expensive materials with abundant sodium and cheaper metals. Following is a list of the top ten companies playing an important industry role in developing sodium-ion batteries and updating existing charging solutions through advances in electrolyte chemistry, cell engineering, and existing lithium-ion production lines. CATL (Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited) A Chinese manufacturing company developing a sodium-ion charging solution as an alternative to lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles, commercial transportation and energy storage systems. The company has shown outstanding performance in developing sodium-ion batteries by achieving a First-generation Cell Spec that reached up to 160 Wh/kg cell energy density, 15-minute charging to 80% battery charge, and overcoming challenges in extreme moisture conditions which cause rapid chemical degradation and structural collapse in sodium-ion batteries. HiNa Battery Technology The company manufactures sodium-ion batteries and battery chemical components using copper-iron-manganese layered oxide cathodes and hard/soft carbon anodes. The company’s headquarters is in Liyang, Jiangsu Province, China specialising in sodium-ion battery research, cell manufacturing and energy storage solutions. This company employs a tabless, double aluminium current collector design to lower internal resistance and improves manufacturing techniques to make sodium-ion cells more efficient and increase energy storage capacity. BYD (Build Your Dreams) BYD is globally recognized for manufacturing electric vehicles and charging solutions. In terms of material and electrochemistry, BYD uses highly stable polyanion materials and electrochemical refinements for the cathode and transition metal chemistries to stabilize layered transition metal oxides and suppress undesirable phase transitions. BYD’s sodium-ion cells operate across wide temperature ranges (-40°C to 80°C) on the 3rd-gen platform and support fast charging/discharging rates paired with its Blade cell architecture. The multi-chemistry approach implemented by BYD in its sodium-ion battery technology enhances overall battery performance and balances cost, durability, extreme-weather conditions, energy density, and cycle life across different applications. Faradion Faradion manufactures sodium-ion battery technology for electric vehicles that lowers reliance on costly metals while offering strong safety and fast charging. The charging solution is designed to run on existing lithium-ion manufacturing lines without cobalt, lithium, or copper while targeting 30% lower cost than lithium-ion. EVE Energy The company commercializes high-durability NF155L sodium-ion cells built on lithium-compatible manufacturing lines. These cells use NFPP chemistry and are designed primarily for stationary battery energy storage systems (BESS) that provide thermal and fire safety by producing less flammable gas under extreme thermal runaway. EVE Energy is also expanding its sodium-ion battery production for electric vehicles by targeting electric two-wheelers with high-durability, low-temperature cells while building a manufacturing facility in Huizhou, Guangdong Province, China, targeting 2 GWh of annual production. Gotion High-Tech Again, a China-based manufacturing company established with a vision of “Build an Energy Science System Based on Materials Science and Digital Science,” and carrying the mission to “Make Green Energy Accessible and Sustainable.” The company is widely popular for its sodium-ion battery technology because of its Gnascent platform launched in May 2026. The platform eliminates the use of an anode as a current receiver, enabling the flow of electric current by using an anode-free structure. This reduces manufacturing costs and increases energy density. The sodium ions release from the cathode, travel through the electrolyte, and deposit directly on the negative current collector as a thin layer of metallic sodium. This plated sodium metal immediately acts as the active anode to complete the internal electrochemical circuit. Tiamat Energy A French company manufacturing sodium-ion battery technology as an alternative to lithium-ion battery technology with features such as fast charging, high power density, and reduced dependence on costly materials. The technology is designed for hybrid systems, buses, and future battery electric vehicles (BEVs), and utilizes a sodium vanadium fluorophosphate (NVPF) cathode and hard carbon anode to provide structural durability along with high power output and fast charging/discharging. artigo.texto: Governor Sherrill's Ponders Data Center "Faustian Bargain' BY COLLEEN O'DEA New Jersey’s U.S. senators both voted last Thursday against a divisive bill that seeks to speed permitting for new energy projects and require data centers to pay for the power they use, while also weakening environmental protections. Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s position on the bill, which still needs to pass the House, where its future is uncertain, is less clear. Her office declined to comment on it. Energy policy has been a priority of hers since taking office 11 months ago. New Jersey needs to increase supply in order to blunt electricity increases – last year, power bills jumped by about 20%. But the state also has strong environmental laws and a population that values the clean water and open spaces in the most densely populated state in the nation. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) combines some clean energy provisions and the promise of jobs with reduced environmental protections. It has pitted the Citizens Climate Lobby and AFL-CIO against the Sierra Club and NAACP. It divided the Democratic caucus, with 14 Democrats joining the Republican majority Thursday to pass the bill 62-33 and send it to the House of Representatives. Only two Republicans opposed the bill. If sent to his desk, President Trump likely would sign it. A policy statement from the White House touted a number of provisions of the bill, saying it would “remove major obstacles to building the infrastructure we need in this country.” The New Jersey State Chamber of Commerce and four regional chambers signed on to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s statement of support for quick action on the bill: “Permitting reform is ultimately about delivering results. When needed investments are delayed, families and businesses face higher costs, longer wait times, and fewer opportunities. Communities wait longer for congestion relief, the broadband connections needed to support work, education, health care, and entrepreneurship, improved access to clean water, and the energy infrastructure needed to meet growing demand. A more efficient permitting process can help deliver these benefits sooner by reducing unnecessary delays and improving certainty while maintaining strong environmental protections and opportunities for community engagement.” But many environmental organizations disagree and oppose some or all of the bill’s provisions to weaken environmental protections. Doug O’Malley, director of Environment New Jersey, called it a “Faustian bargain” that the nation should not accept and he praised Sens. Cory Booker and Andy Kim, both Democrats, for voting against the measure. “This would be a really bad deal for New Jersey and the country,” O’Malley said. “We would be sacrificing the natural environment for the promise of clean energy but there would be a ton of rollbacks of permitting protections for fossil fuel projects.” The bill would weaken a number of environmental protection laws, including the Clean Water Act, making it harder for groups to stop projects that could harm the environment. One such project is the Northeast Supply Enhancement Project or NESE, a proposed expansion of a pipeline carrying natural gas from Pennsylvania through New Jersey to New York and that would require the installation of six miles of pipeline through the Raritan Bay. The project is back before the state Department of Environmental Protection after a federal appeals court vacated state approvals for it two months ago. “It’s a false choice,” O’Malley said of the bill. “We think you don’t think you have to sacrifice environmental protections for clean energy.” While the bill would require data center developers to cover the costs of the electricity they consume, there would still be “huge environmental impacts,” including in water usage that cools the high-capacity computers needed for artificial intelligence processes, O’Malley said. In voting no, both Booker and Kim said that while they support the bill’s clean energy goals, it does not do enough to stop potential abuses of a new permitting system by Trump, including those involving new immigration detention systems. "I believe the climate crisis demands urgent action, and smart permitting reform can unleash a generation of new good-paying union jobs and new technology,” Kim said in a statement. “I voted earlier in the process to allow a debate and amendment process that could improve the bill before final passage. Unfortunately, those improvements, which would rein in the worst impulses of the Trump Administration, were not made, and the potential consequences for New Jersey are unacceptable.” Booker’s statement explaining his “no” vote went further. "I respect the work done on this bill with the goal of accelerating clean energy and building out our grid, but I do not believe it meets the mandate voters have charged us with to put a check on the corruption, chaos and cruelty of Trump's administration,” he said. “I am particularly concerned that the legislation would eliminate the courts’ authority to block the administration’s illegal projects, including ICE detention centers.” As the Senate considered the bill, Kim had proposed several amendments, including one that would allow local communities to challenge immigration facilities that skipped environmental review. One of those is in Roxbury, where federal officials recently signed a contract to advance the conversion of a warehouse to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility despite having agreed to halt work at the site until they conduct required environmental reviews in response to a lawsuit filed by the state and the township. artigo.texto: Squadron Energy has submitted plans for a proposed 1,000MW battery energy storage system at Cullen Bullen, 25km north of Lithgow to the NSW Department of Planning and Environment. The proposed Cullen Bullen Battery would be Australia’s biggest battery, boasting eight hours of long-duration energy storage. Related article: AER grants electricity retailer authorisation for Squadron The Waratah Super Battery in New South Wales is currently Australia’s largest operating battery storage system by output at 850MW/1,680MWh, while Western Australia’s Collie Battery Energy Storage System holds more total storage energy at 2,400MWh. The Cullen Bullen Battery is proposed to connect directly to Transgrid’s existing 500kV transmission network. It would help support a more reliable electricity system by storing clean energy when it is abundant and supplying it when needed. The project is in the early stages of development, with Squadron seeking feedback from the local community to help inform its design and development. Squadron Energy project developer Sean Cross said engaging with the community early and delivering lasting local benefits were priorities for Squadron. “We want to hear from local residents and businesses as we develop this proposal, understand what matters to them and identify opportunities for the project to benefit the wider community,” Cross said. “Squadron is committed to delivering real benefits for local families and businesses through investment in infrastructure, funding for community programs and the creation of local jobs and training opportunities. Related article: Big Canberra Battery fully commissioned and operational “We’re already investing in the local community through our sponsorship program, with funding available to support organisations delivering education and training, community development, health and wellbeing, and environmental initiatives.”

artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Skanska conquista contrato adicional para novo data center na Geórgia Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Pontos-chaveA Skanska registrou o prêmio como novo trabalho contratado, e não como receita já… Ver mais - A Skanska registrou o prêmio como novo trabalho contratado, e não como receita já auferida. - O mais recente prêmio espelha um projeto anterior na Geórgia em capacidade e área de implantação. - Os anúncios da Skanska na Geórgia representam prêmios separados, e não um valor cumulativo de projeto. Skanska anunciou, em 26 de novembro de 2026, que havia recebido de um cliente atual um contrato adicional de US$ 275 milhões para construir um novo data center de 48 MW na Geórgia, nos Estados Unidos. O contrato vale cerca de 2,8 bilhões de coroas suecas (SEK) e será incluído na carteira de pedidos da Skanska nos Estados Unidos no quarto trimestre de 2026. Essa classificação é importante: o anúncio acrescenta trabalho contratado à carteira de pedidos, em vez de contabilizar o valor total como receita já auferida. Escopo da construção e cronograma de entrega A instalação principal terá 244.730 pés quadrados, aproximadamente 22.700 metros quadrados. O escopo da Skanska inclui a construção da estrutura e o acabamento interno de espaços técnicos, áreas de apoio e escritórios. O projeto também inclui um edifício auxiliar de tratamento de água com 860 pés quadrados, aproximadamente 80 metros quadrados. Embora pequeno em comparação com a instalação principal, ele incorpora ao contrato a infraestrutura de apoio necessária para os serviços. A construção começou em novembro de 2026, e a Skanska espera concluí-la em outubro de 2028, o que significa que as obras já estavam em andamento quando o contrato adicional foi anunciado. Contrato de setembro oferece uma comparação próxima O anúncio da Skanska de 22 de setembro de 2026 descreveu um contrato de US$ 84 milhões com um cliente atual, contabilizado na carteira de pedidos da empresa nos Estados Unidos no terceiro trimestre. O anúncio indicava a mesma capacidade de 48 MW e a mesma área de 244.730 pés quadrados do projeto mais recente, além de especificar cinco salas de data center para colocation e espaços administrativos. A previsão era que o projeto de setembro começasse em novembro de 2026 e fosse concluído no terceiro trimestre de 2028; o comunicado mais recente indica outubro de 2028 como mês previsto para a conclusão. O escopo de entrega do projeto de setembro incluía obras civis e estruturais, redes de serviços, instalações elétricas e mecânicas, segurança, comodidades internas e serviços de acabamento, além do comissionamento dos principais equipamentos até a conclusão. Contratos anteriores estabelecem uma sequência de obras na Geórgia Um comunicado de 9 de abril de 2026 divulgou um contrato de US$ 75 milhões, contabilizado no primeiro trimestre, para uma instalação de 22.700 metros quadrados, ou 244.090 pés quadrados. O escopo incluía obras associadas no terreno, redes subterrâneas de serviços, espaços administrativos e cinco salas de data center. A construção começou em março de 2026, e a conclusão estava prevista para o primeiro trimestre de 2028. Em seguida, um anúncio de 23 de junho de 2026 informou um contrato suplementar de US$ 255 milhões, contabilizado no segundo trimestre. O projeto abrangia aproximadamente 245.000 pés quadrados, obras associadas no terreno e redes subterrâneas de serviços, espaços administrativos e cinco salas de data center, com o mesmo cronograma de construção informado, de março de 2026 ao primeiro trimestre de 2028. Esses comunicados estabelecem uma sequência de contratos para data centers na Geórgia ao longo de 2026, mas não informam um valor agregado para um único projeto. A Skanska identifica os clientes apenas como clientes atuais e não afirma explicitamente que todos os anúncios se referem à mesma instalação. Portanto, os valores devem ser considerados contratos distintos, e não um custo acumulado documentado para um único projeto. A importância do contrato mais recente se divide entre dois cronogramas: sua contabilização no quarto trimestre de 2026 para as operações da Skanska nos Estados Unidos e um programa de construção que se estende até outubro de 2028. O primeiro indica o novo trabalho contratado; o segundo acompanhará a transformação desse trabalho em uma instalação concluída de 48 MW, com sua infraestrutura de tratamento de água.

artigo.texto: Batteries delivered 2.75 times as much energy to the all-island grid of Ireland during the first year of the new scheduling and dispatch programme Battery supply during evening peak demand averaged 2.7%, up from 1.1% a year earlier Batteries reached a peak grid supply of 520 MW on January 31, 2026, and increasingly charged during daytime hours between April and September 2026, according to EirGrid Battery energy storage is starting to play a greater role in Ireland’s electricity supply, supported by regulatory framework. Following a scheduling and dispatch update to rules in November 2025, Irish grid operator EirGrid says there was a 2.75-fold increase in energy delivered by batteries to the all-island grid. Between November 13, 2025, and November 3, 2026, batteries supplied an average of 2.7% of electricity demand during the evening peak period from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m., compared with 1.1% during the corresponding period a year earlier. This was an increase of 175% more energy delivered to the grid. Their contribution during this window reached a maximum of 9%. Battery power supplied to the grid peaked at 520 MW on January 31, 2026, EirGrid reported. For context, EirGrid shared that the average peak demand in Galway is around 100 MW, about 83 MW in Drogheda, 75 MW in Limerick, and 69 MW in Athlone. Battery charging patterns also shifted during the reporting period. Between April and September 2026, batteries charged more during the day than overnight, coinciding with periods of higher solar generation. EirGrid attributes this to the successful implementation of changes under the Scheduling and Dispatch Programme (SDP-02) in November 2025, which enable batteries to participate more effectively in the electricity market. The arrangements allow battery operators to respond more actively to electricity system requirements, increasing the energy they deliver to the grid. EirGrid said the ability to store electricity and discharge it when needed helps shift energy to periods when it is most useful to the power system. The increase in battery utilization comes amid wider policy efforts to expand energy storage in Ireland. In June 2026, Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O’Brien shared that the country had installed over 800 MW of grid-scale battery storage since 2018. He stressed that grid-scale batteries place downward pressure on costs as these provide flexibility, reducing the dispatch down of renewables, while moving surplus electricity to times of higher demand. The minister called the first year of EirGrid’s SDU for battery storage a successful one. He added, “Battery storage is now regularly contributing more than 400 MW of generation during evening peak demand periods, which is equivalent in scale to a large gas-fired power station, reducing costs for consumers and emissions for Ireland.” Since October 1, 2026, Ireland’s CRU has eliminated grid connection charges on standalone and co-located battery energy storage systems (BESS). They will be required to pay Generation Transmission Use of System (G-TUoS) charges, consistent with those paid by wind and solar farms. This eliminates the payment of €30/MWh as Demand Transmission Use of System (D-TUoS) charges when importing electricity to charge. Bobby Smith, the Director of Energy Storage Ireland (ESI) believes this reform will reduce balancing costs, curtailment and redispatch on the grid, while supporting increased integration of renewable energy. A study by AFRY commissioned by ESI also examined the potential economic benefits of additional storage capacity in Ireland. In an early-2030s scenario in which renewable energy targets are met, the modelling found that 2 GW of additional six- to eight-hour storage could deliver net annual economic benefits of €102 million. The study also modelled a high-gas-price scenario, in which the net benefit from the same additional storage capacity reached €151 million annually.

artigo.texto: The surge in battery storage projects across the U.S. in the past year included projects in Oklahoma. A new report by the Solar Energy Industries Association and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence showed there was a 20% installation growth nationwide in the first nine months of this year. Most of that capacity is from utility-scale installations, though it includes residential and commercial installations, too, according to Canary Media. One of those projects is a $394 million, 301-MW Frontier Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) near Ponca City. It was approved by the Oklahoma Corporation Commission on a 2-1 vote in August. The BESS is supposed to be in service sometime in late 2027. Commissioners Kim David and Brian Bingman supported the project as proposed but it was opposed by Commissioner Todd Hiett. OG&E stated at the time of the approval that the project was “an important milestone in meeting Oklahoma’s growing energy needs” and it would do so by strengthening grid reliability, improving system efficiency and dispatching power during peak demand. The utility also has a 20-year capacity purchase agreement with the Black Kettle battery storage project near Enid. Rather than owning and operating the facility, OG&E has the capacity purchase agreement, and it was approved in November 2025 by Corporation Commissioners on a 2-1 vote. Canary Media reported that in the last decade, batteries have gotten exponentially cheaper and have rapidly become one of the most important grid technologies. The systems are relatively speedy to install, and their ability to store inexpensive surplus power for later has captivated utilities, data center developers, and households alike. Even without the final three months of data for 2026, 11 states have already seen battery installations reach record levels this year: Alabama, Colorado, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, Massachusetts, Michigan, Mississippi, Montana, Utah, and Virginia. The bad news is that the report predicts residential installations will drop 8% this year compared to 2025. That sector took a hit after the federal government ripped away incentives for home energy storage at the end of last year, though SEIA and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence say business is recovering faster than expected. Despite the residential dip, the report authors expect overall battery capacity additions in 2026 to surpass last year’s figures by 26%. It’s a testament to the tech’s broad appeal — and a bright spot for the energy transition, which will rely on abundant storage to spread wind and solar power through all hours of the day.

artigo.texto: Parceiro institucional: Mercado de carbono: avanços na regulamentação global e brasileira podem redefinir os riscos e as decisões de investimento da indústria (Freepik) CEO da David Canassa - Strategy & Advisory e colunista Publicado em 25 de novembro de 2026 às 13h00. *Por David Canassa Em dezembro de 2015, Paris não entregou apenas um acordo diplomático. Entregou uma arquitetura: cada país definiria sua própria trajetória de redução, submeteria a revisão periódica e, para que o esforço custasse menos, haveria um mercado global de carbono. Quase onze anos depois, a COP31 em Antália encerra com um avanço que passou quase despercebido pelo mundo corporativo — e que muda o cálculo de risco de quem tem ativo industrial no Brasil. O Acordo de Paris fixou o objetivo — manter o aquecimento bem abaixo de 2°C, buscando 1,5°C — e deixou o instrumento para as Partes construírem. O Artigo 6 é esse instrumento. Ele tem dois trilhos: o 6.2, que permite transferência bilateral de resultados de mitigação entre governos, e o 6.4, que criou um mecanismo multilateral de crédito sob supervisão da UNFCCC, substituindo o MDL de Quioto. Até 2024, o Artigo 6 era um texto. A partir de 2025, virou infraestrutura. A COP29, em Baku, declarou o mecanismo plenamente operacional. A COP30, em Belém, fechou o pacote de autorizações, registro e transparência. E 2026 foi o ano em que a máquina começou a girar: três metodologias aprovadas no mecanismo do 6.4, 18 entidades acreditadas para verificação, 129 autoridades nacionais designadas e mais de dois mil projetos do antigo MDL na fila de transição. O ponto que a maioria das análises perdeu em Antália é institucional, não climático. A UNFCCC deixou de ser secretariado de negociação e passou a ser operadora de infraestrutura de mercado. Ela opera o registro do mecanismo do 6.4, o sistema centralizado de contabilidade e reporte, e desde janeiro de 2026 desenvolve, sob contrato plurianual, a camada digital que rastreia e verifica os resultados transferidos entre países. É uma mudança de natureza: a Convenção que organizava conferências agora administra ativos. Isso importa ao Brasil por uma razão direta. Um mercado global de carbono só funciona se houver um registro comum que impeça a mesma tonelada de ser contada duas vezes. É a UNFCCC que garante essa unicidade. Sem ela, o Artigo 6 seria uma coleção de acordos bilaterais sem lastro contábil. O país se comprometeu em Paris com 37% de redução até 2025 e 43% até 2030, e em 2024 elevou a meta para 59% a 67% até 2035, com neutralidade climática em 2050. Mas o movimento decisivo foi doméstico: a Lei nº 15.042, de dezembro de 2024, criou o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões. A lei não é uma declaração de intenções. Ela resolveu a decisão de arquitetura mais consequente — o tipo de teto. O art. 2º, XVI define o limite máximo como limite quantitativo em toneladas de CO2 equivalente, aplicável ao sistema como um todo. É cap absoluto, nacional e centralizado. Não é meta de intensidade, como a China operou até agora, nem baseline agregado, como o Japão. Essa escolha, isolada, já coloca o Brasil na família de União Europeia, Califórnia e Coreia. E o teto não é discricionário. A lei o amarra em cadeia: o art. 2º, XVI remete às metas da Política Nacional sobre Mudança do Clima; o art. 3º vincula o sistema aos compromissos sob a Convenção; e o art. 21, § 1º, VI exige observar a proporcionalidade entre as emissões dos operadores regulados e as emissões totais do País. O denominador vem do Inventário Nacional. O teto tem, portanto, base verificável — o inventário fornece o total, a NDC fornece a trajetória. O arcabouço regulatório brasileiro não é um decreto. É uma cadeia de derivação em quatro elos e um resultado, e cada elo depende do anterior. O primeiro elo é o compromisso internacional: a NDC de novembro de 2024, com redução de 59% a 67% até 2035, equivalente a um teto de 850 milhões a 1,05 bilhão de toneladas naquele ano. O segundo é a tradução doméstica, pela Política Nacional sobre Mudança do Clima. O terceiro é a amarração legal do sistema, nos arts. 2º, 3º e 5º da Lei nº 15.042. O quarto é o denominador quantitativo, o Inventário Nacional mantido pelo MCTI. O resultado é o Plano Nacional de Alocação, com o teto e a distribuição por operador. A cadeia de amarração legal, do compromisso internacional à obrigação da instalação A leitura dessa cadeia revela onde está o risco real, e não é onde o debate está. O Inventário Nacional mais recente cobre até 2022. O Plano de Alocação entra em vigor em 2030. A defasagem é de oito anos, e mesmo com o segundo relatório bienal, previsto para este semestre, cairá para quatro a seis. O sistema terá dado primário anual e verificado das instalações no numerador e um denominador de meia década atrás. É uma inconsistência que precisa ser compreendida e tratada na regulamentação, com regra explícita sobre qual edição do inventário serve de base e como recálculos futuros serão tratados. O debate público sobre o SBCE gira em torno de preço e de custo. Os dois são imateriais no primeiro período. Ao preço de referência do crédito voluntário brasileiro, o custo de conformidade de uma planta eletrointensiva fica abaixo de 0,4% da receita. Não muda decisão de investimento. O que muda é outra coisa: a definição dos benchmarks setoriais e a base de atividade — o que se multiplica pelo benchmark. A alocação gratuita é o produto de dois fatores. O primeiro é o coeficiente de eficiência, o benchmark. Nos sistemas internacionais, a premissa consolidada é calculá-lo sobre o desempenho dos mais eficientes do setor — na União Europeia, a média dos 10% melhores; na Coreia, que partiu do top 37% e apertou para o top 20%. No Brasil, essa definição ainda não existe: a lei menciona “ganhos históricos de eficiência” e custos marginais de abatimento como critérios, mas não nomeia o instrumento nem fixa a metodologia. O benchmark brasileiro será construído no Plano Nacional de Alocação. O segundo fator é a quantidad

The collaboration combines that software with MinTech's inspection hardware, according to Interesting Engineering. MinTech uses electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and in-house diagnostic algorithms. The technology examines batteries' electrical characteristics to reveal potential issues. Operators can receive advanced warning of potential faults from Electra's software-as-a-service platform, which can recognize patterns linked to battery health. If you're facing grid instability and time-of-use electricity prices, whole-home batteries offer backup protection, while battery leases can help homeowners avoid $20,000 or more in upfront costs. EasyHome is a marketplace offering battery shoppers unique prices and exclusive deals from trusted partners. Meaning a developing fault can affect more than a single battery, potentially disrupting the availability of the whole facility. MinTech's diagnostic work spans production, routine operation, reuse, and recycling. Its systems include electric vehicle battery testing and storage that gives used batteries a second life. artigo.texto: UK and EU agree to link Emissions Trading Systems Announced at the 2026 UK-EU Summit, the agreement aims to address differences in carbon markets, regulations and allowance prices. The UK Emission Trading Scheme and EU Emission Trading System (ETS) will become more closely aligned from January 2028. From this point, ETS allowances issued in either the UK or EU can be used for compliance across either scheme. Both systems operate on a cap-and-trade basis, requiring companies covered by the schemes to hold allowances for each tonne of greenhouse gas emissions produced. The UK Government estimates that linking the systems could add up to £3.8bln to the UK economy annually by 2040. The anticipated benefits include a larger carbon market, price stability, reduced trade barriers, lower administrative costs and greater incentives for industrial investment. Linking the systems could benefit energy-intensive industries, including cement, steel and aluminium manufacturing, which face significant costs associated with their carbon emissions. A carbon price therefore creates an additional operating cost for manufacturers, making investments in lower-carbon technologies more financially viable. The ETS linking agreement could give these manufacturers access to a larger carbon market, potentially increasing trading liquidity and improving carbon pricing security. Another aim is to reduce carbon-related trade barriers by enabling exemptions from the UK and EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms (CBAMs) for eligible goods traded between the two markets.

artigo.texto: Eight EU States Urge Early Entry of Road Carbon Market Ministers from eight member states back immediate application of CELE 2, a carbon market covering buildings and road transport fuels. Updated on Nov. 23, 2026 in Transportation Live Poll Should the EU carbon market expand to cover home heating and road transport fuel? Ministers from Denmark, Finland, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden wrote to EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra supporting the European Emission Trading System 2 (CELE 2). Portugal and the other signatories called for its immediate entry into force, while Italy and Poland have urged delaying or easing it. Why it matters The letter frames CELE 2 as an economically efficient way to accelerate decarbonisation of road transport and buildings, and cites recent energy disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz as evidence that Europe must cut reliance on imported fossil fuels. The dispute over timing reflects a split between member states on how quickly to price carbon in these sectors. Eight member states signed the letter urging CELE 2 into force, while the system was created in 2023 with a scheduled start in 2028. The letter does not specify revenue, emissions volumes or price levels, and the outcome of the impact assessment agreed in October 2026 remains unknown. The players Wopke Hoekstra Wopke Hoekstra is the European Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth, responsible for the EU's climate policy and emissions trading framework. Italy Italy is a major EU economy in the Mediterranean whose government has joined calls to delay or ease CELE 2 before its scheduled start. Poland Poland is a Central European EU member state whose fossil-fuel-dependent economy has led it to urge a delay or easing of CELE 2. The details The ministers of Denmark, Finland, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden sent the letter, which Denmark initiated, to Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra. CELE 2 complements the original EU carbon market, which covers power, heat, heavy industry, aviation and shipping, by covering fuel use in buildings and road transport. Timeline - 2023: CELE 2 is created. - October 2026: EU leaders at the European Council summit commit to assess CELE 2's impact before entry into force. - 2028: CELE 2 is initially scheduled to enter into force. Roadmap CELE 2 extends the EU Emissions Trading System, which priced carbon only in power, heavy industry, aviation and shipping, into buildings and road transport. The split between eight member states pushing for early entry and Italy and Poland seeking delay shows how the expansion is being contested as Europe weighs energy security against its decarbonisation timetable. If CELE 2 takes effect earlier, the cost of fuel used for road transport and heating in buildings could rise sooner as carbon pricing reaches those sectors. The timing debate will determine when households and fleet operators begin to feel that cost. The takeaway The debate over CELE 2 is less about whether to price carbon in transport and buildings than about how fast Europe moves, a choice that will shape fuel costs for drivers and homeowners across the bloc. Following the Commission's impact assessment will show which timetable is adopted. What happens next The Commission is expected to carry out the impact assessment agreed at the October 2026 European Council summit before CELE 2's 2028 entry into force. With roughly 10% charge left most days, they asked whether one or two more batteries would be worthwhile. The additions would potentially bring storage to around 36 kWh. "Really happy with the system overall though obviously at the moment we're relying heavily on overnight charging," the original poster wrote. The family wanted to install an air conditioning system that heats the home in winter. artigo.texto: Moment Energy has introduced Nova, a commercial and industrial battery energy storage system rated at 200 kW and 500 kWh that runs on repurposed electric-vehicle batteries, TaiyangNews reported. Each Nova block carries UL 1973 and UL 9540 certifications, and the company has opened orders with first deliveries planned for Q1 2027. The launch lands at a moment when used EV packs are starting to look like an asset instead of a disposal problem. Investors have already floated big numbers for the category, including the 1 TWh used-battery bet from Redwood Energy, and Moment Energy now puts a certified, factory-built product into the same conversation. Below, we break down what the Nova specification confirms, what it leaves open, and how a second-life system stacks up against new-cell storage. Price and named-executive commentary were not available in the reviewed reports, so we flag those gaps instead of guessing. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Moment Energy Nova at a Glance The Moment Energy Nova is a modular storage block aimed at businesses that want to shave peak demand, firm up on-site solar, or ride out grid trouble. It is not a home battery and it is not a utility-scale container. Reports place it squarely in the commercial and industrial tier, which sits between a residential wall unit and a multi-hundred-megawatt-hour grid project. Every headline number comes from the announcement coverage. The table below lists what reports confirm for a single Nova block, plus one figure we calculated ourselves from those inputs. Note that the 2.5-hour figure is a simple division, not a tested runtime. Real duration depends on depth of discharge, temperature, inverter losses, and how the operator sets the state-of-charge window. Moment Energy has not published a round-trip efficiency figure in the coverage we reviewed. How Nova Turns Retired EV Batteries Into Storage An EV battery does not die when a car retires it. Packs usually leave vehicles once they can no longer deliver the range or acceleration drivers expect, but they still hold a large share of their original capacity. A stationary system asks far less of a cell. It does not need to be light, it does not need to deliver sudden bursts for acceleration, and it can sit in a climate-managed enclosure. That mismatch is the whole business case for second-life storage. A pack that is too tired for a car can still cycle once a day on a factory floor for years. Electrek framed Nova in exactly those terms, describing a 500 kWh system that runs on retired EV batteries. The hard part sits between the junkyard and the enclosure. Retired packs arrive with different chemistries, different ages, and different histories. Someone has to test them, sort them, and group compatible units so the finished system behaves predictably. The fact sheet confirms production at Megafactory 1 but does not describe the sorting and grading steps in detail, so we will not invent a process description here. What the reports do establish is the outcome. A buyer gets a finished, certified storage block, not a pile of salvaged modules to engineer into a system. For a facilities manager, that distinction matters more than the cell source. Few plant operators want to own the risk of integrating used packs, and a certified product moves that risk back to the manufacturer. What 200 kW and 500 kWh Mean in Practice Power and energy are different things, and the Nova numbers show why. The 200 kW rating describes how fast the block can move electricity in or out at any instant. The 500 kWh rating describes how much it can hold. Divide one by the other and you get the 2.5 hours mentioned above, a profile that suits daily peak shaving better than multi-day backup. To put 500 kWh in context, it equals the usable energy of several modern passenger-EV battery packs. That is a loose comparison, since pack sizes vary widely by model, but it explains why a stack of retired packs can be repackaged into a single industrial unit. A mid-size warehouse, a cold-storage facility, or a small manufacturing line could plausibly use one block to trim its utility demand charges. Commercial customers often pay for their single highest 15-minute spike of the month, not just total consumption. A battery that discharges during that spike can cut the bill without touching production. Reports describe the target application only as commercial and industrial energy storage, so specific customer types and tariff savings remain our reading of the product class, not a Moment Energy claim. Power-hungry sites with unreliable feeds have similar needs. Our earlier look at technologies that keep data centers running without grid overloads shows how on-site storage has moved from optional to expected for operators with tight uptime targets. Nova targets a smaller scale than a hyperscale campus, yet the logic is the same: buffer the grid and keep the load steady. UL 1973 and UL 9540: Why the Certifications Matter For stationary storage, certification is not decoration. Insurers, fire marshals, and utilities routinely ask for it before they approve an installation. Moment Energy says Nova holds both UL 1973 and UL 9540, and that pairing is the reason the launch drew attention. What the two standards cover UL 1973 addresses the battery system itself, meaning the packs, their management electronics, and their protective features. UL 9540 looks at the energy storage system as a whole, including how the battery, power conversion, and controls work together. A product that clears both has been judged at the component level and at the system level. Why used cells make this harder Certifying a system built from new, uniform cells is routine. artigo.texto: A new peer-reviewed study from MIT researchers estimates that the electricity powering US data centers contributed to about 650 premature deaths in a single year, and that much of the harm landed far from the buildings themselves. The paper, published November 19, 2026 in Environmental Research Letters, puts hard numbers on a question the cloud industry has mostly answered with carbon pledges: what happens to the air that people breathe when data centers pull more power from the grid? According to coverage from Technology Networks and TechRadar, the answer is that data centers worsen air quality across a wide area, including in states that host very few of them. The finding lands at an awkward moment. Cloud and AI demand is pushing grid planners to add capacity, and our earlier look at Goldman’s 52 GW projection for US data centers in 2028 showed how much of that new load analysts expect gas generation to cover. The MIT work gives that story a public-health dimension. It measures not just how much power data centers use, but where the resulting pollution drifts and who inhales it. This analysis walks through what the study reports, what it leaves unanswered, and what it means for cloud buyers, operators and regulators. We stick to the figures confirmed for the paper. Where the public record is silent, such as on specific companies, power plants or emissions tonnage, we say so plainly rather than fill the gap. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What the MIT Study Found on Data Centers and Air Quality The paper is titled “Spatially distributed air quality and health impacts of data center electricity demand in the United States.” Yuang Chen and colleagues are listed as the authors, and the research comes from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. It appeared in Environmental Research Letters on November 19, 2026. The geographic scope is the contiguous United States, and the analysis uses data from 2023. The headline result is an estimate of about 650 premature deaths tied to data center electricity demand. The authors split that total by pollutant. Fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, accounts for an estimated 513 of those deaths. Ground-level ozone accounts for another 137. Both pollutants have well-documented links to respiratory and cardiovascular harm, which is why health researchers treat them as the standard yardsticks for air-quality damage. The second finding matters as much as the first. The study reports that pollution tied to data center demand does not stay local. Emissions from the power plants that supply the grid travel through the atmosphere and cross state lines, which means the communities that absorb the damage can sit well downwind of the data centers causing the demand. MIT co-author Noelle Selin summed up the pattern in a single line reported in coverage of the study: “The impact of data centres on air quality extends over a vast area.” The Numbers: 650 Deaths Split Between PM2.5 and Ozone The two pollutant totals add up cleanly: 513 plus 137 equals 650. Using that arithmetic, PM2.5 accounts for roughly 79 percent of the estimated deaths and ozone for roughly 21 percent. Those percentages are our own calculation from the reported figures, not numbers the authors published, so treat them as a convenience for reading the split rather than a separate finding. PM2.5 dominates because the particles are tiny enough to travel deep into the lungs and, from there, into the bloodstream. They form both directly, as soot from combustion, and indirectly, when gases from smokestacks react in the air. Ozone works differently. It forms when sunlight cooks precursor gases such as nitrogen oxides, and it tends to build over hours and distance. That difference in chemistry is one reason a pollution plume can cause harm far from its origin. A figure of 650 deaths in one year deserves context, because “premature deaths” is a statistical estimate and not a count of named individuals. Health-impact studies of this type combine modeled pollution exposure with established relationships between exposure and mortality. The result is a population-level estimate with uncertainty bands. The public summaries we reviewed report the central numbers, and we will not invent confidence intervals that the fact sheet does not confirm. How Electricity Demand Turns Into Downwind Pollution From the meter to the smokestack A data center does not burn fuel for its servers in the typical case. It draws electricity from the grid, and the grid has to generate that electricity somewhere. The study’s core mechanism follows that chain. When a data center’s demand rises, power plants supplying the grid respond, and any plants that burn fossil fuels release the associated pollutants. The data center is the cause of the demand, but the stack that emits sits elsewhere, often in a different state. This indirect link is why corporate sustainability claims and health outcomes can diverge. A company can buy renewable energy certificates that match its annual consumption and still draw hour-by-hour power from a grid that leans on fossil plants. The study does not accuse any named operator of that. It simply shows that the aggregate effect of data center load on the grid carries a measurable human cost. Why the pollution crosses state lines Once emitted, pollutants ride the wind. The paper reports that atmospheric transport carries the resulting pollution across state lines and affects downwind communities. Air does not respect jurisdictional borders, and neither do the chemical reactions that turn precursor gases into fine particles and ozone. A plume released in one state can add to the pollution burden of residents far from the source. The fact sheet for this story does not give a travel distance in miles, and we will not guess one. artigo.texto: World’s first 300 MW artificial-cavern energy storage plant connects to China’s grid China has connected a 300-megawatt compressed air energy storage plant to the power grid, using four underground chambers excavated in hard rock rather than natural salt caverns. The Yuanchu No. 1 facility in Gansu province is designed to store 1.8 gigawatt-hours of electricity, offering another option for large-scale storage in regions without suitable salt formations. The plant achieved its first grid connection on Nov. 16, according to China Energy Engineering Corporation, the project developer. The company describes it as the world's first grid-connected compressed air energy storage (CAES) facility to use purpose-built underground rock caverns, a claim CGTN reported. China Energy Digital Technology Group, a subsidiary of China Energy Engineering Corporation, developed Yuanchu No. 1. The project cost about $374 million (2.5 billion yuan) and is expected to generate 600 gigawatt-hours annually. Its 300-MW generating unit can discharge stored energy for six hours per cycle. Rock caverns store pressurized air underground The facility's storage system consists of four interconnected chambers excavated about 361 feet (110 meters) below ground. Together, they provide roughly 7.1 million cubic feet (200,000 cubic meters) of storage volume and are designed for pressures of up to 18 megapascals. CAES uses electricity to run compressors that force air into a storage space. When electricity is needed, the compressed air is released and expanded through turbines to generate power. The process allows energy produced at one time to be stored and used later, helping balance fluctuations in supply and demand. Yuanchu No. 1 uses an adiabatic, non-combustion design. Instead of burning natural gas to heat the air before it reaches the turbines, the plant captures heat generated during compression and stores it. During discharge, that heat is returned to the compressed air before it expands through the turbines. The thermal system combines pressurized hot water with molten salt to store heat at different temperatures, according to the project report. Water stores lower- and medium-temperature heat, while molten salt stores higher-temperature heat. Both release heat in stages during power generation. An alternative to salt-cavern storage Many underground CAES systems rely on natural salt caverns, which can provide suitable storage but are available only in certain geological settings. Excavating chambers in hard rock could make the technology viable in more locations, although geology and the cost of excavation and sealing remain important constraints. That flexibility could matter in Yumen, which sits in the Hexi Corridor, a major wind and solar development area in northwest China. The plant is intended to absorb surplus renewable electricity when supply is high and return power to the grid when demand increases. China Energy Engineering Corporation says the station has an electricity-to-electricity conversion efficiency of 72%. However, long-term operating data will be needed to establish how efficiently the plant performs in routine service. The project is part of China's wider expansion of compressed air storage. An October 2026 industry report cited by PV Magazine said 13 CAES projects, totaling 4.95 GW and 23.95 GWh, were under construction. Wider deployment will depend on whether projects can demonstrate reliable cavern performance, competitive construction costs, and sustained efficiency.

artigo.texto: From July this year, if a battery loses more than 0.5% of its mass during a vacuum bake test at {{120ºC}} for six hours, you can't legally call it an all-solid-state unit - at least not in China. That single metric matters more than any press release we've read this decade. For the last five years, automakers have put the "solid-state" label on anything with slightly less liquid sloshing around inside. China closed that marketing loophole with the rollout of GB/T 43568-2026. It establishes a formal threshold that strips away the PR fluff and forces OEMs to show actual factory readiness instead of optimistic lab charts. To secure an official all-solid-state designation, the liquid electrolyte must sit below 5% of the total cell weight. In August 2026, the International Electrotechnical Commission officially approved a China-led proposal to establish global testing and application guidelines for automotive solid-state batteries. The implications stretch into how legacy brands engineer their upcoming platforms. China is effectively shaping global markets without exporting a single battery. If you're a Chinese manufacturer already dominating the electric vehicle supply chain, aligning your export models with a domestic standard reduces compliance friction to zero. Foreign competitors face a reverse burden. European and American automakers now have a choice - they can either adapt to a framework designed without their input, or they can spend years trying to draft a new standard from scratch while the market moves on. There is no dedicated European solid-state standard published yet. Japan has advanced R&D, but lacks an equivalent national mandate to enforce it. We're already seeing the results of this regulatory clarity on the ground. Doctex spun up a manufacturing facility in Tianjin producing certified solid-state cells with an energy density of 350 Wh/kg. Far from being some fragile lab prototypes - they are going straight into production vehicles, offering a 15% to 20% bump in real-world driving range. Not everyone is moving at the same pace. Geely is working to complete full vehicle validation and pack layout integration by the third quarter of 2026. BYD has mapped its solid-state development timelines closer to 2027. Saike Power is still pouring concrete for its 0.1 GWh sulfide pilot line down in Yibin, pushing actual machine testing to the final months of 2026. It highlights the massive capital divide between battery suppliers who are fully industrialized and those still chasing the chemistry. State-backed Dongfeng Motor is prepping a 0.2 GWh plant to integrate its own oxide-polymer hybrid cells into a fleet of 100 demonstration vehicles across Hubei province. They're targeting driving ranges pushing toward the 620 miles mark, which sounds absurd until you look at the validation data. During winter testing up in Mohe - one of the coldest places in China - these cells kept 72% of their energy capacity. They also survived high-temperature {{170ºC}} oven bake evaluations without losing structural integrity. That kind of thermal stability addresses the strict thermal runaway and single-cell failure requirements laid out in the mandatory GB 38031-2025 EV safety rules that arrived this summer. The hardware needed to build these cells is also changing. Gotion High-Tech validated a pilot line using 100% locally manufactured machinery, integrating domestic slot-die coaters and high-pressure rollers into the factory floor. This cuts their reliance on international procurement entirely. When you eliminate overseas logistics bottlenecks and geopolitical tariff friction, the cost of scaling drops dramatically. Upgrading production lines with domestic equipment is projected to save the industry billions. It shifts initial factory budgets down to between RMB 400,000,000 and RMB 500,000,000 (roughly $59,000,000 to $74,000,000) per GWh. That financial insulation gives domestic brands a huge buffer against price wars. Western automakers simply don't have that localized machinery leverage yet. But having machinery readily available is only one part of this monumental shift. China is building a layered regulatory framework that scrutinizes every single component inside the pack. The new GB/Z 214-2026 guidance document issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology targets the solid electrolytes themselves. It establishes a uniform vocabulary and strict material parameters for suppliers, ensuring everyone evaluates the same physical characteristics in the exact same way. If an electrolyte material doesn't meet the baseline, it doesn't get CCC certification, and it won't be sold or imported into China. This prevents cell producers from swapping in cheaper, unverified electrolyte compounds to hit cost targets. It treats individual chemical components as distinct product categories with their own (enforceable) technical expectations. But even with this much manufacturing progress, we need to stay realistic about the timelines. CATL has openly acknowledged that widespread commercialization of true all-solid-state batteries will likely be restricted until 2030 due to anomalies in solid-interface resistance. The physics of moving ions through a solid medium at scale without degradation is still a big problem. For now, conventional liquid setups will continue to reach high-volume delivery records. That is the reality of mass manufacturing - the transition simply won't happen overnight, but the technical and safety definitions are now set in stone. By drawing a hard line with the GB/T 43568-2026 classification and pushing it through the IEC, China has ended the era of vague battery marketing. The unified safety standards are next, and it won’t be long before China gets those rubber-stamped. Automakers who want to sell a premium solid-state electric vehicle will have to build one that passes all the tests. For European and American brands, the pressure might be too much. artigo.texto: Ohio OKs gas plant for data centers despite local voter backlash Ohio regulators just greenlit construction of a big gas plant to power a data center complex, despite local residents’ overwhelming rejection of the projects in this month’s elections. The permit approval itself is not unique: Around the U.S., energy-hungry data center developers are racing ahead with controversial plans to build natural gas–fired generation. But critics of the recent Ohio ruling say it highlights the state’s leniency toward fossil-fuel projects compared with its tight restrictions on solar and wind farms, which are often denied permits due to local opposition. “There’s a huge double standard for fossil fuels and renewables in the state of Ohio,” said state Rep. Tristan Rader, a Democrat who serves as ranking minority member on the Ohio House Energy Committee and took part in the case as a nonvoting member of the Ohio Power Siting Board. The gas plant in question is an 800-megawatt facility to be built at a data center complex under development in the central Ohio village of Ashville. As of now, the plant won’t be connected to the grid at large and will serve just the computing warehouses. The project site is close to homes, as well as a playground, park, and soccer field, Rader noted. “This plant is literally going to be throwing a shadow on these communities,” while spewing health-harming pollution, Rader said during the Power Siting Board’s Nov. 19 meeting. Yet Ohio has more stringent requirements for wind and solar, which emit zero air pollution. Ashville’s Village Council passed a resolution in April to back the data center and gas plant project, after its developer, EdgeConneX, agreed to pay up to $102 million to support municipal, school, and community work. But the deal didn’t sit well with some residents, who gathered enough signatures for a referendum on whether to overturn the resolution. On Election Day, Ashville was one of dozens of U.S. communities to reject data centers, with 81% of the village’s voters opposing the local government’s agreement with EdgeConneX. Even so, the Power Siting Board’s decision OK’ing the gas plant finds that the developer met a statutory requirement that the project is in the public interest. Regulators pointed to factors like the project’s economic benefits, backing from the Village Council and local school district, and the developer’s promises to limit noise and construction hours. That’s sparked frustration from clean energy advocates in the state. The board has denied multiple solar projects on the basis that local opposition outweighs economic benefits or has proposed permit conditions aimed at addressing community concerns, said Chris Tavenor, general counsel for the Ohio Environmental Council, which was not a party to the case. “In this case, the Board does the exact opposite, using those community benefits and conditions to justify ignoring local concerns,” he said in an email. In this decision and those pertaining to renewable energy, critics take issue with the Power Siting Board’s deference to local governments, even when evidence shows they are not necessarily reflecting the wishes of the broader public. In 2025, for example, the Power Siting Board’s staff recommended against the Grange Solar project in Logan County on the basis of pushback from local governments. But a majority of individuals who submitted comments wanted the solar farm. The developer ultimately withdrew its plan and opted to pursue projects elsewhere. And earlier this year, regulators nixed the Crossroads Solar farm in Morrow County because all nearby local governments opposed the project. Although that ruling noted the “presence of strong, united opposition” among the local population, dozens of comments were apparently fake, and an analysis by the developer found that the number of verifiable individuals against the project was not overwhelming in comparison with its supporters. The board’s staff also did an about-face from supporting Crossroads Solar to opposing it after one township changed its position from neutral to opposed. “Ultimately, the Ohio Power Siting Board has demonstrated its hypocrisy,” Tavenor said, “by approving a natural gas facility for a data center where it has denied renewable energy projects with less significant opposition.” Regulators, for their part, acknowledged the Ashville vote in their decision but asserted that they have authority to issue the permit regardless of the outcome of the election. The 108-page opinion also says that conditions agreed to by the village, the developer, and the board staff were enough to deal with public concerns. The board also gave short shrift to opponents’ argument that the gas plant proposal fails to meet a separate legal requirement that projects have minimal environmental impact. Its take stems from the fact that the developer opted for reciprocating internal combustion engines and simple-cycle natural gas turbines over less-polluting combined-cycle turbines or fuel cells, which are more expensive right now. Regulatory staff argued that “minimum” doesn’t demand the lowest environmental impact but depends on a plant’s purpose, available technology, and economics. The board decided that the project meets the requirement, basically punting to the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency’s expected issuance of air permits for the facility. Project opponents have 30 days to ask for reconsideration of the ruling. Unless the Power Siting Board changes its mind, an appeal to the Ohio Supreme Court could follow. Kathiann M. Kowalski is a contributing reporter at Canary Media who covers Ohio.

artigo.texto: O mercado bilionário de data centers vai, finalmente, ganhar velocidade de escala para sair do planeta. A Comissão Federal de Comunicações (FCC) dos Estados Unidos, agência federal dos Estados Unidos que regula o setor no país, autorizou a SpaceX, de Elon Musk, a construir um milhão de equipamentos para levar ao espaço. Segundo a FCC, de acordo com a licença concedida, a SpaceX deve iniciar o lançamento dos foguetes até novembro de 2033, e enviar até 10% do total, o que equivale a 100 mil data centers, em novembro de 2035. Até novembro de 2038, o plano é de enviar até 50% dos equipamentos para o espaço. “Os Estados Unidos estão agindo de forma decisiva para garantir que essa tecnologia inovadora crie oportunidades, impulsione investimentos e traga benefícios duradouros para o povo americano”, diz o presidente da FCC, Brendan Carr, em comunicado divulgado nesta quarta-feira, 25 de novembro. “Essa ação abre uma nova e ousada fronteira para a infraestrutura de computação necessária para impulsionar a liderança e o crescimento dos Estados Unidos”, complementa. A decisão, anunciada um dia antes do feriado de Ação de Graças nos Estados Unidos, representa uma vitória expressiva para a companhia e para Musk, que se aliou ao governo Trump e chegou a ocupar um cargo na Casa Branca. A SpaceX protocolou em janeiro deste ano um pedido junto à FCC para solicitar autorização para lançar os satélites. A rede de satélites com data centers de inteligência artificial (IA), chamada Starmind, tornou-se uma parte importante da apresentação do CEO Elon Musk aos investidores antes do IPO da empresa, em junho. “Ao aproveitar diretamente a energia solar quase constante com baixos custos de operação ou manutenção, esses satélites alcançarão uma eficiência energética e de custos transformadora, reduzindo significativamente o impacto ambiental associado aos centros de dados terrestres”, informa a companhia de Musk à FCC, no documento. A decisão surge em um momento em que a demanda por data centers disparou devido à necessidade de poder computacional dos provedores de hiperescala para impulsionar o desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial. A autorização inclui outros aspectos. A SpaceX propôs operar em seis órbitas, variando de 550 km a cerca de 1.000 km. A empresa solicitou uma isenção das normas da FCC para permitir que satélites acima de 600 km sejam descartados em “órbitas de descarte terrestre ou órbitas heliocêntricas”. Isso significaria que, em vez de queimá-los na atmosfera terrestre, a SpaceX quer a flexibilidade de mover satélites desativados para outras órbitas ao redor da Terra ou, potencialmente, para uma órbita ao redor do Sol. Esta permissão, no entanto, ainda não ocorreu. A decisão da FCC também autoriza a SpaceX a usar links de radiofrequência para telemetria, rastreamento e comando de backup e emergência em todo o sistema de satélites. A SpaceX também pode complementar os links ópticos intersatélites com comunicações de radiofrequência. Antes de iniciar a implantação do sistema Starlink, a SpaceX solicitou aprovação para 42 mil satélites. A rede, em expansão, conta atualmente com pouco mais de 11 mil satélites em órbita. O pedido da SpaceX aposta na redução dos custos da Starship, o foguete reutilizável de próxima geração da empresa, atualmente em desenvolvimento, para ajudar no lançamento de satélites. A concorrente Leo, empresa de satélites da Amazon, criticou o plano, sugerindo que era improvável que a SpaceX implantasse todos os satélites, e que isso poderia levar séculos. Em março, ainda durante a fase de análise, o presidente da FCC rejeitou essas críticas. A FCC afirmou que continua analisando propostas adicionais de data centers orbitais e pretende emitir decisões sobre cada uma delas. Desde que a SpaceX abriu capital na Nasdaq, as ações SPCX acumulam queda de 21,4%. A fabricante de foguetes de Elon Musk tem valor de mercado de US$ 1,7 trilhão.

artigo.texto: A Europa está resgatando suas velhas usinas desativadas para lhes dar uma segunda vida: virar data centers Com 700 MW assegurados e filas de espera que chegam a 10 anos, usinas desativadas na Europa voltam a valer verdadeiras fortunas no boom da IA A energética alemã Uniper planeja converter usinas desativadas no Reino Unido, Alemanha, Suécia e Holanda em data centers. O negócio inicial, que prevê a transformação de uma unidade e negociações avançadas para outras duas, aproveita o espaço e o acesso garantido à transmissão elétrica. Com capacidade estimada em 700 MW, essa infraestrutura pode abastecer cerca de sete data centers de hiperescala, marcando uma nova vida para instalações históricas em resposta à crescente demanda digital europeia. A empresa de energia alemã Uniper está prestes a fechar um negócio que pode dar um verdadeiro salto aos centros de dados na Europa: o plano é converter suas usinas desativadas na infraestrutura mais disputada do momento, como revelou o Financial Times. Essas antigas instalações têm tudo o que um data center precisa: espaço de sobra, boas vias de acesso e, o mais importante, uma conexão garantida à rede de transmissão de energia elétrica. Um acordo cercado de sigilo O negócio ainda é cercado de segredo, mas dois detalhes cruciais já vieram a público. O primeiro é que a energética está a ponto de selar um contrato em uma de suas 10 propriedades paradas — distribuídas entre Reino Unido, Alemanha, Suécia e Holanda — para transformá-la em um centro de processamento de dados, além de manter conversas avançadas sobre outras duas localidades. O segundo é que seu CEO, Michael Lewis, calcula em cerca de 700 MW a capacidade de rede elétrica assegurada nesses pontos. De acordo com a Agência Internacional de Energia (AIE), essa potência seria suficiente para abastecer em torno de sete data centers de hiperescala ou perto de 70 instalações de menor porte. Ainda não se sabe com certeza quais desses 10 locais serão contemplados, embora haja fortes pistas de que as primeiras opções fiquem no Reino Unido e na Alemanha, como o próprio executivo deixou escapar em meados do ano.
