artigo.texto: The clean energy revolution hinges on electrifying the entire global economy just as power-hungry data centers are surging. It’s a challenge delegates from all over the world had to grapple with during the United Nations climate conference, called COP31, that came to a chaotic and unsatisfying close in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday. AI data centers throw another wrench into chaotic UN climate talks Global climate negotiations fell apart as delegates tried to tackle AI’s growing carbon footprint. Each year, attendees try to make good on the commitment to stop climate change as part of the 2015 Paris climate accord. Preventing extreme weather from growing more terrifying, coastal communities from flooding, and droughts from wrecking food and water systems requires slashing greenhouse gas emissions. But in order to power homes or cars with solar and wind instead of oil and gas, they need to go electric. “Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this” To that end, one of the most anticipated outcomes of this year’s negotiations was a deal to raise electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035, compared to about 20 percent today. That becomes harder to do, however, when data centers are causing electricity demand to skyrocket. That made the rush of new AI data centers a climate issue alongside talks on how to transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy. “Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this, and it will inevitably come up in the discussions. It’s part of the broader energy transformation,” Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy and the president of COP31 climate negotiations, told Politico in an interview at the start of the COP31 summit. Despite becoming the longest COP yet, with debates lasting two days longer than scheduled, official negotiations fell apart spectacularly. Delegates ultimately failed to garner enough support to pass the “pact” they’d been bargaining on for two weeks. The EU, UK, and several smaller nations most vulnerable to climate change rejected the deal that they saw as too weak. The pact omitted the term “fossil fuels” despite many nations calling for stronger commitments to phase out oil, coal, and gas. And the US, the epicenter of the data center buildout and the biggest climate polluter historically, was a no-show after the pro-fossil-fuel Trump administration pulled the country out of the Paris accord (twice). With official negotiations falling apart, and countries only making voluntary commitments on AI and electrification, some environmental and humanitarian groups called this year “the worst COP” ever. To meet the Paris goals, nations will need to cut their greenhouse gas emissions roughly in half by 2030 before reaching net zero by the middle of the century. Many tech companies made similar commitments in recent years, including Google, Microsoft, and Meta. But thanks to the AI boom, those goals have fallen by the wayside. Meta is “re-evaluating” its timeline to reach net zero emissions as it focuses on AI, the company said in its annual sustainability report on Thursday. Meta reported a 45 percent year-over-year increase in climate pollution. Google’s and Microsoft’s carbon footprints are also growing despite climate commitments the companies have made. Data centers’ electricity consumption is forecast to double by 2030, according to a forecast by the International Energy Agency. “That is a huge climate risk: rising power demand from data centres is not yet sustainable, and an AI boom cannot be allowed to become a fossil fuel boom,” Bruce Douglas, CEO of the Global Renewables Alliance, tells The Verge in an email. Data centers were “a key topic” at COP31, according to Douglas, whose organization cohosted a panel on the challenges during the event. In the US, the country with the most data centers, power sector emissions could increase 42 percent by 2030 as energy companies build more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a recent analysis by the Sierra Club. Already, hyperscale data centers in the US create more climate pollution than the country of Denmark, a separate study by Harvard researchers recently found. To stop data centers from creating more pollution, they would need to be powered by additional new sources of renewable energy, Douglas says. He adds that data centers are currently competing with everyone else for grid connections, finance, and electricity generation capacity — and against arguably more essential tasks like heating and air conditioning, as well as electrifying transportation. Many tech companies match their electricity use with renewable energy purchases. But unless they’re helping to build new sources of green energy to meet their added electricity demand, they might just end up hogging limited renewable energy capacity. And if more fossil fuels make up the difference, then greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise overall. “Should new green electrons be used for air-conditioning, electrification or data centres?” “In many cases, datacentres are outbidding other consumers to get speed to power,” Douglas says. “Should new green electrons be used for air-conditioning, electrification or data centres?” There was some progress. artigo.texto: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-lofty goal of Elon Musk's rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists. The U.S. Federal Communications Commission lauded its authorization as a historic first amid the artificial intelligence race. It said that SpaceX's one million "orbital compute modules" (forming a data center constellation called "Starmind") would process massive amounts of data that would be used back on Earth — and bring humans closer to harnessing "the full power of the sun." "America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who was appointed by Republican President Donald Trump, said in a statement. He added that Wednesday's move "opens a bold new frontier." A lengthier authorization order published by the FCC noted that the company must deploy at least "one authorized space station" by 2033 — and then gradually add more and more through 2040. Musk welcomed the decision over social media. The world's richest man has long vowed to form vast, solar-powered data centers in space to help run AI tools on Earth. But scientists and industry experts have stressed enormous technical and financial obstacles, as well as a host of environmental concerns. Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and author, called the prospect of launching a million satellites into space to create data centers "a fantasy." "It's not going to happen," he said Wednesday. Proponents of data centers in space argue that capturing the sun's energy would ease pressure on power grids and cut demand for sprawling computing warehouses on Earth (and resources like water needed to cool them). Space seems to offer a solution because it is cold, but it is also a vacuum, trapping heat inside objects much like a thermos. Becker explained that there are "basic physical limits" to otherwise radiating that heat out — and sending lots of smaller satellites could potentially carry the necessary material combined, but it would be expensive and difficult. He and others also point to additional risks, such as atmospheric pollution through launches and reentries, as well as possible in-orbit collisions that could impact other essential satellites. "You could end up with a cascading set of space junk collisions," said Becker, noting such crashes could create "a cloud of debris" in the low Earth orbit — where many weather and telecommunication satellites are also found. In its ruling, the FCC maintained that SpaceX's proposed Starmind constellation operates consistently with its orbital debris rules. It also acknowledged that it had received a "substantial number" of public comments leading up to its authorization Wednesday, including petitions to deny SpaceX's request. But the regulator maintained that deploying the satellites "serves the public interest" — and said that it dismissed topics that it didn't have authority over, such as environmental concerns. The American Astronomical Society, satellite communication company Viasat and Amazon-owned Kuiper Systems were among those who called on the regulator to deny SpaceX's proposed data centers in space. In a statement Wednesday, the AAS said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the FCC's decision. The organization said that SpaceX's proposed position of data centers in low Earth orbit would undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky." "The proposed constellation involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects," AAS said, noting that "these satellites would therefore be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky." Becker echoed that sentiment. "It also is pollution of the night sky to the naked eye," he said. Viasat, Amazon, SpaceX and the FCC did not immediately respond to The Associated Press' requests for further comment Wednesday.

artigo.texto: Despite the recent attention on new electric demand created by data centers, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries sees greater potential for long-term growth in the utilities sector, MHI President and CEO Eisaku Ito said earlier this month. Utilities and independent power producers accounted for 94% of Mitsubishi Heavy Industries’ new gas turbine orders in 2024 and 2025, Ito said. Although many U.S. data center operators say they intend to install their own off-grid generation, Ito argued that these plans rely on smaller gas-fired power plants that cost more to run than the larger plants utilities and IPPs are pursuing. In the long-term, Ito said, the cost differential will push data centers to connect to the grid, ultimately supporting utilities' expansion plans. His comments, made during a call with analysts on Nov. 6, according to a translated transcript, come as fallout from the U.S. midterm elections and stock market volatility raise questions about the future of the artificial intelligence buildout in North America. Ito expressed confidence in utilities' long-term expansion plans, arguing that growing demand for electricity does not rely solely on data centers. “Electricity demand from data centers is expected to grow rapidly in the United States, but data centers still account for only around 10% of the country's total electricity demand,” Ito said. “If some of the anticipated growth in demand does not materialize, there will be some impact, but we believe the effect on our overall GTCC business would be limited.” MHI booked 8 GW in orders for large frame gas turbines in the first half of its 2026 fiscal year, compared to 16 GW of orders in all of FY 2025. Profit for the company’s Energy Systems segment rose 80% on account of increased orders and shifts in the value of the yen, according to the company's financial statements. “We are also beginning to see the benefits of improved pricing on new unit projects, lower loss-related costs and greater production efficiency,” MHI CFO Hiroshi Nishio said. Company executives said they continue to take a conservative approach to forecasting demand and expanding manufacturing capacity. The company expects global demand for gas turbines at all manufacturers and makers to average about 70 GW per year over the next five years — somewhat lower than the 100 GW MHI expects will sell across all manufactuers this year amid what Ito characterized as “exceptionally strong” demand he does not anticipate will continue. But Ito said he remains confident in MHI’s company backlog, noting that the company vets new orders carefully and hasn’t had any order cancellations in the past two years. The company plans to double its gas turbine production capacity by 2030, though most of the additional capacity will come from improved processes and automation at existing plants in the U.S. and Japan. “We are improving productivity and driving other initiatives at a pace that outstrips the growth in orders,” he said. MHI also signaled that it's exploring opportunities to expand into other infrastructure-related markets. Ito said MHI will release additional details in May, but suggested the company is interested in expanding its gas turbine service and repair capabilities, as well as investing in unmanned systems that can operate in harsh environments. At the same time, MHI plans to divest some of its aerospace business, he said. “These examples may seem quite different, but they all share a common theme: resilience,” Ito said. “We aim to identify new business opportunities in infrastructure and industrial machinery through the lens of resilience and turn them into future growth.”

artigo.texto: SpaceX recebe aval dos EUA para lançar até 1 milhão de satélites para data centers de IA Autorização inédita abre caminho para rede de IA em órbita, mas tecnologia ainda não foi testada “Ao levar a capacidade de computação para além da Terra, a SpaceX e os muitos concorrentes que desenvolvem seus próprios data centers orbitais estão respondendo às exigências do momento”, afirmou o presidente da FCC, Brendan Carr, em comunicado. Carr elogia a SpaceX com frequência e acompanhou um lançamento de teste do novo foguete Starship, da empresa, em novembro. A aprovação da FCC elimina um obstáculo regulatório e aproxima a SpaceX de seu ambicioso plano de data centers orbitais. Segundo a empresa, eles podem ser uma alternativa mais barata e menos prejudicial ao meio ambiente do que os data centers em terra. Quais são os desafios dos data centers no espaço A SpaceX enfrenta dificuldades importantes para criar data centers espaciais, que ainda não existem na escala proposta por Musk e pela empresa. Eles vão exigir painéis solares de dimensões muito grandes, tecnologias de resfriamento sofisticadas e sistemas capazes de transmitir para a Terra volumes de dados muito maiores do que os atuais. A SpaceX não respondeu de imediato a um pedido de comentário. Como vão funcionar os data centers orbitais da SpaceX O pedido da empresa, apresentado em janeiro, trazia detalhes sobre a nova rede. Em vez de sistemas de resfriamento que consomem grandes volumes de água, a rede usaria o resfriamento por radiação que ocorre no espaço, que permite dissipar o calor. Também dependeria menos de baterias, já que a energia viria do sol, segundo o documento. Os satélites vão se comunicar entre si por links de laser e serão lançados em altitudes entre 500 e 2.000 quilômetros, em uma órbita que garante acesso quase constante ao sol, de acordo com o pedido. Por que cientistas criticam o projeto O plano de lançar tantos satélites preocupa cientistas e outros participantes do setor espacial. Eles temem que o tamanho da rede deixe a órbita da Terra superlotada, aumente as colisões entre satélites e reduza a visibilidade das estrelas para os astrônomos. A proposta recebeu mais de 1.500 comentários públicos. Entre eles, o da Sociedade Astronômica Americana, que pediu à FCC que negasse o pedido. A Blue Origin, de Jeff Bezos, também pediu autorização à FCC para lançar seus próprios data centers orbitais, mas ainda aguarda aprovação. Nesta quarta-feira (25), a SpaceX também anunciou que vai destinar uma ação ordinária classe A recém-emitida a cada Trump Account ativa. As Trump Accounts são contas de investimento com benefício fiscal criadas para crianças americanas.

artigo.texto: A new study from the University of Oklahoma puts hard numbers behind a question that planning boards across the country keep asking: what draws data centers to a community? According to the University of Oklahoma announcement, researchers examined 212 U.S. data centers run by 11 major technology companies, including Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta. Land-use diversity came out as the strongest factor, ahead of the other signals the team tested. The story is dated November 20, 2026, with an update on November 22. It lands at a moment when cloud and AI operators are hunting for sites faster than most local governments can write zoning rules. Our earlier look at an immersion-only data center pitched at under 30,000 square feet showed how much the building itself is changing. The OU work asks a different question: not how to build the hall, but why a given town gets it. This analysis walks through what the study found, what it left out, and what the findings mean for cloud planners, local officials and anyone who has watched a substation upgrade or a rezoning notice appear at the edge of town. We keep to the facts the university has published. Where the record is thin, we say so. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What the OU Study Actually Measured Kijin Seong, Ph.D., is an assistant professor in the Division of Planning, Landscape Architecture and Design at OU’s Christopher C. Gibbs College of Architecture. He co-authored the research. The team did not survey executives or ask companies to explain their reasoning. Instead, it looked at where 212 existing facilities sit and tested which local characteristics tracked with those locations. The sample spans 11 major technology companies. Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta are named in the announcement, and the other seven are not identified in the material we reviewed. That matters for readers who want company-by-company patterns. The published summary reports aggregate findings, so we cannot say whether Meta favors different communities than Microsoft does. The analysis grouped its explanatory factors into three families: land use, infrastructure and workforce. Land use covers the mix of activities in the surrounding area. Infrastructure covers electrical substations and major roads. Workforce covers concentrations of information technology workers. Those three families gave the researchers a way to compare very different sites on the same terms. Land-Use Diversity: The Strongest Factor in Data Center Site Selection The headline result is the one that surprises people. Land-use diversity, meaning a neighborhood or district that mixes housing, commerce, industry and services, was the strongest factor the analysis identified. Many readers would have guessed that wide-open, single-purpose land wins. The OU team found the reverse pattern holds up better in the data. Why would a mixed area attract a server hall? The study summary does not offer a causal story, and we will not invent one. What we can say is that mixed-use areas tend to come with the things a large facility needs to function: established utility service, road networks, nearby workers and a local government used to permitting different kinds of buildings. A diverse land-use pattern may work as a proxy for all of that. What diversity does and does not mean Diversity here describes the surrounding community, not the data center parcel. A site can sit on a quiet lot and still score high if the district around it mixes uses. For local officials, that distinction changes the pitch. A town does not need to rezone everything for servers. It needs to look like a place where varied development already happens. Practitioners have long published checklists that treat land as a gate. A site selection criteria guide from Base Operations is one example of that genre, which lists the factors developers screen before they commit. The OU analysis adds something those checklists rarely supply: a pattern drawn from where 212 real facilities actually went. Substations, Roads and IT Workers: The Supporting Signals Three more factors helped explain where facilities landed. Proximity to electrical substations, access to major roads and concentrations of information technology workers all showed up in the analysis. None of them beat land-use diversity, but each one added explanatory power. The substation finding fits the physical logic of the business. A data hall is, at its core, a very large electrical load with cooling attached. Sitting close to a substation shortens the path between the grid and the racks. It does not guarantee capacity, and the OU summary reports no megawatt figures, so readers should not read the finding as a statement about how much power any site gets. Major roads matter for less glamorous reasons. Construction crews, generators, cooling equipment and replacement hardware all arrive by truck. Roads also bring staff to the door during shifts. The study treats road access as one measurable proxy for that logistics burden. The IT workforce signal is the most interesting for smaller communities. Facilities cluster where technology workers already live. That suggests that talent, not just land and power, shapes the map. Towns hoping to land a cloud region should ask whether they can supply or attract the people who run it. What Site Selectors Say About Power and Workforce The OU findings line up with how industry practitioners describe the job. Seong himself framed the basics plainly in a report from okcfox.com. He said, “The buildings that hold data centers need land, a lot of electricity, water for cooling and fiber connections.” Note that water and fiber appear in that quote, yet the announcement lists land use, infrastructure (substations and roads) and workforce as the factors the analysis found helpful. artigo.texto: The furor over data centers in Aurora led the City Council to pass a temporary moratorium on projects Monday and one developer to abandon a controversial hyperscale project near the Denver airport. The council adopted a one-year timeout for new data centers in the most developed part of Aurora — south of Interstate 70 and west of Powhaton Road — while more comprehensive data center regulations are developed. At Monday’s council meeting, Mayor Mike Coffman announced that Denver-based Vantage Data Centers has decided to abandon its planned 500-megawatt Trident data center near E-470 and East 48th Avenue. The project was the biggest announced data center in Colorado and it sparked heated opposition by residents, particularly from new residential neighborhoods filling in east of Green Valley Ranch, along Picadilly and Tibet roads. “In response to the recent community concerns, Vantage voluntarily initiated a review of alternative sites, and the examination of viable alternatives continues,” Misty Allen, Vantage vice president for public policy in North America, said in a statement. “While we will no longer pursue the current site for our proposed campus, Vantage remains committed to being a responsible long-term partner in the state,” Allen said. The announcement brought cheers from the audience at the council meeting. Aurora’s moratorium comes as communities along the Front Range are wrestling with proposed data centers and some, including Denver, Boulder County, Longmont and Thornton, have imposed moratoriums or limited development. Concerns include data centers’ large demands for power and in some cases water, as well as their use of land. Another question is whether power-hungry data centers could drive up electric rates. The Colorado Public Utilities Commission has ordered Xcel Energy, the state’s biggest electricity provider, to develop data center rates that protect other customers. In Aurora, the impact on property values of new homes next near the proposed 108-acre Trident site was a major concern. “Had that Trident center gone forward, the value of your properties would have sunk like a rock,” Coffman told homeowners at Monday’s meeting. “I am just grateful the nightmare is over and you have prevailed.” The council twice failed to pass a more comprehensive moratorium that would have covered the entire city. While the revised moratorium is “limited and imperfect,” Council member Alison Coombs said, “this is the moratorium we can pass.” The moratorium covers approvals for new data centers until October 2027, but there are already projects underway including a 160-MW hyperscale center by Sterling, Virginia-based Quality Technology Services, or QTS. The QTS Aurora facility is the largest data center under construction in the state. “I am against moratoriums of any kind,” Council member Stephanie Hancock said. “What we are in disagreement on is putting a blanket moratorium that would impede the progress of something that is inevitable.” “Data centers are here to stay,” Hancock said. “You’ve got to wrap your heads around it.” Hancock’s remarks were met with a round of boos.

artigo.texto: Basing entire business plans on back-of-the-envelope calculations might not seem like the best idea. However, according to a new paper available in preprint on arXiv by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory, that is precisely what the companies touting orbital AI data centers are doing. While on paper, the math looks good, the physical constraints of actually utilizing all the processing power and free energy of the Sun that orbit provides is prohibitive in a number of ways - and it will be a long time before we have the technology to truly capitalize on the advantages of space-based AI. First, letâs dig into what the back-of-the-envelope calculations say. Research from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory suggests that U.S.-based data centers could consume 580 terawatt-hours of electricity over a five-year window, an increase of around 17-46 gigawatts compared to modern levels. But land-based data centers are running into plenty of bottlenecks, from newly elected hostile politicians to hard caps on the electrical gridâs ability to supply all that additional power. So the solution seems obvious - launch the data centers into orbit, where they will be beyond any individual NIMBY protesters, have access to essentially unlimited free solar power, and not have to deal with water cooling systems. Sounds pretty good. Until the actual physics of what that means comes into play. Fraser addresses the idea of data centers in space. There are three main physics hurdles that all culminate into a giant economic one facing data centers, and it all comes down to scale. Size and weight are the first major obstacle. Dr. Turyshev uses a baseline 1-megawatt orbital processing facility as an example. It would hold roughly the processing power of a small commercial server room. But in space it would require 5,640 square meters of deployed solar panels, even in a âdawn-duskâ orbit designed to minimize the time it spends in Earthâs shadow. Thatâs roughly the size of an American football field. On top of that, the spacecraft would need around 2,500 square meters of radiator panels to stop the electronics from frying themselves. Combining the power generation and cooling equipment required would already bring a spacecraft up to 30 metric tons. Adding in structural trusses, control thrusters, and radiation shielding brings the total mass of 1 MW of orbital data capacity is likely between 34 and 59 metric tons. For the purposes of practicality, Dr. Turyshev then drops down to a 100 kW center, since a 1 MW data center would not even fit in many modern rocket fairings. Arguably, since each 100 kW data center wouldnât be exactly 10% of the weight of a 1 MW data center, he uses a rough estimate of around 5 metric tons for a single spacecraft of that size. The problem is, to keep up with demand, we would need to launch between 170,000 and 461,000 of them over the course of five years. And each Falcon 9 can only launch at most four of them. That would require almost 9,000 Falcon 9 launches over the next five years - or roughly 33 of them per week. Fraser talks about turning the Moon into a data center. Even if we had the launch capacity for that sheer scale, there is another bottleneck to contend with - getting the data back to Earth. As we reported earlier this week, weâve made great strides in high-speed optical communications down from orbit lately. However, the headline number of 200 gigabits per second is a single point in time. These âhigh speedâ links realistically deliver around 13 to 26 gigabits per second continuously, in part because they require a direct line of sight to the ground station theyâre communicating with, and they also canât communicate through clouds. Even if we flooded major parts of the Earthâs surface with ground stations, those speeds would severely hobble any interactive cloud apps or data-heavy training runs that require continual syncing with anything on the ground. But even if we solved the communications problem, thereâs still the problem of that omnipresent menace in space - radiation. Cosmic rays are famous for flipping single bits in computer memory, constantly forcing processors to run error-checking algorithms, and thereby eating into usable computer time. According to the paper, over a five-year mission, the cumulative radiation damage and micrometeoroid impacts would continually degrade both the electronics and solar panels, driving up the cost of every calculation completed. With all that in mind, the economic hurdle becomes very clear. On Earth, a high-end AI data center costs between $10,000 and $40,000 per kilowatt of computing capacity. In order for a 40-kilogram per kilowatt orbital satellite to match that pricing, it would need combined launch and manufacturing costs of between $250 and $1,000 per kilogram. For comparison, current dedicated Falcon 9 launches work out to roughly $3,360 per kilogram. So the launch cost alone is three to thirteen times more expensive than the entire combined launch and manufacturing cost of a single data center. Video from Astraveo arguing the same physics as what Dr. Turyshev talks about in the paper. Credit - Astraveo YouTube Channel With all that said, there are some niche applications for orbital computing in the near future, according to the paper. The first is space-native processing, where satellites crunch the raw imagery for Earth-observation satellites or sensor data before broadcasting high-value insights back down to Earth. Another is communications-based edge computing, where processors piggyback on existing constellations like Starlink that already pay for solar arrays, lasers, and ground stations. But ultimately, despite this paper, various organizations are moving forward with their plans for data centers in orbit. artigo.texto: As the engines of artificial intelligence, large data centers can consume as much power as medium-sized cities, straining grids and prompting expensive upgrades to U.S. energy infrastructure. New research finds that residents, and especially lower-income and rural residents, are disproportionately bearing the costs. In the study, published Nov. 9 in Nature Energy, Cornell researchers analyzed growth in energy demand and infrastructure projects for four major U.S. power grids from 2020 to 2025 and found that data centers have hiked wholesale energy prices and on average paid only 38% of the infrastructure costs linked to their growth — $3.12 billion of an $8.25 billion bill in 2025. The remaining $5.13 billion, or 62 percent, fell largely on residents, with the lowest income households seeing extra energy costs up to 28 percent of their incomes. “We were trying to answer a very simple question: With the booming of data centers, who pays for that expansion and who benefits?” said Fengqi You, the Roxanne E. and Michael J. Zak Professor in Energy Systems Engineering in the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering. “It’s not just a question of generating enough electricity but of whether the rules for paying for the grid are keeping pace with who is driving new demand.” The research is the first multi-region, long-term assessment of how data center development impacts infrastructure growth and how costs are distributed across communities. It comes amidst a boom in data center construction. The researchers found that transmission investment in energy infrastructure projects increased from $2 billion in 2020 to $34 billion in 2025, with data centers driving much of that rise. Debates are ongoing – from local communities to state governments to Congress – about who picks up the bill as growth accelerates; data centers are projected to consume between 8% and 17% of U.S. electricity by 2030, with 70% to 80% of that attributed to AI. With first author and postdoctoral researcher Cheng Feng, You also looked at data centers’ economic benefits, finding that each gigawatt of data center capacity can create 15,000 jobs across the economy, with an average 2,700 jobs directly associated with the data center (although not necessarily all on-site). “In a lot of discussions right now, people take one side or the other, completely yes on data centers or completely no,” said You, director of the Cornell AI for Sustainability Initiative. “But there are benefits and costs, and the key issue in the end is how to balance the trade-offs.” Sharing the cost of power infrastructure The team analyzed data from 4,000 existing and proposed data centers, as well as power-price records, rate filings from utilities, power-line plans, and federal household and job data. The major grids they studied encompass regions with the largest clusters of data centers, including the southern San Francisco Bay area; north Texas around Dallas-Fort Worth; the Midwest; and the mid-Atlantic region, including northern Virginia, where the biggest concentration of data centers has been built to date. State incentives for data centers have provided returns on the investments, if inconsistently, the researchers found. Some states, such as California, reaped $180 in worker income for every dollar spent, while Virginia increased income $2 for every dollar invested. The researchers determined that the presence of an existing, qualified workforce was a stronger indicator of high returns than the amount of incentive spending. Data centers also increased wholesale electricity prices, the amounts utilities pay regional power markets before delivering the electricity to homes. In the most-affected hubs, data center growth raised those prices by nearly 10 percent or more by 2025. In Virginia, the costs jumped 15 percent and in California’s southern Bay Area, 20 percent. In contrast, residents in New York and New England, where data center construction has been limited, have not seen clear price increases due to data center expansion, the researchers found. “I think that means we’re at a good starting point in New York to think about the next steps,” You said. “Economic benefits, job benefits, investment, fairly allocating the costs – these are the dimensions and trade-offs we need to consider.” A key problem is how the costs of new infrastructure projects are currently shared: The allocation is often based on previous patterns of energy consumption. “It’s kind of a chicken-and-egg problem,” You said. “Because if you’re going to build a data center, you need to expand this power infrastructure. Otherwise, there’s no electricity for them to run. But before they build, they’re not using energy. So with this model of relying on past consumption, households end up taking on much of the infrastructure costs.” Many more rural and lower-income residents saw proportionally higher bills; the share of rural families shouldering a high energy burden — spending more than 6% of their incomes on energy – rose 76% more than among urban residents. The authors cite a national survey finding that rural residents are also less likely to use AI tools like ChatGPT than urban residents. The impact on energy bills also has a wide geographical reach. For example, residents in New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Ohio help pay for grid upgrades linked to data center growth in Virginia, the researchers said. “You do not have to live next to a data center to help pay for its power infrastructure,” You said. “The grid connects communities across states, and cost-sharing rules connect them financially.” Using insights from the data, You and Feng recommend changes to cost-sharing rules and strategies to lower burdens. In all four regions, they found that, if data centers cut back power use during 22 of the region’s peak demand hours each year, they would relieve strain on the grid and minimize the need to expand. artigo.texto: St. Charles may get a battery storage system meant to reduce energy costs as part of a pilot program with its electricity provider, even while the city’s future with the Illinois Municipal Electric Agency, or IMEA, remains uncertain. The city is looking to work with IMEA, which would pay for and manage the project, on the construction of a battery storage facility that St. Charles would take over management of in the event the city does not continue to get its energy from the electricity provider past 2035. Generally speaking, a battery energy storage system, or BESS, works by storing electrical energy in batteries so it can be used later, said St. Charles Director of Public Works Peter Suhr at a meeting of the St. Charles City Council’s Committee of the Whole on Nov. 16, at which a measure expressing the city’s support for participating in the pilot program was recommended for approval. Such a system can lower utility bills by storing electrical energy when the energy is least expensive, and then discharging that stored energy when prices are at their highest, Suhr said. It can also improve electricity reliability because a system can act as a backup generator during power outages. The measure recently recommended for approval by the Committee of the Whole is essentially a preliminary step to allow St. Charles to work with IMEA on the proposed battery storage project in the city. At this point, the city is looking for council approval for initial analysis work and participation in a request for proposals with IMEA for the project, Suhr said. The project is set to be formalized in a contract around March, Suhr said. St. Charles is one of 32 municipalities across Illinois that are part of IMEA, a nonprofit joint action agency that sells electric power to municipally-owned utilities, per its website. The city began purchasing partial electric power for its electric utility with IMEA in 1999, and entered into its current contract to get all of its electric power from them in 2004. The city is among those served by PJM Interconnection, the regional grid that includes northern Illinois, 12 other states and the District of Columbia. The downstate area is part of the Midwest Independent System Operator grid, or MISO, which also serves 14 other states from Mississippi to North Dakota as well as Manitoba in Canada. As part of a sustainability plan that details its goal of reducing the power supplied to its member municipalities to net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, IMEA has been looking at the feasibility of utility-scale behind-the-meter battery storage on its member distribution systems, according to its website, and it is now looking to pursue pilot projects for this technology. Several months ago, IMEA sent out requests for proposals to all 32 municipalities, with the goal of having one battery storage pilot in the PJM market, and another in the MISO market, Suhr said. According to Suhr, IMEA received responses from both Naperville and St. Charles, but St. Charles was ultimately selected for the planned pilot. The idea behind the pilot program is to allow city staff and IMEA to “dip (their) toes into this technology,” Suhr said. If successful, it could be scaled up in the future. Being part of the pilot would give the city hands-on experience with battery storage technology and help prepare its electric utility for future power supply decisions, a city memo indicated. The program anticipates systems in the range of 1 MW to 5 MW, with a capacity of about four hours’ worth of energy, or less than 1% of St. Charles’ total peak load, Suhr said. The proposed location of the battery storage system is at a substation between Kirk Road and the East Side Sports Complex. This proposal comes as St. Charles’ long-term relationship with IMEA remains uncertain. Last year, the City Council voted against extending its contract with the electricity provider after its current agreement expires in 2035, though returning to IMEA is not necessarily out of the question for good. Among the major concerns raised about the IMEA contract was the potential environmental impact of the city getting its electricity from the cooperative electric supplier. One of IMEA’s primary suppliers is a downstate coal plant called Prairie State that was one of the top 10 biggest polluters in the country, according to 2023 data from the United States Environmental Protection Agency. How nearby Naperville, another IMEA member, will procure its electricity post-2035 is similarly still playing out. Participating in the battery storage pilot with IMEA would not lead to any direct costs to St. Charles until at least 2035, because IMEA would be handling things like construction and maintenance, Suhr said. But, if the city opts not to continue working with IMEA, St. Charles would be responsible for costs associated with the battery storage system. A system like this is expected to cost the city around $100,000 to $200,000 annually, according to Suhr. The measure recommended for approval at the Nov. 16 Committee of the Whole meeting essentially allows the city to move forward with participating in the pilot program. The measure is expected to come to the City Council for final approval on Dec. 7, per the resolution. From there, IMEA would seek vendors for the project, Suhr said, and an official contract would be expected to come back to the City Council for approval around March. mmorrow@chicagotribune.com

artigo.texto: Duke Energy to build new battery storage system in Goldsboro, its largest in NC Duke Energy is building a new battery storage system in Wayne County — the largest of its kind on Duke's power grid — as North Carolina sees a surge in electricity demand. The utility company expects to spend up to $756 million to build the facility, which will be able to store up to 410 megawatts of backup electricity, the company announced on Nov. 18. It will also receive a 50% federal tax credit for "investing in an energy community with domestic content," according to Duke's announcement. Battery storage systems can store excess electricity that's generated from power plants, and release that electricity onto the grid at times of high demand. In recent years, battery storage has emerged as a way to make electric grids stronger and prevent blackouts when energy use spikes. North Carolina's demand is largely due to data centers, but also from population growth. Duke Energy has been planning to drastically scale up its battery storage capacity, building up to 6,500 megawatts of battery storage by 2035. This new plant is a first step toward that goal. With a capacity of 460 megawatts, it will more than double Duke's current battery storage capacity, which currently adds up to about 308 megawatts across 14 facilities in North Carolina. "We're building new resources to keep the Carolinas' economy thriving, while reinvesting in our existing power plant communities that have powered North Carolina and South Carolina for decades," said Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy's North Carolina president, in a Nov. 18 news release. The plant will be built next to the H. F. Lee natural gas plant in Goldsboro, about 50 miles southeast of Raleigh, with construction happening in two phases, according to Duke's announcement. The first battery storage system, which will have capacity to store up to 260 megawatts of electricity, will come online in fall 2028. The second system, which will be able to store up to 150 megawatts of electricity, will come online by the end of 2028. Construction is expected to start early in 2027. Economic impact The new system is expected to generate an estimated $2 million in revenue for Wayne County, on top of the $5.8 million that Duke Energy already pays to the county in taxes for the existing H. F. Lee plant. It's also expected to create nine permanent full-time jobs linked to this facility and "other regional battery and solar resources," according to Duke's announcement. County leaders celebrated the investment last week, and Joe Daugherty, chair of the Wayne County board of commissioners, called it a "significant milestone." "This project will provide substantial long-term tax revenue while reinforcing Wayne County's role in meeting the growing energy needs of our state," Daugherty said. The announcement came after the N.C. Utilities Commission authorized Duke Energy to develop about 2,700 additional megawatts of new battery storage capacity as a part of its Carbon Plan, which outlines what type of energy Duke will invest in over the next several years. Along with increasing battery storage capacity, the Utilities Commission also approved heavy investments in gas, nuclear and solar energy as part of the Carbon Plan ruling. artigo.texto: Citing concerns about its effects on the environment and residents’ health, members of the South Whitehall community on Monday pleaded with officials from the state Department of Environmental Protection to reject a massive data center across the road from Parkland High School. During a three-hour meeting at Cedar Crest College, the DEP fielded questions and listened to testimony from people who live near the proposed $8.9 billion Project Atlas site, or who have children attending the high school. Representatives from Project Atlas developer CDE Acquisitions LLC- Edged US also answered questions about the project, though few in the audience seemed satisfied with their answers. Alice Lenthe, an environmental engineer and member of the South Whitehall Civic Alliance, which is raising money to fight the project in court, urged the DEP to consider the wildlife that would disappear if wetlands on the data center site were destroyed. She noted that Edged has proposed buying wetlands in another part of the Lehigh River watershed through mitigation credits — something that is allowed under the federal Clean Water Act — to make up for the wetlands they’d destroy in South Whitehall, but said that wasn’t enough. “The loss of wetlands is a local issue. While the DEP permits the purchase of credits, those credits do nothing to alleviate the enormous harm that Project Atlas, if approved, would impose on the environment of this community,” she said. Lenthe blasted the developer’s vague answers to her questions about their plan, and said Edged did not respect the community it was trying to become part of. “In this, as with every other aspect of Project Atlas, Edged shows their contempt of local residents and the local environment,” Lenthe said. Monday’s review was a key stepping stone for the proposed 1.5 million-square-foot campus on Cedar Crest Boulevard. At stake are two permits the developer needs to begin construction near tributaries of Coplay Creek and Jordan Creek. There is no deadline for the DEP to rule on the permits. South Whitehall Township manager Tom Petrucci testified that the township is not recommending approval of the project at this time, since the township engineer has identified unresolved issues, including how stormwater would move through the site and affect neighboring properties. Logan Kreglow, another South Whitehall resident, raised concerns about waivers the developer is seeking related to stormwater management at the Mauch Chunk intersection leading into the proposed construction zone. Kreglow, a civil engineer, reminded the DEP representatives that Edged filed their waiver application on Aug. 8, 10 days before Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order mandating that all data centers go through an extended two-part DEP review. Under the order, data centers must get local officials’ approval before seeking DEP permits. “Atlas hurried their application to avoid a more thorough and appropriate permit review process,” Kreglow said. “This is exactly the type of project the executive order is meant to protect us from. Do not let them be grandfathered in.” In a statement posted online after the meeting, the South Whitehall Civic Alliance said they were disappointed that they didn’t get answers from the developer about other environmental concerns, including how soil contaminated with arsenic and lead would be addressed during construction, whether the lithium ion batteries that will be used in the data center operation were safe, as well as questions about noise and air pollution testing. “Residents should not have to ask the same questions repeatedly, only to receive vague assurances instead of substantive answers. If the applicant’s representatives cannot explain these issues at a public meeting, DEP should not consider those concerns resolved,” Alliance members wrote. Project Atlas developers will be back before the planning commission Jan. 13. That meeting will be held at Parkland High School. The deadline for the township to act on the plan is Feb. 28. The DEP will continue to collect written testimony from people affected by the data center project until Dec. 7. Comments can be emailed to pkania@pa.gov.

artigo.texto: Os carros estão cada vez mais parecidos com smartphones sobre rodas e precisam de conectividade para melhorar a experiência dos motoristas. É de olho nessa transformação que a TIM está ampliando sua presença na indústria automotiva. A operadora acaba de fechar uma parceria com a BYD para oferecer conectividade embarcada inicialmente a cerca de 200 mil veículos da montadora chinesa nos próximos dois anos. O acordo também prevê a instalação de uma infraestrutura dedicada de redes 5G e 4G no complexo industrial da BYD em Camaçari – a maior fábrica de veículos eletrificados da América Latina. A parceria faz parte da estratégia da operadora de ampliar sua atuação no mercado corporativo, através da unidade TIM B2B Solutions, oferecendo portfólio de soluções que vão desde a conectividade a serviços de tecnologia. Detalhe: a iniciativa ganha escala em um momento de expansão da BYD no mercado brasileiro. A montadora ultrapassou a marca de 300 mil veículos em circulação no País em 2026. “Hoje, a tecnologia é um dos principais motores de transformação da indústria automotiva e da mobilidade,” disse Alberto Griselli, CEO da TIM Brasil. Nos veículos da BYD, a tecnologia utilizada será o eSIM – uma espécie de chip digital que facilita a ativação remota de serviços. A solução da TIM permitirá interações com motoristas desenvolvidas pela montadora em seu próprio aplicativo e através das mídias no carro. Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente sênior da BYD do Brasil e head de marketing e comercial da BYD Auto, diz que a ideia é que a experiência digital do consumidor continue evoluindo ao longo da vida útil do automóvel. Segundo o executivo, a parceria com a TIM vai permitir à BYD ampliar a oferta de serviços e funcionalidades e garantir que a experiência de quem escolhe a marca continue evoluindo mesmo depois que o veículo sair da concessionária. “O consumidor brasileiro está cada vez mais exigente, e não basta oferecer um carro com tecnologia de ponta se essa experiência não continuar evoluindo ao longo do tempo,” disse Baldy. A outra frente da parceria está em Camaçari, onde a BYD inaugurou sua maior operação industrial fora da China. O complexo ocupa uma área de 4,6 milhões de metros quadrados, que será atendida pela infraestrutura de conectividade da TIM. O projeto prevê a instalação de sete pontos de cobertura externa e 63 equipamentos distribuídos entre os galpões e as áreas operacionais da fábrica. A cobertura dedicada foi planejada para acompanhar o crescimento da produção e conectar não apenas os colaboradores e visitantes, mas também os sistemas operacionais e os próprios veículos ainda durante a fabricação. Com isso, diz o CEO da TIM, diferentes etapas da operação poderão trocar informações em tempo real, facilitando a integração dos processos industriais e abrindo espaço para novas aplicações digitais. A infraestrutura também foi dimensionada para acompanhar a expansão da capacidade produtiva da montadora, combinando conectividade e digitalização industrial. Para a TIM, o acordo com a BYD representa mais um avanço em um mercado que vem ganhando importância com a digitalização dos veículos e das operações industriais. A companhia já conecta mais de 670 mil veículos por meio de soluções da chamada Internet dos Veículos (Internet of Vehicles, ou IoV): uma tecnologia que permite integrar automóveis a redes e serviços digitais. “Esta parceria com a BYD une a digitalização de uma das mais importantes operações industriais em desenvolvimento no Brasil à evolução da conectividade embarcada dos veículos,” disse Griselli. Segundo Griselli, a operadora também oferece soluções de Internet das Coisas (IoT), computação em nuvem, cibersegurança e aplicações com inteligência artificial para apoiar a transformação digital de empresas de diferentes setores – que já são linhas de negócios relevantes dentro da companhia.

artigo.texto: Sellersburg updates zoning rules for data centers, solar farms Sellersburg, Indiana, has unanimously approved new zoning regulations for data centers, solar farms, and energy storage facilities, requiring developers to apply for zoning changes and go through a public approval process. Town leaders passed the ordinance to address what they described as a gray area in the previous development rules. Under the old ordinance, developers could argue that such facilities could be built in industrial zones. The new regulations establish "solar energy district" and "data center district" as specific zoning categories, though no properties are currently zoned for these uses. "Because there are no current zones of those uses, there would have to be a very public process that would have to go to where someone who wanted to potentially do that, if they ever did, they'd have to come through the town process to get something rezoned and basically so they'd have to send out letters," Town Manager Charlie Smith said. "According to state statute, there would be public hearings. They'd have to come to the zoning meeting, present to the zoning planning commission for their zoning change request, and then the planning commission would then make a recommendation to the town council, and the elected town council would have the ultimate final say on those type of uses," he added. Officials noted that only two properties within the town limits have the capacity to accommodate such developments. "I think that our biggest goal was to make sure that we just went on ahead and put it to rest and made everybody understand the fact that they were not in favor of nothing like this, nor do we want anything like this in our community, and to be able to tighten up the rules and regulations a little bit more," Sellersburg Town Council President Brad Amos said. The council president and town manager emphasized that the change ensures decisions remain with elected officials, reducing the likelihood of legal disputes. "This needs to be decided by the people that are appointed and elected by the body with the community's input, which it was. And then we could take this, put it to our standards, eliminate the gray area, and here's what it is. Here's what it's not. Here's the process. If you don't like it, maybe this isn't the community for you," Smith said. The new zoning standards also apply to large-scale energy storage facilities, with the regulation intended to protect properties within the town limits in the future.

artigo.texto: The boundaries between smart home technology, household appliances and residential energy management are becoming increasingly blurred. Midea, a name increasingly familiar to many Australian households through its air conditioners, refrigeration, laundry and other household appliances, is taking another step into that convergence with the launch of its residential energy storage business in Australia. Announced on 24 November 2026, the expansion brings Midea’s PowerInfi and Omni X energy storage solutions to the local market, following their Australian debut at All Energy Australia in Melbourne last month. Under its vision of “Energy Links All”, Midea is positioning its energy storage business around accessible residential energy solutions, drawing on its existing manufacturing capabilities and research and development across the broader household technology ecosystem. PowerInfi: An all-in-one residential energy storage system Leading Midea’s Australian energy storage portfolio is PowerInfi, an all-in-one residential energy storage system. When paired with a suitable rooftop solar installation, residential battery systems allow households to store surplus electricity generated during the day for use later, potentially reducing grid electricity purchases and improving the utilisation of existing solar investments. PowerInfi features a modular design and was recognised with a 2026 Red Dot Design Award, with judges highlighting its robust construction and user-oriented operating system. The system represents a significant expansion of Midea’s existing household technology portfolio, bringing energy storage alongside products that are among the largest consumers of electricity in Australian homes. Omni X provides another option for Australian households Midea is also introducing Omni X, a standalone energy storage solution showcased in a 7kWh battery configuration. Designed with flexibility in mind, Omni X provides installers and homeowners with another option when considering energy storage solutions suited to their household requirements. Australian pricing, available system configurations and detailed technical specifications were not provided as part of the launch announcement. From household appliances to whole-home energy management What makes Midea’s entry into this market particularly interesting to me is not simply the arrival of another residential battery manufacturer. Throughout 2026, DRN has been getting to know Midea across an increasingly diverse range of household appliances, from ice makers and benchtop dishwashers to inverter microwaves and, more recently, the Athena air conditioner. Each represents a different type of household energy demand, from refrigeration cycles and water heating to short bursts of high-power cooking and sustained climate control. In our Midea 3 Place Benchtop Mini Dishwasher Plus review, Peter measured actual electricity consumption across different wash programs, looking beyond the energy efficiency label to understand real-world running costs. Our coverage of the Midea 45L Smart Inverter Microwave explored inverter technology in a household appliance characterised by relatively short periods of high energy demand. The 12kg ice maker, meanwhile, represents another type of discretionary household load, where the timing of operation could potentially be aligned with periods of cheaper electricity or surplus solar generation. Meanwhile, my own experience with the Midea Athena has taken things a step further, integrating the air conditioner into Home Assistant and exploring how its operation can be aligned with my three-hour daily free electricity window. Rather than simply reacting to room temperature, I can begin to consider electricity pricing as part of the decision-making process for heating and cooling the home. (Full review is coming!) These are individual examples of something I have been exploring for some time: how we can move beyond evaluating household appliances in isolation and start considering their collective impact on household energy consumption. Connecting the dots with SMART MASTER and AI ECOMASTER Back in September, DRN covered Midea’s unveiling of its SMART MASTER whole-home AI ecosystem at IFA 2026. Among the technologies showcased in Berlin was AI ECOMASTER, Midea’s approach to coordinating household energy consumption across connected appliances, solar generation and battery storage, taking into account changing household demand and electricity prices. At the time, we identified intelligent energy management as one of the more compelling practical applications of whole-home AI. Today’s Australian residential energy storage announcement adds another important piece to that picture. With Midea now offering both energy storage and many of the appliances that consume electricity throughout the home, the potential exists to bring generation, storage and consumption together under a more coordinated energy management strategy. What remains to be established is how PowerInfi and Omni X fit into Midea’s wider SMART MASTER and AI ECOMASTER ambitions, particularly for Australian households. There are also important questions around interoperability with existing solar installations, third-party appliances, open smart home platforms such as Home Assistant and Australia’s increasingly diverse electricity tariffs. Having spent much of 2026 exploring different parts of Midea’s appliance portfolio, I am particularly interested in seeing how those pieces might eventually work together. The battery itself is only part of the story. The intelligence connecting it to the rest of the household could ultimately be just as important. artigo.texto: The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to send up to a million satellites into orbit for its Starmind data-processing network. In a news release, the FCC touted today’s decision as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space” and echoed the high-flown language that SpaceX used to describe the network in its application 10 months ago. “It promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization — one that can harness the full power of the sun,” the agency said. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the plan “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.” Carr signaled that he was all in on the Trump administration’s support for rapid data center expansion, despite a growing backlash that figured in this month’s midterm elections. He said that “compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership” in artificial intelligence. “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” Carr said. In a post to X, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk told Carr that his praise was “much appreciated.” “This will be a great asset to America and the world,” Musk said. Proponents of solar-powered orbital data centers say such constellations will address the top concerns about terrestrial data centers, including land use, power consumption and water requirements for cooling. Critics point to the engineering challenges, including concerns about cooling the satellites, managing space traffic and dealing with orbital debris. In approving SpaceX’s application, the FCC rejected opposition from Amazon and Viasat, as well as from the American Astronomical Society, which raised concerns about the constellation’s impact on the night sky. The AAS said in a statement that it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s decision. The FCC attached several conditions to its authorization, including requirements for communications backups, regular updates and a detailed plan for orbital debris mitigation. SpaceX was cleared to operate its satellites at orbits ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers (310 to 623 miles) in altitude. The first satellite is to be put into operation no later than 2033, and the FCC calls for the full constellation to be operating by 2040. In August, SpaceX announced that it was partnering with Nvidia to design the compute payload for the Starmind AI1 satellite. “Each of the Starmind satellites will include Nvidia Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs for datacenter-class space compute,” SpaceX said at the time. SpaceX’s facility in Redmond, Wash., makes the satellites for the Starlink telecommunications network — but in a filing related to this year’s initial public offering, SpaceX said its operation in Bastrop, Texas, would be put in charge of producing AI compute satellites. The FCC said it is continuing to review additional orbital data center proposals and intends to issue decisions on each proposal “according to the agency’s regular procedures.” Among other companies planning data-processing satellite constellations are: - Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, which has proposed a 51,600-satellite constellation for its Project Sunrise initiative. - Redmond-based Starcloud, which has applied to the FCC to operate an 88,000-satellite data center constellation. - Cowboy Space, formerly known as Aetherflux, which has applied to deploy a 20,000-satellite constellation. The California-based company is leasing a 291,035-square-foot facility in Kent to serve as its launch vehicle and satellite design hub. “We will be building our rocket engines and solar [power] systems here too,” the company said. - Google, which is testing satellites for a data-processing constellation called Project Suncatcher. Last week, Google announced that its first Project Suncatcher satellites would be launched by Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket, with liftoff planned for no earlier than 2029. - Sophia Space, a California startup with Seattle connections that is planning to create a 10-satellite constellation for high-performance orbital computing. Last week, Sophia Space announced that its orbital operating system was deployed on Kepler Communications’ optical data relay constellation.

artigo.texto: The EU and UK have reached an agreement to link their Emissions Trading Schemes (ETS), with the aim of going operational by 2028. Incineration of waste, excluding landfill, is included among the sectors and activities covered by the linking agreement. EU and UK leaders have committed to applying the agreement as of 1 January 2028, subject to the ratification process and entry into force in the EU and UK. The intention to link the two systems was announced at the first EU-UK Summit in May 2025 and means that the same set of climate rules related to emissions trading will apply in the EU and the UK, creating a level playing field for businesses on both sides of the Channel. The European Commission (EC) says the agreement will also create a ‘larger, more liquid carbon market with a more stable carbon price’. As a result of the agreement, the UK will expand its ETS to include aviation and maritime, which the EC says will cover over 10 million tonnes of additional CO2 emissions as part of the system. The agreement provides the basis for a possible future mutual exemption from the respective carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAM), reducing red tape and costs for companies across the UK and the EU. The UK ETS sets an overall cap on total emissions from in-scope sectors, which is divided into allowances. It currently applies to energy-intensive industries, the power generation sector, and the aviation industry. Operators who are covered by the scheme must acquire allowances through auctions run by the UK ETS Authority, from other participants through secondary markets, or, if eligible, they can obtain UKAs from their free allocation. The scheme creates a market for carbon allowances, allowing operators who decarbonise to trade allowances with those whose operations continue to emit.

artigo.texto: A desaceleração dos data centers O lado positivo de uma pausa na alucinante corrida dos laboratórios de IA Atualizado 24/11/2026 Tenho um amigo que recentemente decidiu tirar um ano de folga de seu cargo de professor titular de matemática para estudar segurança em inteligência artificial (IA). Com a OpenAI divulgando 722 artigos que alegam soluções para 377 questões matemáticas até então não resolvidas, e com os modelos de IA ficando cada vez melhores, ele está preocupado se sua profissão tem futuro. Se um matemático brilhante pode ser substituído com tanta facilidade, por que o resto de nós não está preocupado? Parte da resposta pode ser que, embora a IA possa resolver uma variante da conjectura de Navier-Stokes, meu banco ainda não criou um chatbot confiável capaz de resolver um problema de transferência de fundos sem que eu exija, irritado, falar com um ser humano. Os laboratórios de IA estão usando técnicas recursivas de autoaperfeiçoamento para dotar seus modelos ainda não lançados de capacidades de pesquisa ainda mais milagrosas, e os primeiros a adotar a tecnologia em alguns setores já contam com bots negociando contratos e conciliando faturas com entregas. Mas a adoção por empresas tradicionais está avançando lentamente no geral, e as capacidades de IA que elas podem usar ainda são modestas. Por que, então, tantas empresas de IA estão usando tanta capacidade computacional para desenvolver modelos mais sofisticados, cujas capacidades só algumas poucas conseguem aproveitar em sua plenitude? Além da emoção de criar uma forma nova e mais rápida de inteligência, acredita-se que o primeiro laboratório a criar um modelo totalmente capaz de se autoaperfeiçoar se beneficiará de suas capacidades que melhoram exponencialmente e ficará permanentemente à frente da concorrência. No entanto, parece improvável que os concorrentes não sigam o exemplo em pouco tempo. O líder poderia ter um ou dois meses de vantagem, ainda que com um crescimento exponencial de capacidade, mas os seguidores mais ágeis podem muito bem descobrir técnicas que lhes permitam ultrapassá-lo e assumir a liderança. É exatamente isso que vem acontecendo na corrida pela capacidade de IA, com as posições de liderança dos modelos mudando com frequência. Parece improvável que qualquer vencedor domine para sempre - especialmente se puderem contratar funcionários uns dos outros - a menos que literalmente neutralizem ou destruam seus concorrentes. Esperamos que essa não seja a intenção de ninguém. Outro motivo pode ser simplesmente que nenhum dos líderes dos principais laboratórios de IA confia nos outros para lidar com o poder que vem acompanhado de capacidades extraordinárias de IA. Cada um é motivado não só pelo desejo de vencer, mas também pela sensação de que apenas ele é capaz de lidar bem com esse poder. Outra fonte de impulso é o medo de que a China alcance os EUA. Modelos chineses de IA têm se mantido apenas alguns meses atrás dos modelos líderes dos EUA. Assim como na corrida por capacidades nos EUA, é improvável que fiquem muito mais para trás, a menos que os EUA consigam montar uma campanha mais eficaz para impedir o acesso chinês aos chips mais avançados, tanto na China quanto no resto do mundo. Com os principais laboratórios de IA sob intensa pressão competitiva para continuar expandindo as fronteiras das capacidades dessa tecnologia, a resistência à ampliação dos recursos computacionais não é algo tão ruim Não importa o motivo, o enorme investimento em recursos computacionais para o treinamento de modelos pressiona os laboratórios de IA a gerar mais receita - quanto antes, melhor. Por isso que a Anthropic lançou uma joint venture, a Ode, para impulsionar o uso da IA em empresas não-tecnológicas, usando engenheiros da Anthropic integrados a essas empresas. Isso significa que alguns bancos poderão ter chatbots muito superiores em breve, pressionando todos os bancos a seguirem o exemplo. Quanto tempo levará para que os empregos de atendimento ao cliente se juntem aos de professores de matemática? É claro que há várias maneiras de implementar a IA. É possível substituir os empregos existentes ou redesenhar o trabalho e o treinamento de habilidades para que as capacidades dos funcionários atuais sejam muito ampliadas. A primeira opção gerará receitas mais depressa, mas resultará num desastre social; a segunda exigirá mais tempo e reflexão, mas preservará empregos e estabilidade. As empresas que estão sendo alvo de um aumento no uso da IA estão na melhor posição para implementar uma IA centrada nos funcionários, mas precisam assumir mais responsabilidade pelo futuro de seus funcionários, mesmo que o governo ofereça mais incentivos para que as corporações resistam aos lucros de curto prazo obtidos por meio de demissões. Há muitas ideias viáveis - como impostos sobre o uso de tokens corporativos e créditos para treinamento de funcionários -, mas poucos governos as puseram em prática. A conclusão parece inevitável: a sociedade não está pronta para uma implantação em larga escala da IA. Mas talvez estejamos vendo agora um movimento para desacelerar a enorme expansão da capacidade computacional. Muitos líderes políticos nos EUA estão exigindo uma pausa nas aprovações de novos data centers, ecoando preocupações das comunidades locais e chamando a atenção para as consequências mais amplas de uma implantação descontrolada da IA. Diante da perspectiva de que haja menos recursos computacionais disponíveis para monetizar a IA no médio prazo, investidores serão forçados a limitar a alocação de recursos onerosos para o desenvolvimento de modelos. Uma desaceleração na construção também eleva o custo do uso da IA, o que vai mudar o cálculo por trás das decisões de substituir funcionários. Isso permite que a oferta de chips e memória se equilibre, de modo que os custos não aumentem inexoravelmente no futuro. Além disso, permite que a regulamentação da IA se atualize, de modo que os fundadores de laboratórios de IA não sejam os únicos a det

artigo.texto: ReData deve ser regulamentado nos próximos dias, diz ministro Frederico de Siqueira Filho prevê políticas de data centers e cabos submarinos para 2027 e defende ampliar o papel do MCom na infraestrutura digital. O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, afirmou nesta quarta-feira, 25, que a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (ReData) está na fase final de discussão dentro do governo federal e que a expectativa é de que o processo seja resolvido nos próximos dias. Já as políticas nacionais de data centers e de cabos submarinos deverão ficar para 2027. Em entrevista à imprensa durante o Fórum Dig.IA, em Brasília (DF), o ministro disse que as discussões sobre o ReData envolvem a Casa Civil e a Presidência da República. “Mas a gente acredita que nos próximos dias isso será resolvido, perante a importância do tema”, afirmou Siqueira Filho. Durante seu discurso no encerramento do evento, o ministro destacou a participação do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva nas articulações para viabilizar os incentivos ao setor de data centers. Segundo ele, o Ministério das Comunicações (MCom) também trabalhou na elaboração do regime em conjunto com a Receita Federal, o Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços (MDIC) e o Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME). O objetivo do governo, segundo Siqueira Filho, é transformar o Brasil em um polo de infraestrutura de data centers voltados à inteligência artificial (IA) na América Latina, aproveitando as condições da matriz energética brasileira. Políticas nacionais ficam para 2027 Questionado sobre a possibilidade de publicação das políticas nacionais de data centers e de cabos submarinos ainda em 2026, o ministro descartou a perspectiva. “Não, acredito que não. Isso vai ficar para 2027”, respondeu. Segundo Siqueira Filho, a política nacional de data centers será complementar ao ReData. Entre as medidas em discussão estão a redução da burocracia e a articulação com estados e municípios para simplificar os processos de licenciamento dos empreendimentos. “Balcão único de licenciamento, é isso que a gente está propondo para dar mais visibilidade e segurança jurídica para quem decide investir no Brasil”, afirmou. No caso dos cabos submarinos, o governo trabalha na descentralização das zonas de ancoragem ao longo da costa brasileira, na atualização das cartas náuticas em articulação com a Marinha e na proteção das áreas de chegada dos cabos, considerando seu caráter de infraestrutura crítica. A proposta envolve a participação de órgãos responsáveis pela defesa e pela segurança nacional. O ministro também destacou a necessidade de compatibilizar a presença dos cabos submarinos com as atividades de exploração de petróleo na costa brasileira. Ainda não há definição sobre a necessidade de alterações legislativas para implementar a política. “A gente primeiro está definindo o conceito”, explicou o ministro, acrescentando que o objetivo é reduzir a burocracia e dar agilidade e previsibilidade aos investidores. Infraestrutura digital no próximo governo Lula Siqueira Filho também defendeu que o Ministério das Comunicações amplie sua atuação na agenda de infraestrutura digital durante o próximo mandato do presidente Lula. Na avaliação do ministro, a expansão da inteligência artificial exige investimentos em redes resilientes, tecnologias de comunicação por satélite, cabos submarinos e ampliação da cobertura 5G. “O tema digital está no centro da discussão do governo”, declarou. Segundo o ministro, tratar essas atividades sob a perspectiva da infraestrutura digital contribuirá tanto para o fortalecimento do setor produtivo quanto para o do próprio Ministério das Comunicações. MCom vai ouvir provedores sobre Norma 4 Outro tema abordado pelo ministro foi a discussão sobre a Norma 4. Siqueira Filho afirmou que ainda não tratou pessoalmente do assunto e que pretende conversar com a Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) antes de estabelecer uma posição. O ministro também afirmou que pretende ouvir os provedores de internet e as demais empresas do setor para compreender os impactos da discussão. Funttel destina R$ 150 milhões à inteligência artificial Durante o evento, o Ministério das Comunicações informou a destinação de R$ 150 milhões do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel) a projetos relacionados à inteligência artificial e à infraestrutura digital. Desse montante, R$ 46 milhões são destinados ao desenvolvimento de uma plataforma nacional de inteligência artificial que deverá integrar data centers regionais e ampliar a capacidade computacional no interior do país. Outros R$ 104 milhões são destinados a projetos executados em parceria com o CPQD, no triênio de 2026 a 2028. As iniciativas incluem pesquisas sobre redes 6G, ferramentas de inteligência artificial generativa para operadoras de telecomunicações, soluções de segurança e privacidade digital e aplicações de telemedicina. O ministro afirmou ainda que o Brasil atingiu a marca de 1 gigawatt (GW) de energia elétrica contratada para data centers e ocupa a 12ª posição entre os maiores mercados mundiais do segmento. Siqueira Filho também destacou a ampliação das possibilidades de aplicação dos recursos do Fundo de Universalização dos Serviços de Telecomunicações (Fust), incluindo investimentos em data centers e na modernização das redes de telecomunicações. Segundo ele, mais de R$ 300 milhões foram investidos na recuperação das redes de fibra óptica no Rio Grande do Sul. O ministro citou ainda o lançamento, nesta quarta-feira, do Conecta CRAS, iniciativa de conectividade dos Centros de Referência de Assistência Social com recursos do Fust, que se soma às políticas de atendimento a escolas públicas e unidades básicas de saúde.
