artigo.texto: The South Korean government said it will invest a total of 15 trillion won ($10.2 billion) by 2030 to secure 13.6 gigawatts of battery energy storage systems, a 3.4-fold increase from about 4 gigawatts of installed battery storage capacity at the end of last year. Lee Ho-hyun, vice minister of climate, energy and environment, said at the 24th Energy Strategy Forum held at the Shilla Hotel in Seoul's Jung district on the 24th that it is "now time for an energy storage revolution." He added that the government "will significantly expand policy and budget support to grow the ESS market." To that end, the ministry plans to invest 1.1 trillion won ($749 million) in 2027 alone to build 2.7 gigawatts of new storage capacity. Annual bidding volumes, set at about 0.5 gigawatt under the 11th Basic Plan for Long-Term Electricity Supply and Demand, rose to 1.08 gigawatts last year and 1.18 gigawatts this year. The push for storage reflects the growing importance of flexible power sources that can bridge the gap between electricity generation and consumption as renewables account for a larger share of the mix. "Going forward, producing a lot of energy will not be enough," the vice minister said. "The key to the success or failure of the energy transition is how reliably the electricity we generate can be delivered to the time and place where it is needed." Kim Jae-eon, a professor of electrical engineering at Chungbuk National University, said in a keynote address that the government's large-scale deployment plan must translate into competitiveness for domestic industry. "We need to build an implementation framework so that domestic procurement and demonstration projects lead to actual business," the professor said.

artigo.texto: Em 23 de novembro, a Valencia Plaza informou que a SpainDC ainda finalizava o recurso contra o Real Decreto 1032/2026 e previa apresentá-lo ao Supremo em 25 ou 26 de novembro. A associação havia anunciado em 20 de novembro que contestaria a norma e pediria sua suspensão cautelar. A declaração da SpainDC confirma a intenção da entidade; o relato de 23 de novembro registra o prazo previsto para o protocolo. O que determina o decreto espanhol O Conselho de Ministros aprovou o Real Decreto 1032/2026 em 20 de novembro. A norma foi publicada no Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE) em 21 de novembro e prevê entrada em vigor no dia seguinte. O texto oficial estabelece que a maioria das obrigações se aplica a centros de dados com pelo menos 10 MW de capacidade de acesso à rede, incluindo certos agrupamentos de instalações no mesmo local e sob o mesmo proprietário. Esse limite mede o acesso à rede, não a potência de TI. O artigo 13 tem um patamar separado para obrigações de divulgação de informações: 500 kW de potência de TI. Para entender o alcance da norma, separe a capacidade de acesso à rede da potência de TI: os limites medem coisas diferentes. O decreto também separa duas regras de energia renovável. Uma exige que 80% do consumo total seja coberto por autoconsumo elegível ou contratos de energia renovável que atendam às condições da norma. Em geral, a geração associada deve ter começado a operar no máximo 36 meses antes do início das operações do centro de dados ou do primeiro uso da energia. Os contratos elegíveis precisam durar pelo menos seis anos. A outra regra é horária: em cada hora, ao menos 80% do consumo deve ter cobertura equivalente de eletricidade renovável gerada naquela mesma hora. O texto reconhece, sob condições específicas, autoconsumo, contratos renováveis e armazenamento. Há ainda uma alternativa de transição de cinco anos para instalações elegíveis que participem tecnicamente do sistema automático de redução de potência. Nesse percurso, a cobertura exigida nas horas P1 é de 60% até 31 de dezembro de 2028. A partir de 1º de janeiro de 2029, passa a 70% nas horas P1 e 60% nas P2 até o fim da transição. Antes da aplicação do sistema europeu de etiquetagem, os limites gerais de transição são PUE máximo de 1,25 e WUE máximo de 0,1. O prazo para cumprir a exigência de eficiência energética começa após dois anos de operação; para a de eficiência hídrica, após um ano, conforme o calendário de verificação do decreto. As regras de soberania digital têm escopo específico: abrangem centros de dados que hospedem sistemas do setor público classificados como de nível alto no Esquema Nacional de Segurança da Espanha. A norma prevê condições de localização e acesso na União Europeia e no Espaço Econômico Europeu, além de exceções para operações tecnicamente necessárias. Os argumentos em torno das novas regras O preâmbulo do decreto afirma que a procura por acesso à rede pelos centros de dados pode competir por capacidade limitada. A justificativa do governo é alinhar a expansão digital à rede elétrica e às metas de energia e meio ambiente, com exigências de geração renovável, eficiência e acesso à rede. A SpainDC considera impraticáveis as regras de adicionalidade renovável e de correspondência horária. A associação também argumenta que a alternativa ligada à redução automática de potência pode ameaçar a operação ininterrupta dos centros de dados e afetar investimentos. Essas são as posições da entidade sobre os efeitos da norma.

artigo.texto: According to a MoP proposal, battery storage could be required for rooftop solar systems above 10 kW The proposed requirement is at least 20% of the system's daily energy generation, unless a different proportion is specified The storage provision is expected to take effect from April 1, 2028, under the draft India's Ministry of Power (MoP) has proposed requiring battery energy storage systems (BESS) for rooftop solar installations above 10 kW, with effect from April 1, 2028. The proposal is part of the draft Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Amendment Rules, 2026. It proposes that the storage provision will take effect where State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) have not specified a different capacity threshold. The proposal gives state regulators flexibility to determine the threshold and storage requirements based on local conditions. As per the draft, SERC may prescribe the capacity threshold above which prosumers must install energy storage. The required storage capacity would be at least 20% of the renewable energy system's total daily generation, unless the respective Commission specifies a different proportion. In the absence of a threshold set by a State Commission, the proposed requirement would apply to renewable energy systems with an installed capacity exceeding 10 kW. The ministry said falling battery storage costs, supported by economies of scale, technological innovation and market competition, have improved the economic viability of storage deployment. Integrating batteries with rooftop solar could also help shift surplus electricity to evening hours, support grid stability and ease operational pressure on distribution companies. Additionally, the draft also proposes allowing consumers, including commercial and industrial (C&I) units and MSMEs, to install rooftop solar capacity beyond their sanctioned load. This will be subject to limits set by State Commissions based on local grid capacity and technical requirements. However, consumers would be allowed to feed electricity into the grid only up to their sanctioned load, unless the distribution company approves a higher limit. Power injected beyond the approved limit would not qualify for compensation and could attract penalties. The draft also proposes delaying the rollout of Time-of-Day (ToD) tariffs to align it with smart meter installation. Under the proposal, ToD tariffs would apply to consumers with a load of 10 kW and above from April 1, 2028, and to other non-agricultural consumers from April 1, 2029. This will give state regulators the flexibility to decide solar and peak hours based on electricity demand and generation patterns in their respective states, instead of following fixed timings. Earlier, the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) proposed making co-located energy storage mandatory for new ground-mounted solar and onshore wind projects commissioned after July 1, 2027 (see India May Mandate Storage For Solar, Wind Projects From 2027).

artigo.texto: Two forces are behind falling energy storage costs, which is a boon for the clean energy industry. The market features growing competition among battery manufacturers and a possible lithium surplus in 2027. Here's what to know As SolarQuarter detailed, InfoLink's Energy Storage Supply Chain Price Forecast Report projects a slight lithium surplus in 2027. Battery-grade lithium carbonate prices could fall to about 99,800–117,900 Chinese yuan ($14,945-$17,656) per U.S. ton in the first half of that year. The forecast comes after declines in storage-cell prices. In July 2026, the tax-inclusive average prices for both 280 amp-hour and 314 amp-hour lithium iron phosphate storage cells dropped 4% to 0.36 yuan (around 5 cents) per watt-hour, according to the outlet. Smaller, 100 amp-hour cells averaged 0.44 yuan per watt-hour, down 2.7% from June 2026. For households facing grid instability and time-of-use electricity rates, whole-home batteries can keep essentials running during outages, while leases can help protect homes without upwards of $20,000 in upfront costs. EasyHome is a marketplace connecting battery shoppers with trusted partners offering unique prices and exclusive deals — another avenue for homeowners exploring backup power as storage-cell costs decline. More background The cost of lithium iron phosphate cathode material used in storage applications declined to approximately 47,800 yuan ($7,158) per U.S. ton, bringing tax-inclusive storage-cell production costs to around 0.31 yuan (around 5 cents) per watt-hour, according to SolarQuarter. These declines can translate to savings down the road for consumers looking to tap into their storage systems. Home batteries can also help reduce energy bills by supplying stored electricity during expensive peak-pricing periods. For households seeking a smaller-scale option, Pila offers plug-and-play battery backup at a substantially lower price point than whole-home backup systems. What's being done? Intense competition among battery manufacturers as supply expands is putting additional pressure on storage-cell prices, according to SolarQuarter. Lithium carbonate prices could still rise before the projected surplus in 2027. InfoLink's September and October 2026 price forecast is about 131,500–136,100 yuan ($19,692-20,381) per U.S. ton, above the expected August 2026 average near 127,000 yuan ($19,018) per U.S. ton. The firm expects seasonal demand and restocking to support that increase. According to SolarQuarter, China will begin taxing lithium-ion battery consumption at 2% on September 1, 2026, with the rate rising to 4% on September 1, 2027. Meanwhile, the estimated U.S. tariff rate for lithium-ion battery systems originating in China is around 40.9%. artigo.texto: New solutions address power needs across the source-grid, power-distribution and cabinet-side layers of AI data center infrastructure LAS VEGAS, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As AI workloads scale, data centers are placing new demands on power infrastructure, making reliable electricity supply essential to continuous operations. At RE+ 2026, part of North America's Smart Energy Week, EVE Energy introduced a full-scenario energy storage portfolio for AI data centers (AIDC), with solutions designed to support power requirements from the source-grid side through power distribution to cabinet-level backup. The company also showcased energy storage solutions for commercial and industrial, residential and telecommunications applications, alongside emerging all-solid-state and sodium-ion battery technologies. From the source grid to the cabinet: an integrated AIDC power architecture During the exhibition, EVE held a dedicated AIDC product launch and presented solutions for three application layers: the green zone, or source-grid side; the gray zone, or power-distribution side; and the white zone, or cabinet side. The portfolio includes rack-level battery backup solutions and is designed to address requirements ranging from millisecond-scale load smoothing to long-duration energy management. Source-Grid Side: High-Power Energy Storage and Frequency Regulation. On the green zone's source-grid side, EVE Energy introduced the 1P 5MWh ESS, which the company describes as the industry's first 20-foot, 5 MWh, 1P high-rate energy storage system. The system balances 5 MWh of energy capacity with 1P power capability in a standard 20-foot container. It is rated at 1P, with a peak rate of up to 1.2P, and delivers 20,000 equivalent cycles in frequency-regulation applications. System efficiency reaches 93.6%, while auxiliary power requirements are reduced by 20%, according to EVE. The solution integrates DC, AC and EMS capabilities at the plant level. At a 100 MWh project scale, the configuration can reduce the number of cabinets by three, lower transportation costs by more than 40% and reduce land use by more than 13%. EVE reports annual system availability of 99%, along with higher returns over the system's full lifecycle. The system is equipped with what EVE describes as the industry's first 300+ Ah dedicated frequency-regulation cell, featuring a capacity of 315 Ah and a volumetric energy density of 395 Wh/L. According to EVE, no lithium plating occurs at the cell interface under high-rate operating conditions, helping ensure cell safety and long service life. Also on display was Mr.Giant 3.0, EVE Energy's flagship long-duration energy storage system. Following 700 days of demonstrated operation, the system achieved efficiency of more than 95.5% and a cycle count reaching 10,000 cycles. EVE says the system can deliver lifecycle benefits equivalent to an additional two years. Power-distribution side: backup for transient loads. EVE presented its Fortron 6C/10C backup power cabinet, designed to support short-duration, high-power load events. The cabinet supports continuous discharge at up to 10C and can deliver 660 kW for five minutes. It has a 15-year design life and is compatible with uninterruptible power supply (UPS) backup systems, with support for high-voltage direct current (HVDC) applications. The modular architecture is designed for factory pre-integration and rapid deployment. Safety provisions include a reinforced cell design, compartmentalized thermal isolation, staged overcurrent protection and coordinated fire-suppression systems. These features are intended to help protect the system while supporting fast-response backup applications. Cabinet side: rack-level support for dynamic AI loads. EVE also introduced a rack-level energy storage system combining a battery backup unit (BBU) with a capacitor backup unit (CBU). The BBU uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) high-power cells in a high-density 3U form factor and supports discharge rates of up to 48C. The system is designed to smooth load fluctuations across a 1-millisecond-to-10-second window, while providing backup power transfer in less than 2 milliseconds. According to EVE, The LIC hybrid supercapacitor has a response time of 1 millisecond or less. Building a full-scenario energy storage platform for AIDC Spanning the green zone on the source-grid side, the gray zone for power distribution and the white zone at the rack level, EVE Energy's newly launched AIDC energy-storage portfolio reflects years of sustained investment, development and expertise across the company's full range of battery products. With one of the world's most comprehensive lithium battery product portfolios, EVE Energy is among the few companies capable of directly supplying both battery cells and systems across the entire AIDC power chain. The company's end-to-end capabilities extend from battery cell development through system integration. The integrated approach is intended to simplify procurement and operations for customers. A single-source offering can reduce the number of vendor relationships and streamline purchasing and project decisions. Coordinated development of cells, BMS and system integration can also clarify accountability when issues arise. A unified technical platform and service contact are designed to reduce maintenance complexity and operations and maintenance (O&M) costs for data centers that operate around the clock. EVE says it ranked No. 2 globally in energy-storage cell shipments in the first half of 2026. The company reports cumulative global shipments of 230 GWh and inclusion in S&P Global's Tier 1 list of energy storage system integrators. Building on its strategy of "global manufacturing, global cooperation and global service," EVE says it will continue developing grid-forming capabilities and energy storage products for the full range of AIDC applications. artigo.texto: Data center proposal in Northern New York met with pushback CHAZY, N.Y. (WCAX) - A proposed data center in New York’s North Country is facing resistance from the community. On the shores of Lake Champlain, Chazy is home to large apple orchards and poultry farms. It’s also home to the NorthStar Technology Center. The owners of NorthStar say they are exploring the possibility of building a data center there. While we don’t know much about the project, we do know it would meet state requirements and fall below the threshold of the state’s moratorium, which is 50 megawatts. Despite this, residents in the town say they have concerns and questions about the proposal. “My immediate thoughts were, well, it’s time for action,” said Nelson Pelton of Chazy. Pelton said the prospect of a data center in a place he’s called home for three decades worries him. “Really value things like water for our agriculture, preserving the environment for the amazing habitats we have around here and also keeping our energy bills low for people that are already dealing with already high costs; that’s a big concern to me,” Pelton said. The Rockefeller Institute said New York has around 150 data centers. Molly Ryan, the executive director of the Clinton County Industrial Development Agency, said data centers can bring short-term job creation and potentially lower taxes. “Usually data centers are a couple hundred million dollar investment and therefore property taxes usually end up significantly going down,” Ryan said. But she said data centers also have drawbacks, many of which are top of mind for residents in Chazy. “Concerned about noise pollution, water usage and groundwater contamination, along with energy rates,” said Alex Sweet of Chazy. The owners of the NorthStar Technology Center did not reply to a request for comment. However, WCAX News did obtain a mockup presented to the Chazy Town Board, which shows the preliminary placement of the data center at the existing facility. Neither the town nor the county said they are weighing in just yet. “We believe in local control and every community has to decide what’s right for them and they should be establishing what works in their community,” Ryan said. Town officials have scheduled a public meeting on the proposed data center on Dec. 7. It will be held at the Chazy Central School auditorium at 6 p.m. Copyright 2026 WCAX. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: US Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-NC, has introduced bipartisan legislation to prevent Chinese telecommunications companies previously identified as national security threats from accessing American data centers and cloud services. The Digital Infrastructure Security Act of 2026, House Bill 11100, introduced by Harrigan and US Rep. Dave Min, D-CA, seeks to extend existing federal telecommunications restrictions to digital infrastructure that handles sensitive American financial, medical, and military information. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) previously revoked or denied telecommunications licenses for China Telecom Americas, China Unicom Americas, and China Mobile USA over national security concerns. However, those actions did not automatically remove the companies’ equipment and connections from American data centers. According to Harrigan’s office, investigations identified more than 108,000 instances of Chinese-linked networks redirecting internet traffic between 2018 and 2025, raising concerns about foreign interference and the potential exposure of sensitive information. “China has spent years stealing American technology and targeting our communications networks, and we know they’re not going to stop,” Harrigan said in a press release announcing the legislation. Harrigan said the legislation would address gaps in existing federal restrictions by prohibiting the companies from operating domestic data centers or conducting business with Americans through cloud services, including through subsidiaries and other intermediaries. “What concerns me is that we’ve already identified these companies as national security threats, revoked their licenses, and somehow still allowed them to keep a foothold in our data centers,” he said. “When we’re talking about the systems that handle Americans’ financial information, medical records, and sensitive military data, I think that’s a pretty reasonable safeguard.” Under the legislation, the FCC would enforce the restrictions, with fines of up to $1 million per violation or per day for continuing violations. Existing operations and contracts would have 180 days following enactment to comply. It would also establish a waiver process subject to a federal national security assessment. The legislation comes as North Carolina grapples with the rapid expansion of data centers and their impact on electricity demand, water resources, and local infrastructure. More than 30 local governments across the state have enacted temporary moratoriums on data center development, while state lawmakers repealed the sales tax exemption for electricity consumed by data centers earlier this year. Broader legislation, Senate Bill 730, the Ratepayer Protection Act, remains stalled in the Senate and would establish additional ratepayer protections, water-use standards, and restrictions on data center ownership by entities tied to foreign adversaries, including China. Harrigan criticizes Nvidia CEO’s reinstatement The legislation coincides with heightened scrutiny in Washington over the relationship between American technology companies and China, including Monday’s reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang resigned Nov. 12 following reports of extramarital affairs, including an alleged relationship with a woman suspected by US officials of having ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia’s board of directors unanimously voted to reinstate Huang on Nov. 23 following discussions with Huang and input from senior federal government officials. The company said its board was confident that his reinstatement posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump supported Huang’s reinstatement, while several congressional Republicans, including Harrigan, criticized the decision on X. “For the past two years, I have privately said there is no way Jensen Huang can argue for the exportation of advanced American chips to China without being compromised,” Harrigan wrote in a post on X. “Turns out, well, we all know.” Harrigan argued that Huang’s reinstatement was premature and called for further congressional investigation into the potential national security implications. “His reinstatement today at this juncture is a mistake,” he continued. “There may come a time when forgiveness is warranted, but there are still too many unanswered questions and too much unmitigated risk. Today’s coordinated action between the company and this administration is likely to whitewash this risk.” Harrigan called for investigations by the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence and Foreign Affairs Committees. “Today, we sent a signal that one man’s financial impact on our economy outweighs the importance of good governance, good citizenship, and adherence to the law,” he said. “That is a dangerous precedent to set, and one I believe will come at a significant cost to our country in the long run.” Harrigan’s Digital Infrastructure Security Act was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on Nov. 19.

artigo.texto: Residents in Sutton and neighboring Central Massachusetts communities worry that the giant data center proposed by the Kraft Group would inflate their energy bills. In reality, it could also raise costs for customers across New England. The computer facility, which would support power-intensive artificial intelligence services across a 10-building campus, likely would require hundreds of millions of dollars in upgrades to electricity infrastructure, according to energy specialists. Those kinds of costs have often been passed on broadly to customers in this region and in other states. Many of Sutton’s 9,700 residents are already up in arms about the magnitude of the proposed $16 billion project by the Kraft family, owners of the New England Patriots. A January town meeting is scheduled at which residents may vote to ban data centers, and stall or kill the Krafts’ massive project. According to the proposal, when fully built, the campus would use as much as 900 megawatts of electricity — comparable to what a medium-sized city requires — and would be among the largest such facilities in the country. “The scale of that certainly made my eyes go wide,” said Dan Dolan, president of the New England Power Generators Association. Dolan, whose group represents power plant owners and energy developers, knows how hard it is to get even smaller projects up and running. Developers usually spend months, if not years, prospecting for sites that check all the regulatory boxes. Then they have to go through rigorous studies by energy agencies to determine how a site could get hooked up to the grid and at what cost. “You put all of those elements together” for the Kraft plan, “and this would be a Herculean task,” Dolan said. As Sutton weighs the Kraft project, efforts are already underway locally and across the country to make data centers pay their own way — part of a campaign to block or slow development of the warehouse-sized campuses that have sparked outrage over their impact on electricity bills as well as air, noise, and water pollution. Governor Maura Healey issued an executive order in September requiring data centers to fund the full cost of energy infrastructure upgrades and provide new clean energy to the grid. The order also imposes a fine if developers can’t meet clean energy requirements. And New England’s grid manager, ISO New England, has just proposed a regulation, currently under review by a federal agency, to make large customers like data centers pay for their own upgrades. In Massachusetts, where electricity rates are already among the highest in the nation, the ISO New England proposal, along with the governor’s order, could potentially prevent rates from going even higher as more data centers are built to support growing AI usage, industry experts say. “The standard business model of the industry is to socialize costs of new infrastructure,” said Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard University’s Law School. There’s now progress in putting pressure on the developers to shoulder the costs, he said. But he warns ratepayers may still end up with higher bills. In the proposal presented at a Select Board meeting this month, Town Manager Austin Cyganiewicz emphasized that the full cost of energy supply, infrastructure, and interconnection should be borne by the project developer. “Massachusetts energy consumers, communities, and residents should not bear the costs or burdens of data center development, operations, or energy and water needs,” he said. Robert Kraft’s companies, the Kraft Group and Unified Global Packaging Group, own a 383-acre parcel in an industrial area of the town, sitting directly under a major transmission line. The Kraft Group has long tried to find a tenant to occupy the largest lot on the property, but to no avail. In late October, executives at the companies approached Sutton’s town manager with a proposal to build a data center campus on the site. The proposal made public by Sutton officials does not disclose details on how the Kraft Group plans to power the data center or handle its costs. The proposal said that the developers was in discussions with ISO New England and the local utility company, National Grid. An ISO spokesperson told the Globe that while “a conversation took place” with the Kraft Group, the organization has not received any formal proposal or launched any studies. A National Grid spokesperson said the utility company discussed the project with the Kraft Group, and has begun studying the site. The study will cover energy demand, available grid capacity, and any potential required infrastructure upgrades. The spokesperson added that the customer, in this case the Krafts, covers the cost of such studies. The Kraft Group did not respond to a request for comment. Given the experience of other communities where electric rates have jumped with the arrival of data centers, it’s no surprise Sutton officials and residents were quick to question who would pay for the upgrades needed for the Kraft project, with many voicing staunch opposition in public meetings. And infrastructure upgrades are not the only way consumers could see bills spike. Data centers also can drive up costs for all customers at peak demand times, such as summer heat waves. “When demand goes up, as it’s going to go up for electricity . . . then prices go up, and we all pay those higher market prices,” said Peskoe, of Harvard’s Electricity Law Initiative. In Ohio, which has more than 250 data centers, consumers saw electricity supply prices increase by 10 to 35 percent in June 2025, according to Ohio’s Office of Consumers’ Counsel. The following month, a state utilities organization created a tariff that requires data centers to pay for most of their own electric capacity. artigo.texto: A Europa está resgatando suas velhas usinas desativadas para lhes dar uma segunda vida: virar data centers Com 700 MW assegurados e filas de espera que chegam a 10 anos, usinas desativadas na Europa voltam a valer verdadeiras fortunas no boom da IA A alemã Uniper planeja converter antigas usinas desativadas no Reino Unido, Alemanha, Suécia e Holanda em data centers. O negócio inicial contempla uma de suas dez propriedades, com negociações avançadas para outras duas. A grande vantagem das instalações é a conexão direta à rede de energia, garantindo cerca de 700 MW de potência. Essa capacidade estimada pelo CEO Michael Lewis é suficiente para abastecer até sete data centers de hiperescala, impulsionando a infraestrutura de dados na Europa. A empresa de energia alemã Uniper está prestes a fechar um negócio que pode dar um verdadeiro salto aos centros de dados na Europa: o plano é converter suas usinas desativadas na infraestrutura mais disputada do momento, como revelou o Financial Times. Essas antigas instalações têm tudo o que um data center precisa: espaço de sobra, boas vias de acesso e, o mais importante, uma conexão garantida à rede de transmissão de energia elétrica. Um acordo cercado de sigilo O negócio ainda é cercado de segredo, mas dois detalhes cruciais já vieram a público. O primeiro é que a energética está a ponto de selar um contrato em uma de suas 10 propriedades paradas — distribuídas entre Reino Unido, Alemanha, Suécia e Holanda — para transformá-la em um centro de processamento de dados, além de manter conversas avançadas sobre outras duas localidades. O segundo é que seu CEO, Michael Lewis, calcula em cerca de 700 MW a capacidade de rede elétrica assegurada nesses pontos. De acordo com a Agência Internacional de Energia (AIE), essa potência seria suficiente para abastecer em torno de sete data centers de hiperescala ou perto de 70 instalações de menor porte. Ainda não se sabe com certeza quais desses 10 locais serão contemplados, embora haja fortes pistas de que as primeiras opções fiquem no Reino Unido e na Alemanha, como o próprio executivo deixou escapar em meados do ano. artigo.texto: Haroldo Almeida participa do PodCast AgroAmbiental para debater Caatinga, crédito de carbono e mudanças climáticas Comendador Guardião das Águas de Alagoas, ex-secretário de Meio Ambiente de Delmiro Gouveia, participante da COP30 e presidente da Associação dos Produtores de Crédito de Carbono Social do Bioma Caatinga, o ambientalista é o convidado do 7º episódio. O PodCast AgroAmbiental recebe, nesta terça-feira (24 de novembro), às 20h, o ambientalista Haroldo Almeida, comendador Guardião das Águas de Alagoas, ex-secretário municipal de Meio Ambiente de Delmiro Gouveia, integrante do Fórum Brasileiro de Mudança do Clima e presidente da Associação dos Produtores de Crédito de Carbono Social do Bioma Caatinga. O sétimo episódio traz à discussão temas de grande relevância para o futuro do Semiárido nordestino, como a preservação da Caatinga, a gestão dos recursos hídricos, o avanço da desertificação, o mercado de créditos de carbono e os resultados da 30ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP30), realizada em Belém, no Pará, em novembro de 2025. Com uma trajetória marcada pela participação em iniciativas ambientais, debates institucionais e ações de conscientização, Haroldo compartilha experiências acumuladas ao longo de sua atuação e apresenta propostas que buscam conciliar conservação ambiental, valorização dos recursos naturais e geração de oportunidades econômicas para as populações do Sertão. Trajetória ambiental e defesa dos recursos hídricos Um dos assuntos abordados durante a entrevista é a trajetória de Haroldo Almeida na defesa do meio ambiente, especialmente no Alto Sertão alagoano. Ex-secretário de Meio Ambiente de Delmiro Gouveia e participante das discussões do Comitê de Bacia da Região Hidrográfica do Sertão do São Francisco, o ambientalista trata sobre a importância da gestão participativa das águas, os desafios enfrentados pelos municípios e a necessidade de políticas públicas voltadas à conservação dos recursos hídricos. A conversa também destaca a importância do Rio São Francisco para o desenvolvimento regional, a recuperação de áreas degradadas, a proteção da vegetação nativa e a adoção de medidas capazes de garantir maior segurança hídrica às populações sertanejas. O episódio propõe uma reflexão sobre a relação entre a preservação ambiental e o desenvolvimento econômico, especialmente em uma região que depende diretamente da disponibilidade de água para o abastecimento humano, a agricultura e a pecuária. Desertificação e os desafios da conservação da Caatinga A desertificação é outro tema importante do episódio, considerando os impactos que a degradação ambiental pode provocar sobre a produtividade do solo, a disponibilidade de água e as condições de vida das comunidades rurais. Haroldo participou de um seminário internacional sobre o combate à desertificação, realizado na Câmara dos Deputados, em Brasília, onde foram discutidas estratégias de enfrentamento da degradação das terras e a necessidade de ampliar as ações de recuperação ambiental no Semiárido. Durante a entrevista, são abordadas as diferenças entre a seca, característica natural da região, e os processos de desertificação, que podem ser agravados pelo desmatamento, pelas queimadas, pelo sobrepastoreio e pelo manejo inadequado do solo. O debate também chama a atenção para a importância da Caatinga, bioma exclusivamente brasileiro que possui significativa biodiversidade e desempenha papel fundamental no equilíbrio ambiental do Nordeste. A discussão busca demonstrar que a conservação da vegetação nativa, a recuperação de áreas degradadas e a adoção de práticas produtivas sustentáveis são fundamentais para garantir melhores condições ambientais e econômicas às futuras gerações. Crédito de carbono pode representar oportunidade de renda para agricultores do Sertão Um dos principais destaques do episódio é a proposta de Crédito de Carbono Integral Bio-Sócio-Hidro-Energético, iniciativa idealizada por Haroldo Almeida que busca desenvolver mecanismos de valorização dos serviços ambientais prestados pela Caatinga e pelas comunidades que contribuem para sua conservação. Presidente da Associação dos Produtores de Crédito de Carbono Social do Bioma Caatinga, o ambientalista apresenta os fundamentos da proposta e discute as possibilidades de inserção dos pequenos produtores rurais em iniciativas relacionadas ao mercado de carbono. A entrevista procura esclarecer, de maneira acessível, o que são créditos de carbono, como funciona esse mercado, quais são os critérios para sua geração e de que forma a manutenção da vegetação nativa pode representar uma oportunidade econômica para os proprietários rurais. Também são discutidos os desafios relacionados à quantificação, à certificação e à comercialização desses créditos, além da importância de mecanismos que assegurem transparência, confiabilidade e participação das comunidades locais. Entre os questionamentos levantados está a possibilidade de transformar a preservação ambiental em uma atividade economicamente atrativa, contribuindo para reduzir a pressão sobre a vegetação nativa e estimular a recuperação de áreas degradadas. A discussão propõe uma questão central: será possível que, no futuro, um agricultor do Sertão consiga obter renda pela conservação da Caatinga, mantendo a vegetação em pé? Participação na COP30 e valorização da Caatinga no cenário internacional A participação de Haroldo Almeida na COP30, realizada em Belém, também ocupa espaço importante na entrevista. O ambientalista compartilha experiências de sua passagem pela conferência, considerada um dos principais encontros internacionais sobre mudanças climáticas, reunindo representantes de governos, instituições, pesquisadores e organizações da sociedade civil. Durante o evento, Haroldo participou de discussões e articulações voltadas à valorização da Caatinga, à justiça climática e ao reconhecimento das iniciativas de conservação desenvolvidas no Semiárido nordestino. artigo.texto: Sungrow Renewables and Actuate Energy have signed an agreement for a 380 MW/1,500 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) portfolio in Spain. The transaction covers seven standalone projects located in A Coruña, Almería, Castellón and Navarra. The agreement also establishes a long-term strategic partnership between the two companies to develop, build and operate the projects. The first projects are already under construction, while construction of the remaining projects is expected to begin in the coming months. The portfolio is expected to reach ready-to-build status during 2027, with the projects scheduled to begin commercial operations between 2027 and the first half of 2028. The agreement also allows for further cooperation between the companies on future energy storage projects in Spain. Earlier, in October 2026, Sungrow, ENGIE and Elecnor collaborated on the 150 MW/300 MWh Hazelwood 2 BESS expansion in Victoria, Australia. Sungrow Australia will provide the project’s technology, while Elecnor will handle the balance-of-plant work. The facility will comprise 66 battery storage units from Sungrow’s PowerTitan 2.0 series, 33 power conversion system inverters, and an energy management system.

artigo.texto: A new study finds U.S. hyperscale data centers use about 2% of the nation’s electricity. In Oregon, Virginia and Iowa, the share is above 10%. Data centers’ electricity use is soaring, and in some states it already makes up a large share of the power supply. That’s the finding of a Harvard-led study in Nature Sustainability. The researchers catalogued 403 hyperscale data centers in the U.S. They estimate these facilities use about 82 terawatt-hours a year, roughly 2% of the nation’s electricity and about as much as nearly 8 million homes. The facilities are also tied to about 26 million metric tons of carbon emissions a year. The national number hides big differences between states. In Oregon, the facilities in the study equal about 18.6% of 2024 retail electricity sales. Virginia comes in at about 15.5% and Iowa at about 13.1%. A utility filing suggests Virginia’s real share is closer to 28%. The researchers say their numbers are probably low. The study counts only facilities they could verify. Data centers are also increasingly building their own gas power plants on site, and about 143 GW of those plants have been proposed nationally. Power from those plants doesn’t show up in utility sales data. Better tracking could help. Federal energy surveys don’t count data centers as their own category of customer. A permitting bill now before the Senate would direct the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) to measure how much electricity data centers use. Until that happens, state and local planners won’t have a clear picture of how fast the demand is growing. Locals role in energy policy will be a key conversation during the 2027 MACo Winter Conference. The session, “Powering Local Decisions: The County Role in Maryland’s Energy Future,” will explore where counties fit in the decision-making process, what tools local governments have—and don’t have—and how county leaders can effectively engage with residents, developers, utilities, and state policymakers. MACo’s Winter Conference, “Full Steam Ahead,” will be held at the Hyatt Regency Chesapeake Bay Hotel in Cambridge, MD, on January 6-8, 2027. artigo.texto: Administration Gives SpaceX OK to Launch 1M Data Centers The Trump administration gave SpaceX the green light on Wednesday to turn orbit into an AI server farm, the Wall Street Journal reports. The FCC authorized the company to deploy up to 1 million "Starmind" satellites—AI-focused orbital data centers that CEO Elon Musk says will tap solar power to cut computing costs and sidestep local fights over land- and energy-hungry installations on Earth. The decision "opens a bold new frontier," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement, per the AP. But it's a high-stakes bet on hardware that doesn't yet exist at scale. And there's already organized opposition to putting data centers in space. Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and author, called the prospect of launching a million satellites into space to create data centers "a fantasy," saying on Wednesday, "It's not going to happen." He cited difficulties and risks that include in-orbit collisions that could affect other essential satellites and add to the accumulation of space junk. SpaceX must lean on its Starship rocket to build out the constellation through 2040, over objections from Amazon, Viasat, and astronomers worried about light pollution, per the Journal. The company, already running terrestrial data centers and fresh off a giant IPO, aims to launch the first orbital units in 2027. - Aaron Rodgers is cut after 'stunning interview.' - US Forest Service drops the Bigfoot files. - Vanity Fair hit piece just makes some like Taylor Swift more. - Cat caused a 'situation' on Boston-to-Tampa Delta flight.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - The number of data center projects cancelled in the U.S. more than doubled in the third quarter, compared to the same period last year, according to data released Tuesday from Relae, the climate solutions company formerly known as Carbon Direct. - Sixteen data center projects were stopped in the third quarter due to community opposition, Relae said in a blog post. That’s up from seven in the same quarter of 2025. - Relae, which has a data center cancellation tracker, said there were 70 data center projects “blocked, withdrawn or stalled since 2024,” representing $271 billion in estimated or announced investments. Dive Insight: The rise in cancellations came amid an election season that saw data center pushback — along with affordability and geopolitical concerns — play a role in Democrats flipping both the House of Representatives and Senate. Relae estimated that $64 billion in planned investments were stopped in Q3. Most of the projects were stopped by local governments, with seven stopped with formal denials and four being axed due to zoning bans. The other five projects were cancelled due to developer withdrawals, according to Relae. Relae said three trends have emerged as data centers have drawn an increasing share of the public ire: “more cancellations, greater intervention by local governments, and the importance of transparency (or lack thereof) to communities.” “At present, local opposition is not inherently a broad referendum on AI, although this could quickly change in the future,” Relae said in its blog. “Instead, our research shows that most community concerns are within a project team’s control.” A lack of transparency represented the top concern for communities, representing a leading or secondary theme for 34 of 44 stopped projects that Relae analyzed. Voters approved measures to restrict data center development in jurisdictions across 10 states, and an NBC exit poll found that 76% of voters opposed new data centers being built in their communities. The same exit poll found that 56% said data centers were a crucial or major factor in choosing a congressional candidate. “Data centers have moved to the center of American politics,” Relae said. “As public views of the projects have turned more negative, they have become material for stump speeches, attack ads, and ballot measures.” Of the 47 local ballot measures on data centers this past election, 46 passed that would limit or ban development, the firm said. The success of such measures “shows the growing significance of data center development as a local electoral issue,” Relae said.

artigo.texto: Goleta has begun taking steps toward banning data centers in the Good Land. In a 4-1 vote, the Goleta Planning Commission on Monday moved forward an ordinance that would permanently prohibit data centers in the city. The ordinance will now head to the City Council for review. The city currently doesn’t have regulations on data centers, according to Anne Wells, the city’s advance planning manager. Goleta has not permitted any data centers or received applications, supervising planner Andy Newkirk said. He said that while most people think of data centers as large-scale facilities, they can be the size of a “normal office building,” and it’s “certainly possible” that the city could receive a proposal. The drafted permanent ordinance is a way for Goleta to get ahead “of a potential issue” and “not get caught off-guard,” Newkirk said. While the ordinance would be permanent, the city could revisit the details of the prohibition in the future. “I do think it is a good idea to have an ordinance and to get ahead of it,” Commissioner Jennifer Fullerton said. City staff highlighted water, electricity, noise and air pollution as potential data center impacts. “We are very aware that in other jurisdictions around the country, this is becoming a really big issue, and we know that in other areas of regulation we have been caught unprepared,” said Peter Imhof, planning and environmental review director. Commissioner Rita Serotkin had similar sentiments. She referred to Goodland Guns’ relocation next to a preschool and daycare facility as sneaking “around behind.” Goleta’s proposed ordinance defines a data center as a facility that houses a group of networked computer systems used for data storage and processing, to be used for the storage, processing and/or distribution of data. The facilities may also include air handlers, power generators, water cooling and storage facilities, utility substations, backup batteries, fire suppression systems, enhanced security features and other associated utility infrastructure to support operations, according to city staff. Goleta’s proposed ordinance also includes a lengthy description of what is not considered a data center. A data center is not, according to the staff report: an enclosed room, suite or other accessory space containing computer servers, data storage and processing equipment, network switching equipment, telecommunications equipment, and related supporting equipment, including cooling, electrical, backup power and security systems, that are used to support and facilitate an allowed on-site principal use that takes up no more than 20% of the floor area of the principal use. The 20% allowance considers businesses that may need data center-like facilities on site, according to the city staff report. However, that 20% allowance brought some concerns Monday night. It was later swapped in favor of an exemption that would allow for data center-like facilities that use less than 3 megawatts of energy. Some commissioners had worried about how it would affect local technology companies. “My only concern is the 20% and not having reached out to the tech companies,” Fullerton said. Commissioner Cary Penniman, who voted against the recommendation Monday night but supports preventing “hyperscale data centers” in Goleta, had similar concerns. He worried about how it would impact small startups coming out of UC Santa Barbara. “I don’t think we want to prevent that from happening,” he said. “There are some unintended consequences.” He advocated that city staff develop a tighter definition of a data center. He posted a question to staff that a public commenter had asked earlier in the night: “What are we exactly trying to prevent?” Others were concerned about the energy use from the allowance. “The primary concern for me is sort of the energy and water usage, and so that’s where I feel like the restriction should be,” Commissioner Katie Maynard said. She asked staff why they decided to go with the floor area instead of “focusing on things that are most (concerning) for data centers such as energy or water.” She advocated for the allowance to be 3 megawatts or less. Newkirk said the decision was made to provide some flexibility. “Thinking (of) it as a proxy, it would be fairly consistent over time, where I think the energy demands may be really a standard today might not make much sense tomorrow,” he said. Wells also told the commissioners that city staff looked at other jurisdictions and floor area is a typical measure. Cherie Cabral spoke Monday on behalf of the California Construction Labor Management Trust and urged the Planning Commission against supporting a “blanket ban.” She also encouraged the commission to look at possible advantages that data centers could bring to the city and other cities’ regulations. “It’s entirely doable to create regulations that would address most of the issues, and in fact, many of the issues that are under discussion at the moment are generated out of social media as opposed to something that comes out of studies,” she said. Commissioner Anne Miller acknowledged the commissioner’s concerns about local impact, but insisted that the timing of establishing an ordinance was important. “I think it’s important to get on top of this now before something really disastrous happens in the meantime,” she said. “It’s moving so quickly, and it’s scary, I think.” Monday night’s discussion comes about a month after the Earl Warren Fairgrounds’ CEO put an end to speculation that the fairgrounds were considering a data center.

artigo.texto: Centre Proposes Energy Storage Mandate for Rooftop Solar Ministry of Power has proposed state-level storage mandates for rooftop solar systems exceeding 500 kW. November 24, 2026. By EI News Network The Ministry of Power has proposed empowering State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) to mandate energy storage systems for consumers with renewable energy generation capacities exceeding 500 kW, in a move aimed at strengthening grid stability and improving renewable energy integration. The proposal seeks to address the operational challenges faced by power distribution companies amid the growing adoption of rooftop solar systems across the country. Under the proposed framework, state regulators would be authorised to prescribe energy storage requirements for prosumers, enabling them to store surplus electricity generated during solar hours and utilise it during periods of peak demand. The draft amendments also propose changes to the net-metering framework, allowing state regulators to determine applicable charges. Rooftop solar installations exceeding 5 kW could attract network-related charges, while smaller installations would remain exempt. The proposed mechanism is expected to help distribution companies recover network infrastructure and operational costs while facilitating the continued expansion of distributed renewable energy generation. The Ministry has also proposed revised timelines for implementing Time-of-Day (ToD) tariffs. Commercial and industrial consumers with connected loads exceeding 10 kW would be brought under the tariff framework from April 1, 2027, followed by other consumer categories, excluding agricultural consumers, from April 1, 2028. Electricity tariffs during solar hours would be at least 20 percent lower than normal tariffs, encouraging consumers to shift electricity consumption to periods of higher renewable energy availability. The proposed amendments could drive demand for battery energy storage systems and energy management solutions, particularly among commercial and industrial consumers with large rooftop solar installations. The measures are part of the government's broader efforts to modernise India's electricity distribution network, improve renewable energy utilisation and ensure grid reliability as the country accelerates its clean energy transition. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands (PROPUBLICA) - A dozen Democrats in Congress are calling for limiting or banning the construction of data centers on public lands. The moves follow reporting from ProPublica that revealed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the White House’s artificial intelligence push, has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies. “Our public lands aren’t a piggy bank for Trump’s powerful friends,” Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said in a social media post that pointed to ProPublica’s reporting. Her office told the news organization that the senator, who serves on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, is working on legislation to regulate data centers on public lands and will use the panel’s oversight authority to address concerns about transparency surrounding them. Burgum was asked about ProPublica’s reporting at a recent event hosted by the conservative website Daily Caller. He said that his financial reporting and ethics were “clean as a whistle,” and that he invested in software companies before they turned to AI. “I don’t even know all the names of the companies that are in the portfolio,” he said of his vast wealth. ProPublica found that hundreds of President Donald Trump’s political appointees in the executive branch, or their spouses, held stocks, owned equity or had other financial ties to AI companies and data center developers. Other offices, including the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, defended their political leadership, saying the appointees followed lawyers’ guidance and had not violated ethics rules. Our reporting also found that a U.S. Geological Survey study released earlier this year identified an area of U.S. Department of the Interior land nearly the size of Montana that might be suitable for data centers. Several members of Congress pledged to float legislation to ban data center development on this land. “These lands are treasured and must be protected for future generations to benefit from and enjoy,” Rep. Maxine Dexter of Oregon said in a statement. In mid-November, she filed the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act, which would ban data center construction on land managed by the Interior Department and the Forest Service. Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan in July filed the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act, which would also prohibit their build-out on federally managed land. The measure was dead on arrival in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives. “I’m going to continue building the coalition for our bill, and at the same time, I’m going to push the Oversight Committee to investigate the outrageous corruption of the Trump Administration,” she told ProPublica in a statement. The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the pushback from Democrats in Congress. Also speaking up were Rep. Jared Huffman of California and Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who serve as the ranking members of the natural resources committees in their respective chambers. Huffman and Heinrich are in line to take up the gavel in those committees in January when Democrats retake the majority. “These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Public lands belong in public hands.” Heinrich is pushing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a generational overhaul of the legislation governing how federal agencies permit major developments. Republicans in Congress and the White House support the swift passage of the bill, as do some Democrats. The more environmentally minded members of the Democratic caucus, however, are calling on Heinrich to slow down and force a better deal once Congress reconvenes next year with Democratic majorities. Environmental policy experts agree that permitting reform is desperately needed to address climate change by allowing the faster build-out of renewable electricity generation and transmission lines. But green groups including the Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council and League of Conservation Voters oppose the bill because it would likely also lead to more fossil fuel projects while limiting input on projects from Native American tribes. The legislation presents a mixed bag for data centers. A spokesperson for Heinrich defended the permitting reform bill, pointing out that it would require data center companies to bear their own costs for connecting to and upgrading the electrical grid. But the legislation would also streamline approval of natural gas-fired power plants, which power many data centers. The bill would make it more difficult to take away a permit after it’s issued. Meanwhile, the Interior Department released a five-year strategic plan last week that includes a proposal to sell off public lands or pursue “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges and direct transfer of lands.” It is unclear whether the department intends to offer to sell to companies or only to local, state and tribal governments. Researchers who study natural resources policy told ProPublica that the country’s foundational land management law lays out steps that must be followed to dispose of federal land, steps that will be difficult for the Trump administration to legally navigate. Still, with permits for data centers pending before the Interior Department, the release of the strategic plan sparked fear that developers might try to buy federal land. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for conservation group Save Our Parks, said the plan was another attempt by Burgum to “sell off what’s left to AI data center developers and his extractive resource buddies.” The Interior Department did not respond to a request for comment on its proposal to sell federal land. artigo.texto: Cookeville Planning Commission postponed a vote Monday on proposed data center regulations that would establish zoning restrictions based on facility size. Community Development Director Jon Ward said staff revised the original proposal after reviewing model regulations developed by UT advisors. “One of the primary conclusions from that review is that data centers can vary significantly in scale and impact,” Ward said. “A relatively small facility occupying a few thousand square feet is very different from a larger hyperscale data center campus that may consume tens or even hundreds of megawatts of electricity.” Ward said the amendment divides data centers into five categories based on building size and projected electricity demand. Smaller facilities could operate in some commercial and light manufacturing districts, while the largest facilities would require special exceptions in Heavy Manufacturing districts. “The revised standards place greater emphasis on potential impacts to adjoining properties,” Ward said. “These include measurable noise standards based upon the type of adjoining property, acoustics studies for larger facilities and certain facilities near residential property, screening of generators and mechanical equipment, limitations on routine generator testing, and additional review where exterior equipment could affect adjoining residential uses.” Ward said utility providers would have to confirm they could accommodate a facility operating at full capacity before development could be approved. “It would allow the utility to consider existing demand, previous committed capacities, future developments, planned capital improvements, our system reliabilities, peak conditions, and reasonably anticipated future utility demands elsewhere in the city,” Ward said. Ward said several commissioners expressed concerns about whether residents could face higher utility bills as a result of data center development. The proposed regulations would not obligate the city to pay for infrastructure improvements needed to serve a facility. Ward said recently enacted state legislation generally prevents municipalities and electric utilities from absorbing electrical infrastructure costs for qualifying data centers. The law applies to facilities with projected peak electrical demands of at least 50 megawatts. “We shouldn’t assume that every smaller facility contemplated by the amendment would fall within that statutory protection,” Ward said. Planning staff will consult with utility departments to address commissioners’ concerns before bringing the amendment back for consideration in December. In other business, the commission granted conditional final plat approval for Emerald Forest Estates, which includes 71 residential lots, and amended the commission’s bylaws to require meeting agendas to be posted on the city’s website at least 48 hours before regular meetings.

artigo.texto: Korean researchers have developed an all-solid-state lithium-metal battery that operates reliably at room temperature under low pressure. The technology could ease the high-pressure requirements that are one of the barriers to commercializing all-solid-state batteries and could be used to reduce their weight and size. A team led by Park Su-jin, a chemistry professor at Pohang University of Science and Technology POSTECH, said on the 26th that it had developed an all-solid-state lithium-metal battery that operates at room temperature under pressure of 0.3 megapascals (MPa) or less. The team worked with researchers at Chung-Ang University, Korea Basic Science Institute (KBSI) and Southern Methodist University (SMU) in the United States. The findings were published in the international journal Nature Communications on the 7th, local time. All-solid-state batteries are attracting attention as a next-generation technology that can reduce fire risks by using a solid electrolyte instead of a liquid one. Using lithium metal in the anode can increase energy density, but the lithium expands during charging, creating gaps between the electrode and the electrolyte. In this process, branchlike growths called lithium dendrites can penetrate the electrolyte and cause an internal short circuit. High pressure has been applied to batteries to prevent this, but the equipment needed adds weight and bulk. The researchers addressed the problem by preventing cracks in the solid electrolyte and distributing the pressure caused by lithium expansion. They added thioctic acid (TA) to a sulfide-based solid electrolyte to form a polymer network, suppressing cracks in the electrolyte and the penetration of lithium dendrites. They also applied a porous carbon material with many tiny holes to the anode current collector to provide space for lithium to accumulate. The design distributes the force generated by lithium expansion during charging within the current collector, reducing the strain on the electrolyte. The researchers used the Pohang Light Source to observe the inside of the battery in 3D during charging and discharging. They found that stress from expansion was relieved as lithium filled and left the pores of the current collector. A battery using the technology operated reliably at room temperature and under pressure of 0.3 MPa or less, even in a full cell using a ternary cathode material (NCM811) for electric vehicles. The researchers said it was the first time in the world that such low-pressure operation had been achieved in a sulfide-based all-solid-state lithium-metal full cell with an areal capacity of 2.4 mAh/㎠. "We addressed both the limitations of the brittle sulfide-based solid electrolyte with a polymer network and the stress caused by lithium expansion with a porous current collector," Park said. "This result came from close collaboration with Korean researchers." References Nature Communications(2026), DOI: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-79393-w

artigo.texto: President Donald Trump told reporters at a White House news conference on Friday, November 20, 2026, that U.S. companies building artificial-intelligence data centers in other countries would face a “tremendous tax.” The Trump overseas data center tax threat landed on the largest American cloud providers with almost no detail attached. Yahoo Finance ran several stories on the remarks and reported no tax rate, no start date and no legal mechanism. The wording was blunt. According to NBC News, Trump said, “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country.” Yahoo’s coverage recorded the follow-up: “They can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.” Those two sentences are the entire policy, as of today. Six days later, the idea still sits in threat territory rather than law. For governments courting hyperscale capital, that ambiguity is its own problem, as our earlier story on Australia’s $115 billion AI data centre bet and the Trump tax threat showed. This analysis separates what the record confirms from what remains guesswork, then walks through who is exposed, how a tax could work, and what cloud buyers should do while they wait. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What Trump Said About Data Centers Abroad on November 20 The remarks came during a White House press briefing, in the middle of a broader discussion about U.S. artificial-intelligence infrastructure. Trump framed overseas construction as something his administration would not simply permit. He then softened the point in the same breath, saying companies could still go ahead, but at a price. That pairing of a prohibition and a toll is typical of how he floats trade measures, and it leaves room to land almost anywhere between a symbolic levy and a hard restriction. NBC News said the president went on to describe substantial penalties for companies that try to build abroad. Yahoo News and AP-syndicated Yahoo coverage described the statement as an open-ended threat. Yahoo’s reporting also said Trump argued that overseas construction could end up benefiting China, a point we return to below. None of the outlets we reviewed found a document, draft bill or executive order behind the remarks. That matters because the phrase “data centers abroad” covers a huge range of activity. A hyperscaler can own a facility outright, lease capacity from a local colocation operator, sign a power deal for a campus it never builds itself, or rent capacity inside a partner’s cloud region. Trump’s comments did not say which of those would trigger a tax. They also did not say whether a facility already under construction counts. What the Reports Confirm and What They Leave Open Readers are seeing a lot of confident takes on this story, so a clean ledger helps. The table below lists what the named outlets support and what they do not. Anything marked unconfirmed has no supporting statement in the coverage we reviewed. Two lessons come out of that ledger. First, every operational question, from rate to enforcement, is still open. Second, anyone quoting a percentage or a start date is guessing. Our fact base holds no number of that kind, and neither do the Yahoo Finance and AP-syndicated reports we reviewed. Which Companies Face Exposure From the Overseas Tax Reports name five U.S. companies with international data-center operations that a tax like this could touch: Amazon.com, Inc., Alphabet Inc., Microsoft Corp., Meta Platforms, Inc. and Oracle Corp. The White House has not published its own list, so the grouping reflects journalists’ reading of who has the largest overseas footprint, not an official target list. Amazon and Alphabet Headlines framed the story around Amazon and Google, and Yahoo Finance’s own headline named Amazon, Google and Microsoft. One caution applies. It remains unconfirmed whether Google or Amazon as consumer brands would be the taxpayers, as opposed to the legally registered corporate entities that actually own and operate the facilities. Corporate structure decides who writes the check, and large cloud groups hold their foreign assets through layered subsidiaries. Microsoft, Meta and Oracle Microsoft has been the most visible voice so far, thanks to President Brad Smith’s television comments covered below. Meta and Oracle also appear in the reports as firms with international data-center operations. The coverage we reviewed does not quantify the hit to any single company. Why Hyperscalers Build Data Centers Outside the United States Cloud companies do not go abroad for sport. Latency pushes capacity toward users, because a video call or a trading application runs better when servers sit close by. Data-residency laws push the same way, since many governments require certain records to stay inside national borders. Customers in regulated sectors, such as banking and health care, often refuse to buy from a region they cannot place on a map. Power is the third driver, and it is getting more important. AI training and inference clusters draw enormous electricity, and grid connections in some U.S. markets now take years. Developers therefore look wherever the electrons and the land are available. Our coverage of Goldman’s 52 GW forecast for U.S. data centers in 2028 shows how hard domestic power demand is already climbing, which gives companies an extra reason to look abroad for capacity. Seen through that lens, a tax on foreign sites would not just add a cost line. It would squeeze three strategies at once: serving local customers, meeting local data law and finding spare grid capacity. A company could absorb the levy, shift the build back home, or hand the foreign build to a partner. Each answer carries its own price, and none of them is free. artigo.texto: Data center emissions are worse than we knew, Harvard study confirms This past election, Americans across the country rejected data centers, voting to restrict new projects in their communities. As voters push back against data centers, a new study out of Harvard reveals startling revelations about the severity of the pollution they create. Pollution from data centers is three times higher than previously estimated, according to a new study from the Harvard Data Science Initiative. The study examined 403 "hyperscale" data centers and found that emissions from these facilities were underestimated. In fact, the lead author Gianluca Guidi believes that their research only provides a "floor estimate." When factoring in the thousands of data centers across the country, many of which were not included in the study, the energy use is likely much higher. You May Also Like The study found that the largest data centers in the U.S. use as much energy in a single year as the state of Michigan does. Carbon emissions from these data centers surpassed those of entire countries. Researchers found that 2 percent of all electricity use in the U.S. during the study period came from data centers. A single data center included in the study consumed as much energy as 30,000 homes on average. The best tech deal this week Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission. Certain U.S. states are worse off than others in terms of climate pollution from data centers, according to Harvard researchers. For example, Virginia has the most data centers, and fossil fuel-burning power plants are most common there. Other states, such as Oregon, have green-friendly, eclectic grids, so data centers residing there are likely emitting less pollution. Data centers have become a controversial topic across the U.S. Thanks to the AI boom, the tech industry is looking to build more data centers in the U.S. to provide compute for AI models and research. However, data centers are proving unpopular in many communities. Some state legislatures have taken action to restrict data center buildouts and stiffen regulations around the industry. As previously mentioned, 44 ballot measures to restrict data center buildout were passed by voters during the midterm elections. And the movement against AI data centers appears to only be growing. For example, environmental activist Erin Brockovich launched her own data center tracking initiative earlier this year. The tech and AI industries are currently struggling with a series of other issues. However, based on what studies are finding, it seems the anti-data-center movement will continue to be a thorn in the side of big tech and AI. artigo.texto: ALEXANDRIA — The city of Alexandria continues to study and discuss data center regulations. The Alexandria Planning Commission put together a data center study that includes a draft ordinance. The new zoning district was titled, “Data Center Planned Unit Development” and amended existing city code sections as necessary to accommodate the new district provisions. ADVERTISEMENT The draft was presented for commission discussion and suggested revisions. If the commission desires, the final version will be available for public hearing in either December or January. At an Alexandria Planning Commission meeting , City Planner Mike Weber presented a draft zoning ordinance framework intended to regulate the location, design, operation and approval process for future data center developments in the city. The creation of two categories of data centers were proposed: 1. Small-scale data centers (tentatively up to 2-4 MW) permitted through a conditional use permit process in I-1 "Light Industrial" and potentially B-1 "General Business" zoning districts. 2. Large-scale data centers requiring approval through a specialized data center Planned Unit Development (PUD) process. Development standards under consideration include: Minimum site area requirements. Noise impact studies and mitigation measures. Landscaping and perimeter buffering requirements. Utility and infrastructure capacity studies. Performance guarantees associated with public infrastructure improvements. Project phasing requirements. Decommissioning and site restoration standards. Weber noted that developers will have to present a preliminary proposal that meets the city requirements and utility capacity. Prior to approval of a PUD, there could be requirements for formal studies on noise or environmental concerns. Unlike a conditional use permit, which grants the use permanently and runs with the land, data center Planned Unit Developments could have a sunset date: An approved PUD could expire after five years if no construction was started. Commission members sought clarification on the potential thresholds for distinguishing small and large data center developments. They discussed utility demand and coordination with public utility providers. ADVERTISEMENT Commission members engaged in extensive discussion about the proposed standards regarding noise, visual impacts, and screening requirements. Appropriate building material and architectural standards were considered. Comparisons were drawn to existing industrial uses and how future development standards should be applied. A public hearing is anticipated at a future meeting, with the likelihood of continuing the hearing as additional information and revisions become available. In July, the council voted to place a moratorium on data centers within the city of up to one year for the construction, expansion, application for any permit, or application contemplating construction or expansion for data centers. Data centers are massive centralized hubs used to house computer networks, storage and computing infrastructure. According to information from CBS news, data centers for Artificial Intelligence use huge amounts of electricity and water, driving up costs and causing climate concerns. In other action, the Alexandria Planning Commission talked about a variance that was earlier submitted to Bill Fath on behalf of Fath Family Properties. Chairperson Deb Parrott announced applicant Bill Fath withdrew a variance application on Monday, Nov. 16. No public hearing, discussion or action was taken.
