artigo.texto: Socomec, a specialist manufacturer of low-voltage power management and battery energy storage solutions (BESS), has announced it was selected by KALS Energie Kraftwerk to deliver a first-of-its-kind energy storage system in Tyrol, Austria. The project combines hydropower and photovoltaic generation with Socomec’s BESS to increase renewable energy value and make hybrid generation more dispatchable, profitable, and useful to the local grid. KALS Energie Kraftwerk is an Austrian renewable energy producer operating hydroelectric and photovoltaic generation resources in the Tyrol region. With renewable generation rarely aligning with real-time grid demand, the company sought a solution that would allow it to store surplus hydroelectric and solar energy for optimised dispatch, as well as to unlock new revenue opportunities through supporting positive and negative balancing energy services. Given the plant’s location at an altitude of 2400 m, the solution also needed to deliver reliable performance in demanding conditions, including temperatures ranging from -18˚C to +25˚C and humidity levels of up to 100%. To support these objectives, Socomec deployed its SUNSYS HES XXL BESS as part of an integrated hydropower, photovoltaic and energy storage project. The installation combines 847 kW of hydroelectric generation and 400 kW of photovoltaic generation with Socomec's SUNSYS HES XXL BESS, delivering 1.5 MVA of output power and 3.3 MWh of storage capacity, as well as delivering approximately 90% efficiency. Integrated with an external energy management system (EMS), the BESS continuously analyses grid demand and dispatch opportunities, storing surplus renewable electricity and redistributing it within milliseconds according to market conditions and regional energy requirements. Its high-durability design, complete with a UV-resistant coating, ensures reliable performance even in challenging alpine conditions. Since commissioning, the project has demonstrated strong commercial performance and is expected to deliver a payback period of 5 – 6 years. Socomec’s BESS has so far supported the injection of up to 107 MWh of electricity into the grid per month, while ensuring that surplus renewable generation can be stored and utilised when and where it is needed most. KALS can now actively manage renewable energy production and respond rapidly to electricity market opportunities, improving the overall flexibility, profitability, and efficiency of its renewable assets. “This was a particularly challenging project, combining hydropower, photovoltaic generation and battery storage in a demanding mountainous environment,” said Robert Trenkwalder, CEO of KALS Energie Kraftwerk. “Socomec supported us every step of the way – from the initial design phase, through commissioning, and continuing today with the ongoing operation of the system. Their expertise and commitment gave us confidence throughout the project and they continue to deliver value today.” “Our partnership with KALS Energie Kraftwerk for the Tyrol plant clearly demonstrates how battery storage improves the overall business case for renewable generation,” added Michael Stötzner, Project Execution Manager, Socomec Germany. “The unique combination of hydropower, solar generation and intelligent energy storage provides a practical and replicable model for renewable energy producers across Europe seeking to increase the profitability, flexibility, and the value of their existing assets.” For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine. artigo.texto: CSIRO Urges Australia to Build Battery Manufacturing Scientists say Australia should make battery components locally rather than export critical minerals for overseas processing. Updated on Nov. 24, 2026 in Electric Vehicles Live Poll Should Australia manufacture more batteries domestically rather than exporting raw minerals? CSIRO scientists urged Australia to build a battery manufacturing industry instead of exporting critical minerals. A CSIRO report released in early November identified local manufacturing capabilities that could produce battery components. Why it matters Australia is the world's number one lithium producer, yet it exports raw minerals and ships end-of-life batteries overseas for materials recovery. Building domestic capacity could capture more value from resources the country already holds. More than 600,000 home batteries have been installed under a federal scheme since July 2025. Electric vehicle sales have risen rapidly since March, though the report does not quantify the growth rate. The players CSIRO The Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation is Australia's national science agency, conducting research across industry and environmental fields. The details Australia has nickel, cobalt, manganese, aluminium, copper and graphite, but exports them as raw materials for overseas processing. A CSIRO report released in early November found Australia could manufacture battery casings using aluminium aerosol can expertise and copper foil from scrap wire. Timeline - July 2025: Federal home battery scheme began installations. - March: Electric vehicle sales began rapid growth. - Early November: CSIRO released its battery manufacturing report. - Tuesday: CSIRO scientists delivered the battery manufacturing warning at an event. Roadmap The federal home battery scheme, operating since July 2025, has installed more than 600,000 units and created domestic demand for batteries. The CSIRO report asks whether that demand can support local manufacturing rather than continued reliance on imported finished batteries. Local battery manufacturing could affect the price and availability of home and electric vehicle batteries over time. Households already using the federal scheme may see the supply chain behind their installed batteries change as domestic capacity develops. The takeaway Australia's mineral wealth gives it a head start in battery production, but capturing that value depends on processing and manufacturing at home. Tracking the CSIRO report's proposals will show whether local industry follows. Further reading Explore more on Electric Vehicles to see how battery supply chains are shaping the market. artigo.texto: Residents react to Google data center pause in Botetourt County ROANOKE, Va. (WDBJ) - A judge’s ruling has halted work at the site of a planned Google data center in Botetourt County after finding the county mishandled its agreement with the company. Crews had already begun moving dirt at the site. Under Monday’s ruling, work must stop until public hearings are held in accordance with state law. The Southwest Virginia Data Center Transparency Alliance called the decision a step in the right direction. Alliance member Kathryn Hatam said she believed the county and Google were moving too quickly. “We felt specifically that Botetourt County and Google were rushing the process and that wasn’t fair to the community, it’s not fair to the environment,” Hatam said. Tim Dooley, one of the attorneys behind the lawsuit against Botetourt County, said the ruling gives him hope that changes can be made. Dooley also works closely with the alliance. “There is a degree of fatalism in the public when these these big deals come down and people are not as powerless as they sometimes imagine unfortunately,” Dooley said. Hatam said she wants county leaders to use the ruling as a reason to go back to the drawing board. “The people are watching you now. We have a government here that is supposed to be of, by, and for the people and every local official swore an oath to that effect. So are you taking that oath seriously?” she said. In a statement, Botetourt County said it is reviewing the ruling and considering its next steps. “The county respects the legal process and appreciates the attention the court gave to hearing this matter. The county is reviewing the ruling with its legal counsel and the Board Members and is evaluating its options going forward.” Copyright 2026 WDBJ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: A DSEZA declarou que o projeto da fábrica da Arbin Energy em Da Nang abrange uma área de 5,34 hectares no Parque de Alta Tecnologia de Da Nang, com um investimento total de US$ 117 milhões (equivalente a mais de VND 3,05 trilhões). A fábrica produzirá sistemas de armazenamento de energia alimentados por baterias (BESS), equipamentos para teste de baterias e equipamentos para a produção de baterias. Empresa americana investe US$ 117 milhões na construção de fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) em Da Nang. DNVN - O Conselho de Administração do Parque de Alta Tecnologia e Zonas Industriais de Da Nang (DSEZA) emitiu a Decisão 347/QD-BQL aprovando a política de investimento e reconhecendo a Arbin Energy LLC (EUA) como investidora no projeto da usina da Arbin Energy em Da Nang. A construção da usina da Arbin Energy em Da Nang deverá começar em dezembro de 2026 e a produção no terceiro trimestre de 2028. Este é um dos resultados concretos da visita de trabalho aos Estados Unidos realizada pelo presidente do Comitê Popular de Da Nang, Nguyen Manh Hung, em setembro de 2026. Até o momento, somente o Parque de Alta Tecnologia de Da Nang atraiu 14 projetos de investimento estrangeiro direto (IED), com um capital registrado de US$ 830,5 milhões. Segundo o Departamento de Estatísticas de Da Nang, nos primeiros 10 meses de 2026, a cidade atraiu um total de investimento estrangeiro direto (IED) registrado superior a US$ 800 milhões, incluindo novos registros, ajustes e aportes de capital/aquisições de ações, um aumento de mais de 147% em comparação com o mesmo período do ano anterior. Desse total, 130 projetos foram recém-registrados, totalizando quase US$ 630 milhões em capital, o que representa um aumento de mais de 17% no número de projetos e de mais de 233% no capital. O capital recém-registrado representou 78,3% do capital total atraído e aumentou em US$ 440,7 milhões em comparação com o mesmo período do ano anterior, contribuindo com 92% do aumento total do IED. Em termos de setores econômicos , o capital de investimento estrangeiro direto (IED) recém-registrado em Da Nang durante os primeiros 10 meses de 2026 concentrou-se fortemente no setor imobiliário, com aproximadamente US$ 435,7 milhões, representando 69,2% do total do capital recém-registrado; e nas indústrias de transformação e processamento, com US$ 177,6 milhões, representando 28,2%. Esses dois setores representaram 97,4% do total do capital recém-registrado. No setor imobiliário, os novos aportes de capital estão focados principalmente em projetos de desenvolvimento e operação de infraestrutura para parques industriais e centros comerciais, com destaque para os projetos de infraestrutura dos parques industriais VSIP Da Nang e WHA Da Nang e para o centro comercial AEON MALL Da Nang Hoa Xuan.

artigo.texto: The Town of Selma's planning board is set to meet on Monday evening to consider agenda items related to a proposed data center. The board will consider a conditional rezoning request and special use permit of Montana-based Advanced Manufacturing, Inc.'s application to build a 177,000-square-foot, single-story data center dubbed "Project Volt." Other WRAL Top Stories The developer's rezoning request, according to town documents, encompasses over 100 acres near I-42 and Buffalo Road. People living near the proposed site tell WRAL that they are considering selling their homes if the data center plans become reality. "There's no way you can tell me I'm not going to be able to hear that thing around the clock if I decide to stay," Ron Parrish said. His family, he said, has lived on Eason Lane in Selma for four generations. Parrish told WRAL that neighbors had conversations with the data center developers on Monday about potential property sales. Representatives for Advanced Manufacturing did not respond to WRAL's request for comment. Meanwhile, people at recent public meetings have called for more transparency from town officials, as concerns about the facility's potential water consumption, electricity use, and noise loom. "For a while, it's going to hurt. What that's going to bring, we just don't know and that's what's causing a lot of headache here," Parrish said. Planning documents said that the applicant "will fund the required power infrastructure and reclaimed water system, which will supply all process water used to cool the facility." Selma leaders last month approved new regulations for data center projects in the town. The rules address electricity, water usage and cooling, and noise levels. Mayor Byron McAllister and a town spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment on resident concerns or how the new rules would impact Project Volt. A town staff report on the project said many of the items required in the data center ordinance are not required until a building design is completed. The report goes on to say that an approved electricity study must be completed prior to construction, and that noise levels would be set as a condition of the special use permit. The items would need approval from Selma's town council before becoming final. McAllister indicated a council vote could happen early next month.

The global Quantum Battery Technology market was valued at US$ 18.50 million in 2025 and is anticipated to reach US$ 85.76 million by 2032, witnessing a CAGR of 24.5% during the forecast period 2026-2032. Request a Free Sample Report - Includes Market Forecasts, Manufacturer Profiles, Competitive Analysis and Quantum Battery Technology Insights: https://www.qyresearch.in/request-sample/energy-power-global-quantum-battery-technology-market-insights-industry-share-sales-projections-and-demand-outlook-2026-2032 Quantum battery technology refers to an emerging class of energy-storage and energy-management devices that use quantum-mechanical effects to absorb, store, retain and release energy. The scope of this study focuses on device concepts, prototype systems, enabling materials and research platforms based on quantum coherence, superposition, entanglement, superabsorption, superradiance and strong light-matter coupling. Typical physical implementations include organic microcavities, quantum dots and inorganic nanostructures, perovskite-related platforms, superconducting quantum circuits and qubit-based architectures. The core value proposition lies in faster charging, more efficient energy transfer, low-interference power management and potential integration with quantum computing, microelectronics, sensors, wireless charging and future high-rate energy systems. At the current stage, the industry should not be measured as a conventional battery-cell market; pricing is more appropriately assessed through prototype R&D contracts, customised experimental devices, enabling material supply and early-stage technology licensing rather than standardised cell-level ASP. Based on our research, quantum batteries should be understood as a pre-commercial quantum energy-storage technology rather than a sub-segment of conventional electrochemical batteries. The industry is currently defined by laboratory-scale prototypes, quantum thermodynamics, advanced materials platforms and device-level proof-of-concept work. Its decisive technical variables are quantum-state lifetime, scalable light-matter coupling, usable energy extraction, device stability and system integration, rather than cell manufacturing capacity or battery-pack cost. The 2026 Australian proof-of-concept marked an important step because it demonstrated a full charge-store-discharge cycle, but the present capacity and storage duration remain far from practical battery deployment. The global supply structure is not yet comparable to the lithium-ion or solid-state battery industries. At this stage, the most credible participants are research organisations and deep-tech entities, while quantum-dot materials suppliers and quantum-computing companies should be treated as adjacent or potential participants only when official product evidence supports their relevance. Planckian remains the most notable corporate name historically associated with quantum battery development, but its current public positioning appears more focused on next-generation quantum processors, which requires caution in revenue modelling and ranking. From a demand perspective, near-term adoption is more likely to emerge from quantum computing, microelectronics, sensors, optical energy conversion and low-interference energy-management systems than from electric vehicles or grid-scale storage. Policy support for quantum technologies in Europe, China and the United States can improve the funding environment, but it should not be interpreted as direct evidence of a mature quantum battery market. The sector's outlook is attractive but highly option-like: a single technical breakthrough in storage lifetime or scalable device manufacturing could materially change the market trajectory, while slow progress would keep the market largely confined to research and prototype revenues. artigo.texto: Resumo - Pela 1ª vez, a FCC liberou que data centers em formato de satélite subam ao espaço - Permissão foi concedida à SpaceX, de Elon Musk, para até 1 milhão de equipamentos - Constelação será chamada de 'Starmind' e deve atender à demanda por IA - Satélites processarão dados em órbita, mas para uso no planeta Terra - FCC diz que medida impulsiona a 'economia de superinteligência' dos EUA A Comissão Federal de Comunicações (FCC, na sigla em inglês) dos Estados Unidos autorizou a SpaceX, empresa aeroespacial de Elon Musk, a desenvolver uma constelação de até 1 milhão de satélites que funcionarão como data centers espaciais. A decisão, anunciada nesta quarta-feira (25), representa a primeira autorização desse tipo na história do país. Com o aval, a companhia poderá avançar com o projeto batizado de Starmind. A iniciativa prevê instalar módulos de processamento de dados em órbita para atender à crescente demanda por capacidade computacional, especialmente no desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial (IA). A proposta da SpaceX envolve uma infraestrutura que funciona de maneira diferente dos centros de dados terrestres. Em vez de concentrar servidores em grandes instalações no planeta, a empresa pretende distribuir a capacidade de processamento entre milhares de equipamentos no espaço. A estratégia aproveita dois recursos considerados fundamentais para o projeto: a disponibilidade de energia solar fora da atmosfera e o espaço físico disponível em órbita. Embora operem longe da Terra, os módulos continuarão conectados ao planeta. Afinal, eles deverão processar grandes volumes de informações e transmitir os resultados para usuários e sistemas terrestres. O que a FCC pretende impulsionar? A autorização faz parte de uma estratégia dos Estados Unidos para ampliar sua infraestrutura tecnológica e fortalecer a chamada “economia de superinteligência”. O presidente Donald Trump utiliza o termo superinteligência ao tratar da corrida global pelo desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial. Nesse contexto, a FCC considera os data centers uma estrutura essencial para sustentar o avanço da tecnologia. Em comunicado, o presidente da agência, Brendan Carr, afirmou que os Estados Unidos lideram a nova etapa do desenvolvimento tecnológico. “Essa ação abre fronteiras ousadas para a infraestrutura de computação necessária para impulsionar a liderança e o crescimento da América”, declarou. Com a decisão, a SpaceX poderá desenvolver a constelação Starmind, que prevê até 1 milhão de módulos orbitais de processamento. Segundo a FCC, o objetivo é atender à rápida expansão da demanda por capacidade computacional voltada à superinteligência. A autorização também permite que a companhia utilize frequências de rádio como alternativa de comunicação e emergência. Além disso, os equipamentos poderão complementar suas conexões ópticas entre satélites com transmissões por radiofrequência. Economia de energia e civilização Kardashev tipo II Um dos principais argumentos em favor dos data centers espaciais envolve o aproveitamento da energia solar. Fora da atmosfera terrestre, os equipamentos poderão captar energia diretamente do Sol. Segundo a SpaceX, essa estrutura também poderá reduzir a pressão sobre recursos naturais utilizados pelas instalações terrestres, como eletricidade e água. A FCC relacionou o projeto a um conceito da escala de Kardashev. Essa classificação hipotética mede o nível de desenvolvimento tecnológico de uma civilização conforme sua capacidade de aproveitar energia. Uma civilização do tipo II conseguiria captar e utilizar a energia produzida integralmente por sua estrela. No caso da Terra, isso significaria aproveitar toda a energia emitida pelo Sol. A agência americana mencionou esse conceito ao defender a dimensão tecnológica da iniciativa. Entretanto, a classificação representa uma referência teórica, e não uma condição que o projeto da SpaceX já tenha alcançado. Quando os data centers espaciais serão lançados? Apesar da autorização, a construção da constelação não acontecerá imediatamente. A SpaceX ainda precisará desenvolver a infraestrutura, fabricar os equipamentos e organizar os lançamentos. Além disso, a aprovação regulatória não garante que a companhia consiga colocar todos os 1 milhão de módulos em órbita. A própria viabilidade técnica e econômica de uma operação dessa dimensão ainda representa um desafio. A decisão da FCC, portanto, abre caminho para o desenvolvimento do projeto, mas não significa que toda a estrutura já esteja pronta para funcionar. Por fim, a agência informou que continuará analisando solicitações de outras empresas interessadas em desenvolver data centers orbitais. Dessa forma, a autorização também abre espaço para uma nova disputa tecnológica envolvendo a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial no espaço.

artigo.texto: A new study co-authored by a UCLA Fielding School of Public Health researcher has found that over the course of a year, the largest data centers in the United States use four times as much power as the city of Los Angeles. Findings also indicated that such centers’ electricity consumption and carbon emissions rival those of some U.S. states. The study, published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Sustainability, examined hyperscale data centers (HDCs), the largest and most powerful class of data centers that support services such as cloud computing, large language model training and global deployment of artificial intelligence tools. The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of HDCs’ electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions since the rise of AI. The authors include researchers from Harvard University and Falco Bargagli Stoffi, an assistant professor in the UCLA Fielding Department of Biostatistics. They compared their findings on power usage to electricity sales by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP), which serves approximately 4 million Angelenos. “Our central estimate suggests that the 403 hyperscale data centers we studied across the United States used nearly four times as much electricity as LADWP sells to its customers in a year,” said Bargagli Stoffi, adding that the analysis attributed more than half, or 54%, of the centers’ electricity use to fossil fuels. The study was one of the first to combine fragmented data, helping to better paint a picture of the emissions of individual facilities. “Better public information on electricity use would help communities and policymakers assess the environmental consequences of this industry’s growth,” Bargagli Stoffi said. The researchers noted substantial regional differences, with some HDCs relying much more on carbon-intensive electricity than others. Many of the facilities were concentrated in geographic areas where electricity is heavily generated by coal-fired power plants. The study found that four states — Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa —accounted for more than half of the electricity use studied.

artigo.texto: Brewer holds informational meeting on proposed data center rules BREWER, Maine (WABI) - Brewer residents had a chance Tuesday to learn more about proposed rules for data centers in the city. The city held an informational meeting at the Brewer Auditorium to discuss the proposal and hear from residents. What the proposal includes The Planning Board recommended the changes earlier this month. They would increase the allowable size of data centers from 20 to 50 megawatts in an industrial zone primarily located behind the city landfill. The proposal also includes noise standards, requirements for cooling and wastewater, and a community benefit agreement. Citizens weigh in People on both sides of the issue spoke. Vikas Dhiman, a University of Maine professor, said the proposed size would equal the residential electricity use of Penobscot County. “The regulations are up to 50 megawatt data center. The entire consumption of Penobscot residential electricity usage is 60 megawatts. So it’s the same as the entire county of Penobscot residential consumption. I don’t want a big data center, power-hungry, water-hungry, land-hungry, resource-hungry data center in my neighborhood,” Dhiman said. Jim LeBrecque, an engineer and president of Flexware Control Technology, said data centers help him in his work. “I’m an engineer, and data centers help me out tremendously. I can do in just a matter of a few minutes what took me many months to do before. We could not have the standard of living we have today if it was not for electrification. And the next big jump in our standard of living is going to come from data centers,” LeBrecque said. City’s response and next steps The city said it is not negotiating with any data center developers and that the proposed rules do not approve a specific project. The City Council is scheduled to consider the amendments Dec. 8 and again Jan. 12. Copyright 2026 WABI. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: 24 Novembro 2026 Demanda de energia elétrica foi de 82 TWh, cerca de 1,8% do consumo total de eletricidade do país, com emissões de 26 milhões de toneladas de CO₂. A informação é publicada por ClimaInfo, 24-11-2026. Em um ano, entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025, os 403 maiores centros de dados dos Estados Unidos emitiram mais dióxido de carbono do que a Dinamarca, que tem cerca de 6 milhões de habitantes. É o que mostra um estudo publicado na revista Nature Sustainability na semana passada. A pesquisa é uma das primeiras a estimar o consumo de eletricidade e as emissões de centros de dados hiperescaláveis (HDCs, sigla em inglês) desde o surgimento da inteligência artificial, segundo a Euronews. Em diferentes cenários de carga, esses HDCs consumiram entre 68 e 99 terawatts-hora (TWh) de eletricidade, associados a aproximadamente 21 milhões e 31 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (MtCO₂). No cenário médio, a demanda de eletricidade desses data centers foi de 82 TWh, correspondendo a 1,8% do consumo total de eletricidade dos EUA, com emissões de CO₂ atribuíveis de cerca de 26 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono. Cerca de 54% da geração atribuída foi proveniente de fontes de combustíveis fósseis, principalmente gás e carvão. A estimativa de emissões é de duas a três vezes maior do que a demonstrada em estudos anteriores, afirmou a autora sênior do estudo, Francesca Dominici, professora de bioestatística de Harvard. “É o equivalente à emissão de CO₂ de um pequeno país europeu”, disse a especialista, acrescentando que os planos para mais 2 mil centros de dados tornam essa quantidade ainda mais preocupante para o futuro, destaca a AP. Os HDCs são a maior classe de centros de dados, sendo o tipo que executa serviços em nuvem e treina grandes modelos de IA. Os edifícios da amostra tinham uma capacidade elétrica média de cerca de 40 megawatts, explica a Earth.com. 🔍 Adicione o Instituto Humanitas Unisinos – IHU às suas fontes favoritas do Google Os pesquisadores começaram o estudo com 675 locais candidatos de um banco de dados comercial e mantiveram os 403 que puderam ser confirmados. Cada endereço foi associado a um telhado, e sua área foi verificada no OpenStreetMap. Em seguida, os pesquisadores analisaram imagens de satélite e aéreas em busca de indícios de um centro de dados: grandes telhados uniformes, equipamentos de refrigeração e uma subestação ao lado. Dos HDCs analisados, 142 estão localizados na Virgínia, que abriga mais estruturas desse tipo do que qualquer outro estado dos EUA, 56 no Oregon e 38 em Ohio. Nenhum data center opera em sua capacidade nominal máxima a cada hora, e as empresas não divulgam suas cargas reais. Por isso, a equipe multiplicou a capacidade de cada instalação pelas horas do ano e por um fator de carga. Os pesquisadores executaram quatro versões desse fator, desde uma carga leve até uma destinada a abranger o treinamento pesado de IA, para chegar aos resultados. Agora a equipe planeja examinar os efeitos das emissões associadas aos HDCs na saúde, conta Francesca. “As centrais elétricas movidas a combustíveis fósseis nos sistemas regionais de distribuição de energia, associadas a essa demanda, também liberam outros poluentes, como partículas finas, óxidos de nitrogênio e dióxido de enxofre, que estão diretamente ligados a doenças cardíacas e pulmonares e à morte prematura”, disse a especialista. As pessoas que respiram esses poluentes vivem perto das usinas, que podem estar longe de qualquer centro de dados.

artigo.texto: Oito Estados-membros da União Europeia (UE), incluindo Dinamarca, Finlândia, Alemanha, Luxemburgo, Países Baixos, Portugal , Espanha e Suécia, manifestaram-se em defesa do novo Sistema de Comércio de Emissões (ETS2). Oito países da UE estão se unindo para proteger o mercado de carbono contra pressões para adiá-lo. Oito Estados-membros da União Europeia (UE) defenderam conjuntamente o sistema alargado de comércio de emissões do bloco, alertando que novos atrasos ou ajustes à sua implementação poderão comprometer a segurança energética, prolongar a dependência dos combustíveis fósseis importados e dificultar o investimento em tecnologias limpas. Em carta enviada ao Comissário Europeu para a Ação Climática, Wopke Hoekstra, em 23 de novembro, os ministros do clima argumentaram que a dependência de combustíveis fósseis importados representa riscos econômicos e de segurança significativos. O ETS2 é visto como uma ferramenta para promover a eletrificação nos transportes e na construção civil, reduzindo assim a necessidade de importação de petróleo e gás. A medida surge em meio à pressão da República Tcheca, Hungria, Polônia , Eslováquia, Itália e Grécia para flexibilizar ou adiar o sistema. Na cúpula de outubro, os líderes da UE concordaram em revisar o impacto do ETS2 antes de sua implementação a partir de janeiro de 2028. Segundo esse mecanismo, os combustíveis utilizados no transporte rodoviário e no aquecimento estariam sujeitos a um preço de carbono, o que poderia aumentar os custos para o consumidor. Este é também um ponto de discórdia, tendo em conta os já elevados custos da energia e do custo de vida na Europa. Oito ministros alertaram que ajustes ao ETS2 poderiam comprometer a estabilidade da política climática e impactar os planos de investimento das empresas. Eles também argumentaram que o Fundo Social para o Clima deveria ser mantido para apoiar famílias e empresas vulneráveis que enfrentam custos crescentes. Por outro lado, o vice-primeiro-ministro checo, Karel Havlíček, afirmou que a implementação do ETS2 no atual contexto económico e geopolítico é ilógica. Alertou que a imposição de taxas adicionais seria difícil de ser aceite pela população, uma vez que muitas famílias já enfrentam a pressão do aumento dos preços da energia e do custo de vida.

artigo.texto: Parcerias B.Grimm e NTT buscam oportunidade de desenvolver um centro de dados de IA de 400 MW na Tailândia Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Pontos-chaveO memorando apenas compromete os parceiros a buscar uma oportunidade de 400 MW, em vez… Ver mais - O memorando apenas compromete os parceiros a buscar uma oportunidade de 400 MW, em vez de confirmar a construção. - O negócio existente de geração e distribuição de energia da B.Grimm sustenta o seu papel energético no plano do data center. - O acordo separado da NTT com a Bloom Energy mostra que a disponibilidade de energia agora determina a rapidez com que a capacidade de IA pode ser entregue. A B.Grimm anunciou em 24 de novembro de 2026 que a B.Grimm Power havia assinado um memorando de entendimento com a NTT Global Data Center para buscar uma oportunidade de desenvolver um centro de dados de 400 MW na Tailândia, abrangendo infraestrutura digital, um ecossistema de IA e infraestrutura energética, com investimento estimado em aproximadamente 113 bilhões de THB. O memorando é um acordo para buscar a oportunidade, não uma confirmação de que as obras já começaram. Nopadej Karnasuta, presidente da B.Grimm Power para Tailândia, Malásia e Negócios de Soluções de Energia & Industriais, participou da visita ao Japão durante a qual o documento foi assinado. Segundo a B.Grimm, a visita, liderada pelo vice-primeiro-ministro e ministro das Finanças Ekniti Nitithanprapas, ocorreu de 17 a 21 de novembro de 2026. Conversas no Japão conectam infraestrutura de IA e energia Em um comunicado de 23 de novembro de 2026, o Conselho de Investimentos da Tailândia informa que a delegação esteve em Tóquio de 17 a 20 de novembro de 2026. O Diálogo de Investimento e Negócios Tailândia–Japão BOI–Keidanren reuniu 64 executivos japoneses do setor privado, de 38 empresas de nove setores. As discussões abordaram três cadeias de suprimentos: veículos modernos; infraestrutura de IA e eletrônica avançada; e redes elétricas modernas. Essas prioridades correspondem de perto à combinação de computação e energia prevista no MoU. A delegação também visitou o NTT Data Mitaka EAST Data Center para estudar segurança, continuidade dos sistemas e eficiência energética em infraestruturas que dão suporte à IA. Segundo o relato da B.Grimm, Ekniti destacou que as instalações da NTT no Japão são eficientes, silenciosas, respeitam o meio ambiente e conseguem coexistir com as comunidades locais. A B.Grimm Power também pretende manter essas práticas e compartilhar conhecimentos e tecnologia com a população tailandesa no longo prazo. Operações de geração de energia e digitais da B.Grimm A B.Grimm Power leva para a proposta uma operação consolidada no setor de energia. Seu perfil corporativo informa que a empresa tem capacidade instalada de 5.180 MW, fornece energia por meio de suas próprias redes de distribuição a mais de 400 clientes industriais e tem como meta garantir contratos de compra de energia que totalizem 10.000 MW até 2030. Com sede na Tailândia, a empresa desenvolve, financia, constrói e opera usinas de energia em áreas sem instalações anteriores. Essas operações são relevantes porque o MoU inclui explicitamente a infraestrutura energética, além do centro de dados e do ecossistema de IA. A B.Grimm também tem uma iniciativa de infraestrutura digital industrial. Em 18 de junho de 2026, a subsidiária B.Grimm BeyondBridge e a INET criaram a B.Grimm INET para desenvolver e operar plataformas na Tailândia voltadas à gestão de energia, a sistemas ambientais e de serviços públicos inteligentes, ao monitoramento e à gestão de gases de efeito estufa, à segurança na nuvem e a tecnologias de IA. A iniciativa anterior documenta a expansão da B.Grimm para além da geração de energia, com entrada no setor de plataformas digitais industriais, antes do acordo com a NTT. Expansão regional e estratégia energética da NTT A NTT DATA nomeou Yasuhiro Kajiki em 10 de setembro de 2026 para o cargo de diretor-geral para Japão e Ásia-Pacífico da NTT Global Data Centers, com responsabilidade pelas operações regionais e pela estratégia de crescimento. A empresa associou a ampliação das atribuições do cargo ao aumento da demanda dos clientes por infraestrutura digital preparada para IA na região da Ásia-Pacífico. Um acordo com a Bloom Energy, anunciado em 5 de novembro de 2026, prevê que a NTT instale 900 MW de capacidade de geração de energia no local em vários projetos de centros de dados no mundo todo, com os primeiros envios planejados para 2027. A NTT DATA espera que os sistemas modulares de células a combustível da Bloom permitam disponibilizar energia à medida que as obras avançam e ampliar a capacidade para atender às cargas de trabalho de IA, cada vez mais intensivas em energia. “Nossos clientes estão desenvolvendo recursos de IA em um ritmo que a rede elétrica, sozinha, nem sempre consegue acompanhar, e a rapidez para disponibilizar energia tornou-se um dos fatores decisivos para fornecer capacidade onde e quando ela é necessária”, afirmou Doug Adams, CEO da NTT Global Data Centers. Anunciado separadamente do MoU tailandês, o acordo com a Bloom mostra por que o papel da B.Grimm no setor de energia é importante: para os centros de dados de IA, garantir energia escalável é essencial para fornecer capacidade computacional. A questão em aberto é a execução: será que os parceiros conseguirão combinar a expansão dos centros de dados da NTT com as operações de energia e a experiência em infraestrutura digital da B.Grimm para oferecer a eficiência, a operação silenciosa e a convivência com as comunidades destacadas durante a visita ao Japão? Isso transformaria um memorando firmado durante uma missão de investimento na infraestrutura de IA operacional que a Tailândia busca.

artigo.texto: AOI Announces Multi-Year Long-Term Agreement with Tier-1 Hyperscale Datacenter Customer SUGAR LAND, Texas , Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AOI (NASDAQ: AAOI), a leading provider of advanced optical and HFC networking products that power AI, today announced it has signed a multiyear long-term agreement (LTA) with an existing Tier-1 hyperscale datacenter customer. Under the agreement, AOI will supply the customer with 800G transceiver products as well as laser diodes over the four-year time period from December 2026 through December 2030. Other products may be added depending on future needs. The customer has agreed to purchase a minimum commitment of approximately $1.5 billion of 800G transceivers in 2027 and approximately $0.7 billion in laser diodes between 2028 and 2029. As part of the agreement, AOI will contribute a $2 million one-time expense to accelerate qualification efforts with this customer. The customer made no commitment of capital as part of this LTA. "Securing another LTA with a second hyperscale customer provides us with meaningful long-term revenue and demand visibility, and reinforces our technology leadership, differentiated capabilities in advanced optics, and important role in the AI infrastructure ecosystem," said Dr. Thompson Lin, AOI's Founder, President and Chief Executive Officer. "We believe we are well positioned with our automated manufacturing capabilities and in-house laser technology to support the next phase of AI datacenter deployment." Lin continued, "We have a long history of manufacturing lasers and have strategically curated our portfolio to provide the high-performance optical sources driving the industry's shift toward silicon photonics, near-packaged optics (NPO), and co-packaged optics (CPO). As part of this agreement, we will be supplying our laser diodes, some of which we expect will be used to power CPO architectures, starting in 2028. We believe that in the future, CPO and related technologies will continue to drive increased demand for high-power lasers and we plan to further expand our laser manufacturing capacity in Texas to support this anticipated growth." "The customer's forecast indicates significant demand beyond the purchase commitments specified in the agreement over its four-year term," said Dr. Stefan Murry, AOI's Chief Financial Officer and Chief Strategy Officer. "While not guaranteed, the current level of demand based on long-term discussions with the customer exceeds $10 billion over the four years of the LTA. Expanding our production capacity would position us to serve that demand, but additional sales beyond the $2.2 billion of purchase commitments specified in the agreement will depend on our ability to bring that capacity online and secure additional purchase commitments. Under the LTA, we have committed to supplying volumes needed, including a commitment to ship an agreed-upon quantity of products made in the USA, starting in the first quarter of 2027 and ramping throughout 2027. We believe this agreement supports our ability to further increase our capacity, allocate capital, and invest in advanced technologies with greater confidence. To support this accelerating customer demand, we are continuing to expand our capacity and remain focused on executing on our expansion plans." artigo.texto: Reino Unido e UE concordam em conectar sistemas de comércio de emissões até 2028 O Reino Unido e a União Europeia chegaram a um acordo para conectar seus sistemas de comércio de emissões, com data-alvo de 1º de janeiro de 2028 para que a conexão entre em operação, conforme noticiado pelo ENGINE. A medida foi concebida para se alinhar à extensão programada pelo Reino Unido da precificação de carbono ao transporte marítimo internacional, segundo um explicativo publicado em 20 de novembro pelo Departamento de Segurança Energética e Net Zero do Reino Unido. Como parte da extensão prevista, o Sistema de Comércio de Emissões do Reino Unido passará a abranger metade das emissões de viagens internacionais que conectam portos do Reino Unido e portos de fora do país, para navios de 5.000 toneladas de arqueação bruta ou mais, a partir de 1º de janeiro de 2028. Desde 1º de julho de 2026, o sistema já cobre todas as emissões de viagens domésticas e de embarcações atracadas em portos britânicos. O ETS da UE funciona em bases semelhantes, aplicando-se a 50% das emissões em viagens entre portos da UE e portos de fora do bloco, ao mesmo tempo que obriga as empresas de navegação a responder pela totalidade das emissões de viagens entre portos da UE. Após a conexão, os dois sistemas continuarão a funcionar de forma independente, mas permitirão que as empresas de navegação usem licenças de qualquer um dos mercados para cumprir suas obrigações, o que pode eliminar a necessidade de os operadores abrangidos pelos dois sistemas comprarem licenças britânicas e licenças da UE separadamente. O ETS do Reino Unido também espelhará o tratamento dado pela UE aos portos vizinhos de transbordo de contêineres. Os portos que constam da lista designada pela Comissão Europeia não serão tratados como portos de escala britânicos ao se determinar quais emissões de viagem são cobertas pelo sistema, e essa lista é revisada a cada dois anos. Cronograma de conformidade e alinhamento administrativo O arranjo também pretende tratar das obrigações de emissões relativas a 2027, com o primeiro prazo para o uso intercambiável de licenças fixado em 30 de setembro de 2028. As duas partes buscam ainda um processo administrativo compartilhado que possa permitir às empresas de navegação lidar com a conformidade nos dois sistemas em um único arcabouço. O Reino Unido também pretende eliminar seu preço mínimo de leilão para licenças de carbono assim que a conexão entrar em vigor. O acordo busca alinhar mais estreitamente as regras de navegação do ETS do Reino Unido às do ETS da UE, incluindo os requisitos de monitoramento, relato e verificação. O Reino Unido planeja descontinuar o arranjo temporário que permite às empresas de navegação entregar licenças referentes a apenas 50% das emissões em viagens entre a Grã-Bretanha e a Irlanda do Norte, e espera-se que essas viagens passem a enfrentar a exigência integral de 100% a partir de 2028, igualando outras rotas domésticas britânicas. Espera-se que navios de passageiros e ro-pax que atendem ilhas com menos de 200.000 residentes e sem ligação rodoviária ou ferroviária com o continente sejam elegíveis a uma derrogação temporária de entrega de licenças até pelo menos 31 de dezembro de 2030. Navios com classe de gelo também devem receber uma redução de 5% em suas obrigações de entrega de licenças até pelo menos a mesma data. Combustíveis de menor emissão e revisão da medida global Quanto à contabilização de combustíveis, os operadores poderiam aplicar um fator de emissão zero a biocombustíveis elegíveis, combustíveis renováveis de origem não biológica e combustíveis de carbono reciclado, desde que atendam aos critérios de sustentabilidade e de redução de gases de efeito estufa estabelecidos na Diretiva de Energias Renováveis da UE. O governo britânico também indicou que examinará como suas regras de precificação de carbono interagem com qualquer futura medida global de emissões adotada pela Organização Marítima Internacional. A revisão buscaria evitar a cobrança dupla das empresas de navegação por emissões idênticas, mantendo os requisitos de conformidade viáveis. O departamento afirmou que qualquer revisão considerará mudanças relevantes no ETS da UE, com resultados destinados a sustentar o apoio à descarbonização marítima e a manter a consistência com o net zero. Preparativos técnicos e aprovações legislativas ainda estão pendentes antes que os dois mercados de carbono possam ser unidos até janeiro de 2028.

The Johnson Creek Village Board delayed a vote Monday on a proposed data center in Jefferson County, with the board president saying he wants more information before the board decides whether to move forward. The proposal, called the Johnson Creek Connectivity Hub, is a one-story, 100,000-square-foot edge data center planned for an industrially zoned site near River Drive and County Road Y. The developer, RadiusDC, says the facility would support everyday online services, including video calls, online banking, and streaming. At Monday’s meeting, residents raised concerns about potential water use, noise and environmental effects. Rosa, a community member who spoke at the meeting, asked board members to consider the project’s possible impact on her young daughter. “I will come up to you when I see you and I want you to look my daughter in the eyes and tell her that this is the best option for her,” Rosa said. “She’s 2 years old.” RadiusDC says the project could bring construction and full-time jobs and generate about $500,000 a year in property taxes. The company says construction could begin in 2027, with the facility expected to open in 2029, subject to approvals. Board President John Swisher drew cheers from the crowd when he suggested tabling the vote. He said the time will allow staff to take a closer look at any potential public health impacts and consider operations at similarly sized data centers in other communities. Trustee Rooney Freimund said tabling the vote wouldn't change public opinion. After initially being opposed to the project, he now believes it would benefit Johnson Creek, suggesting it doesn't compare to large-scale projects in other cities. "An airport is an airport, right? Watertown compared to Chicago O’Hare are two different airports," Freimund said. I’ve heard every one of you. I believe you love this community. I love the community too. I believe this project is good for Johnson Creek. We’re going to agree to disagree.” The board is expected to take up the proposal again Jan. 11, 2027.

artigo.texto: Piedmont delays two data center proposals amid utility and zoning concerns PIEDMONT, Okla. (KOKH) — Two proposed data centers in Piedmont will have to wait until December for further consideration after the City Council delayed action on both projects Monday night. Council members voted 3-2 to postpone consideration of Cloverleaf's Project Open Sky until Dec. 3. Later in the meeting, the council also voted 3-2 to bring Beltline Energy's proposal back on the same date while the city attorney reviews questions about changes previously approved by the council. Both developers are seeking to rezone agricultural land for industrial data center developments, but neither project received final approval Monday night. Cloverleaf's Project Open Sky involves a rezoning application from Cimarron ProjectCo LLC and Cimarron DevCo LLC. The developers want to change the property's zoning from A-1 General Agriculture to a Planned Unit Development, or PUD, which would establish development standards for the proposed data center. The application was scheduled for its first ordinance reading Monday night. However, the council voted to postpone further consideration until a special meeting on December 3rd. Beltline Energy is also seeking to rezone agricultural land for its proposed data center. Some Oklahomans raised concerns about whether Piedmont's infrastructure could handle the demands of the proposed developments, particularly when it comes to electricity, water, and sewer services. "The whole thing for me, being retired in utility, is the electric capacity this is gonna take, and also the water and the sewer," said Billy Parker, a Yukon resident. "There's so many questions left that are not answered about the water and the sewer, what it's gonna take for these data centers and so much of that and the electric that they're gonna use." Those concerns were echoed during the council's discussion of Beltline Energy's proposal. One council member urged the city to postpone further action until the development agreement had been fully reviewed. He argued that important details about the project's cooling system remained unresolved. The council member said Beltline previously indicated it was considering moving away from a closed-loop cooling system in favor of air cooling or another alternative. He questioned how much water the original system would hold, whether it would need to be flushed periodically, and what impact a different cooling method could have on noise and electricity demand. "After working on this issue for 10 months, these answers were very disappointing to me, to say the least," he said. He also questioned whether an air-cooled system would require additional fans and how those fans would be powered. "This is all too vague for me personally to take," he said. The council member argued Piedmont should settle the details of the development agreement before moving forward with additional land-use decisions. "First we need to agree on the development plan, then move on to annex or not," he said. The discussion also raised concerns about whether amendments approved during the council's October 26th meeting were accurately incorporated into an ordinance outlining the proposed rezoning for Beltline Energy's project. Council members questioned whether discrepancies between the approved meeting minutes and the ordinance could expose the city to a legal challenge. During the discussion, the city attorney acknowledged that inconsistencies could be challenged. The attorney also explained that the city's required second reading provides an opportunity to review the language and determine whether corrections are needed. A council member proposed directing the city attorney to compare the approved October 26th meeting minutes with the ordinance and identify any differences. His motion called for a report outlining whether the amendments had been properly incorporated and what consequences the city could face if the ordinance did not accurately reflect the council's previous actions. He also proposed preparing a corrected ordinance and holding another first reading if significant changes were necessary. However, another member argued the city could complete that review while keeping the proposal on track for a second reading December 3rd. The council ultimately voted 3-2 to amend the motion, allowing the ordinance to return for a potential second reading at the December meeting while the city attorney reviews the language. If the review identifies significant changes that need to be made, the ordinance may have to return for another first reading rather than moving directly toward final approval. Both data center proposals are expected to return to the Piedmont City Council on December 3rd, when members could take additional action depending on the outstanding reviews and discussions.

artigo.texto: Data centers: Oportunidades e controles de exportação A expansão dos data centers no Brasil ganha impulso com incentivos fiscais, mas enfrenta desafios diante das restrições dos EUA ao acesso a semicondutores. terça-feira, 24 de novembro de 2026 Atualizado em 23 de novembro de 2026 16:03 O Brasil quer atrair data centers com energia renovável e incentivos fiscais. Os Estados Unidos querem controlar quem utiliza os semicondutores que tornam esses investimentos possíveis. As duas políticas agora se encontram nos projetos de empresas que pretendem instalar servidores em território brasileiro. A localização será nacional; parte das condições para funcionamento dependerá de Washington. O REDATA, aprovado pelo Congresso e sancionado em setembro, traz vantagem concreta. Equipamentos importados representam parcela elevada do investimento, e a tributação brasileira encarecia a instalação, enquanto outros países ofereciam benefícios para receber os mesmos projetos. Reduzir esse custo melhora a posição do Brasil numa disputa em que o investidor compara energia, conectividade, impostos e previsibilidade. O REDATA prevê suspensão de tributos federais nas aquisições abrangidas, acompanhada de contrapartidas. Como regra geral, exige destinar ao mercado brasileiro ao menos 10% do fornecimento efetivo de serviços e investir no país o equivalente a 2% das compras beneficiadas, com condições diferenciadas previstas na legislação. Também estabelece requisitos energéticos e limite de consumo de água no resfriamento. Desta forma, o desenho institucional busca vincular a renúncia fiscal a benefícios locais. Como se sabe, a importância dos datacenters ultrapassa o interesse dos fornecedores de equipamentos. Capacidade computacional tornou-se infraestrutura estratégica para empresas, governos e pesquisa. Assim como portos permitem movimentar mercadorias, datacenters permitem processar informações em escala. A inteligência artificial pode parecer imaterial na tela do usuário, mas depende de instalações, cabos e muita eletricidade. O Brasil dispõe de vantagens nessa combinação. Sua matriz elétrica majoritariamente renovável interessa a empresas que precisam conciliar expansão computacional e metas de redução de emissões. A conectividade internacional e o tamanho do mercado interno também contam. Nenhuma dessas vantagens, entretanto, dispensa investimentos em transmissão, armazenamento e segurança do abastecimento. Água exige cuidado semelhante. O REDATA estabelece índice de eficiência hídrica para resfriamento de até 0,05 litro por kWh, medido anualmente. O parâmetro permite avaliar o desempenho das instalações, mas precisa ser acompanhado da análise das condições locais de abastecimento e de fiscalização durante a operação, pois a eficiência de cada unidade não resolve a pressão acumulada sobre uma bacia hidrográfica. Neste tema, a experiência norte-americana traz uma advertência. Levantamento citado pela Agência Internacional de Energia identificou 46 projetos de data centers de inteligência artificial bloqueados, retirados ou paralisados após oposição local, entre janeiro de 2024 e meados de maio de 2026. Estavam associados a mais de US$ 170 bilhões em investimentos anunciados. A esses desafios soma-se uma nova restrição. Em 19 de novembro, o BIS - Bureau of Industry and Security, do Departamento de Comércio norte-americano, publicou uma norma que combina dois controles. Um exige licença para operações abrangidas com determinados semicondutores avançados destinadas a Brasil, Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia. Outro alcança equipamentos utilizados em datacenters que forneçam acesso remoto, acima dos parâmetros definidos, a empresas sediadas, ou com controladora final sediada, em Macau ou nos países do grupo D:5 (China, Rússia, Irã, Coreia do Norte, Cuba e Venezuela). A distinção nesta regulamentação importa: a exigência relacionada ao destino brasileiro não depende apenas de demonstrar atendimento a clientes restritos. A norma prevê exceção condicionada para empresas sediadas nos Estados Unidos, além de obrigações de reporte e diligência. Esta nova regulamentação já entrou em vigor, e receberá comentários até 19 de janeiro de 2027, o que pode ser uma oportunidade para empresas brasileiras interessadas no tema responderem tecnicamente à consulta, buscando regras previsíveis para investimentos futuros. O investidor em datacenters no Brasil terá que atentar para esta regulamentação dos EUA, pois sua lógica é a de monitorar quem utiliza a capacidade computacional, mesmo sem receber fisicamente o chip. Para os contratos, haverá impactos com relação à concessão de licenças, risco de financiamento, contratos de serviços que identifiquem usuários, informações societárias e mudanças na operação. Para o Brasil, surge ainda uma questão concorrencial. Se as condições de acesso aos equipamentos variam conforme a sede e o controle das empresas, projetos instalados no mesmo território podem enfrentar exigências diferentes. Essa assimetria merecerá atenção diplomática, pois se o Brasil oferece incentivos à localização, os EUA consideram a identidade de quem investe e de quem será atendido. Nada disso elimina a oportunidade, para o Brasil, de exportar serviços digitais. Projetos aprovados na Zona de Processamento de Exportação do Pecém mostram que essa possibilidade já integra a agenda de investimentos. Energia, conectividade e processamento podem ser combinados para atender clientes no exterior, respeitadas as condições de cada regime. O Congresso brasileiro criou uma parte das condições para disputar esses investimentos. Agora, autoridades e empresas precisam articular infraestrutura, licenciamento ambiental, proteção de dados e acesso aos equipamentos. Ao governo cabe também tratar com os Estados Unidos das restrições que atingem o Brasil. Aos investidores, cabe incorporar essas condições à avaliação econômica, antes de comprometer capital, sempre relevante quando se trata de um datacenter. Welber Barral Sócio de Barr

artigo.texto: In a late meeting Monday night attended by dozens of people opposing the Trident Data Center, the Aurora City Council approved a ban on giving tax incentives to data center developers. It’s the latest salvo fired against data centers by the City Council. Recommended Stories The vote happened toward the end of the meeting, following the unanimous approval of a temporary data center moratorium and an announcement from Vantage Data Centers that Trident would no longer be built in its initially proposed Aurora location. The ordinance, proposed by Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman, is one effort of many in recent months by the Aurora council to regulate data centers. Aurora’s city code allows the city to use retail tax revenue and construction material use tax revenue generated by qualifying development projects to help finance public improvements and attract businesses. It also allows the city to waive sales or use taxes for certain developers. The ordinance, passed unanimously by the council, would prohibit data center incentives entirely. “There is an unprecedented amount of money behind data centers, largely driven by AI, and they do not need our tax dollars,” Coffman said about his proposed ordinance. Mayor Pro Tem Alison Coombs said she agrees with the ordinance but thinks a broader conversation about development incentives and oversight procedures needs to happen. The council already has the ability to vote on every sales and use tax incentive, including those for data centers, Coombs said, adding that if the council does not want to give incentives to a data center, it can vote against them. Coffman countered that the process, which happens in executive sessions, is not transparent to the public. “I don’t think it’s wise to bind the hand of future councils,” Councilmember Curtis Gardner said in a previous study session, adding that creating a sweeping rule for one industry “is not a good way to do governance.” Four tax incentives have been issued for data centers totaling $83 million. As of earlier this year, about $9 million had been paid out against that potential, City Manager Jason Batchelor said.

artigo.texto: How data center backlash could put banks’ AI bets under pressure 1 / 2 How data center backlash could put banks’ AI bets under pressure Claire Williams 5 min read Key insight: Local opposition to data-center construction could threaten lending and underwriting business for banks, particularly for projects still awaiting permits or approval. Forward look: Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., is pushing for greater disclosure of AI-related financing, a proposal with bipartisan support that could gain traction in the next Congress. WASHINGTON — Along with the election cycle's blue wave that's shifting power on Capitol Hill, voters also delivered a sweeping rebuke to artificial intelligence and a data center build-out that fueled many grassroots movements across the country. In Washington, this means accounting for an upswell in voter anger over AI's projected job losses and having an answer for data centers that many motivated voters do not want to live near. In local and state governments, policymakers are considering moratoriums or additional requirements for data centers that will make them more palatable to their constituents. One of the biggest flashpoints for this debate is Loudoun County, Virginia, said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., in an interview with American Banker. Loudoun County, home to "data center alley," recently paused processing new data center applications for a year. "Loudoun County actually is ground zero," Warner said. "They've got, candidly, the oldest data centers, the loudest, the most inefficient data centers in the country." Warner is not only one of the senators representing Virginia, he's also one of the leaders in the upper chamber on AI policy, particularly as it pertains to banks and other financial companies. "I've been just amazed at the concentration of capital," he said. "I've never seen anything like this. Where anything that has AI attached to it, you know, its valuation gets an extra zero." For the financiers of these data centers who are counting on a coming AI boom and want a piece of that market, a nationwide backlash to the build-out could cause some problems. "Banks should closely monitor and be very concerned about potential limits or moratoriums on AI data centers," said Peter Dugas, CEO of the advisory firm Regulatory Intelligence Group. "Fed Governor Barr recently spoke about potential bank runs due to AI circular financing, and a ban on current data center builds would only add to that stress." For banks, the immediate concern from local opposition in key areas like Loudoun County is more about future or pending business, rather than losses on already-functioning data centers. "I haven't seen anything that suggests there's a credit problem, but certainly it's a potential revenue problem for banks that have been engaged in lending to the sector… and now are questioning what their growth projections look like," said Brian Gardner, a Washington policy strategist at Stifel. The potential headwind mostly depends on the development stage of individual projects. Those that have secured permits and begun construction are less likely to be affected by local opposition than developments that are still awaiting approval. "It shouldn't be a material issue for facilities that are already under construction and are already permitted," Gardner said. "I think it's more for those projects that were on the drawing board or that were in the application phase." And while local moratoriums or other delays might be a problem for data center financiers, depending on the bank or other financial backer, the prospects for national legislation remain slim, especially as President Donald Trump retains veto power for the next two years. "This is a state and local issue, and a federal moratorium is highly unlikely," Gardner said. "I still believe that. I'm probably as confident in that view as I have been." Still, there will be "noise" around a federal moratorium, which presents headline risk for those who want to finance data centers, he said. And there are other ways lawmakers can look at the data-center issue without trying to issue a full moratorium. One of those ways comes from Warner, who late last week introduced a bill alongside Republican Sens. John Kennedy of Louisiana and Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., that would require nonfinancial companies to disclose to the Securities and Exchange Commission all debt arrangements or commitments used to finance AI infrastructure. It's the kind of narrower proposal that, especially with the level of Republican sign-off present in the co-sponsors of the legislation, could make it into law. Warner said in the interview that he's gotten buy-in from some people inside the administration, but that, of course, it's a long way from a bill's introduction to the president's desk, especially in the current political moment. "It's always easier said than done," he said. Warner specifically mentioned special purpose vehicles, or SPVs, that he said allow companies to move potentially risky financing arrangements off their balance sheets, escaping oversight from federal regulators. He said the number of companies using those structures, and the lack of standardization around them, make it harder to assess the concentration of capital flowing into AI. "I'm not accusing that there's something underhanded going on, but this is plain vanilla, 'we need more transparency,'" he said. Warner said he has discussed the proposal with major technology companies and large banks designated as systemically important financial institutions, or SIFIs. While those conversations have involved requests to adjust the language, he said the response has not been outright opposition. "I've talked to hyperscalers, I've talked to some of the big SIFI banks," he said. "They'd like maybe a paragraph slightly different, but nobody starts with 'this is a crazy idea.'"

artigo.texto: California Universities Build Campus AI Data Centers to Control Compute Costs and Data Governance California universities are building campus AI data centers to curb rising vendor cloud costs and protect sensitive student and research data governance. On November 23, 2026, California higher education systems, including the University of California, California State University, and California Community Colleges, accelerated investments in on-campus artificial intelligence data centers and localized open-weight computing clusters. The push establishes institutional digital sovereignty to control escalating commercial software licensing fees, eliminate vendor lock-in, and safeguard sensitive research and student records under strict university governance. What happened Public universities and community colleges across California are deploying on-premises hardware clusters and open-weight artificial intelligence models to counter growing dependence on commercial vendors. According to investigative reports published on November 23, 2026, by CalMatters and partner outlet LAist, institutional leaders across the University of California (UC), California State University (CSU), and the California Community Colleges system are launching on-campus AI data centers and localized computing infrastructure. The push toward local compute is grounded in physical campus deployments. At California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, university leadership unveiled an on-campus computing facility known as the AI Factory, detailed in an official announcement by California Polytechnic State University. Housed in the computer science building, the facility provides dedicated computing power for students and faculty. Simultaneously, the University of California, San Diego expanded its campus AI platform, documented by the University of California San Diego, which operates TritonGPT out of the San Diego Supercomputer Center (SDSC). Concurrently, the California Community Colleges system—representing 116 colleges and the largest postsecondary education network in the United States—submitted a formal budget proposal seeking 21 million dollars in state funding to build an interconnected, sovereign AI compute network. The initiatives represent an institutional effort to control escalating subscription fees and protect student records, even as university systems maintain commercial enterprise agreements. Key details of campus AI deployments Campus computing architectures across California reflect diverse strategies tailored to undergraduate education, high-performance academic research, and statewide community college administration. Cal Poly’s AI Factory was funded by a 3 million dollar gift from the estate of Intel co-founder Robert N. Noyce through the School of Applied Computing. Providing 1,300 terabytes of storage and four NVIDIA DGX B200 systems, it enables faculty like Dr. Jonathan Ventura (drone ecology) and Dr. Paul Anderson (spinal cord genomics) to train models on university-controlled hardware without transmitting protected data externally. At UC San Diego, TritonGPT has evolved into TritonAI, serving administrative and research queries across campus. UCSD shares its underlying software architecture with peer campuses, supporting BearGPT at UC Berkeley and SCOUT at UC Merced. Linking these distributed facilities is the California Research and Education Network (CalREN), an 8,000-mile fiber-optic network operated by CENIC that currently connects approximately 20 community college districts, UC campuses, and CSU universities. Background and commercial cloud tensions The turn toward on-campus compute stems from mounting fiscal and governance friction between public university administrations and commercial artificial intelligence vendors. Systemwide enterprise agreements have grown increasingly expensive. The University of California negotiated enterprise terms for ChatGPT Edu starting at 10 dollars per user per month, with advanced capabilities reaching 30 dollars per user per month. The California State University system signed enterprise contracts with OpenAI extending through 2029 with commitments totaling roughly 56 million dollars. Per-seat commercial licensing creates unpredictable operational expenditures that strain departmental budgets when usage spikes beyond contract quotas. In contrast, acquiring on-premises server hardware converts variable operational costs into amortized capital investments, allowing universities to deploy open-weight models without per-query token fees. Statutory privacy compliance presents an equally critical driver. Public universities manage legally protected records under the FERPA (Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act) and the HIPAA Privacy Rule. Commercial vendor contracts generally stipulate that user data will not be used to train frontier models, but campus administrators remain wary of potential data leakage. On-premises clusters ensure strict data residency within university firewalls. Environmental transparency also shapes compute governance. Assessing the direct compute carbon footprint of closed cloud queries remains difficult due to commercial vendor opacity. Running localized infrastructure under sustainable HPC practices allows university facility managers to monitor power draw and cooling demands directly against institutional sustainability targets. Faculty, student, and governance reactions The expansion of commercial AI contracts and the parallel investment in local compute have triggered significant debate across California academic senates, student groups, and administrative councils. Faculty bodies have voiced skepticism toward top-down commercial software procurement, arguing that automated text tools compromise educational integrity. On November 5, 2026, the Academic Senate of the California State University approved formal resolution AS-3813-26/AA/FA: Reorientation of Faculty Engagement With Generative A.I., calling on CSU leadership

artigo.texto: (The Center Square) – The to-do list for Democrats who will soon control lawmaking in Harrisburg is almost certain to include party staples like a minimum wage increase and reproductive rights legislation, but the biggest question may be how to respond to intense public demand for action on data centers. On Tuesday, a high-profile pollster gave The Center Square a preview of forthcoming poll data that shows Pennsylvanians want lawmakers to act. And, hotspots of public outrage continue to simmer around the state over proposals to build the giant buildings stuffed with servers. In Lackawanna County, Superintendent Patrick Sheehan of Mid Valley School District on Tuesday said his district has gone to court to intervene in a situation in which Olyphant Borough Council voted to drop its traditional "conditional use" public hearing process on a big data center proposal. In exchange for that vote, the developer has agreed to pay more than $100 million for community benefits. In Lehigh County Monday night, the state Department of Environmental Protection hosted a hearing on state permits requested for so-called 'Project Atlas'. The proposed 1.5 million-square-foot data center complex would be built in Lehigh County across the street from the state's fifth-largest high school, Parkland. The project does not yet have full local approvals. Megan McDonough, Pennsylvania director for the advocacy group Food & Water Watch, said Gov. Josh Shapiro and the DEP appear to be "bending over backwards to build this data center." State Senator-elect Mark Pinsley, in a press release issued Tuesday by Food & Water Watch, said he opposed Project Atlas. "A massive data center has no business going across the street from Parkland High School or next to a residential neighborhood," he said. Pinsley was one of four Democratic challengers who beat incumbent Republican senators in the Nov. 3 general election, helping bring an end to more than 30 years of Republican dominance in the Senate. Come January, his party will control the Senate, House, and governor's office. And the public is expecting substantive action on data centers, if new polling overseen by veteran Pennsylvania pollster Chris Borick is any indication. Borick ran a nationally recognized polling operation at Muhlenberg College for many years. In his new post as director of the just-created Lehigh University Opinion Observatory, Borick expects the Bethlehem research center to release data by mid-December on its first polling deep-dive, which is on data centers. The results, he said, are "unquestionable" in showing "the Pennsylvania public is highly concerned with data center development. It played a role with their election decisions this fall and they want actions from policymakers." It would be difficult for the state legislature to do less about data centers than it did in 2026. The House and Senate failed to pass any substantive legislation on the issue. Gov. Josh Shapiro, a possible 2028 presidential candidate, was a high-profile supporter of the data center industry as it mushroomed in Pennsylvania from late 2024 into early 2026. He appeared at the controversial "Project Hazelnut" site in Luzerne County in late 2024 to launch a "fast track" state permitting program that included many big data center proposals. In August, facing the barrage of public negativity, he reversed course and issued an executive order that pulled data centers from the fast track list and put up "guard rails" on the industry. Among other things, the state DEP put into its permit review processes a set of Shapiro-backed safeguards. Minimum wage and reproductive rights legislation got prominent mentions in Democratic post-election press conferences. But references to potential new data center laws were muted. "I refuse to let this be pushed aside, forgotten about, overlooked," state Sen. Katie Muth, a Montgomery County Democrat, said in an interview Tuesday. Muth has pushed unsuccessfully for a three-year moratorium on data center development. She also wants to see elimination of the sales tax break given to data center companies and a legal wall to prevent data centers from being considered public utilities, among other things. The Olyphant Borough Council votes taken on Nov. 17 triggered deep concern in some quarters. One 5-2 vote ratified a legal settlement between the borough and developer Ercor Triboro that does away with the traditional conditional use process involving a public hearing. A separate 5-2 vote approved a community benefits agreement that would dole out $100 million-plus to the community over 15 years. "Residents deserve to have a voice in these decisions and any move to foreclose on that process is wrong," said state Rep. Kyle Mullins, a Democrat whose district includes Olyphant. Mullins said the site originally was supposed to be developed with warehouses with "thousands of jobs" and the switch to data centers means public hearings are necessary. In Harrisburg, he said, "We need urgent action to change the law on data centers." The Mid Valley School District's cluster of buildings is 1.5 miles from the site but Sheehan, the school superintendent, said the location is pretty much "right behind us." Two thousand students as young as five years old and about 200 staffers are on the campus during the day, Sheehan said. The school district has an obligation to protect "the health, safety, and welfare of the students and staff," he said. It would have carried out that obligation by taking part in the public hearing process that has been scrapped, according to Sheehan. Hence, Sheehan said, the district sought to intervene in the court case. A hearing on its participation is scheduled for Dec. 7 in Lackawanna County Court. The district also is seeking proposals on noise and environmental studies to be done at the proposed data center site.
