artigo.texto: TELF AG on How Public Policies Are Reshaping Energy Storage Strategies TELF AG on public policies and energy transition The expansion of renewable energy is prompting governments to reconsider the scope of their energy policies. While the development of wind and solar power remains a central objective, public institutions are increasingly focusing on the infrastructure required to manage renewable electricity efficiently. A recent example comes from the United Kingdom, where the National Wealth Fund has confirmed its support for two large-scale battery storage projects in southern Scotland. The facilities will have a combined power capacity of 1 GW and an energy storage capacity of 2 GWh. The initiative reflects a broader transformation in public energy strategies, with governments increasingly involved in the development of infrastructure that complements renewable electricity generation. “The expansion of renewable energy is encouraging public institutions to address a wider range of infrastructure needs, particularly those associated with the management and distribution of electricity,” says Stanislav Kondrashov. The Changing Scope of Public Energy Policies For several years, many government initiatives related to the energy transition have focused on encouraging renewable electricity production. Regulatory measures, financial incentives and technological development programs have contributed to the construction of wind farms and photovoltaic facilities. However, the increasing availability of renewable electricity is creating new challenges. Electricity generation from wind and solar sources depends on weather conditions, meaning that production does not always coincide with consumption patterns. Governments are therefore paying greater attention to technologies capable of managing these fluctuations. Energy storage systems represent one of the most promising solutions in this area. The British National Wealth Fund has allocated approximately £87 million to support the development of the two Scottish battery storage projects. Their planned locations along electricity transmission corridors connecting Scotland and England could help address some of the challenges associated with renewable electricity distribution. Energy Storage and the Management of Renewable Electricity Scotland has particularly favorable conditions for wind energy generation. Its geographical characteristics and exposure to strong winds have supported the development of both offshore and onshore renewable energy facilities. However, the expansion of generation capacity can place additional pressure on existing transmission networks. When electricity production exceeds the capacity of the grid to transport it, renewable energy facilities may be required to temporarily reduce their output. This phenomenon, known as curtailment, illustrates the importance of developing infrastructure alongside renewable generation capacity. Battery energy storage systems, commonly referred to as BESS, can help address this issue. These facilities store electricity during periods of abundant generation and release it when demand increases or transmission conditions become more favorable. “The Scottish example illustrates how public policies can address some of the operational challenges emerging from the rapid expansion of renewable electricity generation,” explains Stanislav Kondrashov. Storage technologies can also contribute to grid frequency regulation and provide additional flexibility during periods of fluctuating electricity demand. Their effectiveness in addressing transmission congestion depends on their location, operating strategies and the characteristics of the surrounding electricity network. Public Policies and Critical Raw Material Supply Chains The growing attention devoted to energy storage infrastructure also has implications for industrial supply chains. Large-scale battery systems require various raw materials, each performing a specific function within the technology. Lithium is widely used in lithium-ion batteries, while graphite is commonly employed in battery anodes. Copper and aluminum are also used in electrical connections, current collectors and other system components. As governments expand their energy policies to include storage infrastructure, demand for these resources could be influenced by a broader range of public initiatives. This development highlights the relationship between energy policy, industrial planning and raw material availability. Decisions concerning electricity infrastructure may have repercussions across multiple stages of the supply chain, from mineral extraction and processing to battery manufacturing and system installation. “Public energy strategies are becoming increasingly interconnected with industrial policies, technological development and the availability of the materials needed to build modern electricity infrastructure,” concludes Stanislav Kondrashov. The Scottish projects offer an example of how public institutions can participate in this transformation. Rather than focusing exclusively on increasing renewable generation, governments are beginning to address the technical and infrastructural conditions necessary for its effective integration. The future of renewable energy may therefore depend not only on the number of wind turbines and solar panels installed, but also on the ability of public policies to support more flexible, resilient and efficient electricity systems. artigo.texto: A Greenline, empresa brasileira de tecnologia climática, anunciou a adoção de seguro obrigatório para todos os créditos de carbono mensurados e emitidos em suas operações. A iniciativa foi desenvolvida com a participação da corretora Marsh e da Akad Seguros e estabelece um limite inicial de cobertura de US$ 25 milhões por projeto, com o objetivo de reduzir os riscos financeiros associados à comercialização de ativos ambientais. A medida será aplicada aos créditos classificados como ex-post, emitidos após a verificação dos resultados dos projetos. Com isso, a contratação do seguro passa a ser uma condição para a emissão desses ativos nas operações da Greenline. A iniciativa ocorre em um mercado no qual a qualidade dos créditos de carbono, a permanência dos resultados ambientais e a regularidade dos projetos têm ganhado importância nas negociações com compradores corporativos. Entre as preocupações estão a possibilidade de os créditos perderem sua validade e os prejuízos decorrentes de falhas na entrega dos ativos contratados. O seguro foi estruturado para responder a quatro grupos de riscos: descumprimento da entrega dos créditos negociados, falhas estruturais nos projetos responsáveis pela geração dos ativos, perda permanente de sua utilidade e despesas adicionais para aquisição de créditos substitutos. A cobertura para perda de utilidade contempla situações como a desqualificação de metodologias utilizadas na emissão ou de autorizações governamentais. Já a proteção para substituição busca cobrir os custos adicionais enfrentados pelo comprador ou responsável pela operação quando os créditos originais são afetados por um evento previsto na apólice. O produto também prevê despesas emergenciais para mitigação de danos, incluindo custos imediatos com combate a incêndios florestais e auditorias realizadas após desastres naturais, conforme as condições contratadas. Cobertura pode alcançar US$ 25 milhões por projeto O limite inicial estabelecido para a solução é de US$ 25 milhões por projeto. Considerando um preço de referência de US$ 10 por crédito de carbono, o valor corresponde à proteção financeira equivalente a 2,5 milhões de créditos, associados a 2,5 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente. A referência, no entanto, não significa que todos os projetos terão esse volume de créditos emitidos ou que a indenização será automática. A aplicação da cobertura dependerá dos riscos previstos e das condições estabelecidas na apólice. Para Lucio Lopez, fundador e CEO da Greenline, a exigência de seguro está relacionada à necessidade de oferecer maior previsibilidade às empresas que compram créditos de carbono. “Controvérsias sobre a qualidade dos créditos, regularidade fundiária e o risco reputacional do greenwashing tornaram-se tópicos centrais em nossas negociações com grandes compradores corporativos”, afirma. O executivo, a proteção securitária pode contribuir para a estruturação financeira das operações e para a redução das incertezas enfrentadas pelos participantes desse mercado. Além das novas emissões, a Greenline pretende estender a possibilidade de contratação do seguro a projetos que já eram mensurados pela companhia antes da parceria com a Akad Seguros. Nesses casos, a inclusão dependerá de avaliação e aceitação dos riscos pela seguradora. A possibilidade de extensão está relacionada, segundo a empresa, à padronização dos processos de mensuração e ao uso de tecnologias de sensoriamento remoto para acompanhar projetos de conservação de florestas nativas e redução do desmatamento. Embora a Greenline tenha participado da estruturação da demanda e estabelecido a obrigatoriedade do seguro em suas próprias operações, o produto também poderá ser contratado por outros agentes do mercado de ativos ambientais, conforme os critérios de subscrição da Akad. A iniciativa amplia a utilização do seguro como instrumento de transferência de riscos em operações com créditos de carbono. A cobertura financeira, entretanto, não substitui os processos de verificação ambiental nem elimina a necessidade de avaliar a integridade dos projetos e dos ativos negociados. “Estamos transformando ativos ambientais em instrumentos financeiros verdadeiramente bancáveis”, afirma Lopez.

artigo.texto: ACME Solar Completes Commissioning of 255.12 MWh Battery Storage System for NHPC Renewable Energy Project ACME Solar has commissioned part of its battery storage project in Rajasthan. Commercial operations are set to begin later this week. Read more. ACME Solar has commissioned a 63.78 MW battery storage facility in Rajasthan, with an energy storage capacity of 255.12 MWh, under its NHPC renewable energy project. The company completed the commissioning on 25 November, with commercial operations scheduled to begin on 27 November. The commissioning was carried out through ACME Hybrid Urja Private Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of ACME Solar. The project is located at Mehar Nagar village in Pokharan tehsil of Jaisalmer district, Rajasthan. The company said the commissioning covers only the battery storage component of the NHPC FDRE project. ACME Solar Share Price Movement Shares of ACME Solar Holdings were trading higher on Thursday following the development. The stock touched an intraday high of ₹419.60, gaining 0.73% from its previous close of ₹416.55. It opened at ₹417.65 and slipped to an intraday low of ₹413.75 during the session. At 12:32 pm, ACME Solar Holdings shares were down 0.66% on the National Stock Exchange (NSE). What is the Total Battery Storage Capacity of the Project? The commissioned component has a discharge capacity of 63.78 MW and an installed capacity of 300 MWh. It forms part of a larger battery storage installation planned under the project. The total BESS component has a discharge capacity of 280 MW/1,120 MWh, against an installed capacity of 280 MW/1,316 MWh. ACME Solar has signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) with NHPC Ltd for the project. The latest commissioning marks another step in the company's execution of its FDRE project portfolio. However, the exchange filing did not disclose the project cost, expected revenue contribution or the financial impact of the commissioned capacity. How do Battery Energy Storage Systems Support Renewable Energy Projects? Power generation from renewable sources can vary through the day. Battery systems allow companies to store the electricity generated and release it when demand arises. Such systems are an important part of FDRE projects. They aim to provide renewable electricity in line with scheduled power requirements. The commissioned capacity will form part of ACME Solar's battery storage infrastructure for its NHPC project. artigo.texto: Vehicle Solid State Battery Market to Reach USD 29.11 Billion by 2032, Surging at 47.3% CAGR According to QY Research, the latest Global Vehicle Solid State Battery Market Research Report 2026-2032 provides an in-depth assessment of market development, product and technology evolution, competitive positioning, customer demand, regional opportunities and industry-chain changes. The study is designed to help manufacturers, suppliers, distributors, investors, procurement teams and business decision-makers better understand how the Vehicle Solid State Battery industry is changing and where meaningful commercial opportunities may emerge during the forecast period. Rather than focusing only on headline growth, the research evaluates practical issues influencing business decisions, including customer requirements, product differentiation, supply-chain conditions, technology adoption, pricing pressure, qualification barriers and potential routes for market expansion. Get PDF Sample Copy of Report - Includes TOC, Market Forecasts, Company Profiles, Tables and Charts: https://www.qyresearch.in/request-sample/energy-power-global-vehicle-solid-state-battery-market-insights-industry-share-sales-projections-and-demand-outlook-2026-2032 The global Vehicle Solid State Battery market was valued at US$ 1.93 billion in 2025 and is anticipated to reach US$ 29.11 billion by 2032, witnessing a CAGR of 47.3% during the forecast period 2026-2032. In 2025, global Vehicle Solid State Battery production reached approximately 9680 MW , with an average global market price of around US$200 per kilowatt. A vehicle solid-state battery is an advanced energy storage system for electric vehicles that replaces the liquid or gel electrolyte in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a solid electrolyte (ceramic, sulfide, or polymer-based materials). This allows lithium ions to move between electrodes through a solid medium, significantly improving energy density, safety, thermal stability, and cycle life, while reducing fire and leakage risks. Solid-state batteries are considered a next-generation EV battery technology, currently transitioning from R&D to early commercialization. The upstream of vehicle solid-state batteries includes lithium resources, cathode materials (high-nickel NCM, LFP variants), anode materials (silicon-carbon, lithium metal), solid electrolytes (oxides, sulfides, polymers), and current collectors, supplied by companies such as Albemarle, SQM, Ganfeng Lithium, Tianqi Lithium, BASF, Umicore, and CATL material ecosystem partners. The midstream consists of battery manufacturers such as Toyota, QuantumScape, Solid Power, CATL, Samsung SDI, LG Energy Solution, SK On, and Factorial Energy. Downstream applications include electric vehicle OEMs (Tesla, Toyota, Volkswagen, BYD, Mercedes-Benz, NIO) as well as premium energy storage, robotics, and aerospace systems. Vehicle solid-state batteries are currently in a critical transition phase from technology validation to early commercialization. The key drivers include the demand for higher energy density, longer driving range, faster charging, and improved safety in electric vehicles. By replacing liquid electrolytes with solid materials, solid-state batteries fundamentally address safety risks and energy limitations of conventional lithium-ion systems. However, challenges remain, including high interfacial resistance, high material costs, manufacturing scalability issues, and limited cycle stability. The industry is currently adopting a "semi-solid first, full-solid later" roadmap. Future development will focus on lithium-metal anodes, scalable sulfide electrolytes, solid-solid interface engineering, and automotive-grade mass production technologies. Competitive Landscape Competition in the Vehicle Solid State Battery Market is shaped by technology capability, product reliability, manufacturing cost, customer relationships, delivery performance and technical support. Established global companies may benefit from recognized brands, larger customer networks, broader portfolios and long-term qualification histories, while regional manufacturers can compete through faster delivery, competitive pricing, customization and local service. Leading suppliers are increasingly investing in product development, production automation, capacity expansion, regional support and application-specific solutions. Competitive advantage is therefore moving beyond unit price toward the total value a supplier can provide throughout the customer relationship. artigo.texto: Ouça este conteúdo Uma reportagem publicada nesta quarta-feira (25) pela Reuters informou que empresas ligadas a Alice Huang, a empresária apontada como espiã chinesa por agências de inteligência dos EUA e com quem o CEO da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, teve um caso, equiparam grandes data centers de inteligência artificial (IA) na China. De acordo com a agência britânica, registros do banco central chinês indicam que tais empresas obtiveram financiamento oferecendo como garantias 764 servidores e módulos de IA avaliados em US$ 270 milhões e equipamentos usados para conectá-los em grandes redes de computação avaliados em US$ 31 milhões. A Reuters apurou que grande parte desse hardware foi alocada em um grande data center em Xangai, associado a um projeto de computação de IA lançado no âmbito de uma parceria estratégica entre a gigante chinesa de tecnologia Tencent e o governo do distrito de Songjiang. A agência britânica disse que os registros do banco central da China não detalham se tais infraestruturas utilizam chips cuja exportação ao país asiático foi vetada pelos Estados Unidos. Na segunda-feira (23), o Departamento de Comércio dos EUA incluiu a Megaspeed, empresa sediada em Singapura e ligada a Alice Huang, em sua lista negra comercial. A empresa negou qualquer irregularidade e afirmou que Alice Huang deixou a empresa em agosto de 2025. Na segunda-feira, onze dias após ter renunciado, Jensen Huang retornou ao cargo de CEO da Nvidia, com a empresa americana e o governo Donald Trump alegando que a recondução dele não representa riscos à segurança nacional. O presidente americano admitiu que intercedeu junto ao Conselho de Administração da gigante dos chips para que Jensen Huang fosse reconduzido ao posto. A volta do CEO fez as ações da Nvidia dispararem. Segundo informações do jornal britânico Financial Times, Trump, que é acionista da empresa, teria ganhado até US$ 15 milhões com essa movimentação de mercado.

artigo.texto: CMBlu Plans 10 MW Battery System for Imperial Irrigation The German developer's SolidFlow storage project in Winterhaven, California, is set to be the utility's first flow battery deployment. Updated on Nov. 23, 2026 in Energy Live Poll Do you think electricity reliability in your area is getting better? CMBlu, a German battery developer, plans to build a 10 MW/100 MWh SolidFlow battery energy storage system for the Imperial Irrigation District. The California Energy Commission approved a $7.2 million grant this week for the project's first phase. Why it matters The grant is intended to strengthen grid resilience and the reliability of energy supplies for communities across California. The project would give the Imperial Irrigation District its first deployment of flow battery technology. The first phase covers 1 MW of power and 10 MWh of storage, while the full Echo Sands system is planned at 10 MW and 100 MWh, with the $7.2 million California Energy Commission grant funding only the initial phase. The total cost of the full project and the schedule for the second phase have not been disclosed. The players CMBlu CMBlu is a German battery developer that is developing the SolidFlow-based Echo Sands storage project. Imperial Irrigation District The Imperial Irrigation District is a public water and power utility serving California's Imperial Valley region. The details The battery will be installed at a hydroelectric power plant in Winterhaven, California, and is designed to store electricity for more than 10 hours to help supply the Quechan Tribe and surrounding communities. The grant comes from the Community Energy Reliability and Resilience Investment program, which is sourced from federal funds. Timeline - The California Energy Commission approved the $7.2 million grant this week. Energy Landscape The Echo Sands award is one of the grants issued under the Community Energy Reliability and Resilience Investment program to fund grid resilience projects across California. It extends that program's push for longer-duration storage by backing a 10-hour flow battery at a utility's hydroelectric site. For Imperial Valley residents and Quechan Tribe communities, the project aims to keep stored electricity available for more than 10 hours, which could improve power reliability during outages. The grant's first phase is limited to 1 MW and 10 MWh, so the full benefit depends on the planned second phase being completed. The takeaway Longer-duration storage projects like Echo Sands show how state grants can fund early phases of grid resilience work before full deployment. Readers tracking regional energy reliability should watch for updates on the second phase and the full 100 MWh system. Further reading For more on how states are funding grid storage, see the Energy section. Source note: This article includes information reported by pv magazine USA. artigo.texto: Bill would end sales tax exemption for qualifying Texas data centers State Sen.-elect Trent Ashby is a co-author of Senate Bill 293, which lawmakers expect to pass in January AUSTIN, Texas (KCBD) - A bill filed in the Texas Legislature would remove the sales tax exemption for qualifying data centers. State Sen.-elect Trent Ashby, a co-author of Senate Bill 293, said Texas taxpayers should not foot the bill for these projects. Cost of the exemption There have been concerns over data center growth since the sales tax exemption was put in place more than a decade ago. Ashby said that when the law took effect in 2013, the cost was estimated at about $15 million. He said the most recent estimate is that the exemption will cost $3.3 billion in the upcoming biennium. What the bill would do SB 293 would remove the sales tax exemption for qualifying data centers, such as those that are at least 100,000 square feet. Existing exemptions would end when the bill takes effect. “It just doesn’t make sense to continue to subsidize these data center companies that are frankly some of the most capitalized companies in the United States, but in the world,” Ashby said. Economist suggests different approach Texas economist Dr. Ray Perryman said he would rather see additional requirements for data centers to qualify for the exemption than remove it entirely. “Maybe requiring that you have power worked out behind the grid, require you have water supply worked out, those kinds of things,” Perryman said. Perryman said changing the current law could affect rural Texans especially. “It’s enough of an incentive that some of these data centers would go away, and if one goes away, you’re talking about billions in an area, particularly rural, that doesn’t have a lot of development,” Perryman said. Ashby said he does not expect much pushback from businesses. “These companies are so well capitalized, and these data centers are very profitable,” Ashby said. Next steps Enough lawmakers have signed onto the bill for it to pass the state Senate when members convene in January. Ashby also said he wants to look at providing counties with limited regulatory authority over data center development. Copyright 2026 KCBD. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: 24 Novembro 2026 Demanda de energia elétrica foi de 82 TWh, cerca de 1,8% do consumo total de eletricidade do país, com emissões de 26 milhões de toneladas de CO₂. A informação é publicada por ClimaInfo, 24-11-2026. Em um ano, entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025, os 403 maiores centros de dados dos Estados Unidos emitiram mais dióxido de carbono do que a Dinamarca, que tem cerca de 6 milhões de habitantes. É o que mostra um estudo publicado na revista Nature Sustainability na semana passada. A pesquisa é uma das primeiras a estimar o consumo de eletricidade e as emissões de centros de dados hiperescaláveis (HDCs, sigla em inglês) desde o surgimento da inteligência artificial, segundo a Euronews. Em diferentes cenários de carga, esses HDCs consumiram entre 68 e 99 terawatts-hora (TWh) de eletricidade, associados a aproximadamente 21 milhões e 31 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (MtCO₂). No cenário médio, a demanda de eletricidade desses data centers foi de 82 TWh, correspondendo a 1,8% do consumo total de eletricidade dos EUA, com emissões de CO₂ atribuíveis de cerca de 26 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono. Cerca de 54% da geração atribuída foi proveniente de fontes de combustíveis fósseis, principalmente gás e carvão. A estimativa de emissões é de duas a três vezes maior do que a demonstrada em estudos anteriores, afirmou a autora sênior do estudo, Francesca Dominici, professora de bioestatística de Harvard. “É o equivalente à emissão de CO₂ de um pequeno país europeu”, disse a especialista, acrescentando que os planos para mais 2 mil centros de dados tornam essa quantidade ainda mais preocupante para o futuro, destaca a AP. Os HDCs são a maior classe de centros de dados, sendo o tipo que executa serviços em nuvem e treina grandes modelos de IA. Os edifícios da amostra tinham uma capacidade elétrica média de cerca de 40 megawatts, explica a Earth.com. 🔍 Adicione o Instituto Humanitas Unisinos – IHU às suas fontes favoritas do Google Os pesquisadores começaram o estudo com 675 locais candidatos de um banco de dados comercial e mantiveram os 403 que puderam ser confirmados. Cada endereço foi associado a um telhado, e sua área foi verificada no OpenStreetMap. Em seguida, os pesquisadores analisaram imagens de satélite e aéreas em busca de indícios de um centro de dados: grandes telhados uniformes, equipamentos de refrigeração e uma subestação ao lado. Dos HDCs analisados, 142 estão localizados na Virgínia, que abriga mais estruturas desse tipo do que qualquer outro estado dos EUA, 56 no Oregon e 38 em Ohio. Nenhum data center opera em sua capacidade nominal máxima a cada hora, e as empresas não divulgam suas cargas reais. Por isso, a equipe multiplicou a capacidade de cada instalação pelas horas do ano e por um fator de carga. Os pesquisadores executaram quatro versões desse fator, desde uma carga leve até uma destinada a abranger o treinamento pesado de IA, para chegar aos resultados. Agora a equipe planeja examinar os efeitos das emissões associadas aos HDCs na saúde, conta Francesca. “As centrais elétricas movidas a combustíveis fósseis nos sistemas regionais de distribuição de energia, associadas a essa demanda, também liberam outros poluentes, como partículas finas, óxidos de nitrogênio e dióxido de enxofre, que estão diretamente ligados a doenças cardíacas e pulmonares e à morte prematura”, disse a especialista. As pessoas que respiram esses poluentes vivem perto das usinas, que podem estar longe de qualquer centro de dados.

artigo.texto: Shelby County Commission considers data center regulations MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - The Shelby County Commission is discussing its own potential data center regulations Monday, with just over 100 days left on the Memphis City Council’s data center moratorium. Monday’s discussion is the first reading in the full county commission. It passed on first reading 9 ayes and 4 noes. The proposal has two more readings to go through with the full commission. People in the community are on both sides of the issue. Many want stricter boundaries on where data centers can locate. Some in the business community do not want those limits. Commissioner Amber Huett-Garica proposed updating the Memphis and Shelby County unified development code. If passed, the proposal would change zoning options for data centers, set rules on noise from the facilities and outline water usage. Richard Massey, data center accountability manager for the environmental justice organization Young, Gifted, and Green, is pushing for the proposal to pass. He said the proposal may also include zoning for current facilities. “To ensure that at the same time, we are having community sessions for folks to provide recommendations, insight, and testimony about their experience that no hyperscale data center can get grandfathered in beneath the existing zoning laws that have permitted this awful business model to come into Shelby County and effectively run wild without any regulatory oversight,” Massey said. The proposal follows meetings at the city level on data center regulation. The regulation proposal that passed the Memphis City Council differed from what the community pushed for: community input. Massey said he and other community members expect pushback on the county proposal. He said they will continue to push for regulation. “Also, I think it is critical that we pass Commissioner Huett- Garcia’s ordinance because it includes a trove of things that we have been pushing for all along. It includes restrictions on noise, for example; it includes that ban on using the aquifer, for example,” he said. Supporters of data centers in the area see them as a vital economic engine for Memphis and the Mid-South. Click here to sign up for our newsletter! Click here to report a spelling or grammar error. artigo.texto: Peco customers will see electric supply rate increase Dec. 1 because of surge on power grid by data centers Peco said the increase is the result of supply prices set by PJM, the Montgomery County-based regional grid operator for 13 states and Washington, D.C. Peco customers will see a supply rate increase of 10% per kilowatt-hour starting Dec. 1 to cover a strong surge in demand on the region’s power grid. The increase, which will amount to $10 a month on an average bill, is not something Peco sought but rather the result of the wholesale price it pays for power, the company said. Peco passes that onto customers and does not profit from it, the company said. “On Dec. 1, electric supply rates are set to increase as a result of growing demand outpacing available supply across the region,” the utility, which serves 1.7 million customers, said in a statement. Customers of Peco, which serves Southeastern Pennsylvania, are not alone. Customers of most utilities across the state will see increases. The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC) released an independent analysis in September warning about the rapidly growing demand driven by data center development. “Pennsylvania is at an energy crossroads,” wrote PUC Chairman Steve DeFrank. “Electricity demand and supply are moving out of balance, and the status quo is not sustainable.” In the study’s severe scenario, projected new data center demand across PJM between 2029 and 2030 alone exceeds the current annual electricity demand of the entire Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. Rates are determined largely through wholesale power auctions conducted by PJM, the Montgomery County-based regional grid operator for 13 states and Washington, D.C. PJM does not sell power but holds auctions that attempt to match the supply of electricity with demand. The auctions result in wholesale prices utilities like Peco pay power generators, such as power plants. Peco then sends that electricity to customers. However, PJM has struggled in recent years to match the needed power of large-load, hyperscale data centers that run AI across its wide territory. When there is too little supply to meet demand at the capacity auctions, prices rise. In a capacity auction over the summer, PJM said it was short 6,800 megawatts of meeting demand and is seeking ways to increase that. » READ MORE: Where data centers are proposed in the Philadelphia region “Just like many other commodities, prices are high for electricity,” PJM said in a statement. “This is due primarily to the major influx in demand being driven by data centers without commensurate supply being added to the system.” PJM notes that utilities and state utility commissions control who ultimately pays for those costs. A chart PUC released Monday shows the fallout. Customers of 11 of 12 utilities across Pennsylvania will see increases on Dec. 1, just as winter arrives. The PUC chart shows Peco customers facing a rise from 11.76 cents a kilowatt-hour to 12.96 cents — or about 10.3%. Peco said that will translate to a rise of about $9 a month for customers using the average 700 kilowatt-hours per month, or a little more than a 5.3% increase in reality. Candice Womer, a Peco spokesperson, said the 5.3% figure is lower than the 10% in the PUC chart because it reflects the impact on a customer’s total monthly electric bill, which includes a delivery rate and other charges. So the estimated average bill will increase from $166.08 to $174.99. Peco customers pay two separate rates on their bills — one for supply and one for delivery. The supply rate is the one that’s increasing Dec. 1 and typically makes up about half a residential electric bill. Separately, the delivery rate is used to pay for infrastructure and services that bring electric into homes. In March, Peco sought a rate increase in the delivery side of customers’ bills for 2027, saying it needed to increase infrastructure to handle demand, but the request was met with stiff resistance by Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. Peco withdrew that request. » READ MORE: Facing backlash, Peco withdraws request for double-digit rate hike next year In the end, customers’ bills will depend on how much energy they use. If a customer buys electricity or natural gas from a competitive supplier, the supply price could be different. Separately, Peco will make rates for its 553,000 natural gas customers and the estimated impact on bills available this month.

artigo.texto: Sky negocia compra de ativos do braço de data centers da V.tal Operação submetida ao Cade envolve empresa ligada a um dos maiores projetos de infraestrutura digital do Nordeste A Sky, tradicionalmente conhecida por sua atuação no mercado de televisão por assinatura, negocia a aquisição de ativos da Tectodigital II, sociedade de propósito específico ligada ao braço de data centers do grupo V.tal. A operação foi submetida à análise do Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica (Cade) e tornada pública nesta semana. A empresa envolvida na negociação está associada ao Mega Lobster, data center localizado em Fortaleza, no Ceará. O empreendimento é beneficiário de um pacote de financiamento de aproximadamente 233 milhões de reais aprovado pelo Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) para sua expansão. Fortaleza ocupa uma posição estratégica no mercado de infraestrutura digital em razão da concentração de cabos submarinos que conectam o Brasil à América do Norte, à Europa e à África. A negociação ocorre em meio à corrida das empresas de telecomunicações e tecnologia por infraestrutura capaz de atender à crescente demanda por processamento, armazenamento e transmissão de dados. O edital publicado pelo Cade classifica o negócio como uma aquisição de ativos no segmento de tratamento de dados e hospedagem na internet. O valor da transação e o detalhamento dos ativos envolvidos não constam do edital.

artigo.texto: On November 26, 2026, the U.S. Energy Information Administration published a notice of proposed information collection under the Paperwork Reduction Act to launch Form EIA-872, the first federal statistical survey dedicated to measuring facility-level energy consumption across large data centers. The new annual collection directly impacts university high-performance computing centers, national laboratories, and academic energy economists tracking the rapid expansion of power-intensive digital infrastructure. What happened The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) and the Energy Information Administration (EIA) formally initiated public review for the Data Center Energy Consumption Survey (DCECS), designated as Form EIA-872. The agency placed Federal Register Document 2026-24077 on public inspection on November 26, 2026, ahead of scheduled publication on November 27, 2026. Signed in Washington, D.C., on November 23, 2026, by Pushpal Mukhopadhyay, Director of the EIA Office of Statistical Methods and Research, the notice requests Office of Management and Budget (OMB) approval to institute mandatory, facility-level data reporting for high-density computing infrastructure under statutory authorities granted by 15 U.S.C. 772(b) and 42 U.S.C. 7101. According to the official text of Federal Register Document 2026-24077, Form EIA-872 will collect annual operational and physical data from data center facilities across the United States that have an information technology (IT) design capacity of at least 1 megawatt (MW). The survey addresses a critical blind spot in federal statistical programs: while federal statistical agencies track aggregate utility generation and commercial floor-space usage, the government has never collected uniform, facility-level end-use power metrics from large computing installations. Key details The proposed data collection establishes specific structural parameters, operational thresholds, and legal protections that govern which facilities must report and how statistical data will be handled: Qualifying capacity threshold: Mandatory reporting applies to all facilities with an IT design capacity of at least 1 MW. Facilities that fall below this 1 MW design threshold are entirely excluded from the survey scope. Covered facility categories: Eligible sites include enterprise data centers, commercial colocation facilities, hyperscale cloud centers, edge computing hubs, carrier hotels, network gateways, cryptocurrency mining sites, and emerging super intelligence (SI) artificial intelligence computing clusters. Campus definition: The survey defines a data center facility as a dedicated building, multiple buildings, or a delineated portion of a structure whose primary purpose is housing servers, storage, and networking hardware. Functionally integrated multi-building campuses that share common power delivery or cooling infrastructure are treated as unified reporting units. Protection of proprietary data: EIA explicitly stated that it is not proposing to collect confidential business information concerning the commercial customers or computing tenants that these facilities serve. All reported data will be protected under the Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act of 2018 (CIPSEA, 44 U.S.C. 3572), which guarantees that individual responses cannot be disclosed in identifiable form and may only be published in aggregate statistical summaries. Reporting schedule: Data collection will commence in 2027, gathering operational and consumption data for the previous 2026 reference year. The notice outlines the substantial administrative scope and estimated compliance burden across the domestic data center industry: Background and context Historically, the federal government monitored commercial energy use through the Commercial Buildings Energy Consumption Survey (CBECS), a sample-based survey conducted every several years that last gathered field data for the 2018 reference cycle. However, EIA concluded that CBECS is structurally inadequate for evaluating modern computational facilities. Data centers exhibit unprecedented power densities—often exceeding standard office buildings by orders of magnitude—and rely on continuous baseline electrical draws, complex uninterruptible power supply (UPS) arrays, and sophisticated air- or liquid-cooling infrastructures that standard real estate surveys cannot capture. The data gap has become acute as artificial intelligence workloads accelerate electricity demand across regional power grids. Recent Department of Energy assessments of data center electricity demand, supported by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory research, estimated that domestic data centers accounted for approximately 176 to 192 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2023 and 2024, or roughly 4.4% to 4.7% of total national electricity consumption. Projections suggest this figure could reach nearly 12% of total domestic electricity consumption by 2030, driven by the expansion of hyperscale facilities and academic high-performance computing facilities. Reaction and sector perspectives Independent energy economists and grid policy analysts have welcomed the federal initiative while underscoring the severe forecasting challenges confronting utilities and regional transmission organizations. In an analytical study titled The Hype on Hyperscalers: Data Centers and Growing Electricity Demand, published by Resources for the Future, researchers Molly Robertson and Karen Palmer highlighted the extreme uncertainty clouding power growth forecasts. Robertson and Palmer observed that while corporate announcements project massive energy requirements, data centers can be built in two to three years, whereas constructing transmission lines and clean energy generation assets requires five to ten years. The resulting planning friction has prompted utilities to explore specialized clean transition tariffs to shield residential ratepayers from infrastructure upgrade costs. EIA lead

artigo.texto: ANDERSON — As battery energy storage systems proliferate in the United States, officials have sought to dispel what they say are misconceptions about their safety. Battery energy storage systems, or BESS, help stabilize electrical grids by “providing steady power flow despite fluctuations from inconsistent generation of renewable energy sources and other disruptions,” according to the United States Environmental Protection Agency. The Clean Coalition, a nonprofit organization “whose mission is to accelerate the transition to renewable energy and a modern grid through technical, policy and project development expertise,” says BESS helps sources like solar panels and wind turbines reach their full potential by storing excess energy produced during times of high generation and dispersing it when those sources are unavailable. The facilities operate by using lithium-ion batteries to receive and store electrical currents, according to the Indiana Office of Energy Development. “Individual battery cells are grouped together to form battery packs,” according to a study commissioned by the IOED. “Each system has cooling and fire systems to manage safety risks. Each battery storage facility is required to provide emergency response plans as a condition of project approval through Indiana Department of Homeland Security. Operators are required to provide training to first responders, offering instruction on proper responses to battery storage system emergencies.” The Clean Coalition goes on to point out several benefits of BESS, including job creation and the generation of tax revenue for local governments. The Clean Coalition’s website also mentions that BESS is essential in reducing the “environmental footprint of energy generation,” and Rebecca TeKolste, the director of climate and energy at the Hoosier Environmental Council, said BESS is an important tool. “You’re really able to leverage those renewable resources throughout all times of the day, regardless of whether or not the wind is blowing and the sun is shining,” TeKolste said. “Batteries can store any kind of energy. It could be they’re storing energy from gas plants, solar — it really just depends on what the utility has in excess.” TeKolste acknowledged that some people hold safety concerns related to BESS, with several fires breaking out at facilities years ago. TeKolste said batteries are considerably safer now than they were in the past. “There’s always going to be some challenges with safety considerations,” TeKolste said. “Largely, those have been mitigated with the improvements of technology over the last couple of decades. I think now what we are seeing is the primary challenges with batteries rather than safety. Now they’re much more in the supply chain. “Batteries rely on rare Earth metals, and in some cases, there are some concerns about labor when it comes to where those metals are being mined.” Currently, there are nine operating utility-scale battery energy storage systems in Indiana. TeKolste said regulating them is difficult because decisions are typically made through local zoning ordinances. With 92 counties in Indiana, that means up to 92 different potential sets of rules. Sean Coffington, a clean energy organizer at Greenlight America, said that “battery energy storage systems, as part of the electrical grid, are a net environmental positive.” When talking about the placement of BESS facilities, Coffington said their installations near population clusters are logical. “You hear a lot about these systems being built near population centers,” Coffington said. “You can think of it like a water tower on top of an apartment building. We need electricity where the people are, and if we’re producing extra electricity, it makes sense to hold it in storage near where it will need to be used.” TeKolste said when looking at other alternatives, BESS is a better option. “If you look at an apples-to-apples comparison between mining, burning and storing coal ash, that is a known, certain risk to communities, whereas the battery technology has lower risk on almost every metric,” TeKolste said. “Everything has some level of risk, but the level of risk to a battery system is a lot lower than the level of risk of running a coal plant for the same amount of energy. “It’s all part of a system where there are trade-offs,” she continued. “From our perspective, batteries are a solution to get some of these more polluting, more expensive and more carbon-intensive resources offline faster and used significantly less.”

artigo.texto: Justiça Federal nega pedido de suspensão do leilão de baterias ABEEólica questionava principalmente o custeio da contratação das baterias, que por definição legal foi imputado aos geradores de energia A Justiça Federal do Distrito Federal negou nesta quarta-feira (25) um pedido de tutela de urgência que buscava suspender a realização do primeiro leilão para contratação de baterias para o setor elétrico brasileiro, marcado para a próxima semana. Ao negar o pedido, apresentado pela associação de energia eólica ABEEólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica), o juiz Diego Câmara entendeu que não estavam presentes no caso os requisitos para a concessão da medida, como perigo de dano ou o risco ao resultado útil do processo. Na ação civil pública, a ABEEólica questionava principalmente o custeio da contratação das baterias, que por definição legal foi imputado aos geradores de energia. Segundo a entidade, a lei que impôs o ônus aos geradores é inconstitucional. Em paralelo, a ABEEólica também apontava "vícios" na estruturação do certame de baterias pela Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), citando a falta de uma regulamentação sobre o rateio dos custos entre os diferentes geradores. Sobre a questão da inconstitucionalidade, o juiz observou que a entidade também entrou com ação no STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) sobre o tema, e avaliou que "não é prudente que este Juízo... antecipe o juízo sobre a validade de lei federal que a própria parte autora submeteu à Corte Constitucional". Já sobre a alegada ilegalidade do certame, por ter sido convocado antes da definição do rateio do encargo entre os geradores, o juiz disse que não há norma legal ou regulamentar que condicione a realização do leilão à definição prévia pela agência reguladora Aneel do rateio do encargo. O juiz considerou ainda que não há dano iminente aos geradores associado ao leilão, já que a disputa marcada para a próxima semana não corresponde ao início da cobrança de encargos -- algo que somente ocorreria com a entrada em operação dos projetos, em 1º de agosto de 2028. O juiz citou ainda em sua decisão elementos trazidos em defesa da manutenção do leilão pelo governo, como o risco de déficit de potência já a partir do próximo ano.

artigo.texto: Two forces are behind falling energy storage costs, which is a boon for the clean energy industry. The market features growing competition among battery manufacturers and a possible lithium surplus in 2027. Here's what to know As SolarQuarter detailed, InfoLink's Energy Storage Supply Chain Price Forecast Report projects a slight lithium surplus in 2027. Battery-grade lithium carbonate prices could fall to about 99,800–117,900 Chinese yuan ($14,945-$17,656) per U.S. ton in the first half of that year. The forecast comes after declines in storage-cell prices. In July 2026, the tax-inclusive average prices for both 280 amp-hour and 314 amp-hour lithium iron phosphate storage cells dropped 4% to 0.36 yuan (around 5 cents) per watt-hour, according to the outlet. Smaller, 100 amp-hour cells averaged 0.44 yuan per watt-hour, down 2.7% from June 2026. For households facing grid instability and time-of-use electricity rates, whole-home batteries can keep essentials running during outages, while leases can help protect homes without upwards of $20,000 in upfront costs. EasyHome is a marketplace connecting battery shoppers with trusted partners offering unique prices and exclusive deals — another avenue for homeowners exploring backup power as storage-cell costs decline. More background The cost of lithium iron phosphate cathode material used in storage applications declined to approximately 47,800 yuan ($7,158) per U.S. ton, bringing tax-inclusive storage-cell production costs to around 0.31 yuan (around 5 cents) per watt-hour, according to SolarQuarter. These declines can translate to savings down the road for consumers looking to tap into their storage systems. Home batteries can also help reduce energy bills by supplying stored electricity during expensive peak-pricing periods. For households seeking a smaller-scale option, Pila offers plug-and-play battery backup at a substantially lower price point than whole-home backup systems. What's being done? Intense competition among battery manufacturers as supply expands is putting additional pressure on storage-cell prices, according to SolarQuarter. Lithium carbonate prices could still rise before the projected surplus in 2027. InfoLink's September and October 2026 price forecast is about 131,500–136,100 yuan ($19,692-20,381) per U.S. ton, above the expected August 2026 average near 127,000 yuan ($19,018) per U.S. ton. The firm expects seasonal demand and restocking to support that increase. According to SolarQuarter, China will begin taxing lithium-ion battery consumption at 2% on September 1, 2026, with the rate rising to 4% on September 1, 2027. Meanwhile, the estimated U.S. tariff rate for lithium-ion battery systems originating in China is around 40.9%.

artigo.texto: The 2026 midterm elections that swept Democrats into power in Congress and state legislatures also delivered a stunning rebuke to the artificial intelligence industry. Ballot measures that limited the construction of data centers – from California to Kansas to North Dakota – were approved by voters in 40 of 41 instances. These measures included the Kansas prohibition on construction of a type of battery energy storage system, a 180-day moratorium on data centers in Maine, and the outright ban on data center construction in Ohio. Drawing on recent survey data, we suggest that the Democratic sweep and the nationwide rejection of data centers are related. Republicans’ connections with an unpopular AI industry may have contributed to their poor showing at the polls. We are survey researchers. Our August 2026 survey of a nationally representative sample of 1,000 American adults shows that opposition to data centers is widespread. The survey shows that 65% of Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their communities. This opposition is bipartisan, with 76% of Democrats, 67% of independents and 52% of Republicans opposed to the sites. To better understand the sources of this opposition, we asked respondents to explain it in their own words. Twenty-eight percent of respondents voiced concerns about the negative environmental impact of data centers. One respondent stated: “Draining our water reserves significantly with a data center would be catastrophic to our region.” Some respondents, 15%, also expressed concerns about data centers’ negative impact on their quality of life. For example, one respondent said: “Noise issues, energy issues and visual site are three issues that are major concerns for a AI data center to be in the area I live in.” Ten percent of respondents singled out the centers’ connection to increased utility costs. One respondent said that “ever since a data center has been built in my local area the prices of water and electricity have more than doubled.” Finally, 13% of respondents expressed a broad distrust of AI and the industry itself, with one stating, “I think that AI needs to be better regulated and a lot more developed and proven safe before any massive full scale deployment.” Despite mounting public opposition to data centers, President Donald Trump expressed strong support for data center construction before Election Day. He said that if Americans want to live in “crime-infested areas” and “squalor,” they should not have a data center. Days after the midterms, Trump threatened to penalize U.S. companies that build data centers overseas. As widespread opposition to data centers grew through 2026, Republican congressional candidates increasingly had to weigh loyalty to Trump against local backlash. As Election Day neared, many Republican candidates had distanced themselves from unrestricted data center construction. In contrast, many Democrats made opposition to data centers an important theme of their campaigns. Our poll suggests that these efforts may have resonated with voters. Among Americans who expressed opposition to data centers, 48% indicated they would support the local Democratic candidate in the U.S. House of Representatives, compared to 25% for the Republican candidate. And 47% of those living in states that held a Senate election were planning on voting for the Democratic candidate, while 28% planned to vote for the Republican Senate candidate. Even taking partisanship, ideology and demographic characteristics into account, opposition to data centers was associated with an intention to support Democratic House and Senate candidates. Given widespread public concern about data center construction, Democrats have electoral incentives to make AI regulation a part of their legislative agenda in the new Congress. Whether or not they enact new legislation, popular opposition to data centers is unlikely to abate anytime soon. Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links.

artigo.texto: UK and EU aim to link emissions trading schemes by January 2028 The UK and EU have agreed to link their emissions trading systems, targeting 1 January 2028 for the arrangement to take effect alongside the UK's planned expansion of carbon pricing to international shipping. IMAGE: Flags of the UK and the EU. Getty Images The agreement could simplify compliance for shipping companies operating under both schemes by allowing them to use UK and EU carbon allowances interchangeably, the UK's Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said in an explainer on 20 November. Under the planned expansion, the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) is set to cover 50% of emissions from international voyages between UK and non-UK ports for vessels of 5,000 GT and above from 1 January 2028. The UK ETS has already covered 100% of emissions from domestic voyages and emissions at berth in UK ports since 1 July 2026. The EU ETS similarly covers 50% of emissions from voyages between EU and non-EU ports, while requiring shipping companies to account for all emissions on voyages between EU ports. The UK ETS will also adopt the EU's approach to neighbouring container transhipment ports. Ports on the European Commission's designated list will not count as UK ports of call when determining which voyage emissions fall under the scheme. The list is updated every two years. Once linked, the two schemes will continue operating separately but allow shipping companies to use allowances from either market to meet their emissions obligations. This could eliminate the need for operators covered by both schemes to purchase UK allowances (UKAs) and EU allowances (EUAs) separately. The arrangement is also intended to cover emissions obligations for 2027, with the first deadline for using allowances interchangeably scheduled for 30 September 2028. The UK and EU are also working towards a common administrative process that could allow shipping companies to manage compliance under both schemes together. The UK also plans to remove its minimum auction price for carbon allowances when the link takes effect. Impact on shipping The agreement aims to bring UK ETS shipping rules more closely in line with those of the EU ETS, including requirements for monitoring, reporting and verifying emissions. The UK plans to end the temporary arrangement that allows shipping companies to surrender allowances for only 50% of emissions on voyages between Great Britain and Northern Ireland. These voyages are expected to face the full 100% requirement from 2028, bringing them in line with other domestic UK routes. Meanwhile, passenger and ro-pax vessels serving islands with fewer than 200,000 residents and no road or rail connection to the mainland are expected to qualify for a temporary surrender derogation until at least 31 December 2030. Ice-class vessels are also set to qualify for a 5% reduction in their allowance surrender obligations until at least the same date. The agreement also addresses how shipping companies can account for lower-emission fuels. Operators would be able to apply a zero-emission factor to eligible biofuels, renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBOs) and recycled carbon fuels, provided they meet the sustainability and greenhouse gas savings requirements under the EU Renewable Energy Directive. The UK government has also said it will review how its carbon pricing rules interact with any future global emissions measure adopted by the IMO. The review would aim to avoid charging shipping companies twice for the same emissions while keeping compliance requirements manageable. “Any review would take into account any relevant changes to the EU ETS, and its outcomes will maintain support for maritime decarbonisation, and remain consistent with net zero,” the department said. The UK and EU are working towards bringing the two carbon markets together by January 2028, with technical preparations and legislative approvals still required. artigo.texto: Residents in a rural community in southern Wisconsin are calling for the rejection of a new data center proposal. But the developer says the project would be much smaller than the massive data center campuses being built in other parts of the state. Radius DC, a Colorado-based developer, hopes to build a 100,000 square-foot data center on nearly 40-acres in the village of Johnson Creek, located between Madison and Milwaukee. The village board had been set to vote on the proposal this week, but decided to put off making a decision after residents spoke out at the meeting. Residents who spoke with WPR shared concerns ranging from what they described as a lack of transparency from the village to negative impacts to the environment and local wildlife. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. “Everything came about way too fast, and the community wasn’t notified properly, in my opinion,” said Miranda Taylor, a community organizer. “That has created a lot of distrust in this business and the village board itself, and I think that’s where a lot of the opposition is also coming from.” Lindsay Kinateder, who lives in Johnson Creek, said she had too many unanswered questions about the project. “I think we need to slow down, we need to evaluate all of this and we need to make sure that there’s minimal risk and harm to the wildlife, to the environment and to the people that are living close to this area,” she said. The village board is expected to take up the proposal again on Jan. 11. Johnson Creek is in Jefferson County, which passed an 18-month data center moratorium this summer. But that moratorium doesn’t apply to municipalities in the county with their own zoning codes. Jefferson County Board Chair Steve Nass said the county passed the moratorium to give itself time to craft local zoning and regulations on data centers. “We felt that we didn’t have enough information to write a decent ordinance, or really to feel that we could competently regulate it without doing some more study,” Nass said. Some residents feel the Johnson Creek proposal goes against the intent of the moratorium. “It seems (like) a bad faith action to move forward with that, considering the moratorium,” said Cody Stark, who lives kitty-corner from the development site. “I understand the position that the county is in. They can’t actually make any decisions for cities or villages, but — to me — it does go against what I feel like the public wishes were intended to be on that.” Johnson Creek Village Administrator Kyle Ellefson said the village has already passed an ordinance that sets regulations on these types of developments. He said those rules would prevent a hyperscale data center — like those under construction in Mount Pleasant or Port Washington — from coming to the community. Ellefson said the proposed project would be located in a tax increment financing district created last year to support a separate manufacturing project, but would not receive incentives from the village. The village’s proposed development agreement also includes language that would prevent the data center from expanding beyond its proposed 105,000 square feet. Under the agreement, the developer would commit to creating at least $35 million in assessed property value on the site annually for 15 years. “If they don’t meet that level, they will make it up with a payment in lieu of taxes, or a PILOT payment,” Ellefson said. “They also agree that they will not challenge the assessment if it’s at or below 45 million dollars.” The proposal has come as data centers have become increasingly unpopular in Wisconsin. An October Marquette Law School poll found 75 percent of state voters believe the costs of data centers outweigh the benefits. Recent reports from state regulators have raised concerns about spiking electricity demand tied to the developments, while environmental groups have also raised concerns about water usage. But the project in Johnson Creek would use far less water and electricity than two of the data center projects tied to spiking electricity demand, according to the developer. RadiusDC says their data center would require 20 megawatts of power and would use a closed-loop cooling system that would be filled with 30,000-gallons of water. The company says water would be cycled through the system with only occasional top-offs. For context, Microsoft’s data center campus in Mount Pleasant is expected to need 8.4 million gallons of water each year and could need 2.1 gigawatts by 2030. Robert Marchant, a spokesperson for the Wisconsin Partnership for Progress, a pro-data center nonprofit that advocates for responsible development, said the type of facility being considered in Johnson Creek would be roughly the size of a Home Depot. “These can go in existing industrial areas within communities, places that are zoned for business and industry already, and they’re really significantly low impact,” he said. “From a land use standpoint, it’s a relatively small development and building.” The project would create 100 construction jobs, as well as 15 permanent jobs on-site once the facility is operational, according to the developer. Keith Klesner, the vice president of development for RadiusDC, said the company began looking into the project over the summer. He said he’s heard the community’s concerns and that he hopes the company can answer as many of those questions as possible before January. “A lot of the challenges that people think about with data centers on the large-scale may not have the same impact for a data center that’s sized like a big box retailer,” he said. “We’re definitely working to make sure that we’re respecting the watershed, we’re managing noise and any other development concerns for the community.” Wisconsin Public Radio, © Copyright 2026, Board of Regents of the University of Wisconsin

artigo.texto: The FCC has broken new ground, granting SpaceX the first US authorization to launch up to one million satellites as part of the company's Starmind plan to establish orbital data centers that sidestep the physical and regulatory limitations of terrestrial facilities. Modern data centers are the backbone of the world's digital infrastructure, the foundation on which AI, software, communications, commerce, scientific computing, and almost everything we do online depends. They are also central to future computing advances, tomorrow's economy, and even international relations as well. So it's small wonder they sit at the epicenter of economic, social, political, and diplomatic ruckuses, disrupting industries on a scale not seen since Gutenberg rolled out his printing press. Much of this friction stems from the technical and regulatory bottlenecks of building and operating terrestrial facilities. Data centers require continuous, reliable power on a gigawatt scale. Meeting that demand requires not only the power plants to generate the electricity, but also an upgraded grid – right down to the cables and substations – to deliver it. That requires a lot of planning and engineering. It also means developers can't simply plop a data center down anywhere. Facilities must be sited where massive power and water supplies are available, as conventional air cooling is no longer sufficient for modern AI chips. Even when utilities are secured, projects face strict regulations, environmental impact studies, land-use permits, and all manner of local or ideological opposition that can grind construction to a halt. SpaceX's strategy is to bypass these terrestrial hurdles by placing compute capacity in orbit, at altitudes between 310 and 622 miles (500 to 1,002 km), using up to one million satellites linked back to Earth via the Starlink network. Each satellite, spanning 230 to 246 feet (70 to 75 m) when deployed, houses a central rack of radiation-hardened compute modules flanked by two sets of panels. A smaller 1,184-square-foot (110 m²) array circulates liquid through double-sided radiators angled edge-on to the Sun to vent heat into deep space. A larger solar array generates up to 250 kW of peak electrical power. Because the satellites will operate in both 30-degree inclinations and near-polar, sun-synchronous orbits, much of the constellation can harvest near-continuous sunlight while radiating heat away. A modular design also allows SpaceX to upgrade hardware quickly as chip technology evolves. By putting data centers in orbit, Starmind aims to solve terrestrial infrastructure bottlenecks while avoiding local zoning and permitting battles. In a way, it takes moving the factory out of town to avoid the zoning ordinances to a whole new level. The FCC's conditional authorization sets out Starmind's orbital parameters, backup radio frequencies, orbital debris requirements, and deployment milestones through 2040. Under the terms of the license, SpaceX must deploy and operate its first Starmind satellite by November 25, 2033, or forfeit the authorization. Source: FCC

artigo.texto: The Tennessee Valley Authority is set to receive $1.7 billion in aggregate payments from an unnamed data center customer under its new tariff for data centers above 5 MW, the federal utility said in a Nov. 12 U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing. “Capacity commitment charges under the agreement are based on a rate of approximately $1.5 million per MW of requested capacity above 5 MW,” the filing said. “This rate reflects TVA's current cohort-based pricing methodology, which may be revised for future customer cohorts.” The new tariff took effect Oct. 1 and will be phased in through 2029, the filing said. That phase-in period will apply to existing customers to allow them to retain their existing rate structure for a period of time, the Nashville Scene reported in August. TVA CEO Mike Skaggs said during a Nov. 13 earnings call that the change to data center rates has supported the utility’s investments. Those investments include extending the lives of the utility’s existing nuclear units and “helping expand the nuclear fuel and supply hub in the East Tennessee area,” he said. The utility recently received the first small modular reactor construction permit from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission for a BWRX-300 reactor at the Clinch River Site in Oak Ridge, “although TVA has not yet decided whether to construct a reactor at the site,” its filing said. Skaggs came out of retirement to serve as interim CEO following the retirement of former CEO Don Moul and was instated as TVA’s permanent CEO following a Nov. 10 board meeting, TVA’s vice president of financial planning and investor relations Clifton Lowry said on the call. TVA’s filing also noted that in August, the utility’s board approved 1.5 GW of new natural gas generation, “targeted to be online in 2032.” As of Sept. 30, TVA said it “had spent $463 million on long-lead-time equipment associated with previously approved projects, which will now be utilized in connection with the project. TVA could spend up to an additional $3.1 billion on this project.” That previously approved project is TVA’s defunct Middle Tennessee Energy Solution project. In August, TVA said its approval of the new 1.5 GW gas facility “closes out” the previous project, “and all funding has been transferred to the New Gas Facility 2032.” TVA’s President and CFO Tom Rice said that the utility is in a “strong financial position” to executive its $13 billion capital investment plan over the next three years. That investment comes on top of the more than $23 billion in investments since 2020, Rice said. However, TVA’s filing notes that it “continues to experience supply chain pressures resulting from inflation, tariffs and other trade restrictions, material constraints, and labor availability.” “These factors have contributed to project delays, limited availability of critical materials, and increased costs for both materials and labor,” the utility said. “TVA anticipates that inflationary and tariff pressures will persist into 2027. Although these challenges have been managed with limited disruption to business operations thus far, continued or escalating pressures could result in more substantial operational impacts and increased pressure on power rates.”

artigo.texto: Cheyenne Light, Fuel and Power Co. has entered into agreements to build distribution and transmission infrastructure to serve three Microsoft data centers planned for Wyoming, the company said Tuesday in a filing at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The redacted agreements require Microsoft to pay for the infrastructure through “contribution in aid of construction” payments, according to the filing. Cheyenne Light — a subsidiary of Bright Horizon Energy Corp., a utility holding company created by the Nov. 13 merger of Black Hills Corp. and NorthWestern Energy Group — doesn’t believe FERC has jurisdiction over the retail agreements but filed them for review “out of an abundance of caution” due to the agency’s recent statements related to cost recovery agreements for transmission costs caused by large load customers. The Microsoft agreements reflect a massive data center buildout that is underway in southeast Wyoming where Cheyenne Light operates. The utility is executing on a 3-GW data center pipeline, including 600 MW of Microsoft and Meta projects, Black Hills officials said during a Nov. 5 earnings conference call. It is also in initial talks on an additional 2.5 GW of early-stage data center opportunities. Cheyenne Light has about 46,000 retail electric customers in the Cheyenne area and set a peak load record of 439 MW in July, according to Black Hills’ most recent U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission earnings report. The utility in September agreed to supply a Google data center project in Cheyenne with 590 MW and manage 2.1 GW of third-party power supply in a microgrid, Black Hills said in its earnings presentation. The agreements with Google contain cost pass-through mechanisms that protect customers from costs related to the planned data center while protecting utility returns from inflation, interest rate volatility and other cost pressures, Black Hills noted in the SEC filing. Cheyenne Light intends to serve the data centers through its Large Power Contract Service tariff and a proposed Large Customer Transmission Cost Adjustment Mechanism, which are designed to insulate the utility’s customers from the infrastructure costs related to data centers. Black Hills expects the Wyoming Public Service Commission will make a decision on the transmission tariff proposal by mid-2027. Cheyenne Light plans to use the transmission tariff to recover the costs of two recently proposed transmission projects totaling $686 million needed to serve large loads, including the Google data center. Under the tariff, large load customers would pay their share of the transmission expansion. The Google data center is set to begin operating late next year and ramp up to its full load by the end of 2030, according to the SEC filing. To serve it, Cheyenne Light plans to build a $1.8 billion, utility-owned 564-MW gas-fired power plant between 2027 and 2029, through an unregulated affiliate. The company expects the deal with Google will boost its net income by $150 million a year starting in 2030. In its SEC filing, Black Hills warned that the Google deal increases its risk by making it more reliant on one customer. “Our agreements with Google represent a significant long-term growth opportunity and are expected to contribute meaningfully to future revenues, earnings, cash flows and capital investment,” the company said. “As a result, we will have increased exposure to a single large customer and to trends affecting the data center, cloud computing and artificial intelligence industries.” Also, Black Hills said that large load demand forecasts face “significant uncertainty” and could be affected by technological advancements, economic conditions and regulatory developments. “Although the agreements contain customer credit support, termination payment and other investment recovery provisions, those protections may not fully mitigate the impact of reduced customer demand, contract disputes, non-renewal or customer default,” Black Hills said.

artigo.texto: At a bilateral summit on 20 November, EU and UK leaders announced the finalisation of negotiations on creating a joint carbon market. The agreement is set to apply from 1 January 2028, provided it is ratified in both jurisdictions. This was reported by the European Commission on its official website. According to the Commission, the link will create a larger and more liquid market with a more stable carbon price. It is expected to support both sides’ ambitions to achieve climate neutrality, as well as promote more efficient investment decisions and the sustainable development of both economies. The intention to link the systems was first announced at the first EU-UK summit in May 2025. At the same time, the EU Emissions Trading System has been linked to the Swiss system since 1 January 2020, and this link will remain in place. What will change for aviation and maritime transport The UK will extend its emissions trading system to aviation and maritime transport, adding more than 10 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions to it. According to the European Commission, this should stimulate the decarbonisation of these sectors. Both systems will also monitor the non-CO₂ climate effects of aviation. Exemption from CBAM? Linking the systems lays the groundwork for a possible future mutual exemption from each side’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). This would reduce red tape and costs for companies on both sides of the Channel. Recently, EcoPolitic reported that the European Commission adopted rules for deducting carbon prices paid outside the EU from CBAM obligations. This allows producers to avoid paying twice for the same emissions.
