artigo.texto: Residents raise concerns over Brewer’s proposed data center ordinance BREWER, Maine (WABI) — Residents and members of the Maine People’s Alliance gathered outside the Brewer Auditorium on Monday, raising concerns about proposed changes to the city’s data center regulations. “People are really upset about the idea of data centers coming to Maine,” said Megan Smith, Penobscot County community organizer for the Maine People’s Alliance. “We love our outdoors here. We don’t want it spoiled.” The proposed changes would increase the maximum capacity for data centers from 20 megawatts to 50 megawatts. Brewer Planning Board member Joy Sinclair, who attended the demonstration, said the proposal would also increase the allowable level of low-frequency noise near residential properties. The proposal also calls for noise studies and ongoing monitoring, along with closed-loop cooling for server equipment. Sinclair was the only Planning Board member to vote against the proposal. She said she is concerned about the potential impact on homes along the Orrington line and toward Holden. “The information that is available shows that what happens is that these are built. They tear up people’s lives. They make it impossible to live near them. Their property values plummet,” Sinclair said. Demonstrators also raised concerns about potential water and electricity use and said they hope to inform residents about the proposal. The city will hold an informational meeting at 6 p.m. Tuesday at the Brewer Auditorium. Public comment will also be allowed at the Dec. 8 City Council meeting. The proposed changes still need City Council approval. Brewer City Manager, Eric Glidden, provided WABI with a statement regarding the proposal and it is included in full below: “The proposed regulations are more stringent in several respects than what is currently in place. The proposed amendments are available for public review on the City’s website under the “News” section. These changes include additional requirements related to water usage, more comprehensive permitting standards, mandatory connections to the City’s wastewater system to ensure wastewater is properly treated, stricter noise controls, and restrictions limiting data center development to the Industrial 2 (IND-2) zone, which is primarily located behind the City landfill. The proposed increase in allowable capacity from 20 MW to 50 MW is largely driven by economies of scale. Based on discussions with the City’s consultant, larger facilities may be more economically feasible because the substantial upfront costs associated with data center development can be spread across a larger operation. Increasing the allowable capacity would make Brewer more competitive in attracting this type of investment, while the proposed regulations would establish stronger protections for the community. City staff have been making a concerted effort to identify opportunities for responsible economic development, particularly on industrially zoned land that has remained undeveloped for many years. Our goal is to encourage investment that can strengthen the City’s commercial tax base and potentially reduce the tax burden on residential property owners, while ensuring that appropriate safeguards are in place to protect our residents and municipal infrastructure. Ultimately, these are proposed regulations, and the City Council has not yet made a decision on whether to adopt them. We recognize that residents have important questions and concerns, and we welcome their feedback as part of the public review process. All proposed data centers would be required to disclose their anticipated maximum daily water demand, how that water would be used, and any recycling or reuse systems. The developer would also be required to submit a water-use study prepared by a qualified consultant approved by the Brewer Water Department. That study would evaluate whether the City’s water system has sufficient capacity to serve the facility, whether existing infrastructure can deliver the required water, and whether any improvements would be necessary. The proposed regulations also include requirements for closed-loop cooling systems, intended to help manage water consumption. Ultimately, the purpose of these requirements is to ensure that the City has the information necessary to evaluate a proposed development’s impacts on infrastructure, municipal services, and local resources before any decisions are made. Any project would be evaluated based on its specific characteristics and anticipated demands. City staff have been working develop thoughtful and responsible regulations for data centers, with the goal of ensuring that appropriate protections are in place for our community should such development be proposed in Brewer. Our primary goal is to ensure any development is done responsibly. At the same time, we recognize that many residents have strong opinions and concerns about data centers, along with important questions and about their potential impacts. That is precisely why the City is holding a public informational meeting tomorrow evening. We genuinely want to hear from our residents, understand their concerns, answer questions, and receive feedback before the City Council begins its formal consideration of the proposed amendments. At the earliest, the City Council will consider the proposed amendments at its regularly scheduled meeting on December 8, when they are currently scheduled for a first reading. The amendments are then scheduled for a second reading at the January 12 City Council meeting. We are also open to holding additional informational meetings. These meetings will provide additional opportunities for public comment as the Council considers the proposed regulations." Copyright 2026 WABI. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: A comprehensive bibliometric survey examining approximately 3,060 peer-reviewed publications published between 2015 and 2024 has established a unified electrochemical framework that explains how transition metal oxide electrodes transition between surface-dominated pseudocapacitive charge storage and bulk diffusion-controlled battery reactions. Rather than treating rechargeable batteries and electrochemical capacitors as entirely disconnected technological domains with isolated operating principles, the decadal synthesis reveals that transition metal oxides operate along a continuous charge-storage continuum governed by fundamental physicochemical descriptors. These governing descriptors include intrinsic electronic conductivity, solid-state ion diffusion kinetics, the spatial density of electrochemically accessible redox-active sites, surface adsorption energetics, defect chemistry, and crystallographic phase stability under repeated cycling. By evaluating material modifications across both device architectures simultaneously, the unified model demonstrates how structural engineering, morphologic tailoring, and chemical doping systematically shift an electrode’s charge-storage mechanism toward either rapid surface-confined power delivery or high-capacity bulk energy storage, resolving longstanding fragmentation in literature. The extensive analysis underscores that pristine transition metal oxides face an inherent performance trade-off between delivering high theoretical capacitance through multi-electron Faradaic redox transformations and suffering from severe kinetic and mechanical limitations. While conventional graphite anodes in commercial lithium-ion batteries are constrained to a theoretical capacity of 372 milliampere-hours per gram through reversible lithium intercalation, transition metal oxides undergoing multi-electron conversion mechanisms, such as hematite and cobalt oxide, boast theoretical capacities exceeding 800 to 1,000 milliampere-hours per gram. Similarly, single and mixed-valence metal oxides offer specific capacitance values that far outstrip traditional carbon-based electric double-layer capacitors, which rely exclusively on electrostatic charge separation. However, pristine oxides typically exhibit poor intrinsic electronic conductivity, sluggish solid-state ion transport kinetics, substantial volume expansion during repeated cycling, and structural degradation. These interconnected physical constraints induce rapid electrode pulverization, severe capacity fading, and high charge-transfer resistance, preventing pristine bulk oxides from realizing their full theoretical electrochemical capabilities without targeted structural modifications. Within the established framework, electrochemical energy storage systems are distinguished by the kinetic nature of their charge-transfer processes, which can be quantitatively mapped using technique-specific electroanalytical signatures. In electrical double-layer capacitors, energy is stored via electrostatic ion accumulation at the electrode-electrolyte interface without electron transfer, yielding superior cycling stability and elevated power densities but modest energy density. In contrast, battery-type materials undergo diffusion-controlled Faradaic ion intercalation or conversion reactions within the bulk crystalline lattice, producing nonlinear galvanostatic charge-discharge profiles with distinct voltage plateaus and sharp redox peaks in cyclic voltammetry. These physical mechanisms are evaluated through the power-law relationship relating current to voltage scan rate, where a power-law exponent b approaching 1.0 identifies an ideal surface-confined capacitive response, whereas an exponent near 0.5 indicates diffusion-limited bulk storage. Transition metal oxides uniquely span this boundary, frequently exhibiting intermediate exponents between 0.6 and 0.9 that reflect hybrid electrochemical behavior. To overcome the intrinsic conductivity-capacitance trade-off, material synthesis routes dictate the resulting crystal architecture, defect distribution, and electroactive surface area of transition metal oxide electrodes. Hydrothermal and solvothermal synthesis methods typically yield two-dimensional nanosheets or elongated nanorods that provide high specific surface areas and short ion diffusion paths, which facilitate rapid ion transport and elevate pseudocapacitive contributions. Template-assisted synthesis produces hollow, mesoporous structures capable of accommodating mechanical strain during cycling to enhance durability, though often at the cost of synthetic complexity. Chemical vapor deposition deposits high-purity thin films with precisely controlled thicknesses that reduce internal resistance, while electrochemical deposition enables direct electrode growth on conductive substrates to minimize interfacial contact resistance. Complementing these synthesis routes, advanced engineering strategies—such as inducing oxygen vacancies through defect engineering, incorporating conductive carbon frameworks, creating multi-component heterostructures, and introducing aliovalent dopants—alter the underlying electronic band structures, raise charge-carrier concentrations, and lower activation energy barriers. The mechanistic utility of this unified continuum is exemplified in the contrasting behavior of individual transition metal oxides, beginning with nickel oxide and cobalt oxide. Nickel oxide functions as a prototypical hybrid material in alkaline electrolytes, where charge storage is governed by reversible Faradaic redox transitions involving the divalent and trivalent nickel redox couple. At elevated scan rates or within nanostructured architectures, nickel oxide displays surface-confined pseudocapacitive kinetics with power-law exponents between 0.6 and 0.9, while at lower operating rates, deeper proton diffusion into the bulk crystalline lattice triggers battery-type storage. artigo.texto: The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday announced it has given permission to SpaceX to launch 1 million data centers into space. The agency said its decision authorizes SpaceX to “deploy at an unprecedented scale.” It comes as battles brew across the U.S. over where data centers are being built, with residents protesting against construction over noise, environmental and other concerns. The FCC added that the approval will “bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization — one that can harness the full power of the sun.” The Kardashev scale, according to Encyclopedia Britannica, is a “hypothetical measure of an alien civilization’s level of technological advancement,” first coined by Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev. It proposes three levels of civilization, and a Type II civilization — the FCC’s goal — has the capability of using the entire energy output of its star. “Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in SI (super intelligence),” FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement. “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the movement. This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.” “Much appreciated,” SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said on X in response to Carr’s announcement. “This will be a great asset to America and the world.” In July, a coalition of environmental and scientific organizations petitioned the FCC to conduct an environmental review on the effects of data centers in space. The groups, represented by Earthjustice, said that sending that many data centers into space could change the atmosphere and disrupt other satellites already in orbit. “Allowing a million orbiting data centers with no environmental review isn’t just irresponsible — it’s reckless,” Tim Whitehouse, executive director of Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility, said at the time. “The potential for these projects to degrade the atmosphere with pollution and debris and harm wildlife needs to be carefully considered before licensing these projects.” In its authorization, the FCC wrote that it expects SpaceX to launch its first data center into space by November 2033, with all of them being deployed by November 2040. As of July, there are 15,000 active satellites in space, according to Earthjustice. In order for SpaceX to complete its goal, it would be required to launch 5,000 rockets into space a year, or 13 to 14 a day, according to a paper by scientists Eloise A. Marais and Connor R. Barker published in the journal Earth and Space Chemistry.

artigo.texto: Australia has the natural resources and know-how to create a thriving battery manufacturing industry but is missing opportunities by exporting critical minerals rather than turning them into high-value products. Scientists from the CSIRO issued the warning at an event on Tuesday, also recommending more international partnerships and a greater focus on manufacturing individual components rather than trying to make entire batteries. The call comes as Australians embrace battery technology, with more than 600,000 home batteries installed under a federal scheme since July 2025 and rapid electric vehicle sales since March. Speaking at an event called Australia's Battery Opportunity, CSIRO mineral resources principal research scientist Joanne Loh said the nation had enviable access to valuable raw materials. "We have all the minerals needed for batteries, specifically lithium-ion batteries - we're the number one producer in terms of lithium… we have nickel, cobalt, manganese, aluminium, copper, graphite, you name it," she said. "However, we export all of these as raw materials overseas so even though we might have it, we're actually sending it overseas for processing, then importing them back as batteries." The nation also shredded batteries at the end of their lives and exported the materials, Dr Loh said, rather than using them. Australia had also stopped manufacturing elements that could be used in batteries, such as aluminium foil, CSIRO senior research engineer Geoff de Looze said. The nation could re-establish that facility, he said, and target the local production of key components like aluminium casings and copper foil. "We do have some gaps in Australia's capability so when we look at them we need to rank them and work out which ones we can take on and which ones we want to leave alone," Mr de Looze said. "Any of the manufactured parts going into batteries, Australia can take on." A CSIRO report released early in November found Australia could use its expertise in manufacturing aluminium aerosol cans to produce battery casings, for example, or manufacture copper foil from scrap wire. Identifying gaps in the global battery supply chain could allow Australian companies to partner with larger manufacturing firms from the region, CSIRO senior principal research scientist Adam Best said, rather than competing with an established industry. "We need to work closely with our partners in Asia, Pacific, North America, Europe, to find where we fit in this middle part such that we can do… that manufacturing, that value-adding, to capture more value from our resources," he said. "Then Australia does have a brighter future that can lead to a future with energy security." Australian Associated Press

artigo.texto: King George County data center fight turns into a battle over water KING GEORGE COUNTY, Va. (7News) — With 685 data centers either built or planned for construction, Virginia is far and away the nation's data center leader but one of those planned projects, in King George County, has come under greater scrutiny by local leaders and the reason has everything to do with a precious natural resource: water. “Water is the new gold," King George County Administrator Matthew J. Smolnik told the 7News I-Team in a recent interview. "I remember 20 years ago sitting with DEQ [Department of Environmental Quality] and drawing a line in I-95, saying 'If you're east of this line, we're coming for you and they're coming for us.'" RELATED | Lawmakers eye data center moratorium as Virginia environmental coalition ramps up pressure As recently as September 2023, water levels on the Rappahannock River near Fredericksburg, Virginia, had reached historic lows. Back then, you could walk across parts of the Rappahannock without getting wet. The Rappahannock widens ten miles downriver as it winds through King George County. Many in the mostly rural county of just 29,000 were surprised in December 2019 when their Board of Supervisors greenlit plans for an Amazon data center project on the site of the old Birchwood coal-fired power plant. With the purchase, Amazon secured a state DEQ permit allowing it to draw up to 6.6 million gallons of water per day from the Rappahannock River. “The deal the old board struck was a bad deal for King George," state Sen. Richard Stuart, R-Westmoreland, told 7News. “Where people got really upset was, they had no information and the next thing they know, that board voted to approve it and they even gave them data center buildings on the river. I couldn't get any information from the company because they wanted me to sign an NDA and I refused to do it," Stuart added. Amazon has since agreed not to build directly on the bank of the Rappahannock but acknowledged it negotiated the data center deal out of public view, requiring county officials to sign nondisclosure agreements at the time. “Most of the negotiation was done in a closed session. So, little to no information had been brought out to the public to have input on it," David Sullins, Chair of King George County Board of Supervisors, said. In October, Amazon ended its policy of using nondisclosure agreements with local officials on data center projects, according to a company spokesperson. In 2023, Sullins successfully ran for the King George County Board of Supervisors largely because of a lack of transparency surrounding the Birchwood data center project. The board has since tasked Smolnik and Stuart, who’s also the county attorney, with fixing what the men describe as a bad backroom deal, cut by the previous board. King George County sits on the Potomac aquifer, a massive underground water supply that stretches from Fairfax to the north and south to Virginia Beach. SEE ALSO | This week: Two high-stakes data center public hearings in Spotsylvania and Stafford That water source, which is critical to Virginia communities, is declining so much so that Virginia’s Department of Environmental Quality has told King George and other communities east of I-95 they need to start looking elsewhere for water. If King George County is forced to turn to surface water for its drinking water, its only option nearby is the Rappahannock River, and it too is under stress, according to conservation groups. In April 2025, the non-profit conservation group American Rivers issued a report, which placed the Rappahannock as the sixth most endangered river in the United States. "The increasing strain on water resources, and the absence of unified water management, threaten the river’s ability to meet the needs of both people and nature," the American Rivers report read in part. At present, the county does not have its own water intake on the river. Most of the residents are on private wells. That means King George County officials find themselves in the awkward position of having to negotiate with Amazon for the future source of its water, which could flow from the intake Amazon is currently permitted to use on the Rappahannock. “It is a highly unusual situation for a county to have to be negotiating with another entity to share a water intake," Brent Hunsinger, Advocacy and Coastal Programs Director with the non-profit Friends of the Rappahannock, told 7News. Hunsinger said he's not aware of another situation like the one that exists in King George County. He pointed to a July 2026 report by the Virginia Senate, which raised alarms about the declining levels of the Potomac aquifer. “That report has realized that economic development in the future might not be possible," Hunsinger said of the corridor east of I-95. “All the capacity is used. So, there's no additional capacity unless we make adjustments somewhere. That's why so many things are being forced to the river," Stuart said. The I-Team asked Amazon how much water it will use from the Rappahannock for its Birchwood data center. While the company didn’t answer that specific question, in a statement, a spokesperson said: “Our agreement with King George County includes a binding commitment not to build data center buildings next to the Rappahannock River and a $10 million contribution to the county’s new Career and Technical Education School. The surface-water permit came with the former power plant site and sets a maximum, not our expected use. We’ve been clear with the county that we’re willing to provide water to help meet its long-term needs, subject to Virginia DEQ approval, and we’ll continue to be a partner on those needs.” Smolnik, the County Administrator, said Amazon has yet to say just how much water it will use to operate the Birchwood site. “Without a final design of the site, I'm not sure Amazon knows exactly what they're going to need for the site," Smolnik said. “I mean, that's the pr

artigo.texto: Capital Deployment & Mexico's Data Center Competitiveness Mexico could capture part of the US$82.5 billion in projected data center investment through 2031, but global infrastructure capital remains selective due to transmission bottlenecks, permitting delays, and regulatory uncertainty. Developers must deliver energized substations, long-haul fiber connectivity, and clear 20- to 30-year legal frameworks to compete for institutional capital. Global infrastructure funds hold ample capital for digital infrastructure, yet Mexico faces a competitive bottleneck because investors prioritize large-scale projects with ready power and predictable regulations. During his keynote address at the Mexico Data Center Summit 2026 on Nov. 25, 2026, Simón Masri, President and CEO, C3NTRO Telecom, outlined the structural requirements Mexico must meet to convert announced capacity into operational megawatts. While global data center demand is projected to nearly triple from 82 GW in 2025 to 219 GW by 2030, Mexico operates an installed base of 279 MW, with 250 MW concentrated in Queretaro. According to industry data cited by Masri from the Mexican Data Center Association (MEXDC), total capacity could expand roughly eightfold to 2,214 MW over the next five years if announced and under-construction projects materialize, representing an estimated US$82.5 billion investment window between 2026 and 2031. However, Masri warned that capital is not scarce, it is occupied elsewhere. The 10 largest global infrastructure funds hold US$209.4 billion in commitments, while five major technology companies—Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, and Oracle—are projected to spend US$791 billion in capital expenditures in 2026 alone. That annual hyperscaler spending equals roughly 48 times Mexico's five-year data center investment projection. Furthermore, US debt markets closed US$223 billion in data center loans through September 2026, absorbing institutional bandwidth with single-campus transactions such as Meta's US$12 billion debt package in El Paso, Texas. "The capital is not scarce; it is occupied. Mexico has to be easy to understand and easy to approve," says Masri. Substation Readiness and Fiber Bottlenecks Within the five-layer artificial intelligence stack—spanning digital energy, digital infrastructure, chips, models, and applications—Masri noted that Mexico competes in the two physical foundational layers: power generation and transmission, and physical facilities such as data centers, fiber networks, and edge nodes. To attract hyperscalers and neocloud operators, Masri argued that preliminary feasibility letters from the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) or the National Energy Control Center (CENACE) are insufficient. Institutional investors and cloud buyers require substations that are either under construction with confirmed energization dates or already energized. High-voltage substation construction requires significant upfront capital and specialized engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contractors, which remain limited in Mexico. Connectivity presents a parallel constraint. High-density AI workloads require extensive long-haul and metropolitan fiber networks, with US metropolitan fiber deployments scaling from four strands in 2004 to 16,000 strands by 2026. Major US operators and technology firms have pre-ordered massive fiber volumes from manufacturers such as Corning, pushing equipment lead times to 52 weeks. Without dedicated fiber routes, Masri noted, available power capacity cannot be commercialized. Cross-Border Dynamics and Execution Milestones Geopolitical shifts in the United States create both an opening and a policy risk for Mexican operators. Local opposition led to rejections in 40 of 41 US municipal data center ballot measures during the November 2026 midterm elections, alongside calls from congressional leaders for a national moratorium. While stricter US permitting could push demand south under the USMCA framework, Masri highlighted a Nov. 20, 2026 White House proposal to impose tariffs on US firms building data centers abroad, leaving cross-border tax rules undefined. To demonstrate execution viability in Mexico, Masri cited C3NTRO Telecom's Tikva project, a 2,500 km terrestrial fiber backbone connecting Queretaro to Phoenix, Arizona. Financed by European development banks after domestic lenders hesitated over non-real-estate digital assets, the corridor is 84% complete—spanning 2,100 km—and scheduled to be ready for service in the first quarter of 2027. The route integrates 30 carrier-neutral edge data centers across Mexican municipalities from Nogales to Queretaro, providing 10 MW of initial capacity scalable to 60 MW. Looking ahead, Masri identified four priorities to capture long-term compute investment: mixed CFE and private-sector transmission schemes, specialized infrastructure capital, single-window permitting with binding timelines for rights-of-way, and public communication clarifying water and clean-energy management. If Mexico executes on its current 2 GW pipeline by 2030, Masri concluded, the sector should aim for 10 GW of installed capacity by 2035.

artigo.texto: An Asset or a Liability: How Data Center Policy Will Shape ERCOT’s Future By: Joshua Loucks, Kiersten Saathoff, and Brent Bennett Key Points: - Texas is facing unprecedented electricity demand from data centers. ERCOT is tracking over 474 GW of large-load requests, nearly 90% from data centers, on a grid that currently peaks over 90 GW. - Data centers are not the cause of rising electricity bills. Renewable energy mandates and retirements of thermal generation have driven most price increases, while the states adding the most demand have seen some of the smallest rate increases. - Texas is positioned to lead the world in AI infrastructure the way it has led previous energy booms. Getting the integration right turns a decade of private capital into durable grid capacity and economic opportunity. - Data centers can strengthen the ERCOT grid by financing new reliable generation and transmission, but not without changes to current policies that socialize reliability and transmission costs. - The window for getting the design right is closing. Interconnection decisions and transmission commitments made in the next few years will lock in outcomes for decades. Executive Summary Texas is on track to host the largest concentration of data centers in the world. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) is now tracking more than 474 GW of large load interconnection requests, 90% of it from data centers (ERCOT, 2026b). Only a fraction of that queue will ever be built, but the fraction under contract is already substantial: Cushman & Wakefield estimates 3,396 MW operating in Texas today with 4,730 MW under construction, and 28,763 MW planned—more than eight times what is in operation today (Cushman & Wakefield, 2026). Whether that growth becomes an asset or a liability to the ERCOT grid is not a matter of chance. It is a matter of policy design, and the window for getting the design right is now. Data center growth is increasingly being blamed for rising electric bills, but the evidence does not support that claim. California and New York have posted the largest rate increases while losing demand, while Texas and Virginia have added the most data center load in the country without steep price increases. Recent research has found that doubling data center capacity at a fixed level of residential demand lowers residential retail prices by 3.5% (Watten et al., 2026). The drivers of rising bills are elsewhere: mandated retirement of reliable generation, transmission built for distant wind and solar generation, and aging distribution infrastructure (Pyle et al., 2025). The risk to Texas consumers is not the data centers themselves but the electric grid that will serve them. Less than 20% of the 456,578 MW in ERCOT’s generation queue is reliable thermal generation (ERCOT, 2026c). In fact, Texas has not added significant firm dispatchable capacity in over a decade, and wind and solar have been overbuilt to a point that significant amounts are being curtailed (Modo Energy, 2025). Both facts point to a market design that produces a reliability deficit and promotes inefficiency, which ratepayers pay for. Meeting new load with still more intermittent generation would erode reliability and push hyperscalers off the grid—a shift already underway, with more than 40 GW of private grid development announced in Texas (Thomas, 2026a). Islanded capacity enables speed and innovation, but it does not ensure the on-grid reliability residential consumers depend on. Handled well, data centers become the anchor load that funds firm generation and spreads fixed costs across a broader base. Handled poorly, Texas adds inflexible load to an increasingly intermittent fleet. That is the choice facing Texas today, and Texas needs to make the right policy choices to responsibly accommodate data center growth to the benefit of all its citizens. Introduction Texas will likely be home to more data centers than any other state by the end of this decade. While the size and pace of the buildout may seem like a daunting reality, in practice it offers a unique opportunity to improve ERCOT’s ability to handle extreme weather and supply volatility while lowering electricity costs for Texas consumers. Throughout history, technological and industrial advancements that have drastically altered society have also impacted policy, economics, and our environment. From the invention of the cotton gin to the dawn of the internet, American society, culture, and economics have been drastically altered at each turn. Typically, advancements have been tangible or relatively narrow in scope, but artificial intelligence (AI) is bringing rapid and sweeping changes to almost every business sector as well as in our personal lives. AI, particularly the means by which it is powered, presents a historically unique intersection between industry and consumers. The power, water, and even land required to make advanced computing possible is not particularly unique to new industrial advancements . Whether it was textile mills powered through hydropower in Upstate New York in the 1800s or coal-fired steel mills in Pennsylvania, American energy and ingenuity have been the catalyst of growth and opportunity. The challenges data centers present in the 21st century may be more abstract, but in reality, are quite similar to challenges other power-intensive industries have posed in the past. These challenges, if addressed promptly and cohesively through responsible water, land, and electricity production and use agreements, can lead America and the globe into a new era of prosperity and growth. This paper will address the various power and electrical infrastructure needs to provide the computing necessary for the “AI Revolution,” in addition to the economic opportunity these facilities can bring. artigo.texto: Buscando expansão no Nordeste, Tecto anuncia data center no Recife Empreendimento de plataforma controla pelo BTG Pactual terá capacidade escalável de até seis megawatts e integra plano da companhia de investimentos de US$ 2 bilhões até 2028 A Tecto Data Centers, plataforma de data centers controlada pelo BTG Pactual e ligada à V.tal, anunciou nesta terça-feira (24) seu primeiro data center em Pernambuco, o segundo no Nordeste. O empreendimento, batizado de TREC1, será instalado no Recife e terá capacidade inicial de 1 MW (megawatt), com possibilidade de expansão de até 6 MW. Segundo a companhia, com a expansão, a ideia é montar uma estratégia "AI Grid", criando uma rede de data centers regionais, conectando polos do Brasil a pontos estratégicos no exterior. "A estratégia da empresa combina duas camadas: a AI Factory reúne instalações de grande porte e alta densidade, voltadas ao treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial e ao processamento intensivo de dados. E AI Grid distribui a infraestrutura de processamento por meio de data centers regionais interligados, aproximando-a dos locais onde os dados são gerados e consumidos", afirmou em comunicado. A operação está prevista para inicar no primeiro trimestre do ano que vem e atenderá as chamadas "hyperscales", que são operadoras, provedores de nuvem e de conteúdo e empresas do segmento enterprise, oferecendo serviços de colocation, interconexão e serviços gerenciados para operações que demandam alta disponibilidade, segurança e baixa latência. Como mostrou a CNN, com alta demanda do setor e oferta abundante de energia renovável, o Nordeste segue avançando como um forte polo de data centers no país, ampliando a presença do setor para além do eixo Rio-São Paulo. Atualmente, a Tecto opera em Fortaleza (CE) o TFOR3, que é o maior centro de dados em operação da região. Conhecido como "Mega Lobster", o empreendimento fica na Praia do Futuro, e foi inaugurado em outubro do ano passado. Para o CRO da companhia, Tito Costa, a região reúne a conectividade internacional e uma demanda crescente por infraestrutura digital, tendo papel estratégico na expansão da empresa. “Acreditamos que Recife está para Fortaleza, assim como o Rio de Janeiro está para São Paulo. Essa é a lógica da nossa estratégia AI Grid, que conecta data centers, levando capacidade de processamento para perto das empresas e complementando as grandes estruturas do AI Factory”, acrescentou. Com os dois polos conectados (Recife e Fortaleza), os clientes da companhia poderão distribuir suas operações entre diferentes localidades, inclusive para estratégias de recuperação de desastres e continuidade dos negócios, sem sair da região. A capacidade final é de 20 MW (megawatts), com a expansão ocorre em etapas, acompanhando a demanda dos clientes. A previsão da empresa é de aumentar a capacidade inicial de 4 MW para 8 MW até o começo de 2027. A partir da chegada do TREC1, a empresa passará a contar com oito data centers operacionais até 2027, sendo cinco no Brasil (incluindo o de Recife, três em Fortaleza, um no Rio de Janeiro) outros três em Barranquilla, na Colômbia. Além dessas unidades, a companhia segue com o desenvolvimento do TGRU1, em Santana de Parnaíba (SP), com 200 MW, um dos maiores do país em capacidade, que será voltado para aplicações que empregam inteligência artificial e computação em nuvem. Há também o TPOA1, em Porto Alegre (RS), com 20 MW. Ao todo, o plano de investimentos da companhia é estimado em US$ 2 bilhões, previstos entre 2026 e 2028, para acelerar a expansão na América Latina. Brasil deve dobrar capacidade até 2030 Ao todo, dos 660 MW que estão em construção no país, 56% estão pré-locados, segundo levantamento da consultoria JLL. Ainda segundo a consultoria, a ocupação dos data centers brasileiros chegou a 96% no primeiro semestre deste ano. Para a colunista da CNN Infra, Joísa Dutra, o setor busca acelerar os investimentos de forma mais eficiente, buscando alianças internacionais, ao mencionar o lanlamento da AI Energy Management Alliance (AEMA), da qual fazem parte empresas como Emerald AI, Google e NVIDIA, além de outras quase 20 companhias. O objetivo da aliança é criar protocolos e melhores práticas os investimentos. Os esforços dessas empresas são para criar condições para que esses investimentos em data centers possam ocorrer de modo eficiente, possam ocorrer mais rápido no tempo", avaliou a colunista. A iniciativa surge em resposta a um fenômeno já observado em diferentes países, inclusive no Brasil: a resistência de comunidades locais à instalação desses empreendimentos. Joísa descreveu esse comportamento como "nimby" — expressão em inglês que significa "not in my backyard", ou seja, "aqui não, não no meu quintal". Segundo ela, esse tipo de reação, antes associado a plantas de energia ou projetos de transmissão, começa a aparecer também no segmento de data centers. Atualmente, São Paulo concentra o setor, mas a expansão deve alcançar outras regiões, como no Nordeste, impulsionado por incentivos do Redata e pela abundância de energia renovável na região. Para Tito Costa, a concentração paulista decorre da proximidade entre clientes, redes e outros data centers, mas avalia que disponibilidade de energia e terrenos levará o mercado a novos polos à medida que os atuais se saturarem.

artigo.texto: Jensen Huang Reinstated as NVIDIA CEO NVIDIA announced Monday, November 23, that Jensen Huang has been reinstated as president and CEO, effective immediately, reversing a leadership transition that began with his November 12 resignation, previously reported by Data Center Frontier. In an official statement, NVIDIA said its board voted unanimously to restore Huang to his executive position and board seat following discussions with the company's co-founder. The board said it had received input from senior U.S. government officials and was confident that his return posed no national security risk. Harvey C. Jones will remain board chair, while Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, returns to her responsibilities as chief financial officer. "I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in the announcement. NVIDIA emphasized that its independent investigation into reports of a possible foreign intelligence operation targeting Huang will continue. The company has also established additional national security and export-control oversight and plans to appoint a chief compliance officer. Huang's return restores the executive most closely associated with NVIDIA's transformation into the leading supplier of AI computing infrastructure, as the industry continues its rapid expansion of accelerated computing and AI data center capacity. At Data Center Frontier, we talk the industry talk and walk the industry walk. In that spirit, DCF Staff members may occasionally use AI tools to assist with content. Keep pace with the fast-moving world of data centers and cloud computing by connecting with Data Center Frontier on LinkedIn, following us on X/Twitter and Facebook, as well as on BlueSky, and signing up for our weekly newsletters using the form below. About the Author Matt Vincent Matt Vincent is Editor in Chief of Data Center Frontier, where he leads editorial strategy and coverage focused on the infrastructure powering cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and the digital economy. A veteran B2B technology journalist with more than two decades of experience, Vincent specializes in the intersection of data centers, power, cooling, and emerging AI-era infrastructure. Since assuming the EIC role in 2023, he has helped guide Data Center Frontier’s coverage of the industry’s transition into the gigawatt-scale AI era, with a focus on hyperscale development, behind-the-meter power strategies, liquid cooling architectures, and the evolving energy demands of high-density compute, while working closely with the Digital Infrastructure Group at Endeavor Business Media to expand the brand’s analytical and multimedia footprint. Vincent also hosts The Data Center Frontier Show podcast, where he interviews industry leaders across hyperscale, colocation, utilities, and the data center supply chain to examine the technologies and business models reshaping digital infrastructure. Since its inception he serves as Head of Content for the Data Center Frontier Trends Summit. Before becoming Editor in Chief, he served in multiple senior editorial roles across Endeavor Business Media’s digital infrastructure portfolio, with coverage spanning data centers and hyperscale infrastructure, structured cabling and networking, telecom and datacom, IP physical security, and wireless and Pro AV markets. He began his career in 2005 within PennWell’s Advanced Technology Division and later held senior editorial positions supporting brands such as Cabling Installation & Maintenance, Lightwave Online, Broadband Technology Report, and Smart Buildings Technology. Vincent is a frequent moderator, interviewer, and keynote speaker at industry events including the HPC Forum, where he delivers forward-looking analysis on how AI and high-performance computing are reshaping digital infrastructure. He graduated with honors from Indiana University Bloomington with a B.A. in English Literature and Creative Writing and lives in southern New Hampshire with his family, remaining an active musician in his spare time.

artigo.texto: Data centers – A expansão da inteligência artificial (IA) deve provocar um aumento de 70% nas emissões de carbono dos data centers até 2030. A projeção é da Agência Internacional de Energia (AIE), que relaciona o crescimento à necessidade de ampliar a infraestrutura tecnológica para atender à demanda por processamento de dados, principalmente nos Estados Unidos e na China. De acordo com o relatório anual da agência, o consumo de eletricidade de data centers deve dobrar até o fim da década, em comparação com os níveis atuais. A inteligência artificial será responsável por aproximadamente três quartos desse crescimento, devido à necessidade de maior capacidade computacional. LEIA: Nvidia anuncia retorno imediato de Jensen Huang ao comando da empresa A estimativa da AIE é que os data centers voltados à IA consumam 350 terawatts-hora (TWh) adicionais de eletricidade por ano até 2030. O volume supera o consumo anual de energia do Reino Unido. O avanço acontece em um cenário de mudanças no setor energético mundial, que também enfrenta pressões sobre o abastecimento e precisa atender a outras necessidades, como climatização e crescimento populacional. Combustíveis fósseis devem abastecer data centers Mesmo com os investimentos de grandes empresas de tecnologia em fontes renováveis, a geração de eletricidade por meio de combustíveis fósseis deve avançar em ritmo mais acelerado para acompanhar a expansão dos data centers. Na China, a previsão é que aproximadamente metade da eletricidade consumida por essas instalações venha de usinas a carvão até 2030. A parcela restante será fornecida principalmente por fontes renováveis, com participações menores de energia nuclear e gás. Nos Estados Unidos, o gás natural deve representar cerca de 60% da eletricidade destinada aos data centers até o fim da década. Em agosto de 2026, os projetos anunciados para novas usinas a gás vinculadas a essas estruturas somavam aproximadamente 180 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade, número próximo ao de toda a geração a gás atualmente disponível na União Europeia. Infraestrutura mundial cresce com avanço da IA O levantamento da AIE também aponta uma rápida expansão da capacidade global de data centers. Nos últimos dois anos, o indicador aumentou dez vezes, chegando a 17 GW. Com os projetos que estão em construção, a expectativa é alcançar aproximadamente 50 GW. Atualmente, a capacidade instalada mundial é de 120 GW. Outros 120 GW devem ser acrescentados até 2030, sendo que três quartos dessa expansão serão destinados a instalações voltadas à inteligência artificial. O crescimento da infraestrutura reforça o desafio energético associado ao desenvolvimento da IA. Embora a tecnologia amplie a capacidade de processamento e sustente novos serviços digitais, sua expansão também aumenta a demanda por eletricidade e pode prolongar a dependência de fontes de energia responsáveis por emissões de carbono. artigo.texto: Google, Blue Origin Plan Orbital AI Compute Test The 2029 mission will deploy rack-scale computing satellites, with cooling, autonomous recovery, and hardware longevity likely to determine whether orbital infrastructure can support commercial workloads. Google has booked a Blue Origin New Glenn launch for the first quarter of 2029 to advance Project Suncatcher, a test of solar-powered computing satellites designed to evaluate whether space-based infrastructure can support AI workloads at roughly the scale of individual data center racks. The companies announced the agreement Nov. 19, outlining a dedicated heavy-lift mission to place satellites equipped with Google’s Tensor Processing Units into sun-synchronous orbit. Google has described the project as a long-term effort to expand AI infrastructure by tapping solar energy in space. For data center operators and investors, the more immediate questions are how much useful computing the satellites can sustain, how they recover from failures, and whether their operating lives can justify launch and replacement costs. Proving Orbital Reliability Dave McCarthy, IDC’s group vice president for cloud and datacenters, enterprise infrastructure, told Data Center Knowledge that successful deployments will need to demonstrate sustained uptime, autonomous fault recovery, and optical communications capable of keeping pace with the processors. “A server rack in orbit has to prove it can run for long periods of time because you can’t send a technician to swap a failed GPU at 500 kilometers,” he said. Those requirements sharpen the technical and economic questions surrounding Orbital’s planned AI satellites, including radiation resilience and the ability to sustain GPU operations over time. Rob DeMillo, CEO and cofounder of orbital computing company Sophia Space, said the demonstrations must also show that multiple nodes can compute together and run useful customer workloads. “An operator doesn’t necessarily need a demonstration to be large. They need it to demonstrate that the underlying architecture works and can scale,” DeMillo told Data Center Knowledge. “There is a significant difference between putting a computer in space and building computing infrastructure in space.” Cooling May Set the Limits Heat rejection remains the largest engineering obstacle. Because space has no atmosphere to carry heat away, operators must rely on radiators, which add weight and complexity and compete with processors and other components for launch capacity. Bill Ray, distinguished vice president analyst at Gartner, said cooling is only part of the challenge. Radiation protection, micrometeorite shielding, and maneuvering capability to avoid debris in the heavily used sun-synchronous orbital environment are also critical. “Heat is the primary barrier, but not the only one,” Ray told Data Center Knowledge. “Micrometeorite shielding will be essential, along with redundancy to provide radiation resistance.” These constraints also surfaced in orbital infrastructure discussions at September’s AI Infra Summit, where executives highlighted the tradeoffs among radiator size, weight, and launch requirements. DeMillo said designs that simply replicate enclosed terrestrial server racks could create substantial cooling burdens, including the need for pumps and fluid loops. A more viable approach, he said, is to integrate power generation and heat rejection with computing capacity. “Radiation is also a system-level engineering problem,” he said. “Shielding is part of the answer, but so are hardware error correction, fault detection and software that can recover or redistribute workloads when components encounter problems.” The First Workloads Will Follow the Data One of the clearest early commercial applications is processing data already collected in space, reducing the amount of raw information that must be transmitted back to Earth. DeMillo identified wildfire detection, disaster response, weather analysis, and maritime tracking as potential uses for orbital image processing. “Earth observation satellites can collect enormous amounts of imagery,” he said. “Processing that information in orbit and sending down the answer rather than all of the raw data saves bandwidth and, in many cases, more importantly, time.” If more advanced AI workloads move into orbit, ground-to-space communications capacity will become even more important. McCarthy pointed to asynchronous model training and synthetic data generation as possible use cases where computing demand is high but data movement is relatively limited. Ray took a narrower view, saying he expects orbital edge computing to focus on tasks such as screening imagery before transmission and providing security services. Replacement Costs May Decide the Business Case Commercial viability will also depend on how long satellites can provide useful computing before they need to be replaced. The long development timeline for space-based data centers leaves operators balancing potential energy advantages against launch, communications, and maintenance costs. McCarthy said falling launch prices will need to coincide with hardware that can survive at least five years, roughly matching standard data center depreciation cycles. “Abundant solar power in orbit doesn’t automatically offset a steep launch bill,” he said. Radiation damage and thermal wear could shorten that lifespan, increasing the frequency with which operators would need to launch replacement capacity. “If radiation or thermal wear forces operators to replace satellites every two or three years, the unit economics won’t work,” McCarthy said.

artigo.texto: Trump quer os data centers em casa. E o Brasil com isso? Ameaças do líder americano sobre o tema colocam investimentos e a soberania digital do Brasil em xeque Ao retornar da Ásia, Donald Trump disse que empresas americanas que construírem data centers fora dos Estados Unidos poderão pagar impostos muito mais altos. Operadores globais como Equinix e Digital Realty estão na mira, mesmo boa parte da imprensa internacional tendo lido o recado como mais um capítulo da disputa com a China pelo controle da IA. A lei ainda não mudou, mas sim a natureza da decisão. Escolher onde construir um data center era uma conta de engenharia e de custo que mirava energia barata, água, terreno, proximidade dos clientes, dos cabos e fibras óticas. Com a fala de Trump, essa escolha entra na agenda de segurança nacional, ao lado dos chips e dos minerais estratégicos. O volume de dinheiro em jogo explica o interesse. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft e Oracle devem investir juntas cerca de US$ 800 bilhões em 2026 e mais de US$ 1,2 trilhão em 2027, segundo estimativas do Morgan Stanley. Nem tudo isso é data center, mas uma parte grande é. Quem decide onde esse dinheiro vai parar decide também quem fica com os empregos, os impostos e o poder tecnológico da próxima década. As próprias big techs já esbarram em limites de infra e custo dentro dos EUA. As empresas precisam estar perto de clientes no mundo inteiro, para responder rápido, ter cópias de segurança em outros locais e cumprir leis de países que exigem que certos dados fiquem em seu território. O cenário mais provável não é o fim da expansão internacional, mas uma expansão mais seletiva, lenta e negociada, em que cada projeto fora dos Estados Unidos passa a carregar um custo político. Para o Brasil, isso pesa mais do que parece. Boa parte da nuvem que bancos, varejistas, startups e órgãos públicos usam aqui pertence a empresas americanas, que vinham anunciando bilhões em data centers no país. Se cada novo investimento no exterior virar alvo em Washington, alguns desses projetos podem ser adiados ou encolhidos. Na prática, isso significaria menos capacidade instalada no país, serviços de IA mais caros ou mais lentos para empresas brasileiras e mais dados nossos processados no exterior, sob leis de outros países. É uma questão de soberania digital, e também de competitividade. Empresas que pagarão mais pela computação podem vir a inovar menos. O outro lado da moeda é a disputa por capital. Se as americanas hesitarem, o espaço tende a ser ocupado por investidores de outras origens. O país já tem um exemplo dessa diversificação no complexo que a ByteDance, dona do TikTok, constrói no Pecém, no Ceará. Mesmo trazendo dinheiro, coloca o Brasil no meio da rivalidade entre EUA e China, e a escolha de quem constrói e opera um data center pode virar tema diplomático. É nesse cenário que ganham fôlego ideias que pareciam distantes, como os data centers flutuantes — a coreana Samsung Heavy Industries e a cingapuriana Seatrium já têm projetos de dezenas de megawatts —, e pesquisas com resfriamento por água do mar mostram economia relevante de energia, por enquanto apenas em simulações. Nada disso está provado em escala comercial. O Brasil tem litoral, portos já estudados pelo governo para receber a cadeia da energia eólica no mar — Pecém, Suape e Açu — e uma indústria naval e de petróleo que sabe trabalhar offshore. Essas competências podem servir à infraestrutura digital mesmo em terra, com data centers perto de portos, de cabos submarinos e de energia renovável. Nessa esfera, grandes projetos de construção de novos data centers governamentais e privados aqui no país, redundantes ou não, ganham nova pauta para discussões de locais previamente já definidos, uma vez que apenas o terreno se torna parte pequena na conta, e ganham celeridade para serem executados. Provavelmente o caso com que tive muito contato em Vitória, no estado do Espírito Santo, e no Triângulo Mineiro. Para empresas e investidores, a lição é tratar a localização da computação como risco geopolítico, e não apenas técnico. Quem contrata nuvem deve perguntar onde ficam seus dados, o que aconteceria se o fornecedor congelasse a expansão no país e se existe alternativa. Quem investe tem o olhar além das big techs, sendo energia contratada no longo prazo, transmissão, refrigeração, cabos, construção e financiamento de projetos os elos que ganham em qualquer cenário, porque alguém terá de construir, alimentar e resfriar essas máquinas, aqui ou lá. E, para governos, o recado é que atrair data centers exige previsibilidade, regras tributárias estáveis, licenciamento claro e energia firme. Como princípio claro da inteligência vir antes do dinheiro, a ameaça de Trump ainda é só uma frase, mas mostra que o mapa da IA será também orquestrado geopoliticamente. O dinheiro inteligente não vai esperar a regra sair para se reposicionar. O Brasil quer ser apenas um endereço onde outros constroem ou um país que participa da construção? *Marcela Costa é CEO da SM Partner, um ecossistema de investimentos, estrategista, conselheira e engenheira de telecomunicações. Tem mais de 18 anos de experiência executiva em tecnologia, com passagens por IBM e Oracle, e atua com governança, Smart Money e construção de valor em empresas.

artigo.texto: North Carolina is taking an aggressive approach to protecting electric customers from the financial risks of the data center boom, requiring technology companies to put more money on the line for power plants and other infrastructure built to serve them. While much of the attention surrounding last week's North Carolina Utilities Commission decisions focused on Duke Energy's rate increases, regulators also approved sweeping financial safeguards for data centers. Other WRAL Top Stories In interviews with WRAL, Duke Energy, the Data Center Coalition and Utilities Commissioner Floyd McKissick offered new insight into the strength of those protections and how they could affect future development. "I think that's probably one of the most substantial portions of the rate case decision that, to be honest with you, has gotten very little attention," McKissick said. How far North Carolina went Regulators nationwide are grappling with how to accommodate growing electricity demand from data centers without shifting costs onto households and small businesses. North Carolina's requirements go considerably further than a settlement negotiated by Duke Energy, major technology companies and other stakeholders. Under the new rules, qualifying data centers must: - Sign electricity service contracts lasting at least 10 years. - Pay demand charges based on at least 75% of their contracted power capacity, even if they use less. - Pay upfront for certain infrastructure built specifically to serve them. - Provide financial guarantees for transmission upgrades and penalties associated with breaking contracts. - Provide financial security against potential stranded power generation costs. That last provision is particularly significant. A power plant could have an expected lifespan of 35 years, while a data center might only commit to receiving electricity for 15 years. If the facility closes and there isn't enough demand from other customers to replace it, someone still has to pay for that investment. North Carolina is requiring financial safeguards against that possibility. "Oh my gosh, I don't know how much further we could go than what we went," McKissick said. The commission also expanded the reach of the protections by basing their applicability on when qualifying electricity service begins or expands, rather than when a contract was signed. McKissick estimated roughly 20 previously signed agreements would have fallen outside the requirements under the original settlement. Duke Energy and the data center industry respond Duke Energy says it had already incorporated financial protections into agreements with data center developers. "The Utilities Commission wanted to go a step further than the protections that we already have in our contracts," a Duke Energy representative told WRAL on Monday. Duke said it has not received feedback indicating developers plan to abandon projects because of the new requirements. The Data Center Coalition says its members support paying the full cost of the electricity and infrastructure needed to serve their facilities. Its concerns center on why manufacturers and other large electricity users aren't subject to the same requirements and how some of the additional charges will be calculated. "When you single out data centers, you're not doing anything to protect residents from other sources of large load growth on the grid," Dan Diorio, who leads the coalition's state policy efforts, told WRAL. In a written statement, the coalition also called for greater certainty about the costs companies will face. "Cost allocation should rest on what a customer costs the system, not on what kind of business it is, and companies need to know what they will pay before making long-term commitments," said Alex Cutchey, the coalition's director of state regulatory energy policy. McKissick shares one of those concerns. He said he would have preferred to extend the financial safeguards to other large electricity users, including manufacturers. What it means for your electric bill Gov. Josh Stein and Attorney General Jeff Jackson have spent months advocating for stronger ratepayer protections, holding a news conference in October calling on regulators to go beyond Duke Energy's proposed settlement. Stein also called for data centers to bring their own clean energy, a requirement the commission did not adopt. The new safeguards come as Duke Energy prepares to raise electricity rates in January and invest billions of dollars in infrastructure to meet growing demand. While the protections won't prevent electricity bills from rising, they are designed to reduce the risk of customers paying for infrastructure built to serve data centers if those companies fail to fulfill their commitments. McKissick told WRAL on Monday that the rules are already in effect. Some existing data center contracts may need to be renegotiated, and the decision could face appeals. Jackson's office said it is still reviewing the commission's decision.

artigo.texto: A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) prorrogou até esta segunda-feira, 23 de novembro, às 12h, o prazo de inscrição online nos dois leilões de reserva de capacidade para contratação de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias, previstos para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro. Originalmente, o período de inscrições terminaria na sexta-feira, 20, às 23h. A alteração foi comunicada pela Comissão Permanente de Leilões (CPL) da agência na quinta-feira, 19. As demais datas do cronograma foram mantidas, incluindo o prazo para aporte das garantias de proposta, que também termina nesta segunda-feira, às 23h. Leilões de baterias O primeiro certame, marcado para 2 de dezembro, será destinado a sistemas de armazenamento com requisitos de conteúdo nacional, enquanto o segundo, em 4 de dezembro, não terá restrição quanto à nacionalidade dos equipamentos. Os editais foram aprovados pela Aneel em 27 de outubro, com preços-teto de R$ 1,76 milhão por MW ao ano para o leilão nacional e de R$ 1,58 milhão por MW ao ano para o segundo certame. Os contratos terão duração de 15 anos, com início de suprimento previsto para 1º de agosto de 2028. A homologação dos resultados está programada para abril de 2027. Na aprovação dos editais, a agência também reduziu as garantias financeiras exigidas dos participantes e flexibilizou condições de participação, mantendo mecanismos de comprovação da capacidade financeira dos empreendedores.

artigo.texto: Por Agência Minera Brasil 23 de novembro de 2026, às 11:10 A disputa por uma nova fábrica de veículos elétricos mobilizou cidades do Norte de Minas nas redes sociais. Mas o que pesa na decisão de uma montadora? E o que o lítio da região tem a ver com isso? A notícia correu rápido. A BYD, montadora chinesa que já produz carros elétricos e híbridos em Camaçari (BA), avalia investir cerca de R$ 1 bi em uma segunda fábrica no Brasil, desta vez de vans e caminhões elétricos, com previsão de 2 mil empregos. Minas Gerais disputa o projeto com São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro. O governador eleito, Cleitinho Azevedo, afirmou que pretende procurar o presidente da empresa para apresentar o estado. Nas redes sociais, a disputa ganhou contornos locais. Moradores de Araçuaí, Capelinha e outras cidades do Norte de Minas e do Vale do Jequitinhonha passaram a defender que a fábrica fique na sua cidade. Em alguns comentários, a defesa de uma cidade vem acompanhada de ataques à vizinha: uma “não tem água”, outra “não tem estrutura”. A mobilização é legítima e mostra uma região que quer crescer. Mas vale perguntar: até onde essa torcida ajuda, e a partir de que ponto ela atrapalha? O que uma montadora procura Empresas desse porte não escolhem endereço por curtidas. A decisão costuma levar em conta: • Logística: rodovias, ferrovias e acesso a portos, para receber peças e entregar veículos. • Mercado e fornecedores: proximidade dos grandes centros consumidores e das empresas que fornecem componentes. • Infraestrutura: terreno, energia elétrica em quantidade, água e saneamento. • Mão de obra: trabalhadores qualificados ou condições para formá-los. • Segurança jurídica e incentivos: regras estáveis, licenças com prazos previsíveis e condições negociadas com o governo. Camaçari é um bom exemplo. A BYD ocupou o antigo complexo da Ford, num polo industrial já estruturado. E, segundo a imprensa baiana, 86% dos trabalhadores da fábrica são da Bahia: a mão de obra local pesa, desde que esteja preparada. E o lítio? O Norte de Minas e o Jequitinhonha vivem um momento raro. Empresas como Sigma Lithium, CBL, PLS Brasil (Projeto Colina), Lithium Ionic e Atlas Lithium têm minas em operação ou projetos em desenvolvimento na região, de olho no lítio usado em baterias. É natural ligar uma coisa à outra, já que a BYD aposta nas várias etapas da produção, da bateria ao veículo. Mas o lítio sai das minas mineiras ainda como concentrado, e o país tem poucas das etapas que o transformam em bateria. Ter lítio por perto ajuda a contar uma boa história, mas não garante, sozinho, uma fábrica de veículos. Um polo tecnológico no Jequitinhonha? A oportunidade pode ser maior do que uma fábrica. O Vale do Jequitinhonha tem condições de se tornar um polo tecnológico, reunindo no mesmo território: • mineradoras, que extraem e beneficiam o lítio; • empresas de conversão química, que transformam o concentrado em carbonato e hidróxido de lítio; • indústrias que usam esses produtos, como fabricantes de baterias e de veículos; • formação de pessoas, com Senai, cursos técnicos, institutos federais e universidades; • pesquisa e tecnologia, com a academia trabalhando ao lado das empresas. Cada elo atrai o seguinte. Uma fábrica como a da BYD seria uma peça desse polo, não a única. O maior obstáculo hoje é a infraestrutura, em especial as estradas. Para que um polo funcione, a produção precisa chegar com rapidez e segurança aos centros consumidores e aos portos. Em apresentação à Câmara dos Deputados, o próprio Ministério de Minas e Energia listou trechos de rodovias, como a BR-367, entre as obras importantes para o transporte do lítio. Torcida que ajuda, rivalidade que atrapalha Uma cidade que se mobiliza mostra disposição. Mas quem investe olha a região como um todo. Quando cidades vizinhas trocam acusações sem base técnica, o recado que fica é de conflito, não de oportunidade. E a disputa real não é entre Araçuaí, Capelinha ou Salinas: é entre Minas, São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro. Além disso, a cidade vizinha não é concorrente. O desenvolvimento de uma ajuda as outras: trabalhadores circulam entre elas, fornecedores de um município atendem empresas do outro e o dinheiro dos salários se espalha pelo comércio de toda a região. Um grande investimento em qualquer uma delas movimenta também as do entorno. Há um risco maior: transformar cada grande investimento em disputa política ou em boato. Regiões com fama de instáveis, onde a desinformação se espalha e as regras mudam, parecem mais caras e arriscadas para quem decide onde investir. Preparar-se para o desenvolvimento A fábrica pode vir para Minas ou não. Pode vir para o Norte ou para outra região. Mas a lição vale para qualquer cenário: as cidades que se destacam são as que se preparam. Qualificam trabalhadores, organizam dados confiáveis, melhoram a infraestrutura e atuam juntas, como região. artigo.texto: I’m a momentum trader, and I’m always looking for stocks where the potential reward outweighs the risk. Today I’ve got my eye on Vertiv Holdings . I already own a position in Vertiv and I'm looking to buy more. The Ohio-based company provides essential equipment for data centers, including power management and cooling systems that keep servers running. Key points Strong third-quarter earnings and surging orders show demand is still high. Local restrictions could delay data center construction, but they haven't translated into canceled orders. Vertiv generates free cash flow without taking on the same financial risks as its customers. Vertiv shares plunged 25% in the first two trading days after the November midterms amid growing concerns that opposition to data center development could lead to construction restrictions. Shares have continued to slide and are now trading roughly 55% below their May high of $379.94. What's interesting is that while the political rhetoric is getting worse, Vertiv's underlying business is getting stronger. This creates the kind of asymmetric trade I'm looking for. Why I'm buying Business is booming despite the backlash In Vertiv's third-quarter results, revenue surged 61% from a year earlier to $4.31 billion, while adjusted earnings per share came in at $2.21, beating Wall Street's estimate of $1.82 by roughly 21%. Adjusted operating margin reached 25.2%, and organic orders more than doubled from a year earlier. Management also raised its full-year guidance. Those are impressive numbers for a company whose shares have been cut nearly in half. A delay doesn't mean a cancellation There is political opposition to data centers, but there's a key distinction between local opposition and a nationwide slowdown in data center construction. So far, restrictions have been limited to the local level, with bans in towns across six states. There are no statewide bans. I think states and communities that don't want data centers may ultimately reject them, while those that welcome the investment will attract more development. That could change where data centers get built, but it doesn't necessarily eliminate the demand for them. An overlooked advantage Vertiv sells the power and cooling infrastructure that those companies need. It doesn't carry the same construction-related debt burden as the customers financing these massive projects. The company generates positive free cash flow and receives advance payments from customers. That matters in an environment where investors are increasingly questioning the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI infrastructure. VRT YTD mountain Vertiv Holdings, YTD Management also raised its dividend by 60% on November 16, another sign of confidence in the company's cash generation. Why now? Wall Street's consensus price target for Vertiv is approximately $329, implying roughly 92% potential upside from current levels. Given the stock's recent volatility however, I would use stops to protect capital if shares continue to weaken. Bottom line The biggest risk is that the political backlash gains enough traction to produce statewide restrictions or more widespread delays in data center construction. Vertiv's stock is also trading well below its major moving averages, so the technical damage is real. But right now, the company's results aren't showing the deterioration that its stock price suggests. Steven Grasso is the CEO of Grasso Global Inc. artigo.texto: EU, UK Agree to Link Emissions Trading Systems The EU and UK have agreed to link their Emissions Trading Systems (ETS), a statement posted on the European Commission’s (EC) website recently announced. The parties committed to applying this agreement as of January 1, 2028, subject to the ratification process and entry into force in the EU and UK, a separate statement posted on the EC site noted. It highlighted that the intention to link the two systems was announced at the first EU-UK Summit in May 2025. This EC statement pointed out that the UK will expand its ETS, including for aviation and maritime. As a result, over 10 million tons of additional CO2 emissions will be included in the system, “incentivizing decarbonization,” it noted, adding that both the EU and UK ETSs will apply monitoring for aviation’s non-CO2 climate effects. “This linking will provide the basis for a possible future mutual exemption from the respective carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAM), reducing red tape and costs for companies on both sides of the Channel,” the statement highlighted. The statement pointed out that the EU ETS has been linked with Switzerland’s ETS since January 1, 2020. It revealed that this link will remain in place. “Linking the EU and the UK ETS’ brings benefits for both sides,” the EC statement said. “The agreement will ensure that the same set of climate rules related to emissions trading will apply in the EU and the UK, creating a level playing field for businesses on both sides of the Channel,” it added. “It will also create a larger, more liquid carbon market with a more stable carbon price, supporting the EU and the UK on our paths to climate neutrality,” it continued. “A larger carbon market also enables more efficient investment decisions, supporting the sustainable development of the EU and UK economies,” it went on to state. A release posted on the UK government website on November 20 announced that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had agreed a “landmark package” with the European Union at the UK-EU Summit in Brussels and confirmed the linking of the UK and EU’s ETS. “Linking the UK and EU’s emissions trading schemes creates the world’s largest linked carbon market,” this release stated. “It will exempt GBP 6.5 billion [$8.4 billion] of British exports, including steel and aluminum, from the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), removing a major post-Brexit barrier to trade,” it added. “Linking our emissions markets is expected to add up to GBP 3.8 billion [$4.9 billion] a year to the UK economy by 2040,” it continued. A policy paper explaining the EU-UK ETS linking agreement, which was published on the UK government website and pointed out “key features” of the deal, noted that the UK ETS and EU ETS will continue to operate as two separate but linked systems. Industry Reaction In a statement sent to Rigzone, industry body Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) said plans to link the UK and EU Emissions Trading Systems “should only be taken forward on terms that prioritize competitiveness of UK industry, reduce trade barriers, and provide investment certainty”. “Any agreement must also guard against higher UK charges for industrial carbon emitters that could disadvantage domestic operations against international competitors facing lower or no equivalent costs,” OEUK added. OEUK said in its statement that UK industrial competitiveness “must be at the core of any agreement with the EU”, noting that the UK’s oil and gas and renewable energy sectors “are critical to European energy security and are underpinned by closely connected markets, infrastructure, and supply chains”. The industry body also emphasized in the statement that cooperation on energy, carbon markets, and security “must promote increased investment across the UK and Europe”. Enrique Cornejo, OEUK Energy Policy Director, highlighted in OEUK’s statement that “the competitiveness of UK industry must be at the heart of any agreement with the EU”. “Our oil and gas and renewable energy sectors are critical to European energy security,” he added. “Any closer carbon market alignment must strengthen competitiveness, reduce trade barriers and support investment, alongside continued cooperation on energy security and resilience,” he continued. In a separate statement sent to Rigzone, an Ineos spokesperson said linking the UK and EU Emissions Trading Schemes “risks imposing yet another financial burden on British manufacturing at a time when industry is already struggling to survive”. “Linking the EU and UK ETS schemes will add further cost to businesses in addition to sky-high energy prices,” the spokesperson added. “Based on current costs, linking the Emission Trading Scheme to the EU ETS, will mean an additional 10 percent increase in carbon tax for UK businesses who are already paying a 70 percent premium due to speculation of linkage,” the spokesperson continued. This spokesperson highlighted that the EU is reviewing its emissions trading system and said “it makes little sense for Britain to commit to alignment before knowing what the future rules will be, or what influence the UK will have over them”. “This will add to uncertainty for UK industry and further undermine investment confidence,” the spokesperson noted. This spokesperson went on to state that “any agreement must protect the long-term competitiveness of British industry, maintain effective safeguards against carbon leakage and address the growing threat from cheap, high-carbon imports from China and the USA”. “The government argues that closer alignment with Europe will deliver economic growth. But if the result is higher costs, factory closures and the loss of British jobs, in practice the opposite is true,” the spokesperson warned.
