artigo.texto: Data centers, geopolítica e IA: a ameaça de Trump à expansão global da nuvem Empresas como Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta e Oracle sustentam seus serviços em infraestruturas distribuídas globalmente. Por Alessandra Montini* – A inteligência artificial depende de uma base física: data centers, energia, água e chips avançados. Por isso, decisões políticas sobre onde essa infraestrutura pode ser construída têm efeito direto sobre quem consegue desenvolver e usar IA. Em 20 de novembro de 2026, o presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou em coletiva na Casa Branca que não permitirá que empresas americanas construam data centers fora do país e ameaçou aplicar um imposto elevado e outras penalidades severas a quem descumprir a diretriz. A justificativa apresentada foi evitar que a China assuma o controle dessas estruturas no exterior. Quero analisar aqui com vocês os possíveis impactos dessa ameaça sobre a cadeia global de computação em nuvem e IA, com atenção especial às economias emergentes, como o Brasil. Vale ressaltar que, segundo a análise da revista Veja, trata-se de uma intenção política ainda sem regras detalhadas, e o próprio presidente admitiu que não havia discutido o plano formalmente com sua equipe. As consequências descritas abaixo são, portanto, cenários possíveis, e não efeitos já consolidados. Risco para o modelo de expansão das Big Techs Empresas como Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta e Oracle, além de operadoras como Equinix e Digital Realty, sustentam seus serviços em infraestruturas distribuídas globalmente. Essa distribuição serve a dois objetivos: reduzir a latência, aproximando o processamento do usuário, e cumprir leis locais que exigem o armazenamento de dados dentro do território nacional. O caso mais imediato citado pela reportagem é o plano do Google de investir cerca de US$ 15 bilhões em data centers e infraestrutura de IA na Finlândia entre 2027 e 2028, que Trump disse pretender bloquear. Além do impacto sobre projetos específicos, a ameaça de penalidades cria insegurança jurídica para contratos internacionais já firmados e obriga as empresas a reavaliar cronogramas de investimento em escala global. Geopolítica: infraestrutura como ativo de segurança nacional Ao justificar a medida pela necessidade de conter a China, Washington trata a infraestrutura física da internet como ativo estratégico de segurança nacional. Esse movimento se insere em uma disputa tecnológica mais ampla, frequentemente descrita como uma nova “Guerra Fria” e que tende a fragmentar a rede global em blocos. Há, porém, um efeito potencialmente contraditório. Se empresas americanas forem impedidas de investir fora dos Estados Unidos, países em desenvolvimento e mercados emergentes podem passar a depender mais de alternativas chinesas, como Huawei Cloud, Alibaba e Tencent, para atender à sua demanda por processamento de dados. A medida, pensada para limitar a influência chinesa, poderia assim abrir espaço para ela. Impactos sobre economias emergentes e o caso brasileiro Vários países buscavam se posicionar como polos regionais de data centers, atraindo investimentos com energia limpa e incentivos fiscais. O Brasil, com sua matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável, é um exemplo. Esses países enfrentariam agora um duplo obstáculo: a possível proibição de investimentos diretos de empresas americanas e as restrições recentes à exportação de chips avançados de IA. Na mesma semana do anúncio, o Departamento de Comércio dos EUA incluiu o Brasil em uma lista que exige licença prévia para a exportação desses chips, medida que, segundo o material analisado, também atinge Singapura, Malásia, Tailândia e Indonésia. Sem infraestrutura local de ponta, empresas e governos teriam de processar dados a longa distância, o que encarece os serviços de nuvem e retarda a adoção de ferramentas avançadas de IA. Em termos acadêmicos, trata-se de um risco de ampliação da desigualdade tecnológica entre os países que concentram capacidade computacional e os que dependem dela. Gargalo energético e oposição interna nos EUA Concentrar toda a expansão global de data centers em território americano também esbarra em limites internos. De acordo com a reportagem, a resistência de comunidades locais, motivada pelo alto consumo de energia e água e pelo impacto ambiental, já levou ao cancelamento de cerca de US$ 260 bilhões em projetos em 2026. Na própria coletiva, Trump pediu que essas comunidades parem de barrar novos empreendimentos e negociem compensações financeiras com as empresas. O ponto revela uma tensão central: a política de “manter tudo em casa” exige que o país absorva os custos ambientais e energéticos de uma expansão que, até aqui, vinha sendo parcialmente distribuída pelo mundo. A ameaça de Trump evidencia que a computação em nuvem e a IA deixaram de ser apenas questões de mercado e passaram a ocupar o centro da estratégia geopolítica. Entre os efeitos possíveis estão a paralisação de investimentos bilionários, a fragmentação da infraestrutura global, o fortalecimento de concorrentes chineses em mercados emergentes e o aumento de custos e atrasos tecnológicos para países como o Brasil, além de tensões energéticas dentro dos próprios EUA. Como a medida ainda não foi detalhada, o acompanhamento de sua regulamentação é essencial. Para a área de IA, a lição é clara: o desenvolvimento da tecnologia depende de decisões sobre energia, território e soberania digital, e não apenas de avanços em algoritmos. *Alessandra Montini é Diretora do LabData, da FIA Business School

artigo.texto: The Department of the Army recently began soliciting data center proposals for Fort Rucker. The Wiregrass site is one of nine military bases listed in a request for proposals (RFP) released on Friday. “The Department of the Army (“DA”) is issuing this Request for Proposals ('RFP' or 'Solicitation') to solicit competitive proposals from private, public and/or not-for-profit entities interested in leasing non-excess DA land ('Properties') for development of commercial power generation facilities and data centers under a long-term lease agreement(s) ('Enhanced Use Lease' or 'EUL') at Blue Grass Army Depot, Pine Bluff Arsenal, Tooele Army Depot, Sierra Army Depot, Fort McCoy, Fort Bragg, Fort Hood, Fort Rucker, and Joint Base Lewis-McChord ('Installations')," the RFP states. “The EUL(s) that would result from this RFP would be for the purpose of the selected Offeror(s) designing, financing, permitting, developing, constructing, installing, owning, maintaining, operating, securing, and decommissioning a commercial power generation facility and a data center ('Project'). DA’s preference is for integrated power generation facility and commercial data center Projects, but an Offeror can elect to propose power generation only. DA may elect to award one or more EULs pursuant to this RFP.” The 1819 Newsletter Enter your email below to get our top stories delivered straight to your inbox every weekday morning. When asked about the Army's RFP, U.S. Rep. and Sen.-elect Barry Moore (R-Enterprise) told 1819 News in a statement on Tuesday, “My priority is ensuring Fort Rucker remains well-positioned to carry out its critical role in our national defense.” “As the Army moves through this process, I look forward to learning more about the potential opportunities and impacts for both the installation and the surrounding communities,” Moore said. “Any proposed development should be carefully evaluated to ensure it serves the best interests of our military and the people of Alabama.” According to the Army, “Power Generation Facility and Data Center Project” applicants may submit proposals for both power generation and a data center. Proposals are not restricted to any particular data center size or capacity. However, the Army’s preference is for the following data center frameworks: Profile 1: Hardened, physically isolated campuses built to ICD 705 standards for Top Secret/IL6 workloads. Profile 2: Large-scale hyperscale and AI/HPC facilities targeting PUE ≤ 1.15. Offerors electing to integrate commercial data centers alongside generation assets may do so within a unified campus master plan. “Proposed Projects must provide energy resilience capabilities to the DA that will be part of the lease consideration to be provided to DA by the Leassee,” the RFP states. “These capabilities must include the provision of resilient power within one (1) hour of a grid outage and fora minimum of fourteen (14) continuous days, and providing any required improvements to DA’s utility infrastructure that may be required to enable the Installation to accept delivery of the resilient power. For purposes of this RFP, a grid outage is defined as any loss of power from the grid serving the Installation. Preference will be given to Offerors whose Proposal is for the provision of contingency power in excess of fourteen (14) continuous days.” According to the RFP, “projects must avoid draws on water aquifers and must prioritize industrial greywater,treated municipal effluent, or closed-loop cooling towers. Water usage must be net-neutral or better. Offeror shall, at its sole expense, source all industrial process water from non-potable alternative sources, which may include brackish groundwater,reclaimed municipal wastewater (graywater), or treated industrial/agricultural runoff,subject to DA approval and regulatory compliance. DA expects that all power generated and data center capacity (where applicable) will be sold to third-party off-taker(s). The selected Offeror will be responsible for identifying and securing off-taker(s).” Proposals are due by January 18, according to the Army. To connect with the author of this story or to comment, email [email protected].

artigo.texto: MHI and SAKURA sign agreement to explore Japan-based AI data centers The proposed alliance pairs industrial power and cooling technology with cloud operations. Faster construction and greater domestic control remain goals, not delivered results. Loading page… Listen to this story The November 18, 2026 memorandum pairs Mitsubishi Heavy Industries’ engineering capabilities with SAKURA internet’s cloud and data-center operations to examine a strategic alliance. The work could produce Japanese-built infrastructure and modular facility designs, but the agreement funds no announced deployment or new capacity. For AI operators, the proposal addresses dependence on overseas platforms and the practical bottlenecks of power, cooling, construction time, and resilience; any expansion into Asia and Oceania depends on what the exploratory work delivers. The companies will study two workstreams: a domestic computing and service foundation, and reference architectures and modular methods for mechanical and electrical systems. SAKURA already operates data centers in Tokyo, Osaka, and Hokkaido; those facilities are existing capacity, not an outcome of the MOU. Japan’s Digital Agency selected SAKURA as a Government Cloud provider for fiscal year 2026; the companies describe it as the first domestic provider selected. Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and SAKURA internet want to give Japan AI infrastructure that is domestically controlled and faster to build. Their November 18, 2026 announcement establishes an earlier step: a memorandum of understanding to explore collaboration toward a strategic alliance, including modular AI data centers. It is an agreement to investigate development, not a completed deployment. The companies describe their objective as sovereign AI and sovereign cloud: keeping data and AI platforms under a country’s own laws and control. Their proposed collaboration reaches beyond cloud services to the equipment and construction methods needed to support them. They want infrastructure designed, built and operated in Japan, with resilience against disruption as a central requirement. The partners frame overseas cloud dependence as one reason for the effort. They say much of Japan’s AI processing runs on platforms operated by foreign providers, leaving users exposed to sudden service changes or suspensions. Their case for domestic infrastructure is therefore about continued access to computing as well as control over the rules governing its use. Their joint release also identifies a more physical obstacle: AI data centers require large power supplies and advanced cooling. Securing electricity and completing construction can delay operations. The companies say facilities must also withstand disasters and geopolitical uncertainty. Rapid construction and reliable operation are linked goals in the proposal, rather than speed being its only stated measure of success. SAKURA’s announcement divides the exploratory work into two connected areas. One concerns the domestic computing and service foundation; the other concerns how the facilities themselves would be designed and assembled: As AI becomes national infrastructure, that infrastructure has to be resilient in both how it is built and how it is operated. With SAKURA internet, we want to give Japan a sovereign AI foundation that is secure, available when it matters, and fast enough to keep pace with demand. Masayuki Suematsu, executive vice president and chief strategy officer, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries MHI brings engineering capabilities spanning design, manufacturing, controls, simulation and maintenance. Its existing work covers social infrastructure, aviation, defense and space. The company says it is strengthening a data-center business that integrates cooling, power, controls and high-security technologies, with resilience already one of the pillars of its growth strategy. SAKURA supplies the cloud and data-center operating experience. It runs facilities in Tokyo, Osaka and Hokkaido and provides cloud and computing services from its own domestic data centers. That operating footprint is existing background to the agreement, rather than new capacity created by signing it. The announcement also points to SAKURA’s selection by Japan’s Digital Agency as a Government Cloud service provider for fiscal year 2026. The companies describe it as the first domestic cloud provider selected. They present that public-sector credential alongside its facility operations as relevant experience for the proposed domestic infrastructure work. Japan is the initial focus, but the intended market is not exclusively domestic. The companies aim to take products and solutions established through the collaboration into global markets, including Asia and Oceania. That overseas ambition depends on what the exploratory work produces. Loading discussion... Join the conversation Explain how much ownership should matter compared with a provider’s track record. artigo.texto: IQM Quantum Computers Partners with QAI, a South Korean Quantum-AI company to Deploy a Quantum Computer in Their Private AI Data Center in Korea - IQM will deliver an IQM Radiance R3, a 54-qubit quantum computer, to QAI, a South Korean quantum-AI data center and cloud infrastructure company, by the end of 2027. - Once operational, QAI expects to offer the system to its customers through its Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) offering to explore industry use cases. - The order is IQM’s second quantum computer sale in South Korea , following the IQM Spark system atChungbuk National University . SEOUL, South Korea & ESPOO, Finland--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 25, 2026-- IQM Quantum Computers (Nasdaq: IQMX), a global leader in superconducting quantum computers, is partnering with QAI Co., Ltd., a South Korean quantum-AI data center and cloud infrastructure company, to deliver an IQM Radiance R3 54-qubit quantum computer. The order covers a complete on-premises quantum computing solution for QAI’s data center, including an IQM Radiance R3 system and associated services. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261125732569/en/ IQM Quantum Computers partners with QAI, a South Korean quantum-AI company to deploy a quantum computer in their private AI data center in Korea. The 54-qubit quantum computer will be the first IQM quantum computer deployed to a private data center in Asia. The deal brings on-premises quantum computing into QAI’s commercial data center environment, where it will help build applications and a resilient, competitive infrastructure within South Korea’s quantum ecosystem. The IQM Radiance R3 is expected to be delivered and installed on-premises at QAI’s data center in Seoul by the end of 2027. "We are proud to partner with QAI as they bring an IQM Radiance R3 54-qubit quantum computer to their data center in Seoul," said Sylwia Barthel de Weydenthal, Chief Commercial Officer at IQM Quantum Computers. "This sale marks an important milestone for quantum computing in South Korea. With on-premises access to IQM Radiance, QAI will be able to accelerate research, develop commercial applications for businesses and support sovereign quantum capabilities that keep critical technology and data under national control. We look forward to working closely with QAI to build a thriving quantum ecosystem in Korea and across the Asia-Pacific region." QAI builds data centers that combine GPU-based AI computing with quantum computing resources. Once the system is operational, QAI plans to make it available to its customers through its Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) offering. This would give Korean enterprises, research institutions and public organizations access to the IQM Radiance R3 quantum computer hosted in South Korea. The system will initially be used to explore industry use cases in compute-intensive fields such as drug discovery, next-generation materials, including batteries, financial portfolio optimization and scheduling optimization for logistics and energy infrastructure. "By bringing IQM Radiance R3 into our data center in Seoul, we are creating a place where Korean companies and researchers can use GPUs and a quantum computer together to solve real problems,” said Ui-tae Kim, Co-CEO and CTO of QAI. “Together with IQM, we will build an environment where Korea’s industry and research community can work with quantum computing hands-on." IQM Radiance is IQM's most powerful on-premises quantum computer, designed for integration into high-performance computing (HPC) environments, where installing it on site reduces latency for hybrid quantum-classical workloads. The 54-qubit system offers high-fidelity gates and tunable couplers between the qubits, arranged in a square lattice with the highest connectivity available at this scale. Its layout natively supports surface-code error correction. Customers own and operate the system on site, with pulse-level access and the option to upgrade with the latest chips and components as IQM's technology develops. South Korea has made quantum technology a national priority. Under its Sixth Basic Plan for Science and Technology, the government plans to invest more than 200 trillion South Korean won (approximately EUR 135 billion) in research and development between 2026 and 2030, with quantum named as one of ten national strategic technology fields. In January 2026, the Ministry of Science and ICT also set out its first comprehensive plan for the quantum science, technology and industry, which aims to give Korea the world's highest utilization rate of quantum computers by 2035, alongside training 10,000 quantum professionals and fostering 2,000 quantum companies. Reaching those goals will require businesses and researchers in Korea to have hands-on access to quantum computers. With IQM's quantum computer installed on-premises and integrated into its data center offering, QAI will be able to provide that access as a service to customers across Korea. IQM's first quantum computer in South Korea, an IQM Spark at Chungbuk National University, was the first commercial quantum computer installed through the Korean government's official procurement process. IQM opened its Seoul office in June 2025. The QAI order will further extend IQM's installed base across Asia-Pacific, following systems already delivered in South Korea, Taiwan and Japan. About IQM Quantum Computers IQM Quantum Computers (Nasdaq: IQMX) is a global leader in integrated quantum computing, delivering full-stack superconducting quantum computers to enterprises, research institutions, universities, high-performance computing centers and national laboratories worldwide. With more on-premises systems sold than any other manufacturer, IQM gives customers direct ownership and control of quantum computers that integrate with their supercomputing and AI infrastructure, with cloud access also available through IQM Resonance. artigo.texto: Indian solar manufacturer Kosol Energie is looking to make a bigger play in India's battery energy storage system (BESS) market through its subsidiary KoBESS, bringing a portfolio of storage solutions spanning residential, commercial and industrial (C&I), and utility-scale applications to the country. The company is leveraging more than a decade of experience in battery energy storage deployments, with its solutions having been in the market since 2015, primarily catering to the US market. It is now looking to replicate that experience in India, as renewable energy integration, round-the-clock power requirements and energy cost optimisation increasingly drive demand for storage. Speaking to Saur Energy International, Kayan Kalthia, Executive Director – Business Development at KoBESS, said the company sees battery storage playing a critical role in transitioning renewable energy from an intermittent source to firm power. “Renewable energy plus BESS is what gives a firm load and RTC power, round-the-clock power,” Kalthia said, outlining the company's vision for energy storage in the Indian market. A portfolio spanning multiple segments KoBESS is positioning itself across three major market segments, with a manufacturing facility having a capacity of 6 GW, according to Kalthia. Its portfolio includes residential storage solutions ranging from 5 kW to 25 kW, C&I offerings including 250 kWh, 500 kW and 1 MWh systems, and utility-scale battery storage containers with capacities of 5 MWh and 6.2 MWh. The company is seeking to differentiate its offerings through quality assurance and reliability testing, with Kalthia stating that every product and bill of materials used has undergone reliability testing. He also pointed to the company's existing deployments and projects with more than a decade of operating experience as evidence of the technology's maturity. Indigenous EMS at the centre of its offering. A key part of KoBESS's strategy is its energy management system (EMS), which Kalthia described as the company's primary differentiator. Both the hardware and software for its energy management platform have been developed in-house in India, and the technology has been deployed for more than a decade. The EMS is designed to optimise energy consumption, power sourcing and storage utilisation based on a customer's requirements. KoBESS aims to use the software capabilities and historical deployment data to demonstrate the economics of storage to prospective customers, including potential returns on investment. Moving beyond standard BESS sizing KoBESS is also focusing on customised storage solutions rather than recommending battery capacity based on standardised configurations. Kalthia said the company first studies a customer's energy consumption and load profile through a data acquisition system installed at the facility. The data is then analysed through its software to determine the required BESS capacity, the most suitable application, potential savings and the expected payback period. The approach is intended to help customers better understand the economics of battery storage before committing to an investment. Autonomous energy optimisation and market participation The company is also pitching its storage systems as part of a broader energy optimisation platform that can factor in consumption patterns, weather forecasts and holidays to determine the most economical energy mix. Kalthia cited Kosol Energie’s own captive power plant as an example of the approach, describing a planned hybrid installation comprising approximately 12 MW of solar DC capacity and 25 MWh of BESS. The system is intended to match the factory's consumption at 15-minute intervals, moving it towards near-100% renewable power supply. He added that the platform can also support revenue stacking and autonomous energy market participation, including buying and trading electricity in the open market, depending on the applicable market framework and customer requirements. Betting on India's growing storage market KoBESS is introducing its existing international product portfolio to India rather than developing a separate range exclusively for the domestic market. Kalthia said the company sees Indian entrepreneurs and businesses becoming increasingly receptive to new technologies and believes energy storage investments can deliver meaningful returns. With its focus on residential, C&I and utility-scale systems, indigenous energy management technology, and experience in international deployments, Kosol Energie is looking to establish KoBESS as a broader player in India's evolving energy storage market. The company's pitch is that BESS is no longer merely an add-on to renewable energy installations, but increasingly a tool for firming power, optimising energy costs and enabling greater renewable energy integration. artigo.texto: The transaction establishes a long-term strategic partnership between Sungrow Renewables and Actuate Energy, based on the companies’ complementary expertise and capabilities and underpinned by a shared commitment to develop, build and bring into operation Spain’s first large-scale BESS portfolio, comprising seven advanced-stage projects. The first assets are already under construction, while the remainder of the portfolio is expected to commence construction in the coming months, with the full portfolio expected to reach Ready-to-Build (RtB) status during 2027 and enter commercial operation between 2027 and the first half of 2028. The transaction marks the continuation of Sungrow Renewables’ pioneering commitment to energy storage in Spain, which it launched several years ago. The portfolio comprises seven stand-alone BESS projects totalling 380 MW / 1.5 GWh. These include the Valencia Cluster, located in La Vall d'Uixó (Castellón); Santiago, in Lousame (A Coruña); Berja, in the province of Almería; and the Navarra Cluster, located in Olite and Cordovilla. The agreement also leaves the door open to further collaboration on the development of future assets, reflecting both companies’ commitment to continued growth in the energy storage market, strengthening the resilience of Spain’s energy system and reinforcing Spain’s position as a strategic market within Europe. The transaction comes at a time when Spain’s electricity market is in critical need for energy storage, which is reaching a significant level of maturity, with storage becoming the technology with the largest volume of grid connection applications in Spain, ahead of both solar PV and wind. As Daniel Sánchez, CEO of Sungrow Renewables for Western Europe, noted, “This transaction marks a major milestone for Spain’s BESS market. With 380 MW and 1.5 GWh, it is the largest battery energy storage transaction completed to date in Spain and, crucially, is backed by an advanced-stage portfolio of projects already moving into construction. Energy storage in Spain is moving from ambition to execution. “At Sungrow Renewables, we backed this market when it was still a bet on the future and helped pave the way through the development and commissioning of Sanxenxo, Spain’s first stand-alone BESS plant. Today, we are taking a decisive step towards accelerating renewable energy integration and strengthening the stability of the power system, in a transaction that reinforces our long-term commitment to the Spanish market. Energy storage is no longer a promise for Spain: it is strategic infrastructure that we are turning into reality.” Sungrow Renewables’ continued strategy in Spain This latest milestone marks the continuation of Sungrow Renewables’ commitment to Spain and to the integration of energy storage. The company was a pioneer in Spain in the development of hybrid solar PV projects from 2022 onward, moved early into stand-alone BESS with its Sanxenxo project, and currently has stand-alone BESS assets already in operation in the country. Spain remains a strategic market for the company, which operates in more than 20 countries. Actuate Energy focuses on dynamic European energy markets and is committed to supporting an accelerated transition toward renewable energy by investing in and operating energy storage assets that provide stability to the power system. Actuate Energy is backed by NGP, a premier energy private equity firm with over $25 billion of cumulative equity commitments. With this agreement, Spain becomes the starting point for Actuate Energy’s entry into Europe, driven by the country’s high renewable energy penetration, the ongoing need to provide grid stability, and the growth potential of a mature project pipeline.

artigo.texto: Central Virginians urge Henrico leaders: ‘Don’t give water to data centers’ Data centers are popping up across several rural and suburban counties in Central Virginia, banking on one very important and finite resource: water. On Nov. 17, local activists from several Central Virginia counties held a rally along the James River in Henrico, imploring local leaders to protect the area’s limited water resources and quell data center growth in the region. In Central Virginia, water is a geopolitical issue; Henrico currently sells millions of gallons of water each day to nearby rural localities such as Hanover and Goochland. Henrico also owns Cobbs Creek Reservoir in rural Cumberland County, which could be the main water source for Cumberland’s planned natural gas power plant. And over the past year, both Goochland and Hanover have proposed multiple hyperscale data centers near their borders with Henrico – data centers that would require large amounts of water and electricity. While several of Hanover’s proposals were eventually shot down, Goochland’s plans for four data center campuses totaling nearly 3,000 megawatts – less than a mile away from some Western Henrico neighborhoods – are moving forward. Standing alongside the banks of the James River in Varina, one of the last rural areas in the now suburbanized Henrico County, local activist and Henrico resident Aileen Rivera urged Henrico’s Board of Supervisors to prevent Cobbs Creek Reservoir from being used for what will become the second largest natural gas plant in the entire country. “Henrico County has both the ethical and moral responsibility to put the health, safety, and well-being of its residents first,” Rivera said. “Our elected officials have a duty to protect the people they represent, not simply accommodate the needs of powerful industries. Economic development should never come at the expense of public health.” Rivera pointed to last year’s water crisis in Henrico – when nearly half of the county, and almost all residents in Varina, lost access to water for several days after a Richmond water plant failed – as evidence that Henrico cannot afford to sell or provide water to industrial users before ensuring that its own residents have access. “Henrico has already experienced how vulnerable its water system can be when it depends on regional water infrastructure,” she said. “Henrico County must exercise caution. Water is not an unlimited resource, nor should it be treated as a commodity that can be committed to industrial development without a thorough assessment.” At the rally, activists from across Central Virginia – Goochland, Hanover, Cumberland, Fluvanna, and elsewhere – pushed one overarching message: “our individual fights are all connected.” A natural gas plant in Cumberland would provide energy to data centers in Goochland and Hanover, which would require water sold by Henrico. “All of these problems lead back to the data center epidemic that’s plaguing Virginia,” said Jennifer Corpus, a Hanover resident and founder of the anti-data center group, Friends of Hanover. “Every group standing here is fighting a different piece of the exact same problem, and the reason why we are standing here together today is so that everyone can see the whole picture.” Henrico leaders have said that while they are locked into a long-term contract to sell water to Goochland County, there are no plans to sell additional water that could be used to support data center growth. Several Henrico supervisors also have said that although they oppose the planned data centers along the Goochland-Henrico border, it is ultimately under the jurisdiction of Goochland supervisors. Despite reigniting talks with Cumberland last November on a potential water contract that would allow Henrico to sell Cumberland water from Cobbs Creek Reservoir, Henrico officials have said that there is no current water agreement between the two counties and those talks have stalled. Dominion Energy has not yet secured a water source for the new Cumberland natural gas plant. Henrico already has dozens of data center campuses in Varina’s White Oak Technology Park. While Henrico supervisors have passed new measures that prevent data centers from being built outside of the park without a public approval process, those measures came after the rezoning of what will become a large 17-data center campus expansion for tech giant QTS in an area near the park. Rivera called the data center-filled tech park Henrico’s “big mistake” that nearby localities should learn from and avoid. “I urge everybody visiting from out of town, you’re close enough to White Oak Technology [Park] where all the data centers are, go take a look,” she said. “Go take a look and see what happens.” Liana Hardy is the Citizen’s government and education reporter. artigo.texto: Renewable Energy Strategies for Mexico’s Data Center Expansion Panelists at Mexico Data Center Summit 2026 say renewables with storage are becoming a competitive foundation for data center power but must operate within grid-connected hybrid architectures. Atera Energy says about 1,800MW of CENACE's 7,000MW in new demand requests come from data centers, too much for solar alone. GE Vernova identifies transmission as the main bottleneck, while Atlas Renewable Energy says solutions must be designed at the system level. Panelists highlight Mexico's gas price advantage for cogeneration, EMS integration, and Energy-as-a-Service models, while warning that rapidly shifting capacity requirements complicate planning. Renewable generation paired with battery storage is becoming an increasingly competitive foundation for powering Mexico's data centers, but it will not be the only solution. Panelists at Mexico Data Center Summit 2026 say grid-connected hybrid architectures, gas cogeneration, and specialized financing models such as Energy-as-a-Service (EaaS) will be required to meet the sector's demand for stable, continuous electricity. "They are not the definitive solution, and they are not the only solution," says Daniel García, Commercial Director, Atlas Renewable Energy, referring to solar and storage. "Renewable sources are key, and they are among the main solutions, because with the integration of storage they can already be economically competitive." The discussion comes as CFE and MEXDC have established a joint power planning framework to identify the energy and infrastructure needs of new data centers. MBN has also reported that developers must evaluate energy availability and transmission capacity before purchasing land. Luis Felipe Vélez, CEO, Atera Energy, says CENACE currently holds about 7,000MW in requests for new demand, of which close to 1,800MW correspond to data centers alone. A centralized response will not be enough, he says, which strengthens the case for decentralized generation. Solar is the most advanced renewable option in Mexico and gains stability when paired with batteries, but covering that demand with solar alone would require very large installations that may not be economically attractive. Vélez sees solar and storage as a complement that stabilizes systems and reduces pressure on the centralized grid, with nuclear microreactors as a possible future option. Vanessa Varela, Sales Manager GSI – Grid System Integration, GE Vernova, says the right mix depends on the type of facility, since hyperscale, colocation, and edge data centers have different demand profiles. The data center ecosystem has embraced solar and wind partly because combined cycle turbines are not available until 2032, she says, while solar is the fastest technology to deploy. Its challenges include stability, which requires batteries, and supply chains for components such as transformers. The most important challenge, however, is transmission. Even if mixed-investment projects add about 8GW of generation by 2030, that energy must reach the sites where data centers need it, she says. García says the question should be framed at the system level. Isolated on-site renewable systems cannot yet guarantee year-round supply without backup, but most projects plan to remain grid-connected. From a financial standpoint, solar or hybrid solar-wind projects integrated with storage can deliver reliable products compatible with data center demand. "The problem is not that data centers consume energy every hour of the year. The problem is that the system is not like that," he says, adding that high renewable penetration must be complemented by expanded transmission and a broader technology mix. Jimena Ortiz, Commercial Director, Solfium, says diesel backup cannot yet be fully replaced, although battery energy storage systems (BESS) can improve power quality and reduce dependence on it. Scale also matters: each megawatt of solar requires roughly the area of a soccer field, she says. Ortiz adds that operators should start by understanding their consumption profile, and that thermal storage offers an advantage, since cooling, the largest load in a data center, can be shifted across hours. On the demand side, Vélez says Germany now requires new data centers to reach a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.2, compared with a global average of about 1.5 to 1.6, which forces designs built around efficiency from the start. On the supply side, the grid will remain the main stabilizer for years, and Mexico holds a competitive advantage in natural gas. Vélez says Atera recently signed gas contracts at about US25/MMBtu in other markets,while gas in Mexico costs about US4.50/MMBtu. Self-generation alone does not compete with grid tariffs once CAPEX, OPEX, and fuel are included, but cogeneration makes projects financially viable, he says. Mexico's fast-track approval process for projects of up to 20MW is working in most cases, and larger projects can still obtain authorization through a longer process, he adds. Managing these combined sources requires energy management systems (EMS) that coordinate generation forecasts, battery dispatch, and demand, which García says are now far simpler to integrate than five to 10 years ago. Vélez says operators also need hardware, such as flywheels or batteries, to isolate their self-generation systems from grid disturbances and vice versa. Varela says AI loads, which generate power peaks unlike the stable loads of colocation facilities, are leading some governments to require AI data centers to build their own generation to protect the grid. She adds that microgrids and digital twins will be needed to simulate load and electrical behavior. Financing models are also shifting. García says EaaS goes a step beyond PPAs by allowing operators to invest in their core business while transferring risk management to energy specialists. artigo.texto: Two communities in Texas and Arizona are holding votes next month to determine the future of SpaceX data center plans in their areas. On December 9, the Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission in Arizona and the Starbase City Commission are both scheduled to vote on proposals related to the data center project. The two votes center around a special land use authorization and a tax incentive package for the data centers. SpaceX plans to spend more than $74 billion on two AI supercomputing campuses, making them two of the largest data center projects in the country. Read More on AI "These investments will expand local tax bases, generate substantial new revenue for schools and public services, and create economic opportunities that extend far beyond the facilities themselves," SpaceX said on its website. SpaceX Data Center in Texas In Texas, SpaceX plans to invest $24 billion in a 444-acre plot in Brownsville, near its own Starbase rocket site in the Rio Grande Valley. SpaceX said the project has already created more than 3,000 construction jobs, with more than 500 permanent jobs coming once its operations begin. It also pledged $200 million to expand Brownsville's water and wastewater infrastructure. The company added that the facility is designed to "stand on its own" by generating its own electricity rather than pulling from the public power grid. The City Commission of the City of Starbase will convene on December 9 to consider approval of a 10-year, 100 percent property tax abatement. Starbase City officials declined to comment to Newsweek. Last week, the Cameron County commission voted against a tax break for the SpaceX data center. The company sought a tax break in Starbase, where two of the three City Commission members are current SpaceX employees. "As Texas communities consider major supercomputing investments, careful long-term tax planning is essential," SpaceX said. "The proposed abatement was designed to address this challenge: provide the County with substantial, predictable new revenue through payments in lieu of taxes (PILOTs), incentivize continued investment and meet the County’s economic development goals." The project was granted an air pollution permit by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) after outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott directed the regulatory agency to pause all data center permits until it completes its impact evaluations. Newly-elected Governor Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, made halting data center construction a pillar of her campaign to ensure lawmakers can provide adequate protections for Texans. SpaceX Data Center in Arizona SpaceX also plans to build a $50 billion, 747-acre data center in Cochise County, Arizona, about 80 miles east of Tucson. According to the proposal, SpaceX said the plan would reduce electricity bills by up to 20 percent and create 1,000 permanent jobs. This facility would also use a dry cooling system and would not pump groundwater for industrial use, but local residents worry about the already strained aquifer. The Cochise County Planning and Zoning board will vote on the special use authorization for Tombstone Resource LCC, the company building the SpaceX data center. This vote will determine if the project is allowed to proceed under current zoning rules. On November 19, Attorney General Kris Mayes asked the county to postpone the December 9 vote until state and federal agencies could provide a full review of the project. "The people of Cochise County deserve answers before county officials approve a project of this magnitude," Mayes said in a statement. "The company’s proposal raises serious unanswered questions about energy reliability, water use, emergency response capabilities, traffic impacts and effects on surrounding communities. Those issues must be fully examined by the appropriate state and federal agencies before any local approval moves forward." In her letter, Mayes said the project could consume up to six gigawatts of electricity, which is nearly 20 percent of the state's current power-generating capacity, and could strain the local groundwater supplies. She also highlighted concerns about traffic, strains on local emergency service resources and the impact on local wildlife. She said the company's proposal leaves a lot about the project uncertain, saying that "the sheer scale of its power demand and physical size presents exorbitant risks," and reminded the commission of its duty to ensure the development is feasible before construction is approved. Mayes will host a town hall scheduled for Thursday, December 3, for residents to voice concerns. Newsweek reached out to Cochise County officials, Attorney General Mayes and SpaceX for comment. artigo.texto: Tennessee Valley Authority filing references $1.7 billion data center deal It would appear the Tennessee Valley Authority’s new data center rates are paying off. What This Story Is About - A Securities and Exchange Commission filing hints at a major data center project within the Tennessee Valley Authority’s service area. Why It Matters - The deal describes a data center customer prepared to pay the utility almost $2 billion for power. What Happens Next - Many of the details of the project aren’t public, like when the project will begin. For Context - The TVA announced new rates for data centers in September. KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT) - It would appear the Tennessee Valley Authority’s new data center rates are paying off; a new Securities and Exchange Commission filing from the utility implies a large-scale data center may soon be built within the TVA’s service area, netting the country’s largest utility provider a $1.7 billion payday. An annual report form publicly available makes reference to the deal, saying the TVA would see a $31 million primary payment when the agreement is finalized, with the rest to come in 59 installments. That total payoff — $1.7 billion in “aggregate payments” — is important, since it’s the first agreement to fall under the TVA’s new rates. In September, TVA officials announced the new dollar amount data centers would pay for power: $1.5 million per megawatt over five megawatts. Breaking down the numbers — $1.7 trillion worth of megawatts that cost $1.5 million each — the new data center could have a power draw in the neighborhood of 1,100 megawatts. TVA Spokesperson Scott Brooks confirmed the math checked out, but he didn’t go so far as confirming the center’s capacity. Since the TVA is a partially private operation, not all information about the utility is publicly available. “Your understanding is correct, but we wouldn’t speculate on the capacity,” Brooks said. The TVA’s status as a public-private body also means some details of the deal are still under wraps, like which company wants to build the data center and where. Brooks wasn’t able to confirm the information either. “TVA does not disclose confidential business information regarding individual customers or prospective economic development projects,” he said. “Consistent with longstanding practice, we protect commercially sensitive information while working with customers, local power companies and economic development partners.” The filing also doesn’t say when a facility could begin construction, but it does say the TVA expects to log that first $31 million payment in November. artigo.texto: Add military veterans to the growing force demanding a data center reckoning. A national coalition called Veterans for Public Lands is calling on federal powers to immediately pause data center development on public lands until safeguards are in place. “These are our lands,” said Gregg Bafundo, a senior advisor of the coalition and former ranger of the Okanogan Wenatchee National Forest. “If the government’s going to do anything with these, they have to ask the permission of the American people. And right now, the American people don’t want data centers on our public lands.” The coalition launched on Veterans Day, a week after the November midterm elections where at least 69 veterans won election to Congress. “The reality is that veterans themselves … we’re not just a piece of the American pie, we are the American pie,” Bafundo said. “We’re here to protect (public lands) just like we protected (them) in the United States when we were on active duty. The mission, in many regards, hasn’t changed.” The coalition is calling on U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to begin an immediate moratorium. Burgum, a former North Dakota governor, reportedly has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies, according to a Propublica investigation. Burgum’s department recently vowed to sell off public lands to states or tribes in a five-year strategic plan. “Of course he wants to sell them. I mean, the corruption is absolutely blatant,” Bafundo said, noting that Burgum has not responded to the veterans’ request. “They want to dump these lands to the states knowing full well that states have to balance a budget,” he said. Veterans for Public Lands is also calling on the upcoming Congress to advance moratorium legislation on federal public lands within its first 100 days in office. It also wants guardrails in place during development, which include public input, environmental review and tribal consultation. A bipartisan bill slated for a passage vote in the U.S. Senate this week would weaken those protections. Veterans for Public Lands is opening the doors for other veterans to get involved in advocacy work. It is now accepting applications for its Defenders Corps, which trains veterans how to use their voices to help protect and tell the story of America’s public lands. artigo.texto: 2 min leitura Greenvolt constrói projeto solar e de armazenamento de energia nos EUA O projeto, que conta com um investimento de mais de 120 milhões de dólares deverá estar concluído até ao verão de 2028. Este vai ser o maior empreendimento de energia solar e armazenamento em baterias da empresa no país. 25 Nov 2026 - 15:42 2 min leitura A Greenvolt começou a construir um projeto solar combinado com um sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias, num investimento acima de 120 milhões de dólares (109 milhões de euros) no sul dos EUA, divulgou hoje a empresa. “Combinando 100 MWac de produção solar com um sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) de 50 MW [megawatt] / 200 MWh [megawatt-hora], o projeto representa um investimento superior a 120 milhões de dólares (aproximadamente 109 milhões de euros) e constitui um passo importante no desenvolvimento contínuo da atividade da Greenvolt nos Estados Unidos”, refere a empresa em comunicado. No documento, a energética refere que o projeto, denominado Alamogordo, está a ser construído pela Greenvolt Power, empresa do grupo dedicada a projetos de energias renováveis de grande escala. O projeto situa-se no condado de Otero, no estado norte-americano do Novo México e deverá estar totalmente construído até ao verão de 2028, ficando a ser o maior projeto combinado de energia solar e armazenamento de energia em baterias da empresa no país. A Greenvolt acrescenta que assegurou um contrato de aquisição de energia de longo prazo para a venda de eletricidade produzida, garantindo-lhe “receitas contratualizadas e previsibilidade financeira durante um período alargado”. A empresa explica que o sistema de baterias permite armazenar eletricidade “durante um período máximo de quatro horas”, o que possibilitará disponibilizar esta energia produzida durante os períodos de maior produção solar, “maximizando o seu valor e promovendo uma utilização mais flexível das energias renováveis”. Citado no documento, o presidente executivo da Greenvolt, João Manso Neto, garantiu que os EUA vão assumir “um papel cada vez mais importante na concretização do plano de negócios do grupo”, que conta com 341 MW de energia eólica, 686 MW de energia solar e 212 MW de capacidade de armazenamento de energia em baterias. A Greenvolt regista ainda que os trabalhos de engenharia, aprovisionamento e construção são assegurados pela CJR Renewables e pela Dashiell Corporation, estimando criar 370 postos de trabalho durante esta fase. Agência Lusa Editado por Jornal PT Green

artigo.texto: Petrobras avalia extração e refino de minerais críticos para baterias Novo plano de negócios da estatal detalha oportunidades de investimento na cadeia produtiva de baterias, da prospecção mineral à reciclagem A Petrobras avalia investimentos na prospecção, extração e refino de minerais críticos voltados à cadeia produtiva de baterias. A estratégia foi detalhada no Plano de Negócios 2027-2031 da estatal, aprovado na última segunda-feira (23). Embora o interesse da petroleira por minerais críticos não seja novo, a companhia passou a detalhar as etapas da cadeia produtiva em que considera investir, diante da perspectiva de expansão da demanda por veículos elétricos e sistemas de armazenamento de energia. No plano anterior, baterias e minerais críticos figuravam entre as apostas tecnológicas de longo prazo da estatal, dentro de seu portfólio de pesquisa e desenvolvimento. Agora, a Petrobras destaca a “maior valorização de minerais críticos como ativos estratégicos para segurança energética e industrial”. Além das atividades de mineração e refino mineral, a companhia avalia investimentos na montagem de conjuntos de baterias, em sistemas de armazenamento estacionário de energia, infraestrutura de recarga de veículos elétricos, reúso e reciclagem. A montagem de células de baterias, por sua vez, aparece como uma frente de pesquisa e desenvolvimento. A estatal pretende priorizar oportunidades que apresentem maior sinergia com seus negócios no setor energético. A Petrobras também considera favorável o ambiente regulatório brasileiro, citando a recente publicação do decreto que define os minerais críticos e estratégicos para o país, incluindo aqueles utilizados na cadeia de armazenamento de energia. Entre os principais minerais utilizados na fabricação de baterias estão o lítio, o níquel e o grafite, dos quais o Brasil possui reservas relevantes. A eventual entrada da Petrobras nessas atividades faz parte da estratégia de diversificação dos negócios da companhia, que busca ampliar sua atuação em segmentos relacionados à transição energética. O documento, entretanto, não especifica quais minerais deverão ser priorizados pela estatal, nem os valores que poderão ser destinados ao segmento. As oportunidades de investimento ainda estão em fase de avaliação. A possível entrada da Petrobras no setor mineral ocorre em meio a discussões dentro do governo federal sobre a necessidade de ampliar a participação de empresas brasileiras na exploração de minerais críticos e estratégicos. Uma ala do Executivo defende uma atuação mais direta da estatal no segmento, diante do avanço de empresas estrangeiras sobre ativos minerais brasileiros. A preocupação é que o país fique restrito ao fornecimento de matérias-primas, sem capturar parte relevante do valor agregado nas etapas de processamento e industrialização. Em agosto, o presidente do BNDES (Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social), Aloizio Mercadante, defendeu publicamente uma maior participação da Vale e da Petrobras no desenvolvimento das cadeias produtivas de minerais críticos e terras raras no Brasil.

artigo.texto: Legal development Democrats made broad gains nationally on November 3, 2026. For many of the Democratic winners, a key campaign talking point was a commitment to limit or restrict future data center development. Our earlier alert, “Key takeaways for data center developers from the 2026 midterm elections” addressed the national picture. This Legal Development focuses on Texas, where the change in state leadership is likely to have the most immediate consequences for projects already in the pipeline. Developers should prepare for the following: - Utility costs and affordability are likely to drive policy, and Democrats have an opening to act on voter frustration over energy costs. - Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa may inherit ERCOT's pause on energizing new large-load data centers and its delayed Batch Zero classifications and study. TCEQ has stated it has resumed normal permit review. The ambitious platform she has proposed is likely to result in a broader halt soon after inauguration. Her stated scope covers all state permits, including for projects already underway, although the legal mechanism, start date, and duration have not been defined. - Developers should prepare for slower and more searching permit review, even if a formal moratorium does not come to pass. - Grandfathering terms will likely decide which projects go forward, so priority goes to securing power, permits, and site work now. In Texas, the key questions include whether sufficiently complete local permit applications establish vested rights, how the PUCT’s large-load rule applies to projects that had not energized by October 8, 2026, and how 2027 legislation may affect projects already in ERCOT’s Batch Zero study. - Tax exemptions and abatements are at risk, and in Texas, support for repeal crosses party lines; project economics should be tested without them. - As community opposition to data centers accelerates statewide, binding commitments on water, local investment, and transparency, including limits on nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), increasingly decide whether projects move forward. Current state of play: Texas data center directives and key dates Between June and September 2026, Governor Greg Abbott issued four executive directives affecting data center development. On June 10, Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) to pursue measures to protect residential ratepayers from data center-related infrastructure costs, including requiring data centers to pay costs attributable to their electric infrastructure, and directed the PUCT and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) to review their existing authority. On August 3, he directed the PUCT and ERCOT to audit all data centers advancing through ERCOT's interconnection process, requiring information on public financial assistance; power consumption and on-site generation; water consumption, sources, and cooling technology; noise, light, and traffic impacts; and ownership and control. The directive states that any project that fails to comply with PUCT and ERCOT requirements must be denied connection to the grid. For loads of 75 MW or more, the audit overlays ERCOT’s “Batch Zero” process, a one-time, system-wide study under rules the PUCT approved in June that classifies qualifying large-load requests as base load, studied load, or excluded load. ERCOT issued provisional, conditional classifications on September 3, 2026, subject to verification and other conditions. The audit and verification process has affected the timing of Batch Zero classifications and study completion.1 On September 14, Abbott directed the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) to enforce water-use reporting requirements. Noncompliance may result in referral for criminal prosecution and disqualification from obtaining, amending, or renewing Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) water-rights permits under Chapter 11 of the Texas Water Code. On September 21, Abbott directed TCEQ to halt all permits sought by data centers and pause issuance of all permits related to data center projects until ERCOT completes its review. He further directed that no other state agency move forward with regulatory approvals related to data centers until the PUCT, ERCOT, and TWDB information is acquired. In its October 19 compliance update, TCEQ reported that it had paused issuance of all permits related to the construction or development of infrastructure directly supporting data centers, was screening pending applications, and, where possible, was suspending claimed authorizations. TCEQ temporarily shut down its STEERS e-filing portal so that agency staff could review all applications to determine whether they were related to data centers. The STEERS system has now reopened for construction, multi-sector, and concrete production general permits. According to press reports, TCEQ received notice from the governor’s office on November 13 that ERCOT had completed gathering information on potential community impacts from data centers and started normal permit review. On November 16, 2026, TCEQ reportedly issued an air authorization for a gas-fired plant serving planned data centers. Impact of Texas results on data center development In the midterm election, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Governor Greg Abbott, becoming the first Democratic governor of Texas in more than three decades. Democrat Vikki Goodwin defeated Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick, and Democrats won every statewide office on the ballot, including attorney general. Democrats will control the Texas House, while Republicans retain a majority in the Senate. During her campaign, Hinojosa announced a six-point platform for the next legislative session. Governor-Elect Hinojosa’s 'Texans First Data Center Priorities' Status as of November 19, 2026. Planks are campaign proposals; none has been enacted. On October 22, 2026, Hinojosa stated that, as governor, she would issue a moratorium on all data center approvals

artigo.texto: ACME Solar Commissions 63.78 MW Battery Storage Project in Rajasthan; Shares Rise 0.17% Authored By HDFC SKY | Last Modified: Nov 26, 2026 10:07 AM IST ACME Solar Holdings Limited has commissioned 63.78 MW/255.12 MWh of discharge capacity from its Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project in Jaisalmer, Rajasthan. The project, developed through its wholly owned subsidiary ACME Hybrid Urja Private Limited, forms part of a larger 280 MW/1,120 MWh storage component associated with an NHPC power project. Commercial operations for the commissioned capacity are scheduled to begin on November 27, 2026. ACME Solar shares traded marginally higher during morning trading on November 26. Open Free Demat Account Mumbai, November 26: ACME Solar Holdings Limited has announced the commissioning of 63.78 MW/255.120 MWh of discharge capacity under its Battery Energy Storage System project in Rajasthan. The capacity was commissioned on November 25, 2026, through its wholly owned subsidiary, ACME Hybrid Urja Private Limited. The project is part of the NHPC Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE) Power Project in Jaisalmer district. artigo.texto: Exceção dos EUA não garante chips para data center do TikTok no Ceará Restrições já afetam financiamento de 480 milhões de dólares ligado à ByteDance na Ásia O governo dos Estados Unidos abriu uma exceção nas novas restrições à tecnologia de inteligência artificial que pode beneficiar o TikTok, mas deixou de fora uma questão decisiva para o data center de mais de 200 bilhões de reais que a chinesa ByteDance pretende instalar no Ceará: a importação de semicondutores avançados. A regulamentação americana, publicada em 19 de novembro, permite determinadas operações de computação destinadas exclusivamente a sistemas comerciais de recomendação de conteúdo, como os algoritmos utilizados por redes sociais. A exceção, entretanto, não representa uma autorização irrestrita para a compra de chips e servidores. O empreendimento brasileiro continua sujeito às exigências de licenciamento aplicáveis aos equipamentos abrangidos pela norma. A distinção aparece no texto da regulamentação do Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), órgão do Departamento de Comércio responsável pelos controles de exportação. Uma das disposições permite que empresas forneçam capacidade computacional para sistemas que classificam, filtram ou recomendam conteúdos e produtos a usuários, desde que essa seja sua finalidade exclusiva e sejam cumpridas obrigações de comunicação às autoridades americanas. A proteção não se estende a sistemas capazes de produzir textos, imagens, vídeos, softwares e outros conteúdos por meio de inteligência artificial generativa. Outro dispositivo estabelece, de forma independente, a necessidade de licença para exportar determinados semicondutores avançados para cinco países, incluindo o Brasil. Na prática, mesmo um sistema enquadrado na exceção para recomendação de conteúdo poderá depender de autorizações adicionais para receber equipamentos. A dúvida é particularmente relevante para o complexo em construção no Pecém, desenvolvido pela Omnia, do Pátria Investimentos, em parceria com a Casa dos Ventos, para atender à ByteDance. Anunciado como o primeiro data center do TikTok na América Latina, o empreendimento prevê investimentos superiores a 200 bilhões de reais ao longo de suas etapas de implantação e modernização, incluindo 108 bilhões de reais em equipamentos de alta tecnologia até 2035. A primeira fase deverá entrar em operação em 2027. Conforme revelou o Radar Econômico na sexta-feira, 20, a estrutura logística planejada contempla até 15 voos mensais com equipamentos destinados ao complexo. A possibilidade de que parte desses componentes dependa de autorizações americanas introduz uma incerteza sobre o cronograma de implantação. Os efeitos das restrições já começaram a aparecer em outro empreendimento ligado à ByteDance. Segundo reportagem da Bloomberg, bancos interromperam os trabalhos de estruturação de um financiamento de 480 milhões de dólares destinado à compra de processadores avançados da Nvidia para um data center na Malásia que atenderia à companhia chinesa. A operação estava sendo organizada pela Aolani Cloud, de Singapura. De acordo com pessoas familiarizadas com as negociações, representantes de cinco instituições financeiras passaram a discutir a possibilidade de abandonar ou deixar de participar do empréstimo diante do risco de descumprimento das novas regras americanas. O episódio não demonstra que o investimento brasileiro tenha sofrido restrições semelhantes, mas revela que a mudança regulatória já produz consequências concretas para projetos associados à empresa. O alcance das medidas vai além do transporte físico de semicondutores. Washington pretende impedir que empresas sediadas na China tenham acesso a grandes volumes de processamento americano por meio de data centers instalados em terceiros países. A regulamentação exige verificações sobre os beneficiários da capacidade computacional, incluindo estruturas de propriedade e controle indireto. Para o projeto do Ceará, isso torna relevante não apenas a origem dos equipamentos, mas também a finalidade de sua utilização, a capacidade de processamento instalada e as empresas que terão acesso aos servidores. A eventual utilização de modelos de inteligência artificial generativa poderá resultar em exigências diferentes daquelas aplicáveis exclusivamente aos algoritmos de recomendação. A ByteDance foi questionada pelo Radar Econômico sobre a finalidade específica dos sistemas previstos para o Pecém, a possibilidade de utilização da exceção americana, a necessidade de licenças para importação de chips e eventuais mudanças no calendário de implantação. A companhia também foi procurada para esclarecer se os equipamentos da primeira fase já foram contratados e se as entregas dependem de autorizações dos Estados Unidos. Até a conclusão desta versão, não havia respondido aos questionamentos. A definição será importante para determinar se o investimento brasileiro encontrará uma alternativa dentro das próprias regras americanas ou se precisará atravessar um processo adicional de aprovação para colocar seus servidores em funcionamento.

artigo.texto: A expansão das fontes fotovoltaica e eólica na última década diversificou os modais do setor elétrico brasileiro (SEB), historicamente organizado em torno das hidrelétricas. Desse crescimento, porém, deriva o desafio de compatibilizar a geração de eletricidade a partir de fontes não despacháveis à flexibilidade do sistema, sem a qual a assincronia entre oferta de energia e oscilações de consumo exige cortes na geração. Chamados de curtailment, os cortes no sistema interligado nacional passaram de 18 TWh em 2024 para 58 TWh em 2025, segundo o ONS. O mesmo país que investe pesadamente na ampliação da oferta de energia restringiu cerca de 20% da geração potencial solar e eólica no ano passado. Neste cenário, os sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias (Bess), assumem protagonismo no SEB. Eles guardam energia nos períodos de excedente, fornecendo-a nos horários de maior demanda. Desempenham parte das funções de flexibilidade associadas aos reservatórios hidrelétricos e às termelétricas. Enquanto a Lei Federal nº 15.269/2025 garantiu reconhecimento institucional aos sistemas de armazenamento, a Portaria MME nº 136/2026 balizou as regras para os leilões de reserva de capacidade previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro deste ano, criando condições para uma grande expansão do Bess no futuro próximo. Avanços contrastam com regras ambientais ainda em fase embrionária Diante disto, muitos agentes setoriais se apegam à crença de que o licenciamento do Bess será “simples” porquanto sua potencial associação a empreendimentos preexistentes reduziria a extensão das intervenções necessárias à implantação da nova tecnologia. Mesmo admitida a possibilidade de instalação do Bess em áreas antropizadas, os critérios adotados pelas oito unidades da federação que já regularam o enquadramento ambiental da tecnologia impõem limites às expectativas de simplicidade. Piauí e Rio Grande do Sul adotam a área útil, mas classificam o potencial poluidor como médio e baixo, respectivamente, e estabelecem limites distintos de não incidência de licenciamento. Bahia e Pará utilizam a potência; Ceará e Rio Grande do Norte, a capacidade de armazenamento. Goiás e Rio de Janeiro incluem baterias em categorias que também abrangem subestações. Em São Paulo e Minas Gerais, como na maioria dos estados, não foram identificados critérios de enquadramento para o Bess. Não surpreende, portanto, que as primeiras licenças ambientais emitidas para os sistemas de armazenamento de energia abranjam diferentes modalidades. Na Bahia, em julho de 2025, uma licença de alteração incluiu o sistema de armazenamento no Complexo Fotovoltaico Cedro. Em novembro do mesmo ano, o Rio Grande do Sul concedeu licenças prévias e de instalação unificadas aos Bess Pontal e Lagoa, vinculados a complexos eólicos. No dia 27 daquele mês, o Piauí emitiu licença prévia ao Bess Lagoa do Barro Associado, enquadrado em tipologia específica. Esses casos, além de contrariarem a doce ilusão de que a instalação das baterias em áreas intervindas afastaria automaticamente a incidência do rito ordinário, indicam que o Bess não será absorvido de modo homogêneo pelos órgãos licenciadores brasileiros. Os arranjos distintos (autônomo ou integrado) ajudam a explicar essa heterogeneidade, mas a ausência de diretrizes nacionais específicas pode submeter até mesmo projetos comparáveis a exigências severamente desiguais. Normatização do licenciamento do Bess aponta para modelo híbrido Sistemas diretamente associados a usinas solares, parques eólicos ou instalações de transmissão tendem a ser licenciados de forma integrada ao empreendimento principal, enquanto projetos standalone, especialmente aqueles voltados à oferta de potência e à prestação de outros serviços ao sistema, tendem ao enquadramento autônomo. A questão se torna particularmente sensível porque a expansão do Bess e a construção das regras ambientais específicas para a tecnologia coincidem com a reformulação do próprio licenciamento pela Lei Federal nº 15.190/2025. Com dispositivos do novo marco questionados no STF, os vultosos investimentos previstos para o Bess estão à mercê de algum grau de insegurança jurídica. Há, por fim, uma dimensão material que não pode ser subestimada. Baterias de íons de lítio apresentam riscos ambientais concretos (thermal runaway, incêndio e vazamento químico) e, após sua vida útil, tornam-se resíduos que exigem logística reversa, reciclagem e reprocessamento industrial. Essa estrutura permanece frágil no Brasil. O debate setorial avançou mais na dimensão operacional que na construção de uma cadeia robusta de pós-uso para baterias de grande porte. Assim, o desafio do licenciamento alcança tanto o Bess quanto a infraestrutura necessária ao tratamento e à destinação de suas baterias.

artigo.texto: By Staff Reporter | A new data center planning to break ground in Cochise County next year is facing some resistance from Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes. Mayes asked county officials to delay their Dec. 9 vote on Tombstone Resources, the company name used to request a special use permit for Cochise SuperComputer Campus, a proposed SpaceX data center. The attorney general advised the Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission to provide the residents of the county with more answers on the project prior to deciding whether or not to grant SpaceX a special use permit. In a request letter to the commission, Mayes echoed the estimate that the proposed data center would consume an energy equivalent to nearly 20% of the state’s total power generating capacity. “SpaceX’s proposal raises serious questions about energy reliability, water use, emergency response capabilities, traffic impacts, and more,” said Mayes. Mayes advised the officials that the scope of these concerns warranted full examination from state and federal agencies prior to local approval. SpaceX promised to contribute $50 billion in the region’s essential local services, public education, infrastructure, and other undisclosed public goods. The company also stated that it would complete a biological and special-status species assessment before breaking ground. According to SpaceX, the data center campus was designed to not disrupt the natural migratory patterns for sandhill cranes — Cochise County is a recognized wintering area for these birds — and that their company would survey for nesting birds, raptors, and burrowing owls. In conversations with Frank Antenori, chair of the Cochise County Board of Supervisors, SpaceX reiterated their promise to spend $3.6 billion to upgrade the power grid, not rely on groundwater to run the facility, and adhere to the county’s rules on light pollution. SpaceX says the campus will rely on closed-loop cooling, a dry-cooled system with no evaporation spray. Antenori told AZ Family that SpaceX estimated the data center would bring “about 1,000 jobs,” around half only requiring a high school diploma or GED, in addition to 1,500 secondary jobs. SpaceX projects that the data center will bring up to $103 million in new annual property tax revenue, and up to $250 million in a one-time county sales tax benefit. The company also projected a 10% to 40% decrease in electricity bills for all Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative members for the life of the data center development, and an additional annual benefit to those members of approximately $260 million to be used for residential bill relief, the Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative Foundation, and new capital credits for all members. If approved, the data center would become one of the largest in existence in the U.S. It would take up approximately 750 acres of land to house nine supercomputing buildings, each around 500,000 square feet. SpaceX appears confident that the county will approve its special use permit request. Their webpage reports that construction will begin in 2027. Mayes announced a town hall for residents to discuss the proposed data center, scheduled for Thursday, Dec. 3 from 5:30 to 7 p.m. AZ Free News is your #1 source for Arizona news and politics. artigo.texto: A expansão dos data centers voltados à inteligência artificial (IA) exige soluções que reduzam o tempo de conexão à rede elétrica e ampliem a capacidade de processamento sem aumentar a ocupação das instalações. Nesse contexto, uma nova plataforma de energia de média tensão foi desenvolvida para atuar diretamente no ponto de conexão com as concessionárias, reunindo proteção elétrica, estabilização de cargas e continuidade de fornecimento em um único sistema. CONTEÚDO RELACIONADO – Vertiv propõe modelo para levar projetos de IA à produção O Vertiv PowerNexus MV UPS, apresentado pela Vertiv em 19 de novembro, foi projetado para instalações de colocation, neocloud e hiperescala. Com estrutura para instalação externa, o equipamento transfere parte da infraestrutura de energia para fora do data hall, preservando o espaço interno para servidores e sistemas de computação. A plataforma combina um sistema de alimentação ininterrupta (UPS) de média tensão com recursos de ride-through, que permitem suportar distúrbios e falhas temporárias na rede elétrica, e suavização das variações de carga provocadas pelas operações de inteligência artificial. Segundo a fabricante, o sistema alcança eficiência operacional de pico de até 98,5%. Quando integrado a baterias de longa duração, pode oferecer até quatro horas de alimentação de backup, reduzindo a dependência de geradores a diesel. Entre as funcionalidades está a proteção de cargas críticas com qualidade de tensão Classe 1, conforme a norma IEC 62040-3. A solução também foi projetada para absorver variações rápidas de demanda dos sistemas de IA antes que elas sejam transmitidas à rede elétrica, contribuindo para a estabilidade do fornecimento. A arquitetura em skid, fornecida como um conjunto integrado, busca simplificar a instalação e reduzir a necessidade de coordenação entre diferentes fornecedores de UPS, baterias e demais componentes da infraestrutura de energia. A empresa também disponibiliza um modelo de simulação PSCAD para avaliar o comportamento do sistema e sua interação com a rede elétrica antes da implantação. Testes de desempenho A plataforma passou por demonstrações de prova de conceito com a participação de QTS, SoftBank e Rosendin no Centro Global de Pesquisa e Desenvolvimento de Energia e Experiência do Cliente da Vertiv, em Bolonha, na Itália. De acordo com a fabricante, os testes demonstraram estabilidade em cargas de 0% a 100%, precisão de tensão Classe 1 durante mudanças rápidas de demanda e capacidade de suportar distúrbios elétricos. Entre as condições avaliadas estavam uma queda total de tensão por 150 milissegundos e uma sobretensão de 25% durante cinco segundos. A Vertiv também anunciou a criação de um laboratório dedicado a sistemas de média tensão em Bolonha, com previsão de entrada em operação em 2027. A instalação será utilizada para pesquisa e desenvolvimento, testes em tensão plena, treinamento e validação de arquiteturas de energia, incluindo sistemas de média tensão, conversão para 800 VDC e armazenamento em baterias.
