artigo.texto: A Comissão Federal de Comunicações dos Estados Unidos (FCC) autorizou nesta quarta-feira (25) a SpaceX, empresa aeroespacial de Elon Musk, a implantar uma constelação de até 1 milhão de satélites equipados para funcionar como data centers em órbita terrestre. É a primeira vez, na história do país, que o regulador aprova uma constelação desse tipo. A constelação se chamará Starmind e será alimentada por energia solar. O objetivo é ampliar a capacidade de processamento para a inteligência artificial e reduzir o consumo de recursos terrestres. Os equipamentos vão processar grandes quantidades de dados no espaço, mas continuarão atendendo a demandas na Terra. A proposta da empresa é aproveitar a energia solar e o espaço disponível em órbita para diminuir o consumo de água e eletricidade das instalações tradicionais. O presidente da FCC, Brendan Carr, disse que a decisão abre uma nova fronteira tecnológica. Segundo a FCC, o projeto deve ajudar a atender à demanda crescente por capacidade de processamento. Cada satélite terá capacidade computacional média de 175 quilowatts, podendo alcançar 250 quilowatts. Os equipamentos terão a função de processar dados utilizados no planeta. A autorização é válida até 2040, segundo documento publicado no site do órgão regulador. A liberação não garante o lançamento imediato dos satélites, que depende do cumprimento de etapas e prazos exigidos pela FCC. A SpaceX conta com foguetes próprios, que já realizaram centenas de missões.

artigo.texto: The transaction secures capital against contracted, insured delivery of durable removals, proof that high-integrity projects can now access scalable debt beyond equity. State of Sao Paulo, Brazil--(Newsfile Corp. - November 24, 2026) - InPlanet and Idemitsu Americas Holdings (IAH), a wholly owned subsidiary of Idemitsu Kosan (Idemitsu), today announced the closing of one of the first non-recourse project financings in the Enhanced Rock Weathering (ERW) sector. InPlanet and Idemitsu Americas Holdings Close Non-Recourse Debt Facility, Setting a New Standard for Financing ERW Carbon Removal. To view an enhanced version of this graphic, please visit: https://images.newsfilecorp.com/files/8814/324893_f9020ca7c4c68ba6_002full.jpg The debt facility will fund the delivery of more than 28,500 tonnes of contracted Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) and is structured to be repeatable, providing a template for how institutional capital can finance verified CDR at scale. Financing Carbon Removal at Scale Gigaton-scale carbon removal requires financing that can scale deployment beyond equity alone. This agreement was designed to do that, with downside protection backed by an existing carbon removal agreement to remove more than 28,500 tonnes of CO₂ between 2026 and 2028. The financing also includes carbon delivery insurance provided by CFC, covering specified project delivery risks for a defined portion of the delivery. CFC is a specialist insurance provider supporting high-quality carbon market transactions, and the Howden Broking Group provided broking service to InPlanet for this transaction. The financing decision was supported by InPlanet's operating track record, including more than 200,000 tonnes of silicate rock applied across Brazilian farmland. This delivery is enabled by Bedrock OS, InPlanet's AI-powered operating infrastructure, which supports project execution across its portfolio and consolidates logistics, farm, and laboratory data into auditable records for reporting. Each project strengthens the underlying dataset and AI models used to optimize delivery and scale ERW. To view an enhanced version of this graphic, please visit: https://images.newsfilecorp.com/files/8814/324893_f9020ca7c4c68ba6_003full.jpg By linking capital to contracted demand, insured delivery, and the operational infrastructure required to execute at scale, the structure demonstrates how high-integrity carbon removal can be financed like infrastructure and replicated across projects, regions, and buyers as the market matures. For Idemitsu, the partnership forms part of a broader strategy to expand its role in carbon markets as it works toward a carbon-neutral society by 2050. As global demand grows for permanent, measurable, and verifiable removal solutions, Idemitsu is deepening its engagement with durable CDR pathways, with ERW emerging as an area of focus due to its potential for scale. "InPlanet's work in Brazil combines scientific rigor with real operating scale, which is what durable carbon removal needs in order to move beyond pilots,"said Masanori Abe, President of Idemitsu Americas Holdings Corporation." By linking capital to contracted demand and insured delivery, this agreement demonstrates a financing approach we expect to be repeatable. IAH looks forward to building on it as we expand our CDR business." Today, InPlanet operates Brazil's largest ERW program by farmland treated, with access to more than 100,000 hectares through its partners. Working with farmers nationwide, InPlanet applies finely ground silicate rock to agricultural land, accelerating a natural process that permanently captures atmospheric carbon while restoring soil fertility, reducing chemical input costs, and strengthening long-term farm profitability. In December 2024, InPlanet delivered the world's first independently verified ERW carbon removal credits, which subsequently received a post-issuance "A" rating from BeZero Carbon. "In just two years, we went from delivering the world's first independently verified enhanced rock weathering credits to operating the largest ERW program in Brazil. This financing with Idemitsu takes that work to its next level, it shows that carbon removal grounded in solid science can also be financed like real infrastructure," said Felix Harteneck, Founder & CEO of InPlanet. "For us, this is about more than capital. Japan is continuing to develop its carbon market and standards for high-integrity carbon removal, and we look forward to contributing to that dialogue." Compliance Demand in Japan and Brazil Idemitsu and InPlanet will focus on markets where climate ambition and carbon market infrastructure are advancing in step. Japan is continuing to develop its carbon market framework and policies supporting high-integrity carbon removal. Any future use of ERW credits would remain subject to applicable methodologies, regulations, and eligibility requirements. In Brazil, Law 15.042/2024 established the SBCE (Brazilian Greenhouse Gas Emissions Trading System), putting removals on the same legal footing as avoided emissions. Both markets are opening compliance pathways for durable carbon removal, creating long-term, regulated demand for credits that have until now relied almost entirely on voluntary buyers. artigo.texto: CHAMPAIGN — A proposed development just east of the Interstate 57/74 interchange that includes a solar farm, battery storage systems and two small data centers has attracted the concern of a nearby business owner. “It’s an eyesore for one thing, but it’s also a danger,” said Judy Parkinson, co-owner of Research Press Publishers. “The data centers and the batteries are my big concern. Those are not the kind of thing you should have in such a close-to-the-city area. If they did it out in the countryside, it wouldn’t bother me.” She fears that the battery energy storage systems could be a fire hazard that might impact her business if a blaze breaks out. IAG Investments — Champaign Mattis LLC, which is managed by Anthony Donato, seeks to develop approximately 30 acres of vacant land at 2703 N. Mattis Ave. into an industrial site that includes “flex warehouses and a solar farm with accessory battery energy storage systems,” said city of Champaign Associate Planner Mia Trevino. As previously reported by The News-Gazette’s Kathy Reiser, Anthony Donato and Donato Solar have developed several other solar arrays with data farms in and around Champaign-Urbana in recent years. The solar farms are run by Donato Solar and the data centers are operated by Gail Technology. Anthony Donato founded the former company and is the owner of the latter. “The proposed site plan includes five commercial flex warehouses with 3,000 square feet of data centers in proposed Buildings 1 and 5 that are 1.2 (megawatts), approximately 60 percent of the respective buildings’ area,” Trevino wrote in a report to the plan commission. “The performance standards for data centers require a minimum 200-foot setback from residential zone property and are maintained in the proposed site plan. Given that the property is primarily surrounded by interstate right-of-way, and adjacent to industrial and commercial use, a power generation facility would be appropriate at this site.” Peyton Childress, who spoke on behalf of the applicant at a recent plan commission meeting, said that the proposed development is a “behind-the-meter” solar project, with the power generated being used by the buildings on-site. “It will cover all of the energy needed for those five buildings, especially with the batteries on-site, because then during times where the sun is not out, then all of the stored energy from that solar array will be housed in the units of the battery and then can still power the facility itself,” she said. “So any excess energy we’re going to be storing in the battery containers and then we’ll use on-site. So no, I don’t foresee that we will be needing excess energy.” The five battery containers will be located behind the warehouses and out of sight of any potential tenants, she noted. “They do all have fire-suppression systems built in,” Childress said. “There’s a multitude of sensors that send warnings if any element of the container gets too hot, things like that.” According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, there have been lithium battery fires at some battery energy storage system (BESS) facilities. Such fires are very hard to put out and may reignite “hours or days later,” EPA officials said. These blazes can also release harmful gases. “Communities should also note that despite some high-profile incidents, improvements in BESS quality and design have led to a decrease in the number of failure incidents per gigawatt hour deployed,” the agency said. Planning and Development Director Bruce Knight said that fire safety is evaluated as part of the building permit review process. The fire department “has already looked at this development proposal and signed off on it with the assumption that it’ll comply with all building and fire codes,” he added. The subject property is located west of and across the street from 2612 N. Mattis Ave., where Research Press is based. Parkinson co-owns the book-publishing business with her brother and sister; the land on which the business sits is also owned by the family. In addition to fire safety, her other concerns include the facility’s proximity to residences east of her business and potential noise pollution. “They say that sometimes the data centers get noisy because of the cooling,” Parkinson said. Childress told the plan commission that the buildings will be “temperature-controlled.” “A lot of people are worried about water consumption as well, if that’s how we cool any of the server pods — none of that will be taking place here,” she said. “Any water on site would be bathroom or kitchen at inside of the commercial space. So these (data centers) would all be cooled by the temperature-controlled building.” She also noted that the developer will put in the vegetation screening that is required by the city. The proposed project comes as larger data-center developments have come under scrutiny. For instance, an advisory question on the April 6 ballot will ask Champaign County residents if the county should “support the development of large and/or hyperscale data centers, defined as larger than 10 megawatts of total power, within Champaign County.” The county currently has a moratorium on the development of data centers with “at least 10,000 square feet of processing area”; the ban is set to end in April. “They’re only 1.2 megawatts,” Trevino said of the data centers in the proposed project. “People usually consider a normal-size data center to be between 5 to 10 megawatts. Hyperscale’s more like starting at 100 megawatts. So really, this (project) could be seen more as a server room than what we think of as a data center.” Knight later added that the city is looking to impose a one-year moratorium on data centers over 10 megawatts so that staff can research the issue and develop ordinances. He expects the city council to vote on the one-year moratorium on Dec. 15. “Over 10 megawatts, based on our research, is where they start to have any kind of external impacts,” he said. artigo.texto: Virginia stands at a crossroads on data center development. The choice need not be simply between unrestricted growth and a statewide moratorium. A more prudent path is to approve projects when their risks are understood and safeguards can be enforced, while allowing targeted, conditional pauses where essential questions remain unanswered and the government has authority to act. Localities are already taking different approaches. Loudoun County now requires special exceptions in several districts where data centers had been allowed by right. Fairfax County strengthened setbacks and noise protections while retaining some by-right development. These differences matter because every project affects a particular community. But electricity, water, transportation and environmental impacts do not necessarily stop at local boundaries. That leaves Virginia with a larger question: Should development continue under existing rules, be broadly halted or be evaluated project by project using evidence and enforceable conditions? Policy and law makers should consider taking a more comprehensive approach in developing the state’s regulatory framework. The commonwealth’s own research demonstrates why careful evaluation is warranted. The Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission’s 2024 study, “Data Centers in Virginia,” found substantial economic benefits, especially from construction, and significant local tax revenues. It also projected immense growth in electricity demand and identified risks involving infrastructure costs, water use and residential impacts. A subsequent JLARC report released this month estimated that the state received 22 cents in tax revenue for each dollar of the data center sales tax exemption during fiscal years 2021 through 2025, reflecting revised assumptions about how strongly exemptions influence location decisions. Statewide findings, however, cannot determine whether a particular facility belongs on a particular site. That requires examining projected electricity demand, water supply, cooling technology, backup generation, noise, traffic and proximity to homes and schools. A cooling-system label alone cannot establish total resource demands. Virginia has also begun strengthening its regulatory framework. The State Corporation Commission approved Dominion Energy’s GS-5 rate class, effective Jan. 1, for large-load customers meeting specified thresholds. Minimum-demand provisions can reduce risks to other ratepayers, but they cannot eliminate every possibility of cost shifting. Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s Executive Order 22, issued Sept. 18, directs work on community planning, noise protections, cooling-water scarcity, backup-generation impacts, energy affordability and grid reliability. But a directive to develop a regulation or evaluate a problem is not the same as a completed, enforceable safeguard. That distinction matters when communities are deciding whether a project should proceed. Responsible oversight should therefore cover a data center’s entire life cycle. Before approval, officials should evaluate the site, design and cumulative demands on electricity, water, roads and public services. During construction and operation, measurable standards should be backed by reporting, enforcement and corrective action. Planning should also address future expansion, upgrades, closure and potential long-term public liabilities. This is especially important in regions such as western Tidewater and Hampton Roads, where communities share natural resources and infrastructure. Local decisions can have regional consequences. Virginia does not have to choose between technological investment and responsible governance. It can welcome development while insisting on credible evidence, fair allocation of costs, regional coordination and enforceable protections. When critical information is missing, pausing long enough to get the answers is not opposition to progress. It is responsible public policy. Charles W. “Bill” Robinson of Carrollton is a retired U.S. Army officer and civilian employee for the Department of Defense. He has experience with artificial intelligence, data architectures and operational implications.

artigo.texto: India's L&T wins battery storage order in Gujarat In a November 25 filing with the stock exchange, Larsen & Toubro LT (BSE: 500510), the Indian engineering conglomerate, disclosed that it has landed an order for a 300 MW/900 MWh battery storage installation in Khavda, located in Gujarat in the country's west. The facility will soak up excess electricity from renewable sources when output runs high and return it to the grid when consumption peaks. According to the company, this will allow more clean power to be absorbed into India's electricity network while making supply steadier and more dependable. The filing did not name the client or give the exact contract value. The order was won jointly by L&T Electronic Products & Systems (LTEPS) and the company's renewable energy unit, two divisions of the group. Offering 900 MWh of energy capacity alongside 300 MW of power output, the facility can run at maximum output for three hours. According to the filing, the system will rely on liquid cooling, an approach it anticipates will raise power density, improve safety and extend the installation's operating lifespan. L&T said the contract would bolster its standing in the energy storage business. The company added that the award showed clients were confident it could carry out large and complex projects. The Mumbai-based group describes itself as a $32bn multinational working across Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) projects, high-tech manufacturing, products and services in several countries. It has led its main business lines for eight decades, according to the filing.

artigo.texto: PL das baterias pode aumentar conta de luz em R$ 6,2 bi, diz entidade Frente dos Consumidores estima custo de cerca de R$ 94 bilhões em 15 anos e critica proposta que transfere aos consumidores despesas hoje atribuídas aos geradores O projeto de lei das baterias poderá acrescentar até R$ 6,26 bilhões por ano à conta de luz dos consumidores, segundo estimativa da FNCE (Frente Nacional dos Consumidores de Energia). O PL 3.716/2026 tramita em regime de urgência na Câmara dos Deputados e propõe mudar a divisão dos custos da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia. De acordo com a entidade, a despesa poderia chegar a cerca de R$ 94 bilhões ao longo dos 15 anos previstos para os contratos dos leilões de baterias marcados para dezembro. O valor anual corresponde à estimativa de receita fixa que seria cobrada dos consumidores por meio do ERCap (Encargo de Reserva de Capacidade) para remunerar os sistemas contratados. O levantamento da FNCE considerou os preços-teto previstos nos editais e utilizou projeções da EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética) como referência para estimar possíveis contratações de até 5 gigawatts (GW). O custo efetivo dependerá do volume contratado e dos preços obtidos nas disputas. A Lei 15.269/2025 estabeleceu que os custos da contratação de reserva de capacidade por meio de baterias devem ser rateados apenas entre os geradores de energia, conforme regulamentação da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). O projeto propõe retirar essa exclusividade, permitindo que a despesa seja dividida entre os consumidores. planalto.gov.br Para a FNCE, a mudança atingiria inclusive consumidores atendidos por distribuidoras que contratam majoritariamente energia de hidrelétricas e termelétricas. Na avaliação da frente, esses consumidores passariam a pagar por uma necessidade associada à intermitência de fontes como a solar e a eólica. O presidente da FNCE, Luiz Eduardo Barata, afirma que cabe aos geradores arcar com a contratação por considerar que eles são responsáveis pela necessidade de armazenamento. Segundo ele, a transferência da despesa para todos os consumidores pressionaria a inflação e elevaria a conta de luz, especialmente das famílias atendidas por distribuidoras com maior participação de hidrelétricas e térmicas em seus contratos. A Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias) entrou na Justiça contra lei que impõe os custos. A entidade também pediu a suspensão dos dois leilões de reserva de capacidade. A FNCE, por outro lado, defende a manutenção do cronograma dos leilões e classifica como irresponsáveis as tentativas de suspensão das disputas. “Atrasar o leilão pode comprometer o enfrentamento dos cortes de energia e dificultar o equilíbrio do sistema. Não há justificativa técnica ou econômica para mudar o cronograma”, disse Barata, em nota. Os dois leilões estão previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro, com contratos de 15 anos e início do suprimento em 1º de agosto de 2028. Ao aprovar os editais, a Aneel informou que os custos seriam rateados apenas entre os geradores, conforme a legislação vigente.

artigo.texto: The Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX’s request to launch 1 million AI-equipped satellites to create vast data centers in space. SpaceX initially filed an application in May asking for permission to launch the satellites, collectively known as Starmind. The FCC’s approval requires that SpaceX launch its first data center satellite by 2030 and meet the 1 million mark by 2040. “It’s just really abrogating their responsibility to go, ‘Well, this is a project they’re proposing. Is this actually safe?’” Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist who tracks satellite launches, told CNET. “It’s a blank check. Launch as many satellites as you can, and we’ll just see what happens. I think this is a mistake on the FCC’s part.” More from CNET Orbital data centers have long been a goal of SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, becoming a pivotal part of his pitch to investors ahead of the company’s IPO in June. “You’re power-constrained on Earth. Space has the advantage that it’s always sunny,” Musk said in March. On its web page for Starmind, SpaceX touts its high-efficiency solar arrays on the planned satellites and the cooling benefits of space. It says that high-speed laser links will beam the AI results back to Earth through Starlink’s constellation. Space experts I’ve talked to this year about Starmind have been skeptical. The technical challenges alone are dizzying; the scale of SpaceX’s ambitions is hard to swallow. It’s taken seven years for Starlink to grow its constellation to 11,195 satellites, and that was already an unprecedented feat. Is it possible to get to 1 million satellites in 14 years? “We do not have the launch capacity for any of this,” Ian Christensen, senior director at the Secure World Foundation, told me in a previous interview. “Not even within SpaceX to do their own constellation, let alone the other constellations planned.” SpaceX has increasingly prioritized launching its own satellites instead of letting commercial customers hitch a ride on their rockets. Starlink’s share of SpaceX missions has gone from 54% of its Falcon 9 rocket’s missions in 2020 to about 79% in 2026, according to a Reuters analysis. One analysis estimates that SpaceX would have to launch 5,000 Starship rockets a year to meet its goal — a staggering increase from 330 rockets that launched last year in total. Scientists have already been ringing alarm bells about overcrowded orbits as they exist now. The more satellites in space, the more difficult it is for operators to maneuver around each other. A single crash could turn into decades of orbital debris, which could cause a chain reaction that eventually makes space inoperable for everyone. And burning up all those satellites in the atmosphere when they reach the end of their lives has already started to leave ozone-depleting aluminum particles behind. A paper published this week in Earth and Space Chemistry estimated that SpaceX’s data center plan would multiply pollutants in the upper atmosphere by more than 150 times compared to last year. “There are scientific papers out there raising issues,” McDowell said. “Yes, they’re unproven, but if I say, ‘Yeah, we’re not sure if this is going to destroy the atmosphere and kill us all, but it might,’ is the right reaction to go, ‘Well, you haven’t proven it, so we’re just going to ignore it’?” The FCC’s approval came despite objections from Amazon, the environmental nonprofit Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility and the American Astronomical Society. A representative for SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

artigo.texto: Group says data center neighbors should receive direct financial benefits MONTGOMERY, Ala. (WSFA) - A group that creates community benefit packages says people who live near data centers should receive a direct share of the profits as opposition to data centers grows. Meta is expanding its data center in Montgomery. In Lowndes County, residents packed city hall to oppose Project Red Clay. Benefit package proposal Janine Yorio of Community Digital Technologies said cities typically require something beneficial for the community in return for data center construction. She argued those long-term benefits do not always help everyone. “Data centers are not the most beautiful buildings in the world, but they also aren’t puffing out black smoke and creating traffic jams either,” Yorio said. “They are something that does bring a form of prosperity. And if the developers can figure out a way to transfer some of that prosperity locally, it can do a lot for a community.” Community Digital Technologies does not work directly with data centers or the people who oppose them. Yorio said the group creates and administers a benefits package. “So if people get something that looks like a credit card, and the credit card has the benefits on it, you can spend it,” Yorio said. “And it’s tied to when the data center opens. So obviously, both sides have to see both. They have to agree, and then they have to allow the data center to be built in the local neighborhood.” Yorio said making that kind of deal standard could turn data centers from a source of mistrust into a new stream of local prosperity. She said it would require buy-in from companies and local leaders. Meta said it has invested more than $1.5 billion in Montgomery. Cloverleaf, the developer behind Project Red Clay, has pledged up to $10 million to support Lowndes County. Residents respond Some Lowndes County neighbors said no amount of money can address their biggest concerns. “Do we feel there’s a need for money to come our way? Absolutely we do,” said John Urquhart, a Lowndes County resident. “If it drops in my backyard and my property values go away, we absolutely need to be compensated for that. But money’s not going to change the air quality issues, the noise pollution, the light pollution. Money’s not going to take care of any of that.” Urquhart said compensation would not change his outlook on the project. He cited air quality concerns related to diesel generators at operating data centers, as well as potential water contamination. Urquhart said he and his wife own 230 acres in the county. He said property values are falling and that some properties listed for sale in the area have not been viewed since they went on the market. Two Lowndes County women who are suing the Lowndes County Commission over Project Red Clay, a planned data center, are due back in court Dec. 2. Not reading this story on the WSFA News App? artigo.texto: Forest Grove considers new restrictions on data centers near schools and homes How close should a data center be allowed to operate near a school or someone's home? That's one of the questions Forest Grove city leaders will consider Monday night as they work toward new restrictions on future developments. The Forest Grove City Council and Planning Commission will hold a joint work session at 6 p.m. Monday, Nov. 23, to discuss proposed changes to the city's development code. Among the ideas under consideration are requiring greater distances between data centers and nearby neighborhoods, restricting where the facilities can be built and placing additional limits on their operations. The discussion comes more than a month after the city temporarily stopped accepting applications for new data center developments, giving officials time to examine potential impacts on residents, infrastructure and industrial land. While the proposed regulations could change where future data centers are allowed, they also raise another question: What happens to projects that have already received approval? City considers 1,000-foot buffer around schools During an earlier work session on Nov. 9, city planners presented possible restrictions that included a 1,000-foot buffer between data centers and schools and a 250-foot separation from residential areas. City councilors also asked staff to examine larger residential buffers, including 500 feet, and provide maps showing how those distances would affect where data centers could be built. Other options discussed included restricting standalone data centers in certain industrial zones and examining building size, utility demands and backup power systems. No final decisions have been made on those proposals. The discussion reflects growing questions about the impact of large data centers on surrounding communities. Although these facilities support everything from cloud computing to artificial intelligence, they can also require substantial electricity and infrastructure. For families living near proposed developments, concerns include the noise generated by cooling equipment, emissions from backup generators and how industrial facilities might affect nearby schools and neighborhoods. A data center already approved near a middle school One development at the center of the local debate is Crane Data Centers' project on Heather Street, near Neil Armstrong Middle School. The company's planned campus includes multiple phases and more than 100 megawatts of capacity, according to information published by Crane Data Centers. The project has already received land-use approval from the city, meaning the temporary moratorium does not automatically stop it. Crane has described its development as using air-based cooling and biodiesel-fueled backup generators. Those features have become part of the discussion over the facility's potential environmental impacts. Matt Knight, a Forest Grove community advocate and former City Council candidate who has researched the project, has raised questions about the generators' potential emissions, the amount of electricity required and the financial incentives provided for the development. In research published Oct. 16, Knight acknowledged that some of his earlier concerns had been addressed, including questions about water use and noise mitigation. However, he said more information is needed about the project's backup generators, emissions controls and any health-risk assessments. Knight has not claimed that the project has been proven to pose a health hazard. His research also points to the broader question facing city leaders: whether Forest Grove's existing regulations adequately protect surrounding neighborhoods and how those protections should be strengthened for future developments. Forest Grove temporarily pauses new data centers On Oct. 12, the Forest Grove City Council voted to adopt a 120-day moratorium on new data center development. The pause also applies to expansions of existing data centers of 20% or more. According to the city, the moratorium was adopted to give officials time to review the potential impacts of data centers and consider changes to the development code. However, the restrictions are not retroactive to projects that have already received land-use approval. That distinction is significant for the Crane development. Even if Forest Grove ultimately adopts stricter school and residential setbacks, those rules would not automatically overturn the project's existing approval. Whether future modifications or additional phases would require new approvals subject to updated regulations remains a question for city planning officials. The city's temporary moratorium is scheduled to expire Feb. 9, 2027, unless officials take further action. Why Forest Grove temporarily banned new data center development Forest Grove's temporary moratorium goes beyond concerns about data centers being built near schools and homes. City officials say the facilities could also threaten future housing development, strain the electrical grid and limit opportunities for other businesses. In Resolution No. 2026-47, adopted Oct. 12, the City Council outlined several concerns that prompted its decision to temporarily halt new data center development. According to the resolution, Forest Grove's development code currently allows data centers in all industrial zones without regulations specifically designed for those facilities. City officials also raised concerns about the amount of land data centers occupy compared with the relatively small number of permanent jobs they typically create. The resolution warns that allowing too many data centers could consume industrial land needed by other businesses, potentially harming the city's long-term economic health. Another concern involves housing. Forest Grove anticipates that an ongoing housing capacity study will find the city lacks enough buildable residential land to meet demand over the next 20 yea

artigo.texto: A Justiça Federal do Distrito Federal rejeitou nesta 4ª feira (25.nov.2026) o pedido de liminar da Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias) para suspender os leilões de armazenamento de energia em baterias, marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro. A decisão é do juiz Diego Câmara Alves, da 17ª Vara Federal Cível do DF. Eis a íntegra (PDF – 57 kB). A entidade –que representa empresas de geração de energia eólica– havia ajuizado uma ação civil pública contra a União e a Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) em 16 de novembro. A associação argumenta que a contratação de baterias beneficia todo o sistema elétrico e que a atribuição dos custos exclusivamente aos geradores é inconstitucional. Questiona também a realização dos leilões antes da definição dos critérios de rateio dos encargos. O magistrado entendeu, porém, que a realização dos leilões não está condicionada à regulamentação da divisão de custos pela Aneel –que, ao atribuir a conta aos geradores, seguiu o que está determinado na lei. A decisão argumenta que não há risco de dano iminente aos geradores, uma vez que a cobrança do encargo terá início só em agosto de 2028. A suspensão dos leilões, por outro lado, poderia comprometer a segurança do fornecimento de energia elétrica. DISPUTA SOBRE QUEM PAGA A CONTA O impasse em torno dos leilões decorre da reforma do setor elétrico, sancionada em 2025, que atribui exclusivamente aos geradores os custos da contratação de baterias. Associações do setor elétrico articulam a aprovação do PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716 de 2026 antes dos certames. De autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP), o texto retira a obrigação dos geradores e transfere os custos aos consumidores de energia. A proposta tramita em regime de urgência na Câmara dos Deputados e foi designada ao relator Danilo Forte (PP-CE) em 28 de outubro. Entidades que representam os consumidores são contrárias à mudança. A FNCE (Frente Nacional dos Consumidores de Energia) publicou estudo em que estima que a aprovação do projeto possa acrescentar até R$ 6,26 bilhões por ano à conta de luz. Paralelamente à articulação no Congresso, a Abeeólica acionou o STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) em 19 de novembro. Diferentemente da ação civil pública, que busca impedir a realização dos leilões sob as regras atuais, a ADI (Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade) questiona diretamente a validade do dispositivo legal que atribui os custos aos geradores. O relator do processo, ministro Cristiano Zanin, ainda não analisou o pedido de liminar, segundo a decisão da Justiça Federal. https://www.poder360.com.br/poder-justica/justica-rejeita-pedido-de-eolicas-para-suspender-leilao-de-baterias/ ACERCA DEL CORRESPONSAL REDACCIóN CENTRAL Prensa Mercosur es un diario online de iniciativa privada que fue fundado en 2001, donde nuestro principal objetivos es trabajar y apoyar a órganos públicos y privados.

artigo.texto: Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. O Brasil chega aos primeiros leilões de baterias de grande porte com uma contradição. Ao mesmo tempo que reconhece a necessidade de armazenar energia para dar segurança ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), atribui exclusivamente aos geradores o custo desse serviço. A regra foi introduzida pela Lei nº 15.269/2025 e abre uma exceção ao modelo aplicado à reserva de capacidade das termelétricas, cujo custo é repartido entre os usuários finais do sistema. Se a disponibilidade de potência beneficia o conjunto da rede, qual é a justificativa para cobrar por ela de forma tão diferente? Uma bateria pode carregar quando há energia disponível e devolvê-la à rede no início da noite, quando a produção solar diminui e a demanda exige uma resposta rápida do sistema. Essa flexibilidade ajuda a atender aos horários de ponta, contribui para o controle de frequência e, quando o armazenamento é instalado em pontos estratégicos, pode aliviar gargalos de transmissão e reduzir cortes de geração. O benefício aparece na operação do SIN e na confiabilidade do fornecimento a quem depende dele. Em artigo publicado recentemente, o ex-senador e chairman do CERNE Jean Paul Prates chamou atenção para uma condição fundamental do princípio da causalidade econômica. Cobrar de quem provoca determinado custo exige demonstrar tecnicamente a origem desse custo. A variabilidade da geração eólica e solar é parte da equação, assim como o perfil do consumo, a expansão da geração distribuída com controle operacional limitado, as restrições de transmissão e a dificuldade de outras usinas de ajustar sua produção. No nordeste brasileiro, essa discussão tem efeito direto sobre a continuidade dos investimentos. Em determinados períodos, os cortes compulsórios de geração, conhecidos como curtailment, chegaram a superar a faixa de 15% a 20% da produção potencial em ativos eólicos e fotovoltaicos. Esses percentuais dimensionam perdas de geração. O impacto adicional do encargo dependerá da metodologia de rateio e dos valores contratados nos leilões. Para um parque que já perdeu receita, a nova despesa reduz a margem para honrar financiamentos e compromete a previsibilidade dos contratos de venda de energia de longo prazo. Para um projeto que ainda precisa passar pela decisão final de investimento, pode ser suficiente para adiar ou inviabilizar sua implantação. O efeito se estende aos fornecedores, aos empregos e à arrecadação dos municípios potiguares. Adiciona-se a isso um questionamento por parte dos investidores, sobre a necessidade da inclusão dos sistemas de armazenamento (BESS) nos regimes de incentivos tributários estaduais, sendo um fator expressivo no CAPEX dos projetos, e que pode comprometer a viabilidade dos investimentos. A indefinição também afeta os leilões previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro. A Abeeólica pediu à Justiça Federal a suspensão dos certames, questionando a cobrança exclusiva dos geradores e os critérios de rateio em discussão na Aneel. Além do risco para o calendário, há um efeito sobre o preço. Como os sistemas de armazenamento exigem investimento elevado antes de começar a operar, os contratos precisam oferecer previsibilidade suficiente para viabilizar o financiamento. Se a fonte de pagamento está sujeita a litígio e recai sobre agentes já pressionados por perdas de receita, os investidores podem incorporar essa incerteza aos lances. Uma regra criada para concentrar a cobrança pode, assim, encarecer a própria contratação das baterias. Por isso, o CERNE defende a aprovação do PL nº 3.716/2026. O projeto revoga o dispositivo inserido pela Lei nº 15.269/2025 que atribuiu aos geradores o custeio exclusivo do armazenamento contratado como reserva de capacidade. Com a mudança, as baterias voltariam à regra geral de rateio entre os usuários finais, a mesma aplicada à potência contratada das termelétricas no LRCAP de 2026. São tecnologias com características operacionais distintas que, nesse contexto, atendem a uma necessidade comum do sistema. O tratamento do custeio deve refletir esse serviço. O consumidor pode sentir o custo nos dois cenários. Pela regra atual, os geradores tendem a incorporar a nova despesa às ofertas em futuros contratos no mercado livre e nos leilões do mercado regulado, na medida em que as condições de mercado permitirem. Com o projeto, o pagamento ocorre de forma explícita e previsível, por meio do encargo de reserva de capacidade. Essa previsibilidade pode reduzir o prêmio de risco nos lances. Na operação, as baterias também podem evitar, em determinadas horas, o acionamento de usinas de maior custo. O Nordeste precisa de armazenamento para aproveitar melhor a energia que já produz e oferecer condições de fornecimento a novos investimentos industriais e a atividades de demanda elevada, como os data centers, sendo uma oportunidade de preservar uma cadeia produtiva construída ao longo de anos e ampliar o uso econômico da sua geração renovável. Aprovar o PL antes dos certames daria ao primeiro ciclo de contratação de baterias uma base de custeio compatível com o serviço que o país espera delas. Darlan Santos é diretor-presidente do Centro de Estratégias em Recursos Naturais e Energia (CERNE)

artigo.texto: A coalition of six Central Massachusetts legislators is pressing state agencies and utility providers for strict public oversight before issuing permits for the Kraft Group’s proposed $16 billion Unified Parkway Data Center in Sutton. Spanning 10 buildings and requiring 900 megawatts of power, the project would rank as the fourth-largest data center in the U.S., according to one of the lawmakers, if fully built out on property off Boston and Providence roads in Sutton. The state lawmakers representing Sutton and surrounding communities are urging energy, environmental and utility regulators to slow down and answer key infrastructure questions before permits are issued for the data center. The lawmakers sent letters to state agencies, regional planners, National Grid and Aquarion Water Co. The letters call for a transparent review process aligned with Gov. Maura T. Healey’s data center executive order signed in September. Sens. Michael O. Moore and Ryan Fattman, along with Reps. Joseph McKenna, Paul Frost, David Muradian, and Michael Soter representing Sutton and surrounding communities, in letters to the Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs and the Central Massachusetts Regional Planning Commission – as well as the utility companies – urge a public approval process that aligns with the framework laid out in Healey’s data center executive order and request that a slate of important questions be answered before permits are issued. The letters say that Patriots owner and billionaire Robert Kraft’s proposal, if completed as envisioned, is projected to demand the same amount of power as a sizable city and could consume the same amount of water as roughly 23,400 households in an estimate extrapolated from the International Energy Agency’s estimate of typical data center water usage. Though the Kraft Group says it’s in discussions to independently source electricity and is exploring reclaimed water for the project, the letters say critical questions remain unanswered about whether the company will follow through on these promises. The letters sent by lawmakers emphasize the uncertainties and raise additional questions about protections for air and water quality, impacts on utility rates, how the project will change Sutton and neighboring communities, and each organization’s role in the approval process. “Horror stories and broken promises plague hyperscale data centers built by companies like xAI and Meta across the United States,” they stated. “If Robert Kraft wishes to build his data center in our communities, he must make extensive commitments that the Unified Parkway Data Center will not increase electricity rates, affect the local water supply, or disrupt the peaceful neighborhoods we call home,” Moore, D-Millbury, said in a statement. “A government that represents the best interests of its people must ensure a proposal of this scale leaves no questions unanswered. It is our job to make sure that members of the community have ample opportunities to weigh in at every step of the process – and, if the company goes back on its promises, that we have a system set up to hold the Kraft Group accountable.” “While I recognize the potential tax benefits this project could bring, those benefits must be weighed against crucial questions surrounding energy demand, water resources, and quality of life for residents,” Fattman, R-Sutton, said. “A project of this scope deserves an extensive and transparent review, including opportunities for residents to have their voices heard before any decisions are made. As both a Sutton resident and its state senator, I look forward to being fully engaged in that process and guaranteeing these concerns receive the thorough attention they deserve.” While the project is proposed to be built on land owned by the Kraft Group’s Unified Global Packaging Group in Sutton, the data center would border the towns of Millbury and Grafton, with impacts expected to extend to nearby Northbridge, Auburn, Upton, Douglas, Uxbridge, Oxford and Webster. The letters emphasize that constituent concerns in these communities include energy costs, air quality impacts, light and noise pollution, and the disruption of surrounding ponds, rivers and the aquifer it would sit atop. At the time the letters were sent, the Unified Parkway Data Center proposal remained very high-level with scarce details on how the project would affect the region and noncommittal statements on how the company may mitigate energy and water concerns, according to the legislators. “Our constituents deserve to have a full understanding of the potential impacts that this data center complex would have on their cost of living, their communities, and the environment,” the legislators write. “Equally, our regulatory process needs to ensure that if this project moves forward, our constituents are fully protected against those impacts.” Still in preliminary review The data center proposal is still in preliminary review, with no formal applications filed and no agreements negotiated. At a press conference Nov. 17, the governor did not weigh in on the controversial concept, but outlined more of her thinking around local control over the proposal. “It’s a hot topic right now. I’m going to leave it to the people of Sutton,” Healey said at the time. Guardrails of her executive order, which include expectations for securing tax breaks, stipulate that new data centers should directly procure or develop the energy resources to support their operations — without raising energy costs for ratepayers and straining the electric grid. Data centers should also be situated where sufficient water supplies, wastewater and infrastructure exist, and they must minimize air emissions. Communities should also play a “meaningful role” in project planning and development, the Healey administration said. artigo.texto: Ação popular pede liminar para barrar obras de data center em Atibaia Ação popular foi resultado de reportagens publicadas pelo Metrópoles. Entre as exigências está a suspensão de possíveis licenças concedidas São Paulo — Após reportagem do Metrópoles revelar, nesse domingo (22/11), que o projeto de um data center estimado em R$ 3 bilhões de reais está com previsão de ser instalado em Atibaia, interior de São Paulo, uma ação popular apresentada o Ministério Público de São Paulo (MPSP) nesta segunda-feira (23/11) pede a suspensão liminar de eventuais licenças do empreendimento sem a devida avaliação de impacto ambiental. A ação contra o município apresenta uma série de exigências e requerimentos, divididos entre medidas liminares de urgência, obrigações de transparência documental e pedidos definitivos de mérito. Dentro das medidas liminares de urgência, está o pedido de suspensão imediata dos efeitos de eventuais licenças, alvarás ou aprovações municipais concedidas para a implantação do data center, sem a demonstração prévia do cumprimento da legislação ambiental e urbanística e a exigência de que o município se abstenha de permitir qualquer início de obras, supressão de vegetação, movimentação de terra ou intervenção ambiental relacionada ao empreendimento até a comprovação da regularidade dos atos. No âmbito da transparência e exibição de documentos, a pasta exige a apresentação, por parte da prefeitura, de todos os expedientes administrativos existentes sobre o projeto, incluindo consultas preliminares, estudos, pareceres e certidões, a identificação de todas as pessoas físicas e jurídicas envolvidas no projeto, bem como os agentes públicos responsáveis por suas análises e aprovações, e a apresentação de uma declaração administrativa detalhada explicando a situação e informando os registros preliminares existentes, caso a prefeitura confirme a inexistência de processo formal de licenciamento. Entre no canal de WhatsApp do Metrópoles SP O processo ainda solicita: - Anulação definitiva de todos os atos administrativos municipais vinculados ao Data Center Alfa cuja ilegalidade ou lesividade ao meio ambiente, aos recursos hídricos e ao patrimônio local seja comprovada - Extensão da declaração de invalidação a todas as autorizações subsequentes que dependam de atos considerados nulos - Exigência de que o Município observe integralmente, antes de qualquer nova autorização material, os estudos ambientais, a proteção ao uso do solo, o impacto hídrico e a realização de audiências e participação popular quando exigido pela legislação Em nota enviada ao Metrópoles, a Prefeitura de Atibaia afirma que não foi citada, notificada ou tem conhecimento de demanda judicial relacionada à implantação de data center no município. Ademais, como já informado a este veículo em outra oportunidade, não existe pedido de autorização para implantação de empreendimento “data center” no município. Moradores se mobilizam contra instalação de data center O Metrópoles noticiou, neste domingo, que Atibaia, no interior paulista, entrou na mira das grandes empresas de tecnologia e deverá ser a futura sede de um data center de R$ 3 bilhões, em uma região de divisa entre área rural e área urbana da cidade. Temendo possíveis consequências ambientais, os moradores da cidade passaram a se mobilizar contra o projeto, redigindo uma petição que solicita à prefeitura a proibição de data centers de hiperescala no município. O requerimento do movimento popular Fora Data Center pede o envio à Câmara de Vereadores de um projeto de lei complementar para alterar o código de obras e o plano diretor municipal. Um abaixo-assinado do coletivo reuniu, até meados de novembro de 2026, mais de 4 mil assinaturas. A conexão foi autorizada pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) em outubro de 2025. O documento, ao qual o Metrópoles teve acesso, permite a expansão em 15 quilômetros da linha de transmissão e a implantação de dois novos módulos de entrada de linha em 138 kV, com a premissa de atender o Data Center Alfa. A Prefeitura de Atibaia, por sua vez, afirmou à reportagem que não identificou nos registros da Secretaria do Meio Ambiente, pedido de licenciamento ambiental vinculado ao projeto. O movimento Fora Data Center alerta para o risco da retirada de vegetação nativa da Mata Atlântica e de contaminação irreversível do lençol freático, em razão dos reservatórios de óleo diesel no subsolo, utilizados por data centers de hiperescala para alimentar centenas de geradores de emergência (UPS).Os moradores do Bairro do Tanque também temem um estresse hídrico, que pode gerar falta de água, já que o bairro é atendido parcialmente pelo sistema de abastecimento de água encanada e não dispõe de atendimento por rede coletora e tratamento de esgoto.

artigo.texto: The residents of Michigan's Ypsilanti Township are continuing to fight back against what they're calling a proposed "data center" after the University of Michigan's Board of Regents approved funding for a new research computing center last week. The board voted 7-1 on the $785 million construction costs for the $1.25 billion high-performances computing center intended for medical, science, clean energy, engineering and national security research. It's planned for a 124-acre site zoned for industrial use, with an additional 20 acres designated for a DTE electrical substation. The university said this project is not a data center or manufacturing site, but rather a "computing and research hub designed to advance science and education." University Promises Before the vote, University President Domenico Grasso said this project is "a critical step towards realizing one of the University of Michigan's most innovative and needed research initiatives." Read More on AI The university is partnering with Los Alamos National Laboratory and the state to deliver 50 megawatts of power initially, possibly expanding to 100 at full build-out, and is expected to "put Michigan at the forefront of the next generation of scientific discovery, which is where we always want to be." Grasso promised to work closely with the surrounding community to protect the environment, monitor utility usage and preserve the Huron River. He also said the board will commit $5 million over the next five years to the greater Ypsilanti area through its Community Partnership Program. "Leadership is not about pretending we know everything or have the perfect solutions; It is about listening and learning, recognizing where we can improve, and adjusting as appropriate," he said. "We want the people who live and work here to understand our motives and plans, and see the benefits of this partnership." In a letter to Congresswoman Debbie Dingell, Grasso said the university signed a Memorandum of Understanding in late 2024/2025 and said the Los Alamos has made no commitment of funds. “All activities require a separate agreement that will govern specific terms, conditions, funding and any other contractual obligations between U-M [the University of Michigan] and LANL [Los Alamos National Lab]," a spokesperson for Los Alamos told Newsweek. "There is no additional obligation between U-M and LANL. The classified computing center is not currently in the out years' NNSA [National Nuclear Security Administration] budget profile.” According to the Michigan Daily, Los Alamos confirmed that the facility would be used to research nuclear weapons. Community Backlash Critics of the project call it another data center that is set to disrupt the community and local environment. Residents and groups like Stop the Data Center have been protesting this facility for months. Reporting from Planet Detroit highlights outrage from residents, and promises from a local attorney to "use every legal means necessary to stop the data center." “U of M has gone far afield when it comes to the constitutional autonomy which they have enjoyed by virtue of being a university,” attorney Doug Winters said at a Thursday panel discussion. The United Tribes of Michigan (UTM) has also pushed back against the proposal, expressing its desire to preserve Native American cultural and heritage sites in the region and raised concerns about land use, noise levels, water consumption and electrical power needs. It also asked to be included in consultation about the facility's development. "Ypsilanti Township is along the Huron River in Southeastern Michigan and is located in an area that was used by Indian tribes for river and trail travel throughout history," UTM said in a resolution. "The area includes many sites of burials and other locations indicating indigenous usage and Ypsilanti Township is strongly concerned about a proposed data center within its boundaries, particularly about the potential impact on tribal cultural resources." In October, the university released a statement that it is conducting the appropriate due diligence and that a preliminary background search found "no evidence of archeological artifacts or culturally-sensitive materials found at the project site." Regent member Paul Brown, the only no vote, has joined community members protesting the facility. In August, he released a statement calling to stop the super computer site due to a lack of adequate community engagement. "When our development affects communities, we have to take responsibility to involve the people who live there," he said. "The university has failed to engage in an adequate conversation with those most affected and I cannot stand by and support this project being shoved down their throats, in a way that looks like environmental racism." The university is exempt from local building and zoning laws and does not pay property taxes. Michigan House Democrats introduced legislation in June to revoke the school's unilateral authority to circumvent zoning laws and town ordinances to buy land. “My community has been shaken by the university’s decision to quietly buy up land for the massive Los Alamos Data Center,” state Representative Jimmie Wilson of Ypsilanti said in a statement. “Every decision they’ve made was without consultation with local leaders or residents, and when the township board stood up and formally opposed it, U-M just ignored us and bulldozed ahead. "We are the ones who live here, pay taxes here and raise our kids here, but a multi-billion-dollar institution can just decide to drop a massive project in our backyard and expect us to deal with it," he said. "That is a complete betrayal of the public trust, and we’re putting a stop to it.” Local Community Impacts The university said the plan will not draw from or discharge into the Huron River or local groundwater and intends to protect local wildlife around the river. artigo.texto: O Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços (MDIC) defendeu que todos os geradores de energia elétrica participem do rateio dos custos de contratação de baterias para reserva de capacidade, com descontos proporcionais à flexibilidade que cada usina oferece ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). A posição da pasta foi elaborada no contexto da consulta pública nº 037/2026 da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel), que discute a regulamentação do rateio dos custos do leilão de reserva de capacidade na forma de armazenamento de energia (LRCap-SAE). Para o MDIC, a proposta mais adequada é aquela que prevê a aplicação de diferentes níveis de encargos conforme o Índice de Flexibilidade (IF) dos empreendimentos. A contribuição da pasta foi enviada nesta segunda-feira, 23 de novembro, e ocorre em meio a controvérsias jurídicas e econômicas da distribuição dos custos dos sistemas nos LRCap previstos para os dias 2 e 4 dezembro. Posição do MDIC O documento acompanha a avaliação da agência de que a alternativa baseada no índice de flexibilidade é a mais equilibrada do ponto de vista regulatório. Nesse modelo, todos os geradores permanecem na base de custeio, mas aqueles que contribuem mais para a flexibilidade do sistema pagam uma parcela menor do encargo. A proposta estabelece quatro patamares de flexibilidade. Usinas classificadas no nível P1, considerado inflexível, pagariam 100% do encargo unitário. No P2, de baixa flexibilidade, a cobrança seria de 75%; no P3, de alta flexibilidade, de 50%; e no P4, de flexibilidade muito alta, de 25%. Segundo a análise da Aneel, citada pelo MDIC, a terceira alternativa recebeu pontuação de 4,41 na avaliação multicritério, acima da alternativa que restringe o pagamento aos geradores sem flexibilidade, com 3,37 pontos, e da proposta de rateio uniforme entre todos os geradores, com 3,01 pontos. Controvérsia sobre o encargo Em 19 de novembro, a Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica (Abeeólica) acionou o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) contra a regra que atribui exclusivamente aos geradores o custeio das baterias, prevista na Lei 15.269/202. Em paralelo, o Projeto de Lei nº 3.716/2026 tramita em regime de urgência na Câmara dos Deputados para mudar a regra e retirar dos geradores a obrigação exclusiva de custear a contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias como reserva de capacidade. O projeto, segundo estima a Frente Nacional dos Consumidores de Energia (FNCE), pode elevar as despesas com energia em até R$ 6,26 bilhões por ano, ou R$ 94 bilhões em 15 anos, em um cenário de contratação de 5 GW. Já a Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae) contestou a análise e afirmou que a contratação de 4,5 GW em baterias poderia gerar benefícios de até R$ 5,5 bilhões anuais, dos quais cerca de 90% seriam destinados aos consumidores, ao considerar a redução de custos de capacidade, encargos de serviços do sistema e energia vertida. Mudança na lei O MDIC destaca que o apoio à alternativa 3 da Aneel não representa concordância com a regra legal que atribui exclusivamente aos geradores o custeio das baterias, já que, embora considere o modelo de rateio pelo Índice de Flexibilidade o mais equilibrado entre as opções regulatórias, a revogação do dispositivo seria a melhor opção para garantir a segurança do abastecimento e beneficiar todos os consumidores e autoprodutores. Desta forma, o ministério apoia a diferenciação dos encargos entre os geradores enquanto a regra estiver vigente, mas também recomenda mudanças legislativas para rever a responsabilidade pelo financiamento das baterias. A pasta também pondera que os geradores não devem ser responsabilizados pela expansão de fontes intermitentes, como eólicas e solares, contratadas por meio de leilões ou incentivadas no Ambiente de Contratação Livre (ACL). O documento cita ainda os efeitos do curtailment e os prejuízos de R$ 6,5 bilhões dos geradores eólicos em 2025. Revisão de subsídios e tarifas Além da revisão do rateio dos custos das baterias, o MDIC defende um conjunto de medidas para melhorar a alocação dos recursos energéticos e reduzir distorções no setor elétrico. Entre as propostas estão o fim dos subsídios às fontes renováveis, especialmente os descontos nas tarifas de uso do sistema de transmissão e distribuição (Tust e Tusd), e a criação de um limite para os subsídios da micro e minigeração distribuída (MMGD), conforme previsto no Projeto de Lei Complementar (PLP) nº 100/2026. A pasta também defende a redução gradual dos subsídios da MMGD para unidades consumidoras abrangidas pelo artigo 26 da Lei nº 14.300/2022, que estabelece regras de transição. Ainda são propostos o aprimoramento dos sinais de preço no mercado de curto prazo, o fortalecimento do sinal locacional na transmissão e a implementação de tarifa horária para consumidores de baixa tensão, com o objetivo de aproximar os preços da energia das condições de oferta e demanda ao longo do dia. Na conclusão da nota técnica, a pasta defende iniciativas legislativas para revogar o dispositivo que atribui exclusivamente aos geradores o custeio das baterias e para limitar e encerrar subsídios, aprimorar os sinais de preço e implementar a tarifa horária, além do apoio a projetos que contribuam para essas mudanças.

artigo.texto: A new study from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) finds that the expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence (AI) has had substantial negative health and air quality impacts — not just in the areas where most of these centers are being built, but also in regions far away from them. As a result, hundreds of people across the U.S. are dying annually, the study suggests, with researchers finding that pollution from electricity demands of data centers resulted in around 650 premature deaths in 2023 alone. Considering the rapid expansion of data centers since that time, the number could be even higher. “States hosting the largest data center loads do not necessarily experience the highest attributable mortality rates, while some states with little data center demand bear substantial burdens,” a summary of the study states. Researchers compared electricity that was generated from areas with data centers and those without them. They then modeled the electrical output increase due to data centers in both areas, monitoring air pollution rates in various areas of the country. Because the U.S. grid is interconnected, data center electricity demand is more spread out than many people realize. Different types of power plants also emit different amounts of pollution. So, while more data centers are being constructed in states like Virginia and Texas, Midwestern states, including Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas, are seeing higher per capita rates of death as a result of pollution from data centers. “When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors,” said Noelle Selin, senior author of the study. “But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region.” “Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” Selin added. In their findings for 2023, researchers found that data centers likely accounted for 513 premature deaths from fine particulate matter, while 137 deaths were associated with increases in ozone or fog that the data centers helped to create. A separate study published earlier this month also demonstrated the enormous output of electricity — and pollution — due to the explosive growth of data centers in the U.S. In that Harvard-based study, it was determined that data centers across the country emitted a total of 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide per year. That number is equivalent to the output of some countries, including Bolivia and Denmark. Much of the research amounted to “detective work,” the authors of the study said, due to lax federal requirements on public disclosure. “Communities shouldn’t need a team of Harvard researchers to analyze satellite images to understand their environmental impact,” said Harvard scientist Gianluca Guidi, who led the research team. artigo.texto: Proposed Colleton County data center raises questions amid moratorium COLLETON COUNTY, S.C. (WCSC) — A proposed data center development in Colleton County is raising questions about the county’s moratorium and drawing continued opposition from some residents. The first data center development was proposed in the county about a year ago, triggering a lawsuit and a moratorium. The lawsuit was settled last month, establishing restrictions on where data centers can be built. Two more developments have since been proposed. Lighthouse DC plans to purchase approximately 315 acres from Coastal Electric Cooperative near Interstate 95 Exit 62. The property includes the 99-acre site of the former Pomega Battery Systems project and adjacent land. Construction on the first phase is planned for 2027, with delivery targeted for 2028. “Wait, which one? Because there’s so many different things going on at all times and you want to claim that we have a moratorium, then why are we having these conversations right now?” Colleton County resident Alice Banwart said. The county says its moratorium does not affect the two developers considering data centers because both have expressed interest in areas excluded from the moratorium. The moratorium remains in place until the county’s comprehensive plan is updated to reflect areas where digital infrastructure will not be allowed. Under the lawsuit settlement, a new overlay district bans data centers across most of the county’s portion of the ACE Basin and directs development toward industrial areas. Some residents remain concerned about the potential effects on their homes. “It’s still a data center which, you know, none of us really want, but if it’s going to happen, the county is doing the right things and putting it in the right locations,” said Jennifer Singleton, a Colleton County resident and plaintiff in the settled lawsuit. “I would hate to see a situation where we can’t raise our animals, our kids are having problems sleeping and it forces us to the point that we couldn’t even live at the place that we want to call home and if I could be buried there, I would,” Banwart said. Proposed investment, jobs and taxes The county is considering a fee-in-lieu-of-tax agreement, or FILOT, for the redevelopment of the Colleton Industrial Campus. County officials say the project would bring more than $600 million in combined investment, making it the largest capital investment in county history. Lighthouse plans to make at least $400 million in qualifying investment to develop the digital infrastructure campus. The company estimates the initial 20-megawatt phase will include more than $200 million in infrastructure and $400 million in customer equipment. The county estimates the first phase will support approximately 16 direct jobs with an average annual wage of $85,000, 45 indirect permanent jobs in the community and approximately 200 construction workers. It projects employment will grow to more than 200 full-time permanent positions as the campus expands. The county also projects that, at full energization, the project will pay more than $600 million in taxes over the course of the agreement, including more than $288 million to the Colleton County School District. “If we can’t afford the basics of, you know, fire protection, 911, like that’s pretty bad, right? And there’s no industry that’s really breaking down the door saying we want to move to Colleton County,” Singleton said. Colleton County Council Chairman Scott Biering said the project’s industrial location and projected revenue would benefit the county. “This is a landmark investment for Colleton County,” Biering said. “The project is appropriately sited in an existing industrial area, and the revenue generated will assist the county in stabilizing and improving public services, while protecting our existing tax base. The project charts a brighter future for our citizens. It will provide high-quality, long-term employment opportunities for our workforce and fund vital services such as public education, sanitation, law enforcement and emergency services.” Steve Murdaugh, a county council member and chairman of the SouthernCarolina Alliance, also praised the project and the partnerships behind it. “I am excited about the investment by LightHouse DC in Colleton County, both as Chairman of the SouthernCarolina Alliance and as a member of Colleton County Council,” Murdaugh said. “This project represents the largest capital investment in the history of Colleton County and is a tremendous milestone for our community and our region. Beyond the significant investment itself, this project will create new employment opportunities for our citizens and generate substantial revenues for both the County government and our School District, providing additional resources to enhance public services, strengthen our schools, and improve the quality of life for our citizens. I want to commend the Colleton County Economic Alliance staff and thank our partners at Coastal Electric Cooperative, Inc. for their continued commitment, hard work, and partnership in advancing economic development opportunities in Colleton County. Projects of this magnitude are the result of strong partnerships, a shared vision, and a continued commitment to moving our community forward.” Utilities, water and noise Coastal Electric Cooperative CEO Mark Walling said the project would benefit the cooperative and its members. “We expect Lighthouse to have an immediate, positive impact on our community and our cooperative,” Walling said. “The presence of a large, stable user on our system will support the fixed costs to deliver electricity to our members, improve grid reliability and protect our ratepayers.” The proposed utility service framework would require large users to: - Sign contracts of at least 15 years with early termination penalties. - Prepay for necessary electric infrastructure upgrades. - Lower electricity use during potential energy outages or

artigo.texto: Report: Lutnick asked battery startup Pure Lithium to accept US takeover US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s plan marks another attempt by the Trump administration to acquire a stake in an American company. Pure Lithium, however, rejected the proposal, the Reuters report says. US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asked Pure Lithium in July to give Washington a 51% controlling stake in exchange for funds to build a manufacturing plant, which would neither be owned nor controlled by the US battery startup, according to a report by Reuters. Lutnick’s plan marks another attempt by the Trump administration to acquire a stake in an American company. Pure Lithium, however, rejected the proposal, saying such a stake could lead to public scrutiny and risked future capital-raising activities, the Reuters report says, citing documents from July and August. The Trump administration has taken stakes in several companies including Intel, but it has not yet taken a majority stake in any company. The largest equity stake the Trump administration has agreed to would give it a 15% stake in rare earths company MP Materials, the report said. According to Pure Lithium’s website, lithium metal batteries will replace the incumbent lithium-ion battery. The company’s “patented, vertically integrated production process delivers the highest quality Lithium metal anode, contributing to exceptional battery performance.”

Esse risco existe mesmo após a realização do LRCAP (Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência) de março e reforça a necessidade da contratação de baterias, segundo manifestação. A entidade questiona a regra de custeio do certame e pediu, cautelarmente, a suspensão da realização. Na manifestação, assinada no último dia 17, a consultoria jurídica do MME defendeu a legalidade dos certames de baterias e a importância de continuidade do cronograma. A pasta afirmou ainda que não há necessidade de regulamentação prévia sobre o custeio que remunerará as baterias, uma vez que a cobrança só seria iniciada em agosto de 2028. Esse mesmo entendimento foi levado pela ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) no outro processo movido pela Abeeólica, este na Justiça Federal em Brasília. A reguladora também disse que não há necessidade de urgência para definir o encargo e afirmou que uma suspensão do certame atrasaria a entrada das baterias e afetaria os mais de 5 mil projetos cadastrados.

artigo.texto: SpaceX gets approval for 1 million data center satellites - Click here to listen to this article - Share via See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred - The Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX’s plan to launch 1 million satellites for solar-powered data centers, advancing the company’s push to build artificial intelligence infrastructure in orbit. - SpaceX says the project could help meet growing demand for computing power while easing pressure on Earth’s electricity and water supplies. - Amazon’s Kuiper Systems, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society opposed the application, citing collision risks and other concerns about debris and satellite disposal. SpaceX won U.S. government approval to launch 1 million satellites for data centers in space, clearing a regulatory hurdle as the company charges forward with its artificial intelligence ambitions. The Federal Communications Commission, which announced the authorization Wednesday, said in a statement that the go-ahead will help fuel the United States’ efforts to advance AI. The world’s largest tech companies have been investing hundreds of billions of dollars into building data centers, which house computer servers and other infrastructure used to help train and run AI models. The creation of the data centers also has prompted concern that they are draining valuable resources on Earth such as electricity and water. SpaceX’s data center constellation, known as “Starmind,” will harness solar power, the FCC said. Other companies including Google, which announced a project this year to explore the possibility of hosting AI infrastructure in space, are also looking to the skies as part of new moonshot projects. “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement posted on X. “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership and expand prosperity here at home.” Some of SpaceX’s rivals, such as Amazon, have expressed skepticism about SpaceX’s Starlink effort, calling it a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Amazon’s Kuiper Systems, Viasat Inc. and the American Astronomical Society are among the companies that filed petitions to deny SpaceX’s application, according to a new government filing released Wednesday. The filing said concerns about SpaceX’s project in part centered on “collision risk, disposal failures, and casualty risk.” But the company, which relocated its headquarters from California to Texas, committed to “additional measures as core design criteria to ensure the long-term sustainability of space while upholding the highest standards of debris mitigation.” Those measures include deploying satellites at lower altitudes to make sure they’re working before moving to higher altitudes, according to the filing. SpaceX’s Starship is back on Earth, captured in midair by giant mechanical arms at its Texas launchpad. A day earlier its booster exploded, foiling its plans for a double capture. SpaceX didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. In a post on X, SpaceX founder and Chief Executive Elon Musk provided brief remarks in response to Carr’s announcement. “Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world,” Musk wrote. SpaceX shares rose 1.3% on Wednesday to $127.44.
