artigo.texto: Malaysia has stopped waiting for Washington to police its server halls. If you run or rent AI compute in Southeast Asia, one more route to Nvidia's chips for blacklisted buyers just got harder to use. Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, known as MITI, will advise data center operators not to host, lease space to or provide services for seven companies the US added to its trade blacklist this week, according to Bloomberg and Free Malaysia Today on Tuesday, November 24. The seven were put on the Commerce Department's Entity List in a final rule dated November 23, and they are tied to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer at the center of the chip diversion scandal. Three of the listed names are Malaysia-linked: Speedmatrix, MSFusion and PT Megaspeed International. The parent, Megaspeed International Pte Ltd in Singapore, is also listed, along with other affiliates in Singapore and Thailand. MITI says the Malaysian Investment Development Authority will pass the warning to operators. The ministry's line is that Malaysia won't allow itself to be used as a channel to get around export controls, and that it will act against anyone found breaking the law. Notice the word is advise, not ban. No deadline has been set, and the operators who will receive the notice have not been named. MITI also pushed back on the framing. It says PT Megaspeed International is not a Malaysian entity and is neither a data center operator nor a tenant in the country, going by investment agency records, and that Speedmatrix is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Singapore company. Eleven days earlier, on November 13, the ministry had said it never cleared Megaspeed or Speedmatrix of anything, and that Speedmatrix was a tenant at data centers in Malaysia. That's a narrow answer to a broad question: the firms may not be Malaysian by incorporation, but the racks they used sit in Malaysian buildings. Alice Huang, a Chinese national who has since left Megaspeed, was watched by US agencies for about a year after being photographed at dinners with Jensen Huang in Singapore. Nvidia says the contacts were routine and that no chips were diverted. - china recruited megaspeed executive to spy on nvidia - who did china recruit to spy on nvidia Not all Malaysian data centers face the new US chip curb. The one that matters is a separate US rule published on November 19, which requires licenses for data centers supplying large amounts of computing power to companies headquartered in China. Colocation operators feel that rule most, because they rent out the physical space and often can't see who ends up using the compute. Frankly, that blind spot is the whole problem, and it's why a warning letter from MIDA will matter less than whether operators start asking tenants harder questions. Singapore first, now Johor This follows Singapore's own line. Its prime minister, Lawrence Wong, said the city-state won't allow circumvention of export controls and is ready to facilitate US checks on AI chip use. Malaysia is the bigger physical test. Johor, across the causeway, has been the overflow site for Singapore's data center demand, and operators there have built fast on the promise of AI tenants. The scale of what Washington is chasing is large. Bloomberg has reported that Megaspeed imported at least $4.6 billion of Nvidia hardware, based on Malaysian and Indonesian customs data. For Chinese AI developers, the effect is direct. Renting GPU capacity in a neighboring country has been the workaround for the US ban on shipping top chips to China, and every operator that screens tenants more closely narrows it. Nvidia isn't named in the rule, but its customers' customers are now the ones being checked, and a listed buyer can't easily take delivery of new systems. Malaysia has its own money at stake. Tighter US chip rules already cloud the country's data center push, so Kuala Lumpur is balancing Washington's goodwill against an industry it has courted with incentives and a national investment framework. Listing doesn't automatically cover affiliates, one analysis of the rule notes, so operators must screen counterparties themselves rather than wait for a longer list. MITI has not said what happens to existing contracts with the seven firms. Neither Nvidia nor Megaspeed's affiliates had publicly responded to the Malaysian advisory at the time of writing. artigo.texto: AURORA | Audience members of Monday’s city council meeting broke into applause when lawmakers passed a data center moratorium that will prevent construction of new facilities in a majority of the city through September 2027, following months of back and forth. Council voted unanimously for the temporary pause, although Councilmember Curtis Gardner was excused from the meeting. Additionally, the developer behind the controversial Trident data center announced it will relocate the facility. Mayor Mike Coffman congratulated the neighbors of the Trident facility for organizing successfully. “I’m just grateful that the nightmare is over with and that you prevailed,” Coffman said. Under the moratorium, data centers would be prohibited from locating west and south of the intersection of Powhaton Road and Interstate 70 until after Sept. 30, 2027, or until city council determines appropriate land use regulations are in place. The moratorium, like the previous proposals, would not impact data centers that have already had development applications accepted, which includes Trident. The Trident data center has drawn significant backlash from neighbors in the Windler, Green Valley Ranch and Reserve communities over concerns with the potential environmental and health impacts. However, a statement from Vantage Data Centers, which is developing Trident, said it is no longer pursuing the original site on East 48th Avenue, but is continuing to look for an alternative location. It also said Vantage will continue to engage the city on their proposed campus. “In response to the recent community concerns, Vantage voluntarily initiated a review of alternative sites, and the examination of viable alternatives continues,” Misty Allen, vice president of public policy in North America for Vantage, said. “While we will no longer pursue the current site for our proposed campus, Vantage remains committed to being a responsible long-term partner in the state.” While previous iterations of moratoriums failed, council members supported this compromise. Mayor Mike Coffman said he feels it’s a good compromise by exempting the vacant land on the east side of the city while protecting residential communities and allowing the city to continue to draft rules. Councilmember Stephanie Hancock, who opposed past moratoriums, said she thinks Aurora is leading the way on data center regulations, adding “data centers are here to stay.” “I’m not in favor of the word moratorium, that really bothers me and I think it sends a weird message to businesses,” Hancock said. “But we want to keep in mind that our communities want safety, they want to make sure we’re building efficiently and effectively, and I think Aurora is doing a good job of wrapping our arms around this as we’re learning more.” Meanwhile, Councilmember Alli Jackson took issue with the moratorium not going far enough, noting the potential impact of pollution is not limited to nearby communities. She advocated for a total moratorium. “I do have a hard time voting on this because when I listen to the community, and what I hear them say, is that they don’t want data centers in Aurora, period,” Jackson said. “I understand … the votes aren’t going to change for that type of verbiage, so I will vote for this, but when we talk about the safety of our constituents, pollution doesn’t care about (zoning).” The moratorium doesn’t have to last until September 2027, but could end earlier, whenever council decides appropriate rules are in place. The council is already working on changes to the city’s development code regarding data centers, including residential setbacks and a requirement for a noise study. The residential setback would prohibit data centers within 750 feet of residentially-zoned areas and make data centers a conditional use when they’re located between 750 feet and a half-mile from residential areas. Councilmember Amy Wiles said she is exploring other regulations related to vibrations, low frequency noise and community benefit agreements. Councilmember Angela Lawson also noted the state legislature will likely have several bills targeting data centers. Several public commenters spoke in support of the moratorium during the meeting and asked the council to go further and do more to protect neighbors from the potential impacts. A few speakers opposed the moratorium. Chaz Tedesco, representing a local labor union, commented in favor of data centers and against the pause, citing the jobs they provide for local construction workers. “Aurora should not have to choose between protecting neighborhoods and supporting jobs,” Tedesco said. In addition to the moratorium, the council had planned to vote on a resolution stating its support for Trident to move to another location and directing the city manager to facilitate the relocation. However, since Trident announced its plans to move locations, the resolution was pulled from the agenda. Council also voted unanimously on a prohibition on tax incentives for data centers. “I think it’s important to send the message to data center developers that these incentives don’t exist and they can make their decisions accordingly,” Coffman said. Coombs called the ban “performative” because she said the council should have a more general discussion on tax incentives. However, she voted for the prohibition, citing community support for it. The prohibition will end the practices of tax revenue sharing or remitting sales or use tax back to data centers in exchange for jobs, however it would not apply to existing agreements, according to the draft policy. The city has already committed to four incentive agreements, with a maximum total rebate of about $83 million. One of the incentive agreements is for the Trident data center, which could receive up to $39 million in tax rebates. The ban will need one more vote before taking effect.

( McKenzie Patterson / CalMatters ) Topline: On Thursday, the University of California announced another deal with OpenAI to give ChatGPT to students. At the same time, California’s higher education systems are considering building their own data centers and creating in-house alternatives to ChatGPT, Claude, and other commercial AI products. artigo.texto: FCC clears SpaceX to put up to 1 million Starmind data centers in space Elon Musk’s Space Exploration Technologies Corp. today received approval from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to operate as data centers in orbit. Issued by the FCC’s Space Bureau under delegated authority, the order is described by the agency as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space.” “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said. “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.” Replying to Carr on X, Musk wrote that Starmind “will be a great asset to America and the world.” Under the terms of the approval, the Starmind satellites are to sit in six orbital shells, or altitude bands, between 500 and 1,002 kilometers, below the 2,000-kilometer ceiling in SpaceX’s original application. Most communications will run over optical links to other satellites, including those in the Starlink network. The license itself covers a backup Ka-band radio system for emergency telemetry, tracking and command. The approval does come with conditions. SpaceX’s orbital debris plan was found to comply with the agency’s rules only for satellites below 600 kilometers, and four of the six shells sit above that line. Before deploying anything higher, SpaceX is required to file a modification application containing a final debris plan. A request from the company to retire some of those higher satellites into disposal orbits around Earth or the sun, rather than having them re-enter the atmosphere within five years, was deferred for lack of information. To keep the authorization, SpaceX has to have its first Starmind satellite in operation by Nov. 25, 2033. The schedule then calls for 100,000 satellites by 2035, 500,000 by 2038 and the full 1 million by 2040. Missing any of the deadlines would void the license. Petitions to deny the application from Amazon.com Inc.’s Amazon Leo satellite business, Viasat Inc. and the American Astronomical Society were all rejected. In a March filing, Amazon had described the plan as “a lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” According to the bureau, nothing in the FCC’s rules limits how many satellites a single constellation can include. Astronomers’ concerns about the satellites’ brightness in infrared were ruled to fall outside the scope of a radio license. SpaceX first applied for the system in January, shortly before it acquired Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI Corp. Orbital data centers then featured in SpaceX’s pitch to investors ahead of its record initial public offering in June. Built around a space-optimized version of Nvidia Corp.’s Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale system, the first-generation Starmind satellite, known as AI1, could reach orbit as early as the third quarter of next year, according to Musk. The competitors Carr referred to include Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin LLC, which applied in March for Project Sunrise, a planned network of up to 51,600 data center satellites. Starcloud Inc., a startup developing AI data centers in orbit, raised $250 million at a $2.3 billion valuation in August. Shares of SpaceX closed up 1.3% today. artigo.texto: In Depth: Why Oklahomans should prepare to see more data center proposals As part of Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's campaign, she promised a crackdown and more regulations on data centers that she and many others who won earlier this month said they were behind skyrocketing power bills and taking up too much of the state’s water. “We have always been a pro-business state in Texas, but what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans and right now, what has happened is data centers have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans and [they] are being taken advantage of,” said Hinojosa. “So, the difference is we will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections. We can have a strong economy, strong industry, and protections for the people of Texas. Those things are not mutually exclusive, and I’ll make sure as governor, I lead to ensure that happens.” The State of Texas has seen its number of data centers soar in just the last few years. Some of these are hyperscalers, others are more in the traditional sense of data centers and server farms. In 2021, there were 83 operating by the end of the year. At the end of 2025, that number jumped to 145. We don’t have the 2026 numbers yet, but more projects were both built and proposed. Texas and other states have now elected officials that intend to crackdown and regulate data centers. Oklahoma has elected leaders who said we are open for business, and it's time to consider some of these investments. Tulsa Democratic State Representative Amanda Clinton, one of the main lawmakers in Oklahoma City trying to regulate data centers, speaks unedited about why Oklahomans need to be prepared for more data center proposals as these companies and developers look to leave Texas and other states.

artigo.texto: The nation’s largest data centers used at least as much energy in one year as the entire state of Michigan, and were responsible for more carbon emissions than some entire countries, according to a new study from the Harvard Data Science Initiative. The researchers focused on 403 large facilities and found that the climate pollution driven by these “hyperscale” data centers is three times greater than previously estimated. Energy use across the country’s thousand-plus data centers is likely much higher than the study captures, said lead author Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctorate researcher at Harvard. “This paper is just providing a floor estimate,” he said. Data centers contain the servers and computer chips that enable artificial intelligence, online commerce and cloud storage. They require a constant supply of energy to run and cool internal hardware. Communities near data centers have raised concerns about air pollution, and electricity and water use — issues that some political observers believe moved the needle toward Democrats in this month’s midterm elections. Scientists had previously taken a stab at projecting the amount of energy used by data centers, but the Harvard research team said few focused on the large facilities that power AI. Their servers process enormous amounts of data and need enormous amounts of electricity to operate. The average data center in the study consumed as much power as 30,000 homes. The precise amount of electricity used by data centers is difficult to determine because their operators rarely release this information. In this case, the researchers relied on satellite imagery and data from a private company about the facilities’ square footage and their maximum permitted energy use between 2024 and 2025. Then, the researchers used maps to determine which power plants the data centers likely draw electricity from. Based on the types of fuels those facilities burn, the researchers estimated the climate-warming emissions linked to the data centers. “We just wanted to find independent numbers,” said Guidi, “and not just companies’ sustainability claims.” The Harvard team found that the data centers in their sample consumed about 2% of all of the electricity used in the country during the period they studied. And more than half of that energy came from burning fossil fuels. Can Hankendi, a data center researcher at Boston University who was not involved with the study, called the research “very well built.” He said the lack of transparency around data centers’ energy use is a common challenge for researchers in the field. In an email to WBUR, Hankendi said the researchers had to make some assumptions, which he called “reasonable.” “Even though there will be some accuracy issues, they still give us some ballpark numbers to start from,” he wrote. “These estimations are important not only for researchers, but also for policymakers and the public.” The study also suggests that certain parts of the country are more burdened than others by climate pollution driven by data centers. Fossil fuel-burning power plants were more common in Virginia — the state with the most data centers — and Ohio, whereas other states like Oregon have greener electric grids, so data centers there were potentially responsible for less climate-warming gases. The data center industry is evolving so quickly that the numbers in the study “are already outdated in a way,” said Guidi. According to the independent market tracking company Clearview, last year there were 1,163 data centers in operation. That number is expected to skyrocket this year, with 578 new data centers under construction and more proposed. As companies look to build quickly, they are increasingly turning to on-site power generators, said study co-author Francesca Dominici, professor of biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. Some developers have managed to power data centers without connecting to the grid, she said. But the generators they use often rely on fossil fuels like natural gas or diesel, and they may be less efficient and more polluting than traditional power plants. In the coming years, Dominici said she hopes that will change. Some energy experts have suggested the power needs of data centers could spur clean energy development. “In some of the industry the big cloud providers are indeed trying to move into a renewable source of energy,” she said, “but we are not seeing that yet.” “Data center development could become actually a positive thing for the community if it’s done responsibly,” she said. This article was originally published on WBUR.org.

artigo.texto: A EDP condiciona a sua participação no primeiro leilão de baterias do Brasil, a ocorrer nos dias 02 e 04 dezembro, à alteração das regras de pagamento do encargo financeiro decorrente da contratação. Sem a garantia de que o custo seja assumido pelo sistema elétrico global é “muito difícil” licitar, considerou o presidente da EDP América do Sul, João Brito Martins, em conversa com jornalistas em São Paulo. Apesar de ter inscrito 700 MW de projetos para o leilão, a empresa aponta barreiras regulatórias que geram uma dupla penalização aos geradores do mercado livre. “Há uma condição que é crítica para nós podermos ir a leilão, que é a clarificação de como fica o pagamento do encargo”, afirmou o presidente da EDP América do Sul, João Brito Martins. O impasse tem origem na lei aprovada em novembro do ano passado, após uma medida provisória do Governo brasileiro, que atribuiu aos geradores a responsabilidade pelo pagamento dos custos do leilão de baterias. No mercado regulado, esse encargo é repassado automaticamente para os consumidores finais, explicou Brito Martins. Contudo, para os geradores com contratos no mercado livre de energia, como a EDP, não existe qualquer repasse desse custo, segundo explicou. O gestor alertou que os operadores do mercado livre já sofrem com o “curtailment” — a limitação da produção renovável por excesso de oferta ou restrições de rede — e seriam novamente onerados. “Eu já sou penalizado porque tenho curtailment e passo ainda a ser penalizado por suportar um encargo não previsto no momento da decisão de investimento”, explicou Brito Martins. A EDP defende que as baterias trazem estabilidade, flexibilidade e resiliência a toda a rede elétrica, devendo o custo ser repartido pelo sistema como um todo. Um projeto de lei em tramitação no Congresso brasileiro propõe essa alteração, o que poderia exigir o adiamento do leilão para adaptação do edital. No entanto, avalia o gestor, a empresa não conta com aprovação da proposta antes do leilão acontecer na próxima semana. A multinacional reitera que a disciplina de capital sobrepõe-se à assunção de riscos regulatórios que comprometam a receita necessária para cobrir os investimentos. Caso as regras atuais se mantenham, a obrigação de entrega dos equipamentos até agosto de 2028, sob pena de sanções, torna a participação inviável. A EDP já opera 550 MW em baterias globalmente, com presença consolidada nos Estados Unidos e um parque recente de 60 MW no Chile. “Sem a clarificação de que o encargo é suportado pelo sistema, é muito difícil podermos participar nesse leilão”, concluiu o líder da EDP na América do Sul. Para tentar atrair ainda mais empresas a participarem, a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL) reduziu o investimento de referência de 9,8 milhões de reais/MW para 6 milhões de reais/MW, o equivalente a 1,39 milhões de euros/MW para 931 mil euros/MW. Na última terça-feira, a Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae) defendeu a manutenção dos leilões de baterias já na próxima semana, considerando que é “urgente”. O posicionamento da entidade foi em reação a duas ações judiciais apresentadas na semana passada contra o edital na Justiça brasileira pela Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica). Abeeólica pede que o leilão não se realize antes da definição das regras sobre a divisão dos encargos de contratação das tecnologias.

artigo.texto: FCC Approves SpaceX Request to Launch One Million Data Centers into Space The approval comes without any environmental review needed to ensure the project will not cause irreparable harm to the planet Contacts Elizabeth Manning, emanning@earthjustice.org; 907-277-2555 In a stunning decision posted on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving, the Federal Communications Commission has approved a request by SpaceX to deploy a million data center satellites into orbit. The decision was finalized without any environmental review, as required by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). Organizations had previously petitioned the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for a comprehensive review of the environmental risks, impacts, and costs of satellite-based data centers. The petition asks the FCC to pause granting any licenses for these “orbital data centers” until it conducts a programmatic environmental review. The SpaceX proposal is one of several that have in recent months sought a license from the FCC to deploy massive numbers of data centers into space. Putting an unprecedented number of satellites in space risks changing our atmosphere, disrupting our daily activities that rely on satellites currently operating, disturbing wildlife, and fundamentally altering our night sky. “These projects could permanently alter the night sky as we know it,” said Ruskin Hartley, executive director of DarkSky International. “The FCC needs to take seriously its obligation to ensure these projects do not cause unnecessary harm to naturally dark skies, and to our overall environment.” “Allowing a million orbiting data centers with no environmental review isn’t just irresponsible — it’s reckless,” said Tim Whitehouse, executive director of Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility. “The potential for these projects to degrade the atmosphere with pollution and debris and harm wildlife needs to be carefully considered before licensing these projects.” “Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people’s everyday lives as well as the future of our planet,” said Jan Hasselman, senior attorney at Earthjustice. “Agencies that authorize companies looking to space as the next frontier still must operate within the law, and the law requires the FCC to consider all the risks and impacts of these proposals. It is dismaying that the FCC has ignored the law so blatantly and tried to mask the fact with a holiday filing.” The number of satellites in space has grown exponentially in the last several years. In 2015, there were about 1,400 active satellites; as of 2026, there are 15,000 satellites, and that number is projected to grow to an additional 58,000 by 2030. SpaceX’s proposal seeks permission to launch up to a million space-based data centers. Satellites have several known environmental impacts, including emissions from rocket launches and reentries, debris from potential collisions, degradation of the ozone layer, and light pollution that would disrupt and harm our wildlife and negatively affect humans. The Federal Aviation Administration (“FAA”) is following a similar trajectory as the FCC, and recently proposed a rule to exempt space launches from every environmental and resource protection law. Another factor to consider with this authorization is that under the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (“BAAJA”), the proposed permitting reform legislation, a future administration would not be able to revoke the license except in narrow situations. Worse, it would block judges from enforcing environmental review laws even if they found they’d been violated. “This approval to deploy a million data centers in space without any thought to the impacts on earth is just a glimpse of what we’ll see during the next two years of Trump,” said Sam Sankar, Senior Vice President of Earthjustice. “This is great example of why Congress should not pass a flawed bill like BAAJA that would lock in terrible projects like this one. Donald Trump is going to do a lot more dirty and lawless deals over the next years, and BAAJA prevents future presidents from reconsidering them.” Additional Resources About Earthjustice Earthjustice is the premier nonprofit environmental law organization. We wield the power of law and the strength of partnership to protect people's health, to preserve magnificent places and wildlife, to advance clean energy, and to combat climate change. We are here because the earth needs a good lawyer.

artigo.texto: A site built to bury waste is now generating electricity. Holliston, Massachusetts has activated the Marshall Street solar-plus-storage project on its capped municipal landfill, pairing nearly 5,700 solar panels with a 2.75-megawatt-hour battery system. A capped landfill is a closed disposal site sealed with a protective containment layer over buried waste. That design makes it poorly suited for housing or conventional construction, but structurally compatible with solar infrastructure. Nearly 5,700 panels sit on a ballasted mounting system, meaning the equipment is anchored with weight rather than driven stakes, so the protective cap beneath stays intact. Keeping that layer undisturbed is essential: penetrating it would risk compromising the containment separating buried waste from the surrounding environment. Onyx Renewables developed, owns, and operates the project. Town Meeting approval set off roughly seven years of permitting, utility interconnection reviews, financing, and construction before the facility reached activation. The battery carries a 2.75-megawatt-hour rating, a measure of stored energy capacity. That figure is distinct from the array’s 3.4-megawatt generation rating, which describes how much power the panels can produce at a given moment. Storage allows electricity generated during daylight to be dispatched later, adding flexibility to when and how the power reaches the grid. Holliston will receive lease payments and payments in lieu of taxes under agreements running up to 25 years. PILOT, as the latter arrangement is known, is a negotiated fee that replaces standard property taxes on the facility. Specific revenue figures have not been disclosed in the cited project materials. The project sits beside the town recycling center and soccer fields. Closed landfills can become difficult-to-use parcels in communities with limited available land, and placing solar development on them avoids competing with undeveloped forests, farmland, or recreational space. Six completed U.S. landfill-solar projects totaling more than 14 megawatts DC across Connecticut, New York, and Massachusetts make up the company’s current portfolio, according to Onyx. Project cost, annual municipal revenue, power pricing, and participation in Massachusetts’ SMART incentive program were not disclosed in the cited project materials. Holliston Town Manager Frank Gervasio called the installation “a meaningful contribution to our community’s environmental goals,” according to Resource Recycling. The project illustrates how Massachusetts communities can redirect closed waste sites toward productive municipal use, a model that may apply to dozens of similarly capped parcels across the state.

artigo.texto: Introducing a microstructured egg-box topography at the interface between metallic lithium and a Li6PS5Cl solid electrolyte increases the discharge current density at which interfacial voiding commences by a factor of ten. When the operating temperature is elevated to 60 degrees Celsius, the same contoured interfacial configuration successfully accommodates pulsed currents reaching 8 milliamperes per square centimeter while maintaining continuous ionic transport. To evaluate performance under dynamic conditions representative of practical automotive applications, researchers subjected the contoured cells to discharge current profiles derived directly from the Worldwide Harmonized Light Vehicles Test Procedure. Current and voltage time series from battery testing of a Hyundai Ioniq, sourced from Argonne National Laboratory electric vehicle evaluation datasets, were converted into equivalent cell-level areal current densities based on a 77.4-kilowatt-hour total pack energy capacity and an assumed cell areal capacity of 5 milliampere-hours per square centimeter, with regenerative charging currents excluded. Tested at 2 megapascals of stack pressure and 60 degrees Celsius, the egg-box contoured interface successfully sustained the full demanding WLTP discharge profile, which involves peak discharge currents reaching 9 milliamperes per square centimeter. The geometric profile of the microstructured interface was designed as a continuous three-dimensional egg-box pattern generated by sweeping a mathematical cosine function along the trajectory of an identical, perpendicular cosine function. The interfacial surface topography is formally defined by the mathematical expression where the surface elevation f(x,y) equals H multiplied by the cosine of 2 pi x divided by S plus H multiplied by the cosine of 2 pi y divided by S. In this formulation, H represents the peak height or amplitude, fixed at 5 micrometers, while S defines the peak separation or spatial wavelength, set to 30 micrometers. Print trajectories were compiled with NanoWrite software on a commercial Nanoscribe Photonic Professional GT system operating in a dip-in laser lithography configuration, utilizing a 25-times magnification lens with a numerical aperture of 0.8 and liquid IP-S resin. Following optical polymerization, the templates were washed in propylene glycol monomethyl ether acetate of at least 99.5 percent purity to dissolve unpolymerized precursor resin, rinsed with isopropanol of at least 99.5 percent purity, dried under vacuum overnight, and transferred directly into an argon-filled glovebox environment maintained below 1 part per million of oxygen and moisture. Solid electrolyte pellets were fabricated by loading 30 milligrams of Li6PS5Cl argyrodite powder, possessing an average particle diameter of 1 micrometer, together with the microstructured polymer template into a 5-millimeter die set. Applying a uniaxial compaction pressure of 400 megapascals imprinted the egg-box surface topography directly onto the ceramic powder while consolidating the electrolyte disc to an overall thickness of approximately 1 millimeter. After mechanical pressing, the polymeric template was detached from the shaped electrolyte pellet. Both contoured and flat comparative Li6PS5Cl discs subsequently underwent thermal sintering in a muffle furnace at 300 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes to optimize bulk ionic conductivity. Electrochemical validation of interfacial stripping behavior was performed within specialized three-electrode pouch cells assembled inside the inert argon glovebox. Metallic lithium discs measuring 1 millimeter, 0.5 millimeters, and 5 millimeters in diameter served as the working, reference, and counter electrodes, respectively, with an insulating polymer layer isolating the working and reference elements on one face of the electrolyte pellet while the counter electrode resided on the reverse side. The critical current density for stripping was quantitatively tracked using a Gamry 1010E potentiostat via a stepped chronopotentiometry protocol. Cells were initially cycled by electrochemically plating lithium at 0.2 milliamperes per square centimeter and stripping at 0.2 milliamperes per square centimeter to a fixed areal capacity of 0.2 milliampere-hours per square centimeter. In subsequent cycles, the plating current was maintained at a constant 0.2 milliamperes per square centimeter while the stripping current density was increased incrementally by 0.2 milliamperes per square centimeter per cycle. The cathode composite was formulated by mortar-and-pestle blending of LiNi0.83Mn0.06Co0.11O2 powder, Li6PS5Cl solid electrolyte, and conductive carbon nanofibres in a weight ratio of 75 to 22 to 3. artigo.texto: EUA autorizam SpaceX a lançar 1 milhão de satélites para data centers Decisão permite à empresa de Elon Musk instalar data centers em órbita até 2038; projeto enfrenta críticas A FCC (Comissão Federal de Comunicações dos Estados Unidos) autorizou a SpaceX, empresa de Elon Musk, a lançar 1 milhão de satélites para formar uma rede de data centers em órbita. A decisão foi confirmada nesta 4ª feira (25.nov.2026). Batizada de Starmind, a constelação deverá atender à demanda por capacidade computacional para sistemas de inteligência artificial. A autorização estabelece prazos para a implantação da rede. A SpaceX deverá iniciar as operações até novembro de 2033 e colocar 100 mil satélites em órbita até novembro de 2035. A meta é atingir 500 mil unidades até novembro de 2038. As informações são da Reuters. ENERGIA SOLAR A SpaceX afirma que os data centers em órbita terão acesso direto à energia solar, o que reduziria os custos de operação e o impacto ambiental em comparação com as estruturas terrestres. Segundo a big tech, a exposição quase contínua à luz solar permitirá melhorar a eficiência energética dos equipamentos e diminuir os gastos com manutenção. A execução do projeto depende, em parte, da redução dos custos de lançamento da Starship, foguete reutilizável da empresa que ainda está em desenvolvimento. O veículo deverá ser utilizado para transportar os módulos dos data centers ao espaço. CRÍTICAS A unidade de satélites Leo, da Amazon, e outras empresas se opuseram ao projeto. Elas afirmam que a SpaceX dificilmente conseguirá colocar todas as unidades previstas em órbita e que a implantação poderia levar séculos. A SpaceX pediu licença para lançar 42.000 satélites Starlink, mas a rede conta com pouco mais de 11.000 unidades em operação. Atualmente, há cerca de 17.000 satélites em órbita, segundo a FCC. A agência também autorizou pedidos da big tech para ampliar os recursos de comunicação de sua rede óptica.

artigo.texto: AI data centers drive up demand at Britain’s factories The building of artificial intelligence data centers has lifted the UK’s manufacturing output to a 27-month high, according to survey data that shows the economy as a whole continuing to grow. S&P Global’s overall purchasing managers’ index, measuring the health of the UK economy, came in at 52.3 for November in its initial estimate published on Monday. That was down slightly from October’s final reading of 52.9 but still above the 50-mark that indicates economic expansion. Growth in the UK’s dominant services sector slowed to a five-month low, yet this was partly offset by the highest sub-index score for factory output since July 2024 — the same month in which the current Labour government came to power. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is being helped by a surprisingly resilient UK economy, which has outpaced its major European peers so far this year. While surging energy bills are expected to dent consumer confidence over the winter, surveys such as the PMI still show strong business activity — helped by AI. Factory managers “noted stronger sales pipelines, as well as forthcoming investment spending and planned growth in overseas markets,” the S&P report said. “A number of goods producers cited a recent surge in orders related to data center build-outs.” However, there were other causes for concern in the PMI data. Employment shrank again in November, reversing October’s index score — which had been the first increase in more than two years. The UK’s growth this year has failed to drive more hiring, and the survey showed some firms shedding jobs in an effort to boost productivity. Input prices climbed at a slower pace than the previous month but remain elevated at 68.3, while the sub-index for output price growth slid modestly from 57.3 to 56.6. “The combination of resilient output growth and stubbornly elevated inflation meanwhile makes another rate hike by the Bank of England at its December meeting a near certainty, and raises the likelihood of another hike in February,” said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. (By Julian Harris)

artigo.texto: US company to invest $117 mln in battery storage project in central Vietnam U.S.-based Arbin Energy LLC will invest $117 million in a factory producing battery energy storage systems and battery testing equipment at the Danang Hi-Tech Park in Danang city, central Vietnam. The Danang Hi-Tech Park and Industrial Zones Authority (DSEZA) has approved the investment policy and Arbin Energy LLC as the investor for the Arbin Energy Danang Factory project. The project will cover 5.34 hectares at the Danang Hi-Tech Park, with total investment exceeding VND3.05 trillion ($117 million). The factory will focus on manufacturing battery energy storage systems (BESS), battery testing equipment and machinery used in battery production. Its BESS production line will have a designed capacity of 5,000 containers per year, equivalent to 5 GWh annually. The project will add energy storage equipment manufacturing to the hi-tech park's industrial portfolio and create opportunities to connect with supply chains involving companies in power electronics, measurement and automation. Construction is scheduled to begin in December 2026, with production expected to start in the third quarter of 2028. With the latest project, the Danang Hi-Tech Park has attracted a total of 14 foreign direct investment (FDI) projects, with combined registered capital of $830.5 million. In September 2026, during a working visit to the United States, Chairman of the Danang People's Committee Nguyen Manh Hung held a meeting with Arbin Instruments, chaired by its chairman, Chaojiong Zhang. The two sides discussed and updated the company's investment plans in Danang, focusing on project scale, technology, products, infrastructure requirements and implementation timelines. In addition to manufacturing operations, the discussions covered potential cooperation in research and development (R&D), technical training and partnerships with universities and technology companies in the city. The two sides also reviewed investment procedures and agreed on the next steps for implementation. Founded in 1991, Arbin Instruments is headquartered and operates its manufacturing facilities in College Station, Texas, in the United States. Over its 35 years of operations, the company has grown into one of the world's leading manufacturers of battery testing equipment and energy storage system testing solutions. Its core business focuses on researching, designing and manufacturing high-precision battery testing equipment, electric vehicle battery pack testing systems, solutions for industrial-scale battery production, and software systems for data management and analysis. According to the company, its equipment systems are currently used in more than 55 countries. In addition to its approximately 6,000-square-meter headquarters and manufacturing complex in Texas, Arbin Instruments has expanded its operations to Germany, China, India, South Korea, Vietnam and other markets. Its customers include electric vehicle manufacturers, battery producers, consumer electronics companies, universities and research institutes worldwide. In Vietnam, Arbin Energy LLC was established in August 2026, with its registered office at Lot A10, Danang Hi-Tech Park, Lien Chieu ward. The company has initial charter capital of VND52.14 billion ($2 million), and is wholly owned by Chaojiong Zhang, a U.S. citizen born in 1945, who also serves as its chairman. As of August 2026, the United States was one of Danang's key investment partners, with 87 FDI projects worth more than $346 million, ranking seventh among more than 70 countries and territories investing in the city. With support from U.S. diplomatic missions and investment promotion programs, Da Nang has gradually established ties with several leading global technology corporations, including Synopsys, Marvell, Nvidia and Qualcomm. artigo.texto: Trending The cost of state and local state tax breaks for data centers in Ohio is skyrocketing, according to one non-profit group, and has cost the state's public schools $374 million annually. Ohio started granting the state and local sales tax exemptions in 2013 for data center purchases of equipment and construction materials, according to the study by Policy Matters Ohio, a progressive think operating in Cleveland and Columbus. Other groups, however, support the limited use of sales tax incentives with negotiated community benefits. When the tax exemptions were first enacted, "they were designed for an earlier era of smaller data centers and are ill-equipped for the explosion of hyperscale facilities across the state," according to the study. "Since then, the state has signed agreements with the largest technology companies - Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft." Amazon's exemption, according to the study, was signed in 2014 and lasts for the next 40 years. "When the contract was signed, the state agreed to provide Amazon with an estimated $77 million in sales tax breaks in exchange for $1.1 billion in investment," the study states. "In late 2024, the company announced an additional $10 billion investment and said it would invest a total of $23 billion by 2029." But with increased investment comes higher tax breaks. Policy Matters Ohio estimated the actual Amazon subsidy might be 20 times more expensive than originally estimated. Earlier this year, Gov. Mike DeWine directed the Ohio Tax Credit Authority to suspend any new data center tax exemptions. “I fully support the Ohio General Assembly’s work to study the issue and bring forward facts about data centers, including the local benefits to communities when tax exemptions are granted,” DeWine said in a statement. In its study, Policy Matters Ohio calls for making the governor's temporary pause permanent. Ohio currently has 262 data centers, according to the website DataCenterMap. The Buckeye Institute, a conservative think tank in Columbus, supports the sales tax exemptions for goods used in manufacturing, Greg Lawson, institute senior research fellow, told The Center Square. "This is because a sales tax should only be applied at the point of sale of the final good or service," Lawson said. "If you apply it to intermediate goods used to make a final good or service you effectively raise the price of that good or service. This applies to data centers as well because servers and other equipment used inside are not the final good or service, data storage or AI training is. Thus, the sales tax would increase these costs." But he added the tax breaks "deserve hard scrutiny" because they shift costs onto residents. "They should be used sparingly and if they are used, they should be limited in size and length, and communities should negotiate direct benefits, such as payments to the community, before construction begins," Lawson said.

artigo.texto: City Council locks out data centers for 90 days to craft a plan to deal with them QUINCY — The Quincy City Council on Monday put up a temporary “closed for business” sign for any data center companies that might be eying the city. Mayor Linda Moore said as of Monday, the city has not received any applications for a data center, but she noted that she has heard about conversations that have been happening with landowners. In an effort to get ahead of any inevitable applications, the council passed a 90-day moratorium on the applications to give the council a chance to put plans in place requirements that the city would have before a center could even be considered. Moore noted that with solar farms, the city was behind the curve and had to fight after the fact to make changes in city ordinances while trying to meet the requirements put forth by state regulators. One takeaway from the discussion was the belief that data centers are inevitable. Moore noted that any data center built anywhere in the country between Washington D.C. and Quincy will impact the power grid that feeds this region, and so Quincy needs to consider what benefits can be gained in exchange for the inevitable costs. “They’re going to suck our power off the grid,” Moore said. “We’re all on the same grid, so if they’re going to suck the power and raise our rates, why not at least get the economic benefits of them?” Moore said her administration has already been working behind the scenes to try and determine what requirements the city could impose, including zoning requirements, setbacks from neighbors, sound-level controls, and landscaping to name a few. With the 90-day moratorium imposed, Moore anticipates having enough time to get additional information collected such as power-usage information from Ameren Illinois and reviews of other municipalities regulations to see what can be applied to Quincy. Aldermen will have a chance to weigh in before any ordinance is submitted to the city’s Plan Commission. If approved by the Plan Commission, the council will then have three readings of a new ordinance to make final adjustments. The moratorium was on the agenda for the first of three readings on Monday, but aldermen voted to waive the requirement for three readings and passed the moratorium on a vote of 13-0 with Ald. Mike Adkins, R-3, being absent. The council also approved a bid from Leander Construction of Canton, Ill. for the addition of two more pumps into the system at the city’s water treatment plant. At a cost of just over $1.53 million, Director of Public Works Jeffrey Conte said the pumps will reduce the city’s electric bill at the treatment plant by as much as 35% because the pumps being installed are more efficient, though they are also more vulnerable to flooding inside the facility caused by high rain volumes or other events. Conte said the newer pumps that are able to withstand flooding better have proven to be robust in those situations, but he noted they’re not as efficient in their power usage. This new project should provide the plant with strong redundancies while reducing power usage in ordinary operation. A new ordinance up for consideration Monday would see changes put in place in regard to the city’s garbage collection. The changes would eliminate the garbage sticker programs effective as of March 1 and would increase rates for the standard tote from $12.99 per month to $15 per month while the smaller totes offered would have a cost of $10 per month. Conte told the council at the new rates, the city would still subsidize the garbage operations at a rate of around $450,000 in the next fiscal year. He said the break-even point that would eliminate a need for a subsidy right now would be $20 per month for the full-size totes and around $16.50 for the smaller totes, both costs that would still be lower than private-hauler costs. The new ordinance, if passed, would also require private contractors to adjust their pick-up schedules to match the city’s schedules so that residents aren’t dealing with garbage collections from different companies nearly every day of the week.

artigo.texto: Aurora passes partial data center moratorium as Trident data center cancels site plan Aurora community members advocating for an end to data centers saw major wins during Monday night's Aurora City Council meeting, with the passage of a partial temporary moratorium and the cancellation of plans for one controversial facility. It was another Aurora City Council meeting where data centers took center stage. "We all need clean water to drink, we all need clean air to breathe, how can AI possibly be more important than that? It isn't," one community member said during public comment. "Trident mega data center must not be built in our neighborhood," another community member said. But as passionate neighbors spoke, a major announcement came. "Trident just announced they have abandoned the site next to your neighborhood for the data center," said Peter Schulte, city attorney for Aurora. Cheers erupted from an audience full of neighbors there to speak out against the Trident data center. A City of Aurora spokesperson told CBS Colorado, "Neither City Manager Jason Batchelor, City Attorney Pete Schulte nor other members of the city team were aware of that news until it was reported by various outlets near the start of the meeting." "I'm just grateful that the nightmare is over with and that you prevailed, congratulations," Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman said. "Wow, what an announcement, you know," one community member said during public comment, ripping up their printed speech to cheers and laughs from the audience. But many neighbors still want to see a full data center moratorium. "A moratorium gives us all time to reflect, research and hear from those impacted," one community member said at the meeting. Council took a step in that direction, unanimously passing a moratorium on data centers located west and south of the intersection of I-70 and Powhaton Road, covering much of the city. Only a few attendees spoke against that moratorium. One community member responded to the news, saying, "We ask you to consider the full impact of this decision, including the working families whose livelihoods depend on these opportunities." Councilmembers attribute the moratorium passing and Trident data center reversal to the community members who spoke out. "These people right here are proof that you can make a difference if you use your voice," said Aurora Councilmember Amy Wiles. "Thank you for everyone who voted for this. We have a long road to go, but thank you," one community member said during public comment. That moratorium on new data centers in the south and west parts of Aurora goes into effect immediately and will last through September 2027, or until city council takes further action. Monday night, the council also discussed a proposed ordinance to prohibit future sales tax incentives for data centers.

artigo.texto: Após ações judiciais, setor de baterias defende manutenção de leilão Associação de Soluções de Armazenamento afirma que contratações são urgentes e disputas devem ser mantidas nas datas marcadas A Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia) defendeu nesta 2ª feira (23.nov.2026) a manutenção dos leilões de baterias em 2 e 4 de dezembro, datas marcadas inicialmente no cronograma de contratações do governo. A manifestação vem em reação a duas ações judiciais contra o certame apresentadas na última semana à Justiça Federal e ao Supremo Tribunal Federal. Ambos os processos foram protocolados pela Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias), que pede que a disputa não seja realizada antes da definição das regras sobre o rateio dos custos de contratação das tecnologias. A entidade também questiona a constitucionalidade de um trecho da Lei 15.269 de 2025, que determina que os custos de contratação de reserva de capacidade por meio de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias sejam rateados exclusivamente entre os geradores de energia. Segundo a Absae, a contratação de baterias para o Sistema Interligado Nacional é “urgente” e não pode ser adiada. A associação avalia que as ações judiciais “fazem parte do processo e não alteram essa necessidade” e, portanto, podem ser resolvidas no “campo político” depois de já realizados os leilões. A discussão ocorre enquanto tramita na Câmara o PL 3.716 de 2026, que revoga o trecho da lei questionado pelas eólicas e aplica para as baterias a regra geral de divisão de custo entre todos os consumidores, conforme as demais contratações de reserva de capacidade do sistema elétrico. Caso o texto seja aprovado antes do leilão, a Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) pode ter de rever as regras da disputa, o que pode levar ao adiamento do certame. “Os leilões precisam acontecer nas datas previstas. A contratação é urgente para reforçar a segurança do fornecimento, são apenas 18 meses do certame à operação em agosto de 2028. A discussão sobre os encargos deve avançar, mas não pode impedir os certames”, afirma Fabio Lima, diretor-executivo da Absae. A posição vai na contramão do que defendeu a Abeeólica ao pedir o adiamento de todas as etapas do certame, incluindo disputa, adjudicação, homologação e assinatura dos contratos. Segundo a associação, seria impossível para os agentes de geração calcular os riscos e impactos econômicos antes de as regras estarem definidas. ABSAE DEFENDE PROJETO DE LEI Fabio Lima defende que eventuais efeitos do PL 3.716 de 2026 podem ser aplicados mesmo se o texto for aprovado depois do leilão, com as demais etapas da contratação já em andamento. Com isso, a correção alcançaria os contratos da disputa de dezembro e resolveria a controvérsia “na origem”, sem interromper o calendário de contratação, afirma a associação. “A judicialização faz parte do processo, mas não pode adiar uma contratação de que o sistema precisa. Adiar o leilão não elimina a necessidade de potência, só reduz o tempo para atendê-la. A questão do custeio é real e deve ser resolvida no Congresso, e isso pode ser concluído após as sessões públicas, sem prejuízo”, disse Lima. Leia mais: - Abeeólica vai ao STF contra leilão de baterias; - Abeeólica pede suspensão de leilão de baterias na Justiça; - Aneel pode adiar em 30 dias leilão de baterias se Congresso mudar lei; - Câmara aprova urgência de PL sobre divisão de custos de baterias.

artigo.texto: Siga Reset no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Siga Reset no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. O carbono passou a ter preço. Já são 87 impostos e sistemas de comércio de emissões em vigor no mundo, cobrindo 29% das emissões globais. A Europa começou a cobrar pelo carbono embutido nas importações. E o Brasil está regulamentando o seu próprio mercado, o SBCE, que deve estar em plena operação em 2031. O tema se tornou pauta econômica. Hoje influencia decisões de investimento, financiamento e competitividade. Mas, quanto mais ele avança, mais difícil fica entender como as peças se encaixam. - Por que, exatamente, colocar um preço no carbono? - Qual a diferença entre o mercado regulado e o voluntário, e onde eles se cruzam? - Quem será obrigado a reduzir emissões no SBCE, e a partir de quando? - O que são CBE e CRVE? - Como o CBAM europeu e o Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris afetam as empresas brasileiras? - Por que um crédito jurisdicional pode valer três vezes mais que um crédito de projeto? O Guia Reset de Mercados de Carbono responde a essas e outras perguntas de forma didática, mas com a profundidade de quem precisa entender esses mercados na prática. Em quatro capítulos, o guia passa pelos sistemas internacionais, pelo mercado regulado brasileiro e pelo mercado voluntário. No fim, mapeia as oportunidades em sete frentes, do Corsia ao setor financeiro. Muitas dessas oportunidades têm prazo. A aviação internacional entra na fase obrigatória do Corsia em 2027. Os créditos florestais brasileiros têm vantagem enquanto as tecnologias de remoção não ganham escala. E as regras do SBCE ainda estão sendo escritas. Quem se posicionar agora tende a influenciar as regras e os preços do que vem depois. O planeta tem pressa, os negócios também. Clique aqui para baixar.

artigo.texto: Coweta County voters to decide Jan. 12 on $17 billion data center project Probate judge orders special election after petition seeks to repeal county’s approval NEWNAN, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — Coweta County voters will take part in a special election Jan. 12 to decide the fate of a $17 billion data center project and whether data centers should be zoned in the county. Coweta County Probate Judge Carrie B. Markham ordered the election Monday after opponents to the project gathered more than 10,000 signatures seeking to repeal the county’s decision. The county initially approved zoning the project in rural Coweta County. Signs and voices in Newnan Yard signs line home after home along Wagers Mill Road in Newnan, calling to keep data centers out of Coweta County. The project’s future is uncertain as voters will have a chance to weigh in. “I think it’s a good idea, an excellent idea,” Leroy Kenner, who lives in Coweta County, said of the special election. “The voters should have the right to decide whether or not the data centers come to Coweta County or anywhere, period.” Jennifer Tedder said she signed the petition. “I just think it’s not a good thing for us to have in our community here,” Tedder said. What the court order says The petition was filed Oct. 16 in Coweta County Probate Court under the Home Rule provision of the Georgia Constitution, according to Markham’s order dated Nov. 23. The order said the petition seeks an election on whether to repeal one Coweta County zoning ordinance and amend another. The order said 10,971 signatures were required, which is 10% of the 109,703 active electors in Coweta County in the last general election. The county’s director of elections certified in a written report Nov. 20 that 11,065 signatures were verified. Markham found the petition valid. The order directs the Coweta County Board of Elections and director of elections to place this question on the ballot: “Shall the action of the Coweta County Board of Commissioners on April 7, 2026 approving REZONE 24-019 be repealed, and Appendix A. Zoning and Development of the Coweta County Code of Ordinances be amended to delete data centers and data center campuses as permitted and conditional uses in all zoning districts and to prohibit data centers, data center campuses, cryptocurrency data centers, and cryptocurrency mining operations in all zoning districts of Coweta County?” The election will be held Tuesday, Jan. 12, 2027. The order says the Board of Elections and director of elections will administer it under Georgia laws governing special elections. The county will pay for the election, and the court will declare and certify the results, according to the order. “We are thrilled with the Judge’s order,” Vivian Allen, a Citizens for Rural Coweta volunteer, said in a press release. “Thousands of our neighbors signed because they wanted a say, and we can’t wait to see Coweta County turn out on January 12.” “This happened because people stood in parking lots, on sidewalks, and at local events collecting signatures in the summer heat,” Donna Boles, also a volunteer with the group, said in the release. “This vote belongs to them.” About Project Sail Project Sail is a data center proposed by Atlas Development, LLC, according to Development of Regional Impact filings for the project with the Georgia Department of Community Affairs. The filings describe a data center of 13 buildings of about 378,000 square feet each, plus substations. They list the location as “Welcome To Sargent Rd & Wagers Mill” and an estimated completion date of Dec. 31, 2036. The filings estimate the project’s value at build-out at $17,161,900,000. They estimate local tax revenue at $163 million per year. PREVIOUS COVERAGE: Coweta County commissioners approve rezoning for massive data center The filings estimate water demand at 9.1 million gallons per day, sewage flow at 3.03 million gallons per day and solid waste at 800 tons per year. They list the Coweta County Water & Sewer Authority as the water and wastewater provider. According to its website, Atlas Development is based in Buford. The company filed an objection to the petition, which the court received Oct. 23. Markham dismissed the objection in a separate order Nov. 23. The order said the Georgia Supreme Court has made clear that no party has legal standing to object to a petition filed under that provision of the Georgia Constitution. The order also said the objection was not verified. Atlas representatives did not respond to our requests for comment. County response Cathy Wickey, communications manager for Coweta County Government, said in a statement that the county is still assessing the potential implications of the ruling. “The County became aware of this news at the same time as our citizens,” the statement said. “Given the unique nature of this situation, we are still assessing its potential implications. We anticipate that legal questions and challenges may arise among the entities involved.” The statement said the Elections Department will conduct the special election in accordance with state election laws, using normal election equipment and precincts. The election is scheduled for Jan. 12. Copyright 2026 WANF. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Justiça rejeita pedido de eólicas para suspender leilão de baterias Entidade quer revisão da divisão de custos antes do certame, cuja conta deve ser atribuída aos geradores A Justiça Federal do Distrito Federal rejeitou nesta 4ª feira (25.nov.2026) o pedido de liminar da Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias) para suspender os leilões de armazenamento de energia em baterias, marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro. A decisão é do juiz Diego Câmara Alves, da 17ª Vara Federal Cível do DF. Eis a íntegra (PDF – 57 kB). A entidade –que representa empresas de geração de energia eólica– havia ajuizado uma ação civil pública contra a União e a Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) em 16 de novembro. A associação argumenta que a contratação de baterias beneficia todo o sistema elétrico e que a atribuição dos custos exclusivamente aos geradores é inconstitucional. Questiona também a realização dos leilões antes da definição dos critérios de rateio dos encargos. O magistrado entendeu, porém, que a realização dos leilões não está condicionada à regulamentação da divisão de custos pela Aneel –que, ao atribuir a conta aos geradores, seguiu o que está determinado na lei. A decisão argumenta que não há risco de dano iminente aos geradores, uma vez que a cobrança do encargo terá início só em agosto de 2028. A suspensão dos leilões, por outro lado, poderia comprometer a segurança do fornecimento de energia elétrica. DISPUTA SOBRE QUEM PAGA A CONTA O impasse em torno dos leilões decorre da reforma do setor elétrico, sancionada em 2025, que atribui exclusivamente aos geradores os custos da contratação de baterias. Associações do setor elétrico articulam a aprovação do PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716 de 2026 antes dos certames. De autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP), o texto retira a obrigação dos geradores e transfere os custos aos consumidores de energia. A proposta tramita em regime de urgência na Câmara dos Deputados e foi designada ao relator Danilo Forte (PP-CE) em 28 de outubro. Entidades que representam os consumidores são contrárias à mudança. A FNCE (Frente Nacional dos Consumidores de Energia) publicou estudo em que estima que a aprovação do projeto possa acrescentar até R$ 6,26 bilhões por ano à conta de luz. Paralelamente à articulação no Congresso, a Abeeólica acionou o STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) em 19 de novembro. Diferentemente da ação civil pública, que busca impedir a realização dos leilões sob as regras atuais, a ADI (Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade) questiona diretamente a validade do dispositivo legal que atribui os custos aos geradores. O relator do processo, ministro Cristiano Zanin, ainda não analisou o pedido de liminar, segundo a decisão da Justiça Federal.

artigo.texto: Hawaii lawmakers discuss AI safeguards as county weighs data center ban HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - Hawaii lawmakers are weighing the benefits and risks of artificial intelligence as they consider how to promote the technology while protecting the public. State House and Senate committees held a joint briefing on Wednesday to discuss the development and application of AI, its role in government operations and opportunities for the workforce. The meeting came as Hawaii County lawmakers consider a ban on large-scale data centers that run AI models. “Hawaii is not behind when it comes to AI, and we are actually leading the pack considering other states across the country,” Trung Lam of the Hawaii Technology Development Corporation said. Lam added that Hawaii ranks eighth out of 51 in AI usage nationwide. AI and the workforce Experts have estimated that AI could replace or eliminate up to 15% of U.S. jobs in the next five to 10 years. “One of the concerns in AI is workforce, we definitely need to be mindful of how it’s going to affect our community, especially jobs,” said state Rep. Greggor Ilagan, who attended the briefing. After the briefing, Lam said, “I think that for Hawaii, we need to understand that we don’t have a shortage of jobs, we have a shortage of high-paying jobs.” Government use and data security Government entities in Hawaii have been using AI for virtual assistance, to minimize administrative work amid a transition from paper to digital formats, and to monitor and safeguard their data systems. “I’d like to reassure the public that we have safety as one of our top priorities. We understand that the state government has a breadth of data in service of the public,” said Christine Maii Sakuda, state chief information officer and administrator of the Office of Enterprise Technology Services. “How can we understand the breadth of the work that we do within state government by leveraging AI to do it faster.” Proposed data center ban State Sen. Brandon Elefante is drafting legislation to protect government information from data breaches. Elefante also supports Hawaii County Council Bill 170, which proposes a ban on large-scale AI data centers on Hawaii Island. The proposal is distinct from smaller data centers that already exist. “What we’re hearing across the country is these big data centers, consuming electricity, consuming water in our communities, and that is a serious concern,” Elefante said. Lam added, “I think that the concern about these hyper-scale data centers is valid. I do think in Hawaii, it’s less of a concern because our energy costs and water supply is so low.” Bill 170 is set to be heard by the full council on Dec. 2. Copyright 2026 Hawaii News Now. artigo.texto: As communities across Pennsylvania face growing questions about proposed data center developments, Baker, R-Lehman Township, announced she will introduce legislation to strengthen transparency and increase public input, while ensuring residents have access to information before decisions are made regarding projects. "These decisions should be made at the local level, where officials understand the character of their communities and the concerns of their residents," Baker said. "We should be looking carefully at the availability of water and electricity and the capacity for emergency response, along with the suitability of the proposed site. We should also be prioritizing locations such as brownfields and former industrial properties, rather than sacrificing productive farmland and valuable natural resources." Baker's proposed legislation would address several concerns surrounding the development of data centers, including: —Greater transparency: Prohibit public agencies from entering into nondisclosure agreements that prevent the release of information about proposed data center developments. —Meaningful public input: Require at least two public meetings before a municipality approves a data center application, giving residents an opportunity to ask questions and provide comments. —Infrastructure accountability: Require documentation that a data center applicant has applied for electric service and paid the associated application fees and costs before the required public meetings are scheduled. —Protection of ratepayers: Strengthen reporting requirements to ensure data center development does not shift electricity costs onto other classes of customers. Baker also expressed concern about the potential effects of large-scale data center development on rural water supplies, high-value streams and electricity rates, particularly in communities where residents rely on private wells. "Developers should be responsible for the infrastructure necessary to support their projects. Families and small businesses should not be left paying higher utility bills because of the demands of a new data center," she said. "We can support responsible economic development and technological advancement while protecting our natural resources and the quality of life that makes our communities special." Baker said she will be introducing the legislation in the coming weeks. © 2026 The Times Leader (Wilkes-Barre, Pa.). Distributed by Tribune Content Agency, LLC.

artigo.texto: Two business verticals of Larsen & Toubro (L&T) – its Renewables business and L&T Electronic Products & Systems (LTEPS) – have jointly secured an order to develop a 300 MW / 900 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at Khavda in Gujarat. The project will comprise a three-hour battery energy storage facility with a power capacity of 300 MW and an energy storage capacity of 900 MWh. The system will store surplus electricity generated during periods of high renewable energy production and release it when demand peaks. This will help improve the utilisation of clean energy, support grid stability and provide greater flexibility and reliability to the power supply network. The BESS will incorporate advanced liquid-cooling technology, designed to support higher power density, improve safety and extend the operating life of the system. The technology will help maintain operating conditions across the battery installation while supporting efficient performance during charging and discharging cycles. Located at Khavda, the facility will contribute to strengthening India’s power network as renewable energy capacity continues to expand. Energy storage systems are increasingly important for managing variations in solar and wind power generation and matching electricity supply with demand. By storing energy when generation is high and making it available when required, the project will support the integration of a larger share of renewable power into the grid. The order brings together the capabilities of L&T’s Renewables business and LTEPS for the development of a large-scale energy storage facility. It also adds to the company’s work in the energy storage sector and reflects its ability to undertake complex projects involving advanced technologies and integrated execution. The Khavda project is part of the wider development of renewable energy infrastructure in Gujarat, where large-scale generation capacity requires supporting systems to ensure reliable power transmission and distribution. Battery storage can help address fluctuations in renewable generation, improve the use of available electricity and provide additional support during periods of peak consumption. L&T continues to expand its activities across energy and infrastructure, with a focus on engineering, procurement and construction, high-technology manufacturing and specialised products and services. Larsen & Toubro is a USD 32 billion Indian multinational engaged in EPC projects, high-tech manufacturing, products and services. The company operates across diverse business domains and geographies. Its focus on technology, artificial intelligence, customer requirements and quality has supported its leadership across major business segments for eight decades.
