artigo.texto: 5 Things You Didn't Know About BAAJA and Data Centers Key Highlights - Beyond hyperscale: Removal of the original 20-MW threshold potentially extends BAAJA's retail ratepayer protections to smaller data center developments. - Competition for power: States could prioritize electricity service opportunities according to the economic benefits projects deliver to other ratepayers. - Monetizing flexibility: Qualifying behind-the-meter energy resources could gain greater access to wholesale electricity markets. - Measuring actual demand: Federal electricity reporting would begin separately accounting for data center loads. - Community empowerment: DOE would provide local governments with technical assistance and opportunities for independent project analysis. For an industry increasingly accustomed to measuring its growth prospects in gigawatts, the most consequential development in American data center infrastructure this November may have come not from a hyperscaler, a semiconductor manufacturer or an electric utility, but from the floor of the U.S. Senate. On Nov. 19, the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, better known as BAAJA, by a vote of 62-33. The sweeping legislative package seeks to accelerate the development of American energy and transmission infrastructure through changes to federal permitting, environmental review, judicial proceedings and electricity regulation. The legislation now faces consideration in the House. For the data center industry, the appeal of permitting reform is readily apparent. As DCF has reported, transmission infrastructure is emerging as a defining constraint on AI data center development, with the timelines required to construct new electrical infrastructure increasingly at odds with the deployment schedules envisioned by AI infrastructure investors and developers. But a closer reading of the Senate-passed legislation reveals something more consequential than an attempt to accelerate the construction of power plants and transmission lines. BAAJA is also an attempt to establish the economic and regulatory terms under which America's rapidly expanding computational infrastructure will interact with the nation's electricity system and the communities that host it. Here are five provisions that warrant particularly close attention from data center developers, operators, investors and technology suppliers. 1. BAAJA is no longer just about hyperscale data centers One of the more significant changes between the legislation introduced on Sept. 30 and the version passed by the Senate concerns the size of the data centers subject to its ratepayer protection provisions. The original legislation established a 20-megawatt threshold for its retail ratepayer protections, as outlined in an October analysis by attorneys at Foley Hoag. That threshold is absent from the Senate-passed version of Section 2107, which instead defines covered computational facilities primarily by their function. Computing equipment supporting an otherwise unrelated commercial or industrial operation is excluded. The change potentially brings a much broader segment of the industry into the scope of these provisions, including regional colocation facilities, emerging AI infrastructure providers and smaller inference-oriented developments. For new data center interconnections following enactment, the legislation would protect other utility customers against the incremental costs of serving those facilities. Utilities would require financial assurances or contributions ahead of necessary infrastructure investments, while service agreements would provide for continued cost recovery even if a data center customer ceases purchasing electricity before those investments have been recovered. The implications extend beyond electricity pricing. A hyperscaler with an investment-grade balance sheet may be considerably better positioned to accommodate such requirements than an independent developer pursuing a speculative campus or an emerging neocloud seeking to finance its next phase of expansion. As Metlen's Lillian Kasa discussed in a recent interview on the DCF Show, the distinction between announced infrastructure capacity and capacity that can actually be delivered is becoming increasingly important to the industry's investment calculus. BAAJA could add another dimension to that distinction: the ability of a developer or its customers to financially stand behind the electrical infrastructure their projects require. 2. Data centers could find themselves bidding against one another for electricity Perhaps the most striking language in Section 2107 concerns how states could allocate access to electricity among competing data center projects. The legislation explicitly recognizes state authority to use competitive solicitations or open seasons to award electric service opportunities according to the financial benefits projects would provide to other ratepayers, measured on a net present value basis, rather than simply according to the order in which applications were received. States could also establish distinct retail electricity customer classifications for data centers, offer them less favorable service terms or priorities than traditional industrial and manufacturing customers, and condition electric service on commitments to secure additional generation or accept restrictions on grid withdrawals. These provisions would not establish a mandatory national bidding system for data center power. They instead affirm existing state authority and provide a framework that individual jurisdictions could elect to employ. At the federal level, BAAJA would also direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to revise its transmission pricing policy so that eligible data center loads bear both a share of existing transmission costs and an assessment of the additional costs attributable to serving them. artigo.texto: Com expectativa por gás natural, Redata aguarda palavra final de Lula Decreto sobre política para data centers já está na Casa Civil e aguarda decisão do presidente O decreto que regulamenta o Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter) está praticamente pronto e aguarda análise final do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT). A lei que cria os incentivos para empresas que instalarem data centers no Brasil foi sancionada em setembro, mas o início da concessão dos benefícios ainda depende da publicação das regras que serão estabelecidas na regulamentação. O texto é aguardado pelos setores de infraestrutura digital e energia, os principais envolvidos nesse tipo de empreendimento. Segundo apurou o Poder360, uma versão final do decreto já está na Casa Civil, esperando decisão de Lula. O presidente terá a palavra final sobre a definição das fontes de energia que serão permitidas para empreendimentos interessados no programa, um dos pontos mais sensíveis de uma discussão que opôs alas distintas do governo. O texto original estabelecia que apenas data centers abastecidos por energia 100% renovável poderiam receber os incentivos fiscais, mas uma alteração no Senado incluiu também fontes “consideradas de baixa emissão”. Isso abriu brecha para o uso de gás natural, defendido por representantes da indústria, governadores, congressistas e pelo ministro de Minas e Energia, Alexandre Silveira (PSD). A inclusão do gás natural, porém, não foi consenso dentro do governo. Os ministérios da Fazenda e do Meio Ambiente, foram contra permitir o uso de um combustível fóssil, mesmo que o gás tenha menores níveis de emissão. A avaliação era de que seria contraditório com o propósito original do Redata, que condiciona o incentivo tributário ao uso de fontes renováveis. O Ministério de Minas e Energia, por sua vez, defendeu a inclusão do gás, sob a justificativa de que poderia contribuir para dar previsibilidade a investidores por se tratar de uma energia firme, ou seja, de fornecimento ininterrupto, diferentemente da eólica e solar, renováveis normalmente usadas em data centers. Nas últimas semanas, integrantes do Ministério da Fazenda, da Casa Civil e de Minas e Energia participaram de uma série de reuniões sobre o assunto. As negociações já foram concluídas e o tema está “maduro para levar para uma decisão presidencial”, segundo o Assessor Especial do Ministério da Fazenda, Rafael Dubeaux, que falou a jornalistas nesta 4ª feira (25.nov), mas não antecipou qual foi o desfecho das conversas sobre o gás. O presidente, no entanto, ainda não iniciou a análise do tema, que havia sido prometida pela ministra da Casa Civil, Miriam Belchior, para a semana de 16 de novembro, quando Lula voltou de viagem internacional. Também nesta 4ª feira (25.nov.2026), o ministro das Comunicações, Frederico Siqueira, afirmou, sem dar detalhes, que o decreto virá “nos próximos dias”. “É uma discussão que está tendo entre o Ministério, a Casa Civil, o Governo, a Presidência da República. Mas a gente acredita que nos próximos dias isso será resolvido pela importância do tema”, disse a jornalistas depois de participação em evento sobre IA, em Brasília. GÁS NATURAL NO REDATA Feita poucas horas antes da votação do texto no Senado, a alteração que abriu caminho para outras fontes de energia é resultado de uma articulação do setor de gás natural. O movimento também foi apoiado por congressistas que atuavam pelo avanço do texto, inclusive com sugestões de inclusão de outros tipos de fontes, como energia nuclear. Durante a tramitação no Senado, o senador Esperidião Amin (PP-SC) apresentou uma emenda para incluir expressamente geradores movidos a gás natural ou biometano entre as fontes admitidas. O trecho foi rejeitado pelo relator Cid Gomes (PSB-CE). Defensores do uso do gás natural argumentam que o combustível atua como fonte de transição para evitar instabilidade no fornecimento de energia aos data centers. As fontes eólica e a solar, duas das mais usadas no segmento de data centers ao redor do mundo, são intermitentes, ou seja, dependem de variáveis ambientais e não asseguram fornecimento constante ao longo do dia. Como os data centers precisam funcionar ininterruptamente para sustentar o processamento de dados de sites, redes sociais e ferramentas de inteligência artificial, é comum que esses empreendimentos usem sistemas secundários com outros tipos de abastecimento para situações de emergência ou interrupção de fornecimento. Já os críticos da medida afirmam que a inclusão de fontes não renováveis, mesmo que de baixa emissão, contraria as metas de descarbonização e pode reduzir a competitividade do país na atração de empresas de tecnologia.

artigo.texto: Após repercussões em redes sociais e questionamentos levantados por moradores e veículos de comunicação sobre possíveis impactos ambientais e urbanos, a Prefeitura da Estância de Atibaia comunicou oficialmente que não existe nenhum projeto de instalação de data center protocolado na administração municipal para avaliação ou liberação. Ausência de processos técnicos e ambientais Conforme os esclarecimentos do Poder Executivo local, a ausência de pedidos formais significa que não há análises técnicas em andamento nem procedimentos de licenciamento ambiental abertos para contemplar esse perfil de estrutura tecnológica na cidade. A gestão municipal destacou que, no passado, houve apenas uma aproximação informal e de caráter consultivo por parte de interessados no segmento. O contato preliminar, no entanto, não gerou compromissos, tratativas oficiais ou abertura de expedientes administrativos, uma vez que nenhuma documentação foi submetida aos setores competentes. Atratividade logística e exigências legais Situada no entroncamento de duas rodovias estratégicas do Estado de São Paulo, Atibaia registra frequente interesse de empresas dos setores industrial e de tecnologia que buscam expansão. A administração reforçou que eventuais propostas que venham a ser formalizadas no futuro passarão por um rigoroso escrutínio legal. Caso qualquer projeto do gênero venha a ser apresentado, o trâmite exigirá: - Avaliação minuciosa de acordo com a legislação e os ritos administrativos vigentes; - Apreciação técnica pelo Conselho Municipal de Defesa do Meio Ambiente de Atibaia (COMDEMA); - Aprovação e emissão de licenças junto aos órgãos fiscalizadores nas esferas municipal, estadual e federal.

artigo.texto: ZE Energy, a European electricity flexibility provider, has announced the acquisition of the Magliano Alpi battery energy storage system (BESS) project, in the Piedmont region in Italy, from ReFeel New Energy. Fully permitted and ready to build, the 59 MW project will have a storage capacity of up to nearly 480 MWh, equivalent to a duration of up to eight hours. Located in Magliano Alpi, in Piedmont, the project is a standalone BESS connected to the 132 kV high-voltage grid via an existing Terna substation. It will provide the northern Italian grid with long-duration flexibility capacity, able to absorb electricity when generation is abundant and release it during periods of high demand or system stress. In an Italian power system where demand exceeded 300 TWh in 2025, with 15% met by net imports, the accelerated rollout of renewables is increasing the need to connect flexibility systems to the grid. With more than 44 TWh generated in 2025, up 25% y/y, solar PV illustrates this trend: battery storage absorbs surplus energy during production peaks and then releases it to the grid when generation can no longer cover demand. With 59 MW of power and 472 MWh of storage capacity, Magliano Alpi will help balance supply and demand, manage consumption peaks, and keep the northern Italian grid stable. After Sessa Aurunca, in Central-Southern Italy, and Elena, in the South, ZE Energy is expanding and diversifying its Italian portfolio with the acquisition of the Magliano Alpi project, located in the North and sized to meet complementary flexibility needs and markets. This transaction illustrates the company’s ability to source and execute acquisitions of permitted, ready-to-build projects, to which it brings its industrial expertise by integrating the entire value chain (development, engineering, construction, operation). ZE Energy is thus continuing its rollout across Europe, with the goal of reaching 1.5 GW of installed capacity by 2030. Rocco Mauro, Head of M&A and Business Development Italy at ZE Energy, said: “With Magliano Alpi, we are strengthening our presence in Italy through a project that can bring flexibility to the power system, as close as possible to the needs of consumers in the north of the country. “We are delighted to have acquired this project from ReFeel New Energy and would like to commend the quality and constructive spirit of our collaboration throughout this transaction. “Magliano Alpi once again illustrates our ability to grow our portfolio through a strategy of targeted acquisitions, favouring high-quality assets that complement our existing projects and help diversify our geographic footprint. We intend to continue our development in Italy on the basis of this same approach.” For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine. artigo.texto: The European Union and the United Kingdom have announced that they have agreed to strengthen cooperation on steel trade, industrial supply chains and carbon pricing following their second bilateral summit, held in Brussels on November 20, 2026. According to the joint statement issued after the summit, both sides committed to addressing the negative trade effects of global steel overcapacity, developing more resilient industrial supply chains and advancing the integration of their emissions trading systems (ETS). Emissions trading systems aimed to be linked by 2028 The EU and UK welcomed the conclusion of negotiations on linking their respective emissions trading systems, with the agreement intended to enable mutual recognition of carbon allowances. The proposed arrangement would also provide a basis for exempting goods traded between the EU and UK from their respective Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms (CBAM), subject to applicable legislation and procedures. Both sides aim to begin applying the agreement in 2028, following the necessary legal procedures. Stronger cooperation planned to address steel overcapacity The EU and UK reaffirmed their commitment to protecting their steel industries against the negative trade effects of global overcapacity. They agreed to explore additional arrangements to address overcapacity and its impact on steel trade, while strengthening cooperation on diversified and resilient steel supply chains. The two sides also committed to coordinating economic security policies, including measures concerning critical raw materials, supply chain vulnerabilities and potential disruptions. Under the proposed cooperation framework, the EU and UK will seek to minimize the negative effects of their respective trade and industrial measures on each other’s supply chains, with progress in the steel and electric vehicle sectors to be reviewed every four months. The joint statement also highlighted plans to establish a long-term solution for the movement of UK-origin steel into Northern Ireland, taking into account the existing arrangements under the Windsor Framework. The EU and UK also agreed to extend the energy provisions of their Trade and Cooperation Agreement until March 31, 2028. Meanwhile, both sides committed to concluding negotiations on the UK’s participation in the EU’s internal electricity market in 2027, subject to final agreement. According to the joint statement, closer electricity market integration is expected to improve energy security, facilitate cross-border electricity trading and contribute to lower energy costs. The two sides emphasized that closer cooperation on steel, energy and industrial supply chains would support economic resilience and competitiveness while advancing their shared climate objectives. The EU and the UK have finalized negotiations to link their respective emissions trading systems (ETS) effective Jan. 1, 2028. Following Brexit, UK ETS was created in 2021, but there were immediate calls from businesses for the EU ETS and UK ETS to be linked. Negotiations began in late 2025, and a deal was announced at the EU-UK summit on Nov. 20, 2026, in Brussels. “The agreement will ensure that the same set of climate rules related to emissions trading will apply in the EU and the UK,” the European Commission’s Directorate General for Climate Action said on Nov. 20. If the deal is ratified on both sides of the English Channel, it will simplify airline compliance and create a larger market with more stable carbon pricing. The UK will also introduce a “one-stop shop,” so airlines will deal with a single authority for both schemes rather than separate UK and EU regulators. Work is underway to operationalize the agreement, passing any necessary legislation in 2027, with a view to enacting procedures in January 2028. “From this date [Jan. 1, 2028], UK and EU allowances can be used interchangeably across both schemes. The first surrender deadline where UK and EU allowances will be accepted across both schemes will be Sept. 30, 2028, with respect to operators’ obligations for the 2027 compliance year,” the UK government said. The UK ETS and EU ETS will continue to operate as two separate systems, with “dynamic alignment,” and the UK government said it will have an early “decision-shaping role” when the EU develops new EU ETS policies. In July 2026, the European Commission announced plans to extend the EU ETS to cover flights between the EU and non-EU countries within a 5,000 km (3,100 mi.) radius. This drew strong opposition from aviation stakeholders, who see the move as extraterritorial, undermining global efforts through Corsia, the International Civil Aviation Organization’s program to stabilize net CO2 emissions from international flights. The UK Department for Transport acknowledged the draft EU proposal and said it is aligning with “elements” of the EU ETS, including the scope of aviation coverage, to maintain a level playing field. “Both EU and UK ETSs will apply monitoring for aviation’s non-CO2 climate effects,” the European Commission said. The EU ETS has been linked with Switzerland’s ETS since Jan. 1, 2020. This link will remain in place.

artigo.texto: As Bulgaria sets world records in battery energy storage penetration, the government plans to introduce a tax on revenues generated by battery systems. Although the 5% levy, proposed through the 2027 budget bill, aims to bring in additional funding to shield businesses from high electricity prices, it could also discourage investment in the energy storage sector. The government’s proposal, added just before the 2027 budget bill was submitted to parliament, stipulates that the tax would apply only to standalone battery energy storage systems and remain in force throughout 2027, according to a report by Capital. The revenues would replenish Bulgaria’s Electricity System Security Fund (ESS), which compensates businesses for high electricity prices. The government plans a EUR 2 billion package to help households, businesses, and energy-intensive industries cope with high energy prices, with EUR 1.5 billion coming from the fund and the remaining EUR 500 million from the Bulgarian Development Bank. The 5% levy could bring in tens of millions of euros annually Based on recent output and prices, Capital calculated that the 5% levy on standalone batteries would bring in between EUR 28 million and EUR 30 million annually. However, new battery projects are expected to increase average daily output by 20% in 2027, boosting the amount to between EUR 34 million and EUR 36 million. In October, the overall operating power of battery systems in Bulgaria reached 6.23 GW, compared to 5.41 GW in mid-August and 3.43 GW before the end of May, according to data from the Electricity System Operator (ESO). Strong pushback from the sector Although the government’s proposal has yet to be debated in parliament, it is already facing strong opposition from the sector. Dimitar Beleliev, chairman of the Bulgarian Association of Electrical Engineering and Electronics (BASEL), said the group “categorically opposes” the idea, noting that “batteries do not produce electricity, but help balance it and use it more efficiently.” The tax could put the brakes on projects planned for 2027 Investors in some of the largest battery portfolios have told Capital that the new levy could lead to an outflow of projects scheduled for the end of 2027. According to them, the fact that it would be charged on revenues rather than profits is even more worrying. The Association for Production, Storage and Trading of Electricity (APSTE) also strongly opposes the proposal, pointing out that about EUR 3 billion has been invested in battery systems in Bulgaria in the last two years alone.

artigo.texto: Oriana Power reports over 2.7 GWh BESS capacity pipeline Key highlights - Oriana Power reports over 2.7 GWh of BESS capacity, including commissioned, under-construction and allocated projects. - Six named BESS awards total 2.45 GWh, led by a 900 MW/1,800 MWh Maharashtra project. - Four named hybrid projects disclose a combined 450 MWh of storage capacity. - Oriana Power reports more than 1.8 GW of solar energy assets alongside its BESS portfolio. powered by IRIS Oriana Power Limited reports over 2.7 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity, including commissioned, under-construction and allocated projects. Its six named BESS awards total 2.45 GWh, while four named hybrid projects disclose a further 450 megawatt-hours (MWh) of storage whose inclusion in the headline total is not specified. Know Oriana Power inside out Results, valuation, peers and who's buying, in one view. What BESS capacity does Oriana Power report? Oriana Power reports over 2.7 GWh of BESS capacity on its storage page. The presentation states that this figure includes commissioned, under-construction and allocated capacity, but does not split the total between those project stages. One GWh equals 1,000 MWh, so the stated portfolio is above 2,700 MWh. Oriana Power describes BESS as a system that stores surplus solar and wind energy and releases it during periods of peak demand or grid fluctuation. The company says this time-shifting mechanism supports grid stabilisation, system reliability, asset utilisation and continuity of supply for industrial and commercial users. These are intended functions of the storage product rather than reported operating results. The 2.7-GWh figure is expressed as energy capacity, whereas power capacity is stated in megawatts (MW). This distinction matters because the presentation lists the Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited BESS award as 900 MW and 1,800 MWh, showing both the rate at which a system can discharge and the amount of energy it can store. How large are Oriana Power's named BESS awards? Oriana Power's six named BESS awards total 2,450 MWh, or 2.45 GWh, based on the capacities shown for each project. Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited accounts for 1,800 MWh, while the other five listed awards range from 100 MWh to 250 MWh. Oriana Power's Maharashtra award represents about 73% of the 2,450 MWh total across the six named awards. The four 50 MW projects for Rajasthan, Telangana, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu each provide 100 MWh, or two hours of storage at their stated power rating, and together account for 400 MWh. The NTPC Vidyut Vyapar award is also specified as a two-hour system, at 125 MW and 250 MWh. The 2.45-GWh sum of the named awards is at least 250 MWh below Oriana Power's over-2.7-GWh BESS headline. The presentation does not identify the projects or stages accounting for that difference, and does not state contract values, ownership structures, commissioning dates or revenue terms for these awards. Got a follow-up? Ask IRIS Which Oriana Power hybrid projects include battery storage? Oriana Power lists four hybrid projects with 450 MWh of explicitly stated storage capacity: 300 MWh for SECI, 100 MWh for Wonder Cement Limited, 20 MWh for JKCL Gottan and 30 MWh for JKCL Gujarat. The presentation presents these as individual hybrid project entries rather than as a separate aggregate storage portfolio figure. The SECI entry combines 100 MW with 50 MW/300 MWh, making its 300 MWh storage component the largest among the four disclosed hybrid projects. Wonder Cement is listed as 65.5 MW plus 100 MWh, without a separate battery power rating. JKCL Gottan is listed at 27 MW plus 10 MW/20 MWh, while JKCL Gujarat is listed at 50 MW plus 15 MW/30 MWh. Oriana Power defines its hybrid offering as Solar+Wind, Solar+BESS and Wind+BESS configurations. The company says combining complementary generation profiles with storage where applicable is intended to raise annual energy yield, smooth output relative to single-technology plants, and use land, transmission infrastructure and common balance-of-plant more efficiently. The presentation does not say whether the 450 MWh in named hybrid projects is included in the over-2.7-GWh BESS figure, so the two amounts should not be added together. How does BESS fit within Oriana Power's project portfolio? Oriana Power places its over-2.7-GWh BESS capacity alongside more than 1.8 gigawatts (GW) of solar energy assets. Both figures include commissioned, under-construction and allocated capacity, but they measure different things: the solar figure is generating power capacity in GW, while the BESS figure is stored energy capacity in GWh. The solar project list includes 234 MW for Damodar Valley Corporation, 128 MW for Dalmia Cement, 100 MW for Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited and 52 MW for Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited. Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited therefore appears in both portfolios, with a 100 MW solar project and the 900 MW/1,800 MWh BESS award. Oriana Power says it creates a separate special-purpose vehicle (SPV) for every project because customers, states, lenders and contract terms can differ. The company says each SPV has its own approvals, grid connectivity, lender security and cash flows, while different commercial operation dates, loan tenors and repayment schedules can be tracked over 15 to 25 years. The presentation does not identify which SPVs hold the reported BESS or hybrid capacities. Conclusion Oriana Power's presentation shows storage as a substantial disclosed business line alongside more than 1.8 GW of solar assets. The company reports over 2.7 GWh of BESS capacity, while the six named BESS awards add to 2.45 GWh and four named hybrid projects specify 450 MWh. artigo.texto: To give Borough staff time to look into what potential impact data centers could have on Petersburg, the Assembly has been considering a moratorium on issuing permits for the facilities. Last week, assembly members voted 5–2 to broaden the proposed moratorium, so it would apply to “all” data center development. Originally, the temporary freeze was aimed at “certain” projects — data centers that would use uncontained cooling systems, require more power than allowed, or rely on generators instead of Petersburg’s power grid. The Petersburg community has mixed feelings about data centers. The moratorium’s authors are especially concerned about the potential for off-grid operation. Utility Director Steve Harbour, who helped author the ordinance, testified at a public hearing for the moratorium in mid-November. “I don’t know the right answer. I don’t know how we all feel morally on the data center issue. But I do know none of us wants generators running 24/7, and that’s the purpose of this ordinance, and keeping our water clean,” he said. Harbour said the Borough can work on addressing big picture questions, but needs the moratorium in the meantime. “It’s not perfect, and I agree that there’s a lot of mixed emotions and feelings in town. I’ve talked to people that think [a data center could] be good to help with rates. I’ve talked to many that think it’s bad,” he added. “We can have all sorts of public meetings and all that to decide. But we should do that after we pass this ordinance.” Now, that measure is being revised so that the moratorium would apply to “all” data center development, regardless of whether a project runs off or on the local power grid, or what kind of cooling system it uses. Assembly Member Jeff Meucci pitched the amendment. “I think if we’re going to take a moratorium, we’re going to take a real moratorium, and stop any kind of additional building permits for any kind of data center,” Meucci said. Meucci said he didn’t think the moratorium as-written would be broad enough. “I’m afraid that by having a moratorium with leaving a door open, it kind of leaves us exposed,” he said. “I think it’s the Assembly’s responsibility to pass good policy, not to do policy based on a looming threat that is out there.” Meucci proposed the change in previous meetings; it didn’t get enough Assembly support, until now. “I like it. It gives us time, and I will be voting yes,” said Assembly Member James Valentine. Even before the amendment was on the table, Valentine said he wanted the moratorium because there has been a lot of talk, without much clarity to act upon. “I want to add all these protections for us, but we haven’t seen anything in front of us to actually, like, work with,” Valentine said. “At least one moratorium, to start, gives us a breath … so we can actually work on something instead of just talk.” “This has gotten tougher and tougher as time goes on,” said Assembly Member Bob Martin. “I’m becoming more open to the full moratorium. But I still think the biggest open door here, as Member Meucci referenced, is diesel generation.” Martin said he was concerned that broadening the moratorium at this point in the process would be a “big change” without a lot of time to vet the legality. “But, I have noticed public sentiment is heading in the direction of a full moratorium. So I think I’m going to vote for the amendment,” Martin added. But not all assembly members support the change. The Borough Utility has guardrails, like power sale agreements, that protect Petersburg’s grid; but an off-grid facility that runs on diesel generators could technically bypass those protections. Vice Mayor Jeigh Stanton Gregor proposed the original moratorium, focusing on “certain” projects like that, to address the community’s “biggest vulnerabilities.” Weighing in on whether to broaden the moratorium, Stanton Gregor said the change would be unnecessary. “I think the amendment is a solution in search of a problem. I won’t be supporting it,” he said. “I don’t think it’s a necessary thing, given the protections we already have in place. My biggest concern was insulating ourselves from off-grid threats to our community.” Mayor Bob Lynn was also against the amendment. He is the board chair of Southeast Alaska Power Agency, the wholesale hydropower supplier that specifically feeds three communities in the region. As each community has authority to make decisions about proposed projects concerning the town’s power grid, Lynn said he, too, didn’t see the point of broadening the moratorium to apply to on-grid projects. “I’m gonna vote against [the amendment], but there’s still a lot of work to be done, and it’s not going to stop because I know that, from both Ketchikan and Wrangell’s perspective, they’re looking at large loads,” Lynn said. “All of us are going to be looking for power, and all of us are going to be looking to the future of what we can do. So I’m going to vote no, but … we have a lot of work ahead of us, no matter which way it goes.” The Assembly approved the amendment, with Lynn and Stanton Gregor voting against. But the Assembly agreed that there’s still more work to be done. “I think this [amendment] kind of closes the gap. Now, there’s still going to be a ton of work to do until the moratorium expires. We can’t just put this to bed and say we’re good,” said Assembly Member Donna Marsh. “We’ve got to examine every possible scenario, so that we can respect public testimony and public opinion.” The overall ordinance passed unanimously, 7–0, in its second reading. The measure will require one more round of Assembly approval before it can take effect. For now, it’s too early to tell exactly what the updated moratorium will look like, as Borough staff work on a revised version before it is considered once again at the next assembly meeting, which happens Nov. 30 at 6:00 p.m. There will be another public hearing for the proposed moratorium, as amended, during that meeting.

artigo.texto: SiTime Targets Data Center Bandwidth Upgrades with Two New Clock Families The company’s new FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 product families are aimed at surging AI data center bandwidth demands following its strategic acquisition of Renesas timing business. SiTime has announced the the launch of its FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 product families, targeting the surging demand for high-bandwidth clocking solutions in artificial intelligence (AI) and data center networks. The launch follows SiTime’s strategic acquisition of Renesas’s timing business, positioning the company to address a serviceable addressable market (SAM) estimated at $2 billion. These new clock generators and jitter attenuators are designed to meet the rigorous demands of next-generation networking equipment, including 224G SerDes and PCIe Gen7 architectures. To learn more about the news, we spoke with Piyush Sevalia, Executive Vice President, Chief Business Officer at SiTime. Jeff Child, All About Circuits’s Editor-in-Chief and Piyush Sevalia, Executive Vice President, Chief Business Officer at SiTime at Electronica 2026. The Bandwidth Challenge in AI Data Centers The explosive growth of AI workloads is driving an insatiable need for bandwidth within data centers. As GPUs become increasingly powerful and expensive, minimizing their idle time is critical for economic efficiency. “You’ve got to keep the GPUs busy because they are so expensive,” said Sevalia. “And so there is a major upgrade happening in networking both on the Ethernet side as well as on the interconnect side.” This constant pressure for faster data movement is forcing a doubling of bandwidth every two years. Current top-of-rack switches and smart NICs are transitioning to 224G SerDes per lane for Ethernet connectivity, while server motherboards and accelerator interconnects are moving to PCIe Gen7, which doubles the bandwidth of Gen6 to 128 GT/s. These high-speed standards demand extremely low-jitter clocking sources to ensure signal integrity, prevent bit-error rates from climbing, and avoid costly retransmits that degrade system performance. Where the FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 (VC9) clock devices fit in in AI data center designs. FemtoClock 4: Targeting 224G SerDes Top-of-Rack Switches The FemtoClock 4 family (which includes the RC38616, RC38412, RC32418, and RC32412 variants) is aimed squarely at the demanding top-of-rack and spine switch market. According to SiTime, a modern Ethernet switch ASIC can require more than 40 clocks, a number that is only expected to grow. To address this density, the FemtoClock 4 architecture is highly integrated. The flagship RC38616 model, packaged in a compact 10 mm x 10 mm 144-BGA, features: - Up to six independent frequency domains: This allows a single device to synchronize multiple distinct domains within a complex system. - 18 differential output pairs: These outputs can be configured for various signaling standards (CML, LVDS, HCSL, or LVCMOS). - Ultra-low phase jitter: The device delivers an impressive 19 fs RMS phase jitter at 312.5 MHz (measured from 12 kHz to 20 MHz with a 4 MHz high-pass filter) in clock generator mode. The challenge of packing this much functionality into a single die is managing internal crosstalk. “When you have so many different PLLs, there’s a lot of noise in the system. You’ve got to make sure that the noise is isolated,” said Sevalia. “Otherwise, it’s going to creep into the outputs as jitter. And when you’re trying to meet the jitter spec sub 50cond jitter spec for 224G that’s not easy.” The FemtoClock 4 leverages four generations of architectural refinement to isolate internal noise, ensuring solid performance even under noisy power supply conditions typical of dense server environments. FemtoClock 4 (left), VersaClock 8 (right) VersaClock 8: PCIe Gen7 Clocking for Computing and Interconnects Complementing the FemtoClock 4 is the VersaClock 8 family (including the RC31312A, RC31309A, and RC31305A), which is designed for motherboard interconnects, smart NICs, network accelerators, and storage applications relying on PCIe. VersaClock 8 devices are highly flexible, programmable clock generators that offer: - PCIe Gen7 Compliance: They deliver an outstanding 10 fs reference clock jitter, well below the requirements for PCIe Gen7, providing significant timing margin for designers. - Low Phase Jitter: The devices achieve 30 fs RMS phase jitter at 312.5 MHz (12 kHz to 20 MHz, 4 MHz high-pass filter). - Compact Footprint: Available in 5-, 9-, and 12-output variants in QFN packages as small as 4x4 mm. SiTime claims the 12-output variant is roughly 40% smaller than comparable solutions. - High-Temperature Operation: The low-power architecture reduces self-heating, allowing operation up to 105°C board temperature, a crucial feature for densely packed computing boards. The architecture includes a single PLL and fractional output dividers, allowing the generation of up to three distinct frequency domains from a single chip. It supports both Common Clock (CC) and Independent Reference (IR) PCIe clock architectures and can store up to 18 configurations in its internal One-Time Programmable (OTP) memory. A Unified Timing Portfolio With the integration of the Renesas timing business, SiTime is pitching itself as a comprehensive "one-stop-shop" for data center timing. While the FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 handle the complex clock generation and distribution, SiTime’s core MEMS oscillators (such as its TCXOs) provide the fundamental, ultra-stable synchronization pulses required across the network. “Nobody else has that kind of diversity of portfolio,” said Sevalia. “And so it simplifies the customer's job to just buy from us and get everything in place and then move on to the next big problem they have to solve.” Looking ahead, SiTime plans to further integrate these technologies. artigo.texto: Sri Lanka has launched its first comprehensive national facility dedicated to testing modern battery technologies, providing specialised testing services for local manufacturers, importers and technology developers through an investment of approximately Rs. 161.5 million. The Centre for E-Mobility and Battery Technology was officially inaugurated on Monday (23) at the National Engineering Research and Development Centre of Sri Lanka (NERDC), under the patronage of Science and Technology Minister Prof. Chrishantha Abeysena, the Department of Government Information (DGI) said. The facility is expected to improve access to specialised testing services for local manufacturers, importers, researchers and technology developers, while supporting domestic product development and increasing local value addition. According to the DGI, the centre was established to expand Sri Lanka’s testing capabilities beyond conventional battery assessments to cover modern battery technologies. Its services include evaluating the performance, capacity, durability and safety of different battery types and battery systems. The facility will also conduct assessments of battery performance under varying environmental conditions and tests on electric vehicle charging equipment, among other specialised services. Of the total investment of Rs. 161.5 million, Rs. 118 million has been provided through the Government’s National Quality Infrastructure (NQI) Strengthening Project, while NERDC has contributed the remaining Rs. 43.5 million from its own funds. The DGI said the initiative represents a step towards strengthening the country’s quality infrastructure and supporting Sri Lanka’s transition to electric mobility and renewable energy technologies.

artigo.texto: A WEG conseguiu o credenciamento de seu pack de baterias de lítio na rota 2 do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES). O registro posiciona a companhia para participar do primeiro leilão de reserva de capacidade (LRCap) com armazenamento do Brasil, marcado para começar na próxima quarta-feira, 2 de dezembro. Além da fabricante, a Moura obteve aval do banco para a mesma rota, que junto com os caminhos 3 e 4 é proporcional a até 100% de financiamento via Fundo Clima, com custo nominal de 6,5% ao ano. Diferentemente de modalidades que permitem cumprir os requisitos de nacionalização por meio de componentes complementares, essa rota considera processos produtivos ligados ao próprio sistema de baterias, que representa uma parcela expressiva do valor total de um BESS. “É justamente nessa segunda abordagem que nos diferenciamos estrategicamente no mercado. A WEG está indo além da estratégia de nacionalização a partir das células e do atendimento regulatório, pois está contribuindo para estabelecer uma indústria brasileira de armazenamento com maior conteúdo tecnológico, competitividade e autonomia ao mercado. Nossa participação no leilão terá grande importância, pois contribuiremos para atender o sistema energético naquilo que ele precisa, aumentando sua estabilidade e garantindo o uso das fontes renováveis para a transição energética”, diz o diretor de Vendas Solar, BESS e Building, Harry Schmelzer Neto. Para atender à demanda por BESS, a WEG ampliará o parque fabril de Itajaí, em Santa Catarina, construindo uma nova fábrica com capacidade de 4 GWh ao ano. O investimento soma R$ 330 milhões e é feito por meio do programa BNDES Mais Inovação. A previsão é que as operações iniciem no segundo semestre de 2027.

artigo.texto: Ouça este conteúdo A Comissão Federal de Comunicações dos Estados Unidos (FCC, na sigla em inglês) autorizou nesta quarta-feira (25) a SpaceX, empresa aeroespacial de Elon Musk, a implantar uma constelação de até 1 milhão de satélites equipados para funcionar como data centers em órbita terrestre. Batizado de Starmind, o projeto pretende atender à crescente demanda por capacidade computacional para inteligência artificial (IA). A estrutura permitirá que os equipamentos processem grandes volumes de dados no espaço e transmitam os resultados para a Terra. A FCC concedeu a autorização pela primeira vez na história dos Estados Unidos para uma constelação desse tipo. Em comunicado, a agência afirmou que a iniciativa pretende ampliar a infraestrutura computacional necessária ao desenvolvimento da chamada superinteligência. O presidente da FCC, Brendan Carr, disse que a decisão abre uma nova fronteira tecnológica. “Essa ação abre uma nova fronteira para a infraestrutura computacional necessária para impulsionar a liderança e o crescimento dos Estados Unidos”, declarou. A FCC também afirmou que a iniciativa aproxima a humanidade de uma civilização de nível II na escala de Kardashev, conceito teórico que descreve uma sociedade capaz de aproveitar toda a energia emitida por sua estrela. Energia solar e processamento de dados em órbita A SpaceX aposta na disponibilidade de energia solar no espaço para alimentar os equipamentos. A empresa argumenta que a operação orbital poderá reduzir a dependência de recursos terrestres, como água e eletricidade, utilizados em grandes centros de dados convencionais. Os satélites utilizarão conexões ópticas para transmitir informações entre si. A FCC também autorizou o uso de radiofrequências como alternativa para operações de emergência, rastreamento e controle da constelação. Segundo o site Via Satellite, os equipamentos terão capacidade computacional média de 175 quilowatts, podendo alcançar 250 quilowatts. O projeto prevê ainda radiadores líquidos para dissipar o calor gerado pelos sistemas. SpaceX terá até 2038 para colocar metade da constelação em órbita A autorização estabelece prazos para a implantação do projeto. A SpaceX deverá lançar o primeiro satélite da constelação até 25 de novembro de 2033. Depois, terá de colocar 10% dos equipamentos em órbita até novembro de 2035 e metade do total autorizado até novembro de 2038. O prazo para completar a implantação termina em novembro de 2040. A viabilidade do projeto depende, em parte, do desenvolvimento da Starship, foguete reutilizável de grande porte da SpaceX. A empresa aposta no veículo para reduzir os custos de transporte de equipamentos ao espaço. Amazon e outras empresas questionaram o projeto A proposta enfrentou oposição de concorrentes e organizações do setor espacial. Amazon, Viasat e Sociedade Astronômica Americana apresentaram petições contrárias à autorização. Entre as preocupações estavam a viabilidade da constelação, a concentração de satélites em órbita e os possíveis impactos ambientais. A FCC rejeitou os pedidos de veto. A agência argumentou que não cabe ao governo substituir a avaliação das empresas sobre a viabilidade de seus próprios empreendimentos. A SpaceX apresentou o pedido de autorização em janeiro deste ano. A FCC informou que continua analisando propostas de outras empresas interessadas em instalar data centers em órbita e pretende acelerar as decisões.

artigo.texto: A New York City-based developer formalized its plans for the “Project Valley View” data center campus this month in Archbald. PNK Group submitted a conditional use application for two nearly 300,000-square-foot data centers on Archbald Heights Road in the borough’s portion of the Valley View Business Park, officially raising Archbald’s total proposed data centers to 53, though 32 of those data centers — Project Scott and Wildcat Ridge — are tied up in appeals. The borough marked the application as received Nov. 17 on its website. Out of the 53 data centers proposed throughout the borough, PNK Group’s is the first campus slated for the business park in Archbald’s general industrial zoning district, known as an I-2 zone. Project Valley View will be roughly across the street and southeast of Chewy’s warehouse in the business park. The developer also announced on its dedicated project website and through social media ads that it will hold an open house Dec. 8 from 5 to 7 p.m. inside one of the warehouses it developed in the Jessup portion of the Valley View Business Park at 21 Alberigi Drive. The open house will include site plans, renderings and information on the approval process. The developer will have engineers and specialists available to discuss power, noise, water, emergency planning and construction, according to the website, which encourages residents to ask questions and leave comments. “Some details are settled, and others, including acoustic modeling and final site design, are still being studied,” PNK Group wrote on its website. “We’ll be clear about which is which. If we can’t answer a question that night, we’ll follow up, and we’ll post a summary of what we heard at valleyview.pnk.group.” About the application In a conditional use application prepared by engineering firm Kimley-Horn, PNK Group describes two one-story data centers referred to as Building 1 and Building 2. The first data center is approximately 282,471 square feet; the second is approximately 269,691 square feet. An attached will-serve letter from PPL Electric Utilities confirms the utility has the capacity to power Project Valley View with about 300 megawatts of electricity slated for the third quarter of 2029. The campus will have a total of 144 emergency backup diesel generators and 144 chillers to cool its computer hardware, divided into 72 per building, according to PNK Group’s application and accompanying sound study. The campus will also have a roughly 146,360-square-foot substation, two approximately 35,000-square-foot storage buildings and a 1,200-square-foot command center building. There will be two secured entrances and two emergency entrances for first responders, with access coming off Archbald Heights Road. “The Project will not substantially negatively change the character of any surrounding residential neighborhood,” PNK wrote in its application. “The Project is located within the industrial and commercial setting of the Valley View Business Park, which includes high-intensity operations such as Amazon and Chewy, and is expected to generate fewer employee trips and less routine heavy-truck traffic than logistics and distribution uses.” The sound study modeled noise at 12 different receptors throughout the borough, with the nearest residence being more than a mile away at the end of Pike Street. Noise at the residence would be 35.8 dBA during normal operations and 40.3 dBA during an emergency with all 144 generators running, according to the study. The preliminary study also notes that it will consider neighboring Jessup’s noise restrictions. Jefferson Twp. also borders the site to the south, but the township does not have applicable noise standards, according to the sound study. As PNK Group selects its actual equipment, it will “confirm consistency, evaluate whether tonal or pulsating components are present, and determine whether low-frequency noise would be readily distinguishable above measured background conditions,” according to the application. Throughout conditional use hearings for other projects, residents have raised concerns over the impacts of low-frequency and tonal noises from data centers. “If final equipment sound levels exceed the modeled assumptions, the analysis should be updated, and reasonable and feasible mitigation may need to be incorporated as necessary,” PNK Group wrote. Zoning background PNK Group’s site falls into one of four overlay districts that former council members approved in November 2025 to permit data centers as conditional uses. The other overlays span the Wildcat Ridge, Project Scott and Project Green Mountain data center campuses. Residents have advocated for council to limit data centers to industrial land east of the Casey Highway, which would include the site of PNK’s proposed 125.29-acre campus. Archbald is in the midst of further restricting data centers with an amended zoning ordinance that would remove the majority of those overlays, limiting proposals exclusively to land within the Valley View Business Park. PNK Group previously developed two warehouses in the Jessup portion of the business park: a 255,776-square-foot warehouse on Valley View Drive and the 162,907-square-foot warehouse on Alberigi Drive where it will hold its open house. PNK also purchased land in Moosic in July for a 460,000-square-foot warehouse on Davis Street. PNK owns its data center properties under the limited liability companies DC VV and DC VV1. Earlier this month, the developer transferred a 44.47-acre lot it owns in the business park from its PNK P1 LLC to DC VV1 for $4 million. PNK P1 acquired its first Lackawanna County property — the property it transferred to DC VV1 — in February 2024 from the Scranton Lackawanna Industrial Building Company, or SLIBCO, for $3.3 million, according to a property transaction recorded Feb. 8, 2024. SLIBCO is the industrial development arm of the Greater Scranton Chamber of Commerce. SLIBCO developed the Valley View Business Park in 200

artigo.texto: The Philippines’ endorsement of two carbon market initiatives at COP31 has prompted civil society calls for domestic rules that protect communities and uphold developed countries’ climate finance obligations. To continue reading, subscribe to Eco‑Business. Access all our exclusive content and archive — with a 7-day free trial. Then just US$5/month. Cancel anytime. - Exclusive access to training across business and policy topics - Direct access to industry leaders at Eco-Business events - A seat among the decision makers shaping the region's sustainable development The country endorsed the Antalya Statement on Mobilising Private Finance for Climate Action and joined the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets. The statement backs a policy playbook to help governments increase demand for high-integrity carbon credits and attract private investment into climate action. It stresses that companies should use credits alongside – not instead of, or to delay – sustained emissions cuts. The commitments follow President Ferdinand Marcos Jr’s order to develop the Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework through Executive Order No. 127, signed on 13 October 2026. The order directs the Department of Environment and Natural Resources to develop national rules for voluntary carbon markets and international trading under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. John Leo Algo, National Coordinator of Aksyon Klima, described the commitments as signals of the government’s determination to complete its carbon market framework and attract private investment. At a press briefing after the climate conference, he linked the search for alternative funding to what he described as a “stalemate” in climate finance negotiations at COP31. The talks ended without substantive agreement on delivering public climate finance, leaving key funding disputes unresolved. “[The Philippine government] is really keen on tapping into all possible sources of finance and other means of support, so that’s why they’re really going into the private sector investments [for carbon markets],” said Algo, also the lead coordinator for all Philippine civil society organisation delegates at the UN climate conference. The endorsements also offer opportunities to build international partnerships and strengthen the institutions needed to implement carbon markets, he added. “ ‘[The Philippine government] is really keen on tapping into all possible sources of finance and other means of support, so that’s why they’re really going into the private sector investments [for carbon markets].’ John Leo Algo, National Coordinator, Aksyon Klima Carbon credit projects already operate in the Philippines through independent voluntary standards. Singapore-based KenEco’s MinTrees programme in Mindanao, for instance, has secured credits under Verra’s standards rather than a Philippine national crediting system. Algo argued that the domestic framework must clarify what “high integrity” means in the Philippine context. “The release of the carbon market policy framework would be very critical to really defining what high integrity means,” he said. Cheng Pagulayan, Climate Justice Portfolio Manager at Oxfam Pilipinas, said attracting investment must not overshadow the rights of communities affected by carbon projects. “Any investments or involvement in carbon markets must be anchored on equity, on justice, and safeguarding of communities,” he said in the same press briefing, adding that civil society would continue pressing those demands as it examines the new commitments. Pagulayan criticised the prominence given to carbon markets at COP31, arguing that they distracted from climate justice and the responsibility of developed countries to provide climate finance. He pointed to Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, which requires developed countries to provide financial resources to help developing countries cut emissions and adapt to climate change.

O juiz federal Diego Câmara Alves, da 17ª Vara Federal Cível do Distrito Federal, negou nesta quarta (25/11) o pedido de liminar da Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica) para suspender os leilões de reserva de capacidade de baterias, marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Na ação civil pública, a associação questiona a regra da lei 15.269/2025 que põe nos geradores o custo de contratar baterias como reserva de capacidade. No regime geral, essa conta é dos usuários finais de energia. Para o juiz, quem paga a conta foi escolha do legislador. Ele não viu inconstitucionalidade evidente na lei, e os argumentos da associação dependem de premissas técnicas e econômicas que a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e a União contestam e que não têm “solução segura” nesta fase. Se a tese da associação vencer, mudaria quem arca com o custo, e não a validade dos leilões ou dos contratos. A Abeeólica levou a mesma questão ao Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) na ação direta de inconstitucionalidade (ADI) 8.050, que pede a suspensão da norma inclusive nesses leilões. O relator, ministro Cristiano Zanin, pediu informações antes de decidir sobre a liminar. O juiz considerou imprudente antecipar, em decisão provisória de alcance nacional, o julgamento de uma lei que a própria associação submeteu ao Supremo. A decisão cita ainda o PL 3.716/2026, que revoga a regra, como sinal de que o tema está em debate no Congresso, o que recomenda contenção da Justiça. A Abeeólica alegou também que os leilões foram marcados antes da regulamentação que vai definir quanto cada gerador paga. A proposta da Aneel passou por consulta pública e aguarda decisão da diretoria da agência. O juiz não viu norma que condicione os leilões a essa regulamentação, que, segundo a Aneel, tem de estar pronta antes do início do suprimento, em 1º de agosto de 2028. A associação estimou que a cobrança pode chegar a cerca de R$ 17 por MWh, perto de 10% da receita de referência de um gerador no mercado livre. Como os pagamentos começam com o suprimento, o juiz não viu dano iminente aos geradores. Pesou ainda o risco de adiar os leilões, apontado pela União com base em nota do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME). O Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia 2036 e o Plano da Operação Energética 2026 identificaram descumprimento dos critérios de garantia de suprimento de potência a partir de 2027, e o adiamento poderia comprometer a entrada dos projetos nas janelas de acesso à transmissão e atrasar o início da operação. Segundo a Aneel, os leilões têm 5.296 projetos cadastrados no produto Armazenamento Nacional e 5.734 no produto Armazenamento, com garantias de proposta já depositadas. artigo.texto: A Anatel aprovou R$ 375 milhões para um data center de inteligência artificial que a Telebras vai operar, em acórdão publicado em 18 de novembro. A agência exigiu que a fonte do dinheiro para manter o equipamento seja definida antes de qualquer contrato. O Acórdão 325/2026 foi aprovado pelo Conselho Diretor da Anatel em 4 de novembro. A decisão foi publicada 14 dias depois, liberando o valor para um data center com carga elétrica inicial de 2 megawatts e consumo teórico de até 17.520 megawatts-hora por ano. A EAF, Entidade Administradora da Faixa de 3,5 GHz, banca a obra com o saldo do 5G. Depois, ela transfere a estrutura à União e fica proibida de explorar o data center, prestar serviço de IA a terceiros ou ceder capacidade a empresas privadas. À Telebras cabem, depois de pronto, as despesas de energia, manutenção, atualização tecnológica, segurança e suporte. A estatal fechou os primeiros nove meses de 2026 com prejuízo de R$ 90,7 milhões. Recebeu também R$ 169,9 milhões em subvenções do governo no mesmo período. Sem as subvenções, o Ebitda ajustado da Telebras seria negativo em R$ 32,9 milhões no período, segundo o balanço da empresa. Pelos mesmos números, a estatal passa a arcar com os custos permanentes do data center em um período em que ainda depende de subvenção federal para apresentar resultado positivo. O governo vem reduzindo o apoio ano a ano, dentro de um plano de sustentabilidade de cinco anos assinado com o Ministério das Comunicações em 2025. A subvenção cai de R$ 256,3 milhões em 2026 para R$ 86,3 milhões em 2029. Publicidade Só com essa trajetória de corte a Telebras projeta Ebitda positivo sem ajuda federal, e apenas em 2029 ou 2030. A conta de luz do novo data center pode variar de R$ 10,5 milhões a R$ 17,5 milhões por ano, conforme o consumo máximo teórico de 17,52 mil MWh. O valor não inclui manutenção, refrigeração nem a substituição dos aceleradores de IA mais adiante. O investimento acompanha uma corrida mais ampla: o Brasil pode atrair US$ 60 bilhões por ano em data centers até 2050, segundo projeções do setor. O apetite elétrico da inteligência artificial já preocupa em outros projetos: data centers de IA em São Paulo consomem 16,1 bilhões de litros de água por ano para resfriamento. Quando o data center entra em operação? A Telebras estima iniciar a operação até o fim de 2027, mas o local da obra ainda não está definido. O presidente da estatal, Hermano Studart Lins de Albuquerque, já citou Brasília como uma das possibilidades. O projeto prevê um terreno de 5 mil metros quadrados, com 20 racks de 42U, rede de alta velocidade, seis servidores com 48 GPUs e armazenamento all-flash para rodar modelos de inteligência artificial soberanos. O que acontece agora Antes de contratar qualquer etapa, a Telebras precisa confirmar o terreno e a conexão elétrica, validar os projetos de engenharia e cumprir requisitos térmicos, segundo o acórdão da Anatel. Cada fase aprovada não garante automaticamente a seguinte. Faltam ainda o orçamento anual de despesas operacionais, os contratos de prestação de serviço e a definição de como o data center vai se integrar à infraestrutura do Serpro, que já trabalha em IA soberana com a MeetKai, e da Dataprev.

artigo.texto: A SpaceX treina bartenders, varejistas e instaladores de data centers com IA em apenas alguns dias. Na TomorrowX Summit, Elon Musk afirmou que a equipe da ArmyX detalhou o processo para que pessoas com experiência em preparação e venda de bebidas pudessem participar da expansão das unidades Colossus 1 e Colossus 2 em Memphis, EUA. A SpaceX está contratando trabalhadores sem experiência prévia no setor de tecnologia, como bartenders, repositores de supermercado ou cozinheiros de fast-food, para construir seus grandes data centers. A empresa divide o trabalho em etapas simples para que os novos funcionários possam ser treinados em poucos dias. Essa abordagem foi compartilhada pelo bilionário Elon Musk na TomorrowX Summit em Austin, EUA, no último fim de semana. Segundo ele, alguns dos melhores funcionários da equipe de construção de data centers da empresa nunca haviam trabalhado nessa área antes. Eles vinham de profissões menos relacionadas à infraestrutura de tecnologia. ArmyX: Simplificando o processo para ajudar os novos funcionários a começarem rapidamente. Para integrar mão de obra não qualificada em projetos de tecnologia, a SpaceX criou uma equipe interna chamada ArmyX. Essa equipe analisa todo o processo de construção de data centers e o divide em tarefas mais simples. Isso permite que os recém-chegados sejam treinados e concluam o trabalho em poucos dias. Segundo Musk, as empresas não precisam necessariamente contratar pessoas que tenham passado a vida inteira trabalhando com sistemas de cabeamento. Em vez disso, podem criar processos que permitam que funcionários que antes trabalhavam no Starbucks ou repunham prateleiras no Target se adaptem rapidamente a novas funções. Ele também valoriza as habilidades e a ética de trabalho de funcionários dos setores de varejo e alimentação. Ele deu o exemplo dos funcionários da rede de fast-food In-N-Out. Segundo Musk, pessoas acostumadas a fazer hambúrgueres o dia todo conseguem, sem problemas, instalar cabos de rede após o treinamento. Essa estrutura organizacional permite que a SpaceX expanda sua equipe de construção sem depender exclusivamente de pessoal com vasta experiência em data centers. Você também pode gostar Colossus 1 e Colossus 2: A escala das GPUs por trás da demanda da força de trabalho Novos funcionários estão dando suporte à expansão das instalações Colossus 1 e Colossus 2 em Memphis, EUA. Anteriormente, o Business Insider noticiou que a SpaceX ofereceu um aumento salarial de 20% para voluntários que trabalhassem seis semanas em Memphis ou Southaven, Mississippi, cidade que também possui um grande centro de dados. Uma GPU é um processador gráfico, também utilizado em sistemas computacionais para inteligência artificial devido à sua capacidade de processar grandes quantidades de dados em paralelo. Abaixo, seguem informações sobre duas dessas unidades, de acordo com a fonte: Essa escala impõe demandas significativas tanto em mão de obra quanto em cronogramas de construção. Segundo Musk, as operações em Memphis estão se tornando cada vez mais estáveis, com equipes de trabalhadores atuando 24 horas por dia. Ele afirma que pode inspecionar o local à 1h ou 2h da manhã e constatar uma produtividade quase equivalente à das 10h da manhã do dia seguinte. O cronograma de trabalho é mantido continuamente, sete dias por semana. No relatório financeiro de outubro, Musk também mencionou planos para expandir a capacidade de computação. Ele disse que não ficaria surpreso se a empresa adicionasse menos de 13 gigawatts até o final de 2027. Terafab e data centers espaciais: planos ambiciosos Além de Memphis, Musk está investindo em projetos de infraestrutura de maior escala. Segundo a Reuters, ele está construindo duas fábricas no Texas, conhecidas coletivamente como Terafab. Uma das instalações é voltada para os setores automotivo e de robótica humanoide, enquanto a outra atende à sua ambição de desenvolver um centro de dados de IA no espaço. Musk idealiza esses complexos como fábricas avançadas de chips de IA, visando uma capacidade computacional de um terawatt por ano. Esse número é o dobro do meio terawatt que, segundo algumas fontes, é a maior capacidade de uma fábrica nos EUA atualmente. Você também pode gostar No início de 2026, ele fundiu a xAI à SpaceX para apoiar o desenvolvimento de um data center espacial. De acordo com a SpaceX, a instalação de sistemas de computação fora da Terra poderia utilizar energia solar quase contínua, reduzindo assim os custos de operação e manutenção em comparação com instalações terrestres. A empresa também afirma que esse modelo poderia reduzir o impacto ambiental, pois não requer água de resfriamento nem eletricidade da rede elétrica nacional. Nota: Estes são benefícios apresentados pela empresa e não são resultados de operações verificadas de forma independente. A principal lição a ser aprendida com a abordagem de gestão de recursos da SpaceX. Desde o treinamento de ex-bartenders e funcionários do varejo para instalar infraestrutura tecnológica até planos para construir data centers no espaço, as ideias de Musk revelam como ele organiza recursos para projetos de IA em larga escala. O foco dessa abordagem é redesenhar processos para dimensionar a força de trabalho, em vez de simplesmente buscar indivíduos com experiência preexistente.

artigo.texto: Data centers have a reputation for being massive water hogs, fueling plenty of worry over Cheyenne’s recent building boom. Actual usage, however, tells a different story. Frank Strong, engineering and water resource division manager for Cheyenne’s Board of Public Utilities, told Cowboy State Daily that data centers accounted for about 2% of the city’s water sales in 2025. "We sold about 3.5 billion gallons of water in 2025, and 93 million went to data centers,” Strong said. ‘Significantly Less’ Strong said the 93 million gallons was lower than the water usage laid out in the data centers' initial proposals to the city. The difference, he said, comes down to chips, the small processors inside the servers that run the data center's computing. When developers first proposed data center projects to the Cheyenne City Council, the chips they were using needed more water-based cooling to run. “New chip technology can run at higher temperatures,” Strong said. “Newer technology has allowed them to consume less water than they had planned.” Strong did not have the exact difference in gallons between the proposed water usage and what the data centers are using now, but he said it is not a marginal one. “I would say it’s in the significantly less range,” Strong said. Almonds, Golf and AI Cheyenne’s numbers line up with a new report comparing AI water use against everyday habits. The analysis from Enverus Intelligence Research, a Calgary-based energy analytics subsidiary of Enverus, modeled water use per $25 spent across cooling scenarios and consumer benchmarks, finding AI inference uses far less water than golf or almond milk. “The research finds that skipping one almond latte saves more water than spending $100 on AI inference,” the analysis states. “Skipping one round of golf saves more than $16,000 of it.” Ryan Luther, EIR’s director of Energy Transition Research, told Cowboy State Daily that the analysis isn't a pitch for data center developers. It’s just looking at the numbers, he said. "Our reputation lives and dies on our ability to do science-based research,” Luther said. “We have clients on both sides of everything, so we're not trying to pick a side here.” Luther said the analysis was built around four different cooling methods, which he said cover just about every data center operating today. He said it also counted the water used at the power plants that generate the electricity to run those facilities, not only the water used inside the data center itself. About 90% of the water the analysis attributed to AI use was consumed at those power plants. Even with all of it counted, the total water usage still came out low. ”The amount of power used for $25 of compute is pretty low compared to $25 of power,” Luther said. ‘Different Type of Cooling’ The biggest swing in the analysis came down to how a data center is cooled. In the earliest cooling systems, $25 a month of AI use corresponded to about 21 gallons of water. Now that same usage corresponds to about a quarter of a gallon of water, which Luther said is due to modern, closed-loop systems. "There's been a huge improvement on the efficiency,” Luther said. "They still need a lot of cooling, but it's a different type of cooling. It’s not necessarily just pulling in water and evaporating it. It's more like a radiator.” As closed-loop systems become the norm, Luther said, data centers' water use will approach zero, though he said it will take a while for the whole industry to get there. Golf courses and almond farms are widely known as heavy water users. But the analysis found that AI also uses less than household electricity on an all-natural-gas grid. That same $25 a month in household electricity on a grid powered entirely by natural gas corresponded to about 31 gallons of water, compared with about 1.9 gallons for AI use in the base case, according to the analysis. Everyone Hates Infrastructure Still, Luther said some communities have reason to be concerned. As little water as a data center uses, some areas with a low water table don't have any to spare. "In places like Nevada and Utah, you have very real water constraints,” Luther said. Luther started his career in oil and gas at Enverus and has spent years studying energy projects ranging from pipelines and transmission lines to power plants and data centers. Across all of them, he said, community pushback is something he has come to expect. “Generally, the community seems to hate all infrastructure,” Luther said. “No matter what it is, if it's in your backyard or in your community, they'll find reasons to tear it down.” Though the analysis is titled "Setting the Record Straight,” on data center water usage, Luther said he doesn't necessarily expect it to change anyone's minds. But among the concerns people typically have about a new data center in their neighborhood, Luther said water use should rank low on the list. As for the others, like noise and air pollution, he said it could always be worse. “They do have noise, but they're not very loud compared to a power plant," Luther said. “A lot of the communities want the data center to invest in green spaces around them, or sound barrier walls, which I think almost all developers are more than happy to do.” Emma Jane Jackson can be reached at emma@cowboystatedaily.com.

artigo.texto: SpaceX é autorizada a lançar um milhão de satélites para seus data centers no espaço Desde o ano passado, multiplicaram-se os projetos de data centers em órbita O órgão regulador de telecomunicações dos Estados Unidos, a FCC, autorizou nesta quarta-feira (25) a SpaceX a lançar até um milhão de satélites como parte de seu projeto de centros de armazenamento de dados no espaço. Desde o ano passado, multiplicaram-se os projetos de data centers em órbita. Além da SpaceX e de sua constelação Starmind, o Google desenvolve o programa Suncatcher, enquanto a Blue Origin apresentou à FCC um pedido para seu Project Sunrise. Outras empresas emergentes também têm projetos em andamento, em especial a Starcloud, que colocou em funcionamento com sucesso, no fim de 2025, um processador de última geração a partir de um satélite. Em outubro, o Google também alcançou resultado semelhante. A autorização concedida à SpaceX vale até 2040, segundo um documento publicado nesta quarta-feira no site da Comissão Federal de Comunicações (FCC). A SpaceX tem a vantagem de contar com seus próprios foguetes, que já realizaram centenas de missões. Em agosto, Elon Musk, o CEO da SpaceX, prometeu o primeiro lançamento no quarto trimestre de 2027 e uma aceleração do ritmo de implantação em 2028. A empresa firmou um acordo com a Nvidia, que fornecerá processadores de última geração Vera Rubin, projetados especialmente para operar no espaço. A maior parte dos programas de centros de dados espaciais segue uma arquitetura semelhante: uma constelação de satélites em órbita baixa, posicionados próximos uns dos outros para garantir uma conexão confiável. No caso do Starmind, esses satélites se comunicarão com os da constelação de internet Starlink, também da SpaceX, responsável pela transmissão dos dados. O espaço oferece diversas vantagens para a instalação de um data center em comparação com a Terra. Graças a uma órbita conhecida como heliossíncrona, um satélite pode, entre outros benefícios, captar energia solar de forma contínua e com eficiência até oito vezes superior à de uma instalação equivalente em solo terrestre.
